      Chapter 01 · I · Foundations

      🗄️ DBMS Essentials

      Explain in under a minute what a database system is, why plain files are not enough, and what a DBMS really does for you.

      ⏱ 20 minbasicMySQL 8PostgreSQL

      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision

      • Data = raw facts. Information = data with meaning. Database = an organised collection of related data. DBMS = the software that defines, stores, queries and protects that data.
      • File systems fail on 8 things: redundancy, inconsistency, difficult access, data isolation, integrity, atomicity, concurrency, security. Mnemonic: RIDAICS (Redundancy & inconsistency, Isolation, Difficult access, Atomicity, Integrity, Concurrency, Security).
      • A DBMS adds: one shared copy of data, constraints, transactions (ACID), concurrency control, crash recovery, access control, and a declarative query language (SQL).
      • DBMS costs: licence/hardware, complexity, a DBA, some overhead. Do not use a full server DBMS for a tiny single-user config file or a pure blob store.
      • RDBMS = a DBMS built on the relational model: tables, keys, foreign keys, SQL. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server.
      • Data models in history: hierarchical (tree, IBM IMS) → network (graph, CODASYL) → relational (Codd, 1970) → object-oriented / object-relational → NoSQL (key-value, document, wide-column, graph).
      • Metadata (data about data) lives in the data dictionary / system catalog: information_schema in MySQL, pg_catalog in PostgreSQL.
      • SQL sublanguages: DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE), DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), DQL (SELECT), DCL (GRANT/REVOKE), TCL (COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT).
      • Codd's 12 rules (1985) define a "truly relational" system. No real product follows all of them. MySQL bends rules 2, 6, 10 and 12, for example.
      ✏️ This chapter is the "warm-up round". Interviewers use it to judge how clearly you speak. Short, sharp answers win here.

      🗄️ Data, information, database, DBMS

      These four words sound similar. Interviewers like to check that you can separate them cleanly. Think of a library: the books are data, a catalogue card that tells you "this book is on shelf 4" is information, the whole organised building is the database, and the librarian with all the rules is the DBMS. ← the library analogy works for everything in this chapter

      Data
      Raw facts with no context. "Asha", 92, "CSE". Alone, these values say nothing.
      Information
      Data that has been processed and given meaning. "Asha of CSE scored 92, the highest in her class."
      Database
      An organised collection of inter-related data that models some part of the real world (e.g., all students, courses and marks of a college).
      DBMS (Database Management System)
      The software that lets you define, create, store, query, update and protect a database for many users at once. MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, MongoDB.
      Database system
      Database + DBMS + the applications that use them. Some books use this word for the whole package.
      QWhat is the difference between a database and a DBMS?

      A database is the data. A DBMS is the software that manages the data. The database is the stored content: tables, rows, indexes on disk. The DBMS is the program (for example the mysqld server process) that reads and writes that content, checks rules, controls who can see what, runs many users at the same time, and recovers after a crash.

      Example: your college's "student records" is a database. MySQL is the DBMS that stores and serves it.

      ⚠️
      Common mistake

      Saying "MySQL is a database". In casual talk it is fine, but in an interview say "MySQL is a DBMS (an RDBMS). college_db is a database inside it."

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A database is an organised collection of related data, like all the student and course records of a college. A DBMS is the software that manages that data. It lets many users store, query and update the data safely, enforces rules, controls access, and recovers after failures. So MySQL is the DBMS, and my college database is the data it manages.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is data the same as information?

      No. Data is raw facts (92). Information is data with context and meaning ("Asha topped the class with 92"). A DBMS stores data; queries turn it into information.

      ↪Is an Excel sheet a database?

      It holds data, so loosely yes, but it is not a DBMS. It has no real concurrency control, no transactions, weak integrity rules, no fine-grained security and does not scale to millions of rows with many users.

      🗃️ Why not just use files? (the classic opener)

      Before DBMSs, every application kept its own files. This is called a file-processing system. It works for one small program. It breaks as soon as data is shared by many programs and many people.

      🌍
      Mini story: KIIT-style college, no DBMS

      The admissions office keeps students.csv. The hostel office keeps hostel.xlsx with the student's name and phone again. The library keeps members.txt, again with name and phone. Each office has its own little program.

      Asha changes her phone number. Admissions updates it. Hostel does not hear about it (redundancy → inconsistency). The principal asks "list all hostel students with library dues above ₹500" — nobody can answer without writing a new program that reads two files in two formats (difficult access + data isolation). The rule "dues can never be negative" lives inside the library program only; a new script ignores it (integrity). The fee program crashes after debiting the fee account but before crediting the hostel account (atomicity). Two clerks open hostel.xlsx, both allot room 101, last save wins (concurrency). Any clerk who can open the file can also read every student's marks (security).

      QWhat are the problems of a file-processing system? Why do we need a DBMS?

      There are eight standard problems. For each one, know what the DBMS does instead.

      #Problem with filesWhat goes wrong (college example)How a DBMS fixes it
      1Data redundancyName + phone copied in 3 files. Wastes space.One integrated schema; each fact stored once (normalisation, Ch 06).
      2InconsistencyPhone updated in one file, old in two others.Single copy + foreign keys, so there is nothing to go out of sync.
      3Difficult accessEvery new question needs a new program.Declarative query language: one SQL query answers new questions.
      4Data isolationData scattered in CSV, XLSX, TXT with different formats.All data in one managed store with a common data model.
      5Integrity problems"Dues ≥ 0" is buried inside one program's code.Constraints (CHECK, NOT NULL, FOREIGN KEY) declared once, enforced for every app.
      6Atomicity problemsCrash after debit, before credit: money vanishes.Transactions: all-or-nothing with undo/redo logs (Ch 12, Ch 17).
      7Concurrent-access anomaliesTwo clerks read balance 100, each withdraws 50, final = 50 instead of 0.Concurrency control: locks and MVCC (Ch 13).
      8Security problemsWhoever opens the file sees everything.Users, roles, GRANT/REVOKE, views (Ch 18).
      R-I-D-A-I-C-S

      🧠 Redundancy & inconsistency · Isolation of data · Difficult access · Atomicity · Integrity · Concurrency · Security. Say it as "RIDe A ICe Skate".

      🎯
      What they are really testing

      Not the list itself. They want to hear the two "big" ones explained with a mechanism: atomicity (needs a log to undo half-done work) and concurrency (needs locks or versions). Anyone can say "redundancy". Few can say why a file system cannot do atomic multi-file updates.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      With plain files, every application keeps its own copy of the data, so we get redundancy and inconsistent copies. Every new question needs a new program, and rules like "balance cannot be negative" are hidden inside code. Files also cannot give all-or-nothing updates after a crash, cannot safely handle two users changing the same record, and cannot give row-level permissions. A DBMS solves all of this with one shared schema, declared constraints, transactions, concurrency control, recovery logs and access control, plus SQL to ask any new question.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Redundancy is sometimes good. When?

      Yes. Controlled redundancy is fine: replicas for availability (Ch 19), indexes (a sorted copy of some columns), caches, and deliberate denormalisation for fast reads (Ch 06). The problem is uncontrolled redundancy that nobody keeps in sync.

      ↪The OS already has file locks. Why is that not enough for concurrency?

      OS locks are coarse (the whole file) and know nothing about rows, transactions or deadlocks. Locking the whole file serialises every user. A DBMS locks individual rows or uses versions (MVCC), detects deadlocks, and ties locks to transaction commit/rollback.

      ↪How exactly does a DBMS give atomicity after a crash?

      It writes a log record before changing data (write-ahead logging). After a crash, the recovery manager redoes committed changes and undoes uncommitted ones using that log. Details in Chapter 17.

      Advantages and disadvantages of a DBMS

      ✅ Advantages

      • Controlled redundancy and consistent data.
      • Data sharing: many apps, many users, one copy.
      • Integrity constraints declared once, enforced always.
      • Transactions + recovery: ACID, backups, point-in-time restore.
      • Concurrency control: safe parallel reads and writes.
      • Security: users, roles, privileges, views, encryption.
      • Data independence: change storage without rewriting apps (Ch 02).
      • Powerful querying: SQL + a cost-based optimizer.
      • Standards: one language and one set of tools across teams.

      ⚠️ Disadvantages

      • Cost: licences (Oracle, SQL Server), hardware, cloud bills.
      • Complexity: setup, tuning, upgrades, a skilled DBA.
      • Overhead: logging, locking and parsing make tiny jobs slower than a direct file write.
      • Bigger blast radius: one central server failing can stop every app (so you need replicas and backups).
      • Size: a server DBMS needs memory, disk and processes even when idle.
      • Rigid schema (for relational systems): changing structure on huge tables needs care.
      QWhen should you NOT use a DBMS?

      A DBMS is a tool. Use it when data is shared, changing, and valuable. Skip a full server DBMS when its overhead buys you nothing:

      • Small, single-user, rarely changing data: an app's config file (.env, YAML, JSON). Nobody else writes it concurrently.
      • Large binary objects: videos, images, ML checkpoints. Store them in a file system or object storage (S3, GCS) and keep only the path + metadata in the database.
      • Append-only logs / streams at huge volume: log files, Kafka topics. You need sequential writes, not random updates and joins.
      • Hard real-time or tiny embedded systems where a few KB of RAM matter and the timing must be exact.
      • One-off data analysis on a CSV that a script reads once.
      💡
      Middle path: SQLite

      If you need SQL and transactions but not a server, use an embedded DBMS like SQLite. It is a library inside your app (every Android and iOS phone uses it). "No server" ≠ "no DBMS".

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      I would skip a server DBMS when the data is small, used by one program, and rarely changes, like a config file, or when it is big binary data such as videos that belong in object storage with only the metadata in the database. Huge append-only logs also fit better in log files or a streaming system. If I still want SQL without a server, I would use an embedded database like SQLite.

      📋 DBMS vs RDBMS

      QWhat is the difference between a DBMS and an RDBMS?

      DBMS is the general category: any software that manages a database, using any data model (tree, graph, document, key-value, tables). RDBMS is one kind of DBMS that uses the relational model: data lives in tables (relations), rows are linked by key values, rules are declared as constraints, and you query with SQL. Every RDBMS is a DBMS. Not every DBMS is relational.

      AspectDBMS (general / older style)RDBMS
      Data structureFiles, trees, graphs, documents, key-valueTables of rows and columns
      RelationshipsOften physical pointers or noneLogical, through primary/foreign key values
      ConstraintsFew, often in app codePK, FK, UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL built in
      NormalisationNot applicableCore design method
      Query languageNavigational / API callsDeclarative SQL
      Multi-user + ACIDVaries (often limited)Yes, standard
      ExamplesIBM IMS (hierarchical), IDMS (network), file-based stores; modern NoSQL is "non-relational DBMS"MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, SQLite, MariaDB
      ⚠️
      Trap

      Many Indian textbooks write "DBMS = single user, small data; RDBMS = multi-user, large data". That is a simplification of old desktop products (like early dBase). Better answer: the difference is the data model (relations + keys + SQL), not size.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A DBMS is any software that manages a database, whatever the data model. An RDBMS is a DBMS based on Codd's relational model: data is stored in tables, relationships are expressed through primary and foreign keys, integrity rules are declared as constraints, and data is queried with SQL. MySQL and PostgreSQL are RDBMSs; MongoDB is a DBMS but not relational.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is MongoDB a DBMS?

      Yes, a document-oriented (NoSQL) DBMS. It manages data, indexes, replication and even multi-document transactions, but it is not relational. See Chapter 20.

      ↪What exactly makes a system "relational"?

      Data shown only as relations (tables), access by values not pointers, set-based operations (relational algebra / SQL), and declared integrity. Codd formalised this in his 12 rules (below).

      🧩 Data models and types of DBMS

      A data model is a set of concepts for describing data: how it is structured, how items are linked, and what operations and rules apply. The type of a DBMS is named after its data model.

      TypeStructureHow you navigateStrengthWeaknessExamples
      HierarchicalTree: each child has exactly one parent (1:N)Follow parent → child pointersVery fast for fixed top-down pathsM:N impossible without duplication; rigidIBM IMS (late 1960s), Windows Registry, XML/file trees
      NetworkGraph of records; owner–member "sets" allow many parentsNavigate pointer chains in codeModels M:N directlyPrograms depend on physical pointers; complexCODASYL systems, IDMS
      RelationalTables (relations) of rows; links by key valuesDeclarative SQL; optimizer picks the pathSimple, flexible, data independence, strong theoryJoins cost; scaling writes horizontally is harderMySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server
      Object-orientedObjects with identity, attributes, methods, inheritanceFollow object references, like in JavaNo "impedance mismatch" with OO codeNo standard query language; nichedb4o, ObjectDB, GemStone
      Object-relationalTables + user-defined types, arrays, inheritanceSQL with extensionsRelational power + richer typesMore complex than pure relationalPostgreSQL, Oracle (object types)
      NoSQL (teaser)Key-value, document, wide-column, graphAPIs / own query languagesFlexible schema, horizontal scaleWeaker joins; consistency trade-offsRedis, MongoDB, Cassandra, Neo4j
      QWhy did the relational model replace hierarchical and network databases?

      In hierarchical and network systems, programs navigated physical pointers: "go to this department record, then follow the chain to its first student". If the DBA reorganised storage, the programs broke. In 1970 E. F. Codd proposed the relational model: describe data only as tables of values, and let the user say what they want, not how to walk to it. The system (the optimizer) decides the access path. This gave data independence, a simple mental model, and a mathematical base (relational algebra, normalisation). IBM System R and Berkeley Ingres proved it could be fast, and SQL became the standard.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Older hierarchical and network databases made programs follow physical pointers, so any storage change broke the code and many-to-many data was awkward. Codd's relational model stored everything as tables linked by values and let users write declarative queries, while the DBMS chose how to execute them. That gave data independence and a clean mathematical foundation, so it won.

      ℹ️
      Other ways to classify a DBMS

      By users: single-user (SQLite in an app) vs multi-user (MySQL server). By location: centralized vs distributed (Ch 02, Ch 19). By workload: OLTP (many small transactions) vs OLAP (big analytic scans) (Ch 20). By storage: row store vs column store; disk-based vs in-memory.

      📖 Metadata, data dictionary and system catalog

      Metadata is data about data: table names, column names and types, constraints, indexes, users and their privileges, row-count statistics. The DBMS keeps it in the data dictionary (also called the system catalog). When you run CREATE TABLE, the DDL interpreter writes a new entry into the dictionary. When you run a query, the parser and optimizer read the dictionary to check names, permissions and statistics.

      QWhat is a data dictionary? How do you query it in MySQL?

      The data dictionary is the DBMS's own internal database that describes every object in the database. It is read on every query (to resolve names, check privileges, and get statistics for the optimizer) and written by every DDL statement. Because it is stored as tables, you can query it with normal SQL; that is Codd's Rule 4 (dynamic online catalog).

      -- All tables of one database, with InnoDB's estimated row counts
SELECT TABLE_NAME, ENGINE, TABLE_ROWS
FROM   information_schema.TABLES
WHERE  TABLE_SCHEMA = 'college';

-- Columns of one table
SELECT COLUMN_NAME, DATA_TYPE, IS_NULLABLE, COLUMN_KEY
FROM   information_schema.COLUMNS
WHERE  TABLE_SCHEMA = 'college' AND TABLE_NAME = 'student';

-- Shortcut commands that read the same catalog
SHOW TABLES;  DESCRIBE student;  SHOW CREATE TABLE student;
      +------------+--------+------------+
| TABLE_NAME | ENGINE | TABLE_ROWS |
+------------+--------+------------+
| course     | InnoDB |         12 |
| enrolment  | InnoDB |        340 |
| student    | InnoDB |        118 |
+------------+--------+------------+
      🔀
      Engine differences

      MySQL 8.0+: a transactional data dictionary stored in InnoDB tables (older versions used .frm files); you read it through information_schema views. PostgreSQL: native catalog tables in pg_catalog (pg_class, pg_attribute, pg_index) plus the SQL-standard information_schema; \d student in psql. Oracle: USER_TABLES, ALL_TAB_COLUMNS, DBA_* views. SQL Server: sys.tables, sys.columns and INFORMATION_SCHEMA.

      ⚠️
      Gotcha

      TABLE_ROWS for InnoDB is an estimate from statistics, not an exact count. Use COUNT(*) when you need the true number.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Active vs passive data dictionary?

      Active: maintained automatically by the DBMS on every DDL, always in sync (all modern RDBMSs). Passive: a separate document or tool updated by hand, can go stale.

      ↪Who uses the catalog during query execution?

      The parser (does this table/column exist?), the authorization manager (may this user read it?) and the optimizer (row counts, index list, histograms to estimate cost). See Chapter 16.

      👥 Database users and the DBA

      🧑

      Naive / end users

      Use ready-made apps without knowing SQL: a bank teller, an IRCTC passenger, a student checking results.

      ✏️

      Application programmers

      Write the apps: embed SQL in Java/Python/Node, design APIs, use ORMs.

      📊

      Sophisticated users

      Analysts and data scientists who write SQL directly or use BI tools (Power BI, Tableau, notebooks).

      ⚙️

      Specialized users

      Build unusual database apps: CAD, GIS/maps, audio-video, scientific data, vector search.

      🗺️

      Database designers

      Gather requirements, draw the ER model (Ch 03), normalise, choose keys and constraints.

      🛡️

      DBA

      The person with central control over data and the DBMS. Duties below.

      QWhat are the responsibilities of a DBA?
      1. Schema definition — creates the conceptual schema with DDL (often with designers).
      2. Storage structure and access methods — decides tablespaces, file layout, partitions and indexes.
      3. Schema and physical changes — runs safe migrations (ALTERs on big tables, online DDL).
      4. Authorization — creates users and roles, GRANT/REVOKE, least privilege, auditing.
      5. Backup and recovery — schedules full/incremental backups, tests restores, plans RPO/RTO (Ch 17).
      6. Performance tuning — monitors slow queries, adds indexes, tunes the buffer pool and configuration.
      7. Availability — replication, failover, upgrades and patches (Ch 19).
      8. Capacity planning — watches disk space, growth and connections.
      🌍
      Modern twist

      On managed clouds (Amazon RDS, Cloud SQL, Azure Database) the provider does patching, backups and failover. The DBA role shifts to schema design, query tuning, cost control and security. Many startups have no DBA at all; backend engineers do this, which is why SDE interviews ask it.

      ✏️ SQL sublanguages at a glance

      SQL is one language, but its commands are grouped by purpose. Full syntax and traps (DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP, implicit commits) are in Chapter 07.

      GroupFull namePurposeCommandsAuto-commit in MySQL?
      DDLData Definition LanguageDefine / change structure (schema)CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAMEYes — implicit commit before and after
      DMLData Manipulation LanguageChange the rowsINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (+ MERGE in other engines)No — part of a transaction
      DQLData Query LanguageRead dataSELECT— (many books put SELECT under DML)
      DCLData Control LanguagePermissionsGRANT, REVOKEYes in MySQL (account statements commit)
      TCLTransaction Control LanguageGroup changes into transactionsSTART TRANSACTION / BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINTThey are the commit controls
      DDL · DML · DQL · DCL · TCL

      Define the shelves, Move the books, Query the catalogue, Control who enters, Tie it all in one transaction.

      🔀
      Engine differences

      MySQL and Oracle commit implicitly on DDL, so you cannot roll back a DROP TABLE. PostgreSQL has transactional DDL: BEGIN; DROP TABLE t; ROLLBACK; brings the table back. SQL Server also allows DDL inside transactions.

      ⚖️ Codd's 12 rules (actually 13: Rule 0 to Rule 12)

      In 1985 E. F. Codd published 12 rules (plus a foundation Rule 0) in Computerworld, because vendors were calling any product with tables "relational". The rules are a test for a fully relational DBMS. No commercial product passes all of them; what matters in an interview is that you know the important ones and can say where real systems bend them.

      #RuleIn one lineMySQL 8.x
      0FoundationThe system must manage data entirely through its relational capabilities.✔
      1InformationAll information, including metadata, is stored as values in tables.✔ (dictionary in InnoDB tables since 8.0)
      2Guaranteed accessEvery value is reachable by table name + primary key value + column name.~ tables may have no PK and duplicate rows
      3Systematic NULLsNULL means "missing/inapplicable", is distinct from 0 and '' and is handled uniformly.✔ (mostly; non-strict sql_mode can coerce values)
      4Dynamic online catalogThe catalog is queryable with the same language as data.✔ information_schema
      5Comprehensive data sublanguageOne language for definition, manipulation, constraints, authorization and transactions.✔ SQL
      6View updatingEvery view that is theoretically updatable can be updated by the system.~ views with GROUP BY, DISTINCT, aggregates, UNION are read-only
      7High-level insert/update/deleteSet-at-a-time changes, not one record at a time.✔
      8Physical data independenceChanging storage/access methods does not affect apps.✔ (add index, change engine)
      9Logical data independenceChanging tables (e.g., splitting one) does not affect apps.~ partly, via views
      10Integrity independenceConstraints are defined in the catalog, not in application code.~ CHECK was ignored before 8.0.16; MyISAM ignores FKs
      11Distribution independenceApps should not care whether data is on one node or many.~ manual sharding leaks into apps
      12Non-subversionA low-level interface must not bypass integrity rules.✘ SET foreign_key_checks = 0 lets bad rows in
      🧠
      Remember them in 5 groups

      Data representation 0–3 (foundation, information, guaranteed access, NULLs) · Catalog & language 4–5 · Operations 6–7 (view update, set-level DML) · Independence 8–11 (physical, logical, integrity, distribution) · Safety 12 (non-subversion). Rules 8–11 are all "…independence".

      QWhat are Codd's rules? Does MySQL follow all of them?

      Codd's rules are 13 conditions (numbered 0–12) that a DBMS must meet to be called fully relational. No product meets all of them, including Oracle and PostgreSQL. MySQL breaks or bends a few in practice:

      • Rule 2: SQL tables are bags, not sets. You can create a table without a primary key and insert duplicate rows, so a value is not always reachable by a key. (MySQL 8.0.13+ has sql_require_primary_key to forbid PK-less tables.)
      • Rule 6: only simple views (one table, no aggregates/DISTINCT/GROUP BY/UNION) are updatable.
      • Rule 10: before MySQL 8.0.16, CHECK constraints were parsed and silently ignored; MyISAM tables ignore foreign keys.
      • Rule 12: SET foreign_key_checks = 0 lets you insert orphan rows, and turning it back on does not re-check them.
      SET foreign_key_checks = 0;
INSERT INTO enrolment(roll_no, course_id) VALUES (999, 'CS101'); -- roll 999 does not exist
SET foreign_key_checks = 1;   -- no error: the orphan row stays
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Codd's rules, published in 1985, are thirteen rules from zero to twelve that define a fully relational DBMS, such as storing everything in tables, guaranteed access by table, key and column, systematic NULLs, an online catalog, physical and logical data independence, and non-subversion. No real product satisfies all of them. For example MySQL allows tables without a primary key, only simple views are updatable, and turning off foreign_key_checks lets you bypass referential integrity.

      🧭 SQL vs NoSQL — the 30-second teaser

      🗄️ SQL / relational

      • Fixed schema; tables, joins, foreign keys.
      • Strong ACID transactions by default.
      • Scales up easily; scaling writes out needs sharding work.
      • Best for: banking, orders, inventory, anything with relationships and invariants.

      🍃 NoSQL

      • Flexible schema: key-value, document, wide-column, graph.
      • Often built to scale out across many nodes; tunable consistency.
      • Joins limited; you design around access patterns.
      • Best for: caching (Redis), catalogs and user profiles (MongoDB), time-series/IoT writes (Cassandra), social graphs (Neo4j).

      The honest answer is "it depends on the access pattern and the consistency you need", and modern systems blur the line (MongoDB has multi-document transactions; PostgreSQL has JSONB). Full comparison, CAP and NewSQL in Chapter 20 and Chapter 19.

      🌍 Where DBMSs run your life

      🏦

      Banking & UPI

      Accounts, transfers and ledgers. Needs atomic, durable transactions; every rupee must balance.

      🎫

      Railways & airlines

      IRCTC seat booking: thousands of users fight for the same berth. Needs concurrency control.

      🛒

      E-commerce

      Catalog, cart, orders, inventory, payments. Mix of RDBMS (orders) and NoSQL/cache (sessions, catalog).

      🎓

      Universities

      Students, courses, enrolments, results, hostel, library — the classic ER example (Ch 03).

      🏥

      Healthcare

      Patient records, prescriptions, lab results; strict security and audit trails.

      📈

      Analytics & ML

      Data warehouses (OLAP), feature stores, vector databases for AI search.

      📌 Key takeaways

      • Database = data; DBMS = software; RDBMS = DBMS on the relational model (tables + keys + SQL).
      • File systems fail on RIDAICS: redundancy/inconsistency, isolation, difficult access, atomicity, integrity, concurrency, security.
      • For atomicity and concurrency, name the mechanism: write-ahead log for undo/redo; locks or MVCC for parallel access.
      • A DBMS costs money, complexity and overhead; skip it for tiny single-user config, blobs (use object storage) or raw log streams.
      • Relational won because declarative queries over value-linked tables gave data independence.
      • Metadata lives in the data dictionary: information_schema (MySQL), pg_catalog (PostgreSQL).
      • DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, TCL; DDL auto-commits in MySQL and Oracle but is transactional in PostgreSQL.
      • Codd's 12 (+0) rules: no product passes all; MySQL bends 2, 6, 10, 12.

      📚 Go deeper

      • Silberschatz, Korth & Sudarshan — Chapter 1 slides — the source of the classic "file system problems" list.
      • CMU 15-445 Lecture Notes #01: Relational Model — why flat files fail, explained by Andy Pavlo's course.
      • Wikipedia — Codd's 12 rules — full text of every rule.
      • MySQL 8.4 Manual — INFORMATION_SCHEMA — every catalog table you can query.
      • GeeksforGeeks — SQL command categories — quick refresher list.

      Which statement is correct?

      The database is the data; the DBMS is the software. "RDBMS" is about the relational model, not size.

      Two clerks read balance ₹100 at the same time and each withdraws ₹50. Final balance shows ₹50. Which file-system problem is this?

      Both writes were based on the same old read, so one update was lost. Concurrency control (locks/MVCC) prevents it. Atomicity is about partial updates after a failure.

      Which data model allows each child record to have only ONE parent?

      Hierarchical = tree (IBM IMS). The network model (CODASYL) allowed many owners per record through owner–member sets.

      In MySQL, which of these statements can be rolled back?

      DELETE is DML and joins the transaction. TRUNCATE, DROP and ALTER are DDL in MySQL and cause an implicit commit.

      Running SET foreign_key_checks = 0 and inserting orphan rows violates which Codd rule?

      Rule 12 says no low-level path may bypass integrity rules. Disabling FK checks does exactly that.

      Where should a video-streaming app store 4 GB movie files?

      Huge blobs bloat the buffer pool, backups and replication. Keep blobs in object storage and searchable metadata in the DBMS.
      Data vs information?
      Data = raw facts (92). Information = processed data with meaning ("Asha topped with 92").
      Database vs DBMS?
      Database = organised related data. DBMS = software that defines, stores, queries and protects it.
      RIDAICS?
      File-system problems: Redundancy & inconsistency, Isolation, Difficult access, Atomicity, Integrity, Concurrency, Security.
      DBMS vs RDBMS in one line?
      RDBMS is a DBMS based on the relational model: tables, key-based relationships, constraints, SQL.
      Hierarchical vs network model?
      Hierarchical = tree, one parent (IMS). Network = graph, many parents via owner–member sets (CODASYL). Both navigate pointers.
      What is metadata? Where is it kept?
      Data about data (tables, columns, types, constraints, privileges, stats). In the data dictionary / system catalog.
      MySQL vs PostgreSQL catalog?
      MySQL: information_schema views over the InnoDB data dictionary. PostgreSQL: pg_catalog (pg_class, pg_attribute) + information_schema.
      5 SQL sublanguages?
      DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE), DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), DQL (SELECT), DCL (GRANT/REVOKE), TCL (COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT).
      Codd's Rule 2?
      Guaranteed access: every value reachable by table name + primary key + column name.
      Codd's Rule 12?
      Non-subversion: low-level access must not bypass integrity constraints.
      When not to use a DBMS?
      Tiny single-user config, large blobs (object storage), raw append-only log streams, hard real-time tiny devices. Use SQLite if you want SQL without a server.
      Chapter 02 · I · Foundations

      🏛️ Architecture, Schemas & Data Independence

      Draw the three-schema architecture from memory, explain why logical independence is harder, and walk a query through the inside of MySQL and PostgreSQL.

      ⏱ 25 minbasicMySQL 8PostgreSQL

      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision

      • 1-tier: app and DB on one machine. 2-tier: client app talks straight to the DB server. 3-tier: browser → application server → DB (all web apps). 3-tier wins on security, scaling and reuse of business logic.
      • ANSI-SPARC three-schema architecture: external (many user views) → conceptual (one logical schema: tables, keys, constraints) → internal (one physical schema: files, pages, indexes).
      • Two mappings connect the levels: external/conceptual and conceptual/internal. Mappings are what make independence possible.
      • Schema = structure (intension, changes rarely). Instance = data at a moment (extension, changes every INSERT).
      • Physical data independence: change storage (add an index, move files) without changing the logical schema. Logical data independence: change the logical schema (add/split tables) without breaking views and apps. Logical is harder, because apps are written against table and column names.
      • DBMS = query processor (DDL interpreter, DML compiler + optimizer, evaluation engine) + storage manager (authorization/integrity, transaction, file, buffer managers) + disk (data files, dictionary, indexes, statistics).
      • MySQL: one mysqld process, a thread per connection, SQL layer (parser → optimizer → executor) over pluggable storage engines (InnoDB default). No query cache since 8.0.
      • PostgreSQL: process per connection forked by the postmaster, plus background processes (background writer, checkpointer, WAL writer, autovacuum). Many connections → use PgBouncer.
      • Deployment styles: centralized, client-server, distributed (data on many sites), parallel (many CPUs/disks for one job: shared memory / shared disk / shared nothing).

      🖥️ 1-tier, 2-tier and 3-tier architecture

      "Tier" means a separate layer that can run on its own machine. The question is: who talks to the database directly?

      QExplain 2-tier vs 3-tier architecture. Why do web apps use 3-tier?

      2-tier: the client application (UI + business logic) connects directly to the database server and sends SQL. Simple and fast for a few users on a LAN, like a billing app in a shop.

      3-tier: a thin client (browser, mobile app) talks to an application server over HTTP. Only the app server holds DB credentials and sends SQL. The three tiers are presentation, application (business logic) and data.

      2-tier

      • Each client opens its own DB connection → hundreds of connections.
      • DB credentials live on every client machine (security risk).
      • Business logic copied in every client; updating it means reinstalling apps.
      • Good for: small LAN apps, admin tools.

      3-tier

      • App servers pool a few DB connections for thousands of users.
      • Database hidden behind a firewall; clients never see it.
      • Logic in one place; deploy once. App tier scales horizontally behind a load balancer.
      • Cost: one more network hop and more moving parts.
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      In a 2-tier architecture the client application talks directly to the database server. In a 3-tier architecture there is an application server in the middle: the browser talks to the app server, and only the app server talks to the database. Web apps use 3-tier because the database stays hidden and credentials never reach clients, business logic lives in one place, app servers can be scaled out and can pool database connections.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪What is 1-tier? Give an example.

      UI, logic and database all on one machine: an Android app with SQLite inside it, or a developer typing SQL at a local mysql prompt.

      ↪What is n-tier?

      More layers added for scale: CDN, load balancer, API gateway, microservices, cache (Redis), message queue, then the DB. Still the same idea: each layer talks only to its neighbour.

      ↪Why does connection pooling matter in 3-tier?

      Opening a DB connection costs a TCP handshake, authentication and a server thread (MySQL) or a whole process (PostgreSQL). A pool keeps, say, 20 open connections and lends them to requests, so 10,000 users do not mean 10,000 DB connections.

      📦 The three-schema (ANSI-SPARC) architecture

      In 1975 the ANSI/X3/SPARC study group proposed describing a database at three levels. The goal: separate each user's view of the data from the way the data is physically stored. Each level hides the details of the level below it.

      LevelAlso calledDescribesWho caresHow manyMySQL example
      ExternalView levelOnly the part of data a user group needs, in the shape they needEnd users, app developersManyCREATE VIEW, column privileges
      ConceptualLogical levelAll entities, attributes, relationships, constraints, security rules — what is storedDesigners, DBAOneCREATE TABLE … PRIMARY KEY … FOREIGN KEY
      InternalPhysical levelRecord layout, pages, files, indexes, compression, encryption — how it is storedDBA, the storage engineOneENGINE=InnoDB, CREATE INDEX, tablespaces, ROW_FORMAT
      QExplain the three-schema architecture. Why do we need it?

      What: a way to describe one database at three levels of abstraction. The external level has many user views (a student sees her grades, accounts sees fee dues). The conceptual level is the single logical description of the whole database: tables, columns, keys, relationships and constraints, with no storage details. The internal level describes physical storage: files, pages, record formats, indexes.

      Why: so that changes at one level do not force changes at the level above. Users get simplified, secure views. The DBA can tune storage freely. This property is called data independence.

      How: the DBMS stores the definition of every level plus two mappings in its catalog. When a user queries a view, the DBMS uses mapping ① to rewrite it into a query on the conceptual tables, then mapping ② to turn that into page reads on disk.

      💡
      Easy analogy: a restaurant

      The menu is the external level (each customer sees dishes, not recipes; the kids' menu is another view). The recipe book is the conceptual level (what each dish contains). The kitchen layout — which fridge, which shelf — is the internal level. The chef can rearrange the fridge without reprinting menus.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      The three-schema architecture describes a database at three levels. The external level holds the different user views, the conceptual level is the single logical schema of the whole database with all tables, relationships and constraints, and the internal level describes how data is physically stored, like files, pages and indexes. The DBMS keeps mappings between the levels, and those mappings give us data independence: we can change storage or even the logical schema without rewriting every application.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪How many schemas of each level can a database have?

      Many external schemas, exactly one conceptual schema and exactly one internal schema.

      ↪Is a SQL view the external level?

      Yes, a view (plus privileges that hide columns) is the practical way to build an external schema in an RDBMS. See views in Chapter 09.

      ↪What is the cost of three levels?

      Mapping work at query time (view rewriting, translating to page access). Modern optimizers merge views into the main query, so the cost is usually tiny.

      The two mappings

      External schemaview v_fee_due(roll, due)
      ① External/conceptual mappingview definition: SELECT roll, total - paid …
      Conceptual schematable fees(roll, total, paid)
      ② Conceptual/internal mapping"fees is a B+ tree in fees.ibd keyed on roll"
      Internal schemapages, records, indexes

      When something changes, only the mapping is updated. Change storage → fix mapping ②. Change tables → fix mapping ① (rewrite the view). The level above never notices. ← this is the whole trick

      📷 Schema vs instance

      Schema (intension)

      • The design / structure: table names, columns, types, constraints.
      • Defined with DDL; stored in the data dictionary.
      • Changes rarely (ALTER TABLE).
      • Like a variable's type in a program: int x;

      Instance (extension / state)

      • The actual data stored at one moment: a snapshot.
      • Changes with every INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
      • Must always satisfy the schema's constraints (a valid state).
      • Like the variable's value: x = 42
      CREATE TABLE student (
  roll  INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name  VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  dept  CHAR(3)
);
      +------+-------+------+
| roll | name  | dept |
+------+-------+------+
|    1 | Asha  | CSE  |
|    2 | Bilal | ECE  |
+------+-------+------+
      QWhat is the difference between a schema and an instance?

      The schema is the overall design of the database: which tables exist, their columns, types and constraints. It is also called the intension. The instance is the collection of data stored in the database at a particular moment, also called the extension or database state. The schema is fixed by DDL and rarely changes; the instance changes every time a row is inserted, updated or deleted.

      ⚠️
      Word clash

      In MySQL, CREATE SCHEMA is a synonym for CREATE DATABASE. In PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server a schema is a namespace inside a database (public.student, hr.employees). In theory questions, "schema" means "the structure description". Say which meaning you use.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A schema is the structure of the database, like the table definitions with columns, types and constraints. It is defined once and rarely changes. An instance is the actual data in the database at a given moment, and it changes with every insert, update or delete. It is like a variable's type versus its current value.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪What are the types of schema?

      Matching the three levels: physical schema (storage), logical schema (tables and constraints) and view / external schemas (sub-schemas for users).

      ↪What is a "valid state"?

      An instance that satisfies every constraint of the schema (keys unique, FKs matching, CHECKs true). The DBMS rejects any change that would create an invalid state.

      🔓 Data independence: logical vs physical

      Data independence = the ability to change the schema at one level without having to change the schema at the next higher level (and without rewriting application programs).

      🧱 Physical data independence

      • Change the internal schema; the conceptual schema and apps stay the same.
      • Protected by mapping ② (conceptual/internal).
      • Examples: add/drop an index, move data to SSD, change ROW_FORMAT or compression, partition a table, switch from MyISAM to InnoDB, change the buffer pool size.
      • Easy — every modern RDBMS gives it.

      🧩 Logical data independence

      • Change the conceptual schema; external views and apps stay the same.
      • Protected by mapping ① (external/conceptual).
      • Examples: add a column, add a new table, split a table into two (normalisation) and keep the old shape as a view, merge two tables.
      • Hard — only partly achievable.
      QPhysical vs logical data independence — which is harder to achieve, and why?

      Logical data independence is harder. Here is the mechanism:

      1. Physical changes sit below the logical schema. Queries name tables and columns, never pages or files. When you add an index, the optimizer simply sees a new access path. The SQL text does not change, so apps are untouched automatically.
      2. Logical changes touch the very names apps use. Applications and views are written against table and column names and their relationships. If you rename a column, split a table, or drop a column, those names disappear.
      3. Only some logical changes can be hidden. Adding a column is safe (if apps never use SELECT * or column-less INSERT). Splitting a table can be hidden by a view with the old name — but then updates through that view may not be possible (joined views are often not updatable). Removing data that apps need cannot be hidden at all.
      CREATE INDEX idx_student_name ON student(name);   -- same queries, just faster
ALTER TABLE student ROW_FORMAT = COMPRESSED;       -- storage change only
      -- Old design: student(roll, name, dept, hostel_room, hostel_fee)
-- New design: hostel details move to their own table
CREATE TABLE hostel_alloc (roll INT PRIMARY KEY, room VARCHAR(6), fee INT,
                           FOREIGN KEY (roll) REFERENCES student_core(roll));
-- ... migrate data, then rename the old table and create a view with the OLD name
CREATE VIEW student AS
SELECT s.roll, s.name, s.dept, h.room AS hostel_room, h.fee AS hostel_fee
FROM   student_core s LEFT JOIN hostel_alloc h ON h.roll = s.roll;
-- SELECTs keep working. INSERTs through this join view may NOT  <- the leak
      🚫
      Wrong answer that fails interviews

      "Physical is harder because storage is complicated." No — the DBMS hides storage completely. Difficulty is about how much the applications depend on the level being changed.

      🌍
      Production habit that protects you

      Never use SELECT * or INSERT INTO t VALUES (…) without a column list in app code. Then adding a column later is a truly invisible logical change. ORMs and API layers (an extra "external level") give even more independence.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Physical data independence means I can change how data is stored, like adding an index or moving files, without changing the logical schema or the apps. Logical data independence means I can change the logical schema, like adding or splitting tables, without breaking user views and programs. Logical independence is harder because applications are written directly against table and column names, while physical details are already completely hidden by the DBMS. Views help, but not every logical change can be hidden, and joined views are often not updatable.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is adding a column logical or physical? Does it break apps?

      Logical (conceptual schema changes). It breaks only badly written code: INSERT INTO student VALUES (1,'Asha','CSE') now has too few values, and code reading SELECT * by position gets shifted columns.

      ↪Is creating an index a DDL change? Then is it logical?

      It is DDL, but it changes only the internal level (a new access structure). Results of every query stay identical, so it is a physical change. Exception: a UNIQUE index also adds a constraint, which is logical.

      ↪Which Codd rules are these?

      Rule 8 = physical data independence, Rule 9 = logical data independence (Chapter 01).

      P = Plumbing · L = Layout

      Physical independence: you can redo the plumbing (pipes under the floor) and nobody notices. Logical independence: you change the room layout — people bump into walls unless you put up signboards (views).

      ⚙️ Components of a DBMS (inside the box)

      Textbooks (Silberschatz) split a DBMS into two big parts: the query processor (understands and plans your SQL) and the storage manager (moves bytes between disk and memory safely). Below them sit the disk structures.

      QWhat are the main components of a DBMS? Trace a query through them.
      DDL interpreter
      Executes DDL and records the definitions (metadata) in the data dictionary.
      DML compiler + optimizer
      Turns a SQL statement into an evaluation plan of low-level steps and chooses the cheapest of many equivalent plans (query optimization, Ch 16).
      Query evaluation engine
      Runs the plan: index lookups, scans, joins, sorts.
      Authorization & integrity manager
      Checks the user's privileges and that constraints hold.
      Transaction manager
      Keeps the database consistent despite failures (recovery manager + logs) and concurrent users (concurrency-control manager: locks, MVCC).
      File manager
      Manages disk space and the on-disk data structures.
      Buffer manager
      Brings pages from disk into RAM, keeps hot pages cached, writes dirty pages back. Critical because RAM is far faster than disk (Ch 14).
      Disk structures
      Data files (the tables), data dictionary (metadata), indexes (fast lookup), statistical data (row counts, histograms used by the optimizer).
      1. Parsesyntax + names checked against dictionary
      2. Authorizemay this user SELECT?
      3. Optimizeuse statistics, choose index & join order
      4. Executeevaluation engine asks for pages
      5. Bufferpage in RAM? else read from disk
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A DBMS has a query processor and a storage manager. The query processor has the DDL interpreter that records definitions in the data dictionary, the DML compiler with the optimizer that turns SQL into the cheapest execution plan, and the query evaluation engine that runs it. The storage manager has the authorization and integrity manager, the transaction manager for concurrency and recovery, the file manager for disk space, and the buffer manager that caches pages in memory. On disk we have data files, the data dictionary, indexes and statistics.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Which component decides the join order?

      The query optimizer, part of the DML compiler / query processor, using statistics from the catalog.

      ↪Which component guarantees atomicity and durability?

      The transaction manager's recovery part, using the write-ahead log (undo + redo). Isolation comes from its concurrency-control part.

      ↪Why does a DBMS have its own buffer manager instead of trusting the OS page cache?

      It knows more than the OS: which pages are hot index roots, which are dirty and must follow WAL ordering, and when a big scan should not flush the cache. InnoDB is usually configured with O_DIRECT to skip the OS cache. PostgreSQL deliberately uses both its shared buffers and the OS cache.

      🔧 Real engines: MySQL vs PostgreSQL architecture

      The textbook boxes above map onto real servers. Interviewers at product companies love "what happens inside MySQL when I run a query?" and "why does PostgreSQL need PgBouncer?".

      1. Connectors & connection layer — JDBC/Python/Node drivers connect over TCP; the server authenticates and gives each client a dedicated thread. thread_cache_size reuses finished threads; MySQL Enterprise (and Percona/MariaDB) offer a thread-pool plugin.
      2. Parser — checks syntax and builds a parse tree. Resolver/preprocessor — checks that tables and columns exist and that you have privileges.
      3. Optimizer — cost-based: uses index statistics and histograms to choose access paths and join order. See EXPLAIN in Ch 16.
      4. Executor — runs the plan by calling the storage engine through the handler API: "give me the first row from index X", "next row".
      5. Storage engine — chosen per table (ENGINE=InnoDB). InnoDB has the buffer pool, redo/undo logs, row locks and MVCC, clustered PK. MyISAM: table locks, no transactions, no FKs.
      6. Server-level services — the binary log (replication, point-in-time recovery) is written by the server, not by InnoDB, which is why commit uses an internal two-phase commit between redo log and binlog (Ch 17).
      ⚠️
      Outdated answer alert

      Old blog diagrams show a query cache before the parser. It was disabled by default from 5.6 and removed in MySQL 8.0 because every write to a table invalidated its cached results and its global lock hurt multi-core scaling. Saying "MySQL checks the query cache first" shows your notes are from 2015.

      1. Postmaster (the main postgres process) listens on port 5432. For each new connection it forks a backend process ("process per user").
      2. Backend — runs your queries: parser → rewriter (applies views/rules) → planner/optimizer → executor. Backends talk to each other only through shared memory and locks.
      3. Shared memory — shared_buffers (page cache), WAL buffers, lock tables, transaction status.
      4. Background writer — trickles dirty pages to disk so backends rarely have to. Checkpointer — performs checkpoints (flushes all dirty pages, marks a safe redo start point).
      5. WAL writer — flushes WAL buffers to pg_wal/. Archiver — copies finished WAL segments for backups/PITR. WAL sender/receiver — streaming replication.
      6. Autovacuum launcher + workers — PostgreSQL MVCC leaves dead row versions inside the table; VACUUM cleans them, updates statistics and prevents transaction-ID wraparound (Ch 13).
      💡
      Why PgBouncer?

      A process per connection costs several MB of memory and a fork. 5,000 app connections = 5,000 processes. A pooler like PgBouncer keeps a small set of real server connections and multiplexes thousands of client connections onto them.

      QExplain MySQL's architecture. What happens when you run a SELECT?

      MySQL has two big layers. The server (SQL) layer handles connections, parsing, privilege checks, optimization, execution, the binary log and the data dictionary. Below it, through a common handler API, sit pluggable storage engines that actually store and fetch rows. InnoDB is the default.

      Connectauth; thread assigned
      Parsesyntax → tree
      Resolvenames + privileges
      Optimizeindexes, join order
      Executehandler calls to InnoDB
      InnoDBbuffer pool, else disk read
      🔀
      MySQL vs PostgreSQL vs others

      MySQL: thread per connection, many engines per server. PostgreSQL: process per connection, one built-in heap storage (extensible via table access methods), heavy use of background processes. Oracle: instance (SGA memory + background processes such as DBWn, LGWR, CKPT, SMON, PMON) with dedicated or shared server processes. SQL Server: one process with its own scheduler (SQLOS) and worker threads. SQLite: no server at all, a library inside the app.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      MySQL is a single server process with a thread per connection. The SQL layer parses the query, checks names and privileges, lets the cost-based optimizer pick indexes and join order, and then the executor calls the storage engine through the handler API. The storage engine is pluggable per table; InnoDB, the default, gives transactions, row locks, MVCC and crash recovery. PostgreSQL instead forks one process per connection and uses background processes like the checkpointer, WAL writer and autovacuum, which is why it usually needs a pooler like PgBouncer.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Can two tables in one MySQL database use different engines? Is a transaction across them safe?

      Yes, engines are per table. But a transaction touching InnoDB and MyISAM is not atomic: the MyISAM change cannot be rolled back.

      ↪Thread per connection vs process per connection — trade-offs?

      Threads are cheaper to create and share memory directly, so MySQL handles many connections more easily. Processes isolate failures better (one crashing backend does not corrupt another's stack) but cost more memory and fork time, so PostgreSQL relies on poolers.

      ↪Why is SELECT COUNT(*) instant on MyISAM but slow on big InnoDB tables?

      MyISAM stores an exact row count. InnoDB cannot, because under MVCC different transactions see different numbers of rows; it must scan the smallest index.

      Peeking into the catalog (information_schema / pg_catalog)

      Both engines expose their data dictionary through SQL (more in Chapter 01).

      SHOW ENGINES;                                  -- which storage engines are available
SELECT TABLE_NAME, ENGINE FROM information_schema.TABLES
WHERE  TABLE_SCHEMA = 'college';
SELECT TABLE_NAME, COLUMN_NAME, REFERENCED_TABLE_NAME, REFERENCED_COLUMN_NAME
FROM   information_schema.KEY_COLUMN_USAGE
WHERE  TABLE_SCHEMA = 'college' AND REFERENCED_TABLE_NAME IS NOT NULL;
SHOW PROCESSLIST;                              -- one row per connection thread
      SELECT relname, reltuples::bigint AS est_rows
FROM   pg_catalog.pg_class
WHERE  relkind = 'r' AND relnamespace = 'public'::regnamespace;

SELECT pid, backend_type, state, query
FROM   pg_stat_activity;          -- shows client backends AND background processes

      ☁️ Centralized, client-server, distributed and parallel DBMS

      TypeIdeaGood forPainExample
      CentralizedDBMS and data on one computer; users use terminals or the same machineSimple, small orgs, embeddedSingle point of failure; limited by one boxSQLite in an app, one office server
      Client-serverServer machine runs the DBMS; clients send queries over the networkAlmost every app todayServer is still one machine unless replicatedMySQL/PostgreSQL behind a web app
      DistributedData spread over several sites (nodes, maybe in different cities) that cooperate; user sees one databaseScale beyond one box, geo-locality, availabilityNetwork failures, distributed transactions, CAP trade-offsGoogle Spanner, CockroachDB, Cassandra, sharded MySQL (Vitess)
      ParallelMany CPUs and disks (often in one data centre) work on the same query at onceFast big scans and joins (analytics)Coordination, data skewTeradata, Redshift, Greenplum
      🧠

      Shared memory

      All CPUs share RAM and disks. Easy to program; limited to one big machine.

      💽

      Shared disk

      Each node has own RAM, all share a storage network. Oracle RAC, Amazon Aurora storage layer.

      🧩

      Shared nothing

      Each node owns its CPU, RAM and disk; data is partitioned. Scales best. Cassandra, Vitess, Redshift.

      QDistributed vs parallel database — what is the difference?

      A parallel database uses many processors and disks, usually close together and fast-connected, to make one query or workload faster. A distributed database stores data at multiple sites that may be far apart and may fail independently; the goal is scale, locality and availability, and each site can serve local queries on its own. Distributed systems must handle slow networks and partitions (CAP, 2PC, consensus), which parallel systems in one rack mostly ignore. Deep dive in Chapter 19.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A parallel database splits one job across many CPUs and disks, usually in one data centre, to speed it up. A distributed database spreads the data itself across sites that can be geographically apart and fail independently, mainly for scale and availability, so it has to deal with network partitions and distributed transactions.

      📌 Key takeaways

      • 3-tier (client → app server → DB) hides the DB, centralises logic, pools connections and scales the app tier.
      • Three-schema: many external views, one conceptual schema, one internal schema, joined by two mappings.
      • Schema = structure (intension); instance = data at a moment (extension).
      • Physical independence (change storage) is easy; logical independence (change tables) is hard because apps name tables and columns.
      • Components: query processor (DDL interpreter, DML compiler + optimizer, evaluation engine) and storage manager (authorization/integrity, transaction, file, buffer managers).
      • MySQL: thread per connection, SQL layer over a pluggable engine API, InnoDB default, no query cache since 8.0.
      • PostgreSQL: postmaster forks a backend process per connection; background writer, checkpointer, WAL writer, autovacuum; use PgBouncer.
      • Parallel = many CPUs on one job; distributed = data at many independent sites.

      Adding a new index on student(name) is an example of…

      An index changes only the internal level (a new access path). Query results and app code stay the same.

      Which mapping protects applications when you split one table into two and recreate the old shape as a view?

      The view definition is the external/conceptual mapping. Updating it gives logical data independence.

      How many conceptual and internal schemas does one database have?

      Only the external level has many schemas (views). Conceptual and internal are one each.

      In the classic component model, which part chooses the join order?

      The DML compiler produces an evaluation plan and the optimizer picks the cheapest one using statistics.

      Your PostgreSQL server slows down with 4,000 app connections. The standard fix?

      PostgreSQL forks a process per connection; a pooler multiplexes many clients onto few backends. Query cache and MyISAM are MySQL ideas (and the query cache no longer exists).

      Which statement about MySQL 8.0+ is TRUE?

      The query cache was removed in 8.0; MySQL uses threads; the binlog belongs to the server layer.
      2-tier vs 3-tier?
      2-tier: client talks to DB directly. 3-tier: client → app server → DB; better security, scaling, logic reuse.
      Three ANSI-SPARC levels?
      External (user views, many) · Conceptual (logical schema, one) · Internal (physical storage, one).
      Schema vs instance?
      Schema = structure, intension, rarely changes. Instance = data at a moment, extension, changes constantly.
      Physical data independence example?
      Add an index, change file organisation, move to SSD, change ROW_FORMAT — apps unchanged.
      Why is logical independence harder?
      Apps and views are written against table/column names; changing them can only partly be hidden by views.
      Query processor parts?
      DDL interpreter, DML compiler (+ optimizer), query evaluation engine.
      Storage manager parts?
      Authorization & integrity manager, transaction manager, file manager, buffer manager.
      MySQL connection model?
      One mysqld process; one thread per connection; thread cache; thread pool plugin in Enterprise.
      PostgreSQL background processes?
      Background writer, checkpointer, WAL writer, autovacuum launcher/workers, archiver, WAL sender/receiver.
      Shared nothing?
      Each node owns CPU, RAM and disk; data partitioned across nodes. Scales best (Cassandra, Vitess).
      Chapter 03 · I · Foundations

      🧩 ER Model & ER → Tables

      Read and draw any ER diagram (Chen or crow’s-foot), name every symbol, and convert it into the minimum correct set of MySQL tables — including weak entities, M:N, ternary, recursive and inheritance cases.

      ⏱ 35 min🔥 Asked a lotGATE favouriteMySQL 8

      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision

      • ER model = a design-time picture of the real world: entities (rectangles), attributes (ovals), relationships (diamonds). It is converted to tables later.
      • Attribute kinds: simple / composite, single / multivalued (double oval), stored / derived (dashed oval), key (underlined).
      • Cardinality = the maximum (1 or N). Participation = the minimum (0 = partial, single line; ≥1 = total, double line). (min,max) notation shows both.
      • Weak entity (double rectangle) has no key of its own, only a partial key / discriminator (dashed underline). Table PK = owner PK + discriminator, FK ON DELETE CASCADE.
      • Minimum tables: M:N → 3, 1:N → 2, 1:1 → 2 (1 if total on both sides). Multivalued attribute → +1 table. Weak entity → its own table; identifying relationship → no table.
      • 1:N: the FK goes on the N (many) side. M:N: a junction table with composite PK (PKA, PKB).
      • Recursive 1:N (employee–manager) = one table with a self-FK. Recursive M:N (course prerequisite) = 2 tables.
      • EER: specialization (top-down) / generalization (bottom-up), constraints disjoint vs overlapping and total vs partial. Three table strategies: single table, table per type (parent + children), table per concrete class.
      • Aggregation = treat a relationship as an entity so it can join another relationship. Use it instead of a ternary when the third link is optional.
      ✏️ GATE asks “minimum number of tables” every few years. Interviews ask “draw an ER diagram for a library / college / hospital” and then “now give me the tables”. This chapter covers both.

      🧩 What is the ER model and where does it fit?

      Before you write a single CREATE TABLE, you must agree with the business on what things exist and how they are connected. The Entity–Relationship (ER) model, proposed by Peter Chen in 1976, is a simple picture language for exactly that. It sits in the conceptual design step. It does not talk about indexes, data types or storage.

      1. Requirementstalk to users, list nouns & verbs
      2. Conceptual designER / EER diagram
      3. Logical designER → relational tables
      4. Normalizecheck FDs, 3NF / BCNF
      5. Physical designtypes, indexes, partitions
      QWhat is an ER model / ER diagram, and why do we need it if we will build tables anyway?

      What: a high-level, conceptual data model. It describes the data as entity sets (things), attributes (their properties) and relationship sets (how things are connected), plus constraints such as keys, cardinality and participation. The drawing of it is the ER diagram (ERD).

      Why it exists:

      1. Communication — a business person can read boxes and lines. They cannot read DDL. The ERD is the contract between developers and domain experts.
      2. Catch mistakes early — “Can a student take many courses? Can a course have zero students?” are cheap questions on paper and expensive after go-live.
      3. DBMS-independent — the same ERD can become MySQL, PostgreSQL or Oracle tables. It even guides NoSQL modeling.
      4. Mechanical conversion — there are fixed rules (this chapter) that turn an ERD into tables, foreign keys and constraints.

      Analogy: the ERD is the architect’s floor plan; the tables are the bricks. You do not start laying bricks without a plan.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      The ER model is a conceptual design tool. It shows the real-world entities, their attributes and the relationships between them, with constraints like cardinality and participation. We use it before creating tables because it is easy to discuss with non-technical people and catches design mistakes early. Then we convert it to relational tables using standard mapping rules, and normalize the result.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is ER a logical or a physical model?

      Neither — it is conceptual (high-level). The relational schema you get after mapping is the logical model. Indexes, files and partitions are the physical model (see Chapter 02).

      ↪Does every ER diagram produce tables already in 3NF?

      Usually close, but not guaranteed. If an entity hides a dependency (e.g., student(roll, pincode, city) where pincode → city), the mapped table is not in 3NF. That is why step 4 is “normalize” (Chapter 06).

      ↪What tools do people use to draw ERDs?

      MySQL Workbench (EER diagrams, forward/reverse engineering), dbdiagram.io, draw.io, Lucidchart, ERwin, pgModeler. In industry they almost always use crow’s-foot notation; textbooks and GATE use Chen notation.

      Core vocabulary

      Entity
      One real-world thing that can be told apart from others: student Asha (roll 101), the book “DBMS by Korth”, copy #3.
      Entity set
      The collection of all entities of the same type at a moment: all students right now. Becomes a table’s rows.
      Entity type
      The definition / blueprint of an entity set: STUDENT(roll_no, name, dob). Becomes the table schema. (Many books use “entity set” for both; interviewers accept either.)
      Attribute
      A property of an entity or relationship. Each attribute has a domain (set of allowed values).
      Relationship
      An association among entities: Asha enrolls in DBMS. A relationship set is all such associations of one type.
      Degree
      Number of entity sets that take part in a relationship: 1 = unary (recursive), 2 = binary, 3 = ternary.
      Cardinality ratio
      The maximum number of relationship instances an entity can take part in: 1:1, 1:N, N:1, M:N.
      Participation
      Whether every entity must take part (total, “existence dependency”) or may (partial).

      The Chen notation cheat sheet

      🧠 “Double means dependent or many”

      Double rectangle = weak (depends on owner). Double diamond = the relationship it depends through. Double line = must participate. Double oval = many values. Dashed oval = derived (not really stored). Dashed underline = only a partial key.

      📋 Attributes: the six kinds

      QWhat are the types of attributes in the ER model? Give an example of each.

      Attributes are classified on three independent axes, plus two special roles. One attribute can belong to several classes at once (e.g., phone is simple + multivalued + stored).

      AxisKindMeaningExampleSymbolMaps to
      Divisible?Simple (atomic)Cannot be split meaningfullyroll_no, genderovalone column
      CompositeMade of sub-partsname = first + middle + last; addressoval with child ovalsone column per leaf; parent is dropped
      How many values?Single-valuedOne value per entitydobovalone column
      MultivaluedA set of values per entityphone_numbers, skillsdouble ovala separate table (owner PK, value)
      Stored?StoredSaved in the DBdobovalcolumn
      DerivedComputed from othersage from dob; total_amount from line itemsdashed ovalusually not stored: compute in query / view / generated column
      RoleKeyUniquely identifies an entityroll_nounderlinedPRIMARY KEY / UNIQUE
      ComplexComposite + multivalued nesteda person’s many addresses, each with street/citydouble oval with childrenseparate table with several columns

      NULL in ER terms: an attribute value can be “not applicable” (a person with no middle name) or “unknown” (phone exists but not recorded). Both become NULL in SQL, which is one reason designers prefer to avoid nullable columns when a separate table is cleaner.

      -- STUDENT(roll_no, name{first,last}, {phone}, dob, age*)
CREATE TABLE student (
  roll_no    INT PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,          -- composite 'name' flattened
  last_name  VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  dob        DATE NOT NULL
  -- 'age' is derived: NOT stored, it would go stale every birthday
);

CREATE TABLE student_phone (                 -- multivalued 'phone' → own table
  roll_no INT,
  phone   VARCHAR(15),
  PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, phone),
  FOREIGN KEY (roll_no) REFERENCES student(roll_no) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

-- derived value computed when needed
SELECT roll_no, first_name,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(YEAR, dob, CURDATE()) AS age
FROM student;
      ⚠️
      Trap: storing a multivalued attribute as “9876, 9123” in one column

      That breaks 1NF (non-atomic value). You cannot index one phone, cannot put a UNIQUE on it, and WHERE phone = '9123' needs LIKE '%9123%' or FIND_IN_SET (full scan). Always a child table.

      🔀
      Engines bend the multivalued rule

      PostgreSQL has native arrays (TEXT[]) with GIN indexes; MySQL 8.0.17+ has multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays; MongoDB simply embeds an array in the document. These are legal and sometimes handy, but in an ER → relational answer, the textbook (and interview) answer is still “separate table”.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Attributes can be simple or composite, single-valued or multivalued, and stored or derived; and a key attribute identifies the entity. For example, name with first and last parts is composite, phone numbers is multivalued and drawn as a double oval, and age is derived from date of birth and drawn as a dashed oval. When mapping to tables, composite becomes one column per part, multivalued becomes a separate table with the owner’s key, and derived is usually not stored at all.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪When WOULD you store a derived attribute?

      When computing it is expensive and it is read far more than written — e.g., order.total_amount, post.like_count. That is denormalization (Chapter 06): you must keep it in sync (trigger, application code, or a MySQL generated column if it depends only on columns of the same row). age should never be stored: it changes with time, not with data.

      ↪Is “address” always composite?

      It depends on use. If the app never searches by city, one VARCHAR line is fine (simple). If you filter or group by city/pincode, split it. “Atomic” is decided by how the data is used, not by the data itself.

      ↪Can a relationship have attributes?

      Yes — a descriptive attribute. grade belongs to Enrolls, not to Student (a student has many grades) or Course (a course has many grades). It describes the pair. In tables, it goes wherever the relationship goes: in the junction table for M:N, or on the N side for 1:N.

      QEntity vs entity set vs entity type — and how do they map to a table?

      Entity

      • One object: student roll 101, “Asha”.
      • Maps to one row (tuple).

      Entity set

      • All students currently in the DB.
      • Maps to the table instance (all rows now).
      • Changes with every insert / delete.

      Entity type

      • The structure: STUDENT(roll_no, name, dob).
      • Maps to the table schema (intension).
      • Rarely changes.

      Same idea as schema vs instance in Chapter 02, and like class vs object in OOP (entity type ≈ class, entity ≈ object).

      ℹ️
      Strong vs weak in one line

      A strong entity has its own key (STUDENT has roll_no). A weak entity cannot be identified by its own attributes alone (ROOM “101” exists in many buildings). Full treatment in weak entities below.

      🔗 Relationships: degree, roles, cardinality, participation

      Degree of a relationship

      QWhat is mapping cardinality? Explain 1:1, 1:N, N:1 and M:N with examples.

      Mapping cardinality (cardinality ratio) says: at most how many entities on the other side can one entity be associated with through this relationship. It is a business rule you get from requirements, not something you discover from data.

      RatioRead it asExampleWhere the FK goes
      1 : 1an A has ≤ 1 B, a B has ≤ 1 APerson — Passport; Employee heads Departmenteither side, with UNIQUE (prefer the total side)
      1 : Nan A has many Bs, a B has ≤ 1 ADepartment — Employee; Customer — Orderon the N side (employee.dept_id)
      N : 1mirror of 1:NEmployee — Departmenton the N side again
      M : Nan A has many Bs and a B has many AsStudent — Course; Author — Book; Actor — Movieneither — a junction table
      🚫
      Failing answer: “1:N means one table has one row and the other has N rows”

      Cardinality is about how many partners one entity can have, not table sizes. Department has 10 rows and Employee 10,000 — the ratio is still 1:N because each employee has at most one department.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Mapping cardinality is the maximum number of entities one entity can be linked to through a relationship. One-to-one is person and passport, one-to-many is department and employees, and many-to-many is students and courses. It directly decides the tables: for one-to-many the foreign key goes on the many side, and many-to-many needs a separate junction table.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪How do you enforce 1:1 in SQL?

      Put the FK on one side and make it UNIQUE (or make the FK itself the PK of that table). Without UNIQUE, the database happily stores 1:N.

      CREATE TABLE passport (
  passport_no CHAR(8) PRIMARY KEY,
  person_id   INT NOT NULL UNIQUE,      -- UNIQUE turns 1:N into 1:1
  FOREIGN KEY (person_id) REFERENCES person(person_id)
);
      ↪Why can’t we store M:N with an FK on one side?

      Because one student would need many course_ids in one cell (breaks 1NF), or you would duplicate the student row once per course (update anomalies). The only clean way is a third table with one row per (student, course) pair.

      ↪Can you enforce “each department has at least one employee” in MySQL?

      Not with a simple declarative constraint. The FK enforces “every employee has a department” (total on the employee side), but “at least one employee per department” needs a trigger, application logic, or a deferred-constraint trick (PostgreSQL DEFERRABLE FKs help; MySQL has no deferred constraints). This is a classic “ER says more than DDL can express” example.

      QWhat is total vs partial participation? How is it different from cardinality? What is (min, max) notation?

      Participation answers: must every entity take part in the relationship?

      • Total (mandatory, existence dependency) — every entity must participate at least once. Drawn as a double line. E.g., every LOAN must belong to some BRANCH.
      • Partial (optional) — some entities may not participate. Single line. E.g., not every EMPLOYEE manages a department.

      Cardinality = MAX

      • “At most how many?”
      • Values: 1 or N.
      • Decides where the FK goes / whether a junction table is needed.

      Participation = MIN

      • “At least how many?”
      • Values: 0 (partial) or ≥1 (total).
      • Decides whether the FK is NOT NULL, and whether tables can be merged.

      (min, max) notation writes both on each line: (0,N), (1,1), etc. It is more precise than the 1/N + single/double-line style.

      ⚠️
      Trap: (min,max) reads the OPPOSITE way from 1/N labels

      In Chen 1:N style, the “N” is written next to EMPLOYEE (many employees per department). In (min,max) style, the (1,1) is written next to EMPLOYEE (each employee in one department). Both describe the same rule. In GATE questions, first check which convention is used.

      Effect on tables:

      CREATE TABLE employee (
  emp_id  INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  dept_id INT NOT NULL,         -- NOT NULL  = total participation of EMPLOYEE
  FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES department(dept_id)
);
-- If participation were partial (an employee may have no dept yet):
--   dept_id INT NULL
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Cardinality is the maximum — at most one or many. Participation is the minimum — zero means partial, at least one means total, drawn with a double line. For example, every employee must work in a department, so employee has total participation; a department may have no employees yet, so its side is partial. In tables, total participation on the many side becomes a NOT NULL foreign key.
