      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is a weak entity’s participation total or partial?

      Always total in its identifying relationship — it cannot exist without its owner. That is why it is drawn with a double line to the double diamond.

      ↪Does total participation imply a weak entity?

      No. Every EMPLOYEE must be in a DEPARTMENT (total), but EMPLOYEE has its own key emp_id, so it is strong. Weak ⇒ total, but total ⇏ weak.

      Chen vs crow’s-foot notation

      Textbooks and GATE use Chen. Industry tools (MySQL Workbench, dbdiagram.io, Lucidchart) use crow’s-foot (also called IE / Information Engineering). In crow’s-foot, attributes are listed inside the box, relationships are just lines, and the line ends encode (min, max).

      FeatureChenCrow’s-foot (IE)UML class diagram
      Entityrectanglebox with attribute listclass box
      Attributeovalrow inside the boxrow inside the box
      Relationshipdiamond (can have attributes)a line (M:N attributes need an associative entity)association line / association class
      Cardinality1 / N labels or (min,max)line-end symbols0..1, 1..*
      Best forconceptual design, examslogical / physical design, toolsOO + ORM design

      ⛓️ Strong vs weak entities

      QWhat is a weak entity? What is a partial key (discriminator) and an identifying relationship? How do you convert it to a table?

      What: a weak entity set is one that does not have enough attributes to form a primary key of its own. Its existence depends on another entity, called the owner (identifying / strong) entity.

      • Partial key / discriminator — the attribute(s) that tell weak entities apart within one owner. Room “101” is unique inside one building, not across all buildings. Drawn with a dashed underline.
      • Identifying relationship — the relationship linking the weak entity to its owner. Drawn as a double diamond. It is always N:1 (many weak → one owner, occasionally 1:1) with total participation of the weak side.
      • Full key of a weak entity = owner’s primary key + discriminator.
      CREATE TABLE building (
  building_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name        VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE room (
  building_id INT,                     -- borrowed from the owner
  room_no     VARCHAR(10),             -- the discriminator (partial key)
  capacity    INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (building_id, room_no),  -- owner PK + discriminator
  FOREIGN KEY (building_id) REFERENCES building(building_id)
      ON DELETE CASCADE                -- no owner → no room
);
-- No table for 'Has': the FK inside ROOM already stores it.
      building_idroom_nocapacity
      110160
      110240
      2101120

      Classic textbook examples: DEPENDENT of an EMPLOYEE (dependent name is unique only per employee), SECTION of a COURSE (sec_id + semester + year), ORDER_ITEM line number within an ORDER, INSTALLMENT number of a LOAN, EPISODE number of a SERIES.

      Strong entity

      • Has its own primary key.
      • Single rectangle.
      • Exists independently.
      • Participation may be total or partial.

      Weak entity

      • Only a partial key (discriminator).
      • Double rectangle, linked via a double diamond.
      • Existence depends on the owner.
      • Always total participation in the identifying relationship.
      🌍
      In real projects

      Many teams give every table a surrogate id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT, which technically makes ROOM “strong”. That is fine, but you must still add UNIQUE (building_id, room_no) — otherwise the business rule “room numbers are unique within a building” is lost. The weak-entity idea survives as that composite UNIQUE + cascading FK.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A weak entity cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes; it depends on an owner entity. It has only a partial key, or discriminator, which is unique within one owner. For example, room number 101 exists in many buildings, so a room is identified by building ID plus room number. In tables, the weak entity gets its own table whose primary key is the owner’s key plus the discriminator, with a foreign key to the owner, usually ON DELETE CASCADE. The identifying relationship needs no separate table.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Can a weak entity have a primary key?

      In the ER model, no — only a partial key. In the table, yes: the composite PK (owner PK + discriminator).

      ↪Why not just give ROOM a global id and make it strong?

      You can (surrogate key). It is a design choice: the weak model expresses the domain rule directly (rooms have no meaning without a building); the surrogate model makes joins and ORMs simpler. Either way keep the composite UNIQUE.

      ↪Can a weak entity have more than one owner, or own another weak entity?

      Yes to both. A weak entity can be identified through several owners (its key then includes all their keys), and weak entities can nest: BUILDING → FLOOR → ROOM, giving ROOM a key like (building_id, floor_no, room_no).

      ↪Why does the identifying relationship need no table?

      Its information is exactly the owner’s key, which is already inside the weak table’s PK. A separate table would only repeat it — redundant.

      👥 Recursive and ternary relationships

      QWhat is a recursive (unary) relationship? How do you map employee–manager and course–prerequisite?

      A recursive relationship relates an entity set to itself. Because the same set appears twice, each side gets a role name (manager / subordinate, course / prerequisite, follower / followee).

      Each employee has at most one manager → put a self-referencing FK in the same table.

      CREATE TABLE employee (
  emp_id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name       VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  manager_id INT NULL,                       -- NULL for the CEO (partial)
  FOREIGN KEY (manager_id) REFERENCES employee(emp_id)
);

-- Who reports to whom?
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employee e LEFT JOIN employee m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;
      +----------+---------+
| employee | manager |
+----------+---------+
| Asha     | NULL    |
| Ravi     | Asha    |
| Meera    | Asha    |
| Kiran    | Ravi    |
+----------+---------+

      Full hierarchy queries use a recursive CTE (Chapter 09).

      A course can have many prerequisites and be a prerequisite of many courses → junction table with two FKs to the same table.

      CREATE TABLE course (course_id CHAR(6) PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(60));

CREATE TABLE prereq (
  course_id CHAR(6),           -- role: the course
  prereq_id CHAR(6),           -- role: its prerequisite
  PRIMARY KEY (course_id, prereq_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES course(course_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (prereq_id) REFERENCES course(course_id),
  CHECK (course_id <> prereq_id)        -- enforced from MySQL 8.0.16
);

      Same pattern: social “follows” (follower_id, followee_id), “friends”, bill of materials (part contains part).

      ⚠️
      Trap: forgetting role names

      Two columns both named course_id is impossible. Role names become the column names — that is why the ER diagram must show them.

      QWhen do you need a ternary relationship? Can it be replaced by three binary relationships?

      A ternary relationship records a fact that only makes sense with three entities together: “Supplier S supplies Part P to Project J”.

      Can three binaries replace it? In general, NO. Example with three binary tables:

      • CAN_SUPPLY(S, P): S1 supplies bolts; S2 supplies nuts.
      • USES(J, P): J1 uses bolts and nuts.
      • SUPPLIES_TO(S, J): S1 and S2 both supply J1.

      From these you cannot tell whether S1 actually delivered bolts to J1, or whether S2 delivered bolts to J1 too. Joining the three binaries invents combinations that never happened (spurious tuples). The ternary table supplies(s_id, p_id, j_id, qty) stores exactly the real triples. This is the same idea as a join dependency / 5NF (Chapter 06): a ternary can be split into binaries only when a special business rule makes the join lossless.

      CREATE TABLE supplies (
  supplier_id INT, part_id INT, project_id INT,
  qty INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (supplier_id, part_id, project_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (supplier_id) REFERENCES supplier(supplier_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (part_id)     REFERENCES part(part_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (project_id)  REFERENCES project(project_id)
);
      ℹ️
      Ternary PK shrinks with “1” sides

      If the rule were “a given (project, part) is supplied by exactly one supplier”, the PK becomes just (project_id, part_id). Silberschatz allows at most one arrow (“1” side) out of a ternary to keep the meaning unambiguous.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A ternary relationship stores facts that involve three entities at once, like supplier S supplies part P to project J. Three binary relationships are not equivalent in general, because joining them can produce combinations that never happened, so information is lost. It maps to one table holding all three keys, plus the three entity tables.

      🌳 Enhanced ER: specialization, generalization, aggregation, categories

      QWhat are specialization and generalization? What do disjoint / overlapping and total / partial mean?

      Plain ER cannot say “a CAR is a VEHICLE”. Enhanced ER (EER) adds this IS-A (inheritance) idea.

      Specialization (top-down)
      Start from one general entity (EMPLOYEE) and split it into sub-types (ENGINEER, MANAGER) that have extra attributes or relationships.
      Generalization (bottom-up)
      Notice that CAR and TRUCK share attributes (reg_no, price) and pull them up into a super-type VEHICLE. Same picture, opposite direction of thinking.
      Inheritance
      A sub-type gets all attributes and relationships of its super-type, plus its own.
      Disjoint (d) vs Overlapping (o)
      Disjoint: an entity can be in at most one sub-type (a vehicle is a car OR a truck). Overlapping: it can be in several (a person can be STUDENT and EMPLOYEE).
      Total vs Partial (completeness)
      Total (double line): every super-type entity must belong to some sub-type. Partial (single line): some can stay just “general” (an EMPLOYEE who is neither engineer nor manager).
      D-O · T-P

      Two independent switches: Disjoint/Overlapping answers “how many sub-types can one entity be in?”; Total/Partial answers “must it be in one at all?”. So 4 combos exist (e.g. disjoint + total = every vehicle is exactly one of car/truck).

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Specialization and generalization model IS-A relationships. Specialization splits a general entity into sub-types top-down; generalization merges common attributes of similar entities into a super-type bottom-up. Sub-types inherit all attributes and relationships of the super-type. Two constraints describe it: disjoint versus overlapping, meaning whether an entity can belong to more than one sub-type, and total versus partial, meaning whether every entity must belong to some sub-type.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Specialization vs generalization — is the final diagram different?

      No. The diagram looks the same; only the design process differs (refine downward vs abstract upward).

      ↪What is multiple inheritance in EER?

      A shared sub-class with several super-classes, e.g. TEACHING_ASSISTANT is both STUDENT and EMPLOYEE. It inherits from both, and all its super-classes share the same key (one person).

      QHow do you convert specialization/inheritance into tables? Compare the three strategies.

      Three standard ways (ORMs like Hibernate call them SINGLE_TABLE, JOINED, TABLE_PER_CLASS). Example: VEHICLE(reg_no, price) with sub-types CAR(seats) and TRUCK(load_tons).

      CREATE TABLE vehicle (
  reg_no    VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY,
  price     DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  type      ENUM('CAR','TRUCK') NOT NULL,   -- discriminator column
  seats     TINYINT NULL,                  -- only for cars
  load_tons DECIMAL(5,2) NULL,             -- only for trucks
  CHECK ((type = 'CAR'   AND load_tons IS NULL)
      OR (type = 'TRUCK' AND seats     IS NULL))
);

      ✔ No joins, fastest reads. ✘ Many NULL columns; cannot declare seats NOT NULL just for cars (need CHECK). Best when sub-types have few extra columns. A type column fits disjoint; for overlapping use boolean flags (is_car, is_truck).

      CREATE TABLE vehicle (reg_no VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY, price DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE car (
  reg_no VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY,           -- PK is also FK to parent
  seats  TINYINT NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (reg_no) REFERENCES vehicle(reg_no) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
CREATE TABLE truck (
  reg_no    VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY,
  load_tons DECIMAL(5,2) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (reg_no) REFERENCES vehicle(reg_no) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

      ✔ Normalized, no NULL waste, works for overlapping and partial, other tables can FK to vehicle. ✘ Every full read needs a join. The textbook default answer.

      CREATE TABLE car   (reg_no VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY, price DECIMAL(12,2), seats TINYINT);
CREATE TABLE truck (reg_no VARCHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY, price DECIMAL(12,2), load_tons DECIMAL(5,2));

      ✔ No joins for one sub-type. ✘ Only valid if specialization is total (else general vehicles have no home) and ideally disjoint (else overlapping rows are duplicated). Uniqueness of reg_no across both tables is not enforced; “all vehicles” needs UNION ALL; nobody can FK to “any vehicle”.

      StrategyTablesNULLsJoinsOverlapping OKPartial OK
      Single table1✘ many✔ none~ flags✔
      Table per type (joined)1 + n✔ none✘ needed✔✔
      Concrete table per classn✔ none~ UNION for all✘ duplicates✘
      🔀
      Engine note

      PostgreSQL has table inheritance (CREATE TABLE car (...) INHERITS (vehicle)), but PKs, UNIQUE and FKs are not inherited across children, so most teams still use one of the three patterns above. MySQL has no table inheritance.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      There are three options. Single table puts everything in one table with a type column — fast, but full of NULLs. Table per type keeps common columns in a parent table and each sub-type in a child table whose primary key is also a foreign key to the parent — clean and flexible, but needs joins. Concrete table per class gives each sub-type its own complete table — no joins, but only works when the specialization is total and disjoint. I usually choose based on how different the sub-types are and how they are queried.

      QWhat is aggregation in ER? Why is it needed?

      Problem: plain ER cannot connect a relationship to another relationship. Example: EMPLOYEE works_on PROJECT, and some of these (employee, project) assignments are monitored by a MANAGER. Monitoring belongs to the assignment, not to the employee or the project alone.

      Aggregation draws a box around EMPLOYEE — works_on — PROJECT and treats the whole thing as a higher-level entity, which can then take part in monitors with MANAGER.

      CREATE TABLE works_on (
  emp_id INT, proj_id INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (emp_id, proj_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (emp_id)  REFERENCES employee(emp_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (proj_id) REFERENCES project(proj_id)
);
CREATE TABLE monitors (
  emp_id INT, proj_id INT, manager_id INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (emp_id, proj_id),             -- one manager per assignment
  FOREIGN KEY (emp_id, proj_id) REFERENCES works_on(emp_id, proj_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (manager_id) REFERENCES manager(manager_id)
);
      💡
      Why not a ternary (employee, project, manager)?

      A ternary would force every assignment to have a manager (or need NULLs in a key) and would duplicate the assignment fact. Aggregation keeps “works_on” complete on its own and lets monitoring be optional. The FK points at works_on, so you cannot monitor an assignment that does not exist.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Aggregation treats a relationship together with its entities as one higher-level entity, so that it can participate in another relationship. For example, a manager monitors an employee's work on a project. In tables, the monitoring table has a composite foreign key pointing to the works_on table.

      QWhat is a union type (category) in EER, and how is it mapped?

      A category is a sub-class of a union of different super-classes. Example (Elmasri & Navathe): a vehicle OWNER can be a PERSON, a BANK or a COMPANY. An owner is one of them, and the three super-classes have different keys. Drawn with a circle containing ∪.

      Difference from shared sub-class (multiple inheritance): a shared sub-class is in all its super-classes (same key); a category member is in one of them (different keys).

      Mapping: create a surrogate key for the category, give it its own table, and add it as a FK column in each super-class table.

      CREATE TABLE owner   (owner_id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY);
CREATE TABLE person  (aadhaar CHAR(12) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(60),
                      owner_id BIGINT UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY (owner_id) REFERENCES owner(owner_id));
CREATE TABLE bank    (bank_code CHAR(11) PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(60),
                      owner_id BIGINT UNIQUE, FOREIGN KEY (owner_id) REFERENCES owner(owner_id));
CREATE TABLE vehicle_owner (reg_no VARCHAR(12), owner_id BIGINT,
                      PRIMARY KEY (reg_no, owner_id),
                      FOREIGN KEY (owner_id) REFERENCES owner(owner_id));

      🗺️ ER → tables: the complete mapping algorithm

      Earlier sections showed each case on its own. Here is the whole recipe in one place — run it top to bottom on any diagram.

      1. Strong entity → one table; simple attributes become columns; pick the key as PK. Composite attributes → only their leaf parts (first_name, last_name). Derived attributes (age) → usually no column (compute from dob, or a generated column).
      2. Weak entity → own table; PK = owner PK + discriminator; FK to owner ON DELETE CASCADE. Identifying relationship → no table.
      3. 1:1 → put the FK (with UNIQUE) on the side with total participation (so it can be NOT NULL). Total on both sides → you may merge into one table.
      4. 1:N → FK on the N side; relationship attributes go there too. Total participation of the N side → FK NOT NULL.
      5. M:N → new junction table: PK = (PKA, PKB), two FKs, plus relationship attributes.
      6. Multivalued attribute → new table (owner PK, value), PK = both columns.
      7. n-ary (ternary) → new table with all n FKs; PK = keys of the “many” sides.
      8. Recursive → same rules, two role-named columns referring to the same table.
      9. Specialization → single table / table per type / concrete tables (see above). Category → surrogate key table. Aggregation → FK to the aggregated relationship's table.
      ER constructExtra tablesWhere the key/FK goes
      Strong entity1own PK
      Weak entity1PK = owner PK + discriminator
      1:1 relationship0FK + UNIQUE on total side (either side if both partial)
      1:1, total on both sides0 (and the 2 entities merge → 1)one table, one PK
      1:N relationship0FK on N side
      M:N relationship1junction PK (PKA, PKB)
      Multivalued attribute1(owner PK, value)
      Composite / derived attribute0leaf columns / not stored
      Ternary relationship1FKs to all 3
      Identifying relationship0already inside weak table PK
      🚫
      Answer that fails: “1:N needs a separate relationship table”

      It can have one, but it is not minimal and not the standard answer. Also wrong: putting the FK on the “1” side — then one department row would need many employee ids in one column, which breaks 1NF.

      GATE-style “minimum number of tables” — worked problems

      QE1(a1, a2) and E2(b1, b2) are linked by relationship R. Minimum tables if R is M:N? 1:N? 1:1 with total participation on both sides?
      RMin tablesTables
      M:N3E1(a1, a2), E2(b1, b2), R(a1, b1)
      1:N (E1 one, E2 many)2E1(a1, a2), E2(b1, b2, a1)
      1:1, partial on one/both sides2FK (UNIQUE) inside one of them
      1:1, total on both sides1E(a1, a2, b1, b2) — b1 UNIQUE NOT NULL
      🧠
      Memory hook: 3-2-2-1

      M:N → 3, 1:N → 2, 1:1 → 2, 1:1 total-total → 1. Then add one for every multivalued attribute and every M:N or n-ary relationship.

      QEntities A, B, C. A–B is 1:N, B–C is M:N, A has one multivalued attribute, and C has a weak entity D. Minimum tables?
      1. Strong entities A, B, C → 3 tables (B carries FK to A for the 1:N).
      2. M:N B–C → +1 junction table = 4.
      3. Multivalued attribute of A → +1 table = 5.
      4. Weak entity D → +1 table (PK = C's key + discriminator); identifying relationship adds nothing = 6.

      Answer: 6. Technique: count entity tables first, then add 1 per M:N / n-ary / multivalued attribute, 0 per 1:1 or 1:N, and subtract 1 per 1:1 merged because of total-total participation.

      QRecursive M:N on PERSON (“friend_of”) plus 1:N “works_in” from DEPT to PERSON. Minimum tables?

      PERSON (with dept_id FK) + DEPT + FRIEND_OF(person_id, friend_id) = 3. A recursive M:N still needs its own junction table; a recursive 1:N would need 0 extra (self-FK).

      📚 Worked design: a college library, end to end

      Q“Design the ER diagram for a library and give me the tables.”

      Step 1 — requirements (say them aloud): a BOOK (title, ISBN) has many AUTHORS and an author writes many books. The library owns several physical COPIES of a book (copy 1, 2, 3 — a weak entity). A MEMBER borrows a copy; a copy can be borrowed many times over time. Members have several phone numbers.

      Step 2 — map with the recipe: AUTHOR, BOOK, MEMBER (strong) → 3; writes (M:N) → +1; COPY (weak) → +1; phone (multivalued) → +1; borrows → +1 table because the same copy is borrowed many times (history), so it is effectively M:N over time = 7 tables.

      CREATE TABLE author (author_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE book   (isbn CHAR(13) PRIMARY KEY, title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL, pub_year SMALLINT);
CREATE TABLE member (member_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
                     email VARCHAR(120) NOT NULL UNIQUE);

CREATE TABLE book_author (                       -- M:N 'writes'
  isbn CHAR(13), author_id INT,
  PRIMARY KEY (isbn, author_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (isbn)      REFERENCES book(isbn),
  FOREIGN KEY (author_id) REFERENCES author(author_id)
);
CREATE TABLE copy (                              -- weak entity
  isbn CHAR(13), copy_no SMALLINT,
  shelf VARCHAR(10),
  PRIMARY KEY (isbn, copy_no),
  FOREIGN KEY (isbn) REFERENCES book(isbn) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
CREATE TABLE member_phone (                      -- multivalued attribute
  member_id INT, phone VARCHAR(15),
  PRIMARY KEY (member_id, phone),
  FOREIGN KEY (member_id) REFERENCES member(member_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
CREATE TABLE loan (                              -- 'borrows' with history
  loan_id    BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  isbn CHAR(13) NOT NULL, copy_no SMALLINT NOT NULL,
  member_id  INT NOT NULL,
  issue_date DATE NOT NULL, due_date DATE NOT NULL, returned_on DATE NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (isbn, copy_no) REFERENCES copy(isbn, copy_no),
  FOREIGN KEY (member_id)     REFERENCES member(member_id),
  INDEX (member_id, returned_on)
);

-- Which books does member 7 currently hold?
SELECT b.title, l.due_date
FROM loan l JOIN book b ON b.isbn = l.isbn
WHERE l.member_id = 7 AND l.returned_on IS NULL;
      🎯
      What the interviewer is really testing

      (1) Do you separate BOOK (the title) from COPY (the physical item)? (2) Do you notice the loan relationship repeats over time and needs its own key (loan_id) instead of PK (copy, member)? (3) Can you enforce “a copy is out to at most one member at a time”? MySQL has no partial unique index; one trick is a generated column open_flag = IF(returned_on IS NULL, 1, NULL) with UNIQUE(isbn, copy_no, open_flag) — multiple NULLs are allowed in a UNIQUE index. In PostgreSQL use a partial unique index WHERE returned_on IS NULL.

      ⚠️ Common ER mistakes (and what to say instead)

      🔁

      Relationship as an attribute

      Storing dept_name in EMPLOYEE instead of a relationship to DEPARTMENT. Any “thing” with its own attributes is an entity.

      🧮

      Storing derived data

      Saving age or total_marks — goes stale. Store dob / the marks; compute or use a generated column.

      📞

      Comma lists

      phones = '98..,99..' breaks 1NF. A multivalued attribute needs its own table.

      🧷

      FK on the wrong side

      In 1:N the FK belongs on the many side. In M:N there is no “side” — use a junction table.

      🎭

      Missing role names

      Recursive relationships without roles give two identical column names (emp_id, emp_id).

      🔺

      Splitting a ternary blindly

      Three binaries can create spurious tuples. Keep the ternary unless a join dependency allows the split.

      ⏳

      Ignoring time

      Modelling “borrows” or “enrolled” as a set when the same pair repeats over time. Add a surrogate or date to the key.

      🔑

      Weak entity without owner key

      Using only room_no as PK. The discriminator is unique only within the owner.

      📌 Key takeaways

      • ER = design-time picture: entities (rectangles), attributes (ovals), relationships (diamonds). Double = weak / multivalued / total; dashed = derived / partial key.
      • Cardinality is the maximum (1 or N); participation is the minimum (partial 0 / total ≥1). (min,max) shows both.
      • Weak entity table PK = owner PK + discriminator, FK ON DELETE CASCADE; identifying relationship needs no table.
      • Minimum tables: M:N → 3, 1:N → 2, 1:1 → 2, 1:1 total-total → 1; +1 per multivalued attribute and per M:N / n-ary relationship.
      • 1:N → FK on N side; M:N → junction table (PKA, PKB); 1:1 → FK + UNIQUE on the total side.
      • A ternary is not equal to three binaries in general (spurious tuples); aggregation lets a relationship join another relationship.
      • Inheritance → single table (fast, NULLs), table per type (clean, joins), concrete tables (only total + disjoint).
      • In interviews: say requirements aloud, separate thing vs instance (BOOK vs COPY), and watch for relationships that repeat over time.

      📚 Go deeper

      • Silberschatz, Korth & Sudarshan — Database System Concepts (Ch. 6, E-R model) — the standard textbook; slides are free on the site.
      • GeeksforGeeks — Introduction of ER Model — quick revision plus many GATE “minimum tables” problems in linked articles.
      • Lucidchart — ER diagram tutorial — clear visual guide to Chen vs crow’s-foot symbols.
      • MySQL 8.4 manual — FOREIGN KEY constraints — exact rules for the FKs every mapping produces.

      Entities E1 and E2 are linked by an M:N relationship. What is the minimum number of tables?

      One table per entity plus a junction table whose PK is (PK of E1, PK of E2).

      In a 1:N relationship DEPARTMENT (1) — EMPLOYEE (N), where does the foreign key go?

      Each employee has one department, so one FK value per employee row. Putting it in DEPARTMENT would need many values in one cell (breaks 1NF).

      What is the primary key of the table for weak entity ROOM (discriminator room_no, owner BUILDING)?

      Weak entity PK = owner's PK + discriminator. The ER model has only a partial key, but the table has a full composite PK.

      Which inheritance mapping is valid only when the specialization is total (and ideally disjoint)?

      Without a parent table, an entity that belongs to no sub-type has nowhere to live, and overlapping members would be duplicated.

      Why can't a ternary SUPPLIES(supplier, part, project) generally be replaced by three binary relationships?

      The split is lossless only if a join dependency holds (the 5NF idea). Otherwise the join creates spurious tuples.
      Cardinality vs participation?
      Cardinality = maximum (1 or N). Participation = minimum (0 partial, ≥1 total — double line).
      Symbol for a weak entity and its relationship?
      Double rectangle; double diamond for the identifying relationship; partial key with dashed underline.
      How is a multivalued attribute mapped?
      New table (owner PK, value) with PK on both columns and FK to the owner.
      Min tables: 1:1 with total participation on both sides?
      1 — both entities merge into one table.
      How is a derived attribute stored?
      Usually not at all — computed from the base attribute (age from dob) or a generated column.
      Recursive 1:N vs recursive M:N mapping?
      1:N → self-referencing FK in the same table. M:N → junction table with two role-named FKs to the same table.
      Disjoint vs overlapping?
      Disjoint (d): an entity is in at most one sub-type. Overlapping (o): it can be in several.
      What is aggregation?
      Treating a relationship (with its entities) as a higher-level entity so it can take part in another relationship.
      Category (union type)?
      A sub-class of a union of different super-classes (OWNER = PERSON ∪ BANK ∪ COMPANY); mapped with a surrogate key.
      Chen vs crow's-foot in one line?
      Chen: diamonds and ovals, great for teaching/GATE. Crow's-foot: boxes with attribute lists and fork symbols on lines, used in industry tools.
      Chapter 04 · I · Foundations

      🔑 Relational Model, Keys, Constraints & Relational Algebra

      Name every key type without hesitation, answer the “PK vs UNIQUE / NULL / ON DELETE” traps engine by engine, and write any query in relational algebra, including division.

      ⏱ 40 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8PostgreSQLSQL ServerOracle

      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision

      • A relation is a set of tuples: no duplicates, no row order, no column order, atomic values. A SQL table is a bag: duplicates allowed unless a key stops them.
      • Degree = number of columns. Cardinality = number of rows. Schema = structure (stable). Instance = data right now (changes).
      • Keys: Super ⊇ Candidate ⊇ Primary. Candidate key = minimal super key. Alternate = Candidate − Primary.
      • Super keys with one candidate key of k attributes in an n-attribute relation: 2n−k. Two keys: use inclusion–exclusion.
      • PK vs UNIQUE: PK = one per table, never NULL, InnoDB clustered index. UNIQUE = many, NULLs allowed (multiple in MySQL / PostgreSQL / Oracle, only one in SQL Server).
      • An FK may be NULL, may reference a UNIQUE column, and may reference its own table.
      • InnoDB: RESTRICT = NO ACTION (checked immediately). SET DEFAULT is rejected. PostgreSQL can defer NO ACTION to commit.
      • MySQL enforces CHECK only from 8.0.16. A CHECK that evaluates to NULL passes.
      • Relational algebra: 6 fundamental operators σ π ∪ − × ρ. ∩, joins and ÷ are derived. Division answers “for all” questions.
      • SQL is based on (tuple) relational calculus; algebra and safe calculus have equal power (relational completeness).
      ✏️ “Types of keys” + “PK vs UNIQUE” is asked in almost every service-company and campus interview. The follow-ups are where marks are won.

      📖 Where the relational model came from

      In 1970, E. F. Codd at IBM published “A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks”. Before that, databases were hierarchical (IBM IMS) or network (CODASYL). In those systems a program walked pointers from record to record. If the storage layout changed, the program broke.

      Codd’s idea was simple and radical: store all data as values in tables, link tables by matching values (keys), not pointers, and ask questions with a set-based mathematical language. The program says what it wants; the system decides how to fetch it. This is the root of data independence.

      QWhat is the relational model, and why did it replace hierarchical / network databases?

      What: a way to represent data as relations (tables), with keys for identity, constraints for correctness, and relational algebra / calculus for queries.

      Why it won:

      1. Data independence — apps do not depend on pointers or physical layout, so storage can change without rewriting code.
      2. Declarative queries — you state the result; the optimizer picks the access path. One SQL query replaces pages of navigation code.
      3. Mathematical foundation — set theory and predicate logic give precise meaning, so normalization (Chapter 06) and query optimization (Chapter 16) can be reasoned about formally.
      4. Simplicity — one structure (the table) for everything, including metadata (the catalog).
      ℹ️
      Codd’s 12 rules (1985)

      Later, in 1985, Codd published 12 rules (numbered 0–12, so 13 in total) to judge whether a product is “truly relational”. Know these five by name: 1 Information (all data are values in tables), 2 Guaranteed access (table + PK + column reaches any value), 3 Systematic NULLs, 8/9 Physical / Logical data independence, 12 Non-subversion (no low-level path may bypass constraints). No commercial DBMS satisfies all of them. For example, MySQL lets you run SET foreign_key_checks = 0, which bypasses referential integrity.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      The relational model, proposed by Codd in 1970, stores all data as tables and connects them by matching key values instead of pointers. Queries are declarative and based on set theory, so the application says what it wants and the DBMS decides how to get it. That gave us data independence and a formal basis for normalization and query optimization, which hierarchical and network systems lacked.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is SQL the relational model?

      No. SQL is a language inspired by it. SQL departs from the pure model: tables are bags (duplicates allowed), rows can have NULLs (three-valued logic), and column order matters in SELECT *. Purists (Date, Darwen) call SQL only “approximately relational”.

      ↪Who proposed the ER model then?

      Peter Chen, in 1976. ER is a conceptual design model; relational is the logical model you map it into (Chapter 03).

      📋 Relation, tuple, attribute, domain, degree, cardinality

      Interviewers often start with the vocabulary. Every word has a table-world twin. Learn both names; use the formal one, then translate.

      Relation
      A set of tuples that share the same attributes. Shown as a table.
      Tuple
      One row. Formally an ordered list (or a mapping attribute → value) with one value per attribute.
      Attribute
      A named column, e.g. dept.
      Domain
      The set of allowed values for an attribute. In SQL = data type + constraints, e.g. cgpa DECIMAL(3,1) CHECK (cgpa BETWEEN 0 AND 10).
      Degree (arity)
      Number of attributes (columns). Fixed by the schema. Unary = 1, binary = 2, ternary = 3.
      Cardinality
      Number of tuples (rows) right now. Changes with the data. (Do not confuse with relationship cardinality 1:N in ER.)
      Relation schema
      Name + attributes (+ domains + constraints): STUDENT(roll_no, name, dept, cgpa). The intension.
      Relation instance
      The set of tuples at one moment. The extension / state.
      Database schema
      The set of all relation schemas + integrity constraints.
      QWhat is the difference between degree and cardinality? And schema vs instance?

      Degree

      • Number of columns.
      • Changes only with DDL (ALTER TABLE … ADD COLUMN).
      • STUDENT above: 4.

      Cardinality

      • Number of rows.
      • Changes with every DML statement.
      • STUDENT above: 3.

      Schema (intension)

      • The blueprint: names, types, keys, constraints.
      • Rarely changes.
      • Like a class definition.

      Instance (extension / state)

      • The actual rows at time t.
      • Changes all the time.
      • Like an object’s current field values.
      🧠
      Memory aid

      Degree = Down the header (count column names). Cardinality = Count the rows. Cardinality of R × S = |R| × |S|; degree of R × S = deg(R) + deg(S).

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Degree is the number of attributes, so it is fixed by the schema. Cardinality is the number of tuples, so it changes as data is inserted or deleted. The schema is the structure of the relation, like a class; the instance is the set of rows present at a given moment, like the current state of an object.

      QWhat are the properties of a relation? How is a SQL table different?

      Because a relation is a mathematical set of tuples, it has these properties:

      1. No duplicate tuples — a set cannot contain the same element twice. So every relation has at least one key (in the worst case, all attributes together).
      2. Tuples are unordered — “first row” has no meaning.
      3. Attributes are unordered — they are referred to by name, not position.
      4. Values are atomic — each cell holds one indivisible value from the domain (this is 1NF, Chapter 06).
      5. Each attribute name is distinct within a relation.
      6. All values in a column come from the same domain.
      PropertyPure relationSQL table (MySQL / PG / Oracle / SQL Server)
      Duplicate rows✘ impossible (set)✔ allowed (it is a bag / multiset) unless a PK / UNIQUE exists
      Row ordernonenone guaranteed — only an outer ORDER BY fixes order
      Column ordernone (by name)has an order: SELECT *, INSERT … VALUES without column list
      Missing valuesno NULL in Codd’s 1970 modelNULL + three-valued logic (TRUE / FALSE / UNKNOWN)
      Result of projectionduplicates removed automaticallySELECT dept FROM student keeps duplicates; need DISTINCT
      Must have a key?always has oneno — a table with no PK / UNIQUE is legal
       
      CREATE TABLE visit (city VARCHAR(20));      -- no key at all: legal
INSERT INTO visit VALUES ('Pune'), ('Pune'), ('Delhi');
SELECT city FROM visit;            -- 3 rows: Pune, Pune, Delhi   (bag)
SELECT DISTINCT city FROM visit;   -- 2 rows: Pune, Delhi         (set = true projection)
      ⚠️
      Common mistake

      Saying “a table and a relation are exactly the same”. Close, but SQL tables allow duplicates, NULLs and ordered columns. Mentioning “SQL works on bags, not sets” immediately signals depth.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A relation is a set of tuples, so it has no duplicate rows, no row order, attributes are referenced by name, and every value is atomic and drawn from its domain. SQL tables relax this: they are bags, so duplicates are allowed unless a key prevents them, and projection does not remove duplicates unless I write DISTINCT. SQL also adds NULLs with three-valued logic.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Why does SQL allow duplicates if the theory forbids them?

      Removing duplicates costs a sort or a hash on every step. Many queries (like SUM(amount)) need duplicates kept: two ₹500 orders are two orders. So SQL keeps bags by default and makes you ask for DISTINCT / UNION (dedup) vs UNION ALL (keep).

      ↪Then why do we see rows “in insert order” without ORDER BY?

      Coincidence of the physical plan. InnoDB scans the clustered index, so you usually see PK order. A parallel scan, a different index, or a hash join can change it at any time. Never depend on it.

      🔑 Keys: every type, one example table

      A key is a set of attributes whose values identify a row. Keys are how relations “point” to each other without pointers. We will use one running example so every key type has a concrete answer.

      roll_no | email            | aadhaar      | name  | dept
--------+------------------+--------------+-------+-----
101     | asha@iiit.ac.in  | 1111-2222-33 | Asha  | CSE
102     | ravi@iiit.ac.in  | 4444-5555-66 | Ravi  | ECE
103     | meera@iiit.ac.in | 7777-8888-99 | Meera | CSE
Business rules: roll_no, email and aadhaar are each unique per student.
                name and dept can repeat.
      🔑 S ⊇ C ⊇ P

      “Super keys are a Superset.” Candidate = super key with nothing extra to throw away. Primary = the candidate you picked. Alternate = the candidates you did not pick.

      QExplain all the types of keys with an example.
      KeyPlain-English definitionIn STUDENT / other example
      Super keyAny set of attributes whose values are unique for every row. May contain extra, unnecessary attributes.{roll_no}, {roll_no, name}, {email, dept}, all 5 columns…
      Candidate keyA minimal super key: remove any attribute and it stops being unique.{roll_no}, {email}, {aadhaar}
      Primary key (PK)The one candidate key chosen as the row’s official identity. Unique + NOT NULL. At most one per table.roll_no
      Alternate (secondary) keyA candidate key that was not chosen as PK. Usually declared UNIQUE NOT NULL.email, aadhaar
      Composite keyA key made of 2+ attributes (because no single attribute is unique).ENROLL(roll_no, course_id) → PK (roll_no, course_id)
      Compound keyA composite key in which each part is itself a key (usually an FK) of another table. Many books use “compound” = “composite”; say both.ENROLL’s (roll_no, course_id): both parts are FKs
      Unique keyA SQL constraint (UNIQUE) that forbids duplicate non-NULL values. Used to enforce alternate keys.email VARCHAR(80) UNIQUE
      Foreign key (FK)Attribute(s) in one table whose value must match a PK / UNIQUE value in another (or the same) table, or be NULL.ENROLL.roll_no → STUDENT.roll_no
      Natural keyA key that has business meaning in the real world.email, aadhaar, PAN, ISBN, vehicle number
      Surrogate keyA meaningless, system-generated identifier.student_id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT, a UUID
      Partial key (discriminator)In a weak entity: attributes that identify a row only together with the owner’s key.DEPENDENT(emp_id, dep_name): dep_name is the partial key
       
      CREATE TABLE student (
  roll_no  INT          PRIMARY KEY,               -- primary key (natural here)
  email    VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,           -- alternate key via UNIQUE
  aadhaar  CHAR(12)     NOT NULL UNIQUE,           -- another alternate key
  name     VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL,
  dept     CHAR(3)      NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE course (
  course_id CHAR(5) PRIMARY KEY,
  title     VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE enroll (
  roll_no   INT     NOT NULL,
  course_id CHAR(5) NOT NULL,
  grade     CHAR(2),
  PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, course_id),                -- composite / compound key
  FOREIGN KEY (roll_no)   REFERENCES student(roll_no),   -- foreign keys
  FOREIGN KEY (course_id) REFERENCES course(course_id)
);
      🚫
      Answers that fail interviews

      “A table can have two primary keys.” → No: one PK, which may be composite. “Every super key is a candidate key.” → No: only minimal ones. “Foreign key must be unique.” → No: many children can share one parent value.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A super key is any set of columns that uniquely identifies a row. A candidate key is a minimal super key, so nothing can be removed from it. From the candidate keys we choose one as the primary key, which must be unique and not null, and the others become alternate keys, usually enforced with UNIQUE NOT NULL. A composite key has more than one column, a foreign key references a key of another table, and a surrogate key is a system-generated ID with no business meaning.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is every candidate key a super key? Is every super key a candidate key?

      Every candidate key is a super key (yes). Not every super key is a candidate key: {roll_no, name} is unique but not minimal, because roll_no alone is already unique.

      ↪How many candidate keys / primary keys can a table have?

      Many candidate keys (STUDENT has 3). Exactly one primary key in theory, at most one in SQL (a table may have none).

      ↪Can a primary key be composite? Can it be changed?

      Yes, it can be composite: PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, course_id). It can be changed with ALTER TABLE … DROP PRIMARY KEY, ADD PRIMARY KEY (…), but in InnoDB that rebuilds the whole table (the PK is the clustered index) and every secondary index, so it is expensive on big tables. Updating a PK value is also costly: the row physically moves in the clustered B+ tree, and FKs must cascade.

      ↪What is the key of a relation where nothing is unique on its own?

      The combination of attributes that is unique. In the worst case all attributes together form the only candidate key (an “all-key” relation), e.g. STUDENT_HOBBY(roll_no, hobby).

      QComposite key vs compound key vs candidate key — what exactly is the difference?

      They answer different questions:

      • Candidate is about minimality (“is it the smallest unique set?”). A candidate key can be 1 column or many.
      • Composite is about size (“does it have 2+ columns?”). A composite key may be a candidate key or a non-minimal super key.
      • Compound (stricter usage) is a composite key whose parts are each foreign keys / identifiers of other entities, typical of junction tables. Many textbooks and GfG use it as a synonym of composite.
      💡
      Junction-table PK order matters

      For PRIMARY KEY (roll_no, course_id), InnoDB can use the index for “courses of a student” (leftmost prefix) but not for “students in a course”. Add a second index (course_id, roll_no) if you need both directions. See the leftmost-prefix rule in Chapter 15.

      QSurrogate key vs natural key — which would you use for a users table and why?

      Natural key (email, PAN, ISBN)

      • ✔ Has meaning; no extra column.
      • ✔ Prevents duplicate real-world entities by itself.
      • ✘ Can change (user changes email) → cascades through every FK.
      • ✘ Often long (VARCHAR) → every secondary index and FK gets bigger.
      • ✘ May be missing (foreign student with no Aadhaar), reused, or privacy-sensitive (do not put PAN in URLs and logs).

      Surrogate key (AUTO_INCREMENT, UUID)

      • ✔ Stable: never changes.
      • ✔ Compact: 4–8 bytes → small indexes and joins.
      • ✔ Same shape for every table → simpler ORMs and APIs.
      • ✘ Meaningless → needs an extra UNIQUE on the natural key, or duplicates of the same person slip in.
      • ✘ Extra index to maintain; sequential IDs can leak business volume (order #10452).

      Why InnoDB loves short surrogate keys (the mechanism):

      1. The PK is the clustered index — rows are physically stored in a B+ tree ordered by PK.
      2. Every secondary index entry stores the PK value as its row pointer. A 36-byte VARCHAR UUID PK makes every secondary index carry 36 extra bytes per row.
      3. Increasing PK = append-only inserts — AUTO_INCREMENT always goes to the right-most leaf page. A random UUIDv4 lands on a random page → page splits, half-empty pages, more random I/O.
      CREATE TABLE users (
  user_id    BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,   -- surrogate: stable, 8 bytes
  email      VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  phone      VARCHAR(15),
  created_at DATETIME NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_users_email (email)                         -- natural key still enforced
);

-- If you need globally unique IDs (multi-region, offline clients): store UUIDs compactly
-- and time-ordered. UUID_TO_BIN(uuid, 1) swaps the time parts so values increase.
CREATE TABLE device (
  device_id BINARY(16) PRIMARY KEY,                         -- 16 bytes, not CHAR(36)
  label     VARCHAR(50)
);
INSERT INTO device VALUES (UUID_TO_BIN(UUID(), 1), 'phone');
      🔀
      Engine differences

      MySQL: AUTO_INCREMENT; UUID_TO_BIN() / BIN_TO_UUID() since 8.0. PostgreSQL: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY (or legacy SERIAL), native 16-byte uuid type; tables are heaps, so random UUIDs hurt the PK index but not row placement. SQL Server: IDENTITY(1,1), NEWSEQUENTIALID() for ordered GUIDs. Oracle: sequences or GENERATED AS IDENTITY (12c+).

      🌍
      Real-world story

      A team used email as the PK of users, referenced from orders, sessions, reviews and audit logs. When the product allowed “change your email”, one update had to cascade into hundreds of millions of child rows and locked tables for minutes. They migrated to a BIGINT surrogate PK and kept UNIQUE(email). Classic lesson: identity should never change; business attributes do.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      For users I would use a surrogate BIGINT auto-increment primary key and keep email as a UNIQUE NOT NULL alternate key. The surrogate never changes and is only 8 bytes, which matters in InnoDB because the primary key is the clustered index and is copied into every secondary index. The UNIQUE constraint on email still stops duplicate accounts. If I needed globally unique IDs I would use time-ordered UUIDs stored as BINARY(16).

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪AUTO_INCREMENT vs UUID — when is UUID better?

      UUIDs can be generated by any client or shard without coordination, are unguessable in URLs, and make merging databases easy. AUTO_INCREMENT is smaller, ordered and faster, but needs one central counter and leaks counts. Middle ground: time-ordered UUIDs (UUIDv7, or UUID_TO_BIN(…, 1)) or Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs. See sharding in Chapter 19.

      ↪When is a natural key the better PK?

      When it is short, truly immutable and always present: ISO country code 'IN', currency 'INR', a junction table’s (student_id, course_id). Lookup tables with natural codes also save joins because the FK value is already readable.

      ↪Do AUTO_INCREMENT values have gaps?

      Yes. Rolled-back inserts, failed inserts and bulk-insert reservations consume values without reusing them. Never use the ID as a “count” or to assume contiguity.

      QWhat is a partial key? Does a weak entity have a primary key?

      A weak entity cannot be identified by its own attributes. Example: an employee’s DEPENDENT named “Riya”. Two employees can both have a dependent named Riya. dep_name is unique only within one employee. That attribute is the partial key (discriminator), drawn with a dashed underline in ER diagrams.

      When mapped to a table, the weak entity gets a PK = owner’s PK + partial key, and the owner part is also an FK, usually with ON DELETE CASCADE (no employee → no dependents).

      CREATE TABLE dependent (
  emp_id   INT         NOT NULL,
  dep_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,          -- partial key
  relation VARCHAR(20),
  PRIMARY KEY (emp_id, dep_name),         -- owner key + discriminator
  FOREIGN KEY (emp_id) REFERENCES employee(emp_id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

      More on weak entities and identifying relationships in Chapter 03.

      🧮 Counting super keys (GATE favourite)

      A super key is any superset of a candidate key. So counting super keys = counting attribute subsets that contain at least one candidate key.

      1. One candidate key K of k attributes, relation of n attributes — K must be fully present; each of the other n − k attributes is either in or out. Count = 2n−k.
      2. Two candidate keys K1, K2 — inclusion–exclusion: SK(K1) + SK(K2) − SK(K1 ∪ K2). Subtract the sets counted twice (those containing both keys).
      3. Three keys — SK(K1)+SK(K2)+SK(K3) − SK(K1∪K2) − SK(K1∪K3) − SK(K2∪K3) + SK(K1∪K2∪K3).
      4. Maximum possible — if every single attribute is a key, every non-empty subset is a super key: 2n − 1.
      RelationCandidate keysWorkingSuper keys
      R(A,B,C,D)A24−18
      R(A,B,C,D,E)AB25−28
      R(A,B,C,D)A, B23 + 23 − 22 (AB) = 8 + 8 − 412
      R(A,B,C,D)A, BC23 + 22 − 21 (ABC) = 8 + 4 − 210
      R(A,B,C,D)AB, CD22 + 22 − 20 (ABCD) = 4 + 4 − 17
      R(A,B,C,D,E)AB, BC23 + 23 − 22 (ABC) = 8 + 8 − 412
      R(A,B,C,D)A, B, C8+8+8 − 4−4−4 + 2 = 14 (or: 16 subsets − 2 that miss A, B and C)14
      R(A,B,C,D,E,F)AB, AC, AD16+16+16 − 8−8−8 + 428
      R(A1…An)every Aiall non-empty subsets2n − 1
      💡
      Complement trick

      Sometimes it is faster to count the subsets that are not super keys. For keys A, B, C in R(ABCD): a subset is not a super key only if it misses A, B and C, i.e. it is ∅ or {D}. So 16 − 2 = 14. All numbers in the table above were verified by brute force.

      ⚠️
      Trap

      For keys A and BC, people subtract 22 (thinking “A and B and C overlap?”). The overlap set is K1 ∪ K2 = ABC, 3 attributes, so 24−3 = 2. Always compute the union of the keys, then 2n − |union|.

      ⚖️ PRIMARY KEY vs UNIQUE, and NULLs

      QWhat is the difference between a primary key and a unique key?

      Both forbid duplicate values and both create a unique index. The differences are about NULLs, count, and storage.

      PRIMARY KEYUNIQUE
      NULLs✘ never (columns become NOT NULL automatically)✔ allowed; how many is engine-specific (below)
      How many per tableat most 1 (may be composite)many
      Meaningthe row’s official identity (entity integrity)enforces an alternate key / business rule
      InnoDB storagebecomes the clustered index: rows are stored in PK ordera secondary index whose entries carry the PK value
      Index name in MySQLalways PRIMARYyour name or the column name
      FK target?✔✔ (standard SQL, MySQL, PG, Oracle, SQL Server)
      Can be promoted?—yes, if its columns are NOT NULL: ALTER TABLE t ADD PRIMARY KEY (col)
      How many NULLs can a UNIQUE column hold? (the real follow-up)

      Multiple NULLs allowed. MySQL docs: “A UNIQUE index permits multiple NULL values for columns that can contain NULL.” NULL is “unknown”, so two NULLs are not considered equal.

      CREATE TABLE u (phone VARCHAR(15) UNIQUE);
INSERT INTO u VALUES (NULL), (NULL);     -- OK: 2 rows
INSERT INTO u VALUES ('98'), ('98');     -- ERROR 1062: Duplicate entry '98' for key 'u.phone'

      Multiple NULLs by default. PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct. From PostgreSQL 15 you can say otherwise:

      CREATE TABLE u (phone text UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT);
INSERT INTO u VALUES (NULL);   -- OK
INSERT INTO u VALUES (NULL);   -- ERROR: duplicate key value violates unique constraint

      Older versions: use a partial unique index on an expression, e.g. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON u ((phone IS NULL)) WHERE phone IS NULL;.

      Only ONE NULL. SQL Server treats NULLs as equal for UNIQUE constraints. To allow many NULLs but keep non-NULLs unique, use a filtered unique index:

      CREATE UNIQUE INDEX uq_u_phone ON u(phone) WHERE phone IS NOT NULL;

      This is why some websites (written with SQL Server in mind) say “unique allows one NULL”.

      Multiple NULLs allowed for a single-column UNIQUE: Oracle’s B-tree indexes do not store entries whose key columns are all NULL. For a composite UNIQUE, rows with some NULLs and identical non-NULL parts do conflict.

      🚫
      Answer that fails

      “Unique key allows exactly one NULL.” That is SQL Server behaviour only. The SQL standard leaves it implementation-defined. Say “it depends on the engine” and give MySQL + SQL Server as the contrast.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Both enforce uniqueness, but a table can have only one primary key and it can never be NULL, while it can have many unique keys and they accept NULLs. In MySQL and PostgreSQL a unique column can hold many NULLs because NULLs are not equal to each other; SQL Server allows only one. In InnoDB the primary key also becomes the clustered index that physically orders the rows, while a unique key is a secondary index that stores the primary key value.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Then which index becomes the clustered index in InnoDB?

      The PRIMARY KEY. If there is no PK, the first UNIQUE index whose columns are all NOT NULL. If neither exists, a hidden one (next question).

      ↪Is a UNIQUE NOT NULL column the same as a primary key?

      Logically almost — both identify rows. Physically no: in InnoDB only the PK (or the fallback rule) is clustered. Also tools, ORMs and replication treat “the PK” specially, and only one constraint can be named PRIMARY.

      ↪Does UNIQUE create an index? Does PK?

      Yes, both are implemented with a unique B+ tree index in all four major engines. That is how uniqueness is checked quickly on every insert.

      QCan a table exist without a primary key? What does InnoDB do then?

      In SQL: yes. A table is a bag, so a PK is optional. In relational theory: every relation is a set, so it always has at least one candidate key (worst case: all attributes).

      InnoDB must cluster rows on something, so it picks, in order:

      PRIMARY KEY defined?yes → it is the clustered index
      First UNIQUE index with all columns NOT NULL?yes → used as clustered index
      Hidden GEN_CLUST_INDEXon a synthetic 6-byte, monotonically increasing row ID (DB_ROW_ID)

      Why the hidden row ID is bad in production:

      • You cannot use it in queries; secondary indexes point to an ID you cannot see.
      • The row-ID counter is a single instance-wide counter shared by all such tables, which can become a contention point.
      • Row-based replication: updates/deletes on a PK-less table can force the replica to scan to find each row → huge replica lag.
      • Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster require a PK (or equivalent) on every table.
      -- 8.0.13+: refuse to create / alter tables without a PK (default OFF)
SET PERSIST sql_require_primary_key = ON;
CREATE TABLE logs (msg TEXT);
-- ERROR 3750: Unable to create or change a table without a primary key ...

-- 8.0.30+: auto-add an invisible PK instead (default OFF)
SET PERSIST sql_generate_invisible_primary_key = ON;
CREATE TABLE logs (msg TEXT);
SHOW CREATE TABLE logs;
-- `my_row_id` bigint unsigned NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT /*!80023 INVISIBLE */,
-- PRIMARY KEY (`my_row_id`)

-- Find tables that have no PK
SELECT t.table_schema, t.table_name
FROM information_schema.tables t
LEFT JOIN information_schema.table_constraints c
       ON c.table_schema = t.table_schema AND c.table_name = t.table_name
      AND c.constraint_type = 'PRIMARY KEY'
WHERE t.table_type = 'BASE TABLE' AND c.constraint_name IS NULL
  AND t.table_schema NOT IN ('mysql','sys','information_schema','performance_schema');
      🔀
      Engine differences

      PostgreSQL: tables are heaps; rows are addressed by a physical ctid, so no PK is needed for storage — but logical replication needs a PK or REPLICA IDENTITY to replicate UPDATE/DELETE. SQL Server: a table without a clustered index is a heap with RIDs. Oracle: heap tables with ROWID by default; index-organized tables (IOT) require a PK.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      SQL allows it, because tables are bags. But InnoDB always needs a clustered index, so it uses the primary key, else the first unique index on NOT NULL columns, else it creates a hidden 6-byte row ID called GEN_CLUST_INDEX. That hidden key is invisible to queries and hurts replication, so in practice I always define a primary key, and MySQL 8 can enforce that with sql_require_primary_key.

      QCan a candidate key contain NULL?

      In theory, no: a key must identify every tuple, and NULL identifies nothing. In SQL, an alternate key declared only as UNIQUE can hold NULLs, and since NULLs never collide, many rows could be “unidentified”. That weakens the key. Fix: declare alternate keys NOT NULL UNIQUE when they are true candidate keys.

      🔗 Foreign keys and referential actions

      QWhat is a foreign key and what problem does it solve?

      What: a column (or columns) in a child table whose every non-NULL value must exist as a key value in the parent table.

      Why: it enforces referential integrity — no orphans. Without it, an app bug can insert an order for customer 999 who does not exist, or delete a customer who still has orders.

      How the engine enforces it (InnoDB):

      1. Child INSERT / UPDATE of the FK column — look up the value in the parent’s unique index. Not found → error 1452 “Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails”. Found → take a shared lock on that parent index record so nobody deletes it before you commit.
      2. Parent DELETE / key UPDATE — look up matching child rows through the index on the child’s FK column, then apply the referential action (RESTRICT / CASCADE / SET NULL).
      3. Index requirement — InnoDB needs an index on the child FK columns (it creates one automatically if missing) and a unique key on the referenced columns.
      CREATE TABLE dept (dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY, dname VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL UNIQUE);
CREATE TABLE emp (
  emp_id  INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name    VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  dept_id INT NULL,
  mgr_id  INT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_emp_dept FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept(dept_id)
      ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  CONSTRAINT fk_emp_mgr  FOREIGN KEY (mgr_id)  REFERENCES emp(emp_id)
      ON DELETE RESTRICT
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

INSERT INTO emp VALUES (4, 'Zoya', 99, NULL);
-- ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails
-- (`hr`.`emp`, CONSTRAINT `fk_emp_dept` FOREIGN KEY (`dept_id`) REFERENCES `dept` (`dept_id`) ...)
      ⚠️
      Common mistakes

      (1) “FKs make joins faster.” No — joins work on any comparable columns; the FK only enforces integrity (the index it needs helps, the constraint itself does not). (2) “You need an FK to join two tables.” No. (3) Using MyISAM: it parses FK syntax but does not enforce it.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A foreign key is a column in a child table whose values must match a primary or unique key in the parent table, or be NULL. It enforces referential integrity, so there are no orphan rows. On every child insert the engine checks the parent index, and on every parent delete or key update it checks the children and applies the configured action, like RESTRICT, CASCADE or SET NULL.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Can a foreign key be NULL?

      Yes, unless you declare it NOT NULL. NULL means “no relationship yet” — an employee not assigned to a department. The constraint is checked only for non-NULL values. For a composite FK, MySQL and PostgreSQL default to MATCH SIMPLE: if any FK column is NULL, the row is not checked at all. PostgreSQL also supports MATCH FULL (all NULL or none NULL). To force every employee to have a department (total participation), declare dept_id INT NOT NULL.

      ↪Can a foreign key reference a UNIQUE column that is not the PK?

      Yes. Standard SQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and MySQL allow referencing any PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE key, e.g. REFERENCES users(email). What about a non-unique column? Old InnoDB allowed FKs to any indexed column (a non-standard extension). MySQL 8.4 rejects it by default (restrict_fk_on_non_standard_key = ON, error “Missing unique key for constraint…”).

      ↪Can a table reference itself?

      Yes — a self-referencing (recursive) FK: emp.mgr_id → emp.emp_id, category.parent_id → category.id, comment.reply_to → comment.id. The root row has mgr_id = NULL. Query the hierarchy with a self-join or a recursive CTE (Chapter 09). Gotcha: MySQL checks FKs row by row immediately, so deleting a whole tree in one statement can fail under RESTRICT depending on row order; use ON DELETE CASCADE or delete leaves first. MySQL also limits cascades to 15 nested levels.

      ↪Does declaring an FK create an index?

      MySQL InnoDB: yes, if no usable index exists. PostgreSQL: no — it only requires the referenced side to be unique. Without an index on the child column, every parent DELETE scans the child table. Always index FK columns in PostgreSQL.

      ↪How do you bulk-load data with FKs in MySQL?

      SET foreign_key_checks = 0; load, then set it back to 1. Danger: re-enabling does not re-scan existing rows, so orphans loaded meanwhile stay silently. Validate with an anti-join afterwards.

      🔁 ON DELETE / ON UPDATE: CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT, RESTRICT, NO ACTION

      A referential action says what happens to child rows when their parent row is deleted, or when the parent’s key value is updated. You set it separately for DELETE and UPDATE.

      🌊

      CASCADE

      Child follows parent. Delete parent → delete children. Update parent key → update children’s FK.

      🕳️

      SET NULL

      Children stay but their FK becomes NULL. FK column must be nullable.

      🎯

      SET DEFAULT

      FK becomes the column DEFAULT (which must exist in parent). Rejected by InnoDB.

      ✋

      RESTRICT

      Refuse the parent change if any child exists. Checked immediately.

      ⏳

      NO ACTION

      Also refuse — but the standard checks at end of statement, and it can be deferred. Default when nothing is written.

      QWhat happens when you delete a parent row that has children? Walk through each ON DELETE option.

      Setup: DEPT(10 CSE, 20 ECE). EMP: Asha(10), Ravi(10), Meera(20). Run DELETE FROM dept WHERE dept_id = 10;

      FK declared withResult of deleting dept 10Typical use
      ON DELETE CASCADEDept 10 deleted, Asha and Ravi deleted tooOwned data: order → order_items, post → comments, weak entities
      ON DELETE SET NULLDept 10 deleted, Asha and Ravi stay with dept_id = NULLOptional link: employee → dept, ticket → assignee
      ON DELETE SET DEFAULTInnoDB: CREATE TABLE fails. PG / SQL Server: children get the default dept“Unassigned” bucket (PG / SQL Server only)
      ON DELETE RESTRICTError 1451 “Cannot delete or update a parent row”; nothing deletedMoney / audit data: never lose history (customer → invoices)
      ON DELETE NO ACTION / nothingSame as RESTRICT in InnoDBDefault
       
      -- fk_emp_dept: ON DELETE SET NULL ON UPDATE CASCADE
UPDATE dept SET dept_id = 11 WHERE dept_id = 10;
SELECT name, dept_id FROM emp;
      +-------+---------+
| name  | dept_id |
+-------+---------+
| Asha  |      11 |   <- followed the parent
| Ravi  |      11 |
| Meera |      20 |
+-------+---------+
      🔀
      Engine differences

      MySQL InnoDB: CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, NO ACTION (= RESTRICT). SET DEFAULT is parsed but InnoDB rejects the table. Cascaded changes do not fire triggers on the child table.
      PostgreSQL: all five; NO ACTION is checked at end of statement and can be DEFERRABLE; RESTRICT cannot be deferred. PG 15 ON DELETE SET NULL (col) nulls only listed columns of a composite FK.
      SQL Server: NO ACTION (default), CASCADE, SET NULL, SET DEFAULT; no RESTRICT keyword. Rejects FKs that create cycles or multiple cascade paths (error 1785).
      Oracle: only ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL; no ON UPDATE clause at all (default is “no action”). Supports deferrable constraints.

      ⚠️
      CASCADE is dangerous at scale

      One DELETE FROM customer WHERE id = 7 may silently delete thousands of orders, items and payments, all inside one transaction holding locks. Many teams forbid CASCADE on business data and use soft deletes (deleted_at) or explicit cleanup jobs instead.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      The referential action decides what happens to child rows when the parent is deleted or its key changes. CASCADE propagates the change, SET NULL keeps the children but clears the link, SET DEFAULT sets the default value, and RESTRICT or NO ACTION reject the change. In InnoDB RESTRICT and NO ACTION behave the same and SET DEFAULT isn’t supported. In PostgreSQL NO ACTION can be deferred to commit time, which RESTRICT can’t.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪RESTRICT vs NO ACTION — is there any difference?

      In MySQL InnoDB: none. Both are checked immediately, row by row.

      In the SQL standard and PostgreSQL: RESTRICT fails the moment a violating change is made and can never be deferred. NO ACTION is checked at the end of the statement, or at COMMIT if the constraint is DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED. That gives the transaction a chance to fix things first:

      ALTER TABLE emp ADD CONSTRAINT fk_emp_dept FOREIGN KEY (dept_id)
  REFERENCES dept(dept_id) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED;

BEGIN;
DELETE FROM dept WHERE dept_id = 10;            -- children temporarily orphaned: allowed
INSERT INTO dept VALUES (10, 'CSE-new');         -- parent re-created
COMMIT;                                          -- check runs now: passes
      ↪Which option would you choose for order → order_items? customer → orders?

      order_items exist only inside an order → ON DELETE CASCADE. Orders are financial history → RESTRICT (and soft-delete the customer). The choice follows ownership: composition cascades, association restricts or sets NULL.

      ↪What does ON UPDATE CASCADE tell you about the design?

      That the parent key can change — usually a smell (natural key used as PK). With immutable surrogate keys you rarely need ON UPDATE at all.

      QWhat are deferrable constraints? Why can’t MySQL insert two rows that reference each other?

      A deferrable constraint is checked at COMMIT instead of after each statement. Between statements the data may be temporarily invalid.

      Why needed: circular references. Example: dept.head_emp_id → emp and emp.dept_id → dept. The first insert always fails because the other row does not exist yet. Another case: swapping two UNIQUE values (A↔B) in two updates.

      EngineDeferrable?Work-around if not
      PostgreSQL✔ UNIQUE, PK, FK, EXCLUDE (DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED / IMMEDIATE, SET CONSTRAINTS … DEFERRED). NOT NULL and CHECK are never deferrable.—
      Oracle✔ same idea (DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED)—
      MySQL✘ FKs checked immediately, row by rowInsert one side with NULL FK, insert the other, then UPDATE; or SET foreign_key_checks = 0 in the session (risky)
      SQL Server✘NULL-then-UPDATE, or disable with NOCHECK then re-enable WITH CHECK
       
      INSERT INTO dept (dept_id, dname, head_emp_id) VALUES (10, 'CSE', NULL);
INSERT INTO emp  (emp_id, name, dept_id)        VALUES (1, 'Asha', 10);
UPDATE dept SET head_emp_id = 1 WHERE dept_id = 10;

      🛡️ Integrity constraints

      An integrity constraint is a rule that must hold for every legal instance of the database. The DBMS checks it on every change, so bad data cannot get in no matter which app writes it (Codd’s rule 10: integrity independence).

      🗂️

      Domain

      Each value comes from the column’s domain: type, length, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT. age INT CHECK (age BETWEEN 0 AND 150)

      👤

      Entity integrity

      The PK is never NULL (and is unique). Every row is identifiable.

      🔑

      Key constraints

      No two rows share a candidate-key value: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE.

      ⛓️

      Referential integrity

      Every non-NULL FK value matches an existing parent key.

      ⚙️

      Semantic / general

      Any business rule: “salary ≤ manager’s salary”. Needs triggers or app code (assertions are not supported by mainstream engines).

      QWhat are integrity constraints? Entity vs referential integrity?

      Integrity constraints are rules the DBMS enforces so the data stays correct. SQL gives six declarative ones: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, DEFAULT (DEFAULT supplies a value rather than forbidding one, but is usually listed).

      Entity integrity

      • About one table.
      • PK attributes can’t be NULL.
      • Guarantees every row can be found by its PK.
      • Violation: INSERT INTO student(roll_no) VALUES (NULL) → error 1048.

      Referential integrity

      • About two tables (or a table and itself).
      • An FK is NULL or matches a parent key.
      • Guarantees no orphans / dangling references.
      • Violation: enroll a non-existent student → error 1452.
      CREATE TABLE account (
  acc_no     BIGINT        PRIMARY KEY,                           -- entity + key
  ifsc       CHAR(11)      NOT NULL,                              -- domain: NOT NULL
  pan        CHAR(10)      UNIQUE,                                -- key (alternate)
  branch_id  INT           NOT NULL,
  acc_type   ENUM('SAVINGS','CURRENT') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'SAVINGS',-- domain + DEFAULT
  balance    DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  opened_on  DATE          NOT NULL DEFAULT (CURRENT_DATE),      -- expression default (8.0.13+)
  CONSTRAINT chk_balance CHECK (balance >= 0),                   -- domain: CHECK
  CONSTRAINT chk_pan     CHECK (pan REGEXP '^[A-Z]{5}[0-9]{4}[A-Z]$'),
  CONSTRAINT fk_branch   FOREIGN KEY (branch_id) REFERENCES branch(branch_id)  -- referential
);
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Integrity constraints are rules the database enforces on every change. Domain constraints restrict a column’s values through its type, NOT NULL and CHECK. Entity integrity says the primary key can never be NULL, so every row is identifiable. Key constraints make candidate keys unique. Referential integrity says every foreign key value is either NULL or matches an existing parent key, so there are no orphans.

      QDoes MySQL enforce CHECK constraints? Does a CHECK reject NULL?

      Version matters. Before MySQL 8.0.16, CHECK (…) was parsed and silently ignored. People used triggers or ENUMs instead. From 8.0.16 it is enforced (table and column CHECKs).

      NULL passes a CHECK. A row is rejected only if the expression is FALSE. NULL makes the expression UNKNOWN, which is accepted. Add NOT NULL if NULL must be forbidden.

      CREATE TABLE emp2 (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  salary INT CHECK (salary > 0)        -- nullable!
);
INSERT INTO emp2 VALUES (1, -5);    -- ERROR 3819: Check constraint 'emp2_chk_1' is violated.
INSERT INTO emp2 VALUES (2, NULL);  -- OK: NULL > 0 is UNKNOWN, not FALSE

-- Temporarily switch a check off (8.0.16+)
ALTER TABLE emp2 ALTER CHECK emp2_chk_1 NOT ENFORCED;

      Restrictions in MySQL: no subqueries, no non-deterministic functions (NOW(), RAND(), CURRENT_USER()), no stored functions or variables, and a column used in a CHECK cannot also be used in an FK referential action. So “order_date must be in the past” is not a CHECK; use a trigger or the app.

      🔀
      Engine differences

      PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server have enforced CHECK for decades. PostgreSQL also supports CREATE DOMAIN (a reusable type + CHECK) and NOT VALID (add a constraint without checking old rows). SQL Server has WITH NOCHECK for the same purpose.

      🎯
      What they are really testing

      Do you know three-valued logic? CHECK accepts TRUE and UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE. Same expression, opposite treatment of NULL.

      QNOT NULL vs DEFAULT — and what if you insert NULL into a NOT NULL column that has a default?

      NOT NULL forbids NULL. DEFAULT supplies a value when the column is omitted from the INSERT. If you explicitly insert NULL, the default is not used: in strict mode (MySQL 8 default) you get error 1048 “Column cannot be null”.

      CREATE TABLE t (id INT PRIMARY KEY, status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW');
INSERT INTO t (id)         VALUES (1);        -- status = 'NEW'
INSERT INTO t (id, status) VALUES (2, DEFAULT); -- status = 'NEW'
INSERT INTO t (id, status) VALUES (3, NULL);    -- ERROR 1048 (strict mode)
      ⚠️
      Non-strict mode trap

      With sql_mode lacking STRICT_TRANS_TABLES, MySQL converts invalid values to “implicit defaults” (0, '') with only a warning. Old apps that depend on this break when upgraded to strict mode.

      🧮 Relational algebra

      Relational algebra is a set of operators that take one or two relations as input and return a new relation. Because the output is again a relation, operators can be chained like arithmetic: πname(σdept='CSE'(Student)). It is procedural: the expression says which operations to apply, in which order.

      Why learn it if we write SQL? (1) Every SQL query is translated into a relational-algebra tree inside the optimizer (Chapter 16), and rewrites like “push selection below join” are algebra laws. (2) GATE and university exams ask it directly. (3) It forces you to think in sets, which makes hard SQL (division, anti-joins) easy.

      • Music: Meera, John
