      σ = Sigma = Select rows (a horizontal cut). π = Pi = Pick columns (a vertical cut). Fundamental six: “Some People Use Data Carefully, Right?” → Select, Project, Union, Difference, Cartesian product, Rename.

      ① The fundamental operators, worked

      QSelection vs projection — show both with output. Does SQL SELECT equal π?

      σdept='CSE'(Student)

      • 101, Asha, CSE
      • 103, Meera, CSE
      • 2 rows, all 3 columns

      πdept(Student)

      • CSE
      • ECE
      • ME
      • 3 rows (CSE appears once!)
      SELECT * FROM Student WHERE dept = 'CSE';   -- σ
SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM Student;          -- π   (3 rows)
SELECT dept FROM Student;                   -- NOT π: 4 rows, CSE twice (bag)
      ⚠️
      Classic confusion

      The SQL keyword SELECT corresponds to projection π, not selection σ. Selection σ corresponds to WHERE. And π removes duplicates; plain SQL SELECT does not.

      Useful laws (the optimizer uses them):

      • σp∧q(R) = σp(σq(R)) — cascade of selections; σ is commutative.
      • πA(πA,B(R)) = πA(R) — only the outermost projection matters.
      • σp(R ⋈ S) = σp(R) ⋈ S if p uses only R’s attributes — “push selections down”, the most important rewrite.
      QUnion, intersection, difference, product, rename — rules and outputs.
      ExpressionOutputSQL (MySQL 8.0.31+)
      Coding ∪ MusicAsha, Ravi, Meera, JohnSELECT name FROM Coding UNION SELECT name FROM Music
      Coding ∩ MusicMeera… INTERSECT …
      Coding − MusicAsha, Ravi… EXCEPT …
      Music − CodingJohndifference is not commutative
      Student × Course4 × 2 = 8 rows, 3 + 2 = 5 columnsSELECT * FROM Student CROSS JOIN Course
      ρS2(id, nm, d)(Student)same rows, new namesSELECT sid AS id, name AS nm, dept AS d FROM Student S2

      Union compatibility: both inputs have the same degree and the i-th attributes have compatible domains. πsid,name(Student) ∪ πsid(Enroll) is invalid (degree 2 vs 1).

      Why ρ is needed: to combine a relation with itself. “Pairs of students in the same dept”: σS1.dept = S2.dept ∧ S1.sid < S2.sid(ρS1(Student) × ρS2(Student)) → (101, 103). In SQL, the two table aliases are the rename.

      🔀
      Engine differences

      MySQL got INTERSECT and EXCEPT only in 8.0.31; earlier versions need IN/EXISTS and NOT EXISTS/LEFT JOIN … IS NULL. MySQL does not accept MINUS; Oracle traditionally uses MINUS. In MySQL, INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION/EXCEPT. All engines default to DISTINCT semantics; add ALL to keep duplicates.

      QFind the maximum salary using relational algebra (no aggregate functions).

      Classic exam trick. Idea: a salary is not the max if some other salary is bigger. Find all “beaten” salaries, then subtract them from all salaries.

      1. Pair every employee with every other — ρE1(Emp) × ρE2(Emp).
      2. Keep pairs where E1 earns less — σE1.salary < E2.salary(…). Project E1.salary: these are salaries that are beaten.
      3. Subtract — πsalary(Emp) − πE1.salary(σE1.salary < E2.salary(ρE1(Emp) × ρE2(Emp))).
      SELECT DISTINCT e1.salary
FROM emp e1
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary);

      For the second highest: apply the same pattern to (all salaries − max). This is exactly the “Nth highest salary” logic in Chapter 10.

      ② Joins: theta, equi, natural, outer, semi, anti

      All joins are shortcuts built on × and σ: pair everything, then keep the pairs you want.

      QExplain theta join, equi-join and natural join with outputs. How do they differ?

      Equi-join Student ⋈Student.sid = Enroll.sid Enroll keeps both sid columns:

      Student.sid | name  | dept | Enroll.sid | cid
101         | Asha  | CSE  | 101        | C1
101         | Asha  | CSE  | 101        | C2
102         | Ravi  | ECE  | 102        | C1
103         | Meera | CSE  | 103        | C1
103         | Meera | CSE  | 103        | C2        -- 5 rows, 5 columns. John (104) disappears.

      Natural join Student ⋈ Enroll: same rows, but only one sid column (4 columns), because it joins on every attribute with the same name and merges them.

      Theta join uses any comparison (<, ≤, ≠, BETWEEN). Real example: map salaries to grade bands (a non-equi join):

      -- Emp(name, salary): (Asha, 42000) (Ravi, 78000)
-- Grade(grade, lo, hi): (A, 0, 50000) (B, 50001, 100000)
SELECT e.name, e.salary, g.grade
FROM Emp e JOIN Grade g ON e.salary BETWEEN g.lo AND g.hi;
-- Asha 42000 A
-- Ravi 78000 B
      Theta joinEqui-joinNatural join
      Conditionany θ (<, ≥, ≠, …)only == on all same-named attributes (implicit)
      Duplicate join columnsboth keptboth keptmerged into one
      No common attributes?——becomes a Cartesian product!
      🚫
      NATURAL JOIN in production code

      It silently joins on every same-named column. Add an updated_at or name column to both tables later and the query quietly returns wrong or empty results. Use explicit ON or USING (sid).

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A theta join is a Cartesian product followed by a selection on any condition. An equi-join is a theta join where the condition uses only equality, and it keeps both copies of the join columns. A natural join is an equi-join on all attributes that have the same name, and it keeps only one copy; if there are no common attributes it degenerates into a cross product.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪R has m rows, S has n rows. Min and max rows of R ⋈ S? Of R ⟕ S?

      Inner join: 0 to m·n (m·n when every pair matches, e.g. joining on a column with one repeated value). Left outer join: at least m (every R row survives), at most m·n. If the join is on S’s primary key (FK → PK), R ⋈ S has at most m rows and R ⟕ S has exactly m.

      ↪Is the natural join of R and S with no common attributes allowed?

      Yes: it equals R × S (the condition “all common attributes equal” is vacuously true).

      QOuter join, semi-join and anti-join in algebra and SQL.
      OperationOutput on our dataMySQL 8
      Student ⟕ Enrollthe 5 joined rows + (104, John, ME, NULL) = 6 rowsSELECT * FROM Student s LEFT JOIN Enroll e ON s.sid = e.sid
      Student ⋉ Enroll (semi)101 Asha, 102 Ravi, 103 Meera — each once, even though Asha has 2 enrollmentsSELECT * FROM Student s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Enroll e WHERE e.sid = s.sid)
      Student ▷ Enroll (anti)104 John… WHERE NOT EXISTS (…) or LEFT JOIN … WHERE e.sid IS NULL
      Student ⟗ Enroll (full)⟕ ∪ ⟖no FULL JOIN in MySQL: LEFT JOIN … UNION … RIGHT JOIN …
      ⚠️
      Semi-join ≠ inner join

      An inner join repeats Asha twice (two enrollments). A semi-join returns her once. That is why “students who enrolled in something” is written with EXISTS, or SELECT DISTINCT on a join. The anti-join written with NOT IN returns zero rows if the subquery yields any NULL; prefer NOT EXISTS. Details in Chapter 08.

      Outer joins are not part of Codd’s original algebra: they need NULL padding. They are an extended operator, like grouping/aggregation γ.

      ③ Division ÷ — the “for ALL” operator

      Division answers questions with the word all / every: “students who took all courses”, “suppliers who supply every red part”, “customers who bought every product in a category”. For R(X, Y) and S(Y), R ÷ S returns the X values that are paired in R with every Y value in S.

      QFind students who have taken ALL courses — in relational algebra and in SQL.

      Formula with basic operators: R ÷ S = πX(R) − πX( (πX(R) × S) − R )

      1. All candidates — πsid(Enroll) = {101, 102, 103}.
      2. Every combination that should exist — πsid(Enroll) × Course = 3 × 2 = 6 pairs.
      3. Subtract what actually exists — 6 pairs − Enroll = {(102, C2)}: the missing pairs.
      4. Who is missing something? — πsid = {102}: disqualified.
      5. Answer — {101, 102, 103} − {102} = {101, 103}.
      SELECT s.sid, s.name
FROM Student s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (                    -- no course ...
  SELECT 1 FROM Course c
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (                  -- ... that this student has not taken
    SELECT 1 FROM Enroll e
    WHERE e.sid = s.sid AND e.cid = c.cid));
      +-----+-------+
| sid | name  |
+-----+-------+
| 101 | Asha  |
| 103 | Meera |
+-----+-------+

      This is the direct translation of logic: ∀c ∃e ≡ ¬∃c ¬∃e. Works even with duplicate enrollments or stray course IDs.

      SELECT e.sid
FROM Enroll e
JOIN Course c ON c.cid = e.cid               -- ignore enrollments in unknown courses
GROUP BY e.sid
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT e.cid) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Course);

      Shorter and usually faster. Needs DISTINCT (duplicate enrollments would inflate counts) and the join or an FK (an enrollment in a non-existent C9 would also inflate counts).

      🎯
      Gotcha follow-up: what if Course is empty?

      Logically every student qualifies (“took all of zero courses” is vacuously true). The double NOT EXISTS returns all students; the COUNT version compares with 0 and returns nobody (each group has ≥ 1). Mentioning this shows you understand the logic, not just the pattern.

      ⚠️
      Common mistake

      Writing WHERE cid = 'C1' AND cid = 'C2' (always empty: one row cannot have two values) or cid IN ('C1','C2') (that is “any”, not “all”). Division is not a simple join.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      This is relational division. In algebra I take all candidate students, build every student–course pair that should exist with a cross product, subtract the real enrollments to find missing pairs, and remove students who appear in the missing set. In SQL I write it as a double NOT EXISTS: there is no course that the student has not taken. Or I group by student and check that the count of distinct courses equals the total number of courses.

      Click an operator. The widget computes the result live from the tiny dataset above (it really runs the operators, nothing is pre-baked). Tick the box to give Ravi a C2 enrollment and watch division change.

      Pick an operator above.
      QWhich operators are fundamental, and how do you derive the others?

      Fundamental = cannot be expressed with the others. The standard set is σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ (some books leave out ρ by using positional names). Everything else is shorthand:

      Derived operatorDefinition using fundamentals
      R ∩ SR − (R − S)
      R ⋈θ Sσθ(R × S)
      R ⋈ S (natural)πattrs(R) ∪ attrs(S)(σR.a = S.a for all common a(R × S))
      R ⋉ Sπattrs(R)(R ⋈ S)
      R ▷ SR − (R ⋉ S)
      R ÷ SπX(R) − πX((πX(R) × S) − R)

      Practice — write these in algebra:

      • Names of CSE students enrolled in C2: πname(σdept='CSE' ∧ cid='C2'(Student ⋈ Enroll)) → Asha, Meera.
      • Students not enrolled in anything: πsid(Student) − πsid(Enroll) → 104.
      • Courses nobody takes: πcid(Course) − πcid(Enroll) → ∅.
      • Students in C1 or C2 but not both: (πsidσcid='C1'E ∪ πsidσcid='C2'E) − (πsidσcid='C1'E ∩ πsidσcid='C2'E) → 102.
      💡
      Which operators need “−”?

      Any query with “not”, “only”, “all”, “every”, “maximum” needs set difference (or an anti-join). σ, π, × and ∪ alone are monotonic: adding input rows can never remove output rows, so they cannot express negation.

      ℹ️
      Extended operators

      Real optimizers also use γ (grouping + aggregation), τ (sort), δ (duplicate elimination), and bag versions of the operators. Classical algebra cannot count — COUNT, SUM, recursion (transitive closure) are beyond it.

      🧠 Relational calculus (TRC & DRC), safety and completeness

      Relational calculus describes the result you want with a logical formula, not the steps. It is declarative. SQL’s SELECT … FROM … WHERE is closest to tuple relational calculus.

      Tuple relational calculus (TRC)

      • Variables range over tuples.
      • Form: { t | P(t) }
      • CSE students: { t | t ∈ Student ∧ t.dept = 'CSE' }
      • Names of students enrolled in C2:
        { t | ∃s ∈ Student ∃e ∈ Enroll (s.sid = e.sid ∧ e.cid = 'C2' ∧ t.name = s.name) }

      Domain relational calculus (DRC)

      • Variables range over attribute values (domains).
      • Form: { ⟨x1, …, xn⟩ | P(x1, …, xn) }
      • CSE student names: { ⟨n⟩ | ∃s, d (⟨s, n, d⟩ ∈ Student ∧ d = 'CSE') }
      • Basis of QBE (Query-By-Example) and Datalog-style languages.

      Division in TRC (students who took all courses) reads almost like English:
      { s | s ∈ Student ∧ ∀c ∈ Course ( ∃e ∈ Enroll (e.sid = s.sid ∧ e.cid = c.cid) ) }
      Replace ∀ with ¬∃¬ and you get the double NOT EXISTS SQL directly.

      QWhat is a safe expression? What does “relationally complete” mean?

      Unsafe expression: a calculus query whose answer can be infinite or depends on values outside the database. Example: { t | ¬(t ∈ Student) } — “every tuple that is not a student” — includes every possible string and number in the universe.

      Safe expression: every value in the result must come from the relations or constants mentioned in the formula (its domain, dom(P)). Safe TRC requires every component of t to appear in some relation, tuple or constant in P. In practice: every negated or universally quantified variable must be bound to a relation, like ¬∃e ∈ Enroll (…) instead of a free ¬.

      Codd’s theorem: relational algebra, safe TRC and safe DRC have exactly the same expressive power. A query language is relationally complete if it can express every query that relational algebra can. SQL is relationally complete — and goes further (aggregates, recursion via WITH RECURSIVE, ordering).

      Relational algebraRelational calculusSQL
      Styleprocedural (how)declarative (what)declarative
      Unitoperators on relationslogic formulas (∃, ∀, ¬, ∧, ∨)SELECT-FROM-WHERE
      Semanticssetssetsbags + NULLs
      Used forquery plans / optimizertheory, basis of SQL & QBEeverything
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Relational algebra is procedural: I combine operators like selection, projection and join in a specific order. Relational calculus is declarative: I describe the tuples I want with a logical formula, and SQL is based on tuple relational calculus. A calculus expression is safe if its result can only contain values from the database or the query’s constants, so it is always finite. Codd showed that safe calculus and algebra are equally expressive, which is what relationally complete means.

      📌 Key takeaways

      • Relation = set of tuples (no duplicates, no order, atomic values). SQL table = bag, ordered columns, NULLs.
      • Degree = columns (schema); cardinality = rows (instance). Schema = structure; instance = current data.
      • Super ⊇ Candidate ⊇ Primary. Candidate = minimal super key; alternate = candidates not chosen; one PK (maybe composite).
      • Super-key count: one key of size k → 2n−k; several keys → inclusion–exclusion on the union of keys.
      • Prefer a short, immutable surrogate PK + UNIQUE natural key; in InnoDB the PK is the clustered index and lives in every secondary index.
      • UNIQUE NULLs: many in MySQL/PG/Oracle, one in SQL Server; PG 15 NULLS NOT DISTINCT.
      • No PK → InnoDB uses the first NOT NULL UNIQUE index, else a hidden 6-byte GEN_CLUST_INDEX; guard with sql_require_primary_key / GIPK.
      • FKs: may be NULL, may target UNIQUE, may self-reference. InnoDB: RESTRICT = NO ACTION, no SET DEFAULT, no deferral; PG/Oracle can defer.
      • CHECK is enforced in MySQL only from 8.0.16, and NULL passes a CHECK.
      • Algebra: fundamental σ π ∪ − × ρ; derived ∩, joins, semi/anti, ÷. Division = “all candidates minus those missing something” = double NOT EXISTS.

      📚 Go deeper

      • CMU 15-445 Lecture 01 notes — Relational Model & Algebra — crisp, rigorous, short.
      • Silberschatz, Korth, Sudarshan — Database System Concepts slides — Ch. 2 (relational model) and Ch. 27 (relational calculus).
      • MySQL 8.4 — FOREIGN KEY Constraints — referential actions, MATCH, indexes, restrictions.
      • MySQL 8.4 — Clustered and Secondary Indexes — PK choice and GEN_CLUST_INDEX.
      • PostgreSQL — Constraints — NULLS NOT DISTINCT, deferrable constraints, NO ACTION vs RESTRICT.
      • GeeksforGeeks — Relational Algebra — many GATE-style practice questions (cross-check engine claims against docs).

      R(A, B, C, D) has candidate keys A and BC. How many super keys does it have?

      SK(A) = 2³ = 8, SK(BC) = 2² = 4, SK(A ∪ BC = ABC) = 2¹ = 2. 8 + 4 − 2 = 10.

      In MySQL 8, a column declared phone VARCHAR(15) UNIQUE (nullable). How many rows with phone = NULL can you insert?

      MySQL’s UNIQUE index permits multiple NULLs (NULLs are not equal). SQL Server would allow only one.

      An InnoDB table has no PRIMARY KEY and no UNIQUE NOT NULL index. What is its clustered index?

      InnoDB always clusters. Fallback order: PK → first UNIQUE index with all NOT NULL columns → hidden GEN_CLUST_INDEX. CREATE fails only if sql_require_primary_key = ON.

      Which statement about ON DELETE SET DEFAULT in MySQL InnoDB is true?

      InnoDB and NDB reject SET DEFAULT. The default when no action is written is NO ACTION (= RESTRICT in InnoDB). PostgreSQL and SQL Server do support SET DEFAULT.

      MySQL 8.0.20: salary INT CHECK (salary > 0), nullable. INSERT … VALUES (NULL) gives…

      CHECK is enforced since 8.0.16 and rejects only FALSE. UNKNOWN (from NULL) passes. Add NOT NULL to forbid NULL.

      The SQL keyword SELECT (the column list) corresponds to which relational-algebra operator?

      The SELECT list picks columns = π (but without DISTINCT it keeps duplicates). The WHERE clause is σ.

      R(X, Y) has 6 tuples and S(Y) has 2 tuples. What is the maximum number of tuples in R ÷ S?

      Each X in the answer needs one R tuple per S value (2 each). 6 / 2 = 3 is the most possible.

      In PostgreSQL, what is the real difference between ON DELETE RESTRICT and ON DELETE NO ACTION?

      Both prevent orphans. Only NO ACTION can be DEFERRABLE. In MySQL InnoDB they are identical (immediate).
      Degree vs cardinality
      Degree = number of attributes (columns). Cardinality = number of tuples (rows).
      Candidate key
      A minimal super key: unique, and no attribute can be removed.
      Alternate key
      A candidate key not chosen as PK; enforce with UNIQUE NOT NULL.
      Super keys with 1 key of size k in n attributes
      2^(n−k). Two keys: SK(K1) + SK(K2) − SK(K1 ∪ K2).
      Surrogate key
      System-generated meaningless ID (AUTO_INCREMENT, UUID). Stable and compact; pair it with UNIQUE on the natural key.
      Partial key
      Discriminator of a weak entity; unique only with the owner’s key. Table PK = owner PK + partial key.
      GEN_CLUST_INDEX
      InnoDB’s hidden clustered index on a 6-byte row ID, used when there is no PK and no NOT NULL UNIQUE index.
      Can an FK be NULL / reference UNIQUE / reference its own table?
      Yes / yes / yes.
      Entity vs referential integrity
      Entity: PK not NULL and unique. Referential: FK is NULL or matches a parent key.
      Fundamental RA operators
      σ, π, ∪, −, ×, ρ. Derived: ∩, joins, semi/anti-join, ÷.
      Division formula
      R ÷ S = π_X(R) − π_X((π_X(R) × S) − R). SQL: double NOT EXISTS.
      Safe expression
      A calculus query whose result uses only values from the database or the query’s constants, so it is finite.
      Chapter 05 · II · Design

      🧬 Functional Dependencies, Closure & Candidate Keys

      Read a set of FDs like a map: compute any closure in seconds, find every candidate key, shrink FDs to a minimal cover, and prove a decomposition is lossless — the toolkit that every normalization answer stands on.

      ⏱ 40 min🔥 Asked a lotFD · keysminimal cover · chase test

      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision

      • FD X → Y: any two rows that agree on X must agree on Y. It is a business rule for every legal state, never something you prove from sample data.
      • Trivial: Y ⊆ X (always true). Non-trivial: Y ⊄ X. Completely non-trivial: X ∩ Y = ∅.
      • Armstrong's axioms = RAT: Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity — sound (never derive a false FD) and complete (derive every true FD). Derived rules = UDP: Union, Decomposition, Pseudotransitivity.
      • Attribute closure X⁺: start with X, keep firing every FD whose LHS is inside the set, stop when nothing changes. X is a superkey ⇔ X⁺ = all attributes. X → Y holds ⇔ Y ⊆ X⁺.
      • Candidate key = minimal superkey. Attributes that never appear on any RHS are in every key; attributes only on the RHS are in no key.
      • Prime attribute = part of some candidate key. 2NF/3NF only care about non-prime attributes.
      • Minimal cover: split RHS → remove extraneous LHS attributes → remove redundant FDs (in that order). It is the input to 3NF synthesis.
      • Lossless binary split: R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2. A lossy join gives extra (spurious) rows. Dependency-preserving: every FD checkable inside one table.
      • Trap: AB → C does not imply A → C. Decomposition works on the right side only.
      ✏️ In interviews FDs show up as "what is a functional dependency?" plus "find the candidate keys". In GATE-style tests they are MCQs on closure, keys and minimal covers. Same toolkit for both.

      🔗 What is a functional dependency?

      Think of a college office. If you tell the clerk a roll number, they can tell you the student's name. Exactly one name. That is a functional dependency: roll_no → name. The left side (the determinant) decides the right side (the dependent).

      QWhat is a functional dependency? Give an example.

      What: For attribute sets X and Y of a relation R, X → Y holds if, in every legal instance of R, any two rows with the same X value also have the same Y value. Read it as "X functionally determines Y".

      Why it matters: FDs are how we write business rules formally. Keys are defined with them (K is a superkey ⇔ K → R), and every normal form is a rule about which FDs are allowed (Chapter 06).

      How to check one against data: group rows by X; inside each group, Y must have exactly one distinct value.

      SELECT dept_id, COUNT(DISTINCT dept_name) AS names
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT dept_name) > 1;   -- any row returned = FD violated
      +---------+-------+
| dept_id | names |
+---------+-------+
| D2      |     2 |     <- D2 is called both 'HR' and 'Human Res.' : FD broken
+---------+-------+

      Mini-instance: r(A, B) = {(1, 4), (1, 5), (3, 7)}. Here B → A is consistent with the data (each B value appears once), but A → B is false (A = 1 maps to 4 and 5).

      🚫
      Answer that fails

      "Looking at the table, name → roll_no holds, because no two rows share a name." Sample data can only disprove an FD. Tomorrow two students named Priya may join. FDs come from the business rules, and you enforce them with keys and constraints.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A functional dependency X → Y means that whenever two rows have the same X value, they must have the same Y value. For example, roll number determines student name. It is a rule about every valid state of the table, so it comes from the business requirements, not from looking at sample rows. We use FDs to define keys and to decide how to normalize a table.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪How do you enforce an FD in SQL?

      Put X and Y in a table where X is a key: PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE (X). Then two rows cannot share X, so the FD holds automatically. An FD whose LHS is not a key of any table can only be enforced with a trigger or a join check — that is exactly what normalization avoids.

      ↪Is a key the same as an FD?

      A key is a special FD: K → (all attributes). Every key gives FDs, but most FDs are not keys (dept_id → dept_name inside an employee table).

      ↪What does ∅ → A mean?

      A has the same value in every row (a constant column). Rare, but it can appear in GATE questions.

      Types of functional dependency

      TypeRuleExampleWhy you care
      TrivialY ⊆ X{roll_no, name} → name, AB → AAlways true, carries no information. Normal-form tests ignore it.
      Non-trivialY ⊄ Xroll_no → name, AB → BCThese are the real rules.
      Completely non-trivialX ∩ Y = ∅AB → CClean form; every non-trivial FD can be reduced to it by dropping RHS attributes already in X.
      FullX → Y and no proper subset of X → Yroll_no, course_id → gradeWhat 2NF wants for non-prime attributes.
      Partialsome proper subset of X already → Yroll_no, course_id → name (roll_no alone suffices)Partial dependency on a key breaks 2NF.
      TransitiveX → Y, Y → Z, Y not a superkey, Z ⊄ Yemp_id → dept_id → dept_headBreaks 3NF when Z is non-prime.
      Multivalued (MVD)X ↠ Y: a set of Y values per X, independent of the reststudent ↠ hobby, student ↠ languageNot an FD; drives 4NF. See below.
      ⚠️
      Source mismatch to know about

      Some websites call AB → BC "semi non-trivial". The standard textbook split is just trivial vs non-trivial, plus "completely non-trivial" for X ∩ Y = ∅. If asked, give the textbook terms and mention the alias.

      🔨 Armstrong's axioms (and the three derived rules)

      Given some FDs, which other FDs are also guaranteed? Armstrong's axioms are three rules that generate them. Everything else is built from these three.

      🪞

      Reflexivity

      If Y ⊆ X then X → Y. (Gives the trivial FDs.)
      AB → A

      ➕

      Augmentation

      If X → Y then XZ → YZ for any Z. Add the same thing to both sides.
      A → B ⇒ AC → BC

      ⛓️

      Transitivity

      If X → Y and Y → Z then X → Z.
      emp → dept, dept → head ⇒ emp → head

      🧠 RAT + UDP

      Base axioms: Reflexivity, Augmentation, Transitivity — "the RAT is the base". Derived rules: Union, Decomposition, Pseudotransitivity — "UDP is built on top" (like the network protocol). Sound = "never lies". Complete = "never misses".

      Derived ruleStatementProof from RAT (say this if asked "prove it")
      UnionX → Y, X → Z ⇒ X → YZAugment X → Y with X: X → XY. Augment X → Z with Y: XY → YZ. Transitivity: X → YZ.
      DecompositionX → YZ ⇒ X → Y and X → ZReflexivity: YZ → Y. Transitivity with X → YZ: X → Y. Same for Z.
      PseudotransitivityX → Y, WY → Z ⇒ WX → ZAugment X → Y with W: WX → WY. Transitivity with WY → Z: WX → Z.
      Composition (bonus)X → Y, Z → W ⇒ XZ → YWAugment each and chain: XZ → YZ → YW.
      QWhat are Armstrong's axioms, and what do "sound" and "complete" mean?

      They are three inference rules — reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity — for deriving new FDs from a given set F.

      • Sound: every FD you derive with them really holds in every instance that satisfies F. They never produce a false FD.
      • Complete: every FD that is logically implied by F can be derived with them. Nothing is missed.

      So the set of all FDs derivable with the axioms is exactly F⁺, the closure of F. In practice nobody derives F⁺ by hand (it is exponential); we use attribute closure instead.

      🚫
      Classic wrong derivation

      "AB → C, so A → C and B → C." False. Decomposition splits the right side only. Counter-example: (roll_no, course_id) → grade, but roll_no alone does not determine a grade. The opposite is true: A → C does imply AB → C (augmentation + reflexivity).

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Armstrong's axioms are reflexivity, augmentation and transitivity. Using them we can derive every FD implied by a given set — that is completeness — and we never derive a wrong one — that is soundness. Union, decomposition and pseudotransitivity are derived from them. One trap: we can split the right side of an FD, but never the left side.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Prove A → B, BC → D ⇒ AC → D.

      That is pseudotransitivity. Augment A → B with C: AC → BC. Transitivity with BC → D: AC → D. Or the fast way: AC⁺ = AC → +B → +D, and D ∈ AC⁺.

      ↪Is "if X → Y and Z → W then XZ → YW" valid?

      Yes (composition): augment X → Y with Z to get XZ → YZ, augment Z → W with Y to get YZ → YW, then transitivity.

      ↪Is "X → Y and XY → Z ⇒ X → Z" valid?

      Yes. From X → Y, augmentation with X gives X → XY. Then transitivity with XY → Z.

      🧲 Attribute closure X⁺ — the one algorithm you need

      X⁺ (the closure of X under F) is the set of all attributes that X determines. Think of it as a snowball: start with X, and every FD whose left side is fully inside the snowball adds its right side. Roll until it stops growing.

      1. result := X.
      2. Scan every FD L → R in F. If L ⊆ result, add R to result.
      3. Repeat the full scan until a pass adds nothing. (One pass is not enough — a later FD may unlock an earlier one.)
      4. Return result. Cost is polynomial: at most |R| passes over F.

      Three worked closures

      R(A, B, C, G, H, I), F = {A → B, A → C, CG → H, CG → I, B → H}. Find (AG)⁺.

      StepFD firedresult
      start—AG
      1A → BABG
      2A → CABCG
      3CG → HABCGH
      4CG → IABCGHI ✔ = R

      Also: A⁺ = ABCH (no G) and G⁺ = G. So AG is a superkey and no proper subset is ⇒ AG is a candidate key.

      R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {AB → C, B → D, C → E, D → A}. Find B⁺.

      StepFD firedresult
      start—B
      1B → DBD
      2D → AABD
      3AB → C ← unlocked only nowABCD
      4C → EABCDE ✔

      A single attribute B is a key here. Note that AB → C only fired after D → A brought A in — that is why you must keep scanning.

      emp(emp_id, name, dept_id, dept_name, city, state), F = {emp_id → name, dept_id; dept_id → dept_name, city; city → state}.

      • {dept_id}⁺ = {dept_id, dept_name, city, state}. Not all columns ⇒ dept_id is not a key of emp.
      • {emp_id}⁺ = {emp_id, name, dept_id} → + dept_name, city → + state = all ⇒ emp_id is the key.
      • Does F imply emp_id → state? state ∈ {emp_id}⁺ ⇒ yes (a transitive FD — a 3NF problem).
      • Does F imply city → dept_id? {city}⁺ = {city, state} ⇒ no.
      QWhat is attribute closure and what is it used for?

      What: X⁺ is the set of every attribute functionally determined by X under F.

      Why it exists: F⁺ (all implied FDs) can be exponentially large. X⁺ answers the same questions in polynomial time, one X at a time.

      Uses:

      • Superkey test: X is a superkey ⇔ X⁺ contains every attribute of R.
      • Candidate key test: X⁺ = R and, for each attribute a ∈ X, (X − a)⁺ ≠ R.
      • FD membership: F implies X → Y ⇔ Y ⊆ X⁺. (This is how you check an FD without Armstrong proofs.)
      • Building blocks: equivalence of FD sets, minimal cover, BCNF/3NF tests, dependency preservation — all call closure in a loop.
      ⚠️
      Common mistakes

      (1) Stopping after one pass. (2) Firing AB → C when only A is in the set. (3) Forgetting that X ⊆ X⁺ always (reflexivity). (4) Calling a superkey a candidate key without checking minimality.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      The closure of X is everything X determines. I start with X, and repeatedly add the right side of any FD whose left side is already in my set, until nothing changes. If the closure covers all attributes, X is a superkey; and to test whether an FD X → Y follows from the given ones, I just check whether Y is inside X's closure.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Closure of attributes vs closure of an FD set?

      X⁺ is a set of attributes. F⁺ is the set of all FDs implied by F (including trivial ones) — it can have exponentially many members. You can describe F⁺ as {X → Y : Y ⊆ X⁺} over all X.

      ↪How many FDs are in F⁺ for R(A, B) with F = ∅?

      Only trivial ones. With subsets ∅, A, B, AB as LHS: ∅ → ∅; A → ∅, A; B → ∅, B; AB → any of 4 subsets. Total 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9. GATE likes this kind of counting; the general count for F = ∅ is Σ over subsets X of 2^|X| = 3ⁿ.

      🧮 Closure, key & minimal-cover calculator — attributes are single letters; write FDs like AB->C, separated by commas or new lines.

      Pick an action.

      🔑 Finding ALL candidate keys

      Superkey
      Any attribute set X with X⁺ = R (it identifies every row).
      Candidate key
      A minimal superkey: remove any one attribute and it stops being a superkey.
      Primary key
      The one candidate key the designer picks as row identity (NOT NULL). The others are alternate keys.
      Prime attribute
      An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key. Non-prime = belongs to none.
      1. Sort attributes into three bins. Never on any RHS ⇒ must be in every key (nothing can produce them). Only on RHS, never on LHS ⇒ in no key (they never help determine anything). Both sides ⇒ maybe.
      2. Compute (must)⁺. If it is R, the "must" set is the only candidate key. Done.
      3. Otherwise grow it. Add "maybe" attributes one at a time, then pairs, etc. Keep each set whose closure is R. Skip any superset of a key already found (it can't be minimal).
      4. Swap trick for more keys. If K is a key and an FD X → A has A ∈ K, then (K − A) ∪ X is a superkey. Check it for minimality.
      5. List keys, then prime / non-prime. That is the input to every normal-form question.
      ℹ️
      Why step 1 works

      Closure only ever adds attributes that appear on some right-hand side. So an attribute that is on no RHS can enter X⁺ only if it was in X from the start. And an attribute that is on no LHS never triggers an FD, so removing it from a key never shrinks the closure below R minus itself — it can't be needed except to cover itself, which the RHS already does.

      Binsmust / never / maybe
      (must)⁺ = R?yes ⇒ single key
      Growmust + 1 maybe, + 2 …
      SwapX → A, A ∈ K ⇒ try (K−A)∪X

      Four worked key-finding examples

      R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → B, BC → E, ED → A}.

      1. Bins: RHS attributes are B, E, A ⇒ C, D never on RHS ⇒ in every key.
      2. (CD)⁺ = CD. Not R. Grow with one of A, B, E.
      3. ACD⁺ = ACD → +B (A→B) → +E (BC→E) = ABCDE ✔
        BCD⁺ = BCD → +E (BC→E) → +A (ED→A) = ABCDE ✔
        CDE⁺ = CDE → +A (ED→A) → +B (A→B) = ABCDE ✔
      4. Swap check: from key ACD and ED → A ⇒ (CD) ∪ ED = CDE — the same third key, found without guessing.

      Keys: ACD, BCD, CDE. Prime: all five attributes. Non-prime: none ⇒ automatically 3NF; A → B (A not a superkey) ⇒ not BCNF.

      R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → BC, CD → E, B → D, E → A}.

      • Every attribute is on some RHS ⇒ "must" set is empty. Try singles.
      • A⁺ = ABC → +D (B→D) → +E (CD→E) = R ✔. E⁺ = EA… = R ✔. B⁺ = BD ✘. C⁺ = C ✘. D⁺ = D ✘.
      • Pairs without A or E: BC⁺ = BCD → E → A = R ✔. CD⁺ = CDE → A → B = R ✔. BD⁺ = BD ✘.

      Keys: A, E, BC, CD (four!). Lesson: keys can have different sizes. Every attribute is prime ⇒ 3NF; B → D breaks BCNF.

      R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → E, E → A}.

      • B is never on a RHS ⇒ in every key. B⁺ = B.
      • AB⁺ = ABCDE ✔. BC⁺ = BC → D → E → A = R ✔. BD⁺ = BD → E → A → (AB→C) C = R ✔. BE⁺ = BE → A → C → D = R ✔.

      Keys: AB, BC, BD, BE. The cycle C → D → E → A, with A feeding back via AB → C, means any one member of the cycle plus B works.

      R(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, B → C}.

      • Never on RHS: A, D. (AD)⁺ = AD → B → C = ABCD ✔.
      • The must-set alone is a superkey ⇒ AD is the only candidate key. No search needed.
      • C is only on the RHS ⇒ could never have been in a key anyway.
      QGiven R and a set of FDs, how do you find all candidate keys?

      I use attribute closure plus a pruning rule. Attributes that never appear on the right side of any FD must be in every key, because nothing can derive them. Attributes that appear only on the right side are in no key. I compute the closure of the mandatory set; if it covers R, that is the only key. Otherwise I add the remaining "both-side" attributes one at a time, then in pairs, keeping every minimal set whose closure is R and skipping supersets of keys already found. Finally I use the swap trick to make sure I haven't missed any.

      💡
      💡 Exam speed-up

      If the must-set has k attributes and the answer options list keys without one of them, eliminate those options instantly. Many GATE MCQs fall to this alone.

      🔀
      From theory to MySQL

      The theory says "a relation always has at least one candidate key (worst case: all attributes)". In SQL a table is a bag, so it may have no key at all and allow duplicate rows. In MySQL, declare the chosen key as PRIMARY KEY and each alternate key as UNIQUE with NOT NULL columns (UNIQUE allows multiple NULLs in MySQL and PostgreSQL; SQL Server allows only one NULL in a unique index). InnoDB without a PK clusters on the first NOT NULL UNIQUE index, else on a hidden 6-byte row id. See Chapter 04.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪What is the maximum number of candidate keys a relation with n attributes can have?

      C(n, ⌊n/2⌋) — all subsets of size n/2 (keys form an antichain, so Sperner's theorem gives the bound). That exponential count is why testing 3NF is NP-hard in general: it may require knowing all keys.

      ↪Every candidate key is a superkey. Is every superkey a candidate key?

      No. {roll_no, name} is a superkey but not minimal. A candidate key is a superkey with nothing to spare.

      ↪Can two candidate keys have different sizes?

      Yes — A, E, BC, CD in the example above. Minimal means "no proper subset works", not "smallest size".

      Counting superkeys (GATE favourite)

      If K is a candidate key with k attributes in R with n attributes, every superset of K is a superkey: 2n−k of them. With several keys, use inclusion–exclusion so a set containing both keys is counted once.

      RCandidate keysCountSuperkeys
      R(A, B, C, D)A2³8
      R(A, B, C, D)A, B2³ + 2³ − 2² (supersets of AB)12
      R(A, B, C, D)A, BC2³ + 2² − 2¹ (supersets of ABC)10
      R(A, B, C, D)AB, CD2² + 2² − 2⁰ (only ABCD)7
      🧠
      Memory aid

      "Fix the key, flip a coin for every other column": each of the n − k other attributes is either in or out ⇒ 2n−k. For two keys: |S(K1)| + |S(K2)| − |S(K1 ∪ K2)|.

      ✂️ F⁺, equivalent FD sets and the minimal (canonical) cover

      Two FD sets can look different but say exactly the same thing. F and G are equivalent (F ≡ G) if F⁺ = G⁺. Test without building F⁺: F covers G if every FD of G follows from F (check X → Y of G by computing X⁺ under F), and vice versa.

      F = {A→C, AC→D, E→AD, E→H}

      • Under F: A⁺ = ACD ⊇ CD ✔ (gives A → CD)
      • E⁺ = EADHC ⊇ AH ✔ (gives E → AH)
      • ⇒ F covers G

      G = {A→CD, E→AH}

      • Under G: A⁺ = ACD ⇒ A → C ✔, AC → D ✔
      • E⁺ = EAHCD ⇒ E → AD ✔, E → H ✔
      • ⇒ G covers F, so F ≡ G

      A minimal cover (also called canonical cover; some books keep merged RHS for "canonical") is the smallest clean equivalent of F: single-attribute right sides, no extra attribute on any left side, no FD that the others already imply. It is the input to 3NF synthesis, and fewer FDs means cheaper constraint checks.

      1. Split every right side into single attributes: A → BC ⇒ A → B, A → C.
      2. Left-reduce: for each X → A with |X| ≥ 2 and each B ∈ X: if A ∈ (X − B)⁺ (using the current full set), B is extraneous — drop it.
      3. Remove redundant FDs: for each X → A: compute X⁺ using all FDs except this one. If A ∈ X⁺, delete the FD.
      4. (Optional) merge FDs with the same left side using union.
      ⚠️
      Order matters

      Do step 2 before step 3. Removing redundant FDs first and reducing left sides afterwards can leave a redundant FD behind. Also: the minimal cover is not unique — different scan orders can give different, equally correct answers. Say this if the interviewer's answer differs from yours.

      QFind the minimal cover of F = {A → B, C → B, D → ABC, AC → D}.
      1. Split: {A→B, C→B, D→A, D→B, D→C, AC→D}.
      2. Left-reduce AC → D: A⁺ = AB (no D), C⁺ = CB (no D) ⇒ neither A nor C is extraneous.
      3. Redundancy check, one FD at a time with the others:
        • A → B: without it, A⁺ = A ⇒ needed.
        • C → B: without it, C⁺ = C ⇒ needed.
        • D → A: without it, D⁺ = DBC ⇒ no A ⇒ needed.
        • D → B: without it, D⁺ = D → A, C → B (via A → B) ⇒ B reached ⇒ redundant, delete.
        • D → C: without it, D⁺ = DAB ⇒ no C ⇒ needed.
        • AC → D: without it, AC⁺ = ACB ⇒ needed.

      Minimal cover: {A → B, C → B, D → A, D → C, AC → D}. Try it in the calculator above ("Example: cover").

      A second, textbook example (Silberschatz): F = {A → BC, B → C, A → B, AB → C}. Merge to {A → BC, B → C, AB → C}; A is extraneous in AB → C (B → C already) ⇒ {A → BC, B → C}; C is extraneous in A → BC (A → B → C) ⇒ Fc = {A → B, B → C}.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A minimal cover is an equivalent set of FDs with single attributes on the right, no extraneous attributes on the left, and no redundant FDs. I split the right sides, then for each composite left side I check whether dropping an attribute still lets the closure reach the right side, and finally I drop any FD that the remaining ones imply. It's the input to the 3NF synthesis algorithm, and it isn't necessarily unique.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Why do we want a minimal cover at all?

      Each FD is a constraint the DBMS must check on writes. Fewer and smaller FDs mean cheaper checks, and 3NF synthesis creates one table per FD of the cover — redundant FDs would create redundant tables.

      ↪What is an extraneous attribute on the right side?

      In A → BC, C is extraneous if C is still implied after replacing the FD by A → B. Splitting the RHS and removing redundant single-RHS FDs handles both cases at once.

      🧩 Lossless-join decomposition

      When you split R into R1, R2, …, you must be able to join them back and get exactly R. If the join gives back extra rows that were never there, the split was lossy. Those fake rows are called spurious tuples.

      QHow do you test whether a decomposition is lossless?

      Binary split R → R1, R2 (the test everyone asks): lossless if and only if (with only FDs as constraints)

      1. R1 ∪ R2 = R — no attribute dropped;
      2. R1 ∩ R2 ≠ ∅ — they share something to join on;
      3. (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2 — the common attributes are a superkey of at least one side. Check by computing (R1 ∩ R2)⁺.

      Intuition: if the join column is a key of R2, each R1 row matches at most one R2 row, so the join cannot invent combinations.

      Example: R(A, B, C), F = {A → B, B → C}. Split (A, B) + (B, C): common B, B⁺ = BC ⊇ R2 ⇒ lossless. Split (A, B) + (A, C): common A, A⁺ = ABC ⇒ also lossless — but B → C now spans two tables (not preserved, see below). Split (A, C) + (B, C): common C, C⁺ = C ⇒ lossy.

      CREATE TABLE r1 (a INT, b CHAR(1));  INSERT INTO r1 VALUES (1,'x'),(2,'x');
CREATE TABLE r2 (b CHAR(1), c CHAR(1)); INSERT INTO r2 VALUES ('x','p'),('x','q');
SELECT r1.a, r1.b, r2.c FROM r1 JOIN r2 ON r1.b = r2.b ORDER BY a, c;
      +---+---+---+
| a | b | c |
+---+---+---+
| 1 | x | p |
| 1 | x | q |   <- never existed
| 2 | x | p |   <- never existed
| 2 | x | q |
+---+---+---+
      🚫
      Answer that fails

      "A lossy decomposition loses rows when you join." The opposite: you get more rows. The lost thing is the association between values.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A decomposition is lossless if joining the pieces gives back exactly the original table — no missing rows and no spurious extra rows. For a split into two tables the test is simple: the common attributes must be a superkey of at least one of the two tables, which I check with attribute closure. If the common column is a key on one side, each row matches at most one row on that side, so the join can't create fake combinations.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪And for three or more tables?

      Either apply the binary test step by step (join two pieces losslessly, then join the result with the next), or use the chase/tableau test below, which works in one go.

      ↪Is lossless more important than dependency preservation?

      Yes. Lossless is mandatory — without it the design stores wrong information. Dependency preservation is desirable; BCNF sometimes has to give it up (Chapter 06).

      The chase (tableau) test, worked

      R(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, C → D}, decomposition R1(A, B), R2(C, D), R3(A, C).

      1. Build a table: one row per Ri, one column per attribute. Write a (distinguished) where Ri has the attribute, else b with a row subscript.
      2. Chase with each FD X → Y: if two rows agree on X, make their Y entries equal (prefer the a).
      3. Repeat until nothing changes. If some row is all a's ⇒ lossless; otherwise lossy.

      Initial tableau

      ABCD
      R1aab13b14
      R2b21b22aa
      R3ab32ab34

      After chasing

      ABCD
      R1aab13b14
      R2b21b22aa
      R3aaaa
      • A → B: R1, R3 agree on A ⇒ b32 := a
      • C → D: R2, R3 agree on C ⇒ b34 := a
      • R3 is all a ⇒ lossless ✔

      🔒 Dependency preservation

      After a split, can every FD still be checked inside a single table (with a key or UNIQUE constraint)? If yes, the decomposition is dependency-preserving. If not, enforcing the lost FD needs a join on every insert/update — slow, and usually skipped, so the rule silently breaks.

      Formal: let Fi be the FDs of F⁺ that use only Ri's attributes. Preserving ⇔ (F1 ∪ … ∪ Fn)⁺ = F⁺.

      1. Quick check first: if every FD of a minimal cover fits entirely inside some Ri ⇒ preserved. Done.
      2. Otherwise, test the FD X → Y that doesn't fit (polynomial, no F⁺ needed): result := X; repeat: for each Ri, result := result ∪ ((result ∩ Ri)⁺ ∩ Ri), with closure under the full F. Stop when stable.
      3. Preserved ⇔ Y ⊆ result. An FD that doesn't fit any single table may still be implied by the projected FDs, so never say "lost" without this test.
      QR(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, B → C, C → D}, split into (A, B), (B, C), (B, D). Lossless? Dependency-preserving?

      Lossless: (A, B) ⋈ (B, C) on B: B⁺ = BCD ⊇ BC ⇒ lossless, giving ABC. Then ABC ⋈ (B, D) on B: B⁺ ⊇ BD ⇒ lossless. ✔

      Preservation: A → B fits R1, B → C fits R2. C → D fits no table. Test it: result = C. R1: C ∩ AB = ∅, nothing. R2: (C)⁺ ∩ BC = {C} (C⁺ = CD, but D is not in R2). R3: C ∩ BD = ∅. Result stays {C}; D ∉ result ⇒ C → D is not preserved. (R3 does enforce B → D, but that is a different FD.)

      Fix: split as (A, B), (B, C), (C, D) — lossless and preserving. This is exactly what 3NF synthesis would produce.

      🎯
      What the interviewer is really testing

      That you know the two properties are independent: a split can be lossless but not preserving (this one), preserving but lossy, both, or neither. And that BCNF guarantees only the first, while 3NF synthesis guarantees both (Chapter 06).

      ⛓️ Multivalued dependencies (MVD) — a preview

      An FD says "X decides one Y". An MVD X ↠ Y says "X decides a set of Y values, and that set does not depend on the other columns". Example: a student has a set of hobbies and, independently, a set of languages. Stored in one table, every hobby must be paired with every language — that is redundancy no FD can describe.

      studenthobbylanguage
      AshaChessHindi
      AshaChessEnglish
      AshaCricketHindi
      AshaCricketEnglish

      Facts to quote: every FD is an MVD (X → Y ⇒ X ↠ Y); MVDs come in pairs (complementation: X ↠ Y ⇒ X ↠ R − X − Y); and R splits losslessly into (X ∪ Y) and (X ∪ (R − Y)) exactly when X ↠ Y holds. The table above is all-key, so it is in BCNF — yet redundant. 4NF fixes it by splitting into student_hobby and student_language.

      ✏️ If the interviewer asks "can a BCNF table still have redundancy?", the answer is this MVD table. Yes.

      🏆 GATE-style practice (solve, then open)

      QG1. R(A, B, C, D, E, H), F = {A → B, BC → D, E → C, D → A}. Find all candidate keys.

      Never on a RHS: E, H. (EH)⁺ = EHC — not R. Add one more: AEH⁺ = AEHC → B → (BC→D) D = R ✔. BEH⁺ = BEHC → D → A = R ✔. DEH⁺ = DEHC → A → B = R ✔. CEH⁺ = CEH ✘ (C is already in EH⁺, adds nothing). Keys: AEH, BEH, DEH.

      QG2. F = {A → B, BC → D}. Which is implied: (a) A → D (b) AC → D (c) B → D (d) C → D?

      Compute each LHS closure. A⁺ = AB (no D). AC⁺ = ACB → D ✔. B⁺ = B. C⁺ = C. Answer: (b) — it is pseudotransitivity in disguise.

      QG3. R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → B, C → D}. Is the split R1(A, B, C), R2(C, D, E) lossless?

      Common attribute: C. C⁺ = CD. It covers neither R1 (needs A, B) nor R2 (needs E). Lossy. Intuition: E's values attach to C only, and many (A, B) rows share a C, so the join cross-multiplies.

      QG4. R(A, B, C, D) has candidate keys A and BC. How many superkeys?

      Supersets of A: 2³ = 8. Supersets of BC: 2² = 4. Supersets of ABC (counted twice): 2¹ = 2. 8 + 4 − 2 = 10.

      QG5. Are F = {A → B, B → C} and G = {A → B, A → C} equivalent?

      G covers F? Under G, B⁺ = B, so B → C is not implied. Not equivalent. (F covers G, since A⁺ = ABC under F — but equivalence needs both directions.)

      🎯
      🎯 Where this chapter plugs in

      Every "highest normal form" question in Chapter 06 starts with: find all keys (this chapter) → mark prime → classify each FD. Get keys wrong and every later step is wrong. Practise until finding keys takes under a minute.

      📌 Key takeaways

      • X → Y: equal X ⇒ equal Y in every legal instance. FDs are business rules; data can only refute them.
      • Trivial (Y ⊆ X), non-trivial, completely non-trivial (X ∩ Y = ∅); full vs partial vs transitive decides 2NF/3NF.
      • Armstrong's RAT axioms are sound and complete; UDP rules are derived. Split the right side, never the left.
      • X⁺ by repeated FD firing until stable. Superkey ⇔ X⁺ = R. F ⊨ X → Y ⇔ Y ⊆ X⁺.
      • Keys: never-on-RHS attributes are in every key, only-on-RHS in none; grow from the must-set; use the swap trick; keys can differ in size.
      • Superkeys with one key of k attributes: 2n−k; with several keys use inclusion–exclusion.
      • Minimal cover: split RHS → left-reduce → remove redundant FDs (in this order). Not unique.
      • Lossless binary split ⇔ common attributes are a superkey of one side; lossy joins add spurious rows. Chase test for 3+ pieces.
      • Dependency preservation is independent of losslessness; test a non-fitting FD with the projected-closure loop before calling it lost.
      • MVDs (X ↠ Y) capture independent multi-valued facts; they are why BCNF tables can still be redundant (4NF).

      📚 Go deeper

      • Silberschatz et al., Database System Concepts — Ch. 7 slides — closure, canonical cover, lossless join and dependency-preservation algorithms, straight from the standard textbook.
      • GeeksforGeeks: Attribute closure & candidate keys — many extra GATE-style key-finding drills.
      • GeeksforGeeks: Lossless decomposition — more lossless/lossy practice.
      • CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems — rigorous lectures if you want the theory in a systems context.
      • Wikipedia: Armstrong's axioms — compact statement with proofs of the derived rules.

      R(A, B, C, D), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → A}. Which is a candidate key?

      B is never on a RHS, so every key contains B. BD⁺ = BD → A → (AB→C) C = ABCD, and B⁺, D⁺ alone are not R ⇒ BD is a key (so are AB and BC). ABC is a superkey but not minimal.

      From AB → C, which can you conclude?

      Augmentation/reflexivity lets you ADD to the left side. You may never split the left side. ABD → C follows; A → C does not.

      Armstrong's axioms are "complete". That means…

      Complete = never misses an implied FD. "Never derives a false FD" is soundness. F⁺ itself can be exponential in size.

      Splitting R(A, B, C) with F = {A → B} into (A, B) and (B, C). The result is…

      B⁺ = B, which covers neither (A, B) nor (B, C). The join creates spurious rows (more rows, not fewer). The lossless split is (A, B) + (A, C), using A as the join key.

      R(A, B, C, D, E) has a single candidate key AB. How many superkeys?

      Fix A and B; each of the other 3 attributes is in or out: 2³ = 8.

      In the minimal-cover algorithm, which order is correct?

      Removing redundant FDs before reducing left sides can leave redundancy behind. And even with the right order, the minimal cover is not unique.

      An attribute that appears only on right-hand sides of F…

      Any key containing it would still be a superkey without it (the rest already derives it), so the key would not be minimal. Attributes on NO right-hand side are the ones in every key.
      Define X → Y.
      In every legal instance, any two tuples equal on X are equal on Y.
      Trivial vs completely non-trivial FD?
      Trivial: Y ⊆ X (AB → A). Completely non-trivial: X ∩ Y = ∅ (AB → C).
      Armstrong's axioms?
      RAT: Reflexivity (Y ⊆ X ⇒ X → Y), Augmentation (X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ), Transitivity. Sound and complete.
      Derived rules?
      UDP: Union (X→Y, X→Z ⇒ X→YZ), Decomposition (X→YZ ⇒ X→Y), Pseudotransitivity (X→Y, WY→Z ⇒ WX→Z).
      Attribute closure algorithm?
      result := X; repeat: for each L → R with L ⊆ result, add R; until no change.
      Superkey test? FD membership test?
      X superkey ⇔ X⁺ = R. F implies X → Y ⇔ Y ⊆ X⁺.
      Which attributes are in every key? In no key?
      Every key: attributes on no RHS. No key: attributes only on RHS (never on any LHS).
      Prime attribute?
      An attribute that belongs to at least one candidate key.
      Superkeys for one key of size k in n attributes?
      2n−k. Two keys: |S(K1)| + |S(K2)| − |S(K1 ∪ K2)|.
      Minimal cover steps?
      1 split RHS, 2 remove extraneous LHS attributes, 3 remove redundant FDs. Not unique.
      Binary lossless-join condition?
      R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 (common attributes are a superkey of one side).
      Dependency-preserving?
      (F1 ∪ … ∪ Fn)⁺ = F⁺: every FD enforceable within single tables. Independent of losslessness.
      MVD X ↠ Y?
      X determines a set of Y values independent of the other attributes. Every FD is an MVD. Drives 4NF.
      Chapter 06 · II · Design

      🧹 Normalization (1NF → 5NF) & Denormalization

      Spot the anomaly, name the dependency that causes it, split the table the right way — and know exactly when a senior engineer would put the redundancy back on purpose.

      ⏱ 50 min🔥 Asked a lot1NF–3NF basicsBCNF · 4NF · 5NF · algorithmsMySQL 8

      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision

      • Normalization = splitting tables using functional dependencies (FDs) so each fact is stored once. It kills the three anomalies: Insert, Update, Delete (IUD).
      • 1NF: one atomic value per cell, no repeating groups. 2NF: no non-prime column depends on part of a candidate key (partial dependency). 3NF: no non-prime column depends on another non-key column (transitive dependency).
      • Formal 3NF: for every non-trivial X → A, X is a superkey OR A is prime. BCNF drops the "OR": every determinant must be a superkey.
      • BCNF ⊂ 3NF ⊂ 2NF ⊂ 1NF. 3NF and BCNF differ only when there are overlapping composite candidate keys.
      • 3NF synthesis is always lossless + dependency-preserving. BCNF decomposition is always lossless but may lose a dependency. That is why 3NF is the practical target.
      • 4NF removes independent multi-valued facts (MVDs). 5NF removes join dependencies (table splits losslessly only into 3+ pieces). BCNF tables can still be redundant.
      • Mnemonic: "The key (1NF), the whole key (2NF), and nothing but the key (3NF), so help me Codd."
      • Denormalization = adding redundancy on purpose (copied columns, counters, summary tables, materialized views, star schemas) to make reads faster. You pay with write cost and a sync mechanism.
      • Rule: normalize first (3NF/BCNF), measure, then denormalize hot read paths with a clear owner for keeping copies in sync.
      ✏️ Normalization appears in almost every fresher DBMS round. Service companies ask the definitions; product companies say "normalize this table" and then "what would you denormalize?".

      🧹 Why normalize? Redundancy and the three anomalies

      Imagine one big spreadsheet that holds employees and their departments. Every time a department appears, its name and head are copied again. Copies are the problem. When the same fact lives in many rows, the rows can start to disagree. Normalization is the cure: store each fact exactly once, in the table whose key it describes.

      Here is our messy table. Rule of the business: every employee works in one department, and every department has one name and one head.

      emp_id 🔑emp_namedept_iddept_namedept_head
      101AshaD1SalesRavi
      102BilalD1SalesRavi
      103ChenD2HRMeera
      104DivyaD1SalesRavi

      FDs: emp_id → emp_name, dept_id and dept_id → dept_name, dept_head. Key: emp_id. The yellow cells say "D1 is Sales, headed by Ravi" three times. The red cells are the only place where "D2 is HR, headed by Meera" is stored.

      ➕

      Insertion anomaly

      You cannot add a new department D3 Finance until it has an employee. emp_id is the primary key and cannot be NULL. You would need a fake employee.

      ✏️

      Update anomaly

      Sales gets a new head. You must update 3 rows. Miss one and D1 now has two heads. The database contradicts itself.

      🗑️

      Deletion anomaly

      Chen leaves, you delete row 103, and the fact "D2 = HR, head Meera" disappears with him. You lost information you never meant to delete.

      🧪 Anomaly playground — break the messy table yourself, then see how the normalized design behaves.

      One big table: emp_dept
      Normalized: emp + dept

      Pick an action above.

      QWhat is normalization and why do we need it?

      What: Normalization is a step-by-step way to decompose (split) a relation into smaller relations, guided by functional dependencies, so that every fact is stored once and every non-key column describes the key of its own table.

      Why: Redundant copies cause the insert, update and delete anomalies you just saw. They also waste space and make bugs likely (two copies disagree).

      How:

      1. Write the FDs — business rules like dept_id → dept_head. (FDs come from the business, never from sample data; see Chapter 05.)
      2. Find the candidate keys and mark prime / non-prime attributes.
      3. Find the bad FDs — those whose left side is not a key.
      4. Split each bad FD X → Y into its own table (X, Y), keep X in the original as a foreign key.
      5. Check the split: lossless (no spurious rows on join) and dependency-preserving (each FD checkable in one table).

      Three goals of a good decomposition:

      🛡️

      No anomalies

      Each fact once. Insert, update and delete touch one row.

      🔗

      Lossless join

      Joining the pieces gives back exactly the original rows. Must-have, never negotiable.

      🔒

      Dependency preservation

      Every FD can be enforced inside one table (a PK/UNIQUE), with no join. Nice-to-have; BCNF sometimes sacrifices it.

      🚫
      Answer that fails

      "Normalization means removing duplicate rows." No. Duplicate rows are a key problem. Normalization removes duplicate facts spread across different rows (Sales/Ravi repeated three times).

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Normalization is the process of splitting a table based on functional dependencies so that each fact is stored only once. Without it we get insert, update and delete anomalies — for example, changing a department head in one row but not another. We go step by step through 1NF, 2NF, 3NF and BCNF, and each split must be lossless and ideally dependency-preserving. In practice I normalize OLTP schemas to 3NF or BCNF and denormalize only measured hot paths.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Which normal form removes the anomalies in your example?

      3NF. The problem is the transitive dependency emp_id → dept_id → dept_head. Splitting into emp(emp_id, emp_name, dept_id) and dept(dept_id, dept_name, dept_head) fixes all three anomalies.

      ↪Can you find FDs by looking at the data?

      No. Data can only disprove an FD (two rows with same X, different Y). An FD is a rule about every legal state of the table, so it comes from the business requirements.

      ↪Is normalization free?

      No. More tables means more joins on reads. That is the trade-off behind denormalization.

      🧠
      Memory aid: IUD

      The anomalies have the same letters as the DML verbs: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. "Every DML verb has its own way of breaking a redundant table."

      ⭐ The normal-form ladder at a glance

      Each normal form is the previous one plus one more rule. Climbing the ladder removes a new kind of redundancy.

      FormRule in one lineRemovesTypical violation
      1NFEvery cell holds one atomic value; no repeating groupsLists inside cellsphones = "98..., 97..."
      2NF1NF + no non-prime attribute depends on a proper part of a candidate keyPartial dependency(s_id, c_id) → grade but s_id → s_name
      3NFFor every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkey or A is primeTransitive dependencyemp_id → dept_id → dept_head
      BCNFFor every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkeyNon-key determinant of a key partteacher → subject with keys {student, subject}, {student, teacher}
      4NFBCNF + for every non-trivial MVD X ↠ Y: X is a superkeyIndependent multi-valued factsemployee × skills × languages
      5NFEvery join dependency is implied by the candidate keysCyclic 3-way rulessupplier–part–project
      🔑 The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key — so help me Codd

      Bill Kent's line for 1NF → 3NF. Every non-key column must give a fact about…

      • "the key" → 1NF: there IS a key and each cell is one value about it.
      • "the whole key" → 2NF: about the entire composite key, not half of it (no partial dependency).
      • "nothing but the key" → 3NF: not about some other non-key column (no transitive dependency).
      • "so help me Codd" → a pun on the courtroom oath and E. F. Codd, the inventor of the relational model.

      Fine print: the line speaks of one key. Real 2NF/3NF are about every candidate key. BCNF extends it: "every determinant is a key". For the whole ladder use A-W-N-D-M-J: Atomic, Whole, Nothing-but, Determinant, Multivalued, Join.

      Functional dependency X → Y
      If two rows agree on X, they must agree on Y. X is the determinant.
      Superkey
      A set of attributes whose closure is all attributes (it identifies a row).
      Candidate key
      A minimal superkey — remove any attribute and it stops being a key.
      Prime attribute
      An attribute that is part of at least one candidate key. Non-prime = in no candidate key.
      Partial dependency
      A non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key.
      Transitive dependency
      Key → X → A where X is not a superkey and A is non-prime (and not in X).
      Trivial FD
      X → Y with Y ⊆ X (e.g. AB → A). Always true, ignored by NF tests.

      Closure, candidate keys and canonical cover are explained step by step in Chapter 05. This chapter uses them.

      📋 First Normal Form (1NF) — one value per cell

      QWhat is 1NF? What does "atomic" really mean?

      What: A table is in 1NF when every column holds a single, atomic value from its domain, there are no repeating groups (no phone1, phone2, phone3), and each row can be identified (no fully duplicate rows; column order and row order do not matter).

      Atomic means "the database never needs to look inside the value". A date is atomic even though it has day, month and year — because you treat it as one value. A cell "DBMS, OS, CN" is not atomic, because your queries must cut it apart to answer "who takes OS?".

      Before (not 1NF):

      s_ids_namephonescourses
      1Asha98450 11111, 97000 22222DBMS, OS
      2Bilal99000 33333DBMS

      After (1NF): each multi-valued attribute gets its own table, one row per value.

      student

      • (1, Asha)
      • (2, Bilal)

      student_phone (s_id, phone)

      • (1, 98450 11111)
      • (1, 97000 22222)
      • (2, 99000 33333)

      enrollment (s_id, course)

      • (1, DBMS)
      • (1, OS)
      • (2, DBMS)
      -- Non-1NF: "who takes OS?" needs string hacks, cannot use an index, breaks on 'OS2'
SELECT s_name FROM student_bad WHERE FIND_IN_SET('OS', REPLACE(courses, ' ', '')) > 0;

-- 1NF: a plain, indexable equality
SELECT s.s_name
FROM   student s JOIN enrollment e ON e.s_id = s.s_id
WHERE  e.course = 'OS';
      +--------+
| s_name |
+--------+
| Asha   |
+--------+
      ⚠️
      Common mistake

      Saying "1NF means the table has a primary key". The heart of 1NF is atomic values, no repeating groups. Many textbooks also require unique rows (so some key exists), so mention both: "atomic cells, no repeating groups, and rows are uniquely identifiable".

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      A table is in 1NF when every cell holds one atomic value and there are no repeating groups like phone1, phone2, phone3. Atomic means my queries never need to split a value apart. If a student has many phone numbers, I move phones to a separate table with one row per number, keyed by student id and phone.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is phone1, phone2, phone3 a 1NF violation? Each cell is atomic!

      Most textbooks (and Chris Date) call it a repeating group, so yes, a 1NF violation. Some stricter authors call it 1NF-legal but bad design. Either way the problems are real: it caps the count at 3, forces NULLs, and needs WHERE phone1=? OR phone2=? OR phone3=?. Say both views and recommend the child table.

      ↪Is a full name or an address atomic?

      Atomicity depends on use. If you only ever print the address, one column is fine. If you filter or group by city or PIN code, store them as separate columns. "Atomic" is relative to the queries the business needs.

      ↪Does an RDBMS even allow a non-1NF table?

      In theory a relation is always in 1NF. In practice SQL lets you store comma lists in VARCHAR, and modern engines have array and JSON types. So yes, you can break 1NF in a real database — see the JSON debate below.

      QIs a JSON or ARRAY column a 1NF violation? (the modern debate)

      Short answer: it depends on how you use it. If the database treats the JSON as one opaque value (store it, return it whole), it behaves atomically and many people accept it. If your queries filter, join or update inside it, you have hidden a repeating group or a whole child table inside one cell — the classic 1NF smell.

      ✔ Reasonable JSON use

      • Rarely-queried, sparse or vendor-defined attributes (product specs that differ per category).
      • Snapshots kept as documents: shipping_address on an order, options_snapshot on an order line.
      • Raw payloads (webhooks, audit events) stored for later reading.

      ✘ 1NF smell

      • tags or course_ids arrays you search, count and join on.
      • Values that need foreign keys (an array of product ids cannot reference product).
      • Concurrent edits to items inside one document (whole-row write, lost updates).
      🔀
      Engine differences

      MySQL 8: native JSON type; index inside it via generated columns or functional indexes, and multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays (8.0.17+) for MEMBER OF() / JSON_CONTAINS(). PostgreSQL: real ARRAY types and JSONB with GIN indexes — the most mature support. Oracle: JSON stored in a native JSON type (21c+) or text columns with IS JSON checks. SQL Server: JSON stored as NVARCHAR with OPENJSON / JSON_VALUE. Document NoSQL (MongoDB) is deliberately non-1NF: embedding arrays is the normal design.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Strictly, a JSON array that I query into is a repeating group, so it breaks the spirit of 1NF. I use JSON for data I store and return as a whole, like an address snapshot or flexible product attributes. If I need to filter, join, enforce foreign keys or update single elements, I model it as a proper child table.

      🧩 Second Normal Form (2NF) — the whole key

      2NF only cares about composite candidate keys. If a non-prime column depends on just one part of the key, that column is stored once per combination — far too often.

      QWhat is 2NF? Show a violation and fix it.

      Definition: A relation is in 2NF if it is in 1NF and no non-prime attribute is partially dependent on any candidate key — i.e. every non-prime attribute needs the whole of every candidate key.

      Violation: enrollment(s_id, c_id, s_name, c_name, grade), key {s_id, c_id}.

      s_id 🔑c_id 🔑s_namec_namegrade
      1C1AshaDBMSA
      1C2AshaOSB
      2C1BilalDBMSB

      "Asha" is repeated for every course she takes; "DBMS" is repeated for every student in it. You cannot add a new course until someone enrolls (insertion anomaly).

      Fix: move each partial dependency into its own table, keyed by the part of the key it depends on.

      CREATE TABLE student (s_id INT PRIMARY KEY, s_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE course  (c_id CHAR(3) PRIMARY KEY, c_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE enrollment (
  s_id  INT,
  c_id  CHAR(3),
  grade CHAR(2),
  PRIMARY KEY (s_id, c_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (s_id) REFERENCES student(s_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (c_id) REFERENCES course(c_id)
);

      The split is lossless: the common column s_id is the key of student, and c_id is the key of course.

      ⚠️
      Two classic slips

      (1) Checking 2NF only against the chosen primary key. 2NF is about every candidate key. (2) Missing derived partial dependencies: with B → C, C → D and key AB, D also depends on part of the key (B⁺ contains D). Compute the closure of each proper subset of each key.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      2NF says every non-key column must depend on the whole candidate key, not on part of it. It only matters when a key is composite. For example in an enrollment table keyed by student and course, student name depends only on student id, so I move it to a student table. Grade stays because it needs both.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪If a table has a single-column primary key, is it automatically in 2NF?

      Careful: if every candidate key is a single attribute, yes — a single attribute has no proper non-empty subset to depend on. But a table can have a single-column PK and another composite candidate key, e.g. (emp_id) and (dept_id, badge_no). Then check partial dependencies on the composite one too.

      ↪Can a prime attribute depend on part of a key without breaking 2NF?

      Yes. 2NF (and 3NF) only restrict non-prime attributes. A prime attribute depending on part of another key may still break BCNF, not 2NF.

      ↪Does adding a surrogate id column "fix" 2NF?

      No, it only hides it. If {s_id, c_id} is still unique in the business, it is still a candidate key, and s_id → s_name is still a partial dependency on it. The redundancy is unchanged. Surrogate keys do not replace normalization.

      ⛓️ Third Normal Form (3NF) — nothing but the key

      QWhat is 3NF? Give the informal and the formal definition.

      Informal (Codd): 2NF + no transitive dependency: no non-prime attribute depends on a key through another non-key attribute. "Non-key columns must not depend on other non-key columns."

      Formal (Zaniolo, the one to write in GATE / on a whiteboard): R is in 3NF if for every non-trivial FD X → A that holds on R, at least one is true:

      1. X is a superkey of R, or
      2. A is a prime attribute (A belongs to some candidate key).

      The formal version is easier to test: walk the FDs, check two things, done. It also automatically excludes partial dependencies, so 3NF ⇒ 2NF.

      Example and fix: emp_dept(emp_id, emp_name, dept_id, dept_name, dept_head). The FD dept_id → dept_head: is dept_id a superkey? No. Is dept_head prime? No. ⇒ not 3NF. Split on the bad FD:

      CREATE TABLE dept (
  dept_id   CHAR(2) PRIMARY KEY,
  dept_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  dept_head VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE emp (
  emp_id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
  emp_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  dept_id  CHAR(2) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept(dept_id)
);
-- Changing Sales' head is now ONE row:
UPDATE dept SET dept_head = 'Kiran' WHERE dept_id = 'D1';
      Query OK, 1 row affected (0.01 sec)
Rows matched: 1  Changed: 1  Warnings: 0
      ℹ️
      Why the "OR A is prime" escape hatch?

      It is there on purpose so that a lossless and dependency-preserving 3NF design always exists. Without it (that is BCNF) some FDs can no longer be checked inside one table. See BCNF.

      🚫
      Answer that fails

      "3NF means there is no redundancy." Wrong — 3NF can still hold redundancy when a non-key determines part of a key (that is what BCNF fixes), and BCNF can still hold MVD redundancy (4NF fixes that).

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      3NF means non-key columns depend on the key and nothing else — no transitive dependency like emp_id to dept_id to dept_head. Formally, for every non-trivial dependency X → A, either X is a superkey or A is part of some candidate key. To fix a violation I move the dependency into its own table, here a department table, and keep dept_id as a foreign key.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Precisely, what is a transitive dependency?

      K → X and X → A, where K is a key, X is not a superkey (so X ↛ K), A is non-prime and A ∉ X. Then K → A holds only "through" X.

      ↪Is a transitive chain ending in a prime attribute a 3NF violation?

      No. If A is prime, the formal rule is satisfied. That case is exactly "3NF but not BCNF".

      ↪Can a table be in 3NF but not in 2NF?

      No. A partial dependency part-of-key → non-prime has a non-superkey left side and a non-prime right side, so it already fails the formal 3NF rule. Normal forms are cumulative.

      ↪If every attribute is prime, what is the minimum normal form?

      At least 3NF — 2NF and 3NF only restrict non-prime attributes, and there are none. It can still fail BCNF.

      ⚖️ Boyce–Codd Normal Form (BCNF): every determinant is a key

      BCNF is 3NF with the escape hatch removed. If anything determines anything, it must be a superkey. Prime attributes get no exception.

      QWhat is BCNF? Give an example that is in 3NF but not in BCNF.

      Definition: R is in BCNF if for every non-trivial FD X → Y that holds on R, X is a superkey. For a single relation it is enough to check the given FDs. You do not need all of F⁺.

      The classic example is Teaches(student, subject, teacher). The business rules are: (1) each teacher teaches exactly one subject, so teacher → subject; (2) for each subject, a student has exactly one teacher, so {student, subject} → teacher.

      studentsubjectteacher
      AshaDBMSRao
      AshaOSSen
      BilalDBMSKumar
      ChenDBMSRao
      1. Candidate keys: {student, subject} and {student, teacher}. Student plus teacher gives subject, and then everything else. These are two overlapping composite keys.
      2. Prime attributes: student, subject and teacher are all prime. There is no non-prime attribute, so 2NF and 3NF hold automatically.
      3. BCNF check: take teacher → subject. Is teacher a superkey? No, because Rao teaches two students. ⇒ not BCNF.
      4. Redundancy left: the fact "Rao teaches DBMS" is stored twice. If Rao's subject changes, you must update many rows.

      BCNF decomposition: split on the violating FD teacher → subject.

      What did we lose? Insert (Asha, Kumar) into StudentTeacher. Each table looks fine on its own. After a join, though, Asha has two DBMS teachers (Rao and Kumar). No PK or UNIQUE constraint in either table can stop this. You would need a join inside a trigger.

      CREATE TABLE teacher_subject (
  teacher VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY,           -- teacher → subject
  subject VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_ts (teacher, subject)        -- target for the composite FK
);
CREATE TABLE teaches (
  student VARCHAR(30),
  subject VARCHAR(30),
  teacher VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (student, subject),            -- {student, subject} → teacher
  FOREIGN KEY (teacher, subject) REFERENCES teacher_subject (teacher, subject)
);
INSERT INTO teacher_subject VALUES ('Rao','DBMS'), ('Sen','OS');
-- Rao does not teach OS, so this row is rejected:
INSERT INTO teaches VALUES ('Asha', 'OS', 'Rao');
      ERROR 1452 (23000): Cannot add or update a child row: a foreign key constraint fails

      The repeated subject is controlled redundancy. The composite FK guarantees that it always matches the teacher.

      CREATE TABLE teacher_subject (teacher VARCHAR(30) PRIMARY KEY, subject VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE student_teacher (
  student VARCHAR(30), teacher VARCHAR(30),
  PRIMARY KEY (student, teacher),
  FOREIGN KEY (teacher) REFERENCES teacher_subject(teacher)
);
DELIMITER //
CREATE TRIGGER trg_one_teacher_per_subject
BEFORE INSERT ON student_teacher FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF EXISTS (SELECT 1
             FROM student_teacher st
             JOIN teacher_subject ts ON ts.teacher = st.teacher
             JOIN teacher_subject nt ON nt.teacher = NEW.teacher
             WHERE st.student = NEW.student AND ts.subject = nt.subject) THEN
    SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Student already has a teacher for this subject';
  END IF;
END//
DELIMITER ;
      ⚠️
      Concurrency trap

      If two sessions insert at the same moment, both can pass the EXISTS check, because neither sees the other's uncommitted row. A trigger that checks across rows needs locking, for example locking the student's rows with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or SERIALIZABLE isolation. Keys never have this problem, which is one more reason to prefer Option A. See Chapter 13.

      🎯
      What they are really testing

      The interviewer wants to hear three things. BCNF is stricter than 3NF. The gap only appears with overlapping candidate keys. BCNF can cost you dependency preservation. Saying "I would keep 3NF here and enforce both rules with keys" shows real design judgement.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      BCNF says the left side of every non-trivial dependency must be a superkey. 3NF also allows it when the right side is a prime attribute. Take student, subject and teacher, where each teacher teaches one subject. The keys are student-subject and student-teacher, so every attribute is prime and the table is in 3NF. But teacher → subject breaks BCNF. Splitting it is lossless, but it loses the rule "one teacher per subject per student", so in practice I might keep it in 3NF.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪3NF vs BCNF in one line?

      "3NF allows X → A with X not a superkey only if A is prime; BCNF never allows it." Bonus line: "They differ only when a table has overlapping composite candidate keys."

      ↪When is a 3NF table automatically in BCNF?

      When it does not have several overlapping candidate keys (Vincent & Srinivasan, 1993). With a single candidate key, or keys that share no attribute, 3NF ⇒ BCNF. That is why most real OLTP tables that reach 3NF are already in BCNF.

      ↪Is there an FD set for which NO dependency-preserving BCNF design exists?

      Yes: R(A, B, C) with {AB → C, C → B} (Beeri & Bernstein, 1979). Any BCNF split separates C from A, so AB → C can no longer live in one table. Teaches has exactly this pattern.

      ↪Is a BCNF table free of all redundancy?
