      No. BCNF removes only the redundancy caused by functional dependencies. Multivalued and join dependencies can still repeat data. 4NF and 5NF deal with those, as the next sections show.

      3NF

      • Rule: X → A ⇒ X superkey or A prime
      • A lossless, dependency-preserving design always exists (synthesis)
      • Some redundancy may remain (overlapping keys)
      • Practical default for OLTP

      BCNF

      • Rule: X → A ⇒ X superkey, no exceptions
      • A lossless decomposition always exists
      • Dependency preservation is not guaranteed
      • No FD-based redundancy at all

      🎲 Fourth Normal Form (4NF): independent multi-valued facts

      QWhat is a multivalued dependency and what is 4NF? Show an example.

      The problem: an employee has many skills and speaks many languages, and the two lists have nothing to do with each other. If you store them in one table, you must store every skill × every language combination.

      empskilllanguage
      AshaSQLEnglish
      AshaSQLHindi
      AshaJavaEnglish
      AshaJavaHindi

      When Asha learns Odia, you must add two rows (SQL/Odia and Java/Odia). Add only one and the table claims "Asha speaks Odia only when doing SQL", which is nonsense. There is no non-trivial FD here. The only key is all three columns, so the table is already in BCNF. Yet it is still redundant.

      Multivalued dependency (MVD) X ↠ Y: for one value of X, the set of Y values is fixed and does not depend on the other attributes. Formally: if two rows agree on X, the rows you get by swapping their Y values must also exist. Here emp ↠ skill holds, and so does its complement emp ↠ language. MVDs come in pairs, written emp ↠ skill | language.

      4NF: BCNF, plus for every non-trivial MVD X ↠ Y, X is a superkey. An MVD is trivial when Y ⊆ X or X ∪ Y covers all attributes. Here emp is not a superkey ⇒ not 4NF.

      Fix: give each independent list its own table.

      emp_skill(emp, skill)

      • (Asha, SQL)
      • (Asha, Java)

      emp_language(emp, language)

      • (Asha, English)
      • (Asha, Hindi)
      • (Asha, Odia) ← one row
      💡
      The test question

      Ask: "Are these two lists independent?" If the business says "Asha uses SQL only in English", the triple is a real fact (a ternary relationship) and must stay together. MVDs are about independence, not just about having many values.

      ℹ️
      Facts to quote

      Every FD is also an MVD: if X → Y then X ↠ Y. 4NF ⇒ BCNF. Every 2-attribute relation is in 4NF, because any MVD there has X ∪ Y = R and so is trivial. This mistake usually comes from a bad ER mapping, where two multivalued attributes of one entity are squashed into one table (Chapter 03).

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      4NF deals with multivalued dependencies, which means two independent lists about the same key, like an employee's skills and languages. In one table we must store every combination, so adding one language adds several rows, even though the table is in BCNF. 4NF says every non-trivial MVD must have a superkey on the left. So I split the table into employee-skill and employee-language.

      🔗 Fifth Normal Form (5NF / PJNF): join dependencies

      QWhat is 5NF (project-join normal form)? Explain with supplier–part–project.

      Join dependency (JD) *{R1, …, Rn}: R always equals the natural join of its projections on R1…Rn. A table is in 5NF when every non-trivial join dependency is implied by its candidate keys. In plain words: no hidden rule lets you rebuild the table from 3 or more smaller tables, unless that rule comes from the keys.

      Business rule (cyclic): if supplier s supplies part p, part p is used in project j, and s supplies project j, then s supplies p to j.

      supplierpartproject
      SmithBoltProjX
      SmithNutProjY
      AdamskyBoltProjY
      WaltonNutProjZ
      AdamskyNailProjX
      AdamskyBoltProjX
      SmithBoltProjY
      • 3-way join: SP ⋈ PJ ⋈ SJ reproduces exactly the 7 rows ✔.
      • 2-way joins: SP ⋈ SJ adds (Adamsky, Nail, ProjY) and (Smith, Nut, ProjX). SP ⋈ PJ adds (Smith, Nut, ProjZ) and (Walton, Nut, ProjY). SJ ⋈ PJ adds (Adamsky, Nut, ProjY) and (Smith, Nail, ProjX). All three are lossy ✘.
      • The highlighted row (Smith, Bolt, ProjY) is forced by the rule. Delete it and the 3-way join brings it back. That forced, derivable row is the redundancy 5NF removes. The fix is to store the three projections instead.
      💡
      Interview framing

      "4NF matters in real designs, where multi-valued attributes get modelled badly. 5NF is rare, because it needs a cyclic 3-way business rule. I would mention it, show the 3-projection idea, and move on."

      🧭 Beyond 5NF: 6NF, DKNF and EKNF (know the names)

      6️⃣

      6NF

      No non-trivial join dependencies at all (Date, Darwen, Lorentzos). That means roughly one non-key attribute per table. It is used for temporal data, where each attribute changes over time independently, and in anchor-modelled warehouses.

      🧱

      DKNF

      Domain-Key NF (Fagin, 1981): every constraint follows from domain definitions and keys alone. 3NF to 5NF are special cases of it. It is mostly theoretical and not always achievable.

      🔬

      EKNF

      Elementary Key NF (Zaniolo, 1982) sits strictly between 3NF and BCNF. It allows a non-superkey determinant only if the dependent attribute belongs to an elementary key. It is rarely asked, so just know the name.

      The full order: 1NF ⊃ 2NF ⊃ 3NF ⊃ EKNF ⊃ BCNF ⊃ 4NF ⊃ 5NF ⊃ 6NF. DKNF uses a different style of definition; it implies 5NF.

      ✂️ Splitting safely: lossless join and dependency preservation

      Every normalization step is a decomposition: R becomes R1, R2, …. A split is only acceptable if you can glue the pieces back together exactly. Ideally, every rule should also still be checkable inside a single table.

      QWhat is a lossless-join decomposition? How do you test it?

      What: a decomposition is lossless when R1 ⋈ R2 ⋈ … = R for every legal instance. The natural join gives back exactly the original rows: none missing and none extra.

      Binary test (two pieces): R1 ∪ R2 = R, and the common attributes form a key of at least one side:

      (R1 ∩ R2) → R1   or   (R1 ∩ R2) → R2      (check with closure: (R1 ∩ R2)⁺ ⊇ R1 or ⊇ R2)

      Lossy example: R(A, B, C) = {(1, x, p), (2, x, q)}, split into R1(A, B) and R2(B, C). B is not a key of either piece.

      ABC
      1xp✔ original
      1xq✘ spurious
      2xp✘ spurious
      2xq✔ original
      ⚠️
      Classic trick

      "A lossy join loses rows?" No. It produces more rows (spurious tuples). What is lost is information: you can no longer tell which A goes with which C.

      3+ pieces: the chase (tableau) test. Make one row per Ri and one column per attribute. Put a where Ri has the attribute and b elsewhere. Then apply each FD repeatedly: when two rows agree on X, make their Y entries equal, preferring a. If some row becomes all a's, the decomposition is lossless. Example: R(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, C → D}, pieces (A, B), (C, D), (A, C). Row (A, C) picks up B through A → B and D through C → D, so it becomes all a's ⇒ lossless.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪What is dependency preservation and how do you check it?

      Let Fi be the FDs of F⁺ that use only Ri's attributes. The decomposition is dependency-preserving if (F1 ∪ … ∪ Fn)⁺ = F⁺. In practice, every rule can be enforced by a key or constraint inside one table, without a join.

      Exam shortcut: if every FD of a minimal cover fits inside some Ri, the decomposition is preserving. If one does not fit, run the closure test before saying "lost": start with result = X, and for each Ri repeat result ∪= ((result ∩ Ri)⁺ ∩ Ri) until nothing changes. X → Y is preserved if and only if Y ⊆ result.

      ↪Which property is mandatory?

      Lossless join is mandatory, because a lossy split corrupts data. Dependency preservation is highly desirable, and BCNF sometimes has to give it up.

      ↪Is any split into 3NF tables automatically lossless?

      No. The synthesis algorithm guarantees it, because it adds a table that contains a candidate key. An arbitrary split whose pieces happen to be 3NF can still be lossy.

      ⚙️ The two algorithms: 3NF synthesis and BCNF decomposition

      3NF synthesis (Bernstein-style, from a canonical cover)

      1. Compute a canonical cover Fc (Chapter 05): single-attribute RHS, remove extraneous LHS attributes, drop redundant FDs, then merge FDs with the same LHS.
      2. One table per FD: for each X → Y in Fc, create a table with attributes X ∪ Y.
      3. Guarantee losslessness: if no table contains a candidate key of R, add one table that is just a candidate key.
      4. Clean up: remove any table whose attributes are a subset of another table.

      Guarantees: every table is in 3NF, the join is lossless, every FD is preserved, and it runs in polynomial time.

      QWorked example: R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → BC, B → C, AB → D, D → E}. Synthesize a 3NF design.
      1. Split RHS: A → B, A → C, B → C, AB → D, D → E.
      2. Extraneous LHS in AB → D: A⁺ = {A, B, C, D, E} already contains D, so B is extraneous. Replace it with A → D.
      3. Redundant FDs: drop A → C and compute A⁺ with the rest: A → B, then B → C, so C is still reached ⇒ A → C is redundant. Each of A → B, B → C, A → D and D → E is needed: remove any one and its RHS is no longer reachable.
      4. Merge: Fc = { A → BD, B → C, D → E }.
      5. Key: A never appears on a RHS, and A⁺ = ABCDE ⇒ the only key is A.
      6. Tables: R1(A, B, D), R2(B, C), R3(D, E). R1 contains the key A, so no extra table is needed. No table is a subset of another.

      Second mini example (the key step matters): R(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, C → D}. The FDs give (A, B) and (C, D), but the key is AC and neither table contains it. Joining (A, B) with (C, D) would be a cross product, which is lossy. So add R3(A, C). Final: (A, B), (C, D), (A, C).

      💡
      Exam tip

      Forgetting the "add a key table" step is the most common way to lose marks on synthesis questions.

      BCNF decomposition algorithm

      1. Find a violation: in some table Ri, an FD X → Y (projected onto Ri, non-trivial) where X is not a superkey of Ri.
      2. Split it: replace Ri with (X ∪ Y) and (Ri − (Y − X)). Using Y = X⁺ ∩ Ri makes fewer, cleaner splits.
      3. Repeat until every table is in BCNF.
      4. Then check which original FDs are no longer inside a single table. Those are lost.

      Guarantees: always lossless, because each split's common part X is a key of X ∪ Y. Dependency preservation is not guaranteed. The result also depends on which violation you pick first, so several correct answers can exist.

      ⚠️
      Subtle trap

      The "check only the given F" shortcut works for the original relation only. Inside a sub-table you must use FDs projected from F⁺ (closures of subsets of Ri). A violation can hide in a derived FD such as C → B below.

      QWorked example: R(A, B, C, D, E, F), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → B, B → E, E → F}. Decompose into BCNF.

      Keys first: A is never on a RHS. A⁺ = A, AB⁺ = ABCDEF, AC⁺ = ACDBEF, AD⁺ = ADBCEF ⇒ the keys are AB, AC, AD. Prime: A, B, C, D. Non-prime: E, F.

      1. R(ABCDEF): B → E violates BCNF. B⁺ = {B, E, F} ⇒ split into R1(B, E, F) and R2(A, B, C, D).
      2. R1(BEF): the key is B, and E → F violates ⇒ (E, F) and (B, E). Both have 2 attributes, so both are BCNF.
      3. R2(ABCD): the projected FDs include AB → C, C → D, D → B and the derived C → B. C⁺ ∩ R2 = {B, C, D} and C is not a key ⇒ R21(B, C, D) and R22(A, C).
      4. R21(BCD): the key is C, and D → B violates ⇒ (B, D) and (C, D).

      Result: (E, F), (B, E), (B, D), (C, D), (A, C). It is lossless by construction. Dependency check: C → D, D → B, B → E and E → F each sit in one table. For AB → C the closure test gives result = {A, B, E, F}, and C is not in it ⇒ AB → C is lost.

      Compare with 3NF synthesis on the same F: (A, B, C), (C, D), (B, D), (B, E), (E, F). This preserves every FD. The table (A, B, C) has keys AB and AC and the derived FD C → B, so it is 3NF but not BCNF. That is the trade-off in miniature.

      🔍 Finding the highest normal form (GATE-style method)

      1. Assume 1NF (GATE convention: values are atomic).
      2. Find all candidate keys. Attributes that never appear on any RHS are in every key. Grow from there using closures (Chapter 05).
      3. Mark prime and non-prime attributes.
      4. Classify each non-trivial FD X → A (split the RHS into single attributes):
        • X is a superkey ⇒ fine for BCNF.
        • else if A is prime ⇒ fine for 3NF, breaks BCNF.
        • else if X is a proper subset of some candidate key ⇒ partial dependency, breaks 2NF.
        • else ⇒ transitive dependency, breaks 3NF (2NF still holds).
      5. Hidden partial dependencies: for 2NF, also compute the closure of every proper subset of each composite key. If it contains a non-prime attribute, 2NF fails.
      6. Answer = the weakest level any FD forces.
      Non-trivial X → Aone FD at a time
      X a superkey?yes → OK (BCNF) · no ↓
      A prime?yes → 3NF max · no ↓
      X ⊂ some candidate key?yes → partial ⇒ 1NF · no → transitive ⇒ 2NF

      🔬 Normal-form checker: enter a relation and its FDs to get the keys, prime attributes, a verdict for each FD, the highest NF, a 3NF synthesis and a BCNF decomposition.

      Try:

      ↑ Click P1…P7 to check the practice answers below.

      Practice problems (GATE style), with solutions

      QP1. R(A, B, C, D), F = {AB → C, C → D}. Highest normal form?

      A and B never appear on a RHS, and AB⁺ = ABCD ⇒ the key is AB. Prime: A, B. A⁺ = A and B⁺ = B, so there is no partial dependency. C → D: C is not a superkey, D is non-prime, and C is not part of a key ⇒ transitive. Answer: 2NF. Fix: (A, B, C) + (C, D).

      QP2. R(A, B, C, D), F = {AB → C, B → D}. Highest normal form?

      The key is AB. B → D: B is a proper part of the key and D is non-prime ⇒ partial dependency. Answer: 1NF. Fix: (A, B, C) + (B, D).

      QP3. R(A, B, C, D), F = {AB → CD, C → A}. Highest normal form?

      B is never on a RHS. AB⁺ = ABCD, and BC⁺ = BC → A → ABCD ⇒ the keys are AB, BC. Prime: A, B, C. C → A: C is not a superkey, but A is prime ⇒ OK for 3NF, fails BCNF. No subset of a key reaches D. Answer: 3NF. A BCNF split (A, C) + (B, C, D) loses AB → CD.

      QP4. R(A, B, C, D, E), F = {A → B, BC → E, ED → A}. Highest normal form?

      C and D are never on a RHS, so they are in every key. CD⁺ = CD is not enough. ACD⁺ = ABCDE, BCD⁺ = BCDE + A, CDE⁺ = CDEAB ⇒ the keys are ACD, BCD, CDE. Every attribute is prime ⇒ at least 3NF. A → B: A is not a superkey ⇒ BCNF fails. Answer: 3NF.

      QP5. R(A, B, C, D, E, F), F = {AB → C, C → D, D → B, B → E, E → F}. Highest normal form?

      The keys are AB, AC, AD (see the BCNF example above). Non-prime: E, F. B → E: B ⊂ AB and E is non-prime ⇒ partial. Answer: 1NF. Note that B is prime, but that does not help: the test is about the RHS, E.

      QP6. R(P, Q, R, S), F = {P → Q, Q → R, R → S, S → P}. Highest normal form?

      The FDs form a cycle, so each single attribute reaches everything ⇒ the keys are P, Q, R, S. Every LHS is a superkey. Answer: BCNF. Trap: a long chain of FDs looks transitive, but a chain between keys is harmless.

      QP7. R(A, B, C, D, E, F), F = {A → B, B → C, C → A, D → E, E → F, F → D}. How many candidate keys? Highest NF?

      {A, B, C} form one cycle and {D, E, F} form another. A key needs one attribute from each cycle ⇒ 3 × 3 = 9 keys (AD, AE, AF, BD, …, CF). Every attribute is prime ⇒ at least 3NF. A → B: A alone is not a superkey ⇒ BCNF fails. Answer: 3NF. BCNF split: (A, B, C), (D, E, F), (A, D), which happens to preserve every FD.

      🧾 End-to-end walkthrough: one messy order sheet, 0NF → BCNF

      This is the exact task many interviewers give: "Here is a table. Normalize it." Do it out loud, one step at a time. Name the FD you are fixing at each step. That is what earns the marks.

      Start (0NF / unnormalized): a shop keeps orders in a spreadsheet. The items cell holds a list.

      order_idorder_datecust_idcust_namecust_cityitems
      O12026-03-01C7AshaPuneP1 Pen ×2 @10; P2 Notebook ×1 @60
      O22026-03-02C9BilalDelhiP1 Pen ×5 @9
      O32026-03-02C7AshaPuneP2 Notebook ×3 @60

      Business rules (FDs). Note the two prices: list_price is today's catalog price; unit_price is what this order actually paid (O2 got a discount).

      order_id          → order_date, cust_id
cust_id           → cust_name, cust_city
prod_id           → prod_name, list_price
order_id, prod_id → qty, unit_price
      0NFlist inside a cell
      1NFone row per item; key (order_id, prod_id)
      2NFremove partial deps on order_id, prod_id
      3NFremove order_id → cust_id → cust_name
      BCNF?every determinant a key ⇒ yes
      1. 0NF → 1NF: flatten the list. One row per (order, product). Now every cell is atomic. Columns: order_id, order_date, cust_id, cust_name, cust_city, prod_id, prod_name, list_price, qty, unit_price. Neither order_id nor prod_id alone identifies a row, but together they do ⇒ candidate key (order_id, prod_id). O1 now takes 2 rows, and "C7 is Asha from Pune" repeats.
      2. 1NF → 2NF: kill partial dependencies. order_id → order_date, cust_id, cust_name, cust_city depends on half the key. So does prod_id → prod_name, list_price. Move each to its own table:
        • orders(order_id 🔑, order_date, cust_id, cust_name, cust_city)
        • products(prod_id 🔑, prod_name, list_price)
        • order_items(order_id 🔑, prod_id 🔑, qty, unit_price) — only facts about the whole key stay.
      3. 2NF → 3NF: kill transitive dependencies. In orders: order_id → cust_id → cust_name, cust_city. cust_id is not a key of orders, and the city is non-prime ⇒ transitive. Split: customers(cust_id 🔑, cust_name, cust_city) and orders(order_id 🔑, order_date, cust_id).
      4. 3NF → BCNF check. List every determinant in every table: order_id, cust_id, prod_id, (order_id, prod_id). Each is the key of its own table ⇒ all four tables are in BCNF. No MVDs either, so 4NF too.
      5. Verify the split. Each split shares a column that is a key of one side (cust_id, order_id, prod_id) ⇒ lossless. Each FD sits inside one table ⇒ dependency-preserving.
      CREATE TABLE customers (
  cust_id    VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,
  cust_name  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  cust_city  VARCHAR(60)  NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE products (
  prod_id    VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,
  prod_name  VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  list_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL CHECK (list_price >= 0)   -- today's catalog price
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id   VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY,
  order_date DATE NOT NULL,
  cust_id    VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (cust_id) REFERENCES customers(cust_id)
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   VARCHAR(10),
  prod_id    VARCHAR(10),
  qty        INT NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,                           -- price paid on that day
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, prod_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id) REFERENCES orders(order_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (prod_id)  REFERENCES products(prod_id)
);
      SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, c.cust_name, c.cust_city,
       p.prod_name, oi.qty, oi.unit_price
FROM orders o
JOIN customers   c  ON c.cust_id  = o.cust_id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.order_id
JOIN products    p  ON p.prod_id  = oi.prod_id
ORDER BY o.order_id, p.prod_name;
      +----------+------------+-----------+-----------+-----------+-----+------------+
| order_id | order_date | cust_name | cust_city | prod_name | qty | unit_price |
+----------+------------+-----------+-----------+-----------+-----+------------+
| O1       | 2026-03-01 | Asha      | Pune      | Notebook  |   1 |      60.00 |
| O1       | 2026-03-01 | Asha      | Pune      | Pen       |   2 |      10.00 |
| O2       | 2026-03-02 | Bilal     | Delhi     | Pen       |   5 |       9.00 |
| O3       | 2026-03-02 | Asha      | Pune      | Notebook  |   3 |      60.00 |
+----------+------------+-----------+-----------+-----------+-----+------------+
      🎯
      🎯 What the interviewer is really testing

      Can you name the FD behind each split, and do you know that unit_price in order_items is not redundancy? "Delete unit_price, it duplicates products.price" is a classic wrong move: prices change, and an old invoice must not change with them. They are two different facts. More on this under denormalization.

      ⚠️
      Common mistakes in "normalize this table"

      (1) Jumping straight to the final tables without saying which FD each split fixes. (2) Forgetting the junction table and putting prod_ids as a comma list in orders (breaks 1NF). (3) Keeping cust_name in orders "for convenience" — that is denormalization, and you must say so and justify it. (4) Forgetting foreign keys, so the split tables can disagree.

      Q"Normalize this table": Student(roll_no, name, course_id, course_name, instructor, instructor_phone, grade). How do you answer?

      First say the FDs out loud: roll_no → name, course_id → course_name, instructor, instructor → instructor_phone, roll_no, course_id → grade. Key: (roll_no, course_id).

      • 2NF: roll_no → name and course_id → course_name, instructor, … are partial. Split out student(roll_no, name) and course(course_id, course_name, instructor, instructor_phone). Keep enrollment(roll_no, course_id, grade).
      • 3NF: in course, course_id → instructor → instructor_phone is transitive. Split instructor(instructor, instructor_phone); keep course(course_id, course_name, instructor).
      • BCNF: every determinant is now a key. Done: 4 tables.
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      First I'll write the functional dependencies, because normalization is driven by them. The key is roll number plus course id. Student name depends only on roll number and course details only on course id, so those are partial dependencies — I move them to Student and Course tables to reach 2NF. Inside Course, the instructor's phone depends on the instructor, not on the course, so that transitive dependency becomes its own Instructor table for 3NF. Now every determinant is a key, so all four tables are in BCNF, and each split is lossless because the shared column is a key on one side.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪What if a course can have many instructors?

      Then course_id → instructor is no longer an FD. You need a junction table course_instructor(course_id, instructor_id). Always re-check FDs when a cardinality changes.

      ↪Would you use the instructor's name as a key?

      No. Names are not unique and they change. Add a surrogate instructor_id. Normalization theory works on any key, but physical design prefers short, stable keys.

      ↪Which query got slower after your change?

      "Show a student's report card with instructor phones" now joins four tables. With indexes on the keys this is cheap for OLTP. If it were a hot dashboard, you might cache or denormalize it.

      🎲 Tricky truths (rapid-fire traps)

      These one-liners look easy and catch many candidates. Learn the reason, not just the answer.

      StatementVerdictWhy
      Every relation with exactly 2 attributes is in BCNF.✔ TrueIn R(A, B) the only possible non-trivial FDs are A → B and B → A. If A → B holds, A is a key. Same for B. If neither holds, there is no non-trivial FD. (It is also in 4NF: every MVD there is trivial.)
      An all-key relation (the only key is all attributes) is in BCNF.✔ TrueNo non-trivial FD can exist, since its LHS would have to be a superkey = all attributes. But it can still fail 4NF (the student–hobby–language table).
      If every attribute is prime, the relation is at least in 3NF.✔ True2NF and 3NF only restrict FDs whose RHS is non-prime. There are none. BCNF can still fail.
      If every candidate key is a single attribute, the relation is in 2NF.✔ TrueA partial dependency needs a proper subset of a key. A single attribute has none (except ∅). 3NF can still fail.
      A relation in 3NF with no overlapping composite candidate keys is in BCNF.✔ True3NF and BCNF differ only through the "A is prime" escape, which needs overlapping composite keys.
      BCNF means no redundancy at all.✘ FalseBCNF removes FD-based redundancy only. MVDs (4NF) and join dependencies (5NF) can still repeat data.
      A lossy decomposition loses rows.✘ FalseIt adds spurious rows on join. What is lost is the information about which values belong together.
      BCNF decomposition is always dependency-preserving.✘ FalseIt is always lossless, but may lose an FD (the (student, course) → teacher, teacher → course case).
      Normalization always makes queries faster.✘ FalseIt makes writes safe and small. Reads may need more joins. That is why we denormalize hot read paths.
      A higher normal form is always the better design.~ Depends3NF/BCNF is the usual OLTP target. 4NF/5NF fix rare cases. Warehouses deliberately go lower (star schema).
      You can find FDs by looking at the sample rows.✘ FalseData can only disprove an FD. FDs are business rules for every legal state.
      A table with a surrogate id PK is automatically in 3NF.✘ FalseAdding id does not remove zip → city. Hidden FDs between non-key columns still break 3NF, and the old natural key (e.g. email) is still a candidate key.
      2 → BCNF · all-prime → 3NF · 1-attr keys → 2NF

      "Two is always a Boss, all-prime is at least three, single keys can't be partial." Three free answers in GATE MCQs before you compute anything.

      QDoes adding an auto-increment id primary key "normalize" a table?

      No. A surrogate key gives each row a short stable identity. It does nothing about dependencies between the other columns. Example: users(id, email, zip, city). zip → city is still a transitive dependency (id → zip → city), so the table is not in 3NF. And email is still a candidate key — declare it UNIQUE NOT NULL, or two rows can have the same email.

      🚫
      Answer that fails

      "Every table has an id primary key, so it is in BCNF." A surrogate key can even hide duplicates: two rows for the same real person with different ids.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Then why do we use surrogate keys?

      Natural keys can be long (bloating every InnoDB secondary index, which stores the PK) and can change (email, phone). An increasing integer gives short indexes and append-only inserts. Keep the natural key as a UNIQUE constraint. See Chapter 04.

      🚀 Denormalization: putting redundancy back, on purpose

      Normalization optimizes for correct, cheap writes. Some systems mostly read: a product page, a feed, a sales dashboard. If every page view joins five tables and counts a million rows, it is slow. Denormalization means copying or precomputing data so that the hot read touches fewer rows and fewer tables. It is a deliberate step on top of a normalized design, not the same as never normalizing.

      QWhat is denormalization? When and how do you do it?

      What: intentionally storing redundant or precomputed data in a normalized schema to make important reads faster.

      Why: joins and aggregations over big tables cost CPU and I/O on every read. If the same answer is read 10,000 times and changes rarely, compute it once at write time.

      When: read-heavy paths (product pages, feeds, inboxes), dashboards and reports, OLAP/warehouses, NoSQL stores without joins, and caching data from slow or remote services. Not for write-heavy tables with strict consistency needs, and not before you have measured a real problem.

      How (techniques):

      📋

      Redundant column

      Copy a parent attribute into the child: orders.cust_city, appointments.doctor_id. Saves a join, enables an index-only lookup.

      🧮

      Derived / counter column

      posts.comment_count, products.rating_sum + rating_count, orders.total. Avoids COUNT/SUM on every read.

      📊

      Summary / rollup table

      daily_sales(day, store_id, revenue) refreshed by a job. Dashboards read 365 rows, not 50M.

      📦

      Materialized view

      A stored query result the database refreshes for you (PostgreSQL, Oracle; SQL Server indexed views). MySQL: emulate with a summary table.

      🗂️

      Pre-joined / wide table

      Star-schema dimensions in a warehouse, or one document per aggregate in MongoDB/Cassandra (query-first modelling).

      🔨

      Repeating group / array

      Store the last 3 comments, or tags as JSON, inside the parent row for a fast list page. Keep the real table as the source of truth.

      Costs: update anomalies come back (two copies can disagree), extra storage, slower and bigger writes (write amplification), more code or triggers to keep copies in sync, possible stale reads, and harder schema changes.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      Denormalization is adding redundancy on purpose, like a stored comment count or a copied customer name, so that a hot read avoids joins or aggregations. It trades write cost and consistency risk for read speed. I start from a 3NF design, measure the slow queries, and denormalize only those paths. For each copy I name its source of truth and how it stays in sync — the same transaction, a trigger, or an async job — and how to rebuild it if it drifts.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Denormalized vs "never normalized" — what's the difference?

      A denormalized design knows which column is the copy and which is the source, and has a sync path. An unnormalized design has no source of truth, so when copies disagree nobody can tell which is right.

      ↪Before denormalizing, what would you try first?

      Fix the query and the indexes (Chapter 15), check the plan with EXPLAIN (Chapter 16), add a cache (Redis) or a read replica. Denormalize when those are not enough or the aggregate is inherently expensive.

      ↪Is a cache a form of denormalization?

      Yes, in spirit: a copy of data stored elsewhere for fast reads, with the same staleness and invalidation problems. The difference is that it lives outside the database and is usually allowed to be lost.

      ↪"Normalize until it hurts, denormalize until it works" — do you agree?

      Mostly, as a common saying: normalization is the default, denormalization is a targeted optimization. I add: measure the hurt first, and document every denormalized column.

      Keeping copies in sync (MySQL)

      The core problem of denormalization: who updates the copy, and when? Four options, from strongest to weakest consistency.

      The application updates the source and the copy in one transaction. Both commit or neither does. Easy to reason about; the counter row becomes a hot spot under heavy concurrent writes.

      START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO reviews (product_id, user_id, stars) VALUES (42, 7, 5);
UPDATE products
   SET rating_sum = rating_sum + 5,
       rating_count = rating_count + 1
 WHERE id = 42;
COMMIT;

-- Page view: no join, no AVG over millions of rows
SELECT name, rating_sum / NULLIF(rating_count, 0) AS avg_rating
FROM products WHERE id = 42;

      The database keeps the copy in sync, so no code path can forget. Triggers are hidden logic, add work to every write, and are harder to debug (see Chapter 09).

      DELIMITER //
CREATE TRIGGER trg_comment_ins AFTER INSERT ON comments
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE posts SET comment_count = comment_count + 1 WHERE id = NEW.post_id;
END//
CREATE TRIGGER trg_comment_del AFTER DELETE ON comments
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  UPDATE posts SET comment_count = comment_count - 1 WHERE id = OLD.post_id;
END//
DELIMITER ;

      A summary table rebuilt on a schedule. Reads may be up to one interval stale — fine for dashboards. This is how you emulate a materialized view in MySQL (the Event Scheduler must be ON, which is the MySQL 8 default).

      CREATE TABLE daily_sales (
  sale_day DATE,
  store_id INT,
  revenue  DECIMAL(14,2) NOT NULL,
  orders   INT NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (sale_day, store_id)
);

CREATE EVENT ev_refresh_daily_sales
ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 HOUR
DO
  INSERT INTO daily_sales (sale_day, store_id, revenue, orders)
  SELECT * FROM (
    SELECT DATE(o.created_at) AS d, o.store_id AS s,
           SUM(o.total) AS rev, COUNT(*) AS cnt
    FROM orders o
    WHERE o.created_at >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
    GROUP BY DATE(o.created_at), o.store_id
  ) AS x
  ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE revenue = x.rev, orders = x.cnt;

      ↑ only the last 2 days are recomputed — an "incremental refresh" by hand

      The write publishes an event (outbox table, or change data capture from the binlog with a tool like Debezium). A consumer updates the copies — another table, a search index, a cache, a NoSQL read model. Scales best, but copies are eventually consistent and you need retries and idempotent consumers.

      1. Writeorders + outbox row, one txn
      2. Publishrelay / CDC reads outbox or binlog
      3. Applyconsumer updates read model (idempotent)
      🔀
      Materialized views across engines

      MySQL: no materialized views; use summary tables + events/triggers. PostgreSQL: CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW, refreshed manually with REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW (CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index and lets reads continue). Oracle: materialized views with complete or fast (incremental, via MV logs) refresh, on demand or on commit, and query rewrite. SQL Server: indexed views (WITH SCHEMABINDING + unique clustered index) are maintained automatically on every write. NoSQL (Cassandra, DynamoDB, MongoDB): no joins, so you model one table per query and denormalize by design.

      Normalize (OLTP)

      • Many small reads and writes, high concurrency
      • Each fact once ⇒ no update anomalies
      • Small rows, small writes, less locking
      • Reads need joins (cheap with good indexes)
      • Target: 3NF / BCNF

      Denormalize (OLAP / read-heavy)

      • Huge scans and aggregates, few writes (batch ETL)
      • Star schema: fact table + wide dimensions
      • Fewer joins, simpler queries for analysts
      • Redundancy is controlled by the ETL load, not by users
      • See Chapter 20 (star vs snowflake)
      QYour order_items stores unit_price and product_name, but products has them too. Isn't that a 3NF violation?

      No. It looks like a copy, but it is a different fact: "the price this customer paid on 1 March" versus "the price today". There is no FD prod_id → unit_price in order_items, because the same product sells at different prices on different days. The order line depends on its whole key (order_id, prod_id), so it is properly normalized.

      If you joined to products instead, a price change today would silently rewrite every old invoice. Orders, invoices and payslips are historical documents: snapshot what was true at the time.

      🌍
      Real-world story

      E-commerce designs in interviews are graded on exactly this: order lines snapshot the SKU, title and unit price; addresses are copied onto the order at checkout (the customer may move later). The customer's current address belongs in addresses; the shipping address of order O1 belongs to O1.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Then what would be a real denormalization in this schema?

      orders.total (derivable as SUM of lines), orders.cust_name copied for a fast order list, or products.rating_count. Each can drift from its source, so each needs a sync path or a CHECK.

      ↪How do you keep full price history for products?

      A history table product_prices(prod_id, valid_from, valid_to, price) with PK (prod_id, valid_from). That is a type-2 slowly changing dimension in warehouse terms.

      QA viral post gets 5,000 likes per second. Your denormalized like_count column becomes a bottleneck. Why, and what do you do?

      Why: every like does UPDATE posts SET like_count = like_count + 1 WHERE id = ?. InnoDB takes an exclusive row lock on that one row until commit, so all those transactions queue on the same lock (Chapter 13). The redundant counter turned many independent inserts into one serialized hot row.

      1. Move the counter out of the wide posts row into post_stats(post_id, like_count) so it doesn't block edits of the post.
      2. Slotted counters: post_like_slots(post_id, slot, cnt) with, say, 16 slots; each like updates a random slot; reads do SUM(cnt) over 16 rows.
      3. Buffer in memory: Redis INCR, flushed to MySQL every few seconds; display an approximate number ("1.2M").
      4. Rebuild job: periodically recompute from the likes table (the source of truth) to repair drift.
      💡
      The pattern to say

      Every denormalized value needs (1) a source of truth, (2) a sync path, (3) a repair path. Mention all three and you sound senior.

      ✏️ Denormalization answers get marks for the trade-off, not the technique. Always finish with "…and here is how it stays correct."

      🔔 Last-round cross-questions

      QWhich normal form do you actually target in production, and why?

      3NF as the floor, BCNF where it is free. 3NF is always reachable with a lossless, dependency-preserving decomposition (synthesis algorithm), and it removes almost all practical redundancy. When 3NF and BCNF differ (overlapping composite keys), going to BCNF may leave an FD that can only be enforced with a join, trigger or application check — often a worse deal than a tiny bit of redundancy. 4NF matters when you see two independent multi-valued facts in one table; 5NF is rare.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      For OLTP I normalize to at least 3NF, and to BCNF when it doesn't cost dependency preservation. If BCNF would make a business rule impossible to enforce with a simple unique key, I stay at 3NF and accept the small redundancy. Then I denormalize only measured hot read paths, with a documented sync mechanism.

      QWhat is over-normalization? Give an example.

      Splitting further than the business needs, so that common reads need many joins for no integrity gain. Examples: a separate table for first_name; a cities lookup table when you never update city facts; a 6NF-style "one column per table" schema for an OLTP app. Every split should remove a real anomaly; if none exists, the split only adds joins.

      ⚠️
      Trap

      Do not confuse with lookup tables that enforce a domain (order_status, countries). Those are constraints, not over-normalization; an ENUM or CHECK is the alternative.

      QDoes normalization apply to MongoDB or Cassandra?

      The theory still explains the anomalies, but the design rule flips. These stores have weak or no joins and want one read per request, so you model by query and denormalize: embed data that is read together (an order with its lines), duplicate data across tables for different queries, and accept update fan-out. You still reference (normalize) data that changes often or is shared widely (user profiles). See Chapter 20.

      📌 Key takeaways

      • Normalization stores each fact once, guided by FDs, to kill insert/update/delete anomalies. FDs come from business rules, never from sample data.
      • 1NF: atomic cells. 2NF: no partial dependency on a composite key. 3NF: for every X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime. BCNF: every determinant is a superkey.
      • 3NF and BCNF differ only with overlapping composite candidate keys. BCNF splitting is always lossless but may lose dependency preservation; 3NF synthesis keeps both.
      • 4NF removes independent multi-valued facts; 5NF removes join dependencies (lossless only as 3+ pieces). BCNF ≠ zero redundancy.
      • Highest-NF method: find all keys → mark prime → classify each FD (superkey / prime RHS / partial / transitive) → answer is the weakest level.
      • Free answers: 2-attribute relation ⇒ BCNF; all attributes prime ⇒ ≥ 3NF; only single-attribute keys ⇒ ≥ 2NF.
      • "Normalize this table": state FDs, find the key, split partial deps (2NF), then transitive deps (3NF), check BCNF, prove lossless via the shared key.
      • Denormalize only measured hot reads (counters, copied columns, summary tables, materialized views, star schemas); for each copy name the source of truth, sync path and repair path.
      • An order line's unit_price is a historical fact, not redundancy. Snapshots of documents are correct design.

      📚 Go deeper

      • Silberschatz et al., Database System Concepts — Ch. 7 slides (Relational Database Design) — the textbook source for BCNF/3NF algorithms, lossless joins and 4NF.
      • Wikipedia: Boyce–Codd normal form — clean statement of the 3NF vs BCNF difference with the overlapping-keys example.
      • GeeksforGeeks: Normal Forms in DBMS — many GATE-style practice problems on finding the highest NF.
      • CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems — lecture notes and videos for a rigorous, systems-oriented view.
      • PostgreSQL docs: Materialized Views — the built-in alternative to hand-made summary tables.
      • Apache Cassandra: Data modeling — query-first denormalized design, the opposite philosophy.

      R(A, B, C), F = {AB → C, C → B}. What is the highest normal form?

      Keys are AB and AC, so every attribute is prime ⇒ 3NF holds. C → B has a non-superkey LHS ⇒ BCNF fails. This is the classic overlapping-keys case.

      Which statement about BCNF decomposition is correct?

      The BCNF algorithm splits on X → Y into (X ∪ Y) and (R − Y); X is a key of the first piece, so the join is lossless. But an FD spanning both pieces can be lost. 3NF synthesis guarantees both properties.

      A relation has exactly two attributes. Which is guaranteed?

      Any non-trivial FD A → B makes A a key, and if no FD holds the key is AB. So every determinant is a superkey. Any MVD in a 2-attribute relation is trivial, so 4NF too.

      enrollment(roll_no, course_id, student_name, grade), key (roll_no, course_id), roll_no → student_name. What does it violate first?

      student_name (non-prime) depends on roll_no, a proper part of the composite key. Move it to student(roll_no, student_name).

      order_items stores unit_price although products also has a price. Best description?

      The paid price depends on the whole key (order, product) and must not change when the catalog price changes. Syncing it would corrupt old invoices.

      You need a materialized view in MySQL 8. What do you do?

      MySQL has no materialized views. Oracle/PostgreSQL have them; SQL Server uses indexed views (SCHEMABINDING + unique clustered index). In MySQL emulate with a summary table.

      R(A, B, C, D), F = {A → B, B → A, A → C}, key options AD and BD. Highest NF?

      C is non-prime and A → C uses A, a proper subset of key AD ⇒ partial dependency ⇒ 2NF fails. A ↔ B alone would be fine for 3NF (B is prime), but C breaks 2NF.
      The three anomalies?
      Insertion (can't add a fact without an unrelated one), Update (copies disagree), Deletion (deleting one fact loses another). IUD = the DML verbs.
      2NF in one line?
      1NF + no non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of any candidate key (no partial dependency).
      Formal 3NF condition?
      For every non-trivial X → A: X is a superkey OR A is prime.
      BCNF condition?
      For every non-trivial X → Y: X is a superkey. (3NF without the "A is prime" escape.)
      When do 3NF and BCNF differ?
      Only when there are overlapping composite candidate keys, e.g. R(student, course, teacher) with teacher → course.
      3NF synthesis vs BCNF decomposition guarantees?
      3NF synthesis: lossless + dependency-preserving, always. BCNF: lossless always, dependency preservation not guaranteed.
      4NF fixes what?
      Non-trivial multivalued dependencies X ↠ Y where X is not a superkey — independent multi-valued facts stored together (hobbies × languages).
      5NF fixes what?
      Join dependencies not implied by keys: the table splits losslessly only into 3+ projections (agent–company–product).
      Binary lossless-join test?
      R1 ∩ R2 → R1 or R1 ∩ R2 → R2 (the common attributes are a key of one side).
      Every relation with 2 attributes is in…?
      BCNF (and 4NF). All attributes prime ⇒ at least 3NF. Only single-attribute keys ⇒ at least 2NF.
      Denormalization techniques?
      Redundant columns, counters/derived totals, summary/rollup tables, materialized views, pre-joined star dimensions, embedded documents.
      Three things every denormalized value needs?
      A source of truth, a sync path (same txn / trigger / job / async event), and a repair/rebuild path.
      Mnemonic for 1NF–3NF?
      "The key, the whole key, and nothing but the key — so help me Codd."
      Chapter 07 · III · SQL Mastery

      ✍️ SQL Core: Commands, Types, Clauses & Execution Order

      Explain every SQL command family, pick the right data type and defend it, predict exactly what a query returns (NULLs included), and say why WHERE cannot see a SELECT alias.

      ⏱ 45 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8.0 / 8.4PostgreSQLSQL ServerOracle

      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision

      • 5 sublanguages: DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP/TRUNCATE/RENAME), DML (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE), DQL (SELECT), DCL (GRANT/REVOKE), TCL (COMMIT/ROLLBACK/SAVEPOINT).
      • Logical order: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT (window functions here) → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. That is why WHERE cannot use a SELECT alias, but ORDER BY can.
      • DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP: rows (WHERE, triggers, rollback) vs all rows fast (DDL, resets AUTO_INCREMENT, implicit commit in MySQL) vs the whole table. TRUNCATE can be rolled back in PostgreSQL and SQL Server.
      • NULL = unknown: NULL = NULL is NULL, not TRUE. Use IS NULL or <=>. x NOT IN (…, NULL) never returns TRUE.
      • COUNT(*) = COUNT(1) (same speed in InnoDB); COUNT(col) skips NULLs; all other aggregates skip NULLs too.
      • Types: money → DECIMAL, never FLOAT. INT(11)'s 11 is only display width (deprecated). TIMESTAMP converts time zones and dies on 2038-01-19; DATETIME does not.
      • Upserts: MySQL INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE; PostgreSQL ON CONFLICT; SQL Server/Oracle/PG 15+ MERGE. REPLACE = DELETE + INSERT (new row, lost columns, cascades!).
      • MySQL defaults that bite: utf8 = 3-byte utf8mb3 (no emoji); default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is case- and accent-insensitive; non-strict sql_mode silently truncates.
      • Big OFFSET is slow (it reads and throws away rows). Use keyset (seek) pagination: WHERE id < :last ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20.
      ✏️ Every SQL round starts here. Freshers get "DELETE vs TRUNCATE" and "WHERE vs HAVING" in almost every service-company interview.

      All examples below were run on MySQL 8.0 with the default sql_mode (ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, STRICT_TRANS_TABLES, …). The outputs are real. We use one tiny dataset again and again, so you can predict every result in your head.

      CREATE TABLE dept (
  id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE emp (
  id         INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name       VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  dept_id    INT,                       -- nullable on purpose
  salary     DECIMAL(10,2),             -- nullable on purpose
  manager_id INT,
  FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept(id)
);
INSERT INTO dept VALUES (10,'Engineering'),(20,'Sales'),(30,'HR'),(40,'Legal');
INSERT INTO emp (name, dept_id, salary, manager_id) VALUES
 ('Asha', 10, 90000, NULL), ('Ravi', 10, 75000, 1), ('Meera', 20, 60000, 1),
 ('John', 20, 60000, 3),    ('Priya', NULL, 50000, 1), ('Karan', 10, NULL, 2);
      +----+-------+---------+----------+------------+
| id | name  | dept_id | salary   | manager_id |
+----+-------+---------+----------+------------+
|  1 | Asha  |      10 | 90000.00 |       NULL |
|  2 | Ravi  |      10 | 75000.00 |          1 |
|  3 | Meera |      20 | 60000.00 |          1 |
|  4 | John  |      20 | 60000.00 |          3 |
|  5 | Priya |    NULL | 50000.00 |          1 |   <- no department
|  6 | Karan |      10 |     NULL |          2 |   <- unknown salary
+----+-------+---------+----------+------------+

      🧩 SQL sublanguages: DDL, DML, DQL, DCL, TCL

      SQL is one language, but its commands fall into five families. Each family answers a different question: what does the structure look like, what is the data, what do I want to read, who may do it, and when is the work final.

      🔨

      DDL — Data Definition

      Builds and changes structure (schema objects). CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME, plus COMMENT. In MySQL each one commits implicitly.

      ✏️

      DML — Data Manipulation

      Changes rows. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE (not in MySQL), and MySQL's REPLACE. Runs inside transactions, can be rolled back.

      🔍

      DQL — Data Query

      Reads data: SELECT (with WITH, joins, subqueries). Many textbooks put SELECT inside DML; both answers are accepted if you say so.

      🔑

      DCL — Data Control

      Permissions: GRANT, REVOKE (and in MySQL 8 roles: CREATE ROLE, SET ROLE). Who may read or change what.

      🔒

      TCL — Transaction Control

      Makes work final or undoes it: START TRANSACTION/BEGIN, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT, SET TRANSACTION.

      D-D-D-D-T

      Define the box (DDL) → Do things to rows (DML) → Discover rows (DQL) → Decide who (DCL) → Transact (TCL). Or remember the question each answers: shape? content? read? who? final?

      QWhat are DDL, DML, DQL, DCL and TCL? Give the commands in each.

      What: categories of SQL statements grouped by what they act on.

      FamilyActs onMain commandsRollback in MySQL?
      DDLSchema objects: tables, indexes, views, databasesCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME, COMMENT (Oracle)✘ implicit commit before and after
      DMLRows inside tablesINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE*, REPLACE**, CALL, LOAD DATA✔ (InnoDB)
      DQLReading rowsSELECT (+ WITH, TABLE t, VALUES in 8.0.19+)n/a (no change)
      DCLPrivilegesGRANT, REVOKE; MySQL 8 roles✘ (implicit commit in MySQL)
      TCLTransactionsSTART TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, RELEASE SAVEPOINT, SET TRANSACTION—

      * MERGE exists in SQL Server, Oracle and PostgreSQL 15+, not MySQL. ** REPLACE is a MySQL extension.

      CREATE TABLE audit_log (id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, msg VARCHAR(200));  -- DDL
INSERT INTO audit_log (msg) VALUES ('salary review started');                       -- DML
SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 10;                                    -- DQL
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON company.audit_log TO 'report_app'@'%';                      -- DCL
START TRANSACTION;                                                                  -- TCL
  UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE dept_id = 10;
  SAVEPOINT after_eng;
  UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * 1.10 WHERE dept_id = 20;
  ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT after_eng;   -- undo only the Sales raise
COMMIT;                              -- Engineering raise is now permanent
      🔀
      Engine differences

      MySQL & Oracle: DDL (and in MySQL also GRANT/REVOKE) ends the current transaction with an implicit commit. PostgreSQL & SQL Server: most DDL is transactional — you can BEGIN; CREATE TABLE …; ROLLBACK; and the table never existed. Oracle classifies MERGE as DML; some books treat TRUNCATE as DML because it removes data — say "TRUNCATE is DDL in MySQL/Oracle because it recreates the table rather than deleting rows".

      ⚠️
      Common mistake

      Saying "SELECT is DML so it can be rolled back". Plain SELECT changes nothing, so there is nothing to roll back. (A locking SELECT … FOR UPDATE does take locks that last until COMMIT/ROLLBACK — see Chapter 13.)

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      SQL commands fall into five groups. DDL defines structure — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME. DML changes rows — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and MERGE in engines that have it. DQL is SELECT. DCL is GRANT and REVOKE for permissions, and TCL is COMMIT, ROLLBACK and SAVEPOINT. One practical difference: in MySQL every DDL statement auto-commits, so it cannot be rolled back, while DML inside a transaction can.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Is TRUNCATE DDL or DML? Why?

      DDL in MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and PostgreSQL. It does not delete rows one by one; it throws away the table's data storage and starts a fresh, empty one (in InnoDB it is internally like DROP + CREATE of the same definition). Because it works on the object, not on rows, it is DDL — with no WHERE, no row triggers, and a reset AUTO_INCREMENT. Details in DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP.

      ↪What is a SAVEPOINT? Does ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT end the transaction?

      A named marker inside a transaction. ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s undoes only the work after s; the transaction stays open and you still must COMMIT or ROLLBACK. Row locks taken after the savepoint are not necessarily released in InnoDB until the transaction ends.

      ↪Which statements cause an implicit commit in MySQL?

      All DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP/RENAME/TRUNCATE of tables, indexes, views, procedures…), account statements (CREATE USER, GRANT, REVOKE, SET PASSWORD), LOCK TABLES/UNLOCK TABLES, starting a new START TRANSACTION while one is open, and admin statements like ANALYZE TABLE. Exception: CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE does not commit.

      ↪What does autocommit mean?

      With autocommit=1 (MySQL's default) every statement is its own transaction and commits immediately. START TRANSACTION suspends autocommit until the next COMMIT/ROLLBACK. Full story in Chapter 12.

      📦 Data types and the classic comparisons

      A data type is a promise: what values are allowed, how many bytes they take, and how they compare and sort. Wrong types cause wrong answers (FLOAT money), wasted space (BIGINT everywhere), and slow indexes (VARCHAR(255) keys). Interviewers love the comparisons below.

      GroupMySQL 8 typesUse for
      IntegerTINYINT, SMALLINT, MEDIUMINT, INT, BIGINT (± UNSIGNED)ids, counts, flags
      Exact decimalDECIMAL(p,s) = NUMERICmoney, rates, anything that must add up exactly
      ApproximateFLOAT (4 B), DOUBLE (8 B)measurements, science, ML features
      StringCHAR(n), VARCHAR(n), TINYTEXT…LONGTEXTcodes, names, long text
      BinaryBINARY, VARBINARY, TINYBLOB…LONGBLOBhashes, UUID bytes, files (better in object storage)
      Date/timeDATE, TIME, DATETIME(fsp), TIMESTAMP(fsp), YEARevents, birthdays, audit columns
      SpecialENUM, SET, JSON, BIT, spatial (POINT, …)small fixed lists, semi-structured data
      BooleanBOOLEAN/BOOL → really TINYINT(1)flags (0/1)
      QCHAR vs VARCHAR — what is the difference and when do you use each?

      CHAR(n) is fixed length. Shorter values are right-padded with spaces when stored, and those trailing spaces are removed when you read the value back. VARCHAR(n) is variable length: it stores exactly the characters you gave (trailing spaces kept) plus a 1-byte length prefix (2 bytes if the column can exceed 255 bytes).

      CREATE TABLE ch (c CHAR(5), v VARCHAR(5));
INSERT INTO ch VALUES ('ab  ', 'ab  ');          -- two trailing spaces in both
SELECT CONCAT('[',c,']') AS c, CONCAT('[',v,']') AS v, LENGTH(c), LENGTH(v) FROM ch;
      +------+--------+-----------+-----------+
| c    | v      | LENGTH(c) | LENGTH(v) |
+------+--------+-----------+-----------+
| [ab] | [ab  ] |         2 |         4 |   <- CHAR lost the trailing spaces
+------+--------+-----------+-----------+

      CHAR(n)

      • Fixed length, padded with spaces
      • Trailing spaces stripped on read
      • No length byte; max n = 255 characters
      • Best for values that are always the same length: country code 'IN', currency 'INR', MD5 hex (32)
      • With a multi-byte charset (utf8mb4) InnoDB actually stores CHAR(n) in n to 4×n bytes, so the "fixed" saving mostly disappears

      VARCHAR(n)

      • Variable length; n = max characters, not bytes
      • Keeps trailing spaces
      • 1–2 byte length prefix
      • Max 65,535 bytes for the whole row (shared by all columns)
      • Best for names, emails, titles
      💡
      Does VARCHAR(255) vs VARCHAR(50) matter if data is short?

      On disk, not much. But it matters for: (1) in-memory temporary tables and sort buffers, which may allocate the maximum size; (2) index key limits (InnoDB max 3072 bytes per index key; VARCHAR(800) utf8mb4 = 3200 bytes won't fit); (3) the 255-byte boundary that changes the length prefix from 1 to 2 bytes. Size columns honestly.

      🔀
      Engine differences

      PostgreSQL: TEXT and VARCHAR(n) are stored the same way and perform the same; CHAR(n) is usually slower and discouraged. Oracle: use VARCHAR2; Oracle treats '' as NULL. SQL Server: VARCHAR vs NVARCHAR (Unicode, 2 bytes/char) — the N prefix question is common there.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      CHAR is fixed-length: the value is padded with spaces to n and the padding is stripped when read, so it suits codes that always have the same length, like a two-letter country code. VARCHAR stores only the actual characters plus a one- or two-byte length prefix, so it suits names and emails. In MySQL the n in both means characters, not bytes, and with utf8mb4 one character can take up to four bytes.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Does 'abc' = 'abc ' (trailing space) return true?

      It depends on the collation's pad attribute. MySQL 8's default utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is NO PAD, so trailing spaces count: the result is 0 (verified). Older PAD SPACE collations like utf8mb4_general_ci ignore trailing spaces and return 1. This can surprise you after upgrading from 5.7.

      ↪What is the difference between LENGTH() and CHAR_LENGTH()?

      LENGTH() counts bytes; CHAR_LENGTH() counts characters. LENGTH('é') = 2, CHAR_LENGTH('é') = 1; an emoji is 4 bytes, 1 character. Use CHAR_LENGTH for validation rules like "name ≤ 30 characters".

      QWhat are the integer types and their sizes? What does the 11 in INT(11) mean?
      TypeBytesSigned rangeUnsigned maxTypical use
      TINYINT1−128 … 127255flags, small enums, age
      SMALLINT2−32,768 … 32,76765,535year counts, small lookup ids
      MEDIUMINT3−8,388,608 … 8,388,60716,777,215MySQL-only; rarely worth it
      INT4−2,147,483,648 … 2,147,483,6474,294,967,295most ids and counts
      BIGINT8−9.22 × 1018 … 9.22 × 10181.8 × 1019ids of big/fast-growing tables, money in paise

      The INT(11) myth. The number in brackets is display width — a hint for client tools to pad output (only visible with ZEROFILL). It does not limit the value or change the storage. INT(1) still holds 2,147,483,647 and still takes 4 bytes. MySQL 8.0.17 deprecated display width and ZEROFILL; MySQL 8 drops it from SHOW CREATE TABLE (except TINYINT(1), kept so drivers can recognise BOOLEAN).

      CREATE TABLE ty (a INT(11), b TINYINT(1), c BOOLEAN, d INT(5) ZEROFILL);
-- Warning 1681: Integer display width is deprecated and will be removed in a future release.
SHOW CREATE TABLE ty\G
INSERT INTO ty VALUES (2147483647, 5, 7, 42);
SELECT * FROM ty;
INSERT INTO ty (a) VALUES (2147483648);
        `a` int DEFAULT NULL,                       <- (11) is gone
  `b` tinyint(1) DEFAULT NULL,
  `c` tinyint(1) DEFAULT NULL,                <- BOOLEAN became TINYINT(1)
  `d` int(5) unsigned zerofill DEFAULT NULL   <- ZEROFILL also implies UNSIGNED

+------------+------+------+-------+
| a          | b    | c    | d     |
+------------+------+------+-------+
| 2147483647 |    5 |    7 | 00042 |   <- a "BOOLEAN" happily stores 7
+------------+------+------+-------+
ERROR 1264 (22003): Out of range value for column 'a' at row 1
      🚫
      Fails interviews

      "INT(11) stores up to 11 digits" or "INT(5) is smaller than INT(11)". Both are wrong: same 4 bytes, same range.

      🌍
      Real-world story: the INT overflow

      A signed INT AUTO_INCREMENT id stops at 2,147,483,647. High-write tables (events, logs, likes) hit it, and every INSERT fails with a duplicate-key/out-of-range error. Fixing it needs an ALTER … MODIFY id BIGINT that rewrites the table (and every FK column that points to it). Use BIGINT UNSIGNED for ids of tables that can grow fast.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      TINYINT, SMALLINT, MEDIUMINT, INT and BIGINT take 1, 2, 3, 4 and 8 bytes; UNSIGNED doubles the positive range. The 11 in INT(11) is only a display width for zero-padding, it doesn't limit the value, and MySQL 8 has deprecated it. For ids that can grow quickly I use BIGINT UNSIGNED to avoid the 2.1-billion INT ceiling.

      QWhy should money be DECIMAL and not FLOAT or DOUBLE?

      Why: FLOAT and DOUBLE store numbers in binary (IEEE-754). Many decimal fractions like 0.1 have no exact binary form — like 1/3 in decimal — so they are stored as the nearest approximation. Small errors add up and equality checks fail. DECIMAL(p,s) stores the decimal digits exactly (packed, about 4 bytes per 9 digits), so sums of money are exact.

      CREATE TABLE f (x FLOAT, d DOUBLE, m DECIMAL(10,2));
INSERT INTO f VALUES (0.1, 0.1, 0.1), (0.2, 0.2, 0.2);
SELECT SUM(x), SUM(d), SUM(m) FROM f;
SELECT SUM(x) = 0.3, SUM(d) = 0.3, SUM(m) = 0.3 FROM f;
      +---------------------+---------------------+--------+
| SUM(x)              | SUM(d)              | SUM(m) |
+---------------------+---------------------+--------+
| 0.30000000447034836 | 0.30000000000000004 |   0.30 |
+---------------------+---------------------+--------+
+------------+------------+------------+
| SUM(x)=0.3 | SUM(d)=0.3 | SUM(m)=0.3 |
+------------+------------+------------+
|          0 |          0 |          1 |
+------------+------------+------------+

      DECIMAL(10,2) means 10 digits in total, 2 after the point: max 99,999,999.99. Values with more decimals are rounded (and in strict mode, too-large values are an error).

      💡
      Alternative that payment companies use

      Store minor units as an integer: ₹1,234.50 → 123450 paise in a BIGINT, plus a currency column. Integer maths is exact and fast. Either DECIMAL or minor-unit BIGINT is a correct answer; FLOAT never is.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Then when IS FLOAT/DOUBLE the right choice?

      For measured, naturally approximate values where range matters more than exact digits: sensor readings, coordinates, scientific values, ML scores. They are smaller and faster for maths. Never compare them with =; use a tolerance: ABS(a - b) < 1e-9.

      ↪What does FLOAT(7,4) mean?

      A non-standard MySQL syntax (precision, scale) for FLOAT/DOUBLE. It is deprecated since 8.0.17. It only rounds the display; the value is still approximate. Use DECIMAL if you need fixed scale.

      QDATETIME vs TIMESTAMP — which one do you use, and what is the year-2038 problem?

      Both store a date plus a time (optionally with fractional seconds, DATETIME(6)). The difference is what they mean:

      • DATETIME is a "wall-clock" value. What you write is what you read, whatever the session time zone. Range 1000-01-01 00:00:00 to 9999-12-31 23:59:59. 5 bytes (+0–3 for fractions).
      • TIMESTAMP is an instant. MySQL converts it from the session time_zone to UTC when storing, and back to the session time zone when reading. Stored as seconds since 1970 in 4 bytes (+0–3), so the range is 1970-01-01 00:00:01 UTC to 2038-01-19 03:14:07 UTC — the signed 32-bit limit. That is the year-2038 problem.
      CREATE TABLE ts (dt DATETIME, t TIMESTAMP);
SET time_zone = '+00:00';
INSERT INTO ts VALUES ('2026-10-16 10:00:00', '2026-10-16 10:00:00');
SET time_zone = '+05:30';                 -- an Indian client reads it
SELECT * FROM ts;
INSERT INTO ts VALUES ('2040-01-01 00:00:00', '2040-01-01 00:00:00');
      +---------------------+---------------------+
| dt                  | t                   |
+---------------------+---------------------+
| 2026-10-16 10:00:00 | 2026-10-16 15:30:00 |   <- TIMESTAMP shifted by +05:30, DATETIME did not
+---------------------+---------------------+
ERROR 1292 (22007): Incorrect datetime value: '2040-01-01 00:00:00' for column 't' at row 1

      DATETIME

      • No time-zone conversion
      • Year 1000 – 9999
      • 5 bytes + fsp
      • Use for: birthdays, scheduled local events, anything past 2038, UTC instants written by the app

      TIMESTAMP

      • Converted session TZ ↔ UTC
      • 1970 – 2038-01-19 UTC
      • 4 bytes + fsp
      • Use for: "row created/updated at" if every connection sets the right time zone

      Both support automatic values: DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP (DATETIME gained this in MySQL 5.6.5).

      🌍
      Production rule of thumb

      Store instants in UTC: either DATETIME(6) filled by the app with UTC (UTC_TIMESTAMP(6)), or TIMESTAMP(6) with time_zone='+00:00' on every connection. Store local wall-clock times plus an IANA zone ('Asia/Kolkata') for things humans schedule ("open 9:00 local"), because DST rules change. Loan end dates, insurance expiry, mortgages already pass 2038 — TIMESTAMP rejects them.

      🔀
      Engine differences

      PostgreSQL: timestamp (without time zone) ≈ MySQL DATETIME; timestamptz stores UTC and converts on output, range to year 294276 — the recommended type. SQL Server: datetime2 and datetimeoffset; its timestamp/rowversion is not a date at all but a row-version counter. Oracle: DATE includes time to the second; TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE.

      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview

      DATETIME stores the value exactly as given with no time-zone handling and covers years 1000 to 9999. TIMESTAMP stores a UTC instant: it converts from the session time zone on write and back on read, uses 4 bytes, and only goes up to January 2038 because it is a 32-bit epoch counter. I store event times in UTC, usually in DATETIME(6) to avoid the 2038 limit and surprise conversions.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪Which type for a date of birth?

      DATE (3 bytes). A birthday has no time and no time zone; TIMESTAMP would also reject anyone born before 1970.

      ↪How do you query "all orders placed on 15 Oct" on a DATETIME column?

      WHERE placed_at >= '2026-10-15' AND placed_at < '2026-10-16'. Not DATE(placed_at) = '2026-10-15' (a function on the column blocks index use) and not BETWEEN '2026-10-15' AND '2026-10-16' (includes midnight of the 16th). See BETWEEN.

      QTEXT/BLOB vs VARCHAR — when do you need TEXT and what does it cost?
      Text typeBinary twinMax sizeLength prefix
      TINYTEXTTINYBLOB255 bytes1 B
      TEXTBLOB64 KB (65,535 B)2 B
      MEDIUMTEXTMEDIUMBLOB16 MB3 B
      LONGTEXTLONGBLOB4 GB4 B

      TEXT = character data with a charset and collation (compares like strings). BLOB = raw bytes (compares byte by byte). Use them when the value can exceed what fits comfortably in a row — the whole row is limited to 65,535 bytes, and a VARCHAR(20000) in utf8mb4 alone would need 80,000.

      • Storage: with InnoDB's DYNAMIC row format, long values are stored off-page (in overflow pages) with a 20-byte pointer in the row. Reading them costs extra I/O, so SELECT * on a table with big TEXT columns is expensive.
      • Indexes: you can only index a prefix: INDEX (body(100)). For word search use a FULLTEXT index.
      • Defaults: TEXT/BLOB/JSON can have only expression defaults, written in brackets, e.g. DEFAULT ('') (MySQL 8.0.13+).
      • Files: don't store images/PDFs in BLOBs in OLTP tables; store them in object storage (S3/GCS) and keep the URL + checksum.
      QENUM and SET — pros, cons, and what would you use instead?

      ENUM('small','medium','large') stores one value from a fixed list as a 1–2 byte index number. SET('a','b','c') stores any combination as a bitmap (up to 64 members).

      CREATE TABLE en (size ENUM('small','medium','large'));
INSERT INTO en VALUES ('large'), ('small'), ('medium');
SELECT size, size + 0 AS idx FROM en ORDER BY size;   -- sorts by INDEX, not alphabetically
INSERT INTO en VALUES ('huge');
      +--------+-----+
| size   | idx |
+--------+-----+
| small  |   1 |
| medium |   2 |
| large  |   3 |
+--------+-----+
ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'size' at row 1   -- strict mode rejects it
                                                                 -- non-strict mode stores '' (index 0)!

      ✔ Pros

      • Compact (1 byte for ≤255 values)
      • Readable values, built-in validation
      • No join needed

      ✘ Cons

      • Adding a value = ALTER TABLE (cheap only when appended at the end)
      • Sorts by list position, surprising people
      • Can't hold extra info (label, display order, active flag)
      • MySQL-specific; painful to port
      • Numeric-looking ENUMs ('1','2') confuse index vs value

      Alternatives: a lookup table + foreign key (best when values change or carry attributes), or VARCHAR + CHECK (status IN ('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED')) (MySQL 8.0.16+ enforces CHECK). For SET, a proper junction table is usually better (queryable, indexable).

      QHow does MySQL's JSON type work, and what is BOOLEAN really?

      JSON (MySQL 5.7.8+) validates the document on insert and stores it in an optimized binary format, so the server can jump to a key without re-parsing text. Read with -> (returns JSON) or ->> (returns unquoted text).

      CREATE TABLE prof (id INT PRIMARY KEY, data JSON);
INSERT INTO prof VALUES (1, '{"city":"Pune","skills":["sql","go"]}');
SELECT data->'$.city' AS a, data->>'$.city' AS b, JSON_EXTRACT(data, '$.skills[1]') AS c FROM prof;
-- index a JSON field through a functional index (8.0.13+)
ALTER TABLE prof ADD INDEX idx_city ((CAST(data->>'$.city' AS CHAR(30)) COLLATE utf8mb4_bin));
      +--------+------+------+
| a      | b    | c    |
+--------+------+------+
| "Pune" | Pune | "go" |
+--------+------+------+

      Use JSON for genuinely variable attributes (product specs, settings, webhook payloads). Don't use it to dodge schema design: anything you filter, join or constrain on regularly should be a real column. JSON arrays can be indexed with multi-valued indexes (8.0.17+). PostgreSQL's jsonb + GIN index is the richer equivalent.

      BOOLEAN in MySQL is just a synonym for TINYINT(1). TRUE is 1 and FALSE is 0 — and nothing stops you storing 7 (we did above). Add CHECK (flag IN (0,1)) if it matters. PostgreSQL has a real boolean; SQL Server uses BIT; Oracle got a SQL BOOLEAN type only in 23ai (older versions use NUMBER(1) or CHAR(1)).

      🔨 DDL in practice: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, RENAME and constraints

      DDL describes the shape of data. A good CREATE TABLE also encodes the business rules as constraints, so bad data is rejected by the database itself and not by "hopefully every app checks it".

      CREATE TABLE orders (
  order_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT,                 -- surrogate key
  customer_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,                       -- NOT NULL
  order_no     VARCHAR(20)     NOT NULL,
  status       VARCHAR(10)     NOT NULL DEFAULT 'NEW',         -- DEFAULT
  amount       DECIMAL(12,2)   NOT NULL,
  discount     DECIMAL(12,2)   NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  net_amount   DECIMAL(12,2) AS (amount - discount) STORED,    -- generated column
  placed_at    DATETIME(6)     NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  CONSTRAINT pk_orders      PRIMARY KEY (order_id),            -- PRIMARY KEY
  CONSTRAINT uq_order_no    UNIQUE (order_no),                 -- UNIQUE
  CONSTRAINT chk_amount     CHECK (amount >= 0 AND discount <= amount),   -- CHECK
  CONSTRAINT chk_status     CHECK (status IN ('NEW','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED')),
  CONSTRAINT fk_orders_cust FOREIGN KEY (customer_id)          -- FOREIGN KEY
      REFERENCES customers (customer_id)
      ON DELETE RESTRICT ON UPDATE CASCADE,
  INDEX idx_cust_time (customer_id, placed_at)                 -- index (not a constraint)
) ENGINE = InnoDB DEFAULT CHARSET = utf8mb4;
      NOT NULL
      The column must have a value.
      DEFAULT
      Value used when the INSERT does not mention the column.
      PRIMARY KEY
      Unique + NOT NULL row identity; one per table (may be composite). In InnoDB it is also the clustered index (Chapter 15).
      UNIQUE
      No two rows share the value. MySQL and PostgreSQL allow many NULLs; SQL Server allows one.
      CHECK
      A boolean rule per row. Enforced in MySQL only from 8.0.16 — before that it was parsed and silently ignored. A CHECK that evaluates to NULL passes.
      FOREIGN KEY
      Value must exist in the parent table (or be NULL). Actions: CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT/NO ACTION (same in InnoDB). InnoDB auto-creates an index on the FK column if none exists. More in Chapter 4.
      QWhat can ALTER TABLE do? What is the difference between MODIFY, CHANGE and RENAME COLUMN? 
      ALTER TABLE emp ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(100) NULL AFTER name;      -- add column
ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY COLUMN name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL;             -- new type/attributes, same name
ALTER TABLE emp CHANGE COLUMN name full_name VARCHAR(60) NOT NULL;   -- rename AND redefine (must repeat type)
ALTER TABLE emp RENAME COLUMN full_name TO name;                     -- rename only (MySQL 8.0+)
ALTER TABLE emp DROP COLUMN email;                                   -- remove column
ALTER TABLE emp ADD CONSTRAINT uq_emp_name UNIQUE (name);            -- add constraint
ALTER TABLE emp DROP INDEX uq_emp_name;                              -- UNIQUE is dropped as an index in MySQL
ALTER TABLE emp ADD INDEX idx_dept_sal (dept_id, salary);            -- add index
ALTER TABLE emp ALTER COLUMN salary SET DEFAULT 30000;               -- change default only
ALTER TABLE emp RENAME TO employee;                                  -- rename table
ALTER TABLE employee ADD COLUMN note VARCHAR(50), ALGORITHM=INSTANT; -- metadata-only change
      ClauseRenames?Changes definition?Must restate full type?
      MODIFY✘✔✔ (forgetting NOT NULL drops it!)
      CHANGE✔✔✔
      RENAME COLUMN✔✘✘
      ALTER COLUMN … SET/DROP DEFAULT✘default only✘
      ⚠️
      Common mistake

      MODIFY replaces the whole column definition. ALTER TABLE emp MODIFY name VARCHAR(60); silently makes name nullable and drops its default and comment. Always restate everything.

      🌍
      ALTER on a 500 GB table

      MySQL 8 runs many ALTERs as online DDL: ALGORITHM=INSTANT (metadata only: adding a column — 8.0.12+ at the end, 8.0.29+ anywhere; renaming a column — 8.0.28+; changing a default), INPLACE (e.g. adding a secondary index while reads and writes continue), or COPY (rebuilds the table, blocks writes — e.g. changing a column's type). Write ALGORITHM=INSTANT or LOCK=NONE explicitly: if MySQL can't honour it, it errors instead of quietly locking production. For the rest, teams use gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change.

      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      ↪How do you copy a table's structure? Its structure and data?

      CREATE TABLE emp_copy LIKE emp; copies columns, indexes, PK and AUTO_INCREMENT — but not foreign keys. CREATE TABLE emp_copy AS SELECT * FROM emp; (CTAS) copies column types and data but no indexes, no PK, no AUTO_INCREMENT. Best of both: CREATE TABLE … LIKE then INSERT INTO … SELECT. Structure only via CTAS: … SELECT * FROM emp WHERE 1 = 0.

      ↪What does RENAME TABLE give you that two ALTERs don't?

      RENAME TABLE logs TO logs_old, logs_new TO logs; renames several tables atomically — no other session sees a moment where logs doesn't exist. This is the classic "build a cleaned copy, then swap" pattern.

      ✂️ DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP — the deep dive

      This is the single most-asked SQL theory question in campus interviews. The trap is that the "textbook" answer ("TRUNCATE can never be rolled back") is only true for some engines. Learn the mechanism, then the engine table.

      QWhat is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?

      DELETE

      • DML — removes rows
      • Supports WHERE, ORDER BY … LIMIT, JOINs
      • Row by row: each row is locked, written to undo log + redo log
      • Fires ON DELETE triggers; FK cascades run
      • Can be rolled back (inside a transaction)
      • Does not reset AUTO_INCREMENT
      • Space is reused, not returned to the OS
      • Slow for millions of rows

      TRUNCATE

      • DDL — removes all rows, keeps the table
      • No WHERE
      • InnoDB: drops and recreates the table (new empty tablespace) — minimal logging
      • No DELETE triggers fire
      • MySQL: implicit commit → no rollback
      • Resets AUTO_INCREMENT
      • Fails if another table's FK references it
      • Very fast, size-independent

      DROP

      • DDL — removes the table: data, structure, indexes, constraints, triggers, privileges on it
      • Views that use it become invalid
      • MySQL: implicit commit → no rollback
      • Fails if referenced by an FK (drop child/FK first)
      • Only recovery: backup + binlog replay
      PropertyDELETETRUNCATEDROP
      CategoryDMLDDLDDL
      WHERE clause✔✘✘
      Removes structure✘✘✔
      Row-level logging (undo/redo per row)✔✘ (minimal)✘
      DELETE triggers fire✔✘✘
      Resets AUTO_INCREMENT (MySQL)✘✔n/a
      Rollback — MySQL / Oracle✔✘✘ (Oracle: FLASHBACK TABLE from recycle bin)
      Rollback — PostgreSQL / SQL Server✔✔ inside a transaction✔ inside a transaction
      Works on FK-referenced parent✔ (if no child rows block it)✘ (PG: CASCADE)✘
      Speed on 10M rowsslow (minutes)instantinstant

      Proof on MySQL 8 (real output)

      CREATE TABLE a (id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, v VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO a (v) VALUES ('x'),('y'),('z');           -- ids 1,2,3
DELETE FROM a;                                         -- table empty
INSERT INTO a (v) VALUES ('after-delete');
SELECT * FROM a;                                       -- id continues at 4
TRUNCATE TABLE a;
INSERT INTO a (v) VALUES ('after-truncate');
SELECT * FROM a;                                       -- id restarts at 1
      +----+--------------+
| id | v            |
+----+--------------+
|  4 | after-delete |
+----+--------------+
+----+----------------+
| id | v              |
+----+----------------+
|  1 | after-truncate |
+----+----------------+
      START TRANSACTION; DELETE FROM a; ROLLBACK;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a;            -- rows are back      → same count as before

START TRANSACTION; TRUNCATE TABLE a; ROLLBACK;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM a;            -- implicit commit    → 0 (gone for good)

TRUNCATE TABLE dept;   -- ERROR 1701 (42000): Cannot truncate a table referenced in a foreign key
                       --   constraint (`nb`.`emp`, CONSTRAINT `emp_ibfk_1`)
DROP TABLE dept;       -- ERROR 3730 (HY000): Cannot drop table 'dept' referenced by a foreign key
                       --   constraint 'emp_ibfk_1' on table 'emp'.
DELETE FROM dept WHERE id = 10;    -- ERROR 1451: Cannot delete or update a parent row: a foreign key
                                   --   constraint fails (child rows exist)
DELETE FROM dept WHERE id = 40;    -- OK: Legal has no employees
      TimeSession (MySQL)What really happens
      t1START TRANSACTION;transaction T opens
      t2INSERT INTO a (v) VALUES ('ghost');row is uncommitted
      t3CREATE TABLE zz (i INT);❗ implicit COMMIT of T before the DDL runs → 'ghost' is now permanent
      t4ROLLBACK;nothing to roll back; SELECT … WHERE v='ghost' still returns the row (verified)
      🔀
      Engine differences (the part that wins the interview)

      PostgreSQL: TRUNCATE is "transaction-safe" — inside BEGIN … ROLLBACK it is undone; DDL is transactional too. It fires ON TRUNCATE triggers (not ON DELETE).
