      Non-correlated: stands alone — you could run it by itself. Logically evaluated once, then its result is used. Correlated: refers to a column of the outer query (e.dept_id below), so its result is different for each outer row — logically re-evaluated per outer row.
      
      
      SELECT name, salary FROM emp
WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);       -- AVG = 67000 computed once
-- Asha 90000, Ravi 75000
      
      
      SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM emp e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(i.salary)
                  FROM emp i
                  WHERE i.dept_id = e.dept_id);     -- depends on the outer row
-- Asha (90000 > 82500). Dept 20: 60000 is not > 60000.
-- Priya: inner WHERE dept_id = NULL matches nothing → AVG = NULL → UNKNOWN. Karan: NULL salary.
      
      
      
      Is it slow? Logically "once per row", but optimizers are smart: MySQL caches results for repeated inputs in some cases, converts IN/EXISTS to semi-joins, and since 8.0.21 can transform some scalar subqueries into joins with a derived table (optimizer switch subquery_to_derived, off by default). When in doubt, rewrite it yourself:
      
      
      SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM emp e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id) d
  ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > d.avg_sal;

-- or with a window function (MySQL 8.0+): one scan, no join
SELECT name, dept_id, salary FROM (
  SELECT name, dept_id, salary, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS avg_sal FROM emp
) t WHERE salary > avg_sal;
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A non-correlated subquery is self-contained and is evaluated once. A correlated subquery references columns of the outer query, so logically it is evaluated for each outer row — for example comparing each employee with the average of their own department. That can be expensive on large tables, so I check the plan and, if needed, rewrite it as a join to a grouped derived table or use a window function, which computes all department averages in a single pass.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What happens if a scalar subquery returns two rows? Or zero?
          
      Two rows → ERROR 1242 (21000): Subquery returns more than 1 row. Zero rows → the value is NULL (no error). Guard with an aggregate, LIMIT 1 plus ORDER BY, or by correlating on a unique key.
      
        
      ↪Is EXISTS always correlated?
          
      Almost always in practice. An uncorrelated EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders) is just TRUE or FALSE for every row — it either returns the whole outer table or nothing.
      
        
      ↪Where can subqueries appear?
          
      SELECT list (scalar, e.g. (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) AS n), FROM (derived table — MySQL requires an alias: ERROR 1248: Every derived table must have its own alias; PostgreSQL made it optional only in version 16), WHERE / HAVING (scalar, IN, EXISTS, ANY/ALL), and in INSERT … SELECT, UPDATE … SET, DELETE … WHERE.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QShow a subquery in HAVING and a row subquery. What is the NULL catch in "max salary per department"?
    
      
      
      SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);      -- only dept 10 (82500 > 67000)
      
      
      SELECT name, dept_id, salary
FROM emp
WHERE (dept_id, salary) IN (SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) FROM emp GROUP BY dept_id);
      
      
      Asha 10 90000 · Meera 20 60000 · John 20 60000      ← ties both returned
Priya is missing: the group (NULL, 50000) never equals (NULL, 50000) because NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN.
      
      
      A window function (RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC)) would return Priya, since PARTITION BY groups NULLs together. Mention this difference — it shows real understanding.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⚖️ IN vs EXISTS vs JOIN, and the anti-join trio
      

  
      
    QIN vs EXISTS vs JOIN — what is the difference, and which is faster?
    
      
      
      Goal: "customers who placed at least one order". Three ways to write it:
      
      
      -- A) IN (semi-join)
SELECT c.* FROM customers c WHERE c.id IN (SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o);

-- B) EXISTS (semi-join)
SELECT c.* FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);

-- C) JOIN (NOT a semi-join)
SELECT c.* FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id;
      
      
      A and B: Asha, Ravi                 (2 rows — each customer once)
C:       Asha, Asha, Ravi           (3 rows — Asha once per order!)  → needs DISTINCT
      
      
      IN (subquery)EXISTSJOIN
      
        
      Semanticssemi-join: is the value in the set?semi-join: does any matching row exist?all matching pairs
      
        
      Duplicates of outer row✔ never✔ never✘ one per match
      
        
      Can return inner columns✘✘✔
      
        
      Multi-column / complex matchrow IN (a,b) IN (…)✔ any condition✔
      
        
      Stops at first matchyes, conceptually (optimizer: FirstMatch etc.)no
      
      
      
      
      Which is faster? In modern engines, usually none — they get the same plan. MySQL 8.0 rewrites IN (subquery) and (since 8.0.16) EXISTS into a semi-join and picks a strategy by cost:
      
      
      
        
      Table pull-out
      If the inner side can only match once (unique key), turn it into a plain join.
      
        
      FirstMatch
      Nested loop that stops scanning the inner table after the first match.
      
        
      LooseScan
      Read the inner table's index skipping duplicate values, then join.
      
        
      Materialization
      Run the subquery once into a temporary table with a unique index (deduplicated), then look up / join.
      
        
      Duplicate Weedout
      Run as a normal join and remove duplicate outer rows with a temporary table of row ids.
      
      
      
      
      🚫
      "EXISTS is always faster than IN"
      That rule comes from MySQL 5.5 and older, which ran IN (SELECT …) as a dependent subquery once per outer row. Since MySQL 5.6/8.0 (and long before that in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) both are planned as semi-joins. Say: "Logically equivalent for non-NULL cases; modern optimizers produce the same plan; I check EXPLAIN." The real difference is NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS — next question.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      IN and EXISTS are both semi-joins: they return each outer row at most once, as soon as one match exists. A JOIN returns one row per matching pair, so a customer with three orders appears three times and you'd need DISTINCT. On performance, MySQL 8, PostgreSQL and the others rewrite IN and EXISTS into the same semi-join plan, so I choose for readability — EXISTS for correlated multi-column conditions, IN for a simple list — and verify with EXPLAIN. The place where they really differ is the negative form with NULLs.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Does SELECT * vs SELECT 1 inside EXISTS matter?
          
      No. EXISTS only checks whether a row exists; the select list is ignored. SELECT 1 is a readability convention.
      
        
      ↪When would you choose the JOIN version anyway?
          
      When you need columns from the inner table (order amounts), or when the inner side is unique (joining to a primary key can't duplicate rows) — then a join is equivalent and the most direct.
      
        
      ↪How do you see which semi-join strategy MySQL chose?
          
      EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE (8.0.16+) or EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+): look for "semijoin", "FirstMatch", "Materialize with deduplication", "LooseScan" or "Remove duplicates … (weedout)". See Chapter 16.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QNOT IN vs NOT EXISTS vs LEFT JOIN … IS NULL — which one should you use?
    
      
      
      Goal: "customers with no orders" (expected: Meera, John). Remember order 104 has customer_id = NULL.
      
      
      -- 1) NOT IN
SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders);
-- Empty set!   (NULL in the list → every test is FALSE or UNKNOWN)

-- 2) NOT EXISTS
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);
-- Meera, John ✔

-- 3) LEFT JOIN … IS NULL
SELECT c.name FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;                          -- test the PK (never NULL in a real match)
-- Meera, John ✔
      
      
      NOT INNOT EXISTSLEFT JOIN … IS NULL
      
        
      NULL in inner column✘ returns nothing✔ correct✔ correct
      
        
      NULL in outer columnrow dropped (UNKNOWN)row returned (no match exists)row returned
      
        
      MySQL 8 plancan become an anti-join (8.0.17+) with extra NULL checks — the answer is still the NULL-trap answeranti-join (8.0.17+)outer join + filter, often converted to anti-join
      
        
      PostgreSQL plannever an anti-join (hashed subplan; very slow if it doesn't fit in memory)Hash/Merge Anti Joinusually the same Anti Join
      
        
      Readabilityshortclear intentneeds the IS NULL trick explained
      
      
      
      
      💡
      Rule
      Default to NOT EXISTS. Use NOT IN only with a constant list or a subquery column that is declared NOT NULL. In PostgreSQL, NOT IN on a large subquery can be dramatically slower, not just "risky".
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      All three express an anti-join, but they differ with NULLs. NOT IN is true only if the value differs from every value in the list; one NULL makes that unknown, so the query returns no rows. NOT EXISTS just asks whether a matching row exists, so it is NULL-safe, and the optimizers in MySQL 8 and PostgreSQL turn it into an efficient anti-join. LEFT JOIN with WHERE right.pk IS NULL is equivalent and also fine. I use NOT EXISTS by default.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪In the LEFT JOIN version, why test o.id and not o.amount?
          
      If an order had amount = NULL, o.amount IS NULL would wrongly treat that matched customer as "no orders". The primary key (or the join column) is never NULL in a real match.
      
        
      ↪Find orders whose customer does not exist (orphans).
          
      SELECT o.* FROM orders o
WHERE o.customer_id IS NOT NULL
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM customers c WHERE c.id = o.customer_id);   -- order 105
      This is how you clean data before adding a FOREIGN KEY.
      
        
      ↪Can EXCEPT do an anti-join?
          
      For whole rows, yes: SELECT id FROM customers EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM orders → 3, 4 (MySQL 8.0.31+). It treats NULLs as equal and removes duplicates, and only returns the compared columns — so it fits "which ids" questions, not "give me the full rows".
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QHow do ANY / SOME / ALL work? What is the empty-set trap?
    
      
      
      x > ANY (subquery) — TRUE if x beats at least one value (SOME is a synonym). x > ALL (subquery) — TRUE if x beats every value.
      
      
      FormEquivalent to
      
        
      x = ANY (…)x IN (…)
      
        
      x <> ALL (…)x NOT IN (…) (same NULL trap)
      
        
      x > ANY (…)x > MIN(…) (if non-empty, no NULLs)
      
        
      x > ALL (…)x > MAX(…) — except on an empty set
      
      
      
      
      SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 20);
-- Sales salaries {60000, 60000} → Asha, Ravi

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > ALL (SELECT salary FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 30);
-- HR has nobody → empty set → "> ALL of nothing" is TRUE → ALL 6 rows, even Karan (NULL)!

SELECT name FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM emp WHERE dept_id = 30);
-- MAX of nothing = NULL → UNKNOWN → Empty set
      
      
      ⚠️
      Two traps
      (1) ALL over an empty set is TRUE (vacuous truth); ANY over an empty set is FALSE. (2) A NULL in the subquery makes > ALL never TRUE (like NOT IN). The MIN/MAX rewrites behave differently in exactly these cases — mention it if you use them.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🏆 LATERAL derived tables (top-N per group)
      

  
      
    QWhat is a LATERAL join? When would you use it instead of a window function?
    
      
      
      What: a normal derived table in FROM cannot see the other tables of the same FROM clause. Marking it LATERAL lets it reference columns of tables to its left — it becomes a correlated derived table, evaluated per left row, and it may return many rows and many columns (a scalar subquery can return only one value). MySQL 8.0.14+
      
      
      SELECT d.name AS dept, t.name, t.salary
FROM dept d
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
    SELECT e.name, e.salary
    FROM emp e
    WHERE e.dept_id = d.id              -- refers to d: only legal because of LATERAL
    ORDER BY e.salary DESC
    LIMIT 2
) AS t ON TRUE
ORDER BY d.id, t.salary DESC;
      
      
      +-------------+-------+----------+
| dept        | name  | salary   |
+-------------+-------+----------+
| Engineering | Asha  | 90000.00 |
| Engineering | Ravi  | 75000.00 |
| Sales       | Meera | 60000.00 |   (tie with John — order between them is not guaranteed)
| Sales       | John  | 60000.00 |
| HR          | NULL  |     NULL |   <- kept by LEFT JOIN … ON TRUE
| Legal       | NULL  |     NULL |
+-------------+-------+----------+
      
      
      
        
      LATERAL + LIMIT
      • Can stop after N rows per group using an index on (dept_id, salary)
      • Great when groups are few and big ("latest 3 orders per customer")
      • Can return several columns/rows per outer row
      
        
      Window function (ROW_NUMBER)
      • Scans and ranks every row, then filters rn <= N
      • Simpler, more portable, handles ties explicitly (RANK/DENSE_RANK)
      • Great when you need most rows anyway
      
      
      
      
      🔀
      Engines
      PostgreSQL 9.3+: LATERAL. SQL Server: CROSS APPLY (inner) / OUTER APPLY (keeps left rows). Oracle 12c+: both LATERAL and CROSS/OUTER APPLY. MySQL: LATERAL from 8.0.14; with LEFT JOIN you must write an ON clause, hence ON TRUE.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      📦 Set operations: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
      
  
      Joins combine tables side by side (more columns). Set operations stack results on top of each other (more rows) and compare whole rows.
      

  

  
      CREATE TABLE suppliers (name VARCHAR(20), city VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO suppliers VALUES ('Tata','Pune'), ('Infy','Bengaluru'), ('Bharat',NULL);
-- customers.city = Pune, Delhi, Pune, NULL
      

  
      
    QUNION vs UNION ALL — what is the difference? What are the rules?
    
      
      
      SELECT city FROM customers UNION     SELECT city FROM suppliers;   -- Pune, Delhi, NULL, Bengaluru  (4)
SELECT city FROM customers UNION ALL SELECT city FROM suppliers;   -- 4 + 3 = 7 rows, duplicates kept
      
      
      
        
      UNION (= UNION DISTINCT)
      • Removes duplicate rows from the combined result
      • Costs a dedup step (temporary table with unique key / sort / hash)
      • NULLs count as equal: one NULL row survives
      
        
      UNION ALL
      • Keeps everything; just appends
      • Faster, can stream; MySQL 8 avoids the temp table for many UNION ALL queries
      • Use whenever duplicates are impossible or wanted
      
      
      
      
        
        
      1. Same number of columns in every SELECT, matched by position, not by name.
        2. 
        
      2. Compatible types; the result type is widened to fit all branches (e.g. INT + DECIMAL → DECIMAL).
        3. 
        
      3. Column names come from the first SELECT.
        4. 
        
      4. ORDER BY / LIMIT at the end apply to the whole result and can use only output column names/positions. To sort or limit one branch, wrap it in parentheses with its own ORDER BY + LIMIT.
        5. 
        
      5. Mixing: A UNION ALL B UNION C — a DISTINCT UNION removes duplicates from everything to its left too.
        6. 
      
      
      
      (SELECT 'customer' AS kind, name FROM customers ORDER BY name LIMIT 2)
UNION ALL
(SELECT 'supplier', name FROM suppliers ORDER BY name LIMIT 2)
ORDER BY kind, name;
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      UNION stacks the results of two queries and removes duplicate rows, which needs an extra sort or hash step; UNION ALL just appends and keeps duplicates, so it is cheaper and is what I use unless I really need deduplication. Both require the same number of columns with compatible types, the names come from the first query, and an ORDER BY at the end sorts the combined result.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Turn columns into rows (unpivot) with UNION ALL.
          
      SELECT id, 'q1' AS quarter, q1_sales AS sales FROM yearly
UNION ALL SELECT id, 'q2', q2_sales FROM yearly
UNION ALL SELECT id, 'q3', q3_sales FROM yearly
UNION ALL SELECT id, 'q4', q4_sales FROM yearly;
      
        
      ↪UNION vs JOIN in one line?
          
      JOIN combines columns of related rows horizontally using a condition; UNION combines rows of similar result sets vertically with no condition.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QINTERSECT and EXCEPT — how do they work, and how did you emulate them in older MySQL?
    
      
      
      A INTERSECT B = rows in both. A EXCEPT B = rows in A but not in B (Oracle: MINUS; EXCEPT also accepted from Oracle 21c). Both remove duplicates by default; ALL variants keep multiplicities. MySQL 8.0.31+
      
      
      SELECT city FROM customers INTERSECT SELECT city FROM suppliers;   -- Pune, NULL   ← NULL matched NULL!
SELECT city FROM customers EXCEPT    SELECT city FROM suppliers;   -- Delhi
SELECT city FROM suppliers EXCEPT    SELECT city FROM customers;   -- Bengaluru
      
      
      ℹ️
      Set operations treat NULLs as equal
      INTERSECT returns the NULL city, because set operations compare rows with "IS NOT DISTINCT FROM" semantics. A join on c.city = s.city would not match the NULLs. This is the most common trap when people "convert" INTERSECT into a JOIN.
      
      
      -- INTERSECT
SELECT DISTINCT c.city FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM suppliers s WHERE s.city <=> c.city);   -- <=> to match NULLs like INTERSECT

-- EXCEPT
SELECT DISTINCT c.city FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM suppliers s WHERE s.city <=> c.city);
      
      
      Precedence: INTERSECT binds tighter than UNION and EXCEPT (standard SQL, and MySQL 8.0.31+): A UNION B INTERSECT C = A UNION (B INTERSECT C). Use parentheses to be clear.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⚙️ Teaser: how the engine executes a join
      
  
      The result of a join is fixed by its definition; how it is computed is the optimizer's choice. Interviewers love a one-line answer for each. Full detail and EXPLAIN reading in Chapter 16.
      
  
      AlgorithmIdeaBest whenEngines
      
    
      Nested loopfor each outer row, scan the inner tabletiny tablesall
      
    
      Index nested loopfor each outer row, B+ tree lookup in the inner table's index on the join columnsmall outer side + index on inner join column (the typical OLTP join)all (MySQL's main strategy, "eq_ref"/"ref")
      
    
      Hash joinbuild a hash table on the smaller input, probe it with the otherlarge unindexed equi-joins, analyticsMySQL 8.0.18+ (replaced Block Nested Loop in 8.0.20), PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle
      
    
      Sort-merge joinsort both inputs on the key, walk them togetherinputs already sorted (index order), range/inequality joinsPostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle — not MySQL
      
  
      
  
      💡
      Index rule of thumb for joins
      Index the foreign key column on the "many" side (orders.customer_id). InnoDB creates an index automatically when you declare a FOREIGN KEY; PostgreSQL does not — a missing FK index there makes joins and parent DELETEs slow.
      

  
      PAIR → KEEP → PAD → FILTER
      Every join question: Pair all rows, Keep pairs where ON is TRUE, Pad unmatched preserved rows with NULLs (outer joins), then Filter with WHERE. Count rows by multiplying matches per key.
      

  
      ✏️ Whiteboard habit: draw the two tiny tables (with one duplicate key and one NULL) before answering any join question. You will never get the row count wrong again.
      

  
      📌 Key takeaways
        
    
      • A join = Cartesian product filtered by ON; outer joins add back unmatched rows padded with NULLs.
        • 
    
      • Row count = Σ over keys of (left count × right count) + unmatched preserved rows. LEFT JOIN ≥ left rows, never "exactly".
        • 
    
      • Right-table filters of a LEFT JOIN go in ON; in WHERE they turn it into an INNER JOIN. Use COUNT(right.pk), not COUNT(*), to count matches.
        • 
    
      • MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN: LEFT JOIN UNION ALL RIGHT JOIN … WHERE left.pk IS NULL.
        • 
    
      • NULL never matches in ON (use <=> / IS NOT DISTINCT FROM); set operations and GROUP BY treat NULLs as equal.
        • 
    
      • Self-join = two aliases of one table (employee → manager, use LEFT to keep the CEO). NATURAL JOIN is dangerous; prefer ON (or USING).
        • 
    
      • IN/EXISTS are semi-joins (no duplicates) and get the same plan in MySQL 8; JOIN can duplicate outer rows.
        • 
    
      • Anti-join: NOT EXISTS by default. NOT IN breaks on a single NULL; > ALL of an empty set is TRUE.
        • 
    
      • Correlated subqueries are logically per-row; rewrite with a grouped derived table, a window function or LATERAL when slow.
        • 
    
      • UNION dedups (cost), UNION ALL appends; INTERSECT/EXCEPT exist from MySQL 8.0.31; columns match by position, names from the first query.
        • 
  
      

  
      📚 Go deeper
        
    
      • MySQL 8.0 Reference — JOIN Clause — precise syntax, precedence of comma vs JOIN, USING/NATURAL rules.
        • 
    
      • MySQL — Optimizing IN and EXISTS with Semijoin Transformations — FirstMatch, LooseScan, materialization, weedout explained.
        • 
    
      • jOOQ blog — Say NO to Venn Diagrams When Explaining JOINs — the classic argument, with better pictures.
        • 
    
      • Use The Index, Luke — The Join Operation — nested loops, hash and merge joins and the indexes they need.
        • 
    
      • PostgreSQL — Table Expressions — joins, LATERAL and subqueries in the standard's own words.
        • 
    
      • CMU 15-445 — Join Algorithms lecture — how databases really execute joins.
        • 
  
      

  
      
    
      
      
      customers has 4 rows, orders has 5. Asha has 2 orders, Ravi 1, Meera and John none. How many rows does customers LEFT JOIN orders return?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      3 matched pairs (Asha ×2, Ravi ×1) + 2 unmatched customers = 5. A LEFT JOIN can return more rows than the left table.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      T1.x = {1,1,2,NULL}, T2.x = {1,1,1,3,NULL}. Rows from T1 INNER JOIN T2 ON T1.x = T2.x?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      2 × 3 = 6 for key 1; 2 and 3 have no partner; NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN. With <=> it would be 7.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      What does adding WHERE o.amount > 400 to customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON … do?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      NULL-padded rows have o.amount = NULL, and NULL > 400 is UNKNOWN, so WHERE drops them. Put the condition in ON to keep all customers.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      orders.customer_id contains a NULL. What does SELECT name FROM customers WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders) return?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      id <> NULL is UNKNOWN, so the AND chain is never TRUE. NOT EXISTS returns the expected Meera and John.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which statement about IN vs EXISTS in MySQL 8 is most accurate?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      The "EXISTS is faster" rule dates from MySQL 5.5. MySQL 8 transforms IN and EXISTS (8.0.16+) into semi-joins (FirstMatch, materialization, …).
      
    
      
    
      
      
      customers NATURAL JOIN orders where both tables have a column named id (and no other shared names) joins on…
      
      
      
      
      
      
      NATURAL JOIN uses every same-named column — here only id — giving a silently wrong (empty) result.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      customers.city = {Pune, Delhi, Pune, NULL}; suppliers.city = {Pune, Bengaluru, NULL}. What does INTERSECT return?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Set operations treat NULLs as equal and remove duplicates. A join on city = city would not match the NULLs.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      Mechanical definition of a join?
      Cartesian product, keep pairs where ON is TRUE, then (outer joins) add unmatched preserved rows padded with NULLs.
      
    
      Min / max rows of A LEFT JOIN B (m, n rows)?
      Min m, max m × n.
      
    
      FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL?
      A LEFT JOIN B UNION ALL A RIGHT JOIN B WHERE A.pk IS NULL.
      
    
      ON vs WHERE in a LEFT JOIN?
      ON decides matches (left rows always kept); WHERE filters after — a right-table filter there makes it an inner join.
      
    
      Count orders per customer including zero?
      LEFT JOIN + COUNT(o.id) (not COUNT(*), which gives 1 for the NULL-padded row).
      
    
      Does NULL match NULL in a join?
      No (UNKNOWN). Use <=> (MySQL) or IS NOT DISTINCT FROM.
      
    
      Semi-join vs inner join?
      Semi-join (IN/EXISTS) returns each outer row at most once; inner join returns one row per matching pair.
      
    
      Safest anti-join?
      NOT EXISTS (or LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.pk IS NULL). NOT IN fails if the subquery has a NULL.
      
    
      Correlated subquery?
      References outer columns; logically evaluated once per outer row.
      
    
      x > ALL (empty set)?
      TRUE for every row (vacuous truth). x > (SELECT MAX…) on empty set is UNKNOWN.
      
    
      LATERAL?
      Derived table that can reference earlier FROM tables (MySQL 8.0.14+; SQL Server CROSS/OUTER APPLY). Ideal for top-N per group with LIMIT.
      
    
      UNION vs UNION ALL?
      UNION removes duplicate rows (extra dedup work); UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster.
      
    
      INTERSECT / EXCEPT in MySQL?
      Native from 8.0.31; before: EXISTS / NOT EXISTS with DISTINCT (and <=> to match NULLs).
      
    
      Four join algorithms?
      Nested loop, index nested loop, hash join (MySQL 8.0.18+), sort-merge (not in MySQL).
      
  
      

      


      
  
      
    
      Chapter 09 · III · SQL Mastery
      
    
      🪟 Advanced SQL: Window Functions, CTEs, Views, Procedures & Triggers
      
    
      Rank, compare and total rows without losing them, walk hierarchies with recursion, and explain exactly when a view, procedure, function or trigger is the right tool — and when it is a trap.
      
    
      ⏱ 60 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8MySQL 8.0+ for windows & CTEsPostgreSQLOracleSQL Server
      
  
      

  
       
      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
      
    
        
      
      • Window function = a calculation over a group of related rows that keeps every row. GROUP BY collapses rows; OVER (…) does not.
        • 
      
      • Syntax: f() OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY … ROWS|RANGE BETWEEN … AND …). Partition = which rows belong together, ORDER BY = order inside, frame = which rows the current row "sees".
        • 
      
      • Salaries 100, 90, 90, 80 → ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3,4 · RANK 1,2,2,4 · DENSE_RANK 1,2,2,3. Top-N-per-group = rank inside a CTE, then filter.
        • 
      
      • Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW → running totals "just work", but LAST_VALUE looks broken. Fix: give an explicit full frame.
        • 
      
      • Window functions are computed after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING → you cannot filter on them in WHERE. Wrap in a CTE/derived table.
        • 
      
      • CTE = named temporary result for one statement. Recursive CTE = anchor UNION ALL recursive member, repeated until it returns no rows (MySQL guard: cte_max_recursion_depth = 1000).
        • 
      
      • View = saved query, stores no data. Materialized view stores the result (PostgreSQL, Oracle; SQL Server "indexed view"; MySQL has none → summary table + event/trigger).
        • 
      
      • Procedure = called with CALL, can return result sets, OUT params, control transactions. Function = returns one value, usable inside SELECT.
        • 
      
      • Trigger = code fired automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. MySQL: row-level only, BEFORE/AFTER, NEW/OLD, cannot modify its own table. Great for audit logs; dangerous as hidden business logic.
        • 
      
      • Also know: events, prepared statements, temporary tables, generated columns (VIRTUAL vs STORED), pivot with CASE + aggregate, JSON ->/->>/JSON_TABLE, WITH ROLLUP + GROUPING().
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ✏️ The single most asked question of this chapter: "ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK — show me on data." Practise drawing that table from memory.
      

  
      🧰 The advanced-SQL toolbox at a glance
      
  
      Basic SQL (Chapter 07, Chapter 08) answers "give me these rows". Advanced SQL answers harder questions: "rank each employee inside their department", "show the whole reporting chain", "hide salary from the intern team", "log every salary change automatically". Each tool below solves one kind of problem.
      
  
      
    
      📊
      Window functions
      Rank, running total, previous/next row — while keeping every row.
      
    
      🧩
      CTE (WITH)
      Name a sub-result to read top-to-bottom. Recursive CTEs walk trees and generate series.
      
    
      🔍
      View
      A saved SELECT with a name. Abstraction + security. Stores no data.
      
    
      📦
      Materialized view
      A saved SELECT and its stored result. Fast reads, can be stale.
      
    
      ⚙️
      Procedure / Function
      Code stored in the server. Procedure = action (CALL). Function = value (inside SELECT).
      
    
      🔔
      Trigger
      Code that fires by itself on INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE of a table.
      
    
      📅
      Event
      Code that fires on a schedule (MySQL's built-in cron).
      
    
      🗄️
      Extras
      Prepared statements, temp tables, generated columns, JSON, pivot, ROLLUP.
      
  
      

  
      Throughout the chapter we use one small table. Keep it in mind — the outputs refer to it.
      
  
      CREATE TABLE emp (
  id     INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name   VARCHAR(20),
  dept   VARCHAR(10),
  salary INT
);
INSERT INTO emp VALUES
 (1,'Asha','IT',90000), (2,'Bala','IT',75000), (3,'Chen','IT',90000), (4,'Divya','IT',60000),
 (5,'Esha','Sales',70000), (6,'Farid','Sales',70000), (7,'Gopi','Sales',55000),
 (8,'Hana','HR',50000);

CREATE TABLE daily_sales (day DATE PRIMARY KEY, amount INT);
INSERT INTO daily_sales VALUES
 ('2026-01-01',100), ('2026-01-02',130), ('2026-01-03',120), ('2026-01-05',150);  -- note: Jan 4 is missing
      

  
  
      📊 Window functions
      

  
      
    QWhat is a window function, and how is it different from GROUP BY?
    
      
      
      What: a window function computes a value for each row using a set of related rows (the "window"). The rows stay. You only get an extra column.
      
      
      Why it exists: before windows, a question like "show each employee with their department's average salary" needed a self-join or a correlated subquery. That is long, error-prone and often slow. A window function does it in one pass.
      
      
      Analogy: GROUP BY is like a teacher who reads out only the class average. A window function is like a report card that shows your marks and the class average on the same line.
      
      
      
      -- GROUP BY: one row per department
SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS dept_avg FROM emp GROUP BY dept;

-- Window: every employee + the department average + the gap
SELECT name, dept, salary,
       AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept)          AS dept_avg,
       salary - AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS diff
FROM emp
ORDER BY dept, salary DESC;
      
      
      namedeptsalarydept_avgdiff
      
        
      HanaHR5000050000.00000.0000
      
        
      AshaIT9000078750.000011250.0000
      
        
      ChenIT9000078750.000011250.0000
      
        
      BalaIT7500078750.0000-3750.0000
      
        
      DivyaIT6000078750.0000-18750.0000
      
        
      EshaSales7000065000.00005000.0000
      
        
      FaridSales7000065000.00005000.0000
      
        
      GopiSales5500065000.0000-10000.0000
      
      
      
      
      
        
      GROUP BY
      • Rows per group → 1
      • Non-grouped columns can't be selected (ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY)
      • Filter groups with HAVING
      • Works in every MySQL version
      
        
      Window function
      • Rows per group → unchanged
      • Any column can sit next to the result
      • Filter by wrapping in a CTE / derived table
      • MySQL 8.0+ 8.0
      
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistake
      Thinking PARTITION BY is the same as GROUP BY. Both define groups, but PARTITION BY never reduces the number of rows. Also: PARTITION BY here has nothing to do with table partitioning (splitting a table's storage).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A window function calculates something over a set of related rows but, unlike GROUP BY, it does not collapse them. Every input row stays in the output and gets an extra column — for example its rank or its department average. I define the window with OVER: PARTITION BY says which rows belong together, ORDER BY sets the order inside, and the frame says which nearby rows to use. It saves me self-joins and correlated subqueries.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Can you use GROUP BY and a window function in the same query?
          
      Yes. GROUP BY runs first, then the window runs over the grouped rows. You can even nest an aggregate inside a window: SUM(SUM(salary)) OVER () = company total, computed over the per-department sums.
      
          
      SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS dept_total,
       ROUND(100 * SUM(salary) / SUM(SUM(salary)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_company
FROM emp GROUP BY dept;
-- HR 50000 8.93 | IT 315000 56.25 | Sales 195000 34.82
      
        
      ↪What does an empty OVER () mean?
          
      The window is the whole result set (one big partition, no order). COUNT(*) OVER () puts the total row count on every row — handy for "percentage of total" and for pagination ("showing 10 of 2,340").
      
        
      ↪Which clauses can contain a window function?
          
      Only the SELECT list and ORDER BY. Not WHERE, GROUP BY or HAVING — they run before windows are computed (see filtering on a window).
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Anatomy of the OVER clause
      
  
      function_name(args) OVER (
    PARTITION BY dept                 -- 1. split rows into independent groups (optional)
    ORDER BY     salary DESC          -- 2. order rows inside each group (optional)
    ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING          -- 3. frame: which rows around the current row
             AND CURRENT ROW          --    the function may look at (optional)
)
      
  
  
      
    
      Partition
      A group of rows the window function treats independently. No PARTITION BY = the whole result is one partition.
      
    
      Peers
      Rows with the same ORDER BY value (e.g. Asha and Chen, both 90000). Peers matter for RANK and for RANGE frames.
      
    
      Frame
      The subset of the partition used for the current row: e.g. "from the start to me" or "2 rows before me to me". Only aggregate and value functions (SUM, AVG, FIRST_VALUE…) use frames; ranking functions and LAG/LEAD ignore them.
      
  
      

  
      Where windows run in the logical query order
      
  
      
    
      FROM / JOINbuild rows
      
    
      
    
      WHEREfilter rows
      
    
      
    
      GROUP BY / HAVINGgroups
      
    
      
    
      WINDOWcompute OVER()
      
    
      
    
      SELECT / DISTINCTproject
      
    
      
    
      ORDER BY / LIMITsort, cut
      
  
      
  
      Two consequences interviewers love: (1) a WHERE filter changes what the window sees — WHERE dept='IT' makes COUNT(*) OVER () count only IT rows; (2) LIMIT 3 runs after windows, so ranks are computed on the full set first. See Chapter 07 for the full execution order.
      

  
  
      Ranking: ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK
      

  
      
    QExplain ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK on the same data. When do you use each?
    
      
      
      All three number rows in the ORDER BY of the window. They differ only when there are ties (peers).
      
      
        
        
      • ROW_NUMBER() — always 1, 2, 3, … Ties get different numbers, in an arbitrary order unless you add a tie-breaker.
        • 
        
      • RANK() — ties share a number, then the next number skips (like the Olympics: two golds, no silver, next is bronze). Rank = 1 + number of rows strictly ahead of me.
        • 
        
      • DENSE_RANK() — ties share a number, no gaps. Dense rank = 1 + number of distinct values ahead of me.
        • 
      
      
      
      SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, id) AS row_num,   -- id = tie-breaker, repeatable
       RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)     AS `rank`,    -- RANK is reserved in MySQL 8: back-quote
       DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC)     AS dense_rnk
FROM emp
ORDER BY salary DESC, id;
      
      
      namesalaryROW_NUMBERRANKDENSE_RANK
      
        
      Asha90000111
      
        
      Chen90000211
      
        
      Bala7500033 (2 skipped)2
      
        
      Esha70000443
      
        
      Farid70000543
      
        
      Divya6000066 (5 skipped)4
      
        
      Gopi55000775
      
        
      Hana50000886
      
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      Tie-breaker trap
      Notice ROW_NUMBER has , id but RANK/DENSE_RANK do not. If you add id to the RANK window too, Asha and Chen are no longer peers and RANK and DENSE_RANK also become 1..8. Ties exist only on the window's ORDER BY key. A shared WINDOW w AS (…) is convenient, but only when every function really wants the same ordering.
      
      
      🏆 1-2-3-4 · 1-1-3-4 · 1-1-2-3
      ROW_NUMBER = seat numbers (everyone gets a unique seat). RANK = Olympic medals (two golds → next is bronze). DENSE_RANK = "dense" = no holes.
      
      
      TaskUseWhy
      
        
      Exactly one row per group (latest order, dedupe)ROW_NUMBER + unique tie-breakerNever returns 2 rows for "1st"
      
        
      Nth highest distinct salary; "top 3 salaries" incl. tiesDENSE_RANKNo gaps, so 2nd = 2nd distinct value
      
        
      Competition-style ranking (leaderboards)RANKShows how many people are ahead
      
        
      Pagination / numbering rowsROW_NUMBERContiguous numbers
      
      
      
      
      WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, dept, salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr
  FROM emp
)
SELECT dept, name, salary, dr
FROM ranked
WHERE dr <= 2
ORDER BY dept, dr, name;
      
      
      +-------+-------+--------+----+
| dept  | name  | salary | dr |
+-------+-------+--------+----+
| HR    | Hana  |  50000 |  1 |
| IT    | Asha  |  90000 |  1 |
| IT    | Chen  |  90000 |  1 |
| IT    | Bala  |  75000 |  2 |
| Sales | Esha  |  70000 |  1 |
| Sales | Farid |  70000 |  1 |
| Sales | Gopi  |  55000 |  2 |
+-------+-------+--------+----+
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      All of MySQL 8, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server and SQLite (3.25+) support these functions. PostgreSQL accepts AS rank unquoted; MySQL 8 throws ERROR 1064 because RANK became a reserved word in 8.0.2. Snowflake, BigQuery, DuckDB and Teradata add a QUALIFY clause to filter on a window directly — MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server do not have it, so you wrap in a CTE.
      
      
      🚫
      Fails interviews
      Using ROW_NUMBER() = 2 for "second highest salary". If two people tie at the top, row 2 is the same top salary. Use DENSE_RANK() = 2 (or the classic MAX(salary) WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) …)).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      All three number rows by the window's ORDER BY; they only differ on ties. ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique number, so tied rows get arbitrary order unless I add a tie-breaker. RANK gives ties the same number and then skips, like 1, 1, 3. DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number without gaps, like 1, 1, 2. For "Nth highest salary" I use DENSE_RANK; for "exactly one latest row per customer" I use ROW_NUMBER with a unique tie-breaker.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Find the Nth highest salary — with and without window functions.
          
      
            
      -- With windows (returns no row if N is too big)
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr FROM emp
) t WHERE dr = 3;                                  -- 70000

-- Return NULL instead of an empty set (what LeetCode expects)
SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2) AS third;

-- No LIMIT, no windows (Paytm's follow-up): N-1 distinct salaries are bigger
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM emp e1
WHERE 2 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT salary) FROM emp e2 WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary);
      
            
      More variants in Chapter 10.
      
        
      ↪Is ROW_NUMBER deterministic?
          
      Only if the window's ORDER BY is unique. With ties, two runs (or a different plan, or a replica) may number tied rows differently. Always add a unique column (usually the PK) as the last ORDER BY key.
      
        
      ↪Delete duplicate emails but keep the lowest id — with a window.
          
      DELETE FROM person WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM person
  ) t                       -- the extra derived table avoids MySQL ERROR 1093
  WHERE rn > 1
);
      
        
      ↪Does ORDER BY inside OVER sort the final output?
          
      No. It only orders rows for the calculation. The output order is undefined unless the outer query has its own ORDER BY. Rows often come out in window order by accident — never rely on it.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      🧪 Try it: ranking-function comparer
      
    
      Edit the name score list (comma-separated), pick the sort direction and NTILE buckets. Rows with tied scores (peers) are tinted. Tied rows keep your input order here — in a real database that order is arbitrary unless you add a tie-breaker.
      
    
      
      
    
      
    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
    
      
    
      
    
      
    
      
  
      
  
  

  
      NTILE, PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST
      
  
      
    QWhat do NTILE, PERCENT_RANK and CUME_DIST return? Give the formulas.
    
      
      
      
        
      NTILE(n)
      Splits the ordered partition into n buckets as equal as possible and returns the bucket number 1..n. If rows don't divide evenly, the first buckets get one extra row. It looks only at positions, not ties — two equal salaries can land in different buckets.
      
        
      PERCENT_RANK()
      (RANK − 1) / (rows in partition − 1). Range 0..1. The first row is always 0. "What fraction of the others is ahead of me?"
      
        
      CUME_DIST()
      (rows ahead of me + my peers incl. me) / rows in partition. Range (0..1]. The last row is always 1. "What fraction of rows is at my level or better?"
      
      
      
      
      SELECT name, salary,
       NTILE(3)                        OVER w AS bucket,
       ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER w, 3)        AS pct_rank,
       ROUND(CUME_DIST()    OVER w, 3)        AS cume
FROM emp
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary DESC)
ORDER BY salary DESC, id;
      
      
      namesalarybucketpct_rankcume
      
        
      Asha90000100.25
      
        
      Chen90000100.25
      
        
      Bala7500010.2860.375
      
        
      Esha7000020.4290.625
      
        
      Farid7000020.4290.625
      
        
      Divya6000020.7140.75
      
        
      Gopi5500030.8570.875
      
        
      Hana50000311
      
      
      
      
      8 rows into 3 buckets → sizes 3, 3, 2. Use cases: quartiles (NTILE(4)), "top 10% of customers" (CUME_DIST() <= 0.1), percentile dashboards.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Trap
      "Top 25% by NTILE(4)" is not the same as "top 25% by value". NTILE fills buckets by count and can split peers across buckets. If ties must stay together, use PERCENT_RANK/CUME_DIST.
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      For a true median/percentile value, PostgreSQL and Oracle have PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary); SQL Server offers it as a window function (… OVER (PARTITION BY …)). MySQL has no PERCENTILE_CONT/MEDIAN — compute it with ROW_NUMBER and COUNT (see Chapter 10).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      LAG and LEAD — looking at the previous / next row
      
  
      
    QHow do you compute day-over-day change? Explain LAG and LEAD.
    
      
      
      LAG(expr, offset = 1, default = NULL) returns expr from the row offset rows before the current row in the window order. LEAD looks after. If there is no such row (the first row for LAG), you get the default (NULL). They ignore frames.
      
      
      Why it matters: before window functions this needed a self-join on "the previous date", which breaks when dates have gaps and is slow on big tables.
      
      
      SELECT day, amount,
       LAG(amount)  OVER w                                   AS prev_amt,
       amount - LAG(amount) OVER w                           AS change_abs,
       ROUND(100 * (amount - LAG(amount) OVER w) / LAG(amount) OVER w, 2) AS pct_change,
       LEAD(amount) OVER w                                   AS next_amt
FROM daily_sales
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY day)
ORDER BY day;
      
      
      +------------+--------+----------+------------+------------+----------+
| day        | amount | prev_amt | change_abs | pct_change | next_amt |
+------------+--------+----------+------------+------------+----------+
| 2026-01-01 |    100 |     NULL |       NULL |       NULL |      130 |
| 2026-01-02 |    130 |      100 |         30 |      30.00 |      120 |
| 2026-01-03 |    120 |      130 |        -10 |      -7.69 |      150 |
| 2026-01-05 |    150 |      120 |         30 |      25.00 |     NULL |
+------------+--------+----------+------------+------------+----------+
      
      
      ⚠️
      The "previous row ≠ previous day" trap
      Jan 5 was compared with Jan 3 because Jan 4 has no row. LAG moves by rows, not by calendar. If the question says "compared with yesterday" (LeetCode "Rising Temperature"), check the gap DATEDIFF(day, LAG(day) OVER w) = 1, self-join on day = prev.day + INTERVAL 1 DAY, or first fill missing dates with a recursive date series (below).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      LAG gives me a value from an earlier row in the window order and LEAD from a later row, with an optional offset and default. For day-over-day change I compute amount minus LAG(amount) ordered by date. I always check whether "previous" means the previous row or the previous calendar day, because missing dates silently compare the wrong days.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪How would you find 3 consecutive days of rising sales?
          
      Compare with two lags: amount > LAG(amount,1) OVER w AND LAG(amount,1) OVER w > LAG(amount,2) OVER w (plus a date-gap check). For general "streaks", use the gaps-and-islands trick: day - INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY day) DAY is constant inside a run of consecutive days, so GROUP BY that value. Full solutions in Chapter 10.
      
        
      ↪How do you avoid NULL in the first row?
          
      Pass a default: LAG(amount, 1, 0), or wrap with COALESCE. But think first — a NULL "change" for the first day is usually the honest answer; a 0 would claim "no change".
      
        
      ↪Time since the user's previous login?
          
      SELECT user_id, login_at,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(MINUTE,
                     LAG(login_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_at),
                     login_at) AS mins_since_prev
FROM logins;
      Add PARTITION BY so one user's first login is not compared with another user's last login — a very common bug.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE — and the default-frame trap
      
  
      
    QWhy does LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day) just return the current row's amount?
    
      
      
      Because of the default frame. When a window has ORDER BY but no frame, the SQL standard (and MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) uses:
      
      
      RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW   -- "from the start up to me (and my peers)"
      
      
      So the "last" row of the frame is the current row (or its last peer). FIRST_VALUE looks right by luck — the frame always starts at the first row. LAST_VALUE and NTH_VALUE look broken.
      
      
      SELECT day, amount,
  FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day)                       AS first_v,
  LAST_VALUE(amount)  OVER (ORDER BY day)                       AS last_wrong,
  LAST_VALUE(amount)  OVER (ORDER BY day
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS last_right,
  NTH_VALUE(amount,2) OVER (ORDER BY day)                       AS second_default,
  NTH_VALUE(amount,2) OVER (ORDER BY day
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS second_full
FROM daily_sales ORDER BY day;
      
      
      dayamountfirst_vlast_wronglast_rightsecond_defaultsecond_full
      
        
      2026-01-01100100100150NULL130
      
        
      2026-01-02130100130150130130
      
        
      2026-01-03120100120150130130
      
        
      2026-01-05150100150150130130
      
      
      
      
      💡
      Three safe fixes
      (1) Give a full frame ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. (2) Use FIRST_VALUE with the ORDER BY reversed (ORDER BY day DESC) — no frame issue at all. (3) For "first and last per group in one row", use MAX(CASE WHEN rn_asc = 1 …) over two ROW_NUMBERs.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Ties make it even weirder
      With RANGE, the frame ends at the last peer of the current row. If two orders share a date, LAST_VALUE for the first of them already returns the other one's value — and which one is "last" among peers is arbitrary.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      With an ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default frame is RANGE from the start of the partition to the current row and its peers. FIRST_VALUE looks fine, but LAST_VALUE just returns the current row, because the frame ends there. I fix it with ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING, or by using FIRST_VALUE with the order reversed.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What is the default frame when there is NO ORDER BY in OVER?
          
      The whole partition. SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY d) gives the partition total on every row; add ORDER BY and the same expression silently becomes a running total. Adding or removing ORDER BY changes the meaning — say this out loud in interviews.
      
        
      ↪Do ROW_NUMBER, RANK, LAG, LEAD use the frame?
          
      No. Ranking functions, NTILE, PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST, LAG and LEAD work on the whole partition and ignore any frame clause. Frames matter for aggregates (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX…) and FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE / NTH_VALUE.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Aggregate windows: running total, moving average, share of total
      
  
      
    QWrite a running total and a 3-day moving average.
    
      
      
      Any aggregate (SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX) becomes a window function when you add OVER. The frame decides which rows go into the sum.
      
      
      SELECT day, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_total,
  AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)         AS mavg_3_rows,
  AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY day RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 2 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS mavg_3_days,
  ROUND(100 * amount / SUM(amount) OVER (), 2)                                     AS pct_of_total
FROM daily_sales ORDER BY day;
      
      
      dayamountrunning_totalmavg_3_rowsmavg_3_dayspct_of_total
      
        
      2026-01-01100100100.0000100.000020.00
      
        
      2026-01-02130230115.0000115.000026.00
      
        
      2026-01-03120350116.6667116.666724.00
      
        
      2026-01-05150500133.3333135.000030.00
      
      
      
      
      Look at Jan 5. ROWS 2 PRECEDING takes the 3 previous rows (Jan 2, 3, 5 → 400/3). RANGE INTERVAL 2 DAY PRECEDING takes rows whose date is within 2 days (Jan 3, 5 → 270/2). For "last 7 days" business metrics, a RANGE frame on a date is the correct one — gaps don't stretch the window.
      
      
      🌍
      Real-world story
      A dashboard showed a "7-day moving average" with ROWS 6 PRECEDING. During a holiday week with no orders on 3 days, the "7-day" average quietly covered 10 calendar days and looked healthier than reality. Switching to RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (or filling missing dates first) fixed it.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Running total per customer that restarts for each customer?
          
      Add PARTITION BY customer_id: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date, order_id ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING). ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING is short for ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
      
        
      ↪How is a running total computed efficiently?
          
      The engine sorts each partition once and keeps an accumulator, so a running SUM is roughly O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the scan. A correlated subquery (SELECT SUM(…) WHERE d <= t.d) is O(n²). An index on (partition cols, order cols) can remove the sort.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      ROWS vs RANGE frames (and peers)
      
  
      
    QWhat is the difference between ROWS and RANGE in a window frame?
    
      
      
        
        
      • ROWS counts physical rows: "2 rows before me". Peers are treated as separate rows.
        • 
        
      • RANGE works on the value of the ORDER BY key: "rows whose key is within 2 days of mine". All peers of the current row are always inside together. RANGE with an offset needs exactly one numeric/date ORDER BY column.
        • 
      
      
      
      CREATE TABLE sales (id INT PRIMARY KEY, sale_date DATE, amount INT);
INSERT INTO sales VALUES (1,'2026-03-01',100),(2,'2026-03-02',50),(3,'2026-03-02',30),(4,'2026-03-03',20);

SELECT id, sale_date, amount,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date)                                        AS default_range,
  SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY sale_date, id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS rows_frame
FROM sales ORDER BY sale_date, id;
      
      
      idsale_dateamountdefault_rangerows_frame
      
        
      12026-03-01100100100
      
        
      22026-03-0250180150
      
        
      32026-03-0230180180
      
        
      42026-03-0320200200
      
      
      
      
      With the default RANGE frame, rows 2 and 3 are peers, so both already include each other: 100+50+30 = 180. With ROWS, row 2 sees only rows 1–2. Neither is "wrong" — RANGE answers "total up to and including this date", ROWS answers "total up to this row".
      
      
      🎟️ ROWS = seats · RANGE = values
      ROWS counts seats in the queue ("the 2 people in front of me"). RANGE asks "everyone whose ticket time is within 2 minutes of mine" — and your twin with the same ticket time always comes along.
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      MySQL 8 supports ROWS and RANGE (including RANGE … INTERVAL n DAY PRECEDING). PostgreSQL 11+ adds GROUPS frames (count peer groups) and EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW / TIES / GROUP; Oracle 21c also has GROUPS and EXCLUDE. SQL Server supports ROWS fully but RANGE only with UNBOUNDED/CURRENT ROW bounds (no value offsets).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      🧪 Try it: frame visualizer
      
    
      Pick a frame, then click any row to make it the current row. Highlighted rows are inside its frame. The table shows SUM, FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE of amount for every row under that frame.
      
    
      
      
    
      
    
      
    
      
    
      
  
      
  
  

  
      The named WINDOW clause
      
  
      When several functions share a window, name it once. You can also extend a named window by adding a frame or ORDER BY (but not by redefining PARTITION BY).
      
  
      SELECT name, dept, salary,
       RANK()       OVER w                         AS rnk,
       SUM(salary)  OVER (w ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS running_dept_payroll,
       AVG(salary)  OVER d                         AS dept_avg
FROM emp
WINDOW d AS (PARTITION BY dept),
       w AS (d ORDER BY salary DESC);           -- w builds on d
      
  
      Clauses are logically placed after HAVING and before ORDER BY. Supported in MySQL 8, PostgreSQL, SQLite, Oracle 21c+ and SQL Server 2022+.
      

  
      Filtering on a window function (why WHERE fails)
      
  
      
    QWhy can't I write WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) = 1? How do I fix it?
    
      
      
      WHERE runs before window functions are computed (see the order flow). At WHERE time, the rank does not exist yet. The same is true for HAVING. MySQL raises ERROR 3593: You cannot use the window function 'row_number' in this context.
      
      
      -- ✘ WRONG
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) = 1;

-- ✔ RIGHT: compute in an inner query, filter in the outer one
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders o
)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1;
      
      
      Also: you cannot use a SELECT alias of a window in WHERE (aliases don't exist yet either), and you cannot nest a window function inside another window function.
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, DuckDB and Teradata support QUALIFY rn = 1, a "WHERE for windows". MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server need the CTE/derived-table wrapper. Oracle and SQL Server can also do FETCH FIRST 1 ROWS WITH TIES with ORDER BY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (…) as a trick.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING, so the value doesn't exist when WHERE runs. I compute the window in a CTE or derived table and filter on it in the outer query. Some warehouses have QUALIFY for this, but MySQL and PostgreSQL don't.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      MySQL version note and pre-8.0 workarounds
      
  
      🔀
      Version check MySQL 8.0+
      Window functions and CTEs arrived in MySQL 8.0 (MariaDB 10.2). MySQL 5.7 and older have neither. PostgreSQL has had windows since 8.4 (2009), Oracle since 8i, SQL Server since 2005 (full frames 2012), SQLite since 3.25. If an interviewer says "assume MySQL 5.7", you need the workarounds below.
      
  
      
    QHow did people do ranking and running totals before MySQL 8?
    
      
      
      
        
      
        
      
          
      -- RANK inside department = 1 + number of colleagues earning strictly more
SELECT e1.name, e1.dept, e1.salary,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) + 1 FROM emp e2
        WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept AND e2.salary > e1.salary) AS rnk,
       -- DENSE_RANK: count DISTINCT higher salaries instead
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary) + 1 FROM emp e2
        WHERE e2.dept = e1.dept AND e2.salary > e1.salary) AS dense_rnk
FROM emp e1;
      
          
      Correct and portable, but O(n²) per partition. Fine for small tables, painful for millions of rows.
      
        
      
        
      
          
      -- ROW_NUMBER per dept with session variables (the "hacky" 5.x way)
SELECT name, dept, salary, rn FROM (
  SELECT name, dept, salary,
         @rn := IF(@d = dept, @rn + 1, 1) AS rn,
         @d  := dept                       AS d_marker
  FROM emp CROSS JOIN (SELECT @rn := 0, @d := NULL) init
  ORDER BY dept, salary DESC
) t;
      
          
      ⚠️
      Why this is fragile
      It relies on the engine evaluating the SELECT expressions in order and after the ORDER BY — which MySQL never guaranteed. Setting user variables inside expressions is deprecated in MySQL 8.0 (it gives a warning). Mention it to show history, then say "in 8.0 I'd use ROW_NUMBER".
      
        
      
        
      
          
      -- Running total via self-join + GROUP BY
SELECT a.day, a.amount, SUM(b.amount) AS running_total
FROM daily_sales a
JOIN daily_sales b ON b.day <= a.day
GROUP BY a.day, a.amount
ORDER BY a.day;
      
          
      Same O(n²) shape. A window does it in one sorted pass.
      
        
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🧩 Common Table Expressions (WITH)
      
  
      A CTE (Common Table Expression) is a named, temporary result that lives for one statement only. You write it at the top with WITH name AS (…) and then use name like a table below. Think of it as giving a sub-step of your query a name, like a variable in code.
      

  
      Non-recursive CTEs
      
  
      
    QWhat is a CTE and why would you use one instead of a subquery?
    
      
      
      What: WITH x AS (SELECT …) SELECT … FROM x. The CTE is visible only to the statement that defines it. Nothing is saved in the schema.
      
      
      Why it exists:
      
      
        
        
      • Readability — the query reads top-to-bottom, step by step, instead of inside-out like nested subqueries.
        • 
        
      • Reuse in one statement — reference the same CTE twice (e.g. join it to itself) without copy-pasting the subquery.
        • 
        
      • Recursion — only a CTE can refer to itself (WITH RECURSIVE). Derived tables cannot.
        • 
        
      • Filtering on window results — rank inside the CTE, filter outside (see why WHERE fails).
        • 
      
      
      
      WITH dept_avg AS (                       -- step 1: average per dept
  SELECT dept, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
  FROM emp
  GROUP BY dept
),
company AS (                             -- step 2: one number for the company
  SELECT AVG(salary) AS avg_all FROM emp
)
SELECT d.dept, ROUND(d.avg_sal) AS avg_sal, ROUND(c.avg_all) AS company_avg
FROM dept_avg d CROSS JOIN company c
WHERE d.avg_sal > c.avg_all;            -- step 3: compare
      
      
      +------+---------+-------------+
| dept | avg_sal | company_avg |
+------+---------+-------------+
| IT   |   78750 |       70000 |
+------+---------+-------------+
      
      
      Note: one WITH, several CTEs separated by commas. A later CTE may use an earlier one.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistakes
      (1) Writing WITH twice for two CTEs — use one WITH and commas. (2) Putting a semicolon after the CTE — the CTE and its main query are one statement. (3) Expecting the CTE to exist in the next statement — it does not; use a temporary table or a view for that.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A CTE is a named sub-query defined with WITH that lives only for one statement. I use it mainly for readability — I can break a big query into named steps — and to reference the same intermediate result more than once. It is also the only way to write recursive queries, like walking an org chart. It is not stored anywhere; if I need the result across statements I use a temporary table or a view.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Is a CTE faster than a subquery?
          
      Usually neither faster nor slower — it is mostly syntax. In MySQL 8 the optimizer can merge a CTE into the outer query (like a derived table) or materialize it once into an internal temporary table; a CTE referenced twice is materialized once and reused, which can beat repeating a subquery twice. In PostgreSQL ≤ 11 a CTE was always materialized (an "optimization fence"); since PG 12 a simple, side-effect-free CTE used once is inlined. Always check with EXPLAIN (Chapter 16).
      
        
      ↪Can a CTE be used with UPDATE or DELETE?
          
      Yes in MySQL 8: WITH … UPDATE … / WITH … DELETE … work (multi-table form). PostgreSQL goes further: data-modifying CTEs like WITH moved AS (DELETE FROM a … RETURNING *) INSERT INTO b SELECT * FROM moved; — MySQL does not support DML inside a CTE.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Recursive CTEs: series, hierarchies, bill of materials
      
  
      
    QHow does a recursive CTE work? Write one that shows the full org chart with level and path.
    
      
      
      What: a CTE that refers to itself. It has two parts joined by UNION ALL (or UNION):
      
      
      
        
      Anchor member
      The starting rows. Runs once. Example: the CEO (manager_id IS NULL).
      
        
      Recursive member
      Joins the table to the rows produced in the previous step. Runs again and again.
      
        
      Termination
      Stops when the recursive member returns zero new rows. If it never does, you have an infinite loop (MySQL stops you at 1000 levels).
      
      
      
      
      How it runs, step by step (this is what interviewers want to hear):
      
      
        
        
      1. Run the anchor → result set R0 (e.g. Ann the CEO). Put it in the output and in a "working table".
        2. 
        
      2. Run the recursive member using only the working table (the newest rows) → R1 (Ann's direct reports).
        3. 
        
      3. Append R1 to the output; R1 becomes the new working table.
        4. 
        
      4. Repeat step 2–3 with R1 → R2, R2 → R3 …
        5. 
        
      5. Stop when a step produces no rows. Output = R0 ∪ R1 ∪ R2 ∪ …
        6. 
      
      
      
      Despite the name, it is really iteration (a loop over levels, breadth-first), not function-call recursion.
      
      
      
      CREATE TABLE staff (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(20), manager_id INT, INDEX (manager_id));
INSERT INTO staff VALUES (1,'Ann',NULL),(2,'Bob',1),(3,'Cat',1),(4,'Dan',2),(5,'Eve',2),(6,'Fay',4);

WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  -- anchor: the root
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 1 AS lvl,
         CAST(name AS CHAR(500)) AS path        -- widen! column type comes from the anchor
  FROM staff
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  -- recursive member: people whose manager is in the previous level
  SELECT s.id, s.name, s.manager_id, o.lvl + 1,
         CONCAT(o.path, ' > ', s.name)
  FROM staff s
  JOIN org o ON s.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT id, lvl, CONCAT(REPEAT('    ', lvl - 1), name) AS tree, path
FROM org
ORDER BY path;
      
      
      +----+-----+-----------------+-----------------------+
| id | lvl | tree            | path                  |
+----+-----+-----------------+-----------------------+
|  1 |   1 | Ann             | Ann                   |
|  2 |   2 |     Bob         | Ann > Bob             |
|  4 |   3 |         Dan     | Ann > Bob > Dan       |
|  6 |   4 |             Fay | Ann > Bob > Dan > Fay |
|  5 |   3 |         Eve     | Ann > Bob > Eve       |
|  3 |   2 |     Cat         | Ann > Cat             |
+----+-----+-----------------+-----------------------+
      
      
      🚫
      The two errors everyone hits in MySQL
      ERROR 1406: Data too long for column 'path' — the CTE's column types are fixed by the anchor only. name is VARCHAR(20), so the growing path overflows. Fix: CAST(name AS CHAR(500)) in the anchor.
      ERROR 3636: Recursive query aborted after 1001 iterations — your recursion never stops (a cycle, or a missing WHERE in a generator). Fix the logic first; raise SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 10000; only if the data is truly deep.
      
      
      ℹ️
      Rules for the recursive member (MySQL)
      It must not contain aggregate functions, window functions, GROUP BY, ORDER BY or DISTINCT; LIMIT is allowed since 8.0.19. It may reference the CTE only once, and not on the right side of a LEFT JOIN. Do aggregation outside the CTE. Forgetting the word RECURSIVE gives "Table 'org' doesn't exist".
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A recursive CTE has an anchor query that produces the starting rows, then UNION ALL, then a recursive query that joins the table to the rows produced in the previous step. The engine runs the anchor once, then keeps running the recursive part on the newest rows until it returns nothing. For an org chart the anchor is the CEO and the recursive part finds employees whose manager is in the previous level; I carry a level counter and a path string along. I make sure it terminates, I index manager_id, and in MySQL I remember the 1000-level default limit.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Now go the other way: show the chain of command above Fay.
          
      Bottom-up: anchor on Fay, recursive member joins managers to the current row (m.id = c.manager_id).
      
          
      WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (
  SELECT id, name, manager_id, 0 AS hops FROM staff WHERE id = 6
  UNION ALL
  SELECT m.id, m.name, m.manager_id, c.hops + 1
  FROM staff m JOIN chain c ON m.id = c.manager_id
)
SELECT hops, name FROM chain ORDER BY hops;
-- 0 Fay | 1 Dan | 2 Bob | 3 Ann
      
        
      ↪Count everyone (direct + indirect) under each manager.
          
      Build an ancestor→descendant "closure" inside the CTE, aggregate outside (aggregates are banned in the recursive member).
      
          
      WITH RECURSIVE closure AS (
  SELECT manager_id AS ancestor, id AS descendant FROM staff WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.ancestor, s.id FROM closure c JOIN staff s ON s.manager_id = c.descendant
)
SELECT s.name, COUNT(c.descendant) AS total_under
FROM staff s LEFT JOIN closure c ON c.ancestor = s.id
GROUP BY s.id, s.name ORDER BY s.id;
-- Ann 5 | Bob 3 | Cat 0 | Dan 1 | Eve 0 | Fay 0
      
        
      ↪What if the data has a cycle (A manages B, B manages A)?
          
      With UNION ALL the loop never ends → ERROR 3636. Three fixes:
      
          
      • UNION (distinct) instead of UNION ALL — a row already produced is not added again, so the loop stops. Works only if the carried columns repeat exactly (no growing level/path).
        • 
          
      • Visited list — carry a path string and skip rows already in it: WHERE LOCATE(CONCAT(',', s.id, ','), r.visited) = 0.
        • 
          
      • Depth cap — WHERE r.lvl < 20 as a safety net.
      
          
      PostgreSQL 14+ has a built-in CYCLE id SET is_cycle USING path clause and a SEARCH DEPTH/BREADTH FIRST clause; MySQL has neither.
      
        
      ↪How did you do hierarchies before MySQL 8?
          
      Fixed-depth chains of self LEFT JOINs (one per level), a stored-procedure loop, or a different data model: closure table (store every ancestor–descendant pair), nested sets (left/right numbers) or materialized path ('/1/2/4/' + LIKE '/1/2/%'). See Chapter 21 for schema design trade-offs.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QGenerate the numbers 1–10 and a calendar of dates, and use it to fill missing days in a report.
    
      
      
      MySQL has no generate_series() (PostgreSQL does). A tiny recursive CTE is the standard replacement. The classic use: a sales report must show every day, including days with zero sales (our daily_sales is missing Jan 4).
      
      
      -- 1..10
WITH RECURSIVE n AS (
  SELECT 1 AS k
  UNION ALL
  SELECT k + 1 FROM n WHERE k < 10      -- the WHERE is the brake!
)
SELECT k FROM n;

-- Calendar + LEFT JOIN = report with no gaps
WITH RECURSIVE cal AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-01-01' AS day
  UNION ALL
  SELECT day + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM cal WHERE day < '2026-01-05'
)
SELECT c.day, COALESCE(s.amount, 0) AS amount
FROM cal c
LEFT JOIN daily_sales s ON s.day = c.day
ORDER BY c.day;
      
      
      +------------+--------+
| day        | amount |
+------------+--------+
| 2026-01-01 |    100 |
| 2026-01-02 |    130 |
| 2026-01-03 |    120 |
| 2026-01-04 |      0 |   <-- filled
| 2026-01-05 |    150 |
+------------+--------+
      
      
      🔀
      Other engines
      PostgreSQL: SELECT generate_series(DATE '2026-01-01', DATE '2026-01-05', INTERVAL '1 day'). Oracle: SELECT LEVEL FROM dual CONNECT BY LEVEL <= 10 (also CONNECT BY PRIOR for hierarchies). SQL Server: recursive CTE without the word RECURSIVE (default limit MAXRECURSION 100) or GENERATE_SERIES in SQL Server 2022.
      
      
      💡
      Production tip
      For real reporting, keep a permanent calendar (date dimension) table with 10–20 years of dates plus columns like weekday, month, is_holiday. It is faster than regenerating dates and is standard in data warehouses (Chapter 20).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QBill of materials: how many of each basic part do I need to build one bicycle?
    
      
      
      A BOM (bill of materials) is a tree where each edge has a quantity. A bicycle needs 2 wheels; each wheel needs 32 spokes → 64 spokes. The trick: multiply quantities along the path, then sum per part outside the CTE.
      
      
      CREATE TABLE bom (assembly VARCHAR(20), component VARCHAR(20), qty INT);
INSERT INTO bom VALUES
 ('bicycle','wheel',2), ('bicycle','frame',1), ('wheel','spoke',32),
 ('wheel','tyre',1), ('frame','bolt',4), ('wheel','bolt',2);

WITH RECURSIVE parts AS (
  SELECT component, qty AS total_qty
  FROM bom WHERE assembly = 'bicycle'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT b.component, p.total_qty * b.qty           -- multiply down the tree
  FROM bom b JOIN parts p ON b.assembly = p.component
)
SELECT component, SUM(total_qty) AS need
FROM parts
WHERE component NOT IN (SELECT assembly FROM bom)   -- leaf parts only
GROUP BY component;
      
      
      spoke 64 | tyre 2 | bolt 8   (4 from frame + 2×2 from wheels)
      
    
      
  
      

  
      CTE vs subquery vs derived table vs temp table vs view
      
  
      
    QCTE vs subquery vs derived table vs temporary table vs view — when do you use which?
    
      
      
      They all hold "a query result you then query again". The difference is lifetime, reuse and whether data is stored.
      
      
      SubqueryDerived tableCTETemporary tableView
      
        
      Looks likeWHERE x IN (SELECT…)FROM (SELECT…) tWITH t AS (…)CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tCREATE VIEW t AS
      
        
      Lives forone statementone statementone statementthe session (until drop/disconnect)forever (schema object)
      
        
      Visible toits spot onlyits FROM onlywhole statementthis connection onlyeveryone with privilege
      
        
      Reference twice✘ copy-paste✘ copy-paste✔~ not twice in one query (MySQL)✔
      
        
      Recursion✘✘✔✘~ view can contain a recursive CTE
      
        
      Stores datanomaybe (internal temp)maybe (internal temp)yesno
      
        
      Can be indexed✘~ auto-key by optimizer~ auto-key by optimizer✔ you add them✘ (uses base indexes)
      
        
      Best forsimple filters, EXISTS/INone-off intermediate stepreadable multi-step queries, recursionbig intermediate result reused by many statementsreusable abstraction, security
      
      
      
      
      🔀
      Materialize or inline?
      MySQL 8: derived tables and CTEs are either merged into the outer query or materialized into an internal temp table (hints MERGE / NO_MERGE). PostgreSQL 12+: a non-recursive, side-effect-free CTE referenced once is inlined; force a choice with WITH x AS MATERIALIZED (…) or AS NOT MATERIALIZED. Before PG 12 every CTE was an optimization fence — a famous source of slow queries. SQL Server: CTEs are always inlined (never cached) — a CTE referenced 3 times runs 3 times.
      
      
      S · D · C · T · V
      "Small Detours Cost Temporary Visits" — lifetime grows left to right: Subquery, Derived, CTE (statement) → Temp table (session) → View (forever).
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🔍 Views and materialized views
      

  
      
    QWhat is a view? Does it store data? Why use one?
    
      
      
      What: a view is a saved SELECT with a name — a "virtual table". Only the query text (definition) is stored in the data dictionary. A normal view stores no rows. Every time you query it, the engine runs the underlying SELECT against the current base tables.
      
      
      Analogy: a view is a window in a wall. It shows you part of the room (the base table). It does not contain a copy of the room; if furniture moves, the view shows it immediately.
      
      
      Why it exists:
      
      
      
        
      🛡️
      Security
      Grant access to the view, not the table. Hide columns (salary) or rows (other regions).
      
        
      🧩
      Simplicity
      Hide a 5-table join behind one name. Analysts query v_order_summary.
      
        
      🔗
      Logical data independence
      Rename/split tables; keep the old view so old apps still work (Chapter 02).
      
        
      ⚖️
      Consistency
      One official definition of "active customer" instead of 20 copies of the WHERE.
      
      
      
      
      CREATE VIEW v_it_staff AS
SELECT id, name, dept          -- no salary column
FROM emp
WHERE dept = 'IT';

GRANT SELECT ON company.v_it_staff TO 'it_lead'@'%';   -- no grant on emp itself

SELECT * FROM v_it_staff;
-- 1 Asha IT | 2 Bala IT | 3 Chen IT | 4 Divya IT
      
      
      
        
      Simple view
      • One base table
      • No aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY
      • Usually updatable (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE pass through)
      
        
      Complex view
      • Joins, GROUP BY, aggregates, UNION, DISTINCT
      • Usually read-only
      • Great for reporting
      
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistakes
