      (1) Saying "a view makes queries faster" — a normal view is just the stored query; performance is the same as running the SELECT (sometimes worse if the view forces a temp table). (2) Stacking views on views on views — hard to debug, and the optimizer may not merge them well. (3) SELECT * in a view: in MySQL the column list is frozen when the view is created; a column added to the table later does not appear in the view.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A view is a named, stored SELECT — a virtual table. It does not store data; every query on the view runs the underlying query on the current base tables, so it is always up to date. I use views for security, by granting access to a view that hides sensitive columns or rows, for simplicity, by hiding complex joins, and for logical data independence. If I need the result physically stored for speed, that is a materialized view, which MySQL does not have natively.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪If I drop the base table, what happens to the view?
          
      In MySQL the view stays but becomes invalid: querying it gives "View … references invalid table(s) or column(s)". CHECK TABLE v_it_staff reports it. Oracle marks it INVALID and recompiles it automatically if the table comes back. SQL Server can prevent the drop with WITH SCHEMABINDING; PostgreSQL refuses the drop unless you use CASCADE.
      
        
      ↪Can you create an index on a view?
          
      Not in MySQL or PostgreSQL (for a normal view, the base table indexes are used). SQL Server: yes — that makes it an indexed view, i.e. materialized. PostgreSQL: you can index a materialized view.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhen is a view updatable? What does WITH CHECK OPTION do?
    
      
      
      Rule of thumb: a view is updatable when each view row maps to exactly one row of one base table, so the engine knows which physical row to change. In MySQL a view is not updatable if it contains:
      
      
        
        
      • aggregate functions (SUM, COUNT …) or window functions
        • 
        
      • DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING
        • 
        
      • UNION / UNION ALL
        • 
        
      • a subquery in the SELECT list, or certain joins (outer joins)
        • 
        
      • ALGORITHM = TEMPTABLE, or only literal values (no base column)
        • 
      
      
      
      For join views, MySQL lets you UPDATE/INSERT into one base table at a time; DELETE through a join view is not allowed. Columns computed by expressions (salary*12 AS annual) cannot be assigned.
      
      
      The trap that WITH CHECK OPTION fixes: you can insert a row through a view that the view itself cannot see.
      
      
      INSERT INTO v_it_staff (id, name, dept) VALUES (9, 'Ivan', 'Sales');   -- succeeds!
SELECT * FROM v_it_staff WHERE id = 9;   -- empty: the row "disappeared" from the view

CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v_it_staff AS
SELECT id, name, dept FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT'
WITH CHECK OPTION;

INSERT INTO v_it_staff (id, name, dept) VALUES (10, 'Jaya', 'Sales');
-- ERROR 1369 (HY000): CHECK OPTION failed 'company.v_it_staff'
      
      
      
        
      WITH CASCADED CHECK OPTION
      (the default) checks this view's WHERE and the WHERE of every view it is built on.
      
        
      WITH LOCAL CHECK OPTION
      checks this view's WHERE, and underlying views only if they have their own check option.
      
      
      
      
      🔀
      Making "non-updatable" views writable
      MySQL cannot. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server support INSTEAD OF triggers on views: you write the code that decides what INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the view should do to the base tables. PostgreSQL also auto-updates simple views (9.3+) and offers rules.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat are ALGORITHM = MERGE / TEMPTABLE and SQL SECURITY DEFINER / INVOKER in MySQL views?
    
      
      
      CREATE
  ALGORITHM = MERGE              -- UNDEFINED (default) | MERGE | TEMPTABLE
  DEFINER = 'admin'@'localhost'
  SQL SECURITY DEFINER           -- DEFINER (default) | INVOKER
VIEW v_dept_pay AS
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS total FROM emp GROUP BY dept;
      
      
      
        
      MERGE
      • View text is merged into your query (like macro expansion)
      • Your WHERE is pushed into the base table → indexes used
      • Needed for updatable views
      • Impossible with aggregates/DISTINCT/UNION/LIMIT…
      
        
      TEMPTABLE
      • View result is computed into an internal temp table first, then your query runs on it
      • No indexes on the temp table (your WHERE can't use base indexes)
      • Base table locks released earlier
      • View is never updatable
      
      
      
      
      With UNDEFINED, MySQL picks MERGE when it can (in the example above it must use TEMPTABLE because of GROUP BY — asking for MERGE gives a warning and falls back).
      
      
      
        
      SQL SECURITY DEFINER
      • View runs with the creator's privileges
      • That is how a view grants controlled access to a table the user cannot read
      • Risk: if the definer account is dropped, the view breaks
      
        
      SQL SECURITY INVOKER
      • View runs with the caller's privileges
      • Pure convenience view, no privilege escalation
      
      
      
      
      The same DEFINER/INVOKER idea applies to stored procedures and functions (and PostgreSQL's SECURITY DEFINER functions).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QView vs materialized view? MySQL has no materialized views — how would you build one?
    
      
      
      A materialized view (MV) stores the result of its query physically, like a table, and must be refreshed to pick up changes. Reads become very fast (pre-computed joins/aggregates); the price is storage, refresh cost and possible staleness.
      
      
      ViewMaterialized view
      
        
      Storesquery text onlyquery text + result rows
      
        
      Freshnessalways currentas of last refresh (unless auto-maintained)
      
        
      Read speedsame as the queryfast — like reading a table
      
        
      Indexesno (base indexes only)yes
      
        
      Write overheadnonerefresh cost / maintenance on base-table writes
      
        
      Use forsecurity, abstractiondashboards, heavy aggregates, reporting
      
      
      
      
      
        
      
        
      
          
      CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_dept_pay AS
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS total, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM emp GROUP BY dept;

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON mv_dept_pay (dept);          -- required for CONCURRENTLY

REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_dept_pay;              -- full rebuild, blocks readers
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY mv_dept_pay; -- readers keep working; needs unique index
      
          
      Refresh is always a full recomputation (manual or scheduled with cron/pg_cron); no built-in incremental refresh.
      
        
      
        
      
          
      CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW LOG ON emp WITH ROWID, SEQUENCE (dept, salary) INCLUDING NEW VALUES;

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW mv_dept_pay
  REFRESH FAST ON COMMIT          -- incremental, applied when base txn commits
  ENABLE QUERY REWRITE            -- optimizer may answer base-table queries from the MV
AS SELECT dept, SUM(salary) total, COUNT(salary) cnt_sal, COUNT(*) cnt FROM emp GROUP BY dept;
      
          
      Oracle is the richest: fast (incremental) refresh using MV logs, ON COMMIT or ON DEMAND, and query rewrite.
      
        
      
        
      
          
      CREATE VIEW dbo.v_dept_pay WITH SCHEMABINDING AS
SELECT dept, SUM(salary) AS total, COUNT_BIG(*) AS cnt
FROM dbo.emp GROUP BY dept;
GO
CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX ix_v_dept_pay ON dbo.v_dept_pay (dept);
      
          
      An indexed view is maintained synchronously on every base-table write — never stale, but every INSERT/UPDATE pays for it. Many restrictions (SCHEMABINDING, COUNT_BIG, no outer joins…).
      
        
      
        
      
          
      -- 1. A real table holds the "materialized" result
CREATE TABLE mv_dept_pay (dept VARCHAR(10) PRIMARY KEY, total BIGINT, headcount INT);

-- 2a. Periodic full refresh with an EVENT (stale up to 1 hour)
CREATE EVENT ev_refresh_dept_pay
ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 HOUR
DO
  REPLACE INTO mv_dept_pay
  SELECT dept, SUM(salary), COUNT(*) FROM emp GROUP BY dept;

-- 2b. Or keep it exactly in sync with triggers (incremental)
CREATE TRIGGER trg_emp_ai AFTER INSERT ON emp FOR EACH ROW
  INSERT INTO mv_dept_pay VALUES (NEW.dept, NEW.salary, 1)
  ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE total = total + NEW.salary, headcount = headcount + 1;
-- (+ similar AFTER UPDATE / AFTER DELETE triggers)
      
          
      Option 2a is simple but stale; option 2b is fresh but adds write cost and complexity. A REPLACE-only refresh also never deletes departments that vanished — a truncate-and-reload inside a transaction, or a table swap with RENAME TABLE, fixes that.
      
        
      
      
      
      
      🌍
      Real-world scenario
      An e-commerce admin dashboard showing "revenue per category today" scanned 50 M order rows on every page load. Fix: a summary table refreshed every 5 minutes by an event. Page load dropped from seconds to milliseconds; the business accepted 5-minute staleness. That trade-off — freshness vs speed — is exactly what the interviewer wants you to name.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A normal view stores only the query, so it is always fresh but no faster than the query. A materialized view stores the result, so reads are fast and can be indexed, but it must be refreshed and may be stale. PostgreSQL has REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, with CONCURRENTLY to avoid blocking readers; Oracle supports incremental fast refresh and query rewrite; SQL Server has indexed views maintained on every write. MySQL has none, so I create a summary table and keep it updated with a scheduled event or with triggers, depending on how fresh it must be.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⚙️ Stored procedures and functions
      
  
      A stored routine is code (SQL + variables + IF/LOOP) saved inside the database server. There are two kinds: procedures (do an action, called with CALL) and functions (compute and return one value, used inside expressions).
      

  
      
    QWhat is a stored procedure? Write one with IN and OUT parameters.
    
      
      
      What: a named block of SQL statements stored in the database, compiled/parsed once, executed many times with CALL name(args).
      
      
      Why: one network call instead of many round-trips; a single, reusable, permission-controlled entry point ("the app may call transfer() but may not UPDATE accounts directly"); logic close to the data.
      
      
      CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, owner VARCHAR(20), balance DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1,'Asha',1000.00),(2,'Bala',500.00);

DELIMITER $$                                   -- change the client's statement terminator
CREATE PROCEDURE transfer(
    IN  p_from   INT,
    IN  p_to     INT,
    IN  p_amount DECIMAL(12,2),
    OUT p_status VARCHAR(40)
)
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_bal DECIMAL(12,2);

  -- any SQL error: undo everything and re-throw
  DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
  BEGIN
    ROLLBACK;
    RESIGNAL;
  END;

  IF p_amount <= 0 THEN
    SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Amount must be positive';
  END IF;

  START TRANSACTION;
    SELECT balance INTO v_bal FROM accounts WHERE id = p_from FOR UPDATE;   -- lock the row
    IF v_bal < p_amount THEN
      ROLLBACK;
      SET p_status = 'INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS';
    ELSE
      UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - p_amount WHERE id = p_from;
      UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + p_amount WHERE id = p_to;
      COMMIT;
      SET p_status = 'OK';
    END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

CALL transfer(1, 2, 300, @st);
SELECT @st;                                -- OK
CALL transfer(2, 1, 5000, @st);
SELECT @st;                                -- INSUFFICIENT_FUNDS
      
      
      
        
      DELIMITER $$
      A client command (mysql CLI / Workbench), not SQL. The body contains ;, so we temporarily tell the client "the statement ends at $$". GUI tools and drivers usually don't need it.
      
        
      IN
      Value passed in (default). Changes inside are not seen by the caller.
      
        
      OUT
      Starts as NULL inside; the procedure sets it; the caller reads it from a user variable (@st).
      
        
      INOUT
      Passed in and sent back (e.g. a counter you increment).
      
        
      DECLARE
      Local variables, conditions, cursors and handlers — must come first in a BEGIN…END block, in that order (variables/conditions → cursors → handlers).
      
      
      
      
      
        
      VariablesDECLARE v INT DEFAULT 0; SET v = v + 1; SELECT … INTO v
      
        
      
        
      BranchIF … ELSEIF … ELSE … END IF · CASE … END CASE
      
        
      
        
      LoopWHILE … DO · REPEAT … UNTIL · label: LOOP … LEAVE label / ITERATE label
      
        
      
        
      ErrorsDECLARE … HANDLER · SIGNAL · RESIGNAL · GET DIAGNOSTICS
      
      
      
      
      🔀
      Procedural languages per engine
      MySQL: SQL/PSM-style compound statements (no packages, no debugging tools). Oracle: PL/SQL — the richest: packages, exceptions, bulk collect, autonomous transactions. SQL Server: T-SQL — CREATE PROCEDURE … AS BEGIN … END, TRY…CATCH, EXEC proc @p=1. PostgreSQL: PL/pgSQL (plus PL/Python, PL/Perl…); historically only functions — CREATE PROCEDURE with COMMIT/ROLLBACK inside arrived in PostgreSQL 11 and is called with CALL.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A stored procedure is a named block of SQL and control-flow code stored in the database and run with CALL. It can take IN, OUT and INOUT parameters, return result sets, and control transactions. I would use one for a multi-step operation like a money transfer, so it is one network call, it is atomic, and the application only needs EXECUTE permission instead of direct table access. The downside is that the logic is harder to version, test and scale than application code.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Are stored procedures faster than sending the same queries from the app?
          
      Often a bit, for two reasons: fewer round-trips (one CALL instead of 5 queries) and less data shipped to the app. The "pre-compiled" argument is weaker than people think: MySQL caches a procedure's parsed statements per connection, and prepared statements from the app give similar reuse. The big win is network chattiness, not compilation.
      
        
      ↪Do stored procedures prevent SQL injection?
          
      Only if they use parameters as values. A procedure that builds SQL by CONCAT-ing a parameter and runs it with PREPARE is just as injectable (Chapter 18). The real defence is parameter binding, wherever the SQL runs.
      
        
      ↪How does a procedure return a table of rows?
          
      In MySQL and SQL Server, any plain SELECT inside the procedure (not SELECT … INTO) is sent to the client as a result set — a procedure can even return several. Oracle uses a SYS_REFCURSOR OUT parameter; PostgreSQL uses set-returning functions (RETURNS TABLE(…)) or refcursors.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is a cursor? How do handlers and SIGNAL work?
    
      
      
      A cursor lets procedural code walk through a query result one row at a time — like an iterator. MySQL cursors are read-only, forward-only and asensitive (they may or may not see concurrent changes).
      
      
        
        
      1. DECLARE the cursor for a SELECT, and a CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND that sets a "done" flag.
        2. 
        
      2. OPEN it (the query runs).
        3. 
        
      3. FETCH into variables in a loop; stop when done = 1.
        4. 
        
      4. CLOSE it.
        5. 
      
      
      
      DELIMITER $$
CREATE PROCEDURE raise_it()
BEGIN
  DECLARE v_id INT;
  DECLARE v_sal INT;
  DECLARE done INT DEFAULT 0;
  DECLARE cur CURSOR FOR SELECT id, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT';
  DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET done = 1;   -- fires when FETCH runs out

  OPEN cur;
  read_loop: LOOP
    FETCH cur INTO v_id, v_sal;
    IF done = 1 THEN LEAVE read_loop; END IF;
    UPDATE emp
      SET salary = salary * IF(v_sal < 70000, 1.10, 1.05)
    WHERE id = v_id;
  END LOOP;
  CLOSE cur;
END$$
DELIMITER ;
      
      
      ⚠️
      Cursors are usually the slow answer
      The loop above is RBAR — "row by agonizing row". The same work in one set-based statement is much faster: UPDATE emp SET salary = salary * IF(salary < 70000, 1.10, 1.05) WHERE dept = 'IT';. Say: "I'd use a cursor only when each row needs logic SQL can't express, like calling an external procedure per row."
      
      
      ConstructMeaning
      
        
      DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR …Run the handler, then continue with the next statement.
      
        
      DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR …Run the handler, then leave the current BEGIN…END block.
      
        
      FOR NOT FOUND / SQLWARNING / SQLEXCEPTIONClasses of conditions (no row / warning / any error).
      
        
      FOR 1062 or FOR SQLSTATE '23000'A specific MySQL error code (1062 = duplicate key) or SQLSTATE.
      
        
      SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = '…'Raise your own error ('45000' = "unhandled user-defined exception").
      
        
      RESIGNALInside a handler: re-raise the caught error (optionally changed).
      
        
      GET DIAGNOSTICS CONDITION 1 @msg = MESSAGE_TEXTRead details of the last error.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QProcedure vs function — what is the difference? What does DETERMINISTIC mean?
    
      
      
      DELIMITER $$
CREATE FUNCTION tax(p_salary INT)
RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2)
DETERMINISTIC NO SQL                 -- same input → same output, reads no tables
BEGIN
  RETURN CASE
           WHEN p_salary <= 60000 THEN 0
           WHEN p_salary <= 80000 THEN p_salary * 0.10
           ELSE p_salary * 0.20
         END;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

SELECT name, salary, tax(salary) AS tax FROM emp WHERE dept = 'IT';
-- Asha 90000 18000.00 | Bala 75000 7500.00 | Chen 90000 18000.00 | Divya 60000 0.00
      
      
      Stored procedureStored function
      
        
      Called withCALL p(…) — a statement on its owninside expressions: SELECT f(x), WHERE f(x) > 0
      
        
      Returns0..n result sets + OUT/INOUT paramsexactly one value (RETURNS type)
      
        
      ParametersIN, OUT, INOUTIN only
      
        
      Transactionscan START TRANSACTION / COMMIT / ROLLBACKcannot commit or roll back (no statements that cause a commit)
      
        
      Return result sets✔✘
      
        
      Dynamic SQL (PREPARE)✔✘
      
        
      Typical usebusiness operations: transfer, place order, nightly batchreusable calculations: tax, age, format, distance
      
      
      
      
      
        
      DETERMINISTIC
      Same inputs always give the same output (e.g. tax). NOW(), RAND() or reading a table that changes → NOT DETERMINISTIC (the default).
      
        
      NO SQL / READS SQL DATA / MODIFIES SQL DATA / CONTAINS SQL
      What the body does with data. Advisory — MySQL does not verify it.
      
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      ERROR 1418 and replication
      With binary logging on (the default in MySQL 8), creating a function fails with ERROR 1418 unless it is declared DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL or READS SQL DATA (or log_bin_trust_function_creators = 1). Reason: in statement-based replication a non-deterministic function could produce different data on the replica. Never lie with DETERMINISTIC — the optimizer may cache the result.
      
      
      🚫
      Performance trap
      WHERE tax(salary) > 1000 calls the function for every row and cannot use an index on salary. Functions in WHERE on large tables = full scans. Rewrite as a range on the column, or index the expression (generated column / functional index, see below).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A procedure performs an action: it is called with CALL, can have IN, OUT and INOUT parameters, can return result sets and can control transactions. A function computes and returns exactly one value, so it can be used inside a SELECT or WHERE, takes only IN parameters, and cannot commit or return result sets. DETERMINISTIC means the same inputs always give the same output; MySQL needs that declaration for functions when binary logging is on, because of replication safety.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QShould business logic live in stored procedures or in the application?
    
      
      
      
        
      ✔ Logic in the DB (procs/triggers)
      • Fewer round-trips; data never leaves the server
      • One enforcement point for many apps/languages
      • Fine-grained security: grant EXECUTE only
      • Atomic multi-step operations in one call
      • Banks and legacy enterprise systems (Oracle PL/SQL) rely on it
      
        
      ✘ Logic in the app
      • Git, code review, unit tests, CI are natural; DB code tooling is weaker
      • App servers scale horizontally; the DB is the hardest thing to scale — don't burn its CPU on logic
      • Vendor lock-in: PL/SQL ≠ T-SQL ≠ MySQL
      • Harder debugging and deployments (schema migrations for code)
      • Hidden side effects surprise developers
      
      
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      It depends on the system. Modern web teams usually keep business logic in the application because it is easier to test, version and scale, and they keep the database for data integrity — constraints, foreign keys, transactions. I'd still use a procedure for data-heavy batch jobs or operations that need many round-trips, and in organisations where several applications share one database and the rules must be enforced in one place.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🔔 Triggers
      

  
      
    QWhat is a trigger? Write an audit-log trigger for salary changes.
    
      
      
      What: a trigger is stored code that the database runs automatically when a specific event (INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE) happens on a specific table. Nobody calls it — the event fires it.
      
      
      Analogy: a motion-sensor light. You don't press a switch; walking in (the INSERT) turns it on.
      
      
      Timing × event = 6 kinds in MySQL:
      
      
      INSERTUPDATEDELETE
      
        
      BEFORE — runs before the row is written; can change NEW or reject the rowNEW (writable)OLD (read) + NEW (writable)OLD
      
        
      AFTER — runs after the row is written; good for side effects (audit, counters)NEW (read-only)OLD + NEW (read-only)OLD
      
      
      
      
      CREATE TABLE salary_audit (
  audit_id   BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  emp_id     INT,
  old_salary INT,
  new_salary INT,
  changed_by VARCHAR(100),
  changed_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

DELIMITER $$
-- 1) BEFORE UPDATE: validate / fix the incoming row
CREATE TRIGGER trg_emp_bu BEFORE UPDATE ON emp
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NEW.salary < 0 THEN
    SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'Salary cannot be negative';
  END IF;
  SET NEW.name = TRIM(NEW.name);                  -- BEFORE triggers may modify NEW
END$$

-- 2) AFTER UPDATE: write history only when salary really changed
CREATE TRIGGER trg_emp_au AFTER UPDATE ON emp
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NOT (OLD.salary <=> NEW.salary) THEN        -- NULL-safe "changed?"
    INSERT INTO salary_audit (emp_id, old_salary, new_salary, changed_by)
    VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary, CURRENT_USER());
  END IF;
END$$
DELIMITER ;

UPDATE emp SET salary = 95000 WHERE id = 1;
SELECT emp_id, old_salary, new_salary FROM salary_audit;   -- 1 | 90000 | 95000
      
      
      
      🔀
      Trigger differences across engines
      MySQL: only FOR EACH ROW (row-level); BEFORE/AFTER; no triggers on views, no INSTEAD OF; multiple triggers per timing/event allowed since 5.7.2 (order with FOLLOWS/PRECEDES). PostgreSQL: row-level and statement-level (FOR EACH STATEMENT), body is a separate trigger function, INSTEAD OF on views, transition tables (REFERENCING NEW TABLE AS …), event triggers on DDL. SQL Server: statement-level only — the trigger fires once per statement and sees all affected rows in the pseudo-tables inserted and deleted; AFTER and INSTEAD OF; DDL/logon triggers. Oracle: row and statement level, compound triggers, INSTEAD OF on views; the famous ORA-04091 mutating table error when a row trigger queries its own table.
      
      
      ⚠️
      MySQL trigger pitfalls interviewers love
      (1) A trigger cannot modify the table that fired it with a statement (ERROR 1442) — in a BEFORE trigger use SET NEW.col = … instead. (2) Cascading foreign-key actions do not fire triggers in MySQL (ON DELETE CASCADE deletes child rows silently). (3) TRUNCATE does not fire DELETE triggers. (4) No COMMIT/ROLLBACK or dynamic SQL inside a trigger. (5) Writing SQL Server-style code that assumes one row per firing is the classic SQL Server bug — inserted can hold 1,000 rows.
      
      
      
        
      Good uses
      • Audit / history tables
      • Derived data kept in sync (counters, summary tables)
      • Complex validation a CHECK can't express
      • Enforcing rules for every app, even ad-hoc SQL
      
        
      Bad uses / risks
      • Hidden business logic ("why did this row change?")
      • Slower writes — runs per row, inside the transaction
      • Trigger chains: trigger A updates table B whose trigger updates C…
      • Hard to test, easy to forget during bulk loads and migrations
      
      
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A trigger is code the database runs automatically before or after an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table. In MySQL triggers are row-level, and I can read the OLD and NEW row values; a BEFORE trigger can change NEW or reject the row with SIGNAL, and an AFTER trigger is good for side effects like an audit log. They run inside the same transaction, so a failure rolls back the statement. I use them sparingly — mainly for auditing — because hidden logic makes systems harder to debug and slows down writes.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Trigger vs constraint — which do you prefer for validation?
          
      A constraint (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, FK, CHECK — enforced in MySQL since 8.0.16) whenever it can express the rule: it is declarative, visible in the schema, faster and known to the optimizer. A trigger only for rules that need other rows/tables or procedural logic.
      
        
      ↪If the AFTER trigger fails, is the original UPDATE kept?
          
      With InnoDB, no — the statement and the trigger's work are atomic; an error in a BEFORE trigger, the row operation or an AFTER trigger fails the whole statement. With non-transactional MyISAM, rows already changed stay changed.
      
        
      ↪Trigger vs stored procedure?
          
      A procedure is called explicitly and can take parameters, return results and control transactions. A trigger is fired implicitly by a DML event, takes no parameters, returns nothing, and cannot commit.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🔧 Events, dynamic SQL and temporary tables
      

  
      
    QWhat is a MySQL event? How is it different from a trigger?
    
      
      
      An event is a stored block that the server runs on a schedule — MySQL's built-in cron. A trigger is fired by a data change; an event is fired by the clock.
      
      
      SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'event_scheduler';     -- ON by default in MySQL 8.0

CREATE EVENT ev_purge_old_sessions
ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 DAY
STARTS '2026-11-01 02:00:00'
DO
  DELETE FROM sessions WHERE last_seen < NOW() - INTERVAL 30 DAY;

-- one-shot event
CREATE EVENT ev_close_sale ON SCHEDULE AT '2026-12-31 23:59:59'
DO UPDATE products SET on_sale = 0;
      
      
      Uses: purging old rows, refreshing summary tables (the MV emulation above), rotating partitions. Big deletes should be done in batches (LIMIT 10000 in a loop) to avoid long locks and huge undo. Equivalents: PostgreSQL pg_cron extension, SQL Server Agent jobs, Oracle DBMS_SCHEDULER.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat are prepared statements and dynamic SQL? Why do they help against SQL injection?
    
      
      
      A prepared statement is sent to the server in two phases: first the SQL template with ? placeholders is parsed/prepared, then it is executed (many times) with bound values. Values are never parsed as SQL, so ' OR 1=1 -- is just a weird string, not code.
      
      
      PREPARE get_emp FROM 'SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE dept = ? AND salary > ?';
SET @d = 'IT', @s = 70000;
EXECUTE get_emp USING @d, @s;          -- Asha 90000 | Bala 75000 | Chen 90000
DEALLOCATE PREPARE get_emp;
      
      
      Dynamic SQL = building the SQL text at runtime, e.g. when the table or column name is a parameter. Placeholders work only for values, not identifiers, so you must whitelist identifiers yourself:
      
      
      -- inside a procedure: p_col comes from the caller
IF p_col NOT IN ('name','salary','dept') THEN
  SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'bad sort column';
END IF;
SET @sql = CONCAT('SELECT id, name FROM emp ORDER BY ', p_col, ' LIMIT ?');
SET @n = 5;
PREPARE st FROM @sql;
EXECUTE st USING @n;
DEALLOCATE PREPARE st;
      
      
      💡
      In application code
      Use your driver's parameter binding (JDBC PreparedStatement, Python cursor.execute(sql, params)) — same protection, plus plan reuse. Prepared statements are session-scoped in MySQL. Deep dive on injection: Chapter 18.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is a temporary table? How is it different from a CTE or a table variable?
    
      
      
      CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_top_earners AS
SELECT id, name, salary FROM emp WHERE salary >= 75000;

ALTER TABLE tmp_top_earners ADD INDEX (salary);   -- you can index it
SELECT * FROM tmp_top_earners;                     -- usable by many later statements
DROP TEMPORARY TABLE tmp_top_earners;              -- or it vanishes at disconnect
      
      
        
        
      • Scope: visible only to the session that created it; two sessions can each have a tmp_top_earners without clashing. It may even shadow a permanent table with the same name.
        • 
        
      • Lifetime: until DROP or the connection closes (beware connection pools — the session can live long and the table survives into the next "request").
        • 
        
      • MySQL quirk: you cannot refer to the same TEMPORARY table twice in one query (ERROR 1137 "Can't reopen table") — self-joining it fails. A CTE avoids that.
        • 
        
      • Not to confuse with internal temporary tables the optimizer creates for GROUP BY/DISTINCT/UNION/derived tables ("Using temporary" in EXPLAIN).
        • 
      
      
      
      🔀
      Elsewhere
      SQL Server: #local (session) and ##global temp tables in tempdb, plus table variables DECLARE @t TABLE(…). PostgreSQL: CREATE TEMP TABLE … ON COMMIT DROP | DELETE ROWS | PRESERVE ROWS. Oracle: global temporary tables — the definition is permanent, the data is private per session/transaction; 18c added private temporary tables.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🗄️ Power features: generated columns, pivot, JSON, ROLLUP
      

  
      Generated columns (VIRTUAL vs STORED)
      
  
      
    QWhat is a generated column? VIRTUAL vs STORED? How does it help indexing?
    
      
      
      A generated (computed) column is defined by an expression over other columns of the same row. You never write to it; the database computes it. MySQL 5.7+
      
      
      CREATE TABLE orders (
  id         INT PRIMARY KEY,
  price      DECIMAL(10,2),
  qty        INT,
  email      VARCHAR(100),
  total      DECIMAL(12,2) AS (price * qty) STORED,          -- computed on write, saved on disk
  email_dom  VARCHAR(100)  AS (SUBSTRING_INDEX(email,'@',-1)) VIRTUAL,  -- computed on read
  INDEX idx_dom (email_dom)                                   -- index on a virtual column
);

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE email_dom = 'gmail.com';    -- uses idx_dom
      
      
      
        
      VIRTUAL (default)
      • Not stored in the row; computed when read
      • No extra disk; small CPU cost on read
      • InnoDB can still build a secondary index on it (index stores the value)
      
        
      STORED
      • Computed on INSERT/UPDATE and saved like a normal column
      • Uses disk; fast reads
      • Can be in a PRIMARY KEY; needed for some constraints
      
      
      
      
      Why interviewers ask: it is the classic fix for "WHERE LOWER(email) = … doesn't use my index". Index a generated column with the expression, or (MySQL 8.0.13+) create a functional index directly: CREATE INDEX idx_lower_email ON users ((LOWER(email))); — MySQL implements it as a hidden virtual column. PostgreSQL has expression indexes and GENERATED ALWAYS AS (…) STORED (PG 12+; virtual generated columns came in PG 18); SQL Server has computed columns (PERSISTED = stored).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Pivot with CASE + aggregate
      
  
      
    QHow do you pivot rows into columns in MySQL (there is no PIVOT keyword)?
    
      
      
      Pattern: GROUP BY the row label, and for each wanted column write SUM(CASE WHEN category = 'X' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) (or MAX(CASE …) to pick a value). This is "conditional aggregation".
      
      
      SELECT band,
       SUM(dept = 'IT')    AS IT,         -- MySQL: TRUE = 1, so SUM counts matches
       SUM(dept = 'Sales') AS Sales,
       SUM(CASE WHEN dept = 'HR' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS HR   -- portable spelling
FROM (
  SELECT dept,
         CASE WHEN salary >= 80000 THEN 'high'
              WHEN salary >= 65000 THEN 'mid'
              ELSE 'low' END AS band
  FROM emp
) t
GROUP BY band
ORDER BY FIELD(band, 'high', 'mid', 'low');
      
      
      +------+----+-------+----+
| band | IT | Sales | HR |
+------+----+-------+----+
| high |  2 |     0 |  0 |
| mid  |  1 |     2 |  0 |
| low  |  1 |     1 |  1 |
+------+----+-------+----+
      
      
      💡
      Unpivot and dynamic pivot
      Unpivot (columns → rows): SELECT id,'q1' AS q, q1 AS amt FROM t UNION ALL SELECT id,'q2',q2 FROM t …. Dynamic pivot (unknown list of columns): build the CASE list with GROUP_CONCAT into a string and run it with PREPARE. SQL Server and Oracle (11g+) have native PIVOT/UNPIVOT; PostgreSQL has crosstab() in the tablefunc extension or FILTER (WHERE …): COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE dept = 'IT').
      
    
      
  
      

  
      JSON functions and JSON_TABLE
      
  
      
    QHow do you store and query JSON in MySQL? What is JSON_TABLE?
    
      
      
      MySQL has a native JSON type (5.7.8+): the document is validated on insert and stored in an optimized binary format, so reading one key does not re-parse the whole text.
      
      
      CREATE TABLE products (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30), attrs JSON);
INSERT INTO products VALUES
 (1,'Phone','{"brand":"Acme","ram_gb":8,"colors":["black","blue"]}'),
 (2,'Laptop','{"brand":"Zeta","ram_gb":16,"colors":["grey"]}');

SELECT name,
       attrs->'$.brand'   AS brand_json,   -- JSON_EXTRACT  → "Acme" (with quotes)
       attrs->>'$.brand'  AS brand,        -- JSON_UNQUOTE(JSON_EXTRACT(...)) → Acme
       attrs->>'$.colors[0]' AS first_color
FROM products
WHERE attrs->>'$.ram_gb' >= 8;

UPDATE products SET attrs = JSON_SET(attrs, '$.ram_gb', 12) WHERE id = 1;
SELECT name FROM products WHERE JSON_CONTAINS(attrs->'$.colors', '"blue"');   -- Phone

-- JSON_TABLE (8.0.4+): turn a JSON array into relational rows
SELECT p.name, c.color
FROM products p,
     JSON_TABLE(p.attrs, '$.colors[*]' COLUMNS (color VARCHAR(20) PATH '$')) AS c;
-- Phone black | Phone blue | Laptop grey
      
      
      ⚠️
      Indexing JSON
      You cannot index a JSON column directly. Index a generated column (brand VARCHAR(30) AS (attrs->>'$.brand')) or a functional index; for arrays use a multi-valued index (8.0.17+) with MEMBER OF. PostgreSQL's JSONB + GIN index is more powerful here (Chapter 11). And don't put everything in JSON — columns you filter/join on and relationships belong in real columns with constraints.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Subtotals with WITH ROLLUP and GROUPING()
      
  
      
    QHow do you add subtotal and grand-total rows to a GROUP BY report?
    
      
      
      SELECT IF(GROUPING(dept), 'ALL DEPTS', dept) AS dept,
       COUNT(*)    AS headcount,
       SUM(salary) AS payroll
FROM emp
GROUP BY dept WITH ROLLUP;
      
      
      +-----------+-----------+---------+
| dept      | headcount | payroll |
+-----------+-----------+---------+
| HR        |         1 |   50000 |
| IT        |         4 |  315000 |
| Sales     |         3 |  195000 |
| ALL DEPTS |         8 |  560000 |   <-- super-aggregate row (dept was NULL)
+-----------+-----------+---------+
      
      
      WITH ROLLUP adds a super-aggregate row for each level of the GROUP BY list, right to left: GROUP BY year, month WITH ROLLUP gives per-month rows, a subtotal per year, and a grand total. In the extra rows the rolled-up column is NULL. GROUPING(col) (MySQL 8.0.1+) returns 1 for those generated NULLs, so you can tell them apart from real NULL data.
      
      
      🔀
      Engines
      MySQL supports only WITH ROLLUP (and ORDER BY together with it since 8.0.12). PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server support the standard GROUP BY ROLLUP(a,b), CUBE(a,b) (all combinations) and GROUPING SETS ((a),(b),()). In MySQL, emulate CUBE/GROUPING SETS with UNION ALL of several GROUP BYs.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      W · C · V · P · F · T
      Window = rank but keep rows · CTE = name a step (or recurse) · View = saved SELECT, no data · Procedure = CALL an action · Function = one value in SELECT · Trigger = fires by itself on DML. "We Can View Plenty of Fancy Tools."
      

  
      📌 Key takeaways
        
    
      • Window functions add a computed column per row over a partition; they run after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING, so filter on them from an outer query/CTE.
        • 
    
      • ROW_NUMBER = always unique; RANK = ties share, gaps after; DENSE_RANK = ties share, no gaps. Use DENSE_RANK for "Nth highest distinct salary".
        • 
    
      • Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE … CURRENT ROW: great for running totals, wrong for LAST_VALUE — specify the frame.
        • 
    
      • CTE = named sub-result for one statement. Recursive CTE = anchor UNION ALL recursive member, loops until an empty step; widen columns with CAST, guard cycles, mind cte_max_recursion_depth (1000).
        • 
    
      • A view stores only its query (security, abstraction, logical independence); updatable only when rows map 1:1 to a base table; use WITH CHECK OPTION to stop rows "escaping" the view.
        • 
    
      • Materialized views store results (PG REFRESH [CONCURRENTLY], Oracle fast refresh, SQL Server indexed views); MySQL needs a summary table + event or triggers.
        • 
    
      • Procedure = CALL, IN/OUT/INOUT, result sets, transactions. Function = one value inside SQL, no commit. DETERMINISTIC matters for replication (ERROR 1418).
        • 
    
      • Triggers: BEFORE (validate/modify NEW) vs AFTER (audit); MySQL is row-level only, no INSTEAD OF, not fired by FK cascades or TRUNCATE. Use sparingly.
        • 
    
      • Know the extras: events (scheduled jobs), prepared statements (values only, never identifiers), temp tables (session scope), generated columns + functional indexes, CASE pivots, JSON ->>/JSON_TABLE, WITH ROLLUP + GROUPING().
        • 
  
      

  
      📚 Go deeper
        
    
      • MySQL 8.0 manual — Window Functions — exact frame rules and function list.
        • 
    
      • MySQL 8.0 manual — WITH (Common Table Expressions) — recursive CTE restrictions and limits.
        • 
    
      • MySQL 8.0 manual — Updatable and Insertable Views — the full list of rules.
        • 
    
      • MySQL 8.0 manual — Stored Objects — procedures, functions, triggers, events, views in one place.
        • 
    
      • PostgreSQL docs — CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW — and the REFRESH page for CONCURRENTLY.
        • 
    
      • modern-sql.com (Markus Winand) — which engine supports which SQL feature, with clear examples.
        • 
  
      

  
      
    
      
      
      Salaries in a department are 100, 90, 90, 80. What does DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) give for 80?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      DENSE_RANK has no gaps: 1, 2, 2, 3. RANK would give 4 (1, 2, 2, 4); ROW_NUMBER would give 4 too.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      In MySQL, a recursive CTE builds a path string and fails with "ERROR 1406: Data too long for column 'path'". What is the fix?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      The CTE's column types are inferred from the anchor (non-recursive) part only, so the anchor must declare a wide enough type. ORDER BY is not even allowed in the recursive member.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which statement about a normal (non-materialized) view is TRUE?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      A view is a saved SELECT. Simple single-table views are updatable; only materialized views store rows.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which of these can a MySQL stored FUNCTION do?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Functions return exactly one value and are used inside expressions. Result sets, OUT/INOUT parameters and transaction control belong to procedures.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      A parent row is deleted and ON DELETE CASCADE removes 10 child rows in MySQL/InnoDB. The child table has an AFTER DELETE trigger. How many times does it fire?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MySQL documents that cascaded foreign key actions do not fire triggers. An audit trigger on the child table silently misses those deletes — a real production pitfall.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      You need "monthly revenue per category" for a dashboard; slight staleness is fine. Best approach in MySQL?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MySQL has no materialized views. A summary table + event gives fast reads with bounded staleness. A TEMPTABLE view still recomputes on every query.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Why does WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) = 1 fail?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Logical order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window functions → SELECT → ORDER BY. Compute the rank in a CTE/derived table and filter outside (or use QUALIFY in engines that have it, such as Snowflake/DuckDB).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      Window function vs GROUP BY in one line?
      GROUP BY collapses each group to one row; a window function keeps every row and adds the group-level value as a column.
      
    
      ROW_NUMBER / RANK / DENSE_RANK on 100, 90, 90, 80?
      1,2,3,4 · 1,2,2,4 · 1,2,2,3.
      
    
      Default frame when OVER has ORDER BY?
      RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (includes peers). Without ORDER BY: the whole partition.
      
    
      LAG vs LEAD?
      LAG(col, n, default) reads the row n positions before; LEAD reads n positions after, within the partition order.
      
    
      Two parts of a recursive CTE and when does it stop?
      Anchor (runs once) UNION ALL recursive member (joins to the previous step's rows). Stops when a step returns zero rows.
      
    
      MySQL recursion limit variable and default?
      cte_max_recursion_depth = 1000. Exceeding it → ERROR 3636.
      
    
      Does a view store data?
      No — only the SELECT text. A materialized view stores the result and needs refreshing.
      
    
      What does WITH CHECK OPTION do?
      Rejects INSERT/UPDATE through a view if the resulting row would not be visible through that view's WHERE.
      
    
      MySQL view ALGORITHM options?
      UNDEFINED (default), MERGE (inline into query, updatable), TEMPTABLE (compute into temp table first, read-only).
      
    
      Procedure vs function (3 differences)?
      CALL vs used in expressions; IN/OUT/INOUT + result sets vs one RETURN value; can control transactions vs cannot.
      
    
      NEW and OLD in triggers?
      INSERT: NEW only. DELETE: OLD only. UPDATE: both. Only a BEFORE trigger may SET NEW.col.
      
    
      MySQL vs SQL Server trigger granularity?
      MySQL: FOR EACH ROW only. SQL Server: once per statement, rows in the inserted/deleted pseudo-tables. PostgreSQL/Oracle: both.
      
    
      VIRTUAL vs STORED generated column?
      VIRTUAL computed on read (no disk, indexable in InnoDB); STORED computed on write and saved.
      
    
      How to pivot in MySQL?
      GROUP BY the row key + SUM(CASE WHEN col = 'X' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) per output column (conditional aggregation).
      
  
      

      


      
  
      
    
      Chapter 10 · III · SQL Mastery
      
    
      🧪 SQL Interview Problems Lab
      
    
      44 classic interview queries, grouped into 9 patterns. Learn to spot the pattern in 30 seconds, write a correct MySQL 8 answer, defend it against edge cases, and handle every follow-up.
      
    
      ⏱ 90 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8Windows & CTEs need MySQL 8.0+PostgreSQL notesSQL Server notes
      
  
      

  
       
      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
      
    
        
      
      • Almost every interview query is one of 9 patterns: ranking/Nth, top-N per group, duplicates, self-join, anti-join, dates/time series, gaps & islands, aggregation tricks, hierarchies. Name the pattern out loud first.
        • 
      
      • Nth highest = DENSE_RANK() (ties share a rank) or DISTINCT … LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 wrapped in a scalar subquery so "no answer" becomes NULL.
        • 
      
      • Top-N per group = rank inside a CTE with PARTITION BY group, then filter WHERE rnk <= N outside (you cannot filter a window function in WHERE).
        • 
      
      • Delete duplicates keeping lowest id = DELETE p1 FROM t p1 JOIN t p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id. A plain subquery on the same table gives MySQL ERROR 1093 — wrap it in a derived table.
        • 
      
      • "Never did X" = NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN … IS NULL. Avoid NOT IN when the subquery can contain NULL (it returns zero rows).
        • 
      
      • Consecutive / streaks = gaps-and-islands: value − ROW_NUMBER() is constant inside a run. For dates: DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL rn DAY). Dedupe first.
        • 
      
      • Previous row / growth = LAG(). But "yesterday" means the calendar day, not the previous row — join on d = prev + INTERVAL 1 DAY when days can be missing.
        • 
      
      • Rates = AVG(condition) or SUM(CASE …) / COUNT(*). Pivot = MAX(CASE WHEN col='x' THEN val END) per column. Zero-count groups = start from the "all groups" table and LEFT JOIN.
        • 
      
      • Hierarchy of unknown depth = WITH RECURSIVE (anchor UNION ALL recursive step). Missing dates/ids = generate a series with a recursive CTE, then anti-join.
        • 
      
      • Always finish with: edge cases (ties, NULLs, empty table, duplicates), the index you would add, and the pre-8.0 / other-engine alternative.
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ✏️ How to use this lab: read the problem, cover the solution, write your own query on paper (yes, paper — many interviews have no editor), then compare. Do 5 a day and you will finish in 9 days.
      

  
  
      🧭 The 6-step problem-solving framework
      
  
      Interviewers do not only check whether your final query runs. They watch how you get there. A calm, structured approach scores higher than a clever query typed in silence. Use these six steps for every problem in this chapter.
      

  
      
    
      1. Clarifyties? NULLs? duplicates? empty result → NULL or no row?
      
    
      
    
      2. Find the grainone output row = one what? (user, day, dept…)
      
    
      
    
      3. Name the patternrank? anti-join? islands? pivot?
      
    
      
    
      4. Build in CTEssmall named steps, test each
      
    
      
    
      5. Attack edge casestie, NULL, empty, 1 row, gap
      
    
      
    
      6. Optimizeindex, sargable, pre-8.0 / other engine
      
  
      

  
        
    
      1. Clarify the spec. Ask 2–3 short questions. "If two people share the top salary, is the second highest the next distinct value?" "If there is no answer, do you want an empty result or one row with NULL?" These two questions alone fix half of all wrong answers.
        2. 
    
      2. Find the grain (granularity). Say: "The output has one row per department." Now you know what goes in GROUP BY or PARTITION BY.
        3. 
    
      3. Name the pattern. Use the cheat table at the end of this chapter. Saying "this is a gaps-and-islands problem" tells the interviewer you have seen the family before.
        4. 
    
      4. Build in CTEs. Write WITH step1 AS (…), step2 AS (…) SELECT …. Each step is small and testable. It also reads like an explanation.
        5. 
    
      5. Attack your own query. Walk through ties, NULLs, an empty table, a single row, and a missing day. Fix before the interviewer asks.
        6. 
    
      6. Talk about performance. Name one index (for example (dept_id, salary)), say whether the filter is sargable (can use an index), and mention the pre-MySQL-8.0 alternative.
        7. 
  
      

  
      🎯
      🎯 What the interviewer is really testing
      (1) Do you know window functions, joins and GROUP BY well enough to pick the right tool? (2) Do you think about ties, NULLs and empty results without being told? (3) Can you explain your query in plain words? (4) Can you adapt when they change the problem ("now per department", "now without LIMIT", "now on 1 billion rows")? The follow-ups in this chapter are exactly those changes.
      

  
      ⚠️
      Logical execution order — the root of most bugs
      FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → window functions → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. So: you cannot use a window function or a SELECT alias inside WHERE; you cannot use an aggregate in WHERE (use HAVING); LIMIT runs after DISTINCT. When you need to filter on a computed value, wrap the query in a CTE or derived table. Full details in Chapter 07 and Chapter 09.
      

  
      The shared practice dataset
      
  
      Most ranking, self-join and aggregation problems below use these two small tables. Keep them in mind; every expected output in the chapter was computed from them. (Note the tie at 85000, the empty HR department and the NULL manager — these are planted on purpose.)
      
  
      CREATE TABLE Department (
  id   INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE Employee (
  id         INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name       VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  salary     INT NOT NULL,
  dept_id    INT,
  manager_id INT,                    -- NULL for the CEO
  FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES Department(id)
);
INSERT INTO Department VALUES (1,'IT'), (2,'Sales'), (3,'HR');
INSERT INTO Employee VALUES
 (1,'Joe',   85000, 1, 4),
 (2,'Henry', 80000, 2, 4),
 (3,'Sam',   60000, 2, 2),
 (4,'Max',   90000, 1, NULL),
 (5,'Janet', 69000, 1, 4),
 (6,'Randy', 85000, 1, 4),
 (7,'Will',  70000, 1, 5);
      
  
      +----+-------+--------+---------+------------+
| id | name  | salary | dept_id | manager_id |
+----+-------+--------+---------+------------+
|  1 | Joe   |  85000 |       1 |          4 |
|  2 | Henry |  80000 |       2 |          4 |
|  3 | Sam   |  60000 |       2 |          2 |
|  4 | Max   |  90000 |       1 |       NULL |
|  5 | Janet |  69000 |       1 |          4 |
|  6 | Randy |  85000 |       1 |          4 |
|  7 | Will  |  70000 |       1 |          5 |
+----+-------+--------+---------+------------+
Department: 1 = IT, 2 = Sales, 3 = HR (no employees)
      

  
  
      🏆 Pattern 1 · Ranking & the "Nth value"
      
  
      Signal words: "second highest", "Nth", "rank", "top", "without LIMIT". The core decision is how to treat ties. The figure shows the three ranking functions on our salaries.
      

  

  
  
      P01 · Second highest salary
      
  
      🔥 most asked SQL question in India LeetCode 176 TCS · Infosys · Paytm · Walmart
      
  
      Problem. Return the second highest distinct salary as SecondHighestSalary. If it does not exist, return one row containing NULL.
      
  
      Expected output on our dataset: distinct salaries are 90000, 85000, 80000, … → 85000.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM Employee
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);
      
      
      Take the biggest salary that is smaller than the biggest salary. Because MAX() over zero rows returns NULL, the "no second salary" case is handled automatically.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT (
  SELECT DISTINCT salary
  FROM Employee
  ORDER BY salary DESC
  LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1          -- skip 1 row, take 1 row  (same as LIMIT 1,1)
) AS SecondHighestSalary;
      
      
      The outer SELECT ( … ) is a scalar subquery. When the inner query returns no rows, a scalar subquery evaluates to NULL, so you get one row with NULL instead of an empty result.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT MAX(salary) AS SecondHighestSalary
FROM (
  SELECT salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr
  FROM Employee
) t
WHERE dr = 2;
      
      
      DENSE_RANK gives the 85000s rank 2. The outer MAX collapses the two tied rows into one value and turns "no rows" into NULL.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      +---------------------+
| SecondHighestSalary |
+---------------------+
|               85000 |
+---------------------+
      

  
      
    QWalk me through the traps in "second highest salary".
    
      
      
      There are three classic traps, and the interviewer usually plants one of them in the data:
      
      
      Wrong queryWhat goes wrong
      
        
      ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 (no DISTINCT)With a tie at the top (90000, 90000, 85000) it returns 90000 again.
      
        
      SELECT DISTINCT … LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1 without the scalar wrapperOn a one-row table it returns an empty result, not a NULL row. LeetCode marks this wrong.
      
        
      RANK() … WHERE rnk = 2With a tie at the top, ranks are 1, 1, 3 — rank 2 does not exist → NULL.
      
      
      
      
      Edge cases to say out loud: one-row table → NULL; empty table → NULL; all salaries equal → NULL; NULL salaries are ignored by MAX and by ORDER BY … LIMIT they sort last in DESC order in MySQL (NULL is treated as the smallest value).
      
      
      Index: with an index on salary, approach A is two quick index lookups (MySQL reads the max from the end of the B+ tree). B and C must sort the distinct salaries.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      "I'll first confirm we want the second highest distinct salary and NULL if it doesn't exist. The simplest answer is the max salary that is less than the overall max — MAX over no rows gives NULL, so the edge case is free. If you want it to generalize to N, I'd use DENSE_RANK so ties share a rank, or DISTINCT with LIMIT and OFFSET inside a scalar subquery so an empty result becomes NULL."
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Return the employee names who earn the second highest salary.
          
      Find the value, then join back: SELECT name, salary FROM Employee WHERE salary = (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee)); → Joe and Randy. Or with a window: … WHERE dr = 2 without the outer MAX.
      
        
      ↪Do it without LIMIT, without window functions, without MAX.
          
      Use the correlated-count trick (see P03): "a salary is 2nd highest if exactly 1 distinct salary is bigger than it."
      
        
      ↪How would you write it in SQL Server and Oracle?
          
      SQL Server: ORDER BY salary DESC OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY (needs ORDER BY) or TOP. Oracle 12c+: OFFSET 1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY; older Oracle used ROWNUM in nested queries. DENSE_RANK works in all of them.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P02 · Nth highest salary (return NULL when absent)
      
  
      🔥 very common LeetCode 177
      
  
      Problem. Write a function getNthHighestSalary(N) that returns the Nth highest distinct salary, or NULL if there are fewer than N distinct salaries (or N is invalid).
      
  
      Expected: N=1 → 90000, N=2 → 85000, N=3 → 80000, N=10 → NULL.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      DELIMITER //
CREATE FUNCTION getNthHighestSalary(N INT) RETURNS INT
READS SQL DATA
BEGIN
  DECLARE k INT;
  IF N IS NULL OR N < 1 THEN
    RETURN NULL;                       -- guard: OFFSET -1 is a syntax error
  END IF;
  SET k = N - 1;                       -- LIMIT/OFFSET accept variables inside routines,
  RETURN (                             -- but NOT expressions like N-1
    SELECT DISTINCT salary
    FROM Employee
    ORDER BY salary DESC
    LIMIT 1 OFFSET k
  );
END //
DELIMITER ;

SELECT getNthHighestSalary(3);   -- 80000
SELECT getNthHighestSalary(10);  -- NULL
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SET @n = 3;
SELECT MAX(salary) AS nth_salary          -- MAX turns "no rows" into NULL
FROM (
  SELECT salary,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dr
  FROM Employee
) t
WHERE dr = @n;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SET @off = 2;   -- N - 1
PREPARE s FROM
  'SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee
           ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET ?) AS nth_salary';
EXECUTE s USING @off;
DEALLOCATE PREPARE s;
      
      
      In a plain statement, LIMIT needs a literal number. Placeholders (?) in a prepared statement are allowed.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy can't I write LIMIT 1 OFFSET N-1 directly in the function?
    
      
      
      MySQL's LIMIT clause only accepts integer literals, ? placeholders in prepared statements, or local variables / parameters inside stored programs. It does not accept an arithmetic expression like N-1. So you compute k = N-1 first (or do SET N = N - 1) and then use OFFSET k.
      
      
      The N < 1 guard matters: an offset of −1 fails. Also note READS SQL DATA (or DETERMINISTIC): with binary logging on, MySQL refuses to create a function that declares none of DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL or READS SQL DATA (error 1418) unless log_bin_trust_function_creators is set.
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      PostgreSQL accepts expressions in LIMIT/OFFSET (OFFSET n-1 is fine) and would write this as a SQL function. SQL Server: OFFSET @n-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY (expressions allowed). Oracle: OFFSET n-1 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 ROWS ONLY (12c+).
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What if they want the Nth row, not the Nth distinct value?
          
      Then drop DISTINCT / use ROW_NUMBER(). But ask: with ties, "Nth row" is not deterministic unless you add a tie-breaker such as ORDER BY salary DESC, id.
      
        
      ↪Which is faster on a big table, OFFSET or DENSE_RANK?
          
      With an index on salary, DISTINCT … ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET k can walk the index backwards and stop after k+1 distinct values — great for small N. DENSE_RANK ranks the whole table. For huge N, both are linear.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P03 · Nth highest WITHOUT LIMIT or window functions
      
  
      classic "now do it without LIMIT" follow-up GfG classic · Paytm 2018
      
  
      Problem. Find the 3rd highest distinct salary using only basic SQL (works on MySQL 5.x too). Expected: 80000.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- "e1.salary is the Nth highest if exactly N-1 distinct salaries are bigger"
SELECT DISTINCT e1.salary
FROM Employee e1
WHERE 3 - 1 = (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
  FROM Employee e2
  WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary
);
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT e1.salary
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee) e1
LEFT JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM Employee) e2
       ON e2.salary > e1.salary
GROUP BY e1.salary
HAVING COUNT(e2.salary) = 3 - 1;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QExplain how the correlated count works and what it costs.
    
      
      
      For each candidate salary in the outer query, the inner query counts how many distinct salaries are strictly bigger. 90000 has 0 bigger, 85000 has 1, 80000 has 2. We want "2 bigger" for the 3rd highest. COUNT(DISTINCT …) is what makes ties behave like DENSE_RANK.
      
      
      Cost: the inner query runs once per outer row → O(n²) in the worst case. Fine for an interview, slow on millions of rows. An index on salary helps the inner range scan.
      
      
      Edge case: if N is larger than the number of distinct salaries, A returns an empty set. Wrap it: SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT … ) AS nth or SELECT MAX(salary) FROM (…) to get NULL.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common slip
      Writing COUNT(e2.salary) without DISTINCT. With the tie at 85000, 80000 then has 3 bigger salaries (90000, 85000, 85000) and is never found.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P04 · Rank scores (dense ranking)
      
  
      🔥 common LeetCode 178
      
  
      Problem. Rank the scores from highest to lowest. Ties get the same rank and the next rank has no gap. Here we rank salaries.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT name, salary,
       ROW_NUMBER() OVER w AS rn,
       RANK()       OVER w AS rnk,
       DENSE_RANK() OVER w AS drnk
FROM Employee
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary DESC)      -- named window, MySQL 8.0+
ORDER BY salary DESC;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT e1.name, e1.salary,
       (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
        FROM Employee e2
        WHERE e2.salary >= e1.salary) AS drnk
FROM Employee e1
ORDER BY e1.salary DESC;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      +-------+--------+----+-----+------+
| name  | salary | rn | rnk | drnk |
+-------+--------+----+-----+------+
| Max   |  90000 |  1 |   1 |    1 |
| Joe   |  85000 |  2 |   2 |    2 |
| Randy |  85000 |  3 |   2 |    2 |
| Henry |  80000 |  4 |   4 |    3 |
| Will  |  70000 |  5 |   5 |    4 |
| Janet |  69000 |  6 |   6 |    5 |
| Sam   |  60000 |  7 |   7 |    6 |
+-------+--------+----+-----+------+
      
  
      
    QROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK — when do I use which?
    
      
      
      
        
      ROW_NUMBER
      • Always 1, 2, 3, … unique.
      • Ties broken arbitrarily → add a tie-breaker column.
      • Use for: "exactly one row per group", dedupe, latest record, pagination.
      
        
      RANK
      • Ties share; next rank skips (1, 2, 2, 4).
      • Like sports: two silver medals, no bronze.
      • Use for: competition ranking, "position in leaderboard".
      
        
      DENSE_RANK
      • Ties share; no gaps (1, 2, 2, 3).
      • Rank = "which distinct value is this".
      • Use for: Nth highest distinct value, top-N distinct salaries.
      
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      MySQL naming trap
      RANK became a reserved word in MySQL 8.0.2. SELECT …, RANK() OVER (…) AS rank is a syntax error. Use rnk, or quote it with backticks: AS `rank`.
      
      
      ROW · RANK · DENSE
      "Row = roll-call (everyone gets a number). Rank = Olympics (ties share, medals skipped). Dense = no empty seats (ties share, nobody skipped)."
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⭐ Pattern 2 · Greatest-N-per-group & "latest record"
      
  
      Signal words: "in each department", "per customer", "top 3 per", "latest", "most recent", "first". The tool is a window function with PARTITION BY <group>, computed in a CTE, then filtered outside.
      

  
      
    
      CTErank rows inside each group (PARTITION BY)
      
    
      
    
      Ties?keep all → DENSE_RANK / RANK · exactly one → ROW_NUMBER
      
    
      
    
      Outer queryWHERE rnk <= N
      
  
      

  
  
      P05 · Department highest salary (ties included)
      
  
      🔥 very common LeetCode 184
      
  
      Problem. For each department, list the employee(s) with the highest salary. If two people tie, show both.
      
  
      +------------+----------+--------+
| Department | Employee | Salary |
+------------+----------+--------+
| IT         | Max      |  90000 |
| Sales      | Henry    |  80000 |
+------------+----------+--------+
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE (e.dept_id, e.salary) IN (          -- row constructor comparison
  SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary)
  FROM Employee
  GROUP BY dept_id
);
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH x AS (
  SELECT e.*, MAX(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_max
  FROM Employee e
)
SELECT d.name AS Department, x.name AS Employee, x.salary AS Salary
FROM x
JOIN Department d ON d.id = x.dept_id
WHERE x.salary = x.dept_max;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) AS mx
      FROM Employee GROUP BY dept_id) m
  ON m.dept_id = e.dept_id AND m.mx = e.salary
JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.dept_id;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- "no colleague in my department earns more than me"
SELECT d.name AS Department, e.name AS Employee, e.salary AS Salary
FROM Employee e
JOIN Department d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM Employee x
  WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id AND x.salary > e.salary
);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy is SELECT dept_id, name, MAX(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id wrong?
    
      
      
      Because name is not in GROUP BY and is not aggregated. The database does not know which name to show. In MySQL 8 with the default ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY mode you get ERROR 1055. In old MySQL (or with the mode turned off) it silently returned the name from some arbitrary row of the group — often the wrong person. MAX(salary) does not "drag" its row's other columns along.
      
      
      🚫
      Answer that fails the interview
      "I'll just turn off ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY." The interviewer wants you to understand that an aggregate returns a value, not a row. Use one of the four correct approaches above.
      
      
      Index: INDEX(dept_id, salary) makes the GROUP BY dept_id … MAX(salary) a "loose index scan" (MySQL can jump to the last entry of each dept) and makes the join back cheap.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Include departments with no employees (HR) and show NULL.
          
      Start from Department: FROM Department d LEFT JOIN (…ranked employees…) x ON x.dept_id = d.id AND x.rnk = 1. Put the rank filter in the ON clause, not WHERE, or the LEFT JOIN turns back into an INNER JOIN.
      
        
      ↪Only one person per department even if tied (lowest id wins).
          
      ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, id) and keep rn = 1.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P06 · Department top 3 salaries
      
  
      🔥 hot — Amazon, FAANG, product companies LeetCode 185 (Hard)
      
  
      Problem. A "high earner" is someone whose salary is in the top 3 distinct salaries of their department. List them all.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.name, e.salary, e.dept_id,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id
                            ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS drnk
  FROM Employee e
)
SELECT d.name AS Department, r.name AS Employee, r.salary AS Salary
FROM ranked r
JOIN Department d ON d.id = r.dept_id
WHERE r.drnk <= 3
ORDER BY Department, Salary DESC;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT d.name AS Department, e1.name AS Employee, e1.salary AS Salary
FROM Employee e1
JOIN Department d ON d.id = e1.dept_id
WHERE 3 > (
  SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary)
  FROM Employee e2
  WHERE e2.dept_id = e1.dept_id
    AND e2.salary  > e1.salary
);
      
      
      "Fewer than 3 distinct salaries in my department beat me" = I am in the top 3.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      +------------+----------+--------+
| Department | Employee | Salary |
+------------+----------+--------+
| IT         | Max      |  90000 |
| IT         | Joe      |  85000 |
| IT         | Randy    |  85000 |
| IT         | Will     |  70000 |
| Sales      | Henry    |  80000 |
| Sales      | Sam      |  60000 |
+------------+----------+--------+
      
  
      
    QWhy can't I put WHERE DENSE_RANK() OVER (…) <= 3 directly?
    
      
      
      Window functions are evaluated after WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING — they work on the rows that survived filtering. So at WHERE time the rank does not exist yet. MySQL raises error 3593 ("You cannot use the window function 'dense_rank' in this context"). Wrap the ranking in a CTE or derived table and filter outside. (Some engines like Snowflake, BigQuery and DuckDB add a QUALIFY clause for exactly this; MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server do not have it.)
      
      
      Edge cases: a department with fewer than 3 employees returns all of them (Sales: 2 rows); ties can return more than 3 rows (IT: 4 rows). If the interviewer says "exactly 3 people", switch to ROW_NUMBER() with a tie-breaker and confirm.
      
      
      Index: INDEX(dept_id, salary) lets the window sort be read in index order (partition and order columns match the index).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      "This is a greatest-N-per-group problem. I'll compute DENSE_RANK partitioned by department and ordered by salary descending in a CTE — dense rank because the question says top three distinct salaries, so ties should both appear. Then I filter rank ≤ 3 outside, because a window function can't be used in WHERE. Without window functions, I'd use a correlated subquery counting distinct higher salaries in the same department."
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪RANK instead of DENSE_RANK — what changes on this data?
          
      IT ranks become 1, 2, 2, 4, 5. With RANK <= 3, Will (rank 4) disappears, so IT returns only 3 rows. That's the "top 3 people with ties" reading, not "top 3 distinct salaries".
      
        
      ↪Top 3 per department on 500 million rows?
          
      Composite index (dept_id, salary DESC); or, if departments are few, a LATERAL join (MySQL 8.0.14+) that does ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3 per department using the index — it reads only ~3 index entries per department instead of sorting everything.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P07 · Latest record per group, and the second most recent
      
  
      🔥 very common in product & analytics interviews
      
  
      Problem. Using the Orders table below, return each customer's latest order. Variant: return each customer's second most recent order, or their only order if they have just one (LeetCode 1369 style).
      
  
      CREATE TABLE Customers (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(30));
CREATE TABLE Orders (
  order_id INT PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INT, order_date DATE, amount INT
);
INSERT INTO Customers VALUES (1,'Asha'),(2,'Ravi'),(3,'Neha'),(4,'Kabir'),(5,'Zoya');
INSERT INTO Orders VALUES
 (1,1,'2024-01-05',100),(2,2,'2024-01-20',200),(3,1,'2024-02-03',150),
 (4,3,'2024-02-14',300),(5,1,'2024-02-28', 50),(6,2,'2024-03-09',400),
 (7,4,'2024-03-15',200);
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH r AS (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                            ORDER BY order_date DESC, order_id DESC) AS rn
  FROM Orders o
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date, amount
FROM r
WHERE rn = 1;
      
      
      customer_id | order_id | order_date | amount
          1 |        5 | 2024-02-28 |     50
          2 |        6 | 2024-03-09 |    400
          3 |        4 | 2024-02-14 |    300
          4 |        7 | 2024-03-15 |    200
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH r AS (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id)                          AS cnt
  FROM Orders o
)
SELECT customer_id, order_id, order_date
FROM r
WHERE rn = 2 OR (cnt = 1 AND rn = 1);
      
      
      customer_id | order_id | order_date
          1 |        3 | 2024-02-03     ← 2nd most recent of 3
          2 |        2 | 2024-01-20
          3 |        4 | 2024-02-14     ← only order
          4 |        7 | 2024-03-15     ← only order
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- join to the max date per customer (ties on the same date return both)
SELECT o.*
FROM Orders o
JOIN (SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_date) AS mx
      FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id) m
  ON m.customer_id = o.customer_id AND m.mx = o.order_date;

-- or the "no later row exists" anti-join
SELECT o.*
FROM Orders o
LEFT JOIN Orders later
       ON later.customer_id = o.customer_id
      AND later.order_date  > o.order_date
WHERE later.order_id IS NULL;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy add order_id DESC as a tie-breaker?
    
      
      
      If a customer places two orders on the same date, ORDER BY order_date DESC alone does not decide which is "latest". ROW_NUMBER will pick one arbitrarily, and the answer can change between runs. A unique tie-breaker (the PK) makes the result deterministic. Better still, store a DATETIME/TIMESTAMP instead of a DATE.
      
      
      Index: INDEX(customer_id, order_date, order_id) — the window partition + order then matches the index, and the anti-join version becomes an index range probe.
      
      
      🌍
      Production story
      "Current status of every shipment" or "latest price of every product" is this exact query on a history table with hundreds of millions of rows. Teams often keep a separate current_status table updated in the same transaction (a deliberate denormalization) so the hot path never has to rank history. See Chapter 06 on denormalization.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪First AND last order per customer in one row?
          
      Dates only: SELECT customer_id, MIN(order_date), MAX(order_date), COUNT(*) FROM Orders GROUP BY customer_id. Whole first/last rows: FIRST_VALUE(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) and FIRST_VALUE(order_id) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date DESC) — avoid LAST_VALUE with the default frame (it only sees up to the current row).
      
        
      ↪Which approach would you ship?
          
      ROW_NUMBER in a CTE: one pass, handles ties deterministically, easy to change to "top 2". The anti-join is fine with a good index and works on any engine version.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ✂️ Pattern 3 · Duplicates: find, list, delete
      
  
      Signal words: "duplicate", "appears more than once", "keep one", "unique". Finding = GROUP BY … HAVING COUNT(*) > 1. Deleting = pick a survivor per group (smallest id, latest timestamp) and delete the rest.
      
  
      CREATE TABLE Person (id INT PRIMARY KEY, email VARCHAR(50));
INSERT INTO Person VALUES
 (1,'john@example.com'), (2,'bob@example.com'),
 (3,'john@example.com'), (4,'john@example.com');
      

  
  
      P08 · Find duplicate emails (and list the full duplicate rows)
      
  
      🔥 very common — TCS Digital, Infosys LeetCode 182
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM Person
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
-- john@example.com | 3
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- every row whose email occurs more than once (ids 1, 3, 4)
SELECT id, email
FROM (
  SELECT p.*, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY email) AS cnt
  FROM Person p
) t
WHERE cnt > 1
ORDER BY email, id;

-- pre-8.0
SELECT p.*
FROM Person p
JOIN (SELECT email FROM Person GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1) d
  ON d.email = p.email;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- "duplicate" = same first_name + last_name + dob
SELECT first_name, last_name, dob, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM Users
GROUP BY first_name, last_name, dob
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QEdge cases in "find duplicates"?
    
      
      
        
        
      • Case and spaces: MySQL's default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is case- and accent-insensitive, so 'John@x.com' and 'john@x.com' group together. Trailing spaces may also compare equal for PAD SPACE collations. Ask whether that counts as a duplicate; if not, group by BINARY email or a _bin collation. For "normalized" emails: GROUP BY LOWER(TRIM(email)).
        • 
        
      • NULLs: GROUP BY puts all NULLs in one group, so many NULL emails show up as a "duplicate". A UNIQUE index, on the other hand, allows many NULLs. Add WHERE email IS NOT NULL if needed.
        • 
        
      • WHERE vs HAVING: WHERE COUNT(*) > 1 is an error — aggregates are computed after WHERE.
        • 
      
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪How do you stop duplicates from coming back?
          
      ALTER TABLE Person ADD UNIQUE KEY uk_email (email); — after cleaning. Then use INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE or INSERT IGNORE in the app. A check in application code alone is not enough: two concurrent requests can both pass the check (a race condition — see Chapter 13).
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P09 · Delete duplicates, keeping the smallest id
      
  
      🔥 very common LeetCode 196
      
  
      Expected table after the delete: (1, john@example.com), (2, bob@example.com).
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- delete every row that has a twin with a SMALLER id
DELETE p1
FROM Person p1
JOIN Person p2
  ON p1.email = p2.email
 AND p1.id > p2.id;
      
      
      Only the table alias listed before FROM (p1) is deleted from. Flip to p1.id < p2.id to keep the largest id instead.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      DELETE FROM Person
WHERE id NOT IN (
  SELECT keep_id FROM (                      -- extra derived table = the fix
    SELECT MIN(id) AS keep_id FROM Person GROUP BY email
  ) AS k
);
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- best when the "keep" rule is complex (e.g. keep the latest updated_at)
DELETE p
FROM Person p
JOIN (
  SELECT id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn
  FROM Person
