) d ON d.id = p.id
WHERE d.rn > 1;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- a direct subquery on the target table is fine in PostgreSQL
DELETE FROM person
WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM person GROUP BY email);

-- or with USING
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM person
)
DELETE FROM person p USING ranked r
WHERE p.id = r.id AND r.rn > 1;
      
      
      WITH cte AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) AS rn FROM Person
)
DELETE FROM cte WHERE rn > 1;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy does DELETE FROM Person WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM Person GROUP BY email) fail in MySQL?
    
      
      
      MySQL refuses to modify a table while reading the same table in a subquery of that statement:
      
      
      ERROR 1093 (HY000): You can't specify target table 'Person' for update in FROM clause
      
      
      Why: MySQL would be reading rows it is deleting at the same time, and the result could depend on order. Fix: wrap the subquery in one more derived table (SELECT keep_id FROM (…) AS k). That forces MySQL to materialize (compute and store) the list of ids first, then delete. If the optimizer merges the derived table back in, the error returns — the NO_MERGE hint forces materialization. The self-join DELETE (A) avoids the issue entirely.
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      PostgreSQL and SQL Server allow the plain subquery. SQL Server can even DELETE FROM cte. In MySQL, WITH ranked AS (…) DELETE FROM ranked fails with ERROR 1288 ("target table ranked of the DELETE is not updatable"), but WITH ranked AS (…) DELETE FROM Person WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1) works. Also: MySQL does not allow ORDER BY/LIMIT in a multi-table DELETE.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Performance trap
      The self-join is O(k²) inside each duplicate group: an email that appears 10,000 times creates ~50 million join pairs. ROW_NUMBER is one sort. For a huge purge, the MySQL manual suggests copying the rows you keep into a new table and swapping with RENAME TABLE; or delete in batches of a few thousand rows to keep transactions and replication lag small.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      "I'll self-join Person on the same email where my id is bigger than the other id — those are the extra copies — and delete only the left alias. In MySQL I can't delete from a table while selecting from it in a plain subquery, that's error 1093, so if I use the NOT IN version I wrap the subquery in a derived table to force it to materialize. Finally I'd add a unique index on email so this can't happen again."
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Keep the most recently updated row instead.
          
      Use approach C with ORDER BY updated_at DESC, id DESC. The self-join version gets messy with ties on updated_at.
      
        
      ↪Show the rows that would be deleted, without deleting.
          
      Turn the DELETE into SELECT: SELECT p1.* FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id; — note it may list a row more than once (id 4 has two smaller twins), so add DISTINCT. Always run this dry run in production first, inside a transaction.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P10 · Remove exact duplicate rows from a table with NO primary key
      
  
      common follow-up
      
  
      Problem. Logs(user_id, action, ts) has no PK and some rows are 100% identical. Keep one copy of each.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      CREATE TABLE Logs_clean LIKE Logs;
INSERT INTO Logs_clean SELECT DISTINCT * FROM Logs;
RENAME TABLE Logs TO Logs_old, Logs_clean TO Logs;   -- atomic swap
DROP TABLE Logs_old;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      ALTER TABLE Logs ADD COLUMN tmp_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY;
DELETE a FROM Logs a
JOIN Logs b
  ON  a.user_id <=> b.user_id          -- NULL-safe equality!
  AND a.action  <=> b.action
  AND a.ts      <=> b.ts
  AND a.tmp_id  > b.tmp_id;
ALTER TABLE Logs DROP COLUMN tmp_id;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy <=> instead of =, and why can't I use ROW_NUMBER to delete here?
    
      
      
      NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, so two identical rows that both have a NULL column would never match with = and would never be deduplicated. <=> is MySQL's NULL-safe equal (IS NOT DISTINCT FROM in standard SQL/PostgreSQL). DISTINCT already treats NULLs as equal.
      
      
      You can compute ROW_NUMBER over the duplicates, but with no unique column you can't point the DELETE at "copy #2" — every copy looks the same. PostgreSQL can use the hidden ctid, Oracle the ROWID, SQL Server can DELETE FROM cte WHERE rn > 1; MySQL needs a temporary id or the copy-and-swap.
      
      
      Lesson to say: every table should have a primary key. InnoDB secretly creates a hidden 6-byte row id if you don't define one, but you cannot use it in SQL.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🔗 Pattern 4 · Self-joins (a table joined to itself)
      
  
      Signal words: "more than their manager", "pairs", "mutual", "both directions", "same table compares rows". A self-join gives each row a partner row from the same table, using two aliases.
      

  

  
  
      P11 · Employees who earn more than their managers
      
  
      🔥 very common LeetCode 181
      
  
      Expected: Will (70000 vs Janet's 69000).
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT e.name AS Employee
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT e.name AS Employee
FROM Employee e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT m.salary FROM Employee m WHERE m.id = e.manager_id);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhat happens to the CEO (manager_id NULL)? And how do I list everyone with their manager's name?
    
      
      
      The INNER JOIN drops Max because NULL = 4 is never true. For this question that is correct (no manager → can't earn more than one). To list everyone with their manager, use a LEFT JOIN:
      
      
      SELECT e.name AS employee, COALESCE(m.name, '— (top)') AS manager
FROM Employee e
LEFT JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id;
      
      
      Index: m.id is the PK, so each lookup is a single B+ tree probe. An index on manager_id helps the reverse direction ("all reports of X").
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Employees earning more than their manager's manager?
          
      Join a third alias: JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id JOIN Employee g ON m.manager_id = g.id WHERE e.salary > g.salary. For "any manager above me" you need a recursive CTE (Pattern 8).
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P12 · Managers with at least N direct reports
      
  
      🔥 common LeetCode 570 (N = 5) · 1731
      
  
      Problem. Return managers with ≥ 5 direct reports. Our tiny table has fewer, so we demo with N = 3 → Max (4 reports: Joe, Henry, Janet, Randy).
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT m.id, m.name, COUNT(*) AS reports
FROM Employee e
JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT name
FROM Employee
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT manager_id FROM Employee
  GROUP BY manager_id
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
);
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- include people with 0 reports, plus average age/salary of reports (LeetCode 1731 style)
SELECT m.id, m.name,
       COUNT(e.id)             AS reports,     -- COUNT(col) ignores the NULL from LEFT JOIN
       ROUND(AVG(e.salary), 0) AS avg_report_salary
FROM Employee m
LEFT JOIN Employee e ON e.manager_id = m.id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name
ORDER BY reports DESC, m.id;
      
      
      id | name  | reports | avg_report_salary
 4 | Max   |       4 |             79750
 2 | Henry |       1 |             60000
 5 | Janet |       1 |             70000
 1 | Joe   |       0 |              NULL
 ...
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy COUNT(e.id) and not COUNT(*) in the LEFT JOIN version?
    
      
      
      With a LEFT JOIN, a manager with no reports still produces one row whose e.* columns are all NULL. COUNT(*) counts that row → 1 (wrong). COUNT(e.id) skips NULLs → 0 (right). This is the #1 bug in "count including zero" questions (see P33).
      
      
      Also note: GROUP BY m.id, m.name — group by the id, not only the name, because two managers can share a name.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P13 · Mutual follows (pairs in both directions)
      
  
      common in social-app interviews
      
  
      Problem. Follows(follower, followee). List each pair of users who follow each other, once per pair.
      
  
      Follows: (A,B) (B,A) (A,C) (C,D) (D,C) (B,C)
Output :  A | B
          C | D
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT a.follower AS user1, a.followee AS user2
FROM Follows a
JOIN Follows b
  ON  b.follower = a.followee
  AND b.followee = a.follower
WHERE a.follower < a.followee;      -- keep (A,B), drop the mirror (B,A)
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT a.follower AS user1, a.followee AS user2
FROM Follows a
WHERE a.follower < a.followee
  AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Follows b
              WHERE b.follower = a.followee AND b.followee = a.follower);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy a.follower < a.followee? What else could go wrong?
    
      
      
      Without it, every mutual pair appears twice: (A,B) and (B,A). The < keeps exactly one orientation. Same trick for "products bought together" (P44) and any "unordered pair" question. Also check: can a user follow themselves (A,A)? That row would join with itself; the < filter removes it too. Duplicate follow rows would double-count — a PRIMARY KEY (follower, followee) prevents that and is also the index this query needs (the mirror lookup is a PK probe).
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P14 · Who has the most friends?
      
  
      common LeetCode 602
      
  
      Problem. RequestAccepted(requester_id, accepter_id); a friendship counts for both people. Find the person with the most friends. Data: (1,2) (1,3) (2,3) (3,4) → id 3, 3 friends.
      
  
      WITH both_sides AS (
  SELECT requester_id AS id FROM RequestAccepted
  UNION ALL                                  -- ALL! UNION would drop repeated ids
  SELECT accepter_id  AS id FROM RequestAccepted
)
SELECT id, COUNT(*) AS num
FROM both_sides
GROUP BY id
ORDER BY num DESC
LIMIT 1;
      
  
      
    QWhy must it be UNION ALL? And what if two people tie?
    
      
      
      UNION removes duplicate rows, so id 3 (appearing three times) would be counted once. This is the "unpivot two columns into one" trick: stack both columns with UNION ALL, then group. For ties, replace LIMIT 1 with a rank: WHERE num = (SELECT MAX(num) FROM counts) or RANK() OVER (ORDER BY num DESC) = 1.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🔍 Pattern 5 · Anti-joins, semi-joins & relational division
      
  
      Signal words: "never", "did not", "without any", "has no" (anti-join) · "at least one", "who have" (semi-join) · "all", "every" (division).
      

  

  
  
      P15 · Customers who never ordered
      
  
      🔥 very common LeetCode 183
      
  
      Expected (Customers/Orders from P07): Zoya.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
);
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT c.name AS Customers
FROM Customers c
LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;           -- test a NOT NULL column of the right table
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT name AS Customers
FROM Customers
WHERE id NOT IN (
  SELECT customer_id FROM Orders
  WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL      -- without this line, ONE NULL ⇒ ZERO rows
);
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT id FROM Customers
EXCEPT
SELECT customer_id FROM Orders;     -- MySQL 8.0.31+; returns ids (join back for names)
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QExplain the NOT IN + NULL trap step by step.
    
      
      
      Suppose Orders contains one order with customer_id = NULL. Then 5 NOT IN (1, 2, 3, 4, NULL) means 5<>1 AND 5<>2 AND 5<>3 AND 5<>4 AND 5<>NULL. The last part is UNKNOWN, and TRUE AND UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, so Zoya disappears — and so does everyone else. The query silently returns zero rows.
      
      
      NOT EXISTS does not have this problem: the inner o.customer_id = c.id is simply never TRUE for the NULL row, so it does not "match", and the outer row survives.
      
      
      ApproachNULL-safe?Duplicates in output?MySQL 8 plan
      
        
      NOT EXISTS✔✔ neverantijoin (8.0.17+)
      
        
      LEFT JOIN … IS NULL✔✔ never (unmatched rows appear once)outer join + filter
      
        
      NOT IN✘ if subquery can be NULL✔antijoin possible, but the NULL semantics still apply
      
      
      
      
      🚫
      Wrong answer that fails interviews
      LEFT JOIN Orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id WHERE o.amount IS NULL — if amount is nullable, a real order with NULL amount looks like "no order". Always test the right table's join key or primary key for IS NULL.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      "This is an anti-join. I prefer NOT EXISTS: it's NULL-safe and MySQL 8 turns it into an antijoin internally. LEFT JOIN with IS NULL on the right table's key is equivalent. I avoid NOT IN unless the subquery column is NOT NULL, because a single NULL in the list makes NOT IN return nothing."
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Customers who ordered at least once (semi-join) — why not a plain JOIN?
          
      A JOIN returns Asha three times (3 orders). Use WHERE EXISTS (…) or WHERE id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM Orders); each customer appears once. Patching with DISTINCT works but hides the fan-out and costs a dedupe step.
      
        
      ↪Customers who did not order in the last 30 days?
          
      Put the date filter inside the NOT EXISTS (or in the LEFT JOIN's ON clause): … AND o.order_date >= CURDATE() - INTERVAL 30 DAY. Putting it in the outer WHERE of a LEFT JOIN turns it into an inner join.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P16 · Employees whose manager left the company
      
  
      common LeetCode 1978
      
  
      Problem. Find employees with salary < 30000 whose manager_id points to an id that no longer exists in the table. (A dangling reference — possible only when there is no foreign key.)
      
  
      SELECT e.id
FROM Employees e
WHERE e.salary < 30000
  AND e.manager_id IS NOT NULL                 -- the CEO's NULL is not "manager left"
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Employees m WHERE m.id = e.manager_id)
ORDER BY e.id;
      
  
      💡
      Talking point
      A self-referencing FOREIGN KEY (manager_id) REFERENCES Employees(id) ON DELETE SET NULL would make this situation impossible — mention it. The question is really about orphan rows, which happen when integrity is enforced only in application code.
      

  
  
      P17 · Customers who bought ALL products (relational division)
      
  
      🔥 favourite "hard" question LeetCode 1045
      
  
      Customer(customer_id, product_key): (1,5) (2,6) (3,5) (3,6) (1,6)
Product(product_key): 5, 6
Output: 1, 3
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT customer_id
FROM Customer
WHERE product_key IN (SELECT product_key FROM Product)   -- ignore unknown products
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_key) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Product);
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- "there is NO product that this customer has NOT bought"
SELECT DISTINCT c.customer_id
FROM Customer c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM Product p
  WHERE NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM Customer c2
    WHERE c2.customer_id = c.customer_id
      AND c2.product_key = p.product_key
  )
);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy DISTINCT in the count, and what is "relational division"?
    
      
      
      Division (÷ in relational algebra, see Chapter 04) answers "which X are related to every Y". SQL has no ÷ operator, so we use either counting or double negation ("for all" = "not exists one that is missing").
      
      
      COUNT(DISTINCT) matters because a customer who bought product 5 twice has COUNT(*) = 2 = total products, a false positive. The IN (SELECT … FROM Product) filter matters if Customer can contain products that are not in the catalog. Double NOT EXISTS is immune to both problems and is the textbook answer.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Students who took all courses taught by Prof. X?
          
      Same pattern; the "divisor" is now a filtered set: HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Course WHERE prof = 'X'), and only count enrollments in those courses.
      
        
      ↪What if Product is empty?
          
      Logically every customer "bought all of nothing" — double NOT EXISTS returns all customers; the counting version returns none (no customer has 0 distinct products in a GROUP BY). Mention this difference; it shows real understanding.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      📅 Pattern 6 · Dates & time series
      
  
      Signal words: "previous day", "first login", "retention", "monthly", "growth", "running total", "moving average", "every day even with no sales". Tools: LAG/LEAD, SUM() OVER (ORDER BY …), date arithmetic with INTERVAL, DATE_FORMAT, recursive date series.
      
  
      ⚠️
      MySQL date arithmetic gotcha
      DATE('2024-03-01') - 1 returns the number 20240300 in MySQL (the date is converted to 20240301, then 1 is subtracted). Always write d - INTERVAL 1 DAY, DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL 1 DAY) or use DATEDIFF(a, b) (returns whole days). In PostgreSQL, date - 1 really is the previous day.
      

  
  
      P18 · Rising temperature (compare with the previous calendar day)
      
  
      🔥 very common LeetCode 197
      
  
      id | recordDate | temperature
 1 | 2024-01-01 | 10
 2 | 2024-01-02 | 25     ← warmer than 01-01  ✔
 3 | 2024-01-03 | 20
 4 | 2024-01-05 | 30     ← 01-04 is MISSING: no "yesterday" → not included
Expected: id = 2
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT w.id
FROM Weather w
JOIN Weather y
  ON y.recordDate = w.recordDate - INTERVAL 1 DAY   -- or DATEDIFF(w.recordDate, y.recordDate) = 1
WHERE w.temperature > y.temperature;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT id
FROM (
  SELECT id, recordDate, temperature,
         LAG(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_temp,
         LAG(recordDate)  OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_date
  FROM Weather
) t
WHERE temperature > prev_temp
  AND prev_date = recordDate - INTERVAL 1 DAY;      -- the guard that makes LAG correct
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- ✘ returns 2 AND 4: compares 01-05 with 01-03 (the previous ROW, not the previous DAY)
SELECT id FROM (
  SELECT id, temperature, LAG(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_temp
  FROM Weather) t
WHERE temperature > prev_temp;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhat is the trap here, and which index helps?
    
      
      
      "Yesterday" is a calendar concept, LAG is a row concept. They agree only when no day is missing. The data in interviews usually has a gap exactly to catch this. Also check: can a date appear twice? (Then define which reading counts.) An index (ideally UNIQUE) on recordDate makes the self-join an index lookup per row. Note w.recordDate - INTERVAL 1 DAY is on the other side of the comparison from y.recordDate, so the lookup on y stays sargable.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P19 · First login date and the device used at first login
      
  
      common LeetCode 511 / 512
      
  
      CREATE TABLE Activity (player_id INT, device_id INT, event_date DATE, games_played INT,
                       PRIMARY KEY (player_id, event_date));
INSERT INTO Activity VALUES
 (1,2,'2016-03-01',5),(1,2,'2016-03-02',6),(2,3,'2017-06-25',1),
 (3,1,'2016-03-02',0),(3,4,'2018-07-03',5);
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_login
FROM Activity
GROUP BY player_id;
-- 1 | 2016-03-01 · 2 | 2017-06-25 · 3 | 2016-03-02
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT player_id, device_id
FROM (
  SELECT player_id, device_id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY player_id ORDER BY event_date) AS rn
  FROM Activity
) t
WHERE rn = 1;
-- 1 | 2 · 2 | 3 · 3 | 1

-- pre-8.0: row-value IN
SELECT player_id, device_id FROM Activity
WHERE (player_id, event_date) IN (SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      Same "latest/first record per group" pattern as P07. The MIN(event_date) part does not give you the device of that row — classic ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY trap.
      

  
  
      P20 · Day-1 retention (logged in again the day after first login)
      
  
      🔥 hot in analytics / product-company rounds LeetCode 550 (Game Play Analysis IV)
      
  
      Problem. Fraction of players who logged in on the day right after their first login, rounded to 2 decimals. Expected: only player 1 (03-01 → 03-02) qualifies; 1 of 3 players → 0.33.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS first_day
  FROM Activity
  GROUP BY player_id
)
SELECT ROUND(COUNT(a.player_id) / COUNT(*), 2) AS fraction   -- matched / all players
FROM firsts f
LEFT JOIN Activity a
       ON a.player_id  = f.player_id
      AND a.event_date = f.first_day + INTERVAL 1 DAY;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT ROUND(
         COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN event_date = first_day + INTERVAL 1 DAY THEN player_id END)
       / COUNT(DISTINCT player_id), 2) AS fraction
FROM (
  SELECT player_id, event_date,
         MIN(event_date) OVER (PARTITION BY player_id) AS first_day
  FROM Activity
) t;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QHow would you build a full retention cohort table (D1, D7, D30)?
    
      
      
      Cohort = the group of users who started on the same day (or week). For each cohort, count how many came back on day N.
      
      
      WITH firsts AS (
  SELECT player_id, MIN(event_date) AS cohort_day FROM Activity GROUP BY player_id
),
activity AS (
  SELECT f.cohort_day, a.player_id, DATEDIFF(a.event_date, f.cohort_day) AS day_n
  FROM Activity a JOIN firsts f ON f.player_id = a.player_id
)
SELECT cohort_day,
       COUNT(DISTINCT player_id)                                     AS cohort_size,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN day_n = 1  THEN player_id END)       AS d1,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN day_n = 7  THEN player_id END)       AS d7,
       COUNT(DISTINCT CASE WHEN day_n = 30 THEN player_id END)       AS d30
FROM activity
GROUP BY cohort_day
ORDER BY cohort_day;
      
      
      Divide each column by cohort_size for percentages. Clarify: "retained on day 7" (exact day) vs "within 7 days" (rolling) — they give different numbers.
      
      
      Note on division: in MySQL, / always returns a decimal (1/3 = 0.3333). In PostgreSQL and SQL Server, int / int is integer division (1/3 = 0) — multiply by 1.0 first. Use DIV in MySQL for integer division.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P21 · DAU / MAU and "active users in the last 30 days"
      
  
      🔥 hot — product analytics LeetCode 1141
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT DATE(login_ts) AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS dau
FROM Logins
WHERE login_ts >= '2024-03-01' AND login_ts < '2024-04-01'   -- sargable range
GROUP BY DATE(login_ts)
ORDER BY day;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- on our Orders table: monthly active customers
SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m') AS ym,
       COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)      AS mau
FROM Orders
GROUP BY ym
ORDER BY ym;
-- 2024-01 | 2 · 2024-02 | 2 · 2024-03 | 2
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- users active in the 30 days ending 2019-07-27 (inclusive), per day
SELECT activity_date AS day, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS active_users
FROM Activity
WHERE activity_date > '2019-07-27' - INTERVAL 30 DAY
  AND activity_date <= '2019-07-27'
GROUP BY activity_date;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy not WHERE MONTH(login_ts) = 3? And can I sum DAU to get MAU?
    
      
      
      MONTH(login_ts) = 3 wraps the column in a function → the index on login_ts can't be used (not sargable), and it also matches March of every year. Use a half-open range >= '2024-03-01' AND < '2024-04-01'; it also handles DATETIME values at 23:59:59.5 correctly, which BETWEEN '…-01' AND '…-31' does not.
      
      
      No, MAU ≠ sum of DAU: a user active on 20 days would be counted 20 times. Distinct counts are not additive — that's why "DAU/MAU stickiness" needs its own query. A rolling MAU per day needs a self-join or a window over distinct users, which MySQL can't do directly (COUNT(DISTINCT) OVER is not supported); join a date series to the logins within 30 days and count distinct.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P22 · Month-over-month (MoM) and year-over-year (YoY) growth
      
  
      🔥 hot
      
  
      Problem. Monthly revenue and the % change vs the previous month.
      
  
      WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m-01') AS month_start,
         SUM(amount)                         AS revenue
  FROM Orders
  GROUP BY month_start
)
SELECT month_start,
       revenue,
       LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start) AS prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start))
                 / NULLIF(LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month_start), 0), 2) AS mom_pct
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month_start;
      
  
      month_start | revenue | prev_revenue | mom_pct
2024-01-01  |     300 |         NULL |    NULL
2024-02-01  |     500 |          300 |   66.67
2024-03-01  |     600 |          500 |   20.00
      
  
      
    QEdge cases: zero revenue, missing months, and YoY?
    
      
      
        
        
      • Divide by zero: NULLIF(prev, 0) turns 0 into NULL so the result is NULL instead of an error/warning. (MySQL returns NULL for x/0 anyway, with a warning; in strict mode with ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO an INSERT/UPDATE would fail. PostgreSQL raises an error.)
        • 
        
      • Missing month: if April has no orders, there is no April row, and LAG for May would compare with March. Generate a month series with a recursive CTE (P25) and LEFT JOIN, so April shows 0.
        • 
        
      • YoY: with a complete monthly series, LAG(revenue, 12) OVER (ORDER BY month_start). Safer: self-join on prev.month_start = cur.month_start - INTERVAL 1 YEAR, which does not depend on every month being present.
        • 
        
      • Use WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY month_start) to avoid repeating the LAG definition.
        • 
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P23 · Running (cumulative) total
      
  
      🔥 very common
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                         ORDER BY order_date, order_id
                         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running_per_customer,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date, order_id)                    AS running_overall
FROM Orders
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT o.customer_id, o.order_date, o.amount,
       (SELECT SUM(x.amount) FROM Orders x
        WHERE x.customer_id = o.customer_id
          AND x.order_date <= o.order_date) AS running_per_customer
FROM Orders o
ORDER BY o.customer_id, o.order_date;      -- O(n²) — say so
      
    
      
  
      
  
      customer_id | order_date | amount | running_per_customer | running_overall
          1 | 2024-01-05 |    100 |                  100 |             100
          1 | 2024-02-03 |    150 |                  250 |             450
          1 | 2024-02-28 |     50 |                  300 |             800
          2 | 2024-01-20 |    200 |                  200 |             300
          2 | 2024-03-09 |    400 |                  600 |            1200
          3 | 2024-02-14 |    300 |                  300 |             750
          4 | 2024-03-15 |    200 |                  200 |            1400
      
  
      
    QROWS vs RANGE — why did I write the frame explicitly?
    
      
      
      When you give ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE treats rows with the same ORDER BY value (peers) as one block: if two orders share a date, both rows show the total including both. ROWS counts physical rows, so the total grows one row at a time. Add a unique tie-breaker (order_id) or use ROWS when you want a strict row-by-row running sum.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪"Last person to fit in the bus" (LeetCode 1204)?
          
      Running sum of weight ordered by boarding turn, keep rows with running ≤ 1000, take the last: SELECT person_name FROM (SELECT person_name, turn, SUM(weight) OVER (ORDER BY turn) AS w FROM Queue) t WHERE w <= 1000 ORDER BY turn DESC LIMIT 1; On LeetCode's data → John Cena.
      
        
      ↪Reset the running total every month.
          
      Add the month to the partition: PARTITION BY customer_id, DATE_FORMAT(order_date, '%Y-%m').
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P24 · 7-day moving average
      
  
      🔥 hot LeetCode 1321 (Restaurant Growth)
      
  
      Problem. For each day, the average daily sales over that day and the 6 days before it. Only report days that have a full 7-day window.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH daily AS (                                   -- 1 row per day first!
  SELECT visited_on, SUM(amount) AS amount
  FROM Customer
  GROUP BY visited_on
)
SELECT visited_on,
       SUM(amount) OVER w                AS amount_7d,
       ROUND(AVG(amount) OVER w, 2)      AS average_amount,
       COUNT(*) OVER w                   AS days_in_window
FROM daily
WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY visited_on ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)
ORDER BY visited_on;
-- then keep rows WHERE days_in_window = 7 (wrap in a CTE)
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- correct even when some days are missing: the frame is by DATE, not by row count
SELECT visited_on,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY visited_on
                         RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS amount_7d
FROM daily;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT a.visited_on,
       SUM(b.amount)            AS amount_7d,
       ROUND(SUM(b.amount)/7, 2) AS average_amount
FROM daily a
JOIN daily b
  ON b.visited_on BETWEEN a.visited_on - INTERVAL 6 DAY AND a.visited_on
GROUP BY a.visited_on
HAVING a.visited_on >= (SELECT MIN(visited_on) FROM daily) + INTERVAL 6 DAY;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    Q"ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING" — when is it wrong?
    
      
      
      When days are missing. ROWS counts rows, so if 01-04 has no sales row, the "7-row" window actually spans 8 calendar days. Small demo with a 3-day window on sales 01-01:100, 01-02:200, 01-03:300, (01-04 missing), 01-05:500:
      
      
      dayamountROWS 2 PRECEDING avgCorrect 3-calendar-day avg (missing = 0)
      
        
      01-03300200.00200.00
      
        
      01-04—(no row)166.67
      
        
      01-05500333.33 ✘ (01-02, 01-03, 01-05)266.67
      
      
      
      
      Fixes: (1) fill missing days with 0 first (P25), then ROWS works; (2) use RANGE BETWEEN INTERVAL 6 DAY PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW (MySQL 8 supports interval frames on date/time ORDER BY keys); (3) self-join on a date range. Also: AVG over the RANGE frame divides by the number of rows present, so for "average per calendar day" use SUM(…)/7.
      
      
      Two more traps: aggregate to one row per day before the window (multiple visits per day), and decide whether the first 6 days (incomplete window) should be shown.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P25 · Fill missing dates with 0 (recursive date series)
      
  
      🔥 hot — dashboards, reports
      
  
      Problem. Sales has rows for 01-01, 01-02, 01-03, 01-05, 01-06. Show every date from the first to the last, with 0 for days without sales, plus a running total.
      
  
      WITH RECURSIVE days AS (
  SELECT MIN(day) AS d FROM Sales                        -- anchor: first day
  UNION ALL
  SELECT d + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM days                    -- step: next day
  WHERE d < (SELECT MAX(day) FROM Sales)                 -- stop condition
)
SELECT days.d                                   AS day,
       COALESCE(s.amount, 0)                    AS amount,
       SUM(COALESCE(s.amount, 0)) OVER (ORDER BY days.d) AS running_total
FROM days
LEFT JOIN Sales s ON s.day = days.d
ORDER BY days.d;
      
  
      day        | amount | running_total
2024-01-01 |    100 |  100
2024-01-02 |    200 |  300
2024-01-03 |    300 |  600
2024-01-04 |      0 |  600     ← filled
2024-01-05 |    500 | 1100
2024-01-06 |    100 | 1200
      
  
      
    QWhat limits a recursive date series, and what do teams use in production?
    
      
      
      MySQL stops recursion after cte_max_recursion_depth iterations (default 1000) with an error — so a 3-year daily series (≈1096 days) fails until you SET SESSION cte_max_recursion_depth = 5000;. The CTE's column type comes from the anchor; if the anchor is a string literal, cast it: SELECT CAST('2024-01-01' AS DATE).
      
      
      In production, analysts keep a permanent calendar (date dimension) table with one row per day for 50 years plus columns like week, month, is_holiday. It's tiny, indexable and reusable. PostgreSQL has generate_series('2024-01-01'::date, '2024-12-31', '1 day'); SQL Server 2022 has GENERATE_SERIES for numbers.
      
      
      💡
      Same trick, different shape
      Generate a series of numbers, months, hours or ids, then LEFT JOIN the facts → "show zeros". Generate and anti-join → "find what's missing" (P28).
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🏝️ Pattern 7 · Gaps & islands (consecutive runs)
      
  
      Signal words: "consecutive", "in a row", "streak", "continuous range", "missing ids", "gaps". An island is a run of consecutive values; a gap is the hole between two islands.
      
  
      The core trick: number the rows in order with ROW_NUMBER(). Inside a run of consecutive values, value and row number both go up by 1 each step, so value − row_number stays constant. When a gap appears, the difference jumps. Group by that difference → one group per island.
      

  

  
  
      P26 · Consecutive numbers (a value appearing ≥ 3 times in a row)
      
  
      🔥 very common LeetCode 180
      
  
      id : 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
num: 1 1 1 2 1 2 2        → ConsecutiveNums = 1
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM (
  SELECT num,
         LAG(num, 1) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS p1,
         LAG(num, 2) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS p2
  FROM Logs
) t
WHERE num = p1 AND num = p2;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH g AS (
  SELECT id, num,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id)
       - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY num ORDER BY id) AS grp   -- constant inside a run of equal nums
  FROM Logs
)
SELECT DISTINCT num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM g
GROUP BY num, grp
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT DISTINCT l1.num AS ConsecutiveNums
FROM Logs l1
JOIN Logs l2 ON l2.id = l1.id + 1 AND l2.num = l1.num
JOIN Logs l3 ON l3.id = l1.id + 2 AND l3.num = l1.num;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QSelf-join on id + 1 vs LAG — which is right if ids have gaps?
    
      
      
      Ask: does "consecutive" mean consecutive ids or consecutive rows? If id 4 was deleted, the self-join on id + 1 treats 3 and 5 as not adjacent; LAG treats them as neighbours. Neither is wrong — the spec decides. If ids may have gaps and you need row adjacency, generate your own sequence with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id).
      
      
      Approach B is the general "N in a row" solution: change >= 3 to any N. The difference of two ROW_NUMBERs (overall − within-value) is constant while the value doesn't change. DISTINCT is needed because the same number can have several qualifying runs.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Stadium: rows inside runs of ≥ 3 consecutive ids with people ≥ 100 (LeetCode 601).
          
      Filter first (WHERE people >= 100), then island key id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id), then keep rows whose island has COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY grp) >= 3. Returning rows (not groups) is why you use COUNT as a window, not GROUP BY.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P27 · Login streaks: users with ≥ 3 consecutive days, longest streak
      
  
      🔥 hot — FAANG / analytics favourite
      
  
      CREATE TABLE Logins (user_id INT, login_ts DATETIME);
INSERT INTO Logins VALUES
 (1,'2024-03-01 09:00'),(1,'2024-03-01 18:00'),(1,'2024-03-02 08:00'),(1,'2024-03-03 07:00'),
 (1,'2024-03-05 10:00'),(1,'2024-03-06 10:00'),
 (2,'2024-03-01 10:00'),(2,'2024-03-03 10:00'),(2,'2024-03-04 10:00'),
 (3,'2024-02-28 10:00'),(3,'2024-02-29 10:00'),(3,'2024-03-01 10:00'),(3,'2024-03-02 10:00');
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH days AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(login_ts) AS d          -- 1. dedupe same-day logins FIRST
  FROM Logins
),
grp AS (
  SELECT user_id, d,
         DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d) DAY) AS island
  FROM days                                              -- 2. date − rn days = island key
)
SELECT user_id, MIN(d) AS streak_start, MAX(d) AS streak_end, COUNT(*) AS streak_len
FROM grp
GROUP BY user_id, island                                 -- 3. one row per island
ORDER BY user_id, streak_start;
      
      
      user_id | streak_start | streak_end | streak_len
      1 | 2024-03-01   | 2024-03-03 | 3
      1 | 2024-03-05   | 2024-03-06 | 2
      2 | 2024-03-01   | 2024-03-01 | 1
      2 | 2024-03-03   | 2024-03-04 | 2
      3 | 2024-02-28   | 2024-03-02 | 4     ← crosses the leap day correctly
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- (same days + grp CTEs as tab A, then:)
, streaks AS (
  SELECT user_id, COUNT(*) AS len FROM grp GROUP BY user_id, island
)
SELECT user_id, MAX(len) AS longest_streak
FROM streaks
GROUP BY user_id
HAVING MAX(len) >= 3;          -- users 1 (3) and 3 (4); drop HAVING for everyone
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- "the login two distinct days back was exactly 2 days ago" → 3 days in a row
WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(login_ts) AS d FROM Logins)
SELECT DISTINCT user_id
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, d, LAG(d, 2) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d) AS d_2
  FROM days
) t
WHERE d_2 = d - INTERVAL 2 DAY;      -- users 1, 3
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhat breaks if you forget to dedupe, and how do you allow one missed day?
    
      
      
      User 1 logged in twice on 03-01. Without DISTINCT, row numbers become 1,2,3,4 for days 01,01,02,03, so the island keys split the streak incorrectly and lengths are wrong. Always reduce to one row per (user, day) before numbering.
      
      
      Allow one missed day: island keys don't work; use the "flag + running sum" technique — the second classic islands method:
      
      
      WITH days AS (SELECT DISTINCT user_id, DATE(login_ts) AS d FROM Logins),
flags AS (
  SELECT user_id, d,
         CASE WHEN DATEDIFF(d, LAG(d) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d)) <= 2
              THEN 0 ELSE 1 END AS new_streak          -- 1 = a new island starts here
  FROM days
),
numbered AS (
  SELECT user_id, d,
         SUM(new_streak) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY d) AS streak_id
  FROM flags
)
SELECT user_id, streak_id, MIN(d), MAX(d), COUNT(*) AS active_days
FROM numbered GROUP BY user_id, streak_id;
      
      
      The first row has LAG = NULL → DATEDIFF is NULL → the CASE goes to ELSE → 1 (new streak). That's exactly right.
      
      
      Index: (user_id, login_ts). Current streak: the island whose streak_end = CURDATE() (or yesterday, if today's login hasn't happened yet).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      "It's a gaps-and-islands problem. First I reduce logins to one row per user per day. Then I subtract the row number, as days, from the date — inside a streak both go up by one, so that difference is constant and becomes the streak id. Grouping by user and streak id gives start, end and length; then I filter length ≥ 3 or take the max per user."
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P28 · Find missing IDs (gaps in a sequence)
      
  
      common
      
  
      Problem. Table T(id) has 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9. Find the missing ids. Expected: 4, 7, 8 (or as ranges: 4–4, 7–8).
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH RECURSIVE seq AS (
  SELECT 1 AS n
  UNION ALL
  SELECT n + 1 FROM seq WHERE n < (SELECT MAX(id) FROM T)
)
SELECT s.n AS missing_id
FROM seq s
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM T WHERE T.id = s.n);   -- 4, 7, 8
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT id + 1 AS gap_start, next_id - 1 AS gap_end
FROM (
  SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS next_id
  FROM T
) t
WHERE next_id - id > 1;
-- 4 | 4
-- 7 | 8
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- start of each gap: an id whose successor is missing (excluding the max)
SELECT a.id + 1 AS gap_start,
       (SELECT MIN(b.id) - 1 FROM T b WHERE b.id > a.id) AS gap_end
FROM T a
LEFT JOIN T nxt ON nxt.id = a.id + 1
WHERE nxt.id IS NULL
  AND a.id < (SELECT MAX(id) FROM T);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhich approach scales to a table with ids up to 10 billion?
    
      
      
      B (LEAD) reads the existing rows once in index order and reports ranges, so its output stays small even when gaps are huge. A must generate every number up to the max — impossible for billions (and limited by cte_max_recursion_depth). Also say: gaps in AUTO_INCREMENT ids are normal (rolled-back inserts, deleted rows, innodb_autoinc_lock_mode) and are not a bug. Never use ids to count rows.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P29 · Start and end of continuous ranges
      
  
      common LeetCode 1285
      
  
      Problem. Collapse ids 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9 into ranges.
      
  
      SELECT MIN(id) AS start_id, MAX(id) AS end_id, COUNT(*) AS len
FROM (
  SELECT id, id - ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS grp
  FROM T
) t
GROUP BY grp
ORDER BY start_id;
      
  
      start_id | end_id | len
       1 |      3 |   3
       5 |      6 |   2
       9 |      9 |   1
      
  
      🧠
      Memory aid: the two islands recipes
      Recipe 1 — "subtract": value − ROW_NUMBER() is constant inside an island (dates: DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL rn DAY)). Use for strict +1 steps. Recipe 2 — "flag & sum": flag rows where a new island starts (via LAG), then a running SUM of flags is the island id. Use for any custom rule (gap ≤ 2 days, status changes, session timeout of 30 minutes).
      

  
  
      🧮 Pattern 8 · Aggregation tricks
      
  
      Signal words: "above average", "% of total", "per row … as columns", "including zero", "bucket", "median", "most frequent", "rate". Tools: window aggregates (SUM() OVER ()), conditional aggregation (SUM(CASE …)), LEFT JOIN from the full category list.
      

  
  
      P30 · Employees earning more than their department's average
      
  
      🔥 very common
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT name, dept_id, salary, ROUND(dept_avg, 2) AS dept_avg
FROM (
  SELECT e.*, AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg
  FROM Employee e
) t
WHERE salary > dept_avg;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary, ROUND(a.avg_sal, 2) AS dept_avg
FROM Employee e
JOIN (SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
      FROM Employee GROUP BY dept_id) a
  ON a.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > a.avg_sal;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT e.name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM Employee e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM Employee x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      name  | dept_id | salary | dept_avg
Joe   |       1 |  85000 | 79800.00
Max   |       1 |  90000 | 79800.00
Randy |       1 |  85000 | 79800.00
Henry |       2 |  80000 | 70000.00
      
  
      
    QWhy doesn't WHERE salary > AVG(salary) work?
    
      
      
      Aggregates are computed in the GROUP BY step, which runs after WHERE. At WHERE time, AVG doesn't exist yet → MySQL error 1111 "Invalid use of group function". And HAVING salary > AVG(salary) with GROUP BY dept_id doesn't work either, because after grouping there is no single "salary" per group. You need the average as a separate value per row: window AVG, a join to a grouped derived table, or a correlated subquery.
      
      
      Variant: "departments whose average is above the company average" → GROUP BY dept_id HAVING AVG(salary) > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employee).
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P31 · Percentage of department total and of company total
      
  
      🔥 common
      
  
      SELECT name, dept_id, salary,
       ROUND(100 * salary / SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id), 1) AS pct_of_dept,
       ROUND(100 * salary / SUM(salary) OVER (),                     1) AS pct_of_company
FROM Employee
ORDER BY dept_id, salary DESC;
      
  
      name  | dept_id | salary | pct_of_dept | pct_of_company
Max   |       1 |  90000 |        22.6 |           16.7
Joe   |       1 |  85000 |        21.3 |           15.8
Randy |       1 |  85000 |        21.3 |           15.8
Will  |       1 |  70000 |        17.5 |           13.0
Janet |       1 |  69000 |        17.3 |           12.8
Henry |       2 |  80000 |        57.1 |           14.8
Sam   |       2 |  60000 |        42.9 |           11.1
      
  
      
    QWhat does an empty OVER () mean, and how did people do this before MySQL 8?
    
      
      
      OVER () = one window containing all rows of the result, so SUM(salary) OVER () is the grand total repeated on each row. Before 8.0: cross join a one-row total — FROM Employee e CROSS JOIN (SELECT SUM(salary) AS total FROM Employee) t. For "% of total per group" in a GROUP BY query you can nest: SUM(amount) / SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER () — the inner SUM is the group aggregate, the outer is a window over the grouped rows.
      
      
      Trap: in PostgreSQL / SQL Server, 100 * int_col / int_sum is integer division. Use 100.0 *.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P32 · Pivot: rows to columns
      
  
      🔥 common LeetCode 1179 style
      
  
      (Asha,Math,90) (Asha,Physics,80) (Ravi,Math,70) (Ravi,Chem,65)
(Neha,Physics,88) (Neha,Chem,92) (Neha,Math,75)

student | Math | Physics | Chem | total
Asha    |   90 |      80 | NULL |   170
Neha    |   75 |      88 |   92 |   255
Ravi    |   70 |    NULL |   65 |   135
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT student,
       MAX(CASE WHEN subject = 'Math'    THEN marks END) AS Math,
       MAX(CASE WHEN subject = 'Physics' THEN marks END) AS Physics,
       MAX(CASE WHEN subject = 'Chem'    THEN marks END) AS Chem,
       SUM(marks)                                         AS total
FROM Scores
GROUP BY student
ORDER BY student;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- wide table ScoresWide(student, Math, Physics, Chem) → long rows
SELECT student, 'Math'    AS subject, Math    AS marks FROM ScoresWide WHERE Math    IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT student, 'Physics',            Physics          FROM ScoresWide WHERE Physics IS NOT NULL
UNION ALL
SELECT student, 'Chem',               Chem             FROM ScoresWide WHERE Chem    IS NOT NULL;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT student, [Math], [Physics], [Chem]
FROM (SELECT student, subject, marks FROM Scores) s
PIVOT (MAX(marks) FOR subject IN ([Math], [Physics], [Chem])) p;
      
      
      PostgreSQL: conditional aggregation with FILTER — MAX(marks) FILTER (WHERE subject = 'Math'), or crosstab() from the tablefunc extension. MySQL has no PIVOT operator.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy MAX? And what if the list of subjects is not known in advance?
    
      
      
      Each CASE returns the mark for the matching row and NULL for all others. Inside one student's group there is (at most) one non-NULL value per column, and MAX picks it (aggregates skip NULL). SUM works too for numbers, but MAX also works for strings. If a student could have two Math rows, decide: MAX? SUM? latest? — ask.
      
      
      Unknown columns: SQL needs the column list at parse time. Build the query text dynamically: SELECT GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT CONCAT('MAX(CASE WHEN subject = ''', subject, ''' THEN marks END) AS `', subject, '`')) INTO @cols FROM Scores; then CONCAT it into a statement and run it with PREPARE/EXECUTE. Mention SQL-injection risk if subject values come from users, and that group_concat_max_len (default 1024) may truncate the list. Often the honest answer: "pivot in the reporting tool, not in SQL".
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P33 · Count per group, including groups with zero
      
  
      🔥 very common — "show HR with 0" LeetCode 1280 (Students and Examinations)
      
  
      SELECT d.name AS department, COUNT(e.id) AS headcount
FROM Department d
LEFT JOIN Employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY d.id;
-- IT 5 · Sales 2 · HR 0
      
  
      
    QThree ways people get HR wrong — name them.
    
      
      
        
        
      1. Starting from Employee (FROM Employee GROUP BY dept_id): HR has no employee rows, so it can never appear. Start from the table that lists all groups.
        2. 
        
      2. COUNT(*) instead of COUNT(e.id): the LEFT JOIN creates one all-NULL row for HR, and COUNT(*) counts it → HR = 1.
        3. 
        
      3. Filtering the right table in WHERE: WHERE e.salary > 50000 removes HR's NULL row → HR vanishes again. Put right-table filters in the ON clause: LEFT JOIN Employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id AND e.salary > 50000.
        4. 
      
      
      
      Students × Subjects variant: every student must appear with every subject, even with 0 attended exams → Students CROSS JOIN Subjects to build all pairs, then LEFT JOIN Examinations on both columns and COUNT(ex.subject_name).
      
      
      SELECT s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name,
       COUNT(ex.subject_name) AS attended_exams
FROM Students s
CROSS JOIN Subjects sub
LEFT JOIN Examinations ex
       ON ex.student_id = s.student_id AND ex.subject_name = sub.subject_name
GROUP BY s.student_id, s.student_name, sub.subject_name
ORDER BY s.student_id, sub.subject_name;
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P34 · Histogram buckets, including empty buckets
      
  
      common LeetCode 1907 (Count Salary Categories)
      
  
      Problem. Accounts(income): 108939, 12747, 87709, 91796. Categories: Low (< 20000), Average (20000–50000), High (> 50000). Every category must appear. Expected: Low 1, Average 0, High 3.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH cats AS (
  SELECT 'Low Salary' AS category UNION ALL
  SELECT 'Average Salary'         UNION ALL
  SELECT 'High Salary'
),
labeled AS (
  SELECT CASE WHEN income < 20000  THEN 'Low Salary'
              WHEN income <= 50000 THEN 'Average Salary'
              ELSE 'High Salary' END AS category
  FROM Accounts
)
SELECT c.category, COUNT(l.category) AS accounts_count
FROM cats c
LEFT JOIN labeled l ON l.category = c.category
GROUP BY c.category;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT 'Low Salary' AS category, SUM(income < 20000) AS accounts_count FROM Accounts
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Average Salary', SUM(income BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000) FROM Accounts
UNION ALL
SELECT 'High Salary',    SUM(income > 50000) FROM Accounts;
-- SUM(boolean) works in MySQL because TRUE = 1, FALSE = 0.
-- On an EMPTY table SUM returns NULL → wrap in COALESCE(…, 0) or use COUNT(CASE …).
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- equal-width buckets of 10,000: 0–9999, 10000–19999, …
SELECT FLOOR(income / 10000) * 10000 AS bucket_start,
       COUNT(*)                     AS n
FROM Accounts
GROUP BY bucket_start
ORDER BY bucket_start;      -- empty buckets missing → join a number series (P25) to show 0
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P35 · Median (overall and per group)
      
  
      🔥 hot — "MySQL has no MEDIAN()" LeetCode 569 / 571
      
  
      Expected on our 7 salaries (60000, 69000, 70000, 80000, 85000, 85000, 90000): median = 80000. Per dept: IT (69000, 70000, 85000, 85000, 90000) = 85000; Sales (60000, 80000) = 70000 (average of the middle two).
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH r AS (
  SELECT salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER ()                AS cnt
  FROM Employee
)
SELECT AVG(salary) AS median
FROM r
WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((cnt + 1) / 2), FLOOR((cnt + 2) / 2));
-- cnt = 7 → rn IN (4, 4) → 80000 ;  cnt = 8 → rn IN (4, 5) → average of the two middles
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH r AS (
  SELECT dept_id, salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)                 AS cnt
  FROM Employee
)
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS median
FROM r
WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((cnt + 1) / 2), FLOOR((cnt + 2) / 2))
GROUP BY dept_id;
-- 1 | 85000.0000 · 2 | 70000.0000
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- PostgreSQL (ordered-set aggregate)
SELECT PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) FROM employee;
-- Oracle also has MEDIAN(salary).
-- SQL Server: PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id)
--             (a window function there — add DISTINCT or TOP 1 to get one row)
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhy FLOOR? Why not rn = cnt/2?
    
      
      
      In MySQL / returns a decimal: (7+1)/2 = 4.0000 but (8+1)/2 = 4.5000, which matches no row. FLOOR (or integer division DIV) makes both formulas integers. The two formulas give the same middle row for odd counts and the two middle rows for even counts; AVG handles both cases. ROW_NUMBER (not RANK) is required so duplicate salaries still get distinct positions.
      
      
      Frequency-table variant (LeetCode 571): numbers stored as (value, frequency). Compute a running sum of frequency; the median values are those where running_sum >= total/2 and running_sum - frequency <= total/2; average them.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P36 · Mode (most frequent value), with ties
      
  
      common
      
  
      Problem. Values: 3, 7, 7, 2, 3, 7, 9 → mode = 7 (3 times). If several values tie, return all of them.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SELECT v, n
FROM (
  SELECT v, COUNT(*) AS n,
         RANK() OVER (ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC) AS rnk     -- window over a grouped result
  FROM Vals
  GROUP BY v
) t
WHERE rnk = 1;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      WITH freq AS (SELECT v, COUNT(*) AS n FROM Vals GROUP BY v)
SELECT v, n FROM freq
WHERE n = (SELECT MAX(n) FROM freq);
      
    
      
  
      
  
      Avoid ORDER BY COUNT(*) DESC LIMIT 1 unless the interviewer confirms ties don't matter — it silently drops tied modes. Same pattern: "customer with the most orders" (LeetCode 586), "most popular product per category" (add PARTITION BY category).
      

  
  
      P37 · Cancellation rate (Trips and Users)
      
  
      🔥 "hard" classic LeetCode 262
      
  
      Problem. For each day, the cancellation rate of trips where neither the client nor the driver is banned. Rate = cancelled (by anyone) / total, rounded to 2 decimals.
      
  
      Users: clients 1,2(banned),3,4 · drivers 10,11,12,13(banned)
Trips: 2024-10-01 → (1,10,completed) (2,11,cancelled_by_driver) (3,12,completed) (4,13,cancelled_by_client)
       2024-10-02 → (1,10,completed) (2,11,completed) (3,12,cancelled_by_driver) (4,13,completed)
Expected: 2024-10-01 → 0.00   (only trips 1,3 count)
          2024-10-02 → 0.50   (trips 5,7 count; 7 cancelled)
      
  
      SELECT t.request_at AS Day,
       ROUND(AVG(t.status <> 'completed'), 2) AS `Cancellation Rate`
FROM Trips t
JOIN Users c ON c.users_id = t.client_id AND c.banned = 'No'
JOIN Users d ON d.users_id = t.driver_id AND d.banned = 'No'
WHERE t.request_at BETWEEN '2024-10-01' AND '2024-10-03'
GROUP BY t.request_at;
      
  
      
    QExplain AVG(condition) — and the portable version.
    
      
      
      In MySQL a comparison returns 1 (true), 0 (false) or NULL. The average of 0/1 values is the fraction of 1s — that's the rate. Portable form: SUM(CASE WHEN status <> 'completed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) * 1.0 / COUNT(*). In PostgreSQL: AVG((status <> 'completed')::int) or COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE …).
      
      
      Traps: the Users table must be joined twice (once as client, once as driver) — two roles, one table. Days where all trips are by banned users disappear from the result; ask whether they should show 0 or be absent. A NULL status would make AVG ignore that trip — check whether status is NOT NULL.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P38 · Confirmation rate and friend-request acceptance rate
      
  
      common LeetCode 1934 · 597
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- users with no confirmation messages must show 0.00 → LEFT JOIN from Signups
SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS confirmation_rate
FROM Signups s
LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON c.user_id = s.user_id
GROUP BY s.user_id;
-- user 7: 3/3 = 1.00 · user 2: 1/2 = 0.50 · user 3: 0/2 = 0.00 · user 6 (no rows): 0.00
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- count DISTINCT pairs: the same request may be sent/accepted twice
SELECT ROUND(
         COALESCE(
           (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT requester_id, accepter_id FROM RequestAccepted) a)
         / NULLIF((SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT sender_id, send_to_id FROM FriendRequest) r), 0),
         0), 2) AS accept_rate;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      Why CASE … ELSE 0 in A? For user 6 the LEFT JOIN produces one row with c.action = NULL; the CASE maps it to 0, so AVG = 0.00 instead of NULL. Why NULLIF(…, 0) + COALESCE in B? No requests at all → avoid dividing by zero and return 0.00 as specified.
      

  
  
      🌳 Pattern 9 · Hierarchies (recursive CTEs)
      
  
      Signal words: "all levels", "chain of command", "indirect reports", "category tree", "bill of materials", "path from root". A self-join handles a fixed number of levels; for unknown depth use WITH RECURSIVE.
      

  

  
  
      P39 · Org chart with level and path
      
  
      🔥 hot at product companies
      
  
      WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  -- anchor member: the root(s)
  SELECT id, name, manager_id,
         1 AS lvl,
         CAST(name AS CHAR(500)) AS path            -- widen! the anchor fixes the column type
  FROM Employee
  WHERE manager_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  -- recursive member: children of the rows found in the previous iteration
  SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id,
         o.lvl + 1,
         CONCAT(o.path, ' > ', e.name)
  FROM Employee e
  JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id
)
SELECT id, CONCAT(REPEAT('    ', lvl - 1), name) AS tree, lvl, path
FROM org
ORDER BY path;
      
  
      id | tree           | lvl | path
 4 | Max            |   1 | Max
 2 |     Henry      |   2 | Max > Henry
 3 |         Sam    |   3 | Max > Henry > Sam
 5 |     Janet      |   2 | Max > Janet
 7 |         Will   |   3 | Max > Janet > Will
 1 |     Joe        |   2 | Max > Joe
 6 |     Randy      |   2 | Max > Randy
      
  
      
    QWhy CAST(name AS CHAR(500))? What about cycles?
    
      
      
      In MySQL the column types of a recursive CTE are decided by the anchor member only. name is VARCHAR(30), so a longer path in later iterations would be truncated or, in strict mode, raise "Data too long for column 'path'". Casting to a wide type in the anchor fixes it.
      
      
      Cycles: if bad data says A manages B and B manages A, the recursion never ends. MySQL stops it at cte_max_recursion_depth (1000) with an error. Protect yourself by tracking the path and refusing to revisit: add WHERE FIND_IN_SET(e.id, o.id_path) = 0 with an id_path column built like path. PostgreSQL 14+ has a built-in CYCLE clause; SQL Server uses OPTION (MAXRECURSION n) (default 100).
      
      
      Index: INDEX(manager_id) — every iteration looks up children by manager_id.
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      PostgreSQL/MySQL need the word RECURSIVE; SQL Server does not use it (WITH org AS (…) is recursive automatically). Oracle also has the older CONNECT BY PRIOR id = manager_id START WITH manager_id IS NULL with LEVEL and SYS_CONNECT_BY_PATH.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      "A recursive CTE has an anchor and a recursive part joined by UNION ALL. The anchor selects the root — manager_id is null. The recursive part joins the employee table to the rows found in the previous step, adding one level. It repeats until a step returns no rows. I carry a level counter and a path string, cast wide in the anchor, and I'd guard against cycles with the recursion depth limit or a visited-path check."
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Chain of command upward for Will (bottom → top)?
          
      Reverse the direction: anchor WHERE id = 7, recursive step JOIN org o ON e.id = o.manager_id → Will, Janet, Max.
      
        
      ↪How would you store hierarchies to avoid recursion?
          
      Adjacency list (manager_id — simple, needs recursion), materialized path ('/4/5/7/', query with LIKE '/4/5/%'), nested sets (left/right numbers — fast reads, painful writes), or a closure table (one row per ancestor–descendant pair — fast and flexible, more storage). See Chapter 21.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P40 · All direct and indirect reports of a manager (total headcount)
      
  
      common LeetCode 1270
      
  
      WITH RECURSIVE under AS (
  SELECT id, name FROM Employee WHERE manager_id = 4      -- direct reports of Max
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name
  FROM Employee e JOIN under u ON e.manager_id = u.id    -- their reports, and so on
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_reports FROM under;             -- 6 (everyone except Max)
      
  
      ⚠️
      LeetCode 1270's twist
      There the head of the company has manager_id = id (reports to himself), not NULL. A naive recursion from the head then loops forever on the head's own row. Exclude it in the anchor and the step: WHERE manager_id = 1 AND id <> 1. The problem also says depth ≤ 3, so a 3-way self-join works without recursion.
      

  
  
      🧩 Pattern 10 · Classic puzzles & string tricks
      

  
  
      P41 · Swap values with one UPDATE · Exchange adjacent seats
      
  
      🔥 common LeetCode 627 · 626
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- one statement, no temp table
UPDATE Salary
SET sex = CASE sex WHEN 'm' THEN 'f' WHEN 'f' THEN 'm' ELSE sex END;

-- alternative: IF(sex = 'm', 'f', 'm')   |   CHAR(ASCII('m') ^ ASCII('f') ^ ASCII(sex))
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- swap students 1↔2, 3↔4, …; an odd last seat stays
SELECT CASE
         WHEN id % 2 = 1 AND id = (SELECT MAX(id) FROM Seat) THEN id   -- last odd seat
         WHEN id % 2 = 1 THEN id + 1
         ELSE id - 1
       END AS id,
       student
FROM Seat
ORDER BY id;
-- (1 Abbot, 2 Doris, 3 Emerson, 4 Green, 5 Jeames)
-- → 1 Doris, 2 Abbot, 3 Green, 4 Emerson, 5 Jeames

-- window version
SELECT id,
       CASE WHEN id % 2 = 1 THEN COALESCE(LEAD(student) OVER (ORDER BY id), student)
            ELSE LAG(student) OVER (ORDER BY id) END AS student
FROM Seat;
      
    
      
    
      
      
      -- ✘ MySQL evaluates SET assignments left to right using the NEW value:
UPDATE t SET a = b, b = a;     -- both columns end up = old b!
-- ✔ MySQL-safe swap via a self-join on the PK
UPDATE t t1 JOIN t t2 ON t1.id = t2.id
SET t1.a = t2.b, t1.b = t2.a;
-- PostgreSQL / SQL Server: SET a = b, b = a works (uses OLD values, as the standard says)
      
    
      
  
      
  
      🔀
      A great "gotcha" to mention
      The MySQL manual says single-table UPDATE assignments are evaluated left to right, and a later assignment sees the already-updated value. That's non-standard. Showing you know this difference is a strong signal in MySQL-heavy interviews.
      

  
  
      P42 · Fetch odd / even rows, every Nth row
      
  
      service-company classic (GfG list)
      
  
      -- even POSITIONS (2nd, 4th, …) — tables have no inherent order, so we define one
SELECT *
FROM (
  SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY id) AS rn
  FROM Employee e
) t
WHERE rn % 2 = 0;          -- MOD(rn, 2) = 0 ; for every 3rd row: rn % 3 = 0

-- if they mean even ID values (simpler, but different!)
SELECT * FROM Employee WHERE id % 2 = 0;
      
  
      Point to make: a relational table is an unordered set. "Odd rows" only means something after you choose an ORDER BY. Ids can have gaps, so id % 2 is not "every other row". Oracle folks may suggest MOD(ROWNUM, 2) — note that ROWNUM = 2 style filters never match because ROWNUM is assigned as rows pass the filter.
      

  
  
      P43 · Fix name capitalization · string cleanup
      
  
      common warm-up LeetCode 1667
      
  
      -- 'aLice' → 'Alice', 'bOB' → 'Bob'
SELECT user_id,
       CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT(name, 1)), LOWER(SUBSTRING(name, 2))) AS name
FROM Users
ORDER BY user_id;

-- related one-liners
SELECT TRIM(name), LENGTH(name), CHAR_LENGTH(name),            -- bytes vs characters!
       SUBSTRING_INDEX(email, '@', -1) AS domain,                  -- text after '@'
       REPLACE(phone, '-', '')        AS digits
FROM Users;
      
  
      LENGTH counts bytes; CHAR_LENGTH counts characters. For 'José' in utf8mb4: LENGTH = 5, CHAR_LENGTH = 4. SUBSTRING positions start at 1, not 0. Patterns like "emails with a valid domain" use REGEXP (MySQL 8 uses the ICU regex library): WHERE mail REGEXP '^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_.-]*@leetcode[.]com$' (LeetCode 1517) — but note REGEXP follows the column's collation, so it is case-insensitive by default; use REGEXP_LIKE(mail, pattern, 'c') for case-sensitive matching.
      

  
  
      P44 · Products frequently bought together (pair counting)
      
  
      🔥 hot — e-commerce interviews (Amazon, Flipkart)
      
  
      order 1: bread, butter, milk   order 2: bread, butter
order 3: milk, bread           order 4: butter, bread

p1     | p2     | together
bread  | butter | 3
bread  | milk   | 2
butter | milk   | 1
      
  
      SELECT a.product AS p1, b.product AS p2, COUNT(*) AS together
FROM OrderItems a
JOIN OrderItems b
  ON  a.order_id = b.order_id
  AND a.product  < b.product          -- each unordered pair once, no (x, x)
GROUP BY a.product, b.product
ORDER BY together DESC, p1, p2
LIMIT 10;
      
  
      
    QHow does this scale, and what if an order has the same product twice?
    
      
      
      An order with k items produces k(k−1)/2 pairs. A 200-item order → 19,900 pairs. On billions of order lines this self-join explodes; production systems compute pair counts offline (Spark/warehouse) and store them in a summary table. If the same product can appear twice in an order (two lines), dedupe first: SELECT DISTINCT order_id, product. Interviewers may extend to "support / confidence" (association rules): confidence(A→B) = together(A,B) / orders_with(A).
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      P45 · Biggest single number (NULL if none)
      
  
      common LeetCode 619
      
  
      Numbers 8, 8, 3, 3, 1, 4, 5, 6 → numbers that appear exactly once: 1, 4, 5, 6 → biggest = 6. If every number repeats, return NULL.
      
  
      SELECT MAX(num) AS num                 -- MAX over zero rows → one row with NULL
FROM (
  SELECT num FROM MyNumbers
  GROUP BY num
  HAVING COUNT(*) = 1
) singles;
      
  
      Same "aggregate turns empty into NULL" trick as P01. ORDER BY num DESC LIMIT 1 alone would return an empty set instead of NULL.
      

  
  
      P46 · Product price at a given date (latest change on or before a date)
      
  
      common LeetCode 1164
      
  
      Problem. Products(product_id, new_price, change_date) logs price changes. Every product starts at price 10. Return each product's price on 2019-08-16.
      
  
      WITH last_change AS (
  SELECT product_id, new_price,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY product_id ORDER BY change_date DESC) AS rn
  FROM Products
  WHERE change_date <= '2019-08-16'                 -- filter BEFORE ranking
)
SELECT p.product_id, COALESCE(lc.new_price, 10) AS price
FROM (SELECT DISTINCT product_id FROM Products) p     -- all products, even with no change yet
LEFT JOIN last_change lc
       ON lc.product_id = p.product_id AND lc.rn = 1;
      
  
      This is the "as-of" (point-in-time) lookup — the same idea as slowly changing dimensions in warehouses (Chapter 20). Key moves: filter by date before ranking, start from the full product list, and default missing values with COALESCE.
      

  
  
      📋 Pattern-recognition cheat table
      
  
      Read the question, spot the trigger words, name the pattern out loud, then reach for the tool. This table maps all 46 problems above to their family.
      
  
      
    
      Trigger words in the questionPatternGo-to tool (MySQL 8)Problems
      
    
      
      "Nth highest", "second highest", "rank", "return NULL if none"RankingDENSE_RANK(); MAX() over a subquery to force NULL; LIMIT 1 OFFSET n-1 on DISTINCTP01–P04, P45
      
      
      "top N per…", "highest in each department", "latest per user"Top-N per groupROW_NUMBER()/DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY …) in a CTE, filter rn <= NP05–P07, P46
      
      
      "duplicate", "appears more than once", "keep the smallest id"DuplicatesGROUP BY … HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; DELETE with self-join or ROW_NUMBER() > 1 via derived tableP08–P10
      
      
      "than their manager", "pairs", "both directions", "follows each other"Self-joinJoin the table to itself on the relationship column; a.x < b.x to avoid mirrored pairsP11–P14, P44
      
      
      "never", "without any", "not in", "who did not"Anti-joinLEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL or NOT EXISTS (never NOT IN with NULLs)P15, P16
      
      
      "bought all", "took every course"Relational divisionGROUP BY … HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT x) = (SELECT COUNT(*) …)P17
      
      
      "previous day", "compared with yesterday", "next login"Row-to-row comparisonLAG()/LEAD() or self-join on DATE_ADD(d, INTERVAL 1 DAY)P18, P20
      
      
      "first", "earliest", "retention", "returned next day"First event + follow-upMIN(date) per user, then join backP19, P20
      
      
      "running total", "cumulative", "moving average", "MoM / YoY"Window framesSUM() OVER (ORDER BY d), ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, LAG(x, 12)P21–P24
      
      
      "including days with no sales", "fill missing dates", "show 0"Generate a seriesWITH RECURSIVE date/number series + LEFT JOIN + COALESCE(x, 0)P25, P28, P33, P34
      
      
      "consecutive", "streak", "in a row", "continuous ranges"Gaps & islandsvalue − ROW_NUMBER() = group key, then GROUP BY keyP26–P29
      
      
      "more than the average of their…", "% of total", "share"Group vs rowAVG()/SUM() OVER (PARTITION BY …); multiply by 100.0 before dividingP30, P31
      
      
      "one column per month", "rows to columns"PivotSUM(CASE WHEN … THEN x END) or SUM(x * (cond))P32
      
      
      "median", "most frequent", "mode"Order statisticsROW_NUMBER() + COUNT() OVER(), keep middle rows; HAVING COUNT(*) = MAX(…)P35, P36
      
      
      "rate", "ratio", "acceptance", "cancellation"Conditional ratioROUND(AVG(cond), 2) or SUM(cond) / COUNT(*); guard divide-by-zero with NULLIFP37, P38
      
      
      "all reports", "org chart", "levels", "path to CEO"HierarchyWITH RECURSIVE anchor + step, carry level and pathP39, P40
      
      
      "swap", "exchange", "odd rows", "capitalize"Puzzles / stringsCASE in one UPDATE; ROW_NUMBER() % 2; CONCAT(UPPER(LEFT…), LOWER(SUBSTRING…))P41–P43
      
          
  
      
  
      R-D-S-A-W-G
      Rank · Duplicates · Self-join · Anti-join · Windows (dates, running totals) · Gaps & islands — "Real Developers Solve All Window Games". Six families cover about 80% of SQL rounds.
      
  
      ✏️ Before typing: say the pattern name, list the edge cases (ties, NULLs, empty result, missing dates), then write the query.
      

  
      📌 Key takeaways
        
    
      • Every SQL interview problem belongs to a small family. Recognise the family first; the query follows.
        • 
    
      • DENSE_RANK() handles ties for "Nth highest"; wrap in MAX() or a scalar subquery so an absent answer becomes NULL, not an empty set.
        • 
    
      • Top-N per group = window function in a CTE, then filter. You cannot filter a window function in the same WHERE.
        • 
    
      • Anti-joins: use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN … IS NULL. NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery has a NULL.
        • 
    
      • MySQL refuses DELETE/UPDATE on a table you also read in a subquery (error 1093): use a multi-table DELETE … JOIN or wrap the subquery in a derived table.
        • 
    
      • Gaps & islands: value − ROW_NUMBER() is constant inside a consecutive run.
        • 
    
      • "Include zeros" always means: generate the full list (recursive CTE or dimension table), then LEFT JOIN and COALESCE.
        • 
    
      • Ratios: use AVG(condition) or multiply by 1.0; watch integer division in other engines and divide-by-zero.
        • 
    
      • Always state edge cases (ties, NULLs, duplicates, empty tables) and an index that would help — that is what separates a pass from a strong pass.
        • 
  
      

  
      📚 Go deeper
        
    
      • LeetCode — Top SQL 50 — most problems in this chapter come from this list; do all 50 in MySQL.
        • 
    
      • DataLemur SQL interview questions — real FAANG-style problems with company tags and hints.
        • 
    
      • HackerRank SQL track — graded practice used by many Indian service companies in online tests.
        • 
    
      • StrataScratch — data-analyst/engineer interview questions from real companies.
        • 
    
      • MySQL 8 manual — Window functions — exact frame and ranking semantics.
        • 
  
      

  
      
    
      
      
      Salaries are 300, 200, 200, 100. What does "second highest distinct salary" return?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Distinct values are 300, 200, 100. The second highest is 200. DENSE_RANK() = 2 gives 200; ROW_NUMBER() would also hit 200 here but fails for other tie layouts.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Why can WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT customer_id FROM Orders) return zero rows?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      x NOT IN (1, NULL) means x <> 1 AND x <> NULL; the second part is UNKNOWN, so no row passes. Use NOT EXISTS.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      In gaps-and-islands, what is constant across one run of consecutive days?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Both the day and the row number grow by 1 inside a run, so their difference stays the same and becomes the island key.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      MySQL error 1093 ("You can't specify target table for update in FROM clause") appears when you…
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Fix it with DELETE p1 FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2 … or by wrapping the subquery in a derived table so MySQL materialises it first.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      "Show daily sales for every day of March, with 0 for days without sales." Which pattern?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      GROUP BY can only produce groups that exist in the data. Missing days must be generated first, then joined.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      Nth highest salary that returns NULL when absent?
      SELECT MAX(salary) FROM (… DENSE_RANK() …) t WHERE rnk = N — an aggregate over zero rows returns one NULL row.
      
    
      Top 3 per department, ties included?
      DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) in a CTE, then WHERE rnk <= 3.
      
    
      Delete duplicate emails keeping the smallest id (MySQL)?
      DELETE p1 FROM Person p1 JOIN Person p2 ON p1.email = p2.email AND p1.id > p2.id;
      
    
      Safest anti-join?
      NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id) — NULL-safe, usually planned as an anti-join.
      
    
      Gaps & islands key?
      DATE_SUB(day, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user ORDER BY day) DAY) — same value for every day of one streak.
      
    
      7-day moving average frame?
      AVG(amt) OVER (ORDER BY d ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) — on a gap-free daily series.
      
    
      Relational division ("bought ALL products")?
      GROUP BY customer HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product) = (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Product)
      
    
      Cancellation / acceptance rate one-liner?
      ROUND(AVG(status <> 'completed'), 2) — in MySQL a boolean is 0/1, so AVG gives the ratio.
      
    
      Why does UPDATE t SET a = b, b = a fail to swap in MySQL?
      MySQL applies assignments left to right using new values, so both become old b. Use a self-join UPDATE.
      
    
      Recursive CTE skeleton for an org chart?
      WITH RECURSIVE org AS (anchor: WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL step: JOIN Employee e ON e.manager_id = org.id), carry level + 1.
      
  
      

      


      
  
      
    
      Chapter 11 · III · SQL Mastery
      
    
      🔀 SQL Dialects & Engines: MySQL vs PostgreSQL vs Oracle vs SQL Server
      
    
      Explain how the big relational databases really differ — MVCC, isolation, storage, DDL, syntax — compare InnoDB with MyISAM, and justify which database you would pick for a given job.
      
    
      ⏱ 30 minMySQLPostgreSQLOracleSQL ServerSQLite
      
  
      

  
       
      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
      
    
        
      
      • Default isolation: MySQL/InnoDB = REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server = READ COMMITTED; SQLite = serializable (one writer at a time).
        • 
      
      • MVCC styles: InnoDB & Oracle update in place and keep old versions in undo (cleanup = purge / undo retention; Oracle's failure = ORA-01555 "snapshot too old"). PostgreSQL writes a new row version in the table → needs VACUUM (bloat, XID wraparound). SQL Server locks by default; RCSI/SNAPSHOT add versions in tempdb.
        •
