      • Storage: InnoDB table = clustered index on the PK. SQL Server: PK is clustered by default (optional). PostgreSQL and Oracle: heap tables by default (Oracle IOT optional).
        • 
      
      • Transactional DDL: PostgreSQL and SQL Server can ROLLBACK a CREATE/ALTER. MySQL and Oracle commit implicitly on DDL (MySQL 8 has only per-statement atomic DDL).
        • 
      
      • Syntax: LIMIT (MySQL/PG/SQLite) · TOP (SQL Server) · FETCH FIRST (standard; Oracle 12c+, PG, SQL Server with OFFSET) · ROWNUM (old Oracle). Upsert: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE / ON CONFLICT / MERGE.
        • 
      
      • MySQL's missing trio "FPM": no FULL OUTER JOIN, no Partial indexes, no Materialized views. PostgreSQL is the feature-rich one (JSONB+GIN, partial/expression/INCLUDE indexes, extensions).
        • 
      
      • Oracle trap: '' (empty string) IS NULL. WHERE col = '' never matches.
        • 
      
      • InnoDB vs MyISAM: InnoDB = transactions, row locks, MVCC, FKs, crash recovery, clustered PK. MyISAM = table locks, no transactions/FKs, fast COUNT(*) (stored row count). Use InnoDB.
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ✏️ You will rarely get "recite the comparison table". You WILL get "why does PostgreSQL need VACUUM?", "MySQL's default isolation?" and "InnoDB vs MyISAM?". Learn 5 talking points, not 50 cells.
      

  
  
      🗺️ Meet the five engines
      
  
      All five speak SQL and follow the relational model, but each grew up solving different problems. Their dialects (syntax details) and engines (how data is stored, locked and versioned) differ in ways interviewers love to probe.
      
  
      
    
      🐬
      MySQL
      Most popular open-source DB for web apps. Server layer + pluggable storage engines (InnoDB default). Simple, fast for OLTP, huge ecosystem. GPLv2 / commercial dual licence (Oracle owns it).
      
    
      🐘
      PostgreSQL
      "The most advanced open-source DB". Very standards-compliant, rich types (arrays, ranges, JSONB), extensions (PostGIS, pgvector). Permissive PostgreSQL licence.
      
    
      🏦
      Oracle Database
      Enterprise heavyweight in banks and telecom. PL/SQL, RAC clustering, Data Guard, partitioning. Proprietary and expensive.
      
    
      🖥️
      SQL Server
      Microsoft's RDBMS. T-SQL, tight .NET/Windows/Azure integration, strong BI tooling, columnstore. Proprietary (free Express/Developer editions).
      
    
      🪶
      SQLite
      Not a server — a library inside your app (every phone and browser). Whole DB = one file. One writer at a time. Public domain.
      
  
      

  
  
      ⚙️ Architecture & internals compared
      
  
      AspectMySQL (InnoDB)PostgreSQLOracleSQL ServerSQLite
      
    
      Connection modelThread per connection (+ thread cache; thread pool in Enterprise/Percona/MariaDB)Process per connection (postmaster forks a backend) → use PgBouncerDedicated or shared server processesWorker threads scheduled by SQLOSIn-process library, no server
      
    
      Default isolationREPEATABLE READREAD COMMITTEDREAD COMMITTEDREAD COMMITTED (locking)SERIALIZABLE
      
    
      MVCCIn-place update; old versions in undo logs; purge threadsNew tuple version in the heap; VACUUM/autovacuumUndo segments; undo retentionOff by default (locking); RCSI / SNAPSHOT → version store (tempdb, or PVS with ADR)WAL mode: readers see a snapshot
      
    
      Table storageClustered on PK (always)Heap (+ one-off CLUSTER)Heap; IOT optionalPK → clustered by default; heap if nonerowid B-tree; WITHOUT ROWID
      
    
      Transactional DDL✘ implicit commit (atomic per statement in 8.0+)✔ (except CREATE DATABASE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY…)✘ commits before and after DDL✔ (mostly)✔
      
    
      Redo / WALRedo log + binlog (internal 2PC); doublewrite bufferWAL + full_page_writesOnline redo logs (LGWR) + archive logsTransaction log (VLFs) + recovery modelsRollback journal or WAL

      ReplicationBinlog; async default, semi-sync, Group Replication / InnoDB ClusterPhysical streaming (WAL) + logical replicationData Guard, GoldenGate; RAC for shared-disk clusteringAlways On AGs, log shipping, transactional replicationNone built in

    QHow does MVCC differ between InnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server? Why does PostgreSQL need VACUUM?
    
      
      
      MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) means a writer creates a new version of a row instead of blocking readers; each reader sees the version that matches its snapshot. Readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers (Chapter 13 has the deep dive). The engines differ in where the old versions live and who cleans them up.
      
      
      
      EngineHow an UPDATE worksCleanupTypical failure mode
      
        
      InnoDBRow changed in place; the old value is copied to undo; row header has DB_TRX_ID + DB_ROLL_PTR (pointer to undo chain). Readers walk the chain using their read view.Background purge threads drop undo no snapshot needs.A long-running transaction keeps old undo alive → "history list length" grows, everything slows.
      
        
      OracleSame idea: block changed in place, before-image in undo segments; readers rebuild a consistent block as of their SCN (System Change Number).Undo is reused after UNDO_RETENTION.ORA-01555 "snapshot too old": a long query needs undo that was already overwritten.
      
        
      PostgreSQLWrites a whole new tuple in the heap; old tuple gets xmax set. Visibility decided by xmin/xmax vs the snapshot. No undo log; ROLLBACK is cheap (aborted tuples are just invisible).VACUUM / autovacuum removes dead tuples, updates the visibility map, freezes old XIDs.Bloat (table/indexes grow) and transaction-ID wraparound (32-bit XIDs) if vacuum falls behind.
      
        
      SQL ServerBy default no MVCC: readers take shared locks under READ COMMITTED. With RCSI (statement snapshot) or SNAPSHOT (transaction snapshot), old versions go to the version store.Version store cleanup in tempdb (or PVS in the user DB with ADR, 2019+).tempdb growth; update conflicts (error 3960) under SNAPSHOT.
      
      
      
      
      👻 House vs Attic
      PostgreSQL keeps ghosts in the house (dead tuples in the table → VACUUM sweeps). InnoDB and Oracle keep ghosts in the attic (undo → purge / retention). SQL Server has no ghosts unless you invite them (RCSI/SNAPSHOT).
      
      
      🚫
      Answers that fail interviews
      "PostgreSQL has an undo log" (core PG does not). "SQL Server uses MVCC by default" (only Azure SQL Database turns RCSI on by default). "VACUUM FULL is what autovacuum runs" (autovacuum never runs VACUUM FULL; FULL rewrites the table under an exclusive lock).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      All of them want readers and writers not to block each other, but they keep old versions in different places. InnoDB and Oracle update the row in place and keep the previous version in undo, so a reader rebuilds the old version from undo; cleanup is purge in InnoDB, and Oracle can throw "snapshot too old" if undo is overwritten. PostgreSQL writes a brand-new row version in the table and marks the old one dead, so it needs VACUUM to reclaim space and to freeze transaction IDs against wraparound. SQL Server uses locking by default and only versions rows if you enable read committed snapshot or snapshot isolation.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What is a HOT update in PostgreSQL?
          
      Heap-Only Tuple: if the UPDATE changes no indexed column and the new version fits on the same page, PostgreSQL chains it inside the page and adds no new index entries. Encourage it by not indexing frequently-updated columns and by leaving free space (fillfactor < 100).
      
        
      ↪Which design is better?
          
      Trade-off. Undo-based: table stays compact, no vacuum tuning, but rollback of a big transaction is slow (must apply undo) and long readers can hit "snapshot too old". PostgreSQL's design: instant rollback and simple code, but write amplification (new index entries) and vacuum management. Uber's well-known 2016 move from PostgreSQL to MySQL cited write amplification; many others went the other way for features.
      
        
      ↪Why is SELECT COUNT(*) slow on a huge InnoDB or PostgreSQL table?
          
      Under MVCC different transactions can see different row counts at the same moment, so the engine cannot keep one stored number; it must scan an index (InnoDB picks the smallest secondary index; PG may use an index-only scan if the visibility map is fresh). MyISAM has no MVCC, so it stores an exact count and answers instantly.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is the default isolation level in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server? Why does it matter when you migrate?
    
      
      
      "My RR, everyone else RC"
      MySQL = Repeatable Read. PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server = Read Committed. SQLite = Serializable.
      
      
      MySQL InnoDBPostgreSQLOracleSQL Server
      
        
      DefaultREPEATABLE READREAD COMMITTEDREAD COMMITTEDREAD COMMITTED
      
        
      READ UNCOMMITTEDreal dirty readsbehaves as RCnot offeredreal dirty reads (NOLOCK)
      
        
      REPEATABLE READsnapshot + next-key/gap locks for locking readssnapshot isolation (no phantoms)not offeredlocking (S locks held)
      
        
      SERIALIZABLEplain SELECT → FOR SHARE (locking)SSI — optimistic; retry on SQLSTATE 40001really snapshot isolation (ORA-08177 on conflict)range locks
      
        
      Extra——READ ONLYSNAPSHOT, RCSI (option)
      
      
      
      
      🌍
      Migration story
      An app moved from MySQL to PostgreSQL. A report that read the same table twice in one transaction suddenly saw different numbers — RR became RC. Another job that relied on InnoDB gap locks to stop duplicate inserts now raced. Fix: set the isolation explicitly per transaction, and use unique constraints instead of relying on locking side-effects.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QIs the table stored as a clustered index or a heap? Compare InnoDB, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and Oracle.
    
      
      
      
        
      Clustered (index-organized)
      • InnoDB: always. Rows live in the leaf pages of the PK B+tree. No PK → first NOT NULL UNIQUE index → else hidden 6-byte row id.
      • Secondary indexes store the PK value → a second lookup ("bookmark lookup") into the clustered index.
      • SQL Server: PK becomes the clustered index by default (you can say NONCLUSTERED).
      • Oracle: opt-in IOT (ORGANIZATION INDEX).
      
        
      Heap
      • PostgreSQL: always a heap; every index (incl. PK) is secondary and points to a physical TID (page, slot).
      • Oracle: heap by default; indexes store ROWID.
      • SQL Server: a table without a clustered index is a heap (RID).
      • PG CLUSTER reorders once; it is not maintained.
      
      
      
      
      Why it matters: in InnoDB the PK choice is a performance decision. A random UUIDv4 PK inserts in random places → page splits, fragmentation; a long PK makes every secondary index bigger. Prefer a short, increasing key (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT, or UUIDv7 / ordered UUIDs). In PostgreSQL range scans on the PK do not get "rows next to each other" for free. Details: Chapter 15.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QCan you roll back a CREATE TABLE or ALTER TABLE? (Transactional DDL)
    
      
      
      
        
      
        
      
          
      BEGIN;
CREATE TABLE audit_tmp (id int);
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
ROLLBACK;
-- both changes are gone: audit_tmp does not exist, orders has no "note"
      
          
      Whole schema migrations can be all-or-nothing. Exceptions: CREATE/DROP DATABASE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM cannot run inside a transaction block.
      
        
      
        
      
          
      START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (101, 'pending');
CREATE TABLE audit_tmp (id INT);   -- implicit COMMIT happens here!
ROLLBACK;
-- the INSERT is committed, audit_tmp exists
      
          
      MySQL 8.0's atomic DDL only guarantees that one DDL statement fully happens or not at all (crash-safe data dictionary, InnoDB only). It does not let you group DDL with other statements.
      
        
      
      
      
      
      Oracle behaves like MySQL (commits before and after DDL). SQL Server supports DDL inside transactions (with restrictions under snapshot isolation). Practical effect: in MySQL a failed migration halfway leaves a half-migrated schema, so tools write "down" migrations and use online schema change tools (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QThread per connection vs process per connection — why does PostgreSQL need PgBouncer?
    
      
      
      
      A PostgreSQL backend is a full OS process with its own memory, so thousands of idle connections waste RAM and add context-switch and snapshot overhead. PgBouncer (transaction pooling) lets thousands of app connections share a few dozen backends. MySQL threads are cheaper, but at large scale a pool (app-side HikariCP, ProxySQL, or the thread-pool plugin) is still recommended. Defaults to remember: max_connections = 151 in MySQL, 100 in PostgreSQL.

    QWrite "top 3 highest-paid employees" in MySQL, SQL Server and Oracle. What is the ROWNUM trap?
    
      
      
      
        
      
        
      
          
      SELECT name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 3;
      
        
      
        
      
          
      SELECT TOP (3) name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC;
SELECT TOP (3) WITH TIES name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC;   -- include ties
-- standard style (2012+): needs ORDER BY and OFFSET
SELECT name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC OFFSET 0 ROWS FETCH NEXT 3 ROWS ONLY;
      
        
      
        
      
          
      -- 12c+
SELECT name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS WITH TIES;

-- WRONG (pre-12c habit): ROWNUM is assigned BEFORE ORDER BY
SELECT name, salary FROM emp WHERE ROWNUM <= 3 ORDER BY salary DESC;  -- 3 arbitrary rows, then sorted

-- RIGHT pre-12c: sort in a subquery first, then apply ROWNUM
SELECT * FROM (SELECT name, salary FROM emp ORDER BY salary DESC) WHERE ROWNUM <= 3;
      
        
      
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      Two more traps
      (1) WHERE ROWNUM = 2 returns nothing in Oracle: the first candidate row gets ROWNUM 1, fails the test, so no row ever gets number 2. (2) LIMIT/TOP without ORDER BY gives an arbitrary set — never rely on "insertion order".
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QHow do you write an upsert (insert or update) in each database?
    
      
      
      Goal: add 1 to a product's stock if the row exists, otherwise insert it. Needs a unique key on sku so the engine can detect the conflict atomically (no race between "check" and "insert").
      
      
      
        
      
        
      
          
      INSERT INTO stock (sku, qty) VALUES ('A1', 1) AS new       -- row alias: 8.0.19+
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE qty = stock.qty + new.qty;
-- older style (deprecated since 8.0.20): ... UPDATE qty = qty + VALUES(qty)

-- ignore duplicates entirely
INSERT IGNORE INTO stock (sku, qty) VALUES ('A1', 1);
      
          
      Affected-rows = 1 for insert, 2 for update. Beware REPLACE INTO: it deletes the old row and inserts a new one (fires DELETE triggers, cascades FKs, loses other columns).
      
        
      
        
      
          
      INSERT INTO stock (sku, qty) VALUES ('A1', 1)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = stock.qty + EXCLUDED.qty
RETURNING *;

INSERT INTO stock (sku, qty) VALUES ('A1', 1) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING;
      
          
      EXCLUDED = the row you tried to insert. SQLite (3.24+) uses the same syntax. PostgreSQL 15+ also has standard MERGE (not a drop-in replacement for ON CONFLICT in concurrent use).
      
        
      
        
      
          
      MERGE INTO stock AS t
USING (SELECT 'A1' AS sku, 1 AS qty) AS s
   ON t.sku = s.sku
WHEN MATCHED THEN
  UPDATE SET t.qty = t.qty + s.qty
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
  INSERT (sku, qty) VALUES (s.sku, s.qty);   -- SQL Server requires the final semicolon
      
          
      Oracle uses the same MERGE shape (USING (SELECT 'A1' sku, 1 qty FROM dual) s ON (t.sku = s.sku)). In SQL Server, MERGE under concurrency can still race — add WITH (HOLDLOCK) on the target or use UPDATE-then-INSERT inside a serializable transaction.
      
        
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QMySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN. How do you emulate it?
    
      
      
      -- all students and all courses, matched where possible
SELECT s.id, s.name, e.course
FROM students s LEFT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
UNION ALL
SELECT s.id, s.name, e.course
FROM students s RIGHT JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
WHERE s.id IS NULL;          -- only the rows the LEFT half missed
      
      
      LEFT JOIN … UNION … RIGHT JOIN also works, but plain UNION removes legitimate duplicate rows too and costs a sort/dedupe. The UNION ALL + WHERE s.id IS NULL version is exact. More join patterns: Chapter 08.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is special about empty strings and NULL in Oracle?
    
      
      
      Oracle treats a zero-length string as NULL. So:
      
      
      INSERT INTO users (id, middle_name) VALUES (1, '');
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE middle_name = '';      -- 0  (comparison with NULL is UNKNOWN)
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE middle_name IS NULL;   -- 1
SELECT 'abc' || NULL FROM dual;                         -- 'abc' (NULL acts like '')
      
      
      In MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server, '' and NULL are different values. Porting code from or to Oracle: check every = '', every NOT NULL column that receives empty strings (Oracle rejects them!), and every concatenation.
      
      
      🔀
      Other "same name, different behaviour" traps
      Oracle DATE stores time too (to the second). MySQL || is logical OR unless sql_mode has PIPES_AS_CONCAT. MySQL string comparison is case-insensitive with the default collation (utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci); PostgreSQL and Oracle compare case-sensitively (PG has ILIKE); SQL Server depends on collation (default case-insensitive). Division: SELECT 7/2 → 3.5000 in MySQL, 3 in PostgreSQL and SQL Server (integer division).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QHow do identifier case and quoting differ? Why does PostgreSQL say "relation "Users" does not exist"?
    
      
      
      Unquoted names are…Quote withGotcha
      
        
      MySQLColumn names case-insensitive; table names follow the file system (lower_case_table_names: case-sensitive on Linux, not on Windows/macOS by default)`backticks` ("…" only with ANSI_QUOTES)Works on a Windows laptop, breaks on a Linux server
      
        
      PostgreSQLFolded to lowercase"double quotes" (then case-sensitive)Created as "Users" → must always write "Users"
      
        
      OracleFolded to UPPERCASE"double quotes"Data dictionary shows EMP, not emp
      
        
      SQL ServerDepends on database collation (usually case-insensitive)[brackets] or "…"Same collation also makes data comparisons case-insensitive
      
      
      
      
      💡
      Portable habit
      Use lowercase snake_case names, never quote, avoid reserved words (order, user, rank — the last became reserved in MySQL 8.0).
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    Q"MySQL ignores CHECK constraints" — true or false?
    
      
      
      Outdated. Before MySQL 8.0.16, CHECK (…) was parsed and silently ignored — a famous trap. From 8.0.16 CHECK constraints are enforced (and can be declared NOT ENFORCED). MariaDB enforces them since 10.2. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server have always enforced CHECK.
      
      
      CREATE TABLE accounts (id INT PRIMARY KEY, balance DECIMAL(12,2) CHECK (balance >= 0));
INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1, -5);
-- MySQL 8.0.16+: ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'accounts_chk_1' is violated.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⭐ Feature comparison: indexes, JSON, materialized views, extensions, replication
      
  
      FeatureMySQL 8PostgreSQLOracleSQL Server
      
    
      Index typesB+tree, FULLTEXT, SPATIAL (R-tree); HASH only in MEMORY/NDB; adaptive hash (internal)B-tree, Hash, GIN, GiST, SP-GiST, BRIN (+ extensions)B-tree, bitmap, function-based, reverse-key, IOT, domainClustered/nonclustered B+tree, columnstore, full-text, spatial, XML
      
    
      Partial / filtered index✘✔ WHERE~ via function-based index (all-NULL keys not indexed)✔ filtered index
      
    
      Expression index✔ functional key parts (8.0.13+)✔✔ function-based~ index a computed column
      
    
      INCLUDE columns✘ (secondary index carries PK)✔ (11+)✘✔
      
    
      Invisible index✔ (8.0)✘✔~ disable
      
    
      JSONBinary JSON type, ->/->>, JSON_TABLE, multi-valued indexesjson (text) & jsonb (binary, GIN-indexable, rich operators)JSON type (21c+), JSON-relational duality (23ai)Functions since 2016 on NVARCHAR; native json type in 2025 / Azure
      
    
      Materialized views✘ (summary table + event/trigger)✔ manual REFRESH [CONCURRENTLY]✔ fast refresh, ON COMMIT, query rewrite~ indexed views (auto-maintained)
      
    
      ExtensibilityPlugins / components, storage enginesCREATE EXTENSION: PostGIS, pgvector, pg_stat_statements, TimescaleDB, Citus, custom types & operatorsOptions/packs (Spatial, Partitioning…) — often extra-costCLR integration, built-in ML Services
      
    
      Row-level security✘ (views/app)✔ policies✔ VPD✔ security policies

    QJSON vs JSONB in PostgreSQL — and how does MySQL's JSON compare?
    
      
      
      
        
      PG json
      • Stores the exact text (whitespace, key order, duplicate keys kept)
      • Re-parsed on every access → slower to query
      • Fast to insert; use only when you must keep the original text
      
        
      PG jsonb
      • Decomposed binary form; drops whitespace, key order and duplicate keys (last wins)
      • Fast lookups, containment @>, existence ?
      • GIN index on the whole document
      • "Most applications should prefer jsonb" (PG docs)
      
        
      MySQL JSON
      • Binary format like jsonb (validated, quick key access)
      • Index via generated columns / functional indexes, multi-valued indexes for arrays
      • No whole-document GIN-style index
      
      
      
      
      CREATE INDEX idx_attrs ON products USING GIN (attrs);
SELECT name FROM products WHERE attrs @> '{"brand":"Acme"}';   -- uses the GIN index
      
      
      MariaDB note: its JSON is an alias for LONGTEXT with a validity CHECK — text, not binary.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QName some index types MySQL doesn't have. When would you use GIN, BRIN or bitmap indexes?
    
      
      
      
        
      GIN (PostgreSQL)
      Generalized Inverted Index: maps each element (array item, JSON key, word) to the rows containing it. For JSONB, arrays, full-text search, trigram LIKE '%abc%' (pg_trgm).
      
        
      GiST / SP-GiST (PostgreSQL)
      Balanced/space-partitioned search trees for geometry (PostGIS), ranges, nearest-neighbour searches, exclusion constraints ("no two bookings overlap").
      
        
      BRIN (PostgreSQL)
      Block Range INdex: stores min/max per range of pages. Tiny; great for huge append-only tables where the column follows physical order (timestamps in a log table).
      
        
      Bitmap (Oracle)
      One bitmap per distinct value; very compact for low-cardinality columns (gender, status) in data warehouses; terrible for concurrent OLTP writes (locks many rows).
      
        
      Columnstore (SQL Server)
      Stores data column-by-column, compressed; batch-mode execution for analytics on the same OLTP database.
      
      
      
      
      MySQL InnoDB has B+tree, FULLTEXT and SPATIAL; its "adaptive hash index" is built automatically in memory, you cannot create it. Deep dive on B+trees: Chapter 15.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QHow does replication differ between MySQL and PostgreSQL?
    
      
      
      
        
      MySQL
      • Logical: the server writes changes to the binary log (ROW format by default); replicas pull and re-apply them
      • Async by default; semi-sync waits for ≥1 replica to receive the event
      • Group Replication / InnoDB Cluster: Paxos-based, single- or multi-primary
      • Replica can have different indexes, even a different MySQL version
      
        
      PostgreSQL
      • Physical streaming: ships WAL bytes; replica is a byte-identical hot standby (same major version)
      • synchronous_commit + synchronous_standby_names for sync replicas
      • Logical replication (publications / subscriptions, 10+) for selected tables, cross-version upgrades
      • HA via external tools (Patroni, repmgr)
      
      
      
      
      Oracle uses Data Guard (redo shipping to standbys) and RAC (several instances sharing one storage). SQL Server uses Always On Availability Groups and log shipping. Concepts (sync vs async, lag, failover) in Chapter 19.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      📦 MySQL storage engines
      
  
      MySQL is unusual: the server layer (connections, parser, optimizer, binlog) talks to a pluggable storage engine through a handler API. The engine is chosen per table (ENGINE=InnoDB). Check what is available with SHOW ENGINES;.
      
  

  
      
    QInnoDB vs MyISAM — what are the differences, and when (if ever) would you use MyISAM?
    
      
      
      InnoDBMyISAM
      
        
      Transactions / ACID✔ COMMIT / ROLLBACK / savepoints✘ every statement is final
      
        
      LockingRow-level (+ gap / next-key locks in RR)Table-level (writers block everyone; "concurrent inserts" at the end only)
      
        
      MVCC (non-blocking reads)✔✘
      
        
      Foreign keys✔✘ (parsed, ignored)
      
        
      Crash recoveryAutomatic: redo log, undo, doublewrite bufferNone built in — tables may be marked crashed, need REPAIR TABLE / myisamchk
      
        
      Storage layoutClustered index on PK (rows inside the PK B+tree)Heap data file .MYD + index file .MYI; indexes point to row offsets
      
        
      CachingBuffer pool caches data and index pagesKey cache for indexes only; data relies on the OS cache
      
        
      COUNT(*) without WHEREScans the smallest indexInstant (stored row count)
      
        
      Full-text search✔ (5.6+)✔
      
        
      Atomic DDL (8.0)✔✘
      
        
      Max table size64 TB (16 KB pages)256 TB
      
      
      
      
      When MyISAM? Almost never today. Historically: read-mostly tables with no concurrent writes, or full-text search before InnoDB had it (5.6). Since MySQL 8.0 even the system tables (data dictionary) are InnoDB. MyISAM's only remaining "wins" — instant COUNT(*), slightly smaller footprint — rarely beat losing transactions and crash safety.
      
      
      🚫
      Answers that fail
      "MyISAM is faster, so use it for reads" (with any concurrent writes, table locks make it slower; and InnoDB's buffer pool caches data, MyISAM doesn't). "I can mix MyISAM and InnoDB in one transaction" (it runs, but the MyISAM changes are not rolled back — atomicity is broken; you get warning ER_WARNING_NOT_COMPLETE_ROLLBACK).
      
      
      I = Integrity · M = Minimal
      InnoDB = Integrity (transactions, FKs, recovery, row locks). MyISAM = Minimal (table locks, no transactions, no FKs).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      InnoDB is the default and the right choice for almost everything: it supports ACID transactions, row-level locking with MVCC so reads don't block writes, foreign keys, and automatic crash recovery using its redo and undo logs; the table is stored as a clustered index on the primary key. MyISAM has only table-level locks, no transactions, no foreign keys and no crash recovery. Its one advantage is that it stores the exact row count, so COUNT(*) without a WHERE is instant. I would not use MyISAM in a new system.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪How do you convert a table from MyISAM to InnoDB?
          
      ALTER TABLE t ENGINE = InnoDB; — it rebuilds the table (copy), so on a big table use an online schema-change tool. Check first: add a primary key (InnoDB clusters on it), review full-text indexes, and expect COUNT(*) to get slower.
      
        
      ↪Why does InnoDB need a primary key so badly?
          
      The PK is the table's physical order, and every secondary index stores it. Without one InnoDB uses the first NOT NULL UNIQUE index or invents a hidden 6-byte row id (shared global counter, not usable by you, and a contention point). Always define a short, ideally increasing PK.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat are MEMORY, ARCHIVE, CSV, BLACKHOLE, NDB and MyRocks used for?
    
      
      
      EngineWhat it isUse it forWatch out
      
        
      MEMORY (HEAP)Data in RAM; HASH indexes by default (BTREE optional)Small lookup / scratch tablesData lost on restart (definition stays); table locks; no TEXT/BLOB; fixed-length rows. MySQL 8 uses the TempTable engine for internal temp tables.
      
        
      ARCHIVEzlib-compressed rows; only INSERT and SELECTWrite-once logs, audit historyNo UPDATE/DELETE; no indexes (except on an AUTO_INCREMENT column); reads are full scans
      
        
      CSVTable = a plain .CSV fileData exchange with spreadsheets/ETLNo indexes; all columns NOT NULL
      
        
      BLACKHOLEAccepts writes, stores nothing — but they are written to the binlogReplication relay/filter servers; measuring binlog overheadSELECT always returns empty
      
        
      NDB (MySQL Cluster)Distributed, shared-nothing, mostly in-memory; synchronous replication between data nodes; auto-shardingTelecom-style high availability, very high write throughputDifferent behaviour from InnoDB (READ COMMITTED only, join limits); complex to run
      
        
      MyRocksRocksDB (LSM-tree) engine from Facebook; in Percona Server & MariaDB, not Oracle MySQLWrite-heavy, storage-bound workloads — better compression, lower write amplificationSlower range reads than B+tree; different tuning; fewer features
      
        
      FEDERATED / MERGEProxy to a table on another server / union of identical MyISAM tablesLegacy tricksRarely a good idea now
      
      
      
      
      B+tree vs LSM-tree (why MyRocks writes faster) is covered with storage in Chapter 14.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QIs MariaDB the same as MySQL?
    
      
      
      MariaDB was forked from MySQL in 2009 by MySQL's original creator (Monty Widenius) over concerns after Oracle agreed to buy Sun (which owned MySQL). Early versions were drop-in replacements; since MySQL 5.6/5.7 they have diverged and are no longer guaranteed compatible.
      
      
      
        
      MySQL (Oracle)
      • Transactional data dictionary (8.0)
      • Binary JSON, JSON_TABLE, multi-valued indexes
      • InnoDB Cluster / Group Replication, document store (X DevAPI)
      • Thread pool, audit, encryption extras in Enterprise edition
      
        
      MariaDB
      • Extra engines: Aria, ColumnStore, MyRocks, Spider
      • Galera synchronous multi-primary cluster built in
      • Sequences, system-versioned (temporal) tables, RETURNING, Oracle-compat mode (sql_mode=ORACLE)
      • Thread pool in community edition; JSON stored as text; own GTID format
      
      
      
      
      Takeaway: check the exact product and version before assuming a feature. Percona Server is a third variant: MySQL-compatible with performance and observability extras.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🧭 Choosing a database
      
  
      
    
      Runs inside an app / device, one user, no server?yes → SQLite (mobile, desktop, tests, edge)
      
    
      
    
      Data is relational and needs transactions?no (huge key-value, flexible documents, analytics only) → NoSQL / columnar (Chapter 20)
      
    
      
    
      Need rich features — GIS, JSONB queries, custom types, vector search, complex SQL?yes → PostgreSQL
      
    
      
    
      Microsoft / .NET / Azure shop with BI needs?yes → SQL Server
      
    
      
    
      Large enterprise already licensed, needs RAC / Data Guard / PL/SQL estate?yes → Oracle
      
    
      
    
      Otherwise: classic web OLTPMySQL or PostgreSQL — pick what the team knows and what the managed cloud offers (RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL)
      
  
      

  
      
    QMySQL or PostgreSQL for a new project — how would you decide?
    
      
      
      
        
      Lean MySQL when…
      • Simple, read-heavy web OLTP (CRUD, primary-key lookups)
      • Team and tooling already MySQL (Vitess, PlanetScale, ProxySQL, gh-ost)
      • You want clustered PK storage and undo-based MVCC (no vacuum tuning)
      • Huge hosting/replica ecosystem
      
        
      Lean PostgreSQL when…
      • Complex queries, analytics-ish SQL, CTEs, window functions galore
      • JSONB, arrays, ranges, full-text, PostGIS, pgvector
      • Strict standards & correctness: transactional DDL, partial indexes, CHECK/EXCLUDE constraints, RLS
      • Permissive licence, extension ecosystem
      
      
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Both are mature and fine for most OLTP apps, so I start from requirements and team skills. If I need advanced features — JSONB with indexing, geospatial with PostGIS, partial indexes, transactional migrations, or complex SQL — I pick PostgreSQL, and I plan for connection pooling and autovacuum. If it is a straightforward high-traffic web workload and the team knows MySQL, I pick MySQL with InnoDB, designing a short increasing primary key because the table is clustered on it. Oracle or SQL Server make sense mainly when the organisation already runs them.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What breaks when you port an app from MySQL to PostgreSQL?
          
      • Isolation default RR → RC; gap-lock tricks stop working.
      • AUTO_INCREMENT → IDENTITY; LAST_INSERT_ID() → RETURNING.
      • ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE → ON CONFLICT.
      • Backticks → double quotes; case-sensitive string comparison; 7/2 becomes integer division.
      • GROUP BY must list every non-aggregated column (PG is always strict).
      • DDL in migrations becomes transactional (good!).
      
        
      ↪What about Aurora, Cloud SQL or PlanetScale — are they different engines?
          
      They are managed services that speak the MySQL or PostgreSQL wire protocol and dialect. Aurora replaces the storage layer with a distributed, replicated log-structured storage service; PlanetScale runs MySQL behind Vitess sharding. The SQL dialect differences in this chapter still apply.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      5 talking points
      ① My RR, others RC. ② Undo (InnoDB/Oracle) vs heap + VACUUM (PG) vs locking (SQL Server). ③ InnoDB & SQL Server cluster by PK; PG & Oracle use heaps. ④ PG & SQL Server roll back DDL; MySQL & Oracle auto-commit it. ⑤ MySQL lacks "FPM": Full join, Partial index, Materialized view.
      

  
      📌 Key takeaways
        
    
      • MySQL InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to READ COMMITTED (SQL Server's is locking unless RCSI is on).
        • 
    
      • MVCC: InnoDB/Oracle keep old versions in undo (purge; ORA-01555); PostgreSQL stores versions in the heap (VACUUM, bloat, XID wraparound); SQL Server versions rows only with RCSI/SNAPSHOT.
        • 
    
      • InnoDB tables are clustered on the PK; SQL Server clusters the PK by default; PostgreSQL and Oracle use heaps — so PK choice matters most in InnoDB.
        • 
    
      • Transactional DDL: PostgreSQL and SQL Server yes; MySQL (atomic per statement only) and Oracle commit implicitly.
        • 
    
      • Know the syntax pairs: LIMIT / TOP / FETCH FIRST / ROWNUM; AUTO_INCREMENT / IDENTITY / SEQUENCE; ON DUPLICATE KEY / ON CONFLICT / MERGE; CONCAT vs ||; MINUS vs EXCEPT.
        • 
    
      • Oracle treats '' as NULL; MySQL's || is OR; MySQL CHECK is enforced only from 8.0.16; MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN, partial indexes or materialized views.
        • 
    
      • PostgreSQL's strengths: JSONB + GIN, partial/expression/INCLUDE indexes, GiST/BRIN, extensions, RLS. Its costs: process per connection (pool!) and vacuum management.
        • 
    
      • InnoDB beats MyISAM on transactions, row locks, MVCC, FKs and crash recovery; MyISAM's only edge is instant COUNT(*). Other engines (MEMORY, ARCHIVE, CSV, BLACKHOLE, NDB, MyRocks) are niche tools.
        • 
  
      

  
      📚 Go deeper
        
    
      • MySQL 8.4 manual — Alternative Storage Engines — the official feature table for InnoDB, MyISAM, MEMORY, NDB and friends.
        • 
    
      • PostgreSQL docs — Routine Vacuuming — why VACUUM exists, bloat and wraparound.
        • 
    
      • Oracle Concepts — Data Concurrency and Consistency — undo-based read consistency and Oracle's isolation levels.
        • 
    
      • SQL Server — SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL — locking RC vs RCSI vs SNAPSHOT.
        • 
    
      • Wikipedia — Comparison of RDBMSs — a broad feature matrix (verify version details in vendor docs).
        • 
    
      • modern-sql.com — which standard SQL features each engine supports.
        • 
  
      

  
      
    
      
      
      Which database's default isolation level is REPEATABLE READ?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      InnoDB defaults to REPEATABLE READ. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to READ COMMITTED.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Why does PostgreSQL need VACUUM while InnoDB doesn't expose an equivalent command you must manage?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Dead tuples live in PG's heap, so VACUUM must reclaim them and freeze XIDs. InnoDB's purge threads do the cleanup of undo automatically.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      In Oracle, what does SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE nickname = '' return when 10 rows were inserted with nickname ''?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Oracle stores '' as NULL, and NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, so no row matches. Use IS NULL.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Inside a MySQL transaction you INSERT a row, then run CREATE TABLE, then ROLLBACK. What happens?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MySQL (like Oracle) performs an implicit commit around DDL. PostgreSQL and SQL Server would roll both back.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which feature is NOT available in MySQL 8?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MySQL has no CREATE INDEX … WHERE. It does have windows and recursive CTEs (8.0) and enforces CHECK from 8.0.16. Remember "FPM".
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which statement about MyISAM is TRUE?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MyISAM is table-locked, non-transactional and has no crash recovery, but keeps a stored row count. InnoDB has been the default since 5.5.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Oracle (pre-12c): SELECT * FROM emp WHERE ROWNUM <= 3 ORDER BY sal DESC returns…
      
      
      
      
      
      
      ROWNUM is assigned as rows are fetched, before ORDER BY. Sort in a subquery first, or use FETCH FIRST 3 ROWS ONLY in 12c+.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      Default isolation: MySQL / PG / Oracle / SQL Server?
      RR / RC / RC / RC (locking unless RCSI). SQLite: serializable.
      
    
      Where do old row versions live in InnoDB vs PostgreSQL?
      InnoDB: undo logs (purge cleans). PostgreSQL: in the table heap as dead tuples (VACUUM cleans).
      
    
      What is ORA-01555?
      "Snapshot too old": a long Oracle query needed undo that was already overwritten.
      
    
      What is XID wraparound?
      PG transaction IDs are 32-bit; without VACUUM freezing old tuples, old rows could appear to be "in the future" and vanish.
      
    
      Which engines cluster tables on the PK by default?
      InnoDB (always) and SQL Server (PK → clustered index by default). PG and Oracle use heaps (Oracle IOT optional).
      
    
      Which DBs have transactional DDL?
      PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite. Not MySQL (only atomic DDL per statement) or Oracle (implicit commit).
      
    
      Top-N syntax in 4 engines?
      MySQL/PG: LIMIT n. SQL Server: TOP (n). Standard/Oracle 12c+: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY. Old Oracle: ROWNUM in an outer query.
      
    
      Upsert syntax: MySQL / PG / SQL Server & Oracle?
      INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE / INSERT … ON CONFLICT (k) DO UPDATE / MERGE.
      
    
      MySQL's missing trio "FPM"?
      FULL OUTER JOIN, Partial indexes, Materialized views.
      
    
      json vs jsonb?
      json = exact text, reparsed each time. jsonb = binary, no key order/dupes, fast operators, GIN-indexable. Prefer jsonb.
      
    
      Why PgBouncer?
      PostgreSQL forks one OS process per connection; a pooler lets many app connections share few backends.
      
    
      InnoDB vs MyISAM in one line?
      InnoDB: ACID, row locks, MVCC, FKs, crash recovery, clustered PK. MyISAM: table locks, none of those, but instant COUNT(*).
      
    
      BLACKHOLE engine?
      Stores nothing but writes changes to the binlog — used for replication relays/filters.
      
  
      

      


      
  
      
    
      Chapter 12 · IV · Transactions & Concurrency
      
    
      💳 Transactions, ACID & Schedules
      
    
      Explain what a transaction is, how InnoDB and PostgreSQL actually deliver each ACID letter, the MySQL transaction gotchas that trip people up, and solve any GATE schedule question (precedence graphs, view serializability, recoverability) in under two minutes.
      
    
      ⏱ 60 min🔥 Asked in almost every interviewMySQL 8.0 / 8.4PostgreSQLbasicsinternals + GATE
      
  
      

  
       
      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
      
    
        
      
      • A transaction is a group of reads/writes that runs all-or-nothing. Classic example: a bank transfer = debit A + credit B.
        • 
      
      • States: Active → Partially committed → Committed, or Active/Partially committed → Failed → Aborted (then restart or kill). Many Indian textbooks add Terminated.
        • 
      
      • A = undo log (rollback) · C = constraints + your business rules · I = locks + MVCC (Ch 13) · D = redo log / WAL flushed with fsync at COMMIT (Ch 17). Memory hook: “Undo for Atomicity, Redo for Durability”.
        • 
      
      • MySQL durability knobs: innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 + sync_binlog=1 = “double 1” (default, safest). 2 can lose ~1 s on an OS crash; 0 can lose ~1 s even on a mysqld crash.
        • 
      
      • MySQL gotchas: autocommit is ON; DDL causes an implicit commit; an error inside a transaction rolls back only that statement (PostgreSQL instead marks the whole transaction “aborted”); rolled-back AUTO_INCREMENT values are never reused; ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT does not release row locks.
        • 
      
      • Conflict = same item, different transactions, at least one write (RW, WR, WW). Two reads never fight.
        • 
      
      • Conflict-serializable ⇔ precedence graph has no cycle; a topological sort gives the equivalent serial order(s).
        • 
      
      • View-serializable = same initial reads, reads-from, final writes. It is a superset of conflict-serializable; the extra schedules always contain blind writes. Testing it is NP-complete.
        • 
      
      • Recoverability: Serial ⊂ Strict ⊂ Cascadeless ⊂ Recoverable. Serializability and recoverability are two independent axes.
        • 
      
      • Counting: k transactions → k! serial schedules; total schedules = (n₁+…+nₖ)! / (n₁!·…·nₖ!).
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ✏️ “Explain ACID with a real example” is the #1 DBMS question for freshers. Have the bank-transfer answer ready in 30 seconds.
      

  
  
      🏦 What is a transaction, and why do we need one?
      

  
      Start with a story. Asha sends ₹500 to Ben. The bank's program runs two steps:
      
  
        
    
      1. Debit — UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE name = 'Asha';
        2. 
    
      2. Credit — UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE name = 'Ben';
        3. 
  
      
  
      Now imagine the server loses power between step 1 and step 2. Asha has lost ₹500. Ben never received it. The money has simply vanished. ← this is the whole reason transactions exist
      

  
      
    
      1. Debit Ashabalance 1000 → 500 ✔
      
    
      
    
      💥 Power cutserver dies here
      
    
      
    
      2. Credit Bennever runs ✘
      
    
      
    
      Result₹500 vanished — DB is now wrong
      
  
      

  
      A transaction wraps both steps into one unit. The database promises: either both updates become permanent, or neither does. After the crash, recovery sees that the transaction never committed and puts Asha's ₹500 back.
      

  
      
    
      TimeTransfer txn (T1)Database engine
      
    
      t1START TRANSACTION;gives T1 an id; nothing written yet
      
    
      t2UPDATE … Asha − 500writes OLD value (1000) to undo log, NEW value (500) to redo log buffer, changes page in memory
      
    
      t3💥 crash before COMMITno commit record on disk
      
    
      t4restart → recovery finds T1 has no commit → uses undo → Asha = 1000 again ✔
      
  
      

  
      
    
      R(X) / read(X)
      Transaction reads data item X (a row, a value) into its local memory.
      
    
      W(X) / write(X)
      Transaction writes its local value of X back to the database (buffer).
      
    
      COMMIT
      “I am done, make everything permanent.” After success, the changes must survive any crash.
      
    
      ROLLBACK / ABORT
      “Cancel everything I did.” The database restores the old values.
      
    
      Logical unit of work
      A set of operations that only make sense together (debit + credit, order + payment + stock decrement).
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is a transaction? Why does a DBMS need them?
    
      
      
      What: A transaction is a logical unit of work: a sequence of reads and writes that the database executes as one indivisible step. It ends with either COMMIT (make it permanent) or ROLLBACK (undo it all).
      
      
      Why: Two enemies break data:
      
      
        
        
      • Failures — crashes, power cuts, errors in the middle of a multi-step change leave half-done work (the transfer story).
        • 
        
      • Concurrency — many users change the same data at the same time and overwrite or see each other's half-done work.
        • 
      
      
      
      Transactions solve both with four guarantees: ACID.
      
      
      How (one line): the engine logs every change (undo + redo), controls who can touch what (locks / MVCC), and on COMMIT forces the log to disk.
      
      
      CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      INT PRIMARY KEY,
  name    VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL,
  balance DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT chk_bal CHECK (balance >= 0)      -- enforced from MySQL 8.0.16
) ENGINE = InnoDB;

INSERT INTO accounts VALUES (1,'Asha',1000.00), (2,'Ben',200.00);

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 500 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

SELECT * FROM accounts;
      
      
      +----+------+---------+
| id | name | balance |
+----+------+---------+
|  1 | Asha |  500.00 |
|  2 | Ben  |  700.00 |
+----+------+---------+
      
      
      ⚠️
      Only transactional engines
      InnoDB is transactional. MyISAM is not: if you mix a MyISAM table into a transaction and ROLLBACK, MySQL warns that some non-transactional changes could not be rolled back (ER_WARNING_NOT_COMPLETE_ROLLBACK).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A transaction is a logical unit of work — a group of reads and writes that must happen completely or not at all. For example, a money transfer is a debit plus a credit; if the system crashes after the debit, the transaction is rolled back so money is not lost. Transactions protect data from two things: failures in the middle of work, and many users changing the same data at once. The database delivers this through the ACID properties.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Is a single SELECT or UPDATE a transaction?
          
      Yes. In InnoDB, “all user activity occurs inside a transaction”. With autocommit ON (the default), each single statement is its own transaction: it is wrapped in an invisible START TRANSACTION … COMMIT. If the statement fails half-way (say it updates 1000 rows and fails on row 600), the whole statement is rolled back — statement-level atomicity.
      
        
      ↪Can a committed transaction be undone?
          
      Not by ROLLBACK. Once committed it is durable. To “undo” it you run a new compensating transaction (e.g., a reverse transfer). This idea returns in Sagas for microservices (Chapter 19).
      
        
      ↪Why not just write a careful program that does both updates?
          
      No program can stop a power cut between two disk writes. Only the database, with a log written before the data (write-ahead logging), can know after restart what was half-done and clean it up.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Transaction states (the state diagram)
      
  
      Every transaction walks through a small state machine. Interviewers (and university exams) ask you to draw it.
      

  

  
      
    
      StateWhat is happeningReal MySQL moment
      
    
      
      ActiveInitial state. Statements are executing.After START TRANSACTION, while UPDATEs run.
      
      
      Partially committedThe last statement has run, but changes may still be only in memory / the log buffer.You typed COMMIT; the redo log is being flushed.
      
      
      CommittedCommit record is on stable storage. Changes are permanent.COMMIT returned Query OK.
      
      
      FailedNormal execution cannot continue (error, deadlock victim, crash, user abort).ERROR 1213: Deadlock found, or power cut.
      
      
      AbortedRollback finished; DB is back to the state before the transaction.ROLLBACK completed.
      
      
      TerminatedTransaction has left the system (after commit or abort).Session moves on to the next transaction.
      
          
  
      

  
      
    QExplain the states of a transaction.
    
      
      
      A transaction starts Active. When its last statement finishes it becomes Partially committed. When the commit record is safely on disk it is Committed. If anything goes wrong while Active or Partially committed, it becomes Failed; the DBMS then rolls it back using the undo information and it becomes Aborted. From Aborted, the system either restarts it (as a brand-new transaction — only sensible if the failure was not caused by the transaction's own logic, e.g., a deadlock or a hardware hiccup) or kills it (logic error, bad input). Committed and Aborted both lead to Terminated.
      
      
      A → P → C  |  F → A → T
      “All Programs Commit, or Fail, Abort and Terminate.” Two paths: the happy path on top, the sad path below.
      
      
      🎯
      What they are really testing
      Whether you know that partially committed ≠ committed. The difference is durability: until the log is on disk, a crash still rolls the transaction back.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A transaction is Active while it runs. After its last statement it is Partially committed — the work is done but may still be only in memory. Once the commit record is forced to the log on disk, it is Committed. If an error happens before that, it goes to Failed, the database undoes its changes, and it becomes Aborted; then the system either restarts it as a new transaction or kills it. Both Committed and Aborted end in Terminated.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Why is “partially committed” not already “committed”?
          
      Because the changes may still sit in RAM (buffer pool and log buffer). A crash at that moment loses them, and recovery will treat the transaction as uncommitted. Only when the commit record reaches stable storage does the DBMS promise durability.
      
        
      ↪When would the DBMS restart vs kill an aborted transaction?
          
      Restart when the cause was external and temporary: deadlock victim, lock-wait timeout, serialization failure, hardware/software crash. Kill when the cause is inside the transaction: bad input, constraint violation, a bug — re-running it would just fail again. In practice, the application does the restarting (a retry loop, see patterns).
      
        
      ↪Can a transaction go from Partially committed to Failed?
          
      Yes. Example: the disk fails while the commit record is being written, or (in PostgreSQL) a deferred constraint check fails at COMMIT time. The transaction then goes Failed → Aborted.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🛡️ ACID — the four promises (and how they are really kept)
      

  
      A · C · I · D
      All or nothing · Correct rules stay true · Invisible to each other · Don't forget after COMMIT. Implementation hook: Undo → Atomicity, Redo → Durability (“UA-RD”), Locks/MVCC → Isolation, Constraints + app → Consistency.
      

  
      
    
      📦
      Atomicity
      Means: all steps or none.
      Without it: debit happens, credit lost.
      InnoDB: undo log + rollback.
      
    
      ⚖️
      Consistency
      Means: valid state → valid state.
      Without it: negative balance, orphan rows.
      Who: constraints and the application.
      
    
      🔒
      Isolation
      Means: concurrent txns don't see each other's half-done work.
      Without it: dirty reads, lost updates.
      InnoDB: row locks + MVCC.
      
    
      🗄️
      Durability
      Means: after COMMIT OK, a crash can't erase it.
      Without it: “paid” orders vanish after reboot.
      InnoDB: redo log + fsync (+ doublewrite).
      
  
      

  
      
    
      PropertyWhat breaks without it (bank example)MySQL InnoDB mechanismPostgreSQL mechanismWho is responsible
      
    
      
      AtomicityCrash after debit → ₹500 vanishesUndo log records (before-images) in rollback segments; rollback walks them backwardsNo undo log: new row versions are written; abort just marks the XID “aborted” in the commit log (pg_xact); VACUUM cleans dead rowsDBMS
      
      
      ConsistencyBalance goes negative; transfer to non-existent accountPK, UNIQUE, FK, NOT NULL, CHECK (8.0.16+), triggers; plus A + I + DSame, plus deferrable constraints and exclusion constraintsDBMS (declared rules) + application (business rules)
      
      
      IsolationTwo transfers read the same balance and one overwrites the otherRow/gap/next-key locks + MVCC read views; default REPEATABLE READMVCC snapshots + row locks; SSI for SERIALIZABLE; default READ COMMITTEDDBMS, tuned by the isolation level you choose
      
      
      DurabilityCOMMIT said OK, then a reboot loses the transferRedo log (WAL) fsynced at commit; binlog (sync_binlog); doublewrite buffer for torn pagesWAL fsynced at commit (synchronous_commit); full_page_writes for torn pagesDBMS + config + honest hardware
      
          
  
      

  
      
    QExplain ACID with one real example.
    
      
      
      Use one example for all four letters — the transfer of ₹500 from Asha to Ben. Interviewers specifically like a one-line real example per property.
      
      
        
        
      • Atomicity — the debit and the credit happen together or not at all. If the server crashes after the debit, the debit is undone.
        • 
        
      • Consistency — the total money in the bank is the same before and after, no balance goes below zero, and Ben's account must exist (FK). The transaction moves the DB from one valid state to another valid state.
        • 
        
      • Isolation — if someone checks the total money while the transfer is half done, they never see ₹500 “missing”. Two simultaneous transfers from Asha don't both read 1000 and both succeed.
        • 
        
      • Durability — once the app shows “Transfer successful”, the money stays moved even if the data centre loses power one second later.
        • 
      
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Take a bank transfer of 500 rupees from A to B. Atomicity means the debit and credit both happen or neither does — the database uses an undo log to roll back a half-done transfer. Consistency means rules like “balance can't go negative” and “total money is unchanged” hold before and after. Isolation means other transactions never see the in-between state where money has left A but not reached B — the database uses locks and MVCC for that. Durability means once COMMIT returns, the transfer survives a crash, because the redo log was flushed to disk at commit.
      
      
      🚫
      Answers that fail interviews
      “Consistency means all replicas have the same data.” — That is CAP consistency (linearizability), not ACID consistency. “Durability means data is written to disk at commit.” — Only the log is forced at commit; data pages are written later.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Which mechanism gives atomicity? Which gives durability?
          
      Atomicity: undo logging (before-images). Durability: redo / write-ahead logging, with the log flushed at commit. Note the overlap: after a crash, recovery uses redo to replay history and undo to remove unfinished transactions, so the log serves both.
      
        
      ↪Power fails right after COMMIT returns. Is the data safe?
          
      Yes — if the log was flushed at commit (MySQL innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1, PostgreSQL synchronous_commit=on, both defaults) and the disk honours fsync. With relaxed settings you can lose roughly the last second of commits. Saying “always yes” is the trap. Details in Durability.
      
        
      ↪Does MongoDB / NoSQL support ACID?
          
      Single-document operations in MongoDB were always atomic, and multi-document ACID transactions exist since 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters) — with a performance cost. “NoSQL = no transactions” is outdated. See Chapter 20.
      
        
      ↪Can you keep ACID across two microservices with separate databases?
          
      Not with local transactions alone. Options: two-phase commit (atomic but blocking, slow) or a Saga of local transactions with compensating actions plus the outbox pattern (non-blocking, but no isolation, eventually consistent). See Chapter 19.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      ⚛️ Atomicity — all or nothing, via the undo log
      
  
      Plain definition: every operation of the transaction is reflected in the database, or none is. There is no “half”.
      
  
      What breaks without it: partial updates — debited but not credited; order row inserted but stock not decremented; 600 of 1000 rows updated.
      

  

  
      
    QHow does a database actually implement atomicity? (InnoDB vs PostgreSQL)
    
      
      
      Idea: before you change something, remember how it looked. If you must cancel, put the old values back.
      
      
        
        
      1. Before changing a row, InnoDB writes an undo log record holding the old values (the before-image) into a rollback segment.
        2. 
        
      2. The row's hidden DB_ROLL_PTR points to that undo record; DB_TRX_ID records which transaction last changed it.
        3. 
        
      3. The row is updated in place in the buffer pool. The change itself is also described in the redo log (and so are the undo pages — undo is protected by redo).
        4. 
        
      4. On ROLLBACK: InnoDB walks this transaction's undo records from newest to oldest and restores each before-image. For an INSERT, the “undo” is a delete.
        5. 
        
      5. On crash: restart replays the redo log (which also rebuilds undo pages), then a background thread rolls back every transaction that had no commit record, using undo.
        6. 
        
      6. On COMMIT: insert-undo can be thrown away at once; update-undo is kept until no MVCC reader needs the old version, then the purge thread frees it.
        7. 
      
      
      
      🔀
      PostgreSQL does it differently
      PostgreSQL has no undo log. An UPDATE writes a new tuple version in the heap (new xmin) and stamps the old one with xmax. If the transaction aborts, PostgreSQL just records “XID aborted” in the commit log (pg_xact); readers then ignore its tuples. So ROLLBACK is instant in PostgreSQL, but the dead tuples stay until VACUUM removes them (table bloat). In InnoDB, rollback costs time proportional to the work done — a 2-hour batch can take a long time to roll back. Oracle, like InnoDB, uses undo segments.
      
      
      ℹ️
      Atomicity also exists at statement level
      Even inside a transaction, every single statement is atomic: if UPDATE … WHERE dept=10 fails on the 600th row (say a duplicate key), the first 599 changes of that statement are undone. Whether the transaction is then rolled back is a different question — see the error gotcha.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistake
      “Undo is only for rollback.” In InnoDB the same undo records also serve MVCC consistent reads: an old snapshot reconstructs the row version it is allowed to see by following the roll-pointer chain.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Atomicity is implemented with undo logging. Before InnoDB changes a row it writes the old value into an undo log and links it from the row through a hidden roll pointer. If the transaction rolls back, or the server crashes before commit, InnoDB walks those undo records backwards and restores the old values. PostgreSQL does it differently: it keeps old and new row versions in the table and an abort just marks the transaction ID as aborted, so rollback is instant but VACUUM must clean up later.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What is a “before-image” vs an “after-image”?
          
      Before-image = the value before the change (needed to undo). After-image = the value after the change (needed to redo). A textbook log record <T1, A, 1000, 500> holds both.
      
        
      ↪Why would a long rollback block other users?
          
      The rolling-back transaction still holds its row locks until rollback finishes. After a crash, InnoDB opens for connections first and rolls back in the background — other sessions that need those rows wait. The manual warns this rollback can take several times longer than the transaction had been running, and it cannot be cancelled.
      
        
      ↪What is shadow paging and why don't big engines use it?
          
      Shadow paging gives atomicity without undo: write changed pages to new locations, then atomically switch a root pointer at commit. It fragments data and makes concurrency hard, so mainstream OLTP engines use WAL instead (copy-on-write ideas live on in LMDB and some file systems). See Chapter 17.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      ⚖️ Consistency — the “C is the application's job” nuance
      
  
      Plain definition: a transaction that starts from a valid database leaves it valid. “Valid” = every rule (invariant) holds.
      
  
      What breaks without it: negative balances, orders pointing to deleted customers, two bookings for the same seat, total money in the bank changing.
      

  
      
    
      🗄️ Rules the DBMS enforces (declared)
        
      
      • PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL
        • 
      
      • FOREIGN KEY (InnoDB only)
        • 
      
      • CHECK (balance >= 0) — enforced since MySQL 8.0.16 (earlier versions parsed and silently ignored it!)
        • 
      
      • Data types, triggers, generated columns
        • 
      
      • The DB rejects the statement → the invariant can't break
        • 
    
      
    
      🧑‍💻 Rules only the application knows
        
      
      • “Total money before = total money after a transfer”
        • 
      
      • “At least one doctor must be on call”
        • 
      
      • “A user may hold at most 5 active bookings”
        • 
      
      • “Debit and credit amounts must match”
        • 
      
      • If the app writes a wrong transaction, the DB happily commits it
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWho guarantees consistency — the database or the application?
    
      
      
      Both, and saying so is the senior answer.
      
      
        
        
      • The textbook definition (Silberschatz): “execution of a transaction in isolation preserves the consistency of the database.” Notice the assumption — each transaction is correct on its own. Writing a correct transaction is the programmer's job.
        • 
        
      • The DBMS enforces every rule you declare (constraints). And by giving you A, I and D, it makes sure correct transactions stay correct even with crashes and concurrency.
        • 
        
      • Martin Kleppmann (Designing Data-Intensive Applications) goes further: consistency is a property of the application, so “the letter C doesn't really belong in ACID”. A, I and D are database properties; C is what you achieve using them.
        • 
        
      • Fun twist: MySQL's own “ACID model” page maps C mostly to crash-protection internals (doublewrite buffer, crash recovery) — i.e., never leaving the data files in a corrupt state.
        • 
      
      
      
      ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT chk_bal CHECK (balance >= 0);

START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 5000 WHERE id = 1;   -- Asha has only 500
      
      
      ERROR 3819 (HY000): Check constraint 'chk_bal' is violated.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Trap: a constraint error does NOT end the MySQL transaction
      Only the failing statement is rolled back. The transaction is still open; you must ROLLBACK yourself. See the error gotcha.
      
      
      💡
      Some invariants need isolation too
      “At least one doctor on call” spans many rows. Two transactions can each check “2 doctors on call, OK”, each remove a different doctor, and both commit — zero doctors. No single-row constraint catches this write skew. You need SERIALIZABLE, explicit locks on the rows you read, or a materialized conflict row. This is the bridge to Chapter 13.
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      PostgreSQL can defer FK/unique checks to COMMIT (DEFERRABLE INITIALLY DEFERRED) and has exclusion constraints (e.g., no overlapping room bookings). MySQL checks constraints immediately and has no deferrable constraints. Oracle also supports deferrable constraints; SQL Server supports CHECK and FK but not deferral.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Consistency means a transaction takes the database from one valid state to another. The database enforces the rules I declare — primary keys, foreign keys, NOT NULL, CHECK constraints — and atomicity, isolation and durability make sure correct transactions stay correct under crashes and concurrency. But business rules that the schema cannot express, like “total money is unchanged” or “one doctor must be on call”, are the application's responsibility. That's why people say the C in ACID is really the application's job.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Is ACID's C the same as CAP's C?
          
      No. ACID C = integrity invariants hold. CAP C = linearizability: every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy of the data. Completely different ideas that share a word. See Chapter 19.
      
        
      ↪Why still add a CHECK constraint if the app already validates?
          
      Defence in depth. Many apps, scripts, admins and future developers write to the same table. A constraint is the last line of defence that no code path can bypass.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🔒 Isolation — locks + MVCC (full story in Chapter 13)
      
  
      Plain definition: each transaction should behave as if it were running alone. Ideally the result equals some one-after-another (serial) order — that is serializability, the theory in the second half of this chapter.
      
  
      What breaks without it: anomalies. The classic is a dirty read:
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1 (transfer)T2 (audit: total money)
      
    
      t1BEGIN; UPDATE Asha −500 (1000→500)
      
    
      t2SELECT SUM(balance) → ₹500 short ❗ read uncommitted data (dirty read)
      
    
      t3UPDATE Ben +500
      
    
      t4COMMITaudit report already printed with a wrong total
      
  
      
  
      
    QHow does InnoDB provide isolation?
    
      
      
      The MySQL manual: InnoDB “aims to combine the best properties of a multi-versioning database with traditional two-phase locking”.
      
      
        
        
      • Plain SELECT = consistent non-locking read: it reads a snapshot (read view) rebuilt from undo — readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers.
        • 
        
      • Writes (UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT) and locking reads (SELECT … FOR UPDATE / FOR SHARE) take row locks (record, gap, next-key) on index records, held until COMMIT/ROLLBACK.
        • 
        
      • The isolation level tunes the trade-off: READ UNCOMMITTED, READ COMMITTED, REPEATABLE READ (InnoDB default), SERIALIZABLE.
        • 
      
      
      
      🔀
      Defaults differ
      MySQL InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ. PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server: READ COMMITTED. PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE uses SSI (serializable snapshot isolation) and aborts a transaction with SQLSTATE 40001 instead of blocking.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Isolation means concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted work. InnoDB uses two tools: MVCC, so plain SELECTs read a consistent snapshot from the undo log without locking, and row-level locks, held until commit, for writes and SELECT FOR UPDATE. How strict it is depends on the isolation level; InnoDB's default is REPEATABLE READ.
      
      
      ➡ Anomalies, isolation levels, gap locks, MVCC internals and deadlocks are all in Chapter 13.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      💾 Durability — redo log (WAL) + fsync at COMMIT
      
  
      Plain definition: once COMMIT returns success, the change survives any crash — process crash, OS crash, power loss.
      
  
      What breaks without it: the user sees “Payment successful”, the server reboots, the payment is gone.
      
  
      Why not just write the changed data pages to disk at commit? A transfer touches pages scattered all over the disk (two account rows, index pages, a ledger row). Writing them all at each commit = many slow random writes. Instead the DB appends a short description of the change to a sequential log and forces only that to disk. Data pages are written later, lazily, by background flushing. This is write-ahead logging (WAL): “write in the diary before you touch the house”.
      

  

  
      
    QHow is durability implemented? What do innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit and sync_binlog do?
    
      
      
      Mechanism (InnoDB):
      
      
        
        
      1. Every change is described in a redo log record (physical/physiological: “on page P, change these bytes”) placed in the in-memory log buffer.
        2. 
        
      2. On COMMIT, the log buffer is write()-n to the redo log file and fsync()-ed so it is really on the platter/flash — then the client gets OK.
        3. 
        
      3. Dirty data pages stay in the buffer pool and are flushed later (fuzzy checkpoints). The doublewrite buffer protects against a torn 16 KB page half-written during a crash.
        4. 
        
      4. After a crash, InnoDB starts from the last checkpoint LSN and replays redo (roll-forward) before accepting connections, then rolls back uncommitted work using undo. Details: Chapter 17.
        5. 
      
      
      
      
        
      innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commitAt each COMMITmysqld crashOS crash / power lossSpeed
      
        
          
      1 (default)write + fsync redo✔ no loss✔ no lossslowest (one fsync per commit group)
      
          
      2write to OS cache; fsync ≈ once per second✔ no loss (data is in OS cache)✘ up to ~1 s lostfaster
      
          
      0nothing; write + fsync ≈ once per second✘ up to ~1 s lost✘ up to ~1 s lostfastest
      
              
      
      
      
      0 = lazy · 1 = safe · 2 = trust the OS
      And “double 1” = innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 + sync_binlog=1 = fully durable (both are the defaults).
      
      
      sync_binlog controls the binary log (the server-level logical log used for replication and point-in-time recovery). 1 (default) = fsync the binlog at every commit group; 0 = leave it to the OS; N = fsync every N commit groups. Without 1, an OS crash can lose the last binlog events — the replica and your PITR backups then miss transactions that InnoDB itself kept.
      
      
      Why two logs need to agree: MySQL uses an internal two-phase commit between InnoDB redo and the binlog: (1) InnoDB Prepare (redo with XID, fsync), (2) Binlog write + fsync, (3) InnoDB Commit mark. On recovery, a prepared transaction is committed if and only if its XID is in the binlog. Memory hook: P-B-C — “Please Be Consistent”.
      
      
      Group commit: fsync is slow (~0.1–10 ms). If 50 sessions commit within the same millisecond, one leader performs one fsync that covers all 50 commit records. MySQL's binlog group commit runs in three stages (Flush → Sync → Commit) and keeps commit order identical to binlog order. That is why “double 1” is affordable under concurrency.
      
      
      🔀
      PostgreSQL equivalent
      PostgreSQL flushes WAL at commit when synchronous_commit = on (default). synchronous_commit = off returns before the flush and can lose the last few hundred milliseconds (up to 3 × wal_writer_delay) of commits — but never corrupts data: the lost transactions look as if they were cleanly aborted. fsync = off is different and dangerous: a crash can corrupt the cluster. Torn pages are handled by full_page_writes (a full page image goes into WAL on first change after a checkpoint) instead of a doublewrite buffer. Group commit happens naturally; commit_delay (default 0) can widen the batch.
      
      
      🌍
      Production story
      A team set innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2 and sync_binlog=0 on a payments primary “for speed”. A host power loss wiped about a second of commits — orders that customers had already seen confirmed. Worse, InnoDB and binlog lost different transactions, so the promoted replica disagreed with the old primary. Relaxed settings are fine for a bulk-loading replica or analytics box, not for money.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Durability also depends on hardware
      If the disk or RAID controller acknowledges a write that is only in a volatile cache, fsync lies and no setting can save you. MySQL's ACID page lists battery-backed caches, UPS, and backups as part of durability.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Durability comes from write-ahead logging. Every change is first recorded in the redo log, and on commit the database fsyncs the log to disk before telling the client OK; the actual data pages are written later in the background. If the server crashes, recovery replays the redo log. In MySQL the setting innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 makes this happen at every commit — 2 or 0 are faster but can lose about a second of commits — and sync_binlog=1 does the same for the binary log used by replicas. Group commit batches many commits into one fsync so this stays fast.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Why do we need both redo and undo?
          
      Because real engines use steal + no-force. Steal: the buffer pool may write a page with uncommitted changes to disk (to free memory) → after a crash those must be undone. No-force: committed changes need not be on the data pages at commit → after a crash they must be redone. Hook: “Steal → Undo, No-Force → Redo”.
      
        
      ↪Why the doublewrite buffer if we already have a redo log?
          
      Redo records say “apply this change to page P” — they assume P is a valid page. If power fails while a 16 KB page is half-written (torn page), redo can't repair it. InnoDB first writes pages to the doublewrite area (one sequential write + fsync), then to their real place; a torn page is restored from the copy, then redo is applied. “Photocopy before you paint.”
      
        
      ↪What is the difference between redo log, undo log and binlog?
          
      Redo: InnoDB, physical, circular, crash recovery (roll forward). Undo: InnoDB, before-images, rollback + MVCC. Binlog: MySQL server layer, logical events (ROW format by default), all engines, used for replication and point-in-time recovery. “Redo = Replay, Undo = Unwind, Binlog = Broadcast.”
      
        
      ↪When is it OK to relax durability?
          
      When you can re-create the data: bulk loading into a fresh instance, a replica that can be rebuilt, caches, staging/analytics. Never on the primary for financial/order data. (MySQL even lets you ALTER INSTANCE DISABLE INNODB REDO_LOG for initial loads — never in production.)
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🧾 What exactly happens when you type COMMIT in MySQL?
      
  

  
      
    
      💾 Durability knob simulator — what survives the crash?
      
    
      
      
      
      
    
      
    
      
  
      
  
  

  
      🍃 ACID vs BASE — a teaser
      
  
      
    
      ACID (classic RDBMS)
        
      
      • Correctness of each transaction first
        • 
      
      • Strong consistency, serializable options
        • 
      
      • Scales up easily; scaling out needs care (distributed transactions)
        • 
      
      • Banking, orders, inventory, bookings
        • 
    
      
    
      BASE (many NoSQL systems)
        
      
      • Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent
        • 
      
      • Availability and partition tolerance first
        • 
      
      • Replicas may disagree for a while, then converge
        • 
      
      • Feeds, likes counters, product catalogs, telemetry
        •
