      It is a spectrum, not a binary: MongoDB has multi-document ACID transactions, Cassandra offers lightweight transactions, and NewSQL systems (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB) give ACID at scale. Full treatment in Chapter 20 and distributed transactions (2PC, Saga) in Chapter 19.
      

  
  
      ⚙️ Controlling transactions in MySQL
      
  
      Theory is nice, but interviewers also check that you know the actual commands and the surprising defaults. In MySQL every statement runs inside a transaction — the only question is who decides where it starts and ends: MySQL (autocommit) or you (explicit transaction).
      

  
      CommandWhat it doesNote
      
    
      START TRANSACTION / BEGINOpens an explicit transaction; autocommit is suspended until COMMIT/ROLLBACKPrefer START TRANSACTION (standard; BEGIN means something else inside stored programs)
      
    
      COMMITMakes all changes permanent and visible; releases locksDurability point (redo flushed, see above)
      
    
      ROLLBACKUndoes all changes of the transaction using the undo log; releases locksCannot undo DDL that already caused an implicit commit
      
    
      SAVEPOINT s1Puts a named bookmark inside the transactionSame name again = moves the bookmark
      
    
      ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s1Undoes only the work after s1; transaction stays openRow locks taken after s1 are not released
      
    
      RELEASE SAVEPOINT s1Deletes the bookmark (no commit, no rollback)
      
    
      START TRANSACTION READ ONLYDeclares no writes; InnoDB skips assigning a transaction id and some bookkeepingWrites to normal tables fail with ERROR 1792
      
    
      START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOTCreates the MVCC read view immediately (normally it is created at the first read)Used by mysqldump --single-transaction
      
    
      COMMIT AND CHAINCommits and immediately opens a new transaction with the same isolation levelRarely asked
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is autocommit? Is it ON or OFF by default, and what does it mean for a multi-statement update?
    
      
      
      What: with autocommit = 1 (the default in MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server), every single statement is its own transaction: MySQL starts it, runs the statement, and commits it at once.
      
      
      Why it matters: if you send UPDATE A and then UPDATE B as two separate statements without START TRANSACTION, they are two transactions. A crash between them leaves the debit done and the credit missing — atomicity across the two is lost.
      
      
      SELECT @@autocommit;            -- 1 (default)

-- ❌ two independent transactions
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 1;   -- committed NOW
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 500 WHERE id = 2;   -- crash before this? money vanished

-- ✅ one atomic unit
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 500 WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;

-- Turning autocommit off: every statement now silently opens a txn
SET autocommit = 0;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = 0 WHERE id = 3;   -- not committed yet!
-- ...if the session disconnects now, this change is rolled back
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      Oracle has no autocommit at the server level: a transaction starts implicitly at the first DML and lasts until you COMMIT (SQL*Plus has a client setting SET AUTOCOMMIT, OFF by default). PostgreSQL: autocommit unless you BEGIN; psql has \set AUTOCOMMIT off. SQL Server: autocommit by default; SET IMPLICIT_TRANSACTIONS ON gives Oracle-like behaviour. JDBC drivers default to autocommit true — conn.setAutoCommit(false) starts manual mode.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Trap: SET autocommit=0 + forgotten COMMIT
      With autocommit off, even a plain SELECT opens a transaction that stays open. The session keeps an old read view (purge cannot clean undo) and any locks it took. Classic cause of a growing history list and of "my changes disappeared" when the connection pool closes the session.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Autocommit is on by default in MySQL, so each statement is its own transaction and is committed immediately. If several statements must succeed or fail together — like a debit and a credit — I wrap them in START TRANSACTION and COMMIT. If anything fails I ROLLBACK. Oracle is the odd one out: it always works in implicit-transaction mode and waits for an explicit COMMIT.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Does a plain SELECT run inside a transaction too?
          
      Yes. In InnoDB every statement runs in a transaction. With autocommit on, a SELECT is a tiny read-only transaction that ends right away. Inside an explicit transaction, the SELECT uses the transaction's read view (at RR, the snapshot taken at the first read).
      
        
      ↪What happens to an open transaction if the client disconnects?
          
      The server rolls it back. Uncommitted work never survives a session ending — that is atomicity at work.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🔖 Savepoints — partial rollback
      
  
      A savepoint lets you undo part of a transaction. Think of it as "Ctrl+Z back to this bookmark" while the transaction stays open. Useful in long batch jobs: if one optional step fails, undo only that step.
      
  
      START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO orders(id, cust_id, amount) VALUES (101, 7, 900);
SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
UPDATE coupons SET used = used + 1 WHERE code = 'DIWALI50';
-- coupon turns out to be expired -> undo only the coupon step
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
COMMIT;                       -- order 101 is saved, coupon change is not

SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE id = 101;
      
  
      +-----+--------+
| id  | amount |
+-----+--------+
| 101 |    900 |
+-----+--------+
      
  
      ⚠️
      Two savepoint traps
      (1) ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT in InnoDB undoes the changes but keeps the row locks taken after the savepoint until the whole transaction ends. (2) Savepoints are destroyed by COMMIT, ROLLBACK, or any implicit commit — a DDL in the middle kills them all.
      

  
      🫥 Implicit commits — the silent COMMIT
      
  
      
    QCan you roll back a DROP TABLE or ALTER TABLE in MySQL?
    
      
      
      No. In MySQL most DDL statements cause an implicit commit: MySQL commits your open transaction before running the DDL (and the DDL itself commits after). So the DDL is not undoable, and neither is the DML you ran before it in the same transaction.
      
      
      START TRANSACTION;
DELETE FROM orders WHERE created_at < '2020-01-01';   -- 40,000 rows
CREATE INDEX idx_amt ON orders(amount);               -- implicit COMMIT happens here!
ROLLBACK;                                             -- too late: the DELETE is already committed
      
      
      Statements that implicitly commit (the ones to remember):
      
      
        
        
      • DDL: CREATE / ALTER / DROP / RENAME / TRUNCATE TABLE, CREATE / DROP INDEX, CREATE / DROP DATABASE, views, procedures, triggers (CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE is an exception and does not commit).
        • 
        
      • User/privilege statements: CREATE USER, GRANT, REVOKE, ALTER USER.
        • 
        
      • Transaction control: START TRANSACTION / BEGIN while a transaction is already open (it commits the old one — there is no nesting), SET autocommit = 1 when it was 0.
        • 
        
      • Locking/admin: LOCK TABLES, UNLOCK TABLES (if tables were locked), ANALYZE / OPTIMIZE / REPAIR TABLE, LOAD DATA (for non-transactional engines).
        • 
      
      
      
      🔀
      Transactional DDL elsewhere
      PostgreSQL and SQL Server support transactional DDL: BEGIN; DROP TABLE t; ROLLBACK; brings the table back (exceptions in PG: CREATE DATABASE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM cannot run in a transaction block). Oracle behaves like MySQL: DDL commits before and after. MySQL 8.0 introduced atomic DDL — a single DDL statement either fully happens or not at all (crash-safe data dictionary) — but it still implicitly commits and cannot be rolled back by you.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      In MySQL and Oracle, DDL like ALTER or DROP causes an implicit commit, so you cannot roll it back, and it also commits whatever DML was pending in that transaction. PostgreSQL and SQL Server have transactional DDL, so there you can roll back a DROP TABLE. MySQL 8.0's atomic DDL only means the single statement is crash-safe, not that you can undo it.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Is TRUNCATE DDL or DML? Can it be rolled back?
          
      In MySQL, TRUNCATE is DDL (drop + recreate the table internally), causes an implicit commit, and cannot be rolled back. In SQL Server and PostgreSQL it can be rolled back inside an explicit transaction. Details in Chapter 7.
      
        
      ↪Does MySQL support nested transactions?
          
      No. A second START TRANSACTION commits the first. Use savepoints to emulate nesting; frameworks (Spring's NESTED propagation, Django's nested atomic()) do exactly that.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      💥 The error gotcha: an error does NOT roll back a MySQL transaction
      
  
      This is the single most surprising MySQL behaviour. When a statement inside a transaction fails, MySQL rolls back only that statement. The transaction stays open, and earlier successful statements are still there, waiting for your COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO accounts(id, bal) VALUES (5, 100);   -- OK
INSERT INTO accounts(id, bal) VALUES (5, 200);   -- ERROR 1062: Duplicate entry '5'
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 1 WHERE id = 1;  -- still runs fine!
COMMIT;                                          -- commits row 5 (bal 100) AND the update
      
      
      Only the failing statement was undone. If your code catches the error and then calls COMMIT by mistake, you commit half a business operation. Your code must call ROLLBACK explicitly on error.
      
      
      Exceptions — errors that roll back the whole transaction: a deadlock (ERROR 1213) always rolls back the entire victim transaction. A lock wait timeout (ERROR 1205) rolls back only the statement by default; set innodb_rollback_on_timeout=ON to roll back the whole transaction instead.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      BEGIN;
INSERT INTO accounts(id, bal) VALUES (5, 100);   -- OK
INSERT INTO accounts(id, bal) VALUES (5, 200);   -- ERROR: duplicate key value
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 1 WHERE id = 1;
-- ERROR: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block
COMMIT;                                          -- actually performs ROLLBACK
      
      
      PostgreSQL marks the whole transaction aborted (SQLSTATE 25P02 for later commands). Nothing more can run, and COMMIT turns into ROLLBACK. To survive a single failing statement, wrap it in a savepoint and ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT (this is what psql's ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK does for you).
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Default SQL Server behaviour is like MySQL: many errors abort only the statement. With SET XACT_ABORT ON (recommended), any run-time error rolls back the whole transaction. Use BEGIN TRY … BEGIN CATCH … ROLLBACK in T-SQL.
      
      
      SET XACT_ABORT ON;
BEGIN TRY
  BEGIN TRAN;
  UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 1;
  UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 500 WHERE id = 2;
  COMMIT;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
  IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0 ROLLBACK;
  THROW;
END CATCH;
      
    
      
  
      
  
      🚫
      Wrong answer that fails interviews
      "If any query in a transaction fails, the database automatically rolls back the whole transaction." — Not in MySQL (and not by default in SQL Server). Say: "In MySQL the failed statement is rolled back; the application must ROLLBACK the transaction. PostgreSQL forces it by putting the transaction in an aborted state."
      
  
      The stored-procedure way in MySQL is an exit handler:
      
  
      DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE transfer(IN p_from INT, IN p_to INT, IN p_amt DECIMAL(12,2))
BEGIN
  DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION
  BEGIN
    ROLLBACK;
    RESIGNAL;            -- re-throw so the caller sees the error
  END;
  START TRANSACTION;
  UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - p_amt WHERE id = p_from;
  UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + p_amt WHERE id = p_to;
  COMMIT;
END //
DELIMITER ;
      

  
      🔢 AUTO_INCREMENT and ROLLBACK — why IDs have gaps
      
  
      
    QI inserted a row and rolled back. The next insert got id 6, not 5. Why? Is it a bug?
    
      
      
      Not a bug. An AUTO_INCREMENT value is handed out when the insert happens and is never given back on rollback. Why? If T1 took 5 and T2 took 6, and then T1 rolls back, the database cannot "reuse" 5 safely without making every inserter wait for every other one to finish — that would serialize all inserts. Gaps are the price of concurrency.
      
      
      START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO orders(cust_id) VALUES (7);   -- gets id 5
ROLLBACK;
INSERT INTO orders(cust_id) VALUES (8);   -- gets id 6  (5 is lost forever)
      
      
      Other gap sources: failed inserts (duplicate key), INSERT IGNORE/ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE that reserved a value, bulk inserts that pre-allocate a batch, and innodb_autoinc_lock_mode=2 (the 8.0 default, "interleaved") where concurrent bulk inserts get interleaved values.
      
      
      🔀
      Same story everywhere
      PostgreSQL SEQUENCE/IDENTITY, Oracle sequences and SQL Server IDENTITY are all non-transactional and leave gaps on rollback. Also: before MySQL 8.0 the counter lived only in memory and was reset to MAX(id)+1 on restart (deleted top IDs could be reused); since 8.0 it is persisted via the redo log.
      
      
      💡
      Need gap-free numbers (invoice numbers by law)?
      Use a counter row updated inside the same transaction (SELECT … FOR UPDATE on invoice_counter, then increment). It is gap-free because it rolls back with the transaction — but it serializes all invoice creation on that one row.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      📖 READ ONLY transactions
      
  
      START TRANSACTION READ ONLY tells InnoDB you will not write. InnoDB then does not assign a transaction id or add the transaction to internal write lists, which saves work for reporting queries. Writes to normal tables fail with ERROR 1792 (25006): Cannot execute statement in a READ ONLY transaction (temporary tables are still allowed). With autocommit on, plain SELECTs are already treated as read-only automatically. In PostgreSQL, BEGIN READ ONLY works the same way, and SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE lets a long report run with no risk of serialization failure (it waits for a "safe" snapshot).
      

  
  
      ⏳ Why long transactions hurt
      
  
      A transaction that stays open for minutes (a forgotten COMMIT, a batch job, a user "thinking" between screens) is one of the most common production problems. It costs you in five ways:
      
  
      
    
      🔒
      Locks held
      Row locks are held until COMMIT. Other writers wait, then time out (ERROR 1205) or deadlock.
      
    
      📦
      Undo / bloat grows
      InnoDB purge cannot delete old row versions the old read view might still need → history list length grows, reads walk longer version chains. PostgreSQL: VACUUM cannot remove dead tuples → table bloat.
      
    
      🔨
      DDL stuck
      An open transaction holds a metadata lock on every table it touched. ALTER TABLE waits ("Waiting for table metadata lock"), and every new query queues behind the ALTER. See Chapter 13.
      
    
      🕐
      Slow rollback & recovery
      Rolling back 10 million changed rows takes about as long as making them. After a crash, recovery must undo it too.
      
    
      🖥️
      Replication lag
      The binlog is written at commit, so a huge transaction arrives at replicas as one big chunk and replays slowly.
      
  
      
  
      SELECT trx_id, trx_state, trx_started,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, trx_started, NOW()) AS age_s,
       trx_rows_locked, trx_rows_modified, trx_mysql_thread_id
FROM information_schema.innodb_trx
ORDER BY trx_started
LIMIT 5;
-- then, if needed:  KILL <trx_mysql_thread_id>;
      
  
      💡
      Fixes
      Keep transactions short; batch big deletes/updates (e.g. DELETE … LIMIT 5000 in a loop, committing each batch); never wait for user input inside a transaction; set timeouts (innodb_lock_wait_timeout, max_execution_time; in PG idle_in_transaction_session_timeout, statement_timeout); monitor information_schema.innodb_trx / pg_stat_activity.
      

  
  
      🔧 Application patterns that interviewers expect
      
  
      Knowing ACID is half the answer. The other half is writing application code that uses transactions correctly. Four patterns cover most "design a payment / booking / wallet" follow-ups.
      

  
      
    
      1. Lock what you readSELECT … FOR UPDATE (or atomic UPDATE)
      
    
      
    
      2. Same lock orderalways lower id first
      
    
      
    
      3. Idempotency keya retry never double-charges
      
    
      
    
      4. Retry on deadlock1213 / 40001 → rerun whole txn
      
    
      
    
      5. No network calls insidekeep the txn short
      
  
      

  
      
    QWrite a money transfer that is safe under concurrency. What can go wrong with a naive version?
    
      
      
      Naive version (broken): read the balance with a plain SELECT, check it in the app, then write the new value. Two concurrent transfers both read 1000, both pass the check, both write — one debit is lost (lost update), or the account goes negative.
      
      
      bal = q("SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id = %s", a)      # both txns read 1000
if bal >= amt:
    q("UPDATE accounts SET bal = %s WHERE id = %s", bal - amt, a)  # last writer wins
      
      
      Correct version — pessimistic, with consistent lock order:
      
      
      START TRANSACTION;
-- lock BOTH rows, always in ascending id order (prevents A->B vs B->A deadlocks)
SELECT id, bal FROM accounts WHERE id IN (3, 7) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

-- app checks: account 7 has bal >= 500, both accounts active ...
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 7;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 500 WHERE id = 3;
INSERT INTO ledger(txn_ref, from_id, to_id, amount) VALUES ('tr_9f2c', 7, 3, 500);
COMMIT;
      
      
      Even simpler — let one atomic UPDATE do the check:
      
      
      UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500
WHERE id = 7 AND bal >= 500;      -- check + write in ONE statement (row is X-locked)
-- ROW_COUNT() = 0  -> insufficient funds: ROLLBACK
-- ROW_COUNT() = 1  -> continue with the credit, then COMMIT
      
      
      Why this works: the UPDATE takes an exclusive row lock and re-reads the latest committed value (a "current read", see Chapter 13), so the condition is evaluated on fresh data and no other transaction can slip in between the check and the write.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistakes
      Using FLOAT for money (use DECIMAL(p,s) or integer paise); forgetting a ledger row (balances must be explainable); locking rows in request order (A→B and B→A deadlock); and doing the balance check with a plain SELECT at REPEATABLE READ — that reads the snapshot, which may be stale.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      I put the debit, the credit and the ledger insert in one transaction. I lock both account rows with SELECT FOR UPDATE, always in ascending id order so two opposite transfers cannot deadlock. Or I do the debit as a single conditional UPDATE where balance is at least the amount, and check the affected row count. The request carries an idempotency key so a retry never charges twice, and if I get a deadlock error I retry the whole transaction.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Would SERIALIZABLE isolation alone fix the naive version?
          
      In MySQL, SERIALIZABLE turns plain SELECTs into FOR SHARE reads; both transactions hold S locks and then both try to upgrade to X → one gets a deadlock error and must retry. In PostgreSQL SSI, one gets a serialization failure (40001). So yes, it becomes correct, but only with a retry loop, and with more aborts than explicit FOR UPDATE.
      
        
      ↪What about an optimistic version?
          
      Add a version column: UPDATE accounts SET bal = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If 0 rows are affected, someone else changed the row — reload and retry. Good when conflicts are rare; bad for hot rows. Full comparison in Chapter 13.
      
        
      ↪The two accounts are in different databases / services. Now what?
          
      A local transaction can no longer cover both. Options: two-phase commit (XA) or, more commonly, a Saga (debit, then credit, with a compensating refund if the credit fails) plus the transactional outbox pattern. See Chapter 19.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QThe client timed out and retried the payment request. How do you make sure the customer is not charged twice?
    
      
      
      Problem: a timeout does not tell the client whether the server committed or not. Retrying blindly can run the transfer twice. Solution: idempotency key — the client generates a unique id per logical operation (a UUID) and sends it with every retry. The server stores it under a UNIQUE constraint in the same transaction as the business change.
      
      
      CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  idem_key     CHAR(36) PRIMARY KEY,
  response     JSON,
  created_at   TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO idempotency_keys(idem_key) VALUES ('6f1c…-retry-safe');
-- ERROR 1062 duplicate? -> ROLLBACK, then SELECT response and return it (already done)
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 500 WHERE id = 7 AND bal >= 500;
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 500 WHERE id = 3;
UPDATE idempotency_keys SET response = JSON_OBJECT('status','ok') WHERE idem_key = '6f1c…-retry-safe';
COMMIT;
      
      
      Because the key insert and the money movement commit atomically, either both exist or neither does. A second request with the same key hits the unique constraint (or waits on the first one's lock and then fails), so the money moves exactly once.
      
      
      🌍
      Real world
      Payment APIs such as Stripe and Razorpay accept an idempotency key header for exactly this reason. UPI and card networks use a unique transaction reference for the same purpose.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QHow should application code handle deadlocks and serialization failures?
    
      
      
      Treat them as normal, retryable events, not bugs. The database already rolled the victim back; the app should re-run the whole transaction from the beginning (re-reading data), with a small randomized backoff and a retry limit.
      
      
      RETRYABLE = {1213, 1205}          # MySQL deadlock, lock wait timeout
                                  # (PostgreSQL: SQLSTATE 40001, 40P01)
def run_in_txn(fn, max_tries=5):
    for attempt in range(1, max_tries + 1):
        try:
            conn.begin()
            result = fn(conn)         # ALL reads and writes happen in here
            conn.commit()
            return result
        except DBError as e:
            conn.rollback()
            if e.code not in RETRYABLE or attempt == max_tries:
                raise
            time.sleep(random.uniform(0, 0.05 * 2 ** attempt))   # jittered backoff
      
      
      ⚠️
      Retry the transaction, not the statement
      After a deadlock MySQL has rolled back everything the transaction did. Retrying only the failed statement and then committing would commit a half-done operation. Also make fn free of side effects (emails, HTTP calls) or those will repeat.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🌍
      ⚠️ Never make external calls inside a transaction
      A checkout that does START TRANSACTION → reserve stock → call payment gateway (3 s) → COMMIT holds row locks on the stock rows for the entire HTTP call. Under a sale, every buyer of that product queues behind those locks, the connection pool fills up, and the site falls over. If the gateway call times out you also cannot know whether to commit. Fix: commit a "PENDING" order first, call the gateway outside any transaction, then run a second short transaction to mark it PAID (or let a webhook/worker do it), and use the outbox pattern for messages that must go out only after commit.
      
  
      ✏️ Golden rule: a transaction should contain only database work, and finish in milliseconds.
      

  
  
      📅 Schedules — the theory behind isolation (GATE favourite)
      
  
      Now the textbook half. A schedule is the order in which the operations of several transactions actually run, interleaved on one timeline. The question every schedule problem asks: "Is this interleaving as good as running the transactions one after another?"
      
  
      
    
      Notation
      R1(A) = T1 reads item A · W2(B) = T2 writes B · C1 = T1 commits · A1 (or Abort1) = T1 aborts. Read left to right = time order.
      
    
      Serial schedule
      Transactions run one at a time, no interleaving (T1 fully, then T2). Always correct, but no concurrency. With k transactions there are k! serial schedules.
      
    
      Concurrent (non-serial) schedule
      Operations of different transactions are interleaved. Faster (CPU works while another waits on disk/locks), but may be wrong.
      
    
      Serializable schedule
      A concurrent schedule whose effect equals some serial schedule. This is the correctness goal.
      
    
      Complete schedule
      Every transaction in it ends with a commit or abort.
      
  
      

  
      ⚔️ Conflicting operations
      
  
      Two operations conflict if all three are true: (1) they belong to different transactions, (2) they touch the same data item, and (3) at least one is a write. Conflicting operations cannot be swapped without possibly changing the result. Non-conflicting adjacent operations can be swapped freely.
      
  
      Pair (same item, different txns)Conflict?WhyAnomaly if reordered
      
    
      R1(A), R2(A)✔ no conflictReads never change data—
      
    
      R1(A), W2(A)✘ RW conflictT1 sees the old or new value depending on orderNon-repeatable read
      
    
      W1(A), R2(A)✘ WR conflictT2 reads T1's value or the old oneDirty read
      
    
      W1(A), W2(A)✘ WW conflictThe final value depends on who writes lastLost update / dirty write
      
    
      R1(A), W2(B)✔ no conflictDifferent items—
      
  
      
  
      🧠 "Same item, different txn, one writes"
      Only RR is peaceful. Any pair that contains a W on the same item fights.
      

  
      🔁 Conflict serializability
      
  
      Two schedules are conflict-equivalent if one can be turned into the other by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations (equivalently: every pair of conflicting operations appears in the same order in both). A schedule is conflict-serializable (CS) if it is conflict-equivalent to some serial schedule.
      
  
      Swapping by hand is slow. The fast test is the precedence graph (also called serialization graph or conflict graph):
      
  
        
    
      1. One node per transaction (T1, T2, …). Usually only committed transactions are considered.
        2. 
    
      2. For every conflicting pair where an operation of Ti comes before an operation of Tj, draw an edge Ti → Tj ("Ti must come before Tj in any equivalent serial order"). Check RW, WR and WW pairs, item by item.
        3. 
    
      3. Look for a cycle. Cycle → NOT conflict-serializable. No cycle → conflict-serializable.
        4. 
    
      4. If acyclic, topologically sort the graph. Every topological order is an equivalent serial schedule.
        5. 
  
      
  
      💡
      Exam speed trick
      Go item by item. Write the operations on A in order, draw edges from each write to every later read/write by other txns and from each read to every later write by other txns. Then do B, C… This avoids missing pairs.
      

  
      Worked example 1 — two transactions, cycle
      
  
      S1: R1(A) W2(A) R2(B) W1(B)
      
  
      • Item A: R1(A) before W2(A) → T1 → T2.
      • Item B: R2(B) before W1(B) → T2 → T1.
      
  
  
      Verdict: not conflict-serializable. (And since S1 has no blind writes, it is not view-serializable either — see below.)
      

  
      Worked example 2 — three transactions, acyclic
      
  
      S2: R2(A) W2(C) W1(A) R3(C) R3(A) W3(B)
      
  
        
    
      • Item A: R2(A) … W1(A) → T2 → T1; W1(A) … R3(A) → T1 → T3; R2(A), R3(A) are both reads → no edge.
        • 
    
      • Item C: W2(C) … R3(C) → T2 → T3.
        • 
    
      • Item B: only W3(B) → nothing.
        • 
  
      
  
  
      Verdict: conflict-serializable, equivalent to the serial schedule T2 → T1 → T3.
      

  
      Worked example 3 — three transactions, a 3-cycle
      
  
      S3: R1(A) W2(A) R2(B) W3(B) R3(C) W1(C)
      
  
      • A: R1 before W2 → T1 → T2.
      • B: R2 before W3 → T2 → T3.
      • C: R3 before W1 → T3 → T1.
      
  

  
      
    QHow do you test whether a schedule is conflict-serializable, and how do you find the equivalent serial order?
    
      
      
      Build the precedence graph: one node per transaction, an edge Ti → Tj for every conflicting pair (same item, at least one write) where Ti's operation comes first. If the graph has a cycle, the schedule is not conflict-serializable. If it is acyclic, any topological sort gives an equivalent serial schedule. Cycle detection is a DFS — O(V + E) — so this test is cheap (polynomial).
      
      
      How many equivalent serial orders? As many as there are topological sorts. Example: edges T1 → T2 and T1 → T3 only → T1 first, then T2/T3 in either order → 2 serial orders (T1 T2 T3 and T1 T3 T2).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      I draw a precedence graph. Each transaction is a node, and for each pair of conflicting operations — same item, different transactions, at least one write — I draw an edge from the one that happened first. If there is no cycle the schedule is conflict-serializable, and a topological sort of the graph gives the equivalent serial order. If there is a cycle it is not conflict-serializable.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Does a real database build precedence graphs at run time?
          
      Not in that form — checking after the fact would be too late. Databases use protocols that only allow serializable schedules: strict two-phase locking guarantees an acyclic graph; PostgreSQL's SSI tracks "rw-antidependency" edges and aborts a transaction when it sees a dangerous structure (two consecutive rw edges), which is a cheap approximation of cycle detection. See Chapter 13.
      
        
      ↪Is every serial schedule conflict-serializable? Is every CS schedule serial?
          
      Every serial schedule is CS (it is equivalent to itself). Not every CS schedule is serial — S2 above interleaves operations yet is CS.
      
        
      ↪Two schedules with the same final result — are they conflict-equivalent?
          
      Not necessarily. Equivalence is defined on the order of conflicting operations, not on the specific values. Two schedules may give the same numbers by coincidence (e.g. both T1 and T2 add 0) yet not be conflict-equivalent. Result-equivalence is too weak to be useful.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🧪 Try it: precedence-graph builder
      
  
      Type any schedule (e.g. R1(A) W2(A) C2 C1) or pick a preset. The builder lists every conflict, draws the precedence graph, gives all equivalent serial orders, checks view serializability by brute force, and — if you add commits (C1) / aborts (A1) — classifies recoverability.
      
  
      
    
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
      
    
      
    
      
    
      
      
      
      
      
    
      
  
      
  
  

  
      👁️ View serializability and blind writes
      
  
      Conflict serializability is slightly too strict: it rejects some schedules that are actually correct. View serializability is the looser (bigger) class. Two schedules S and S′ over the same transactions are view-equivalent if these three conditions hold for every data item:
      
  
        
    
      1. Same initial reads — if Ti reads the initial value of A in S, it also does in S′.
        2. 
    
      2. Same reads-from — if Ti reads a value of A written by Tj in S, it reads the value written by Tj in S′ too.
        3. 
    
      3. Same final writes — the transaction that performs the last write on A in S also does it in S′.
        4. 
  
      
  
      A schedule is view-serializable (VS) if it is view-equivalent to some serial schedule. Intuition: every transaction "sees" the same values and the database ends in the same state.
      
  
      I · R · F
      Initial read, Reads-from, Final write — "I Really Fear view serializability".
      

  
      Worked example 4 — view-serializable but not conflict-serializable
      
  
      S4: R1(A) W2(A) W1(A) W3(A)
      
  
        
    
      • Conflict test: R1(A)→W2(A) gives T1 → T2; W2(A)→W1(A) gives T2 → T1. Cycle → not CS.
        • 
    
      • View test against serial T1 → T2 → T3: initial read of A: T1 in both ✔. Reads-from: there are no other reads ✔. Final write of A: T3 in both ✔. → view-serializable.
        • 
    
      • Why does it work? W2(A) and W1(A) are blind writes (written without reading A first), and their values are overwritten by T3 before anyone reads them. Nobody can tell which order they happened in.
        • 
  
      
  
      🧠
      The blind-write rule (saves time in GATE)
      A blind write = a write on an item the transaction never read before. If a schedule is VS but not CS, it must contain a blind write. So: not CS + no blind writes ⇒ immediately not VS. Only when there are blind writes do you need the I-R-F check.
      
  
      
    
      Conflict serializability
        
      
      • Test: precedence graph, cycle check
        • 
      
      • Polynomial time — O(V + E)
        • 
      
      • Smaller class (stricter)
        • 
      
      • What real protocols (2PL) guarantee
        • 
    
      
    
      View serializability
        
      
      • Test: compare I-R-F with every serial order (n! of them)
        • 
      
      • NP-complete in general
        • 
      
      • Bigger class (CS ⊂ VS)
        • 
      
      • Mostly theoretical; extra schedules need blind writes
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ♻️ Recoverability: recoverable, cascadeless, strict
      
  
      Serializability assumes everyone commits. Recoverability asks a different question: "If a transaction aborts, can we clean up correctly?" These are two independent axes — a schedule can be serializable but not recoverable, and vice versa.
      

  
      ❌ Irrecoverable schedule
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2
      
    
      t1W1(A)  (A: 100 → 50, not committed)
      
    
      t2R2(A) → 50 (dirty read)
      
    
      t3COMMIT ✅ (pays out based on 50)
      
    
      t4ABORT ❌ — A goes back to 100T2 already committed a decision on a value that never existed. Cannot undo a commit ❗
      
  
      
  
      Recoverable rule: if Tj reads data written by Ti, then Ti must commit before Tj commits. (Tj may still read early — it just must not commit early.)
      

  
      ⚠️ Recoverable, but with cascading rollback
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2T3
      
    
      t1W1(A)
      
    
      t2R2(A) — reads T1's dirty A
      
    
      t3W2(B)
      
    
      t4R3(B) — reads T2's dirty B
      
    
      t5ABORTmust abort (read T1's A)must abort (read T2's B) — cascade ❗
      
  
      
  
      Nobody committed early, so it is recoverable. But one abort drags down a chain of others — wasted work that can snowball. Cascadeless (avoids cascading aborts, ACA) rule: read only committed data — Tj may read A written by Ti only after Ti has committed.
      

  
      ✅ Strict schedule
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2
      
    
      t1W1(A)
      
    
      t2W2(A)? R2(A)? — must WAIT ⏳
      
    
      t3COMMIT
      
    
      t4R2(A), W2(A) ✔ allowed now
      
  
      
  
      Strict rule: no transaction may read or write an item until the last transaction that wrote it has committed or aborted. Why bother beyond cascadeless? Because undo can then simply restore the before-image. In W1(A) W2(A) A1 (cascadeless — no reads), undoing T1 by restoring A's old value would wipe out T2's write too. Strict schedules make "restore the before-image" always correct, which is exactly how the undo log works. Strict 2PL (hold X locks until commit — what InnoDB does) produces strict schedules.
      

  

  
      
    QExplain recoverable, cascadeless and strict schedules. How are they related?
    
      
      
      Recoverable: a transaction commits only after every transaction it read from has committed. Cascadeless: transactions read only committed data, so one abort never forces others to abort. Strict: no read or write of an item until its last writer has finished, so undo is a simple before-image restore. Each is a subset of the previous: Strict ⊂ Cascadeless ⊂ Recoverable, and every serial schedule is strict.
      
      
      ScheduleRecoverableCascadelessStrict
      
        
      W1(A) R2(A) C2 C1✘✘✘
      
        
      W1(A) R2(A) C1 C2✔✘✘
      
        
      W1(A) W2(A) C1 C2✔✔✘
      
        
      W1(A) C1 R2(A) W2(A) C2✔✔✔
      
      
      
      
      🔀
      Real engines
      No mainstream engine allows irrecoverable schedules. Even at READ UNCOMMITTED in InnoDB, writes still take X locks held to commit (strict for writes); only reads may be dirty. PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data at all (its READ UNCOMMITTED behaves like READ COMMITTED), so its schedules are always cascadeless.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Recoverable means nobody commits on top of data from a transaction that might still abort. Cascadeless is stronger: you only read committed data, so one abort never causes a chain of aborts. Strict is stronger again: you cannot even overwrite uncommitted data, so rollback is just restoring the old value. Strict two-phase locking, which InnoDB uses, gives strict schedules.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Can a schedule be conflict-serializable but not recoverable?
          
      Yes: W1(A) R2(A) C2 C1 has one edge T1 → T2 (CS, equivalent to T1 T2) but T2 commits before T1 — not recoverable. That is why the two properties are separate axes.
      
        
      ↪Is every cascadeless schedule recoverable?
          
      Yes. If you only read committed data, the writer committed before you read, hence before you commit.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🔢 Counting schedules
      
  
      QuestionFormulaWhy
      
    
      Serial schedules of k transactionsk!Just choose the order of whole transactions
      
    
      All schedules (serial + concurrent) when Ti has nᵢ operations(n₁ + n₂ + … + nₖ)! / (n₁! · n₂! · … · nₖ!)Arrange all operations, but each transaction's own operations must keep their order (divide by each nᵢ!)
      
    
      Concurrent (non-serial) schedulestotal − k!
      
  
      
  
      Example: T1 has 3 operations, T2 has 2 → total = 5!/(3!·2!) = 10; serial = 2! = 2; non-serial = 8.
      
  
      Example (how many are CS?): T1 = R1(A) W1(A), T2 = R2(A) W2(A). Total = 4!/(2!·2!) = 6. Any interleaving (like R1 R2 W1 W2) has R1→W2 (T1→T2) and R2→W1 (T2→T1) — a cycle. So only the 2 serial schedules are conflict-serializable. This is exactly the lost-update pattern. If instead T2 worked on a different item B, there would be no conflicts at all and all 6 schedules would be CS.
      

  
      🎓 GATE-style practice questions
      
  
      
    QGATE 1: S = R2(X) R1(Y) W2(X) R3(X) W1(Y) W3(Y). Is it CS? How many conflict-equivalent serial schedules?
    
      
      
      X: R2(X), W2(X) are the same txn; W2(X) → R3(X) gives T2 → T3. Y: R1(Y) → W3(Y) and W1(Y) → W3(Y) give T1 → T3. No other edges. Acyclic → CS. T3 must be last; T1 and T2 are unordered → 2 serial orders: T1 T2 T3 and T2 T1 T3.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QGATE 2: S = R1(A) W2(A) W1(A). It has a blind write. Is it view-serializable?
    
      
      
      Conflict graph: R1→W2 gives T1 → T2, W2→W1 gives T2 → T1 → not CS. View check: serial T1 T2 has final write by T2, but S's final write is by T1 ✘. Serial T2 T1: T1 would read A from T2, but in S it reads the initial value ✘. → not VS. Lesson: a blind write is necessary for VS-but-not-CS, not sufficient. (Add W3(A) at the end and it becomes VS — Worked example 4.)
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QGATE 3: S = R1(X) W1(X) R2(X) W2(X) C1 C2. Classify: CS? recoverable? cascadeless? strict?
    
      
      
      All conflicts go T1 → T2 → CS (≡ T1 T2). T2 reads X written by uncommitted T1 → not cascadeless (and so not strict). T1 commits before T2 → recoverable. Answer: CS and recoverable, but not cascadeless.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QGATE 4: T1 has 2 operations, T2 has 3, T3 has 1. How many non-serial schedules?
    
      
      
      Total = 6! / (2!·3!·1!) = 720 / 12 = 60. Serial = 3! = 6. Non-serial = 54.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QGATE 5: Which are TRUE? (a) Every view-serializable schedule is conflict-serializable. (b) Basic 2PL guarantees conflict serializability. (c) Basic 2PL guarantees freedom from cascading rollback. (d) Strict 2PL produces strict, conflict-serializable schedules. (e) Testing view serializability is polynomial.
    
      
      
      True: (b) and (d). (a) is reversed — every CS schedule is VS. (c) is false: basic 2PL may release a lock before commit, so others can read uncommitted data → cascading aborts; strict 2PL fixes that. (e) is false — it is NP-complete. Neither basic nor strict 2PL prevents deadlocks.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QGATE 6: Edges in a precedence graph are T1 → T2, T1 → T3, T2 → T4, T3 → T4. How many equivalent serial schedules?
    
      
      
      T1 first, T4 last, T2 and T3 in either order in the middle → 2 (T1 T2 T3 T4 and T1 T3 T2 T4).
      
    
      
  
      
  
      ✏️ GATE checklist: CS? → graph. Not CS? → blind writes? If none → not VS. Then recoverability separately, using the commit positions.
      

  
  
      📌 Key takeaways
        
    
      • A transaction is an all-or-nothing unit of work. States: active → partially committed → committed, or failed → aborted (restart or kill).
        • 
    
      • InnoDB: A = undo log, C = constraints + app rules, I = locks + MVCC, D = redo log flushed at COMMIT (innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1, sync_binlog=1).
        • 
    
      • MySQL autocommit is ON; DDL implicitly commits; a failed statement rolls back only itself (PG aborts the whole txn); deadlocks roll back the whole txn; AUTO_INCREMENT values are never reused.
        • 
    
      • Safe app code: lock rows in a fixed order or use one atomic conditional UPDATE, use idempotency keys, retry the whole transaction on 1213/40001, and never call external services inside a transaction.
        • 
    
      • Conflict = same item + different txns + at least one write. CS ⇔ acyclic precedence graph; topological sorts = equivalent serial orders.
        • 
    
      • VS checks initial reads, reads-from and final writes; CS ⊂ VS; VS-but-not-CS needs blind writes; testing VS is NP-complete.
        • 
    
      • Strict ⊂ Cascadeless ⊂ Recoverable — independent of serializability. Strict 2PL gives strict + CS schedules.
        • 
    
      • Counting: k! serial; (Σnᵢ)! / Πnᵢ! total.
        •

      In MySQL (InnoDB), a duplicate-key error occurs on the 2nd of 3 statements inside START TRANSACTION. What state is the transaction in?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MySQL rolls back only the failed statement; the app must ROLLBACK. The "aborted, commands ignored" behaviour is PostgreSQL's.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which statement does NOT cause an implicit commit in MySQL?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE is the documented exception. Normal DDL, TRUNCATE and a second START TRANSACTION all commit the open transaction.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      S = R1(A) R2(B) W2(A) W1(B). The schedule is:
      
      
      
      
      
      
      R1(A)→W2(A) gives T1→T2; R2(B)→W1(B) gives T2→T1: a cycle. There are no blind writes (each writes an item it read), so it cannot be VS either.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      W1(A) R2(A) C1 C2 is…
      
      
      
      
      
      
      T2 reads uncommitted A (dirty read → not cascadeless), but T1 commits before T2 commits, so it is recoverable.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Three transactions with 2, 2 and 2 operations. How many schedules are possible in total?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      6! / (2!·2!·2!) = 720 / 8 = 90. Only 3! = 6 of them are serial.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      With innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 2, what can be lost?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Value 2 writes the redo to the OS cache at each commit (survives a mysqld crash) but fsyncs only about once per second, so an OS crash can lose ~1 s.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      A payment API client times out and retries. What guarantees the customer is charged only once?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Isolation and locks handle concurrent transactions, not a repeated request. The unique idempotency key, committed atomically with the payment, makes the retry a no-op.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      Which InnoDB log gives Atomicity, and which gives Durability?
      Undo log → Atomicity (rollback). Redo log (WAL) → Durability (replay after crash).
      
    
      What does "double 1" mean in MySQL?
      innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit = 1 and sync_binlog = 1: redo and binlog fsynced at every commit — no committed transaction lost on crash.
      
    
      Does ROLLBACK undo an ALTER TABLE in MySQL?
      No. DDL causes an implicit commit (before and after). PostgreSQL and SQL Server have transactional DDL.
      
    
      What does ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT NOT do in InnoDB?
      It does not release row locks taken after the savepoint, and it does not end the transaction.
      
    
      Which MySQL error rolls back the whole transaction automatically?
      Deadlock (ERROR 1213). Lock wait timeout (1205) rolls back only the statement unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout = ON.
      
    
      Why do AUTO_INCREMENT ids have gaps?
      Values are handed out at insert time and never returned on rollback/failure — reusing them would serialize all inserts.
      
    
      When do two operations conflict?
      Different transactions, same data item, at least one is a write (RW, WR, WW).
      
    
      Test for conflict serializability?
      Precedence graph: edge Ti→Tj for each conflict where Ti's op is first. Acyclic ⇔ CS; topological sort = serial order.
      
    
      Three conditions of view equivalence?
      Same initial reads, same reads-from, same final writes (I-R-F).
      
    
      What is a blind write and why does it matter?
      A write to an item the txn never read. Every VS-but-not-CS schedule contains one.
      
    
      Recoverable vs cascadeless vs strict?
      Recoverable: commit only after those you read from commit. Cascadeless: read only committed data. Strict: no read or write until the last writer finishes.
      
    
      Total schedules for k transactions with n₁…nₖ operations?
      (n₁+…+nₖ)! / (n₁!·…·nₖ!). Serial ones: k!.
      
  
      

      


      
  
      
    
      Chapter 13 · IV · Transactions & Concurrency
      
    
      🚦 Concurrency Control: Isolation, Locks, MVCC & Deadlocks
      
    
      Walk an interviewer from "two users click Buy at the same time" all the way down to read views, next-key locks and wait-for graphs, and say exactly what MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server really do.
      
    
      ⏱ 75 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL InnoDBPostgreSQLOracleSQL Serverdeepest chapter
      
  
      

  
       
      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
      
    
        
      
      • Anomalies: dirty write, dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, read skew, write skew. ANSI names only three (dirty, non-repeatable, phantom).
        • 
      
      • ANSI levels: RU → RC (no dirty read) → RR (no non-repeatable read) → SERIALIZABLE (no phantom). Defaults: MySQL InnoDB = REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server = READ COMMITTED.
        • 
      
      • InnoDB RR = one MVCC snapshot per transaction (taken at the first read) + next-key locks for locking reads. Phantoms are blocked for plain reads and locking reads, but lost update and write skew are still possible.
        • 
      
      • PostgreSQL RR = snapshot isolation: a conflicting update raises a serialization error (40001), so lost updates are caught. PG SERIALIZABLE = SSI (aborts, never blocks on reads). Oracle SERIALIZABLE is really snapshot isolation.
        • 
      
      • MVCC: readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers; only writers block writers. InnoDB: DB_TRX_ID + DB_ROLL_PTR → undo version chain, filtered by a read view. PostgreSQL: xmin/xmax tuple versions + VACUUM.
        • 
      
      • InnoDB locks index records: record, gap, next-key = record + gap before it, insert-intention. No usable index ⇒ every scanned row gets locked.
        • 
      
      • 2PL (grow, then shrink) ⇒ conflict serializable. Strict 2PL (hold X locks till commit) ⇒ no cascading aborts. Only conservative 2PL avoids deadlock.
        • 
      
      • Deadlock = cycle in the wait-for graph. InnoDB detects it instantly and rolls back the transaction that changed the fewest rows (ERROR 1213). Wait-die: old waits, young dies. Wound-wait: old wounds, young waits.
        • 
      
      • Real-world rule: don't read-then-write. Write with a condition (UPDATE … WHERE stock > 0), lock with FOR UPDATE, or use a version column. Then check affected rows and retry on 1213 / 40001.
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ✏️ Product companies love this chapter. The usual chain is "isolation levels → does MySQL RR stop phantoms? → how? → gap locks → deadlock". Learn the chain, not just the definitions.
      

  
      🚦 The big picture: why concurrency control exists
      
  
      A database serves many users at once. If every transaction ran alone, one after another, nothing could go wrong, but the database would be very slow. So the DBMS interleaves operations from many transactions. Interleaving creates races. Concurrency control is the part of the DBMS that lets transactions overlap in time while making the result look as if they ran one by one (the I in ACID, see Chapter 12).
      
  
      Think of a shared Google Sheet with 50 editors. Without rules, two people type into the same cell and one edit silently vanishes. You can fix it in two broad ways: make people wait their turn (locks) or let everyone work on their own copy and check for clashes at the end (optimistic methods, MVCC snapshots).
      

  
      
    
      🔒
      Pessimistic: locking
      Take shared (S) / exclusive (X) locks before touching data. Two-phase locking (2PL) makes it serializable. Risk: waiting and deadlocks.
      
    
      🕐
      Timestamp ordering
      Give each transaction a timestamp. Conflicting operations must happen in timestamp order, or the late one is aborted. No locks, no deadlocks.
      
    
      ✏️
      Optimistic (OCC)
      Work in a private copy, validate at commit, then write. Great when conflicts are rare.
      
    
      📷
      MVCC
      Keep old row versions so readers read a snapshot without locks. Real engines combine MVCC with locks (InnoDB, SQL Server) or with SSI validation (PostgreSQL).
      
  
      

  
      
    
      1. Anomalieswhat can go wrong
      
    
      
    
      2. Isolation levelswhich anomalies you accept
