      Transaction (Tx, T1, T2)
      A unit of work that must be all-or-nothing and isolated.
      
    
      Conflict
      Two operations from different transactions on the same item where at least one is a write (R-W, W-R, W-W).
      
    
      Serializable
      The result equals the result of some serial (one-at-a-time) order. It does not mean the transactions literally ran one by one.
      
    
      Snapshot
      A consistent, frozen view of committed data as of some moment. Readers of a snapshot need no locks.
      
    
      Locking read / current read
      A read that takes locks and sees the latest committed version (SELECT … FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, and the read part of UPDATE/DELETE).
      
  
      

  
      🐞 The concurrency anomalies (with timelines)
      
  
      An anomaly (also called a phenomenon or read/write phenomenon) is a bad interleaving: the result could never happen if the transactions ran one after another. ANSI SQL-92 defined isolation levels using only three of them. In 1995 Berenson, Bernstein, Gray and others ("A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels") showed four more were missing. Interviewers who know databases well will ask about the extra ones, especially lost update and write skew.
      
  
      All examples use a tiny accounts(id, bal) table: A = 500 and B = 500 unless stated. Read the timelines top to bottom; each row is a moment in time.
      

  
      CodeAnomalyHistory patternOne-line meaningIn ANSI table?
      
    
      P0Dirty writew1[x] … w2[x] … (c1 or a1)Overwrite someone's uncommitted write✘ (assumed impossible)
      
    
      P1Dirty readw1[x] … r2[x] … (c1 or a1)Read someone's uncommitted write✔
      
    
      P2Non-repeatable (fuzzy) readr1[x] … w2[x] … (c1 or a1)Same row, read twice, different value✔
      
    
      P3Phantomr1[P] … w2[y in P] … (c1 or a1)Same predicate, read twice, different set of rows✔
      
    
      P4Lost updater1[x] … w2[x] … w1[x] … c1Two read-modify-writes; one silently erases the other✘
      
    
      A5ARead skewr1[x] … w2[x] … w2[y] … c2 … r1[y]See half of a change: x from before, y from after✘
      
    
      A5BWrite skewr1[x] … r2[y] … w1[y] … w2[x] … (c1 and c2)Both read overlapping data, write different rows, break a rule together✘
      
  
      
  
      w1[x] = T1 writes x, r2[x] = T2 reads x, c1 = T1 commits, a1 = T1 aborts.
      

  
      1 · Dirty write (P0)
      
  
      T2 overwrites a value that T1 wrote but has not committed. If T1 now rolls back, what should the value become? Restoring 500 erases T2's write; keeping 200 means T1's rollback did not really happen. Undo becomes impossible to define, so every real engine forbids dirty writes at every isolation level: the first writer holds an X lock until commit.
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2
      
    
      t1BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal=100 WHERE id='A'; (not committed)
      
    
      t2UPDATE accounts SET bal=200 WHERE id='A'; ⏳ blocked by T1's X lock
      
    
      t3ROLLBACK; (if t2 had NOT waited: restore 500 and lose T2's 200, or keep 200 and break T1's undo?) ❗
      
    
      t4…now runs on the restored 500 ✔
      
  
      

  
      2 · Dirty read (P1)
      
  
      T2 reads data that T1 has changed but not committed. If T1 rolls back, T2 acted on a value that never officially existed. Only READ UNCOMMITTED allows this.
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2
      
    
      t1BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal=0 WHERE id='A';
      
    
      t2SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id='A'; → 0 ❗ dirty read (READ UNCOMMITTED)
      
    
      t3ROLLBACK; -- bal is 500 again
      
    
      t4Blocks the card: "balance is 0" ❗ the 0 never existed
      
  
      

  
      3 · Non-repeatable read (P2, fuzzy read)
      
  
      T1 reads the same row twice and gets different values, because T2 updated (or deleted) it and committed in between. Allowed at READ COMMITTED.
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2
      
    
      t1BEGIN; SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id='A'; → 500
      
    
      t2UPDATE accounts SET bal=300 WHERE id='A'; COMMIT;
      
    
      t3SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id='A'; → 300 ❗ (READ COMMITTED)
      
    
      t3′Same SELECT under InnoDB REPEATABLE READ → 500 ✔ (same snapshot)
      
  
      

  
      4 · Phantom read (P3)
      
  
      T1 runs the same range / predicate query twice and new rows "appear" (or vanish), because T2 inserted (or deleted) matching rows and committed. The rows are like ghosts: they were not there when you looked, so you could not have locked them. Row locks alone cannot stop phantoms; you need predicate / range / gap / next-key locks or a snapshot.
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2
      
    
      t1BEGIN; SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE dept=10; → 3
      
    
      t2INSERT INTO emp(name, dept) VALUES ('Ravi', 10); COMMIT;
      
    
      t3SELECT COUNT(*) FROM emp WHERE dept=10; → 4 ❗ phantom (READ COMMITTED)
      
    
      t3′InnoDB RR plain SELECT → 3 ✔ (snapshot). With FOR UPDATE at t1, T2's INSERT would have waited on a gap lock.
      
  
      

  
      5 · Lost update (P4)
      
  
      Two transactions read the same value, each computes a new value in the application, and each writes it back. The second write is based on a stale read, so the first update is lost. This is the most common real-life bug (stock counts, wallet balances, like counts).
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1 (buyer 1)T2 (buyer 2)
      
    
      t1BEGIN; SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE id=1; → 10
      
    
      t2BEGIN; SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE id=1; → 10
      
    
      t3UPDATE stock SET qty=9 WHERE id=1; -- app did 10−1
      
    
      t4UPDATE stock SET qty=9 WHERE id=1; ⏳ waits for T1's X lock
      
    
      t5COMMIT;…unblocked, writes 9
      
    
      t6COMMIT; → qty = 9 ❗ two units sold, stock dropped by one
      
  
      
  
      🔀
      Who stops the lost update?
      MySQL InnoDB RR: does NOT. Its UPDATE waits, then silently writes over the latest version. PostgreSQL RR: T2 gets ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update at t5. Oracle SERIALIZABLE: ORA-08177. SQL Server RR/SNAPSHOT: blocked by held S locks (RR) or error 3960 (SNAPSHOT). Portable fixes: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 (atomic), SELECT … FOR UPDATE, or a version column.
      

  
      6 · Read skew (A5A)
      
  
      T1 reads two related items but sees them from different moments: A before a transfer and B after it. Each value is committed and correct, yet together they are inconsistent. A per-transaction snapshot (InnoDB RR, PG RR, SQL Server SNAPSHOT) prevents it; READ COMMITTED allows it everywhere.
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1 (audit report)T2 (transfer ₹100 A→B)
      
    
      t1BEGIN; SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id='A'; → 500
      
    
      t2UPDATE A SET bal=400; UPDATE B SET bal=600; COMMIT;
      
    
      t3SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id='B'; → 600 ❗ total = 1100, ₹100 "created"
      
  
      

  
      7 · Write skew (A5B) — the doctors-on-call problem
      
  
      Rule: at least one doctor must be on call. Alice and Bob are both on call and both feel ill. Each transaction checks "are there at least 2 on call?", sees 2, and takes itself off. They write different rows, so there is no write-write conflict. Snapshot isolation only checks write-write conflicts, so both commit and nobody is on call.
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1 (Alice)T2 (Bob)
      
    
      t1SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call AND shift=1; → 2
      
    
      t2SELECT COUNT(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call AND shift=1; → 2
      
    
      t3UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false WHERE name='Alice';
      
    
      t4UPDATE doctors SET on_call=false WHERE name='Bob'; -- different row, no conflict
      
    
      t5COMMIT ✔COMMIT ✔ → 0 doctors on call ❗
      
  
      
  
      Write skew is…Engines / levels
      
    
      ✘ AllowedPostgreSQL RR (SI), Oracle SERIALIZABLE (SI), SQL Server SNAPSHOT, MySQL RR with plain SELECT, every RC
      
    
      ✔ PreventedPostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE (SSI aborts one), MySQL SERIALIZABLE (SELECT becomes FOR SHARE → S-lock conflict → deadlock → one rolled back), SQL Server RR and SERIALIZABLE (held S locks), SELECT … FOR UPDATE on the rows you read
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is the difference between a non-repeatable read and a phantom read?
    
      
      
      Non-repeatable read = the same row changes its value between two reads (someone UPDATEd or DELETEd it). Phantom = the set of rows matching a condition changes (someone INSERTed a new matching row, or deleted/updated a row out of the range).
      
      
      
        
      Non-repeatable read
      • Unit: one existing row
      • Cause: UPDATE / DELETE
      • Fix: hold a read lock on that row, or read from a snapshot
      • Prevented at RR (ANSI)
      
        
      Phantom
      • Unit: a predicate / range (WHERE dept=10)
      • Cause: INSERT (or DELETE / UPDATE moving rows in/out)
      • Fix: lock the gap / range / predicate, or read from a snapshot
      • Prevented only at SERIALIZABLE (ANSI); InnoDB RR also blocks it
      
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistake
      "Phantom = a row got updated." No, that is a non-repeatable read. A phantom needs a range query and a row that was not in the result before.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A non-repeatable read is about one row: I read it twice and its value changed because another transaction updated it and committed. A phantom is about a range: I run the same WHERE query twice and new rows appear because someone inserted matching rows. Locking the rows I read fixes the first one, but not the second, because the new rows did not exist when I locked. For phantoms you need range or gap locks, or a snapshot.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Why can't ordinary row locks stop phantoms?
          
      You can only lock rows that exist. The phantom row is inserted later, into empty space. So the DB must lock the space (a gap between index keys, a key range, or the predicate itself). InnoDB does this with gap and next-key locks; SQL Server with key-range locks; PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE with non-blocking predicate (SIRead) locks.
      
        
      ↪Can a DELETE cause a phantom?
          
      Yes. If a matching row disappears between two range reads, the set changed. Also an UPDATE that moves a row into the range (e.g. dept 20 → 10) creates a phantom for WHERE dept=10.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is a lost update and which isolation level prevents it?
    
      
      
      What: two transactions do read → compute → write on the same row; the second write is based on a stale read and wipes out the first. Why it is tricky: the ANSI table does not even list it, so "which level prevents it" depends on the engine.
      
      
      Engine / levelLost update?Why
      
        
      Any engine, READ COMMITTED✘ possibleno check on concurrent modification
      
        
      MySQL InnoDB REPEATABLE READ (default)✘ possibleUPDATE does a current read of the latest row; no "first updater wins" check
      
        
      PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ✔ preventedSI first-updater-wins → error 40001, retry
      
        
      Oracle SERIALIZABLE✔ preventedORA-08177
      
        
      SQL Server RR / SNAPSHOT✔ preventedheld S locks (RR, usually ends in a deadlock victim) / update-conflict error 3960 (SNAPSHOT)
      
        
      Any SERIALIZABLE✔ preventedby definition
      
      
      
      
      -- Fix 1: atomic read-modify-write in ONE statement (best for counters / stock)
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = 1 AND qty > 0;   -- check affected rows

-- Fix 2: pessimistic lock - read with the lock you will need for the write
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT qty FROM stock WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;              -- others wait here
UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = 1;
COMMIT;

-- Fix 3: optimistic lock - version column compare-and-set
UPDATE stock SET qty = 9, version = version + 1
 WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7;                              -- 0 rows = someone beat you: reload, retry
      
      
      🚫
      Fails interviews
      "REPEATABLE READ prevents lost updates." True for PostgreSQL, false for MySQL's default. Always name the engine.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A lost update happens when two transactions read the same value, both compute a new value in the app, and the second write overwrites the first. ANSI levels don't mention it. In MySQL even REPEATABLE READ allows it, because UPDATE just waits and writes the latest row. PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ catches it with a serialization error. My fix is engine-independent: do the math inside one UPDATE statement, or use SELECT FOR UPDATE, or a version column, and always check the affected row count.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Why is UPDATE … SET qty = qty - 1 safe without explicit locking?
          
      It is one statement. InnoDB takes an X lock on the row and evaluates qty - 1 (and any WHERE qty > 0) on the latest committed version, not on an old snapshot. A second concurrent decrement waits for the lock, then re-reads the new value. So the read and write cannot be split by another writer.
      
        
      ↪What is "cursor lost update" (P4C) and cursor stability?
          
      The same lost update but via a cursor read. Cursor stability (IBM DB2's default) keeps a lock on the row under the cursor until the cursor moves, which stops P4C. It sits between RC and RR.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is write skew, and why doesn't snapshot isolation prevent it?
    
      
      
      Write skew: two transactions read an overlapping set of data, each makes a decision based on what it read, and they update different rows. Each one alone keeps the rule; together they break it.
      
      
      Why SI misses it: snapshot isolation only aborts on write-write conflicts (two transactions writing the same row: first-committer-wins / first-updater-wins). In write skew the conflict is read-write: T1 read Bob's row which T2 wrote, and T2 read Alice's row which T1 wrote. SI does not track reads, so it sees nothing wrong.
      
      
        
        
      1. Lock what you read — SELECT … FROM doctors WHERE shift=1 AND on_call FOR UPDATE. Now T2 waits for T1.
        2. 
        
      2. Materialize the conflict — make both transactions update one shared row (e.g. UPDATE shifts SET version=version+1 WHERE shift_id=1). Now it is a write-write conflict that every engine catches.
        3. 
        
      3. Use a constraint — e.g. PostgreSQL exclusion constraints for "no overlapping bookings".
        4. 
        
      4. Use true SERIALIZABLE — PostgreSQL SSI aborts one transaction (SQLSTATE 40001), so you retry.
        5. 
      
      
      
      🧠
      Memory aid
      Read skew = I saw a torn picture. Write skew = we each painted a different corner and ruined the picture together.
      
      
      🌍
      Real-world write skews
      Meeting-room booking (two people each check "room free 3–4 pm?" and both insert a booking), "max 5 active coupons per user", "username must be unique" without a UNIQUE index, "account total across 2 wallets must stay ≥ 0".
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Is meeting-room double-booking write skew or phantom?
          
      Both ideas meet here. Each transaction checks that no row matches "overlapping booking" and then inserts a new row. The rows that conflict did not exist when read, so it is a write skew caused by a phantom. Locking existing rows does not help; you need a range lock, a materialized "room-day" row to lock, or a constraint.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      D · N · P → L · S · S
      Do Not Panic (Dirty, Non-repeatable, Phantom — the ANSI three, fixed by RC → RR → SERIALIZABLE), then remember the hidden three: Lost update, read Skew, write Skew. "Lost update = last writer wins, first writer cries."
      

  
      🛡️ Isolation levels: the standard vs what engines really do
      
  
      An isolation level is a contract: "I accept these anomalies in exchange for more speed and less waiting." Stronger levels block or abort more. Weaker levels let more anomalies through.
      

  
      The SQL-standard (ANSI SQL-92) table
      
  
      Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantomTypical mechanism (textbook)
      
    
      READ UNCOMMITTED✘ possible✘ possible✘ possibleno read locks; write locks to commit
      
    
      READ COMMITTED✔ prevented✘ possible✘ possibleshort read locks (released after each read) or a snapshot per statement
      
    
      REPEATABLE READ✔✔ prevented✘ possibleread locks held to commit (rows only) or a snapshot per transaction
      
    
      SERIALIZABLE✔✔✔ preventedrange/predicate locks + strict 2PL, or SSI
      
  
      
  
      Dirty write is forbidden at every level. The standard's own default is SERIALIZABLE, but almost no engine ships with it as the default.
      
  
      🧠
      Staircase memory
      Each step up removes exactly one ANSI anomaly: RU (none removed) → RC removes Dirty → RR removes Non-repeatable → SER removes Phantom. "D-N-P, one per step."
      

  
      Why the ANSI table is not enough (the Berenson critique)
      
  
      The 1995 paper "A Critique of ANSI SQL Isolation Levels" made three points interviewers like:
      
  
        
    
      1. Missing anomalies — dirty write, lost update, read skew and write skew are not in the table.
        2. 
    
      2. Snapshot isolation (SI) does not fit — SI avoids all three ANSI phenomena (phantoms mostly), yet it is not serializable because it allows write skew. So "no dirty, no non-repeatable, no phantom" ≠ serializable.
        3. 
    
      3. RR and SI are incomparable — lock-based RR allows phantoms but blocks write skew; SI blocks phantoms (for reads) but allows write skew. Neither is "stronger".
        4. 
  
      

  
      Real behavior per engine
      
  
      Every engine below implements isolation differently. This is where most candidates lose points. Click through the tabs.
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
      MySQL Default REPEATABLE READ. All four levels exist.
      
      
        
        
      • READ UNCOMMITTED: plain SELECTs may read the newest, uncommitted version (dirty read). Otherwise it behaves like RC.
        • 
        
      • READ COMMITTED: each consistent read (even inside one transaction) builds a fresh read view. No gap locks for searches (only for foreign-key and duplicate-key checks), so phantoms are possible. Locks on rows that do not match the WHERE are released after the WHERE is checked. UPDATE uses a "semi-consistent" read. Requires row-based binary logging.
        • 
        
      • REPEATABLE READ: all consistent reads in a transaction reuse one read view, created at the first read. Locking reads, UPDATE and DELETE take next-key locks on the scanned range (record-only lock for a unique-index equality hit). Phantoms blocked; lost update and write skew not blocked.
        • 
        
      • SERIALIZABLE: like RR, but every plain SELECT is silently turned into SELECT … FOR SHARE when autocommit is off. It is pure lock-based strict 2PL: lots of blocking and deadlocks.
        • 
      
      
    
      
    
      
      
      PostgreSQL Default READ COMMITTED. Internally only three levels: READ UNCOMMITTED behaves exactly like READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads ever).
      
      
        
        
      • READ COMMITTED: each statement sees a snapshot taken when the statement started. If an UPDATE finds a row being changed by another transaction, it waits; if that one commits, PG re-evaluates the WHERE on the new row version and applies the update to it. So UPDATE … SET bal = bal + 100 is safe.
        • 
        
      • REPEATABLE READ: true snapshot isolation, snapshot taken at the first statement. No phantoms in reads. If you UPDATE/DELETE a row that someone else changed and committed after your snapshot: ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update (SQLSTATE 40001). Retry the transaction. Read-only transactions never get this error.
        • 
        
      • SERIALIZABLE: SSI (Serializable Snapshot Isolation, PostgreSQL 9.1+). Same as RR plus tracking of read-write dependencies with SIRead "locks" that never block. On a dangerous pattern: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions (40001).
        • 
      
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Oracle Default READ COMMITTED. Offers only READ COMMITTED, SERIALIZABLE and a READ ONLY mode. No dirty reads, ever.
      
      
        
        
      • Statement-level read consistency always: each query sees data as of its start (rebuilt from undo using the SCN, the system change number).
        • 
        
      • "Readers never block writers; writers never block readers; a writer blocks another writer of the same row."
        • 
        
      • SERIALIZABLE is really snapshot isolation: updating a row changed by a transaction that committed after yours began gives ORA-08177: can't serialize access for this transaction. Write skew is still possible.
        • 
      
      
    
      
    
      
      
      SQL Server Default READ COMMITTED using locks (on-premises). Five levels.
      
      
        
        
      • READ UNCOMMITTED (= the NOLOCK hint): dirty reads.
        • 
        
      • READ COMMITTED: with READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT OFF, S locks are taken and released after each read, so readers block on writers. With RCSI (READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON) each statement reads row versions instead. RCSI is ON by default in Azure SQL Database.
        • 
        
      • REPEATABLE READ: S locks held to commit; phantoms possible.
        • 
        
      • SNAPSHOT: transaction-level snapshot (needs ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON). Update conflicts raise error 3960.
        • 
        
      • SERIALIZABLE: key-range locks. Also: SQL Server escalates to a table lock at about 5,000 locks per statement on one object.
        • 
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      The "real behavior" master table
      
  
      ✔ = prevented, ✘ = possible. Based on the vendor docs and Martin Kleppmann's Hermitage tests.
      
  
      Engine · levelDirty readNon-rep. readPhantomLost updateWrite skewHow
      
    
      MySQL RC✔✘✘✘✘read view per statement; record locks only
      
    
      MySQL RR ★✔✔✔ ~✘✘read view per transaction + next-key locks (DML can still "see" new rows)
      
    
      MySQL SERIALIZABLE✔✔✔✔✔plain SELECT → FOR SHARE (lock-based)
      
    
      PostgreSQL RC ★✔✘✘✘✘snapshot per statement; WHERE re-check on update
      
    
      PostgreSQL RR✔✔✔✔ (error)✘snapshot isolation
      
    
      PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE✔✔✔✔✔ (abort)SSI
      
    
      Oracle RC ★✔✘✘✘✘statement-level consistency via undo
      
    
      Oracle SERIALIZABLE✔✔✔✔ (ORA-08177)✘really SI
      
    
      SQL Server RC ★✔✘✘✘✘short S locks (or RCSI versions)
      
    
      SQL Server RR✔✔✘✔✔S locks held to commit
      
    
      SQL Server SNAPSHOT✔✔✔✔ (error 3960)✘row versions, transaction snapshot
      
    
      SQL Server SERIALIZABLE✔✔✔✔✔key-range locks
      
  
      
  
      ★ = default level of that engine
      

  
      
    QName the isolation levels and what each one prevents. What are the defaults?
    
      
      
      Four ANSI levels, each removing one more anomaly: READ UNCOMMITTED (nothing prevented), READ COMMITTED (no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (also no non-repeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (also no phantoms; equivalent to some serial order).
      
      
      Defaults: MySQL InnoDB = REPEATABLE READ. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server = READ COMMITTED (SQL Server: locking RC on-prem, RCSI in Azure SQL Database).
      
      
      Why not always SERIALIZABLE? It costs throughput: more locks held longer (MySQL, SQL Server) or more aborts and retries (PostgreSQL SSI). Most apps choose RC or RR and protect their few critical read-modify-write paths explicitly with FOR UPDATE, atomic updates or constraints.
      
      
      🚫
      Fails interviews
      "SERIALIZABLE means transactions run one at a time." No. It means the result equals some serial order. Transactions still run in parallel.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      There are four standard levels. Read uncommitted allows dirty reads. Read committed only shows committed data, but a re-read can change. Repeatable read guarantees the same row reads the same, but the standard still allows phantoms. Serializable makes the result equal to some serial order. MySQL InnoDB defaults to repeatable read; Postgres, Oracle and SQL Server default to read committed. And I'd add that real engines differ from the table: for example MySQL's repeatable read blocks phantoms but still allows lost updates.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Why does MySQL default to RR when everyone else uses RC?
          
      History and replication. For years MySQL replicated by re-running SQL statements (statement-based binlog). For a replica to get the same result, a statement like INSERT … SELECT or UPDATE … WHERE range must not be affected by concurrent inserts. RR with gap locking gave that. MySQL's docs state that RC supports only row-based binary logging. Today row-based logging is the default, and many teams switch to RC to get fewer gap locks and deadlocks.
      
        
      ↪Is RC enough for a banking app?
          
      Isolation level alone is not the answer. Under RC you get lost updates and read skew if you do read-then-write. But with correct patterns (row locks via FOR UPDATE, atomic guarded updates, constraints) RC is fine and is what most banks' OLTP engines run. Reports that need a consistent picture of many rows should use a transaction-level snapshot (RR / SNAPSHOT).
      
        
      ↪Does PostgreSQL support READ UNCOMMITTED?
          
      You can request it, but it behaves exactly like READ COMMITTED. PostgreSQL never shows uncommitted data to other transactions.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QDoes MySQL InnoDB's REPEATABLE READ prevent phantom reads?
    
      
      
      Short answer: mostly yes, in two different ways, with one famous loophole. ANSI RR allows phantoms, but InnoDB goes further.
      
      
      
        
      Plain SELECT (consistent read)
      • Reads from the transaction's single read view (snapshot)
      • Rows committed after the snapshot are invisible
      • ⇒ no phantoms, and no locks at all
      
        
      Locking read / UPDATE / DELETE
      • Takes next-key locks on every index record scanned + the gap before it
      • Other sessions' INSERTs into those gaps wait
      • ⇒ no phantoms because nobody can insert into the range
      
        
      The loophole: mixing them
      • A plain SELECT reads the snapshot (old)
      • A later UPDATE/DELETE does a current read (latest committed rows)
      • ⇒ the UPDATE can touch rows the SELECT never showed, and afterwards they become visible
      
      
      
      
      
        
      TimeT1 (REPEATABLE READ)T2
      
        
      t1START TRANSACTION; SELECT * FROM t WHERE c2='abc'; → 0 rows
      
        
      t2INSERT 10 rows with c2='abc'; COMMIT;
      
        
      t3SELECT * FROM t WHERE c2='abc'; → 0 rows ✔ (snapshot)
      
        
      t4UPDATE t SET c2='cba' WHERE c2='abc'; → 10 rows affected ❗ (current read)
      
        
      t5SELECT * FROM t WHERE c2='cba'; → 10 rows ❗ they "appeared" (own changes are visible)
      
      
      
      
      This exact example is in the MySQL manual ("Consistent Nonlocking Reads"): the snapshot applies to SELECT statements, not necessarily to DML statements. The manual also says mixing locking and non-locking statements in one RR transaction is not recommended.
      
      
      🔀
      PostgreSQL RR in the same situation
      PG RR is pure snapshot isolation: the UPDATE at t4 only sees rows visible in its snapshot, so it updates 0 rows. If it had tried to update a row changed after the snapshot, it would get a serialization error instead of silently using the new row.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      The ANSI standard allows phantoms at repeatable read, but InnoDB blocks them in practice. Plain selects read one MVCC snapshot for the whole transaction, so newly inserted rows are invisible. Locking reads, updates and deletes take next-key locks, which also lock the gaps between index records, so other transactions can't insert into the range. The catch is that UPDATE and DELETE read the latest data, not the snapshot, so if I mix a plain select with a later update I can modify rows my select never saw. And RR still allows lost updates and write skew.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪When exactly is the RR snapshot taken?
          
      At the first consistent read in the transaction, not at START TRANSACTION. If another session commits between your BEGIN and your first SELECT, you will see that change. Use START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT to take it immediately (this is what mysqldump --single-transaction relies on).
      
        
      ↪So is InnoDB RR serializable?
          
      No. Two plain SELECTs followed by writes to different rows (write skew) both commit. Read-modify-write without locks loses updates. For serializable behavior use SERIALIZABLE (lock-heavy in MySQL) or explicit FOR UPDATE on what you read.
      
        
      ↪What does INSERT INTO t2 SELECT … FROM t1 read at RR?
          
      Statements like INSERT … SELECT, UPDATE … (SELECT) and CREATE TABLE … SELECT without a locking clause lock the rows they read from t1, and the manual says the SELECT part "acts like READ COMMITTED": it reads the latest committed data.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QHow is SERIALIZABLE implemented in MySQL vs PostgreSQL?
    
      
      
      
        
      MySQL SERIALIZABLE (pessimistic)
      • RR + every plain SELECT becomes SELECT … FOR SHARE (if autocommit is off)
      • Shared next-key locks on everything read, held to commit = strict 2PL
      • Conflicts show up as waiting and deadlocks (ERROR 1213)
      • With autocommit ON, a lone SELECT is still a non-locking consistent read
      
        
      PostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE (optimistic, SSI)
      • Runs on snapshot isolation; reads never block
      • Records reads as SIRead predicate "locks" that never block
      • Detects two consecutive read-write dependencies (a "dangerous structure") and aborts one transaction with SQLSTATE 40001
      • Can have false positives; the app must retry
      
      
      
      
      💡
      Tip
      PostgreSQL's wiki gives the best one-liner: if your transaction is correct when run alone, under SERIALIZABLE it is correct in any mix, or it gets rolled back with an error. You just write the retry loop.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Setting and checking the isolation level
      
  
      -- 1) Check current values (tx_isolation was REMOVED in 8.0.3; use transaction_isolation)
SELECT @@GLOBAL.transaction_isolation, @@SESSION.transaction_isolation;

-- 2) Next transaction only (no GLOBAL/SESSION keyword). Not allowed inside an open transaction:
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
START TRANSACTION;  ...  COMMIT;        -- the one after this goes back to the session level

-- 3) Rest of this session
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
SET SESSION transaction_isolation = 'READ-COMMITTED';      -- same thing (note the dash)

-- 4) All NEW sessions (needs CONNECTION_ADMIN / SUPER); existing sessions keep theirs
SET GLOBAL TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;

-- 5) Server startup, my.cnf
-- [mysqld]
-- transaction-isolation = READ-COMMITTED

-- 6) Snapshot right now instead of at the first SELECT
START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT;
      
  
      mysql> START TRANSACTION;
mysql> SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
ERROR 1568 (25001): Transaction characteristics can't be changed while a transaction is in progress
      
  
      
    
      
    
      BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;          -- per transaction
-- or: BEGIN; SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;  (must be first statement)
SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SHOW transaction_isolation;
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE;  -- long report: waits for a safe snapshot, never aborts
      
    
      SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT;     -- per session
ALTER DATABASE shop SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;   -- RCSI for the whole DB
ALTER DATABASE shop SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON;  -- allow SNAPSHOT level
SELECT * FROM orders WITH (NOLOCK);           -- table hint = READ UNCOMMITTED for this table
      
    
      SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;   -- first statement of the transaction
ALTER SESSION SET ISOLATION_LEVEL = SERIALIZABLE;
SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY;                        -- consistent read-only snapshot
      
  
      
  
      ⚠️
      Gotchas
      (1) SET GLOBAL does not change sessions that are already open (connection pools!). (2) In config files the value uses dashes: READ-COMMITTED. (3) Changing to RC in MySQL needs binlog_format=ROW (with MIXED, the server switches to row logging automatically).
