      🎯
      What the interviewer is really testing
      Can you explain why a level prevents an anomaly (snapshot vs lock), and do you know that "prevented" can mean either "returned the old value" (MVCC) or "made someone wait" (locks)? Run the simulator at RR and SERIALIZABLE side by side: same correctness for reads, completely different waiting behavior.
      

  
      📷 MVCC deep dive: how readers avoid locks
      
  
      MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) keeps several versions of a row. A writer creates a new version; a reader picks the version that was committed "as of" its snapshot. So a reader never has to wait for a writer, and a writer never has to wait for a reader. Writers still wait for other writers on the same row.
      
  
      R ⟂ W · W ⟂ R · W ⟷ W
      "Readers don't block writers, writers don't block readers; only writers block writers." Analogy: a newspaper archive. While the editor writes tomorrow's edition, you can still read today's printed copy.
      

  
      
    QWhat is MVCC and why do databases use it?
    
      
      
      What: a technique where each update creates a new version of a row instead of overwriting it in a way that destroys the old value. Each transaction (or statement) reads from a consistent snapshot: the latest version committed before its snapshot moment.
      
      
      Why: with pure locking, a long report holding S locks would block every writer, and every writer's X lock would block readers. Most workloads are read-heavy, so this waiting kills throughput. MVCC removes read-write blocking entirely. Bonus: consistent backups without locking (mysqldump --single-transaction, pg_dump).
      
      
      How (four design choices, CMU 15-445):
      
      
        
        
      1. Concurrency protocol for writers — MVCC is only the storage half. Writers are still coordinated by 2PL (InnoDB, SQL Server), timestamp ordering, or snapshot isolation + SSI (PostgreSQL).
        2. 
        
      2. Version storage — append-only in the table (PostgreSQL), "time-travel" / undo storage (InnoDB undo logs, Oracle undo segments, SQL Server version store), or deltas.
        3. 
        
      3. Garbage collection — old versions must be removed once no snapshot needs them: InnoDB purge, PostgreSQL VACUUM, Oracle undo retention.
        4. 
        
      4. Index management — do indexes point to the newest version, or to every version?
        5. 
      
      
      
      🚫
      Fails interviews
      "MVCC means no locks." Writers still take row X locks, and SELECT … FOR UPDATE still locks. MVCC only removes locks for plain reads.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      MVCC keeps old versions of rows so that each reader sees a consistent snapshot without taking read locks. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers; only two writers on the same row wait for each other. InnoDB keeps old versions in the undo log and decides visibility with a read view; Postgres keeps old versions as dead tuples in the table and cleans them with VACUUM.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What is the cost of MVCC?
          
      Extra storage for versions, background cleanup work (purge / VACUUM), longer version chains to walk if cleanup falls behind, and in PostgreSQL table/index bloat. Also, a snapshot read can return stale data: correct as of the snapshot, but not the newest.
      
        
      ↪Why doesn't InnoDB keep an exact row count for COUNT(*)?
          
      Because of MVCC, different transactions can legally see different numbers of rows at the same moment. There is no single "true" count to store, so InnoDB scans the smallest index. (MyISAM, which has no transactions, stores the count.)
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      InnoDB: hidden columns and the undo version chain
      
  
      Every row in InnoDB's clustered index carries hidden system columns:
      
  
      Hidden columnSizeMeaning
      
    
      DB_TRX_ID6 bytesID of the last transaction that inserted or updated this row. (A delete is an update that sets a "deleted" bit.)
      
    
      DB_ROLL_PTR7 bytesRoll pointer: points to the undo log record that can rebuild the previous version.
      
    
      DB_ROW_ID6 bytesOnly when the table has no PRIMARY KEY and no NOT NULL UNIQUE key: InnoDB generates this hidden clustered-index key.
      
  
      
  
      InnoDB updates the row in place in the clustered index, and copies the old values into an undo log record. Each undo record has its own trx id and roll pointer, so the versions form a linked list from newest → oldest: the version chain.
      

  

  
      The read view and the visibility algorithm
      
  
      A read view is a small object InnoDB creates for a consistent read. It answers one question for any version: "was the transaction that wrote this version already committed when I took my snapshot?" It stores four things (names from the InnoDB source; the manual does not document them):
      
  
      
    
      m_ids
      List of transaction ids that were active (started, not committed) when the view was created. Their changes are invisible.
      
    
      m_up_limit_id (low water mark, "min_trx_id")
      The smallest id in m_ids. Any id below it had committed before the view: visible.
      
    
      m_low_limit_id (high water mark, "max_trx_id")
      The next trx id to be assigned at view creation. Any id ≥ it started after the view: invisible. (Yes, the "low limit" is the high mark. Confusing InnoDB naming.)
      
    
      m_creator_trx_id
      The id of the transaction that owns the view. Its own changes are always visible. (Read-only transactions get no real trx id; InnoDB assigns one only when a transaction first writes.)
      
  
      
  
        
    
      1. Take the version's DB_TRX_ID (call it id).
        2. 
    
      2. If id == m_creator_trx_id → visible (my own change).
        3. 
    
      3. If id < m_up_limit_id → visible (committed before any active transaction started).
        4. 
    
      4. If id ≥ m_low_limit_id → invisible (started after my snapshot).
        5. 
    
      5. Else (in between) → invisible if id is in m_ids (was still running), otherwise visible (it committed before my snapshot).
        6. 
    
      6. If invisible → follow DB_ROLL_PTR to the previous version in undo and repeat. If no version is visible, the row did not exist for me (inserted after my snapshot), so skip it. If the visible version is delete-marked, the row is deleted for me.
        7. 
  
      

  

  
      Version written by trxRule that firesVisible to T118?
      
    
      9595 < up_limit 100✔
      
    
      100in m_ids (was active)✘ → walk undo
      
    
      105between, not in m_ids (committed before view)✔
      
    
      112in m_ids✘ → walk undo
      
    
      118== creator✔ (own change)
      
    
      133≥ low_limit 130 (started after view)✘ → walk undo
      
  
      

  
      RC vs RR: when the read view is created
      
  
      This single difference explains the whole RC/RR behavior in InnoDB.
      
  
      
    
      READ COMMITTED
      • New read view for every consistent read statement
      • "One new photo per statement"
      • Sees everything committed before each statement → non-repeatable reads, phantoms
      • Old undo can be purged sooner
      
    
      REPEATABLE READ
      • One read view per transaction, created at the first consistent read (not at BEGIN)
      • "One photo per transaction"
      • Re-reads always return the same data
      • A long transaction pins old undo → history list grows
      
  
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1T2T3
      
    
      t1START TRANSACTION; -- no snapshot yet!
      
    
      t2UPDATE acct SET bal=300 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
      
    
      t3SELECT bal … → 300 (read view created HERE)
      
    
      t4UPDATE acct SET bal=999 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
      
    
      t5SELECT bal … → RR: 300 · RC: 999
      
  
      
  
      ⚠️
      Trap question
      "Under RR, does T1 see T2's update at t3?" Most candidates say no because "the snapshot is taken at BEGIN". Wrong for InnoDB: the snapshot is taken at the first read, so T1 sees 300. Only START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT takes it at BEGIN. (PostgreSQL likewise takes the RR snapshot at the first statement, not at BEGIN.)
      

  
      Consistent (snapshot) read vs current (locking) read
      
  
      
    
      Consistent read
      • Plain SELECT at RC / RR
      • Reads the version visible in the read view (may be old)
      • Takes no locks, never waits
      • "Consistent reads ignore any locks set on the records"
      
    
      Current read (locking read)
      • SELECT … FOR UPDATE, SELECT … FOR SHARE, UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT checks
      • Reads the latest committed version, ignoring the snapshot
      • Takes S or X locks (next-key at RR) and may wait
      • Needed for correct read-modify-write
      
  
      
  
      
    QInside one RR transaction, a SELECT returns 500 but SELECT … FOR UPDATE returns 300. How?
    
      
      
      The plain SELECT is a consistent read: it uses the transaction's read view, made before another transaction committed 300. The FOR UPDATE read is a current read: it must lock the row, and you can only lock the real, latest row, so it returns the latest committed value 300. Both are "correct" for their purpose. This is why the MySQL manual warns against mixing locking and non-locking reads in one RR transaction.
      
      
      -- Session A (RR)                       -- Session B
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;   -- 500
                                         UPDATE acct SET bal=300 WHERE id=1; -- autocommit
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;   -- 500  (snapshot)
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE;  -- 300 (current read)
SELECT bal FROM acct WHERE id=1;   -- 500  (still the snapshot!)
COMMIT;
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      InnoDB has two kinds of reads. A plain select is a snapshot read from the read view and takes no locks. A locking read, and the read inside UPDATE or DELETE, is a current read: it reads the latest committed row and locks it. So in one transaction you can see 500 from the snapshot and 300 from the locking read. For read-then-write logic I always use the locking read.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Purge and the history list length
      
  
      Undo records cannot be deleted while any read view might still need them. Two kinds of undo exist: insert undo (only needed for rollback, discarded at commit) and update undo (also needed by consistent reads). Background purge threads read the history list (undo logs of committed transactions) and remove undo records and delete-marked rows that no open read view can see anymore. Deleted rows are physically removed only by purge.
      
  
      The backlog is shown as History list length in SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS:
      
  
      ------------
TRANSACTIONS
------------
Trx id counter 48812345
Purge done for trx's n:o < 41200017 undo n:o < 0 state: running but idle
History list length 5123456          <-- millions = purge is stuck behind an old read view
      
  
      🌍
      Production story: the forgotten transaction
      At 08:00 someone opens a SQL client with autocommit off, runs a SELECT, and goes to lunch. That read view is pinned. All day, millions of updates commit, but purge cannot remove any undo newer than 08:00. History list length climbs into millions, the undo tablespace grows, and every consistent read walks longer chains, so the whole server slows down. Fix: find the old transaction (information_schema.INNODB_TRX ORDER BY trx_started), commit or kill it. Prevent: short transactions, commit read-only ones too, timeouts on idle sessions. The MySQL manual names mysqldump --single-transaction during heavy DML as another classic cause.
      
  
      SELECT trx_id, trx_state, trx_started,
       TIMESTAMPDIFF(SECOND, trx_started, NOW()) AS age_s,
       trx_mysql_thread_id, trx_rows_modified, trx_query
FROM information_schema.INNODB_TRX
ORDER BY trx_started
LIMIT 5;
-- KILL <trx_mysql_thread_id>;   -- last resort: rolls the transaction back
      
  
      ℹ️
      Secondary indexes and MVCC
      Secondary index records have no hidden trx columns and are not updated in place: an update delete-marks the old entry and inserts a new one. If a secondary-index page was changed by a newer transaction (or the entry is delete-marked), InnoDB must visit the clustered index to check visibility, so a "covering index" read can lose its advantage on hot data.
      

  
      PostgreSQL MVCC: xmin, xmax, VACUUM, HOT and wraparound
      
  
      PostgreSQL stores every version as a full row (tuple) in the table itself. An UPDATE is basically "mark the old tuple dead + insert a new tuple". Each tuple carries system columns:
      
  
      
    
      xmin
      ID of the transaction that created this tuple version.
      
    
      xmax
      ID of the transaction that deleted / replaced it (0 if alive). It may be non-zero on a visible row if the deleter has not committed or rolled back.
      
    
      ctid
      Physical location (page, slot). The old tuple's ctid link points to its newer version.
      
    
      Snapshot
      xmin:xmax:xip_list: oldest still-running XID, first not-yet-assigned XID, and the list of in-progress XIDs (see pg_current_snapshot()). Same idea as InnoDB's read view. Commit status of each XID is looked up in the commit log (pg_xact).
      
  
      
  
  
      
    
      🧹
      VACUUM / autovacuum
      Removes dead tuples no snapshot can see, makes space reusable, updates the visibility map (for index-only scans) and freezes old XIDs. Plain VACUUM runs alongside normal traffic and usually does not shrink the file. VACUUM FULL rewrites the table under an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock: not routine maintenance.
      
    
      📦
      Bloat
      Heavy UPDATE/DELETE + slow vacuum (or a long transaction holding back the "xmin horizon") leaves many dead tuples. Tables and indexes grow, scans read more pages. Uber's 2016 move from Postgres to MySQL cited write amplification from this design.
      
    
      ⚡
      HOT updates
      Heap-Only Tuple: if no indexed column changes and the new tuple fits on the same page, PG skips creating new index entries; the index still points to the old tuple, which links to the new one. A lower fillfactor leaves room on pages to make HOT updates more likely.
      
    
      ⏳
      XID wraparound
      XIDs are 32-bit and compared in a circle: about 2 billion "older", 2 billion "newer". Without freezing, old rows would suddenly look like they are "in the future" and vanish. Autovacuum forces an anti-wraparound vacuum at autovacuum_freeze_max_age (200 million by default); PG warns 40 million XIDs before the limit and refuses new XIDs 3 million before it.
      
  
      

  
      
    QCompare MVCC in MySQL InnoDB and PostgreSQL. What happens to each with a long-running transaction?
    
      
      
      AspectMySQL InnoDBPostgreSQLOracle
      
        
      Newest version livesin place, clustered indexnew tuple in the heapin place, data block
      
        
      Old versions liveundo logssame heap pages (dead tuples)undo segments
      
        
      Visibility metadataDB_TRX_ID + read viewxmin/xmax + snapshot + commit logSCN + undo
      
        
      Cleanuppurge threadsVACUUM / autovacuumundo retention, automatic reuse
      
        
      Long reader causes…history list grows, undo grows, reads slow downdead tuples can't be removed → bloat; wraparound riskthe long query itself fails with ORA-01555
      
        
      Write-write conflict at RR/SIwaits, then updates latest (no error)error 40001ORA-08177 (SERIALIZABLE)
      
        
      UPDATE costin-place + undo; secondary indexes touched only if their columns changenew tuple; every index gets an entry unless HOT appliesin-place + undo
      
      
      
      
      🧠
      One-liner
      "With a long transaction, MySQL keeps undo and slows down, Postgres keeps dead tuples and bloats, Oracle throws away undo and fails the long query (ORA-01555)."
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪What is ORA-01555 "snapshot too old"?
          
      Oracle rebuilds older block versions from undo for read consistency. If a long query needs undo that other writers have already overwritten (undo is a circular, reused space), Oracle cannot rebuild the old image and the query fails with ORA-01555. Fix: raise UNDO_RETENTION and undo tablespace size, or shorten the query.
      
        
      ↪What is "idle in transaction" and why do DBAs hate it?
          
      A PostgreSQL session that ran BEGIN and some statements but is now doing nothing, with the transaction still open. It holds its snapshot (blocking VACUUM cleanup) and its locks. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to kill such sessions. MySQL's equivalent symptom is a growing history list plus held metadata locks.
      
        
      ↪Where does SQL Server keep row versions?
          
      When RCSI or SNAPSHOT is enabled, old versions go to a version store (traditionally in tempdb; with Accelerated Database Recovery, a persistent version store in the user database). Each row gets a 14-byte versioning tag.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🔒 Locking: who waits for whom
      
  
      MVCC lets plain reads skip locks. But writes (and locking reads like SELECT … FOR UPDATE) still need locks, because two writers cannot both change the same row at the same time. A lock is a note in the lock manager's memory: "transaction T holds mode M on resource R". Anyone asking for an incompatible mode on R waits in a queue.
      

  
      Shared (S) and exclusive (X) locks
      
  
      
    
      S — shared (read) lock
        
      
      • "I am reading this; don't change it."
        • 
      
      • Many transactions can hold S on the same row together
        • 
      
      • MySQL: SELECT … FOR SHARE (old: LOCK IN SHARE MODE); also taken by FK checks
        • 
    
      
    
      X — exclusive (write) lock
        
      
      • "I am changing this; nobody else may lock it."
        • 
      
      • Only one holder; conflicts with S and X
        • 
      
      • Taken by UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT, SELECT … FOR UPDATE
        • 
    
      
  
      
  
      Held ↓ / Requested →SX
      
    
      S✔ grant✘ wait
      
    
      X✘ wait✘ wait
      
  
      
  
      Lock upgrade: a transaction holding S that now wants X must wait for other S holders to leave. If two transactions both hold S and both want X, each waits for the other — the classic upgrade deadlock. That is why "read with the lock you will need" (FOR UPDATE, not FOR SHARE) is the rule for read-then-write.
      
  
      ℹ️
      Remember: plain SELECT takes no row locks in InnoDB (except at SERIALIZABLE)
      At RU/RC/RR a normal SELECT is a consistent (snapshot) read — no S lock. So an X lock held by a writer does not block plain readers; they just read the older version from undo. Only locking reads and writes wait.
      

  
      Lock granularity and intention locks (IS, IX, SIX)
      
  
      Problem: one transaction holds X locks on a few rows. Another wants to lock the whole table (say, LOCK TABLES t WRITE). How does it know some row is locked without scanning millions of row locks? Answer: intention locks. Before locking a row, a transaction first puts an intention lock on the table: "I intend to lock some rows inside you". A table-level request then checks one table-level entry.
      
  
      
    
      IS (intention shared)
      I will take S locks on some rows below.
      
    
      IX (intention exclusive)
      I will take X locks on some rows below.
      
    
      SIX (shared + intention exclusive)
      I read the whole table (S) and will update a few rows (IX). Textbook mode; not used by InnoDB.
      
  
      
  
      Held ↓ / Req →ISIXSSIXX
      
    
      IS✔✔✔✔✘
      
    
      IX✔✔✘✘✘
      
    
      S✔✘✔✘✘
      
    
      SIX✔✘✘✘✘
      
    
      X✘✘✘✘✘
      
  
      
  
      "Intentions never fight each other"
      IS/IX are compatible with IS/IX (two transactions updating different rows of one table must both proceed). They only clash with real table-level S/X. Rule of thumb: IX vs S ✘ (someone reading the whole table blocks row writers), IS vs X ✘, X vs everything ✘.
      
  
      Protocol (multiple-granularity locking): lock from the root down (database → table → page → row): to get S or IS on a node you need IS (or IX) on its parent; to get X, IX or SIX you need IX (or SIX) on its parent. Release bottom-up. In InnoDB, SELECT … FOR SHARE takes IS on the table, writes and FOR UPDATE take IX; they show up in performance_schema.data_locks as LOCK_TYPE = TABLE.
      

  
      InnoDB row locks: record, gap, next-key, insert-intention
      
  
      The single most important fact: InnoDB locks index records, not "rows" in the abstract. A lock is placed on the index entries that a statement scans (clustered or secondary). Gaps between index entries can be locked too — that is how InnoDB stops phantoms at REPEATABLE READ.
      
  
  
      LockWhat it coversWhy it existsdata_locks.LOCK_MODE
      
    
      Record lockOne index recordProtect a row you read/updateX,REC_NOT_GAP / S,REC_NOT_GAP
      
    
      Gap lockThe open interval between two index records (no record itself)Stop inserts into a range → no phantoms. Gap locks never conflict with each other; they only block inserts.X,GAP
      
    
      Next-key lockRecord + the gap before it, e.g. (10, 20]Default lock for scans at RRX / S
      
    
      Insert-intention lockA special gap lock taken by INSERT on the gap it inserts intoMany inserts into one gap at different positions don't block each other, but they wait for a gap/next-key lock held by someone elseX,INSERT_INTENTION
      
    
      AUTO-INC lockTable-level, shortHand out AUTO_INCREMENT values (see below)—
      
  
      

  
      Worked examples — what gets locked? (REPEATABLE READ)
      
  
      Table emp(id PK, age INT, name VARCHAR, KEY idx_age(age)) with rows (1,10,'Asha') (2,20,'Ravi') (3,30,'Meena').
      
  
      #StatementLocks takenEffect on others
      
    
      1SELECT * FROM emp WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATERecord lock on PK 2 only (unique index + equality + row exists → no gap needed)Only row 2 is blocked
      
    
      2SELECT * FROM emp WHERE id = 5 FOR UPDATE (no such row)Gap lock on the gap after id 3 (up to supremum)INSERT id=4 or id=9 waits
      
    
      3UPDATE emp SET name='X' WHERE age = 20Next-key (10, 20] on idx_age + gap (20, 30) on idx_age + record lock on PK 2Inserting age 15 or 25 waits; age 35 is fine
      
    
      4SELECT * FROM emp WHERE age BETWEEN 15 AND 25 FOR UPDATENext-key locks on idx_age covering (10, 20] and the next gap up to 30 (exact boundary handling has been refined across 8.0 versions) + PK record 2No new rows can appear in 15–25 → no phantoms
      
    
      5UPDATE emp SET age = 21 WHERE name = 'Ravi' (no index on name)Full clustered-index scan → next-key lock on EVERY row and gapEffectively a table lock: all other writers and inserts wait
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhy did one UPDATE on a single row block the whole table in MySQL?
    
      
      
      Because InnoDB locks the index records it scans, not just the rows it finally changes. If the WHERE column has no usable index, InnoDB scans the whole clustered index and puts a (next-key) lock on every record it touches. At REPEATABLE READ these locks stay until COMMIT, so the "single-row" UPDATE behaves like a table lock.
      
      
      
        
      TimeT1T2
      
        
      t1BEGIN; UPDATE emp SET age=21 WHERE name='Ravi';  (no index on name)
      
        
      t2UPDATE emp SET age=11 WHERE id=1;  ⏳ waits — row 1 was scanned and locked
      
        
      t3INSERT INTO emp VALUES (9,40,'Zoya');  ⏳ waits — gap to supremum locked
      
        
      t4COMMIT;both proceed
      
      
      
      
      Fixes: add an index on the filter column (CREATE INDEX idx_name ON emp(name)) so only matching entries are locked; or update by primary key; or use READ COMMITTED, where InnoDB drops gap locks and releases locks on non-matching rows right after evaluating the WHERE ("semi-consistent read").
      
      
      🔀
      PostgreSQL is different
      PostgreSQL locks only the rows it actually modifies (the lock lives in the tuple header, xmax), never gaps or scanned-but-not-matching rows. A sequential scan UPDATE is slow, but it does not block unrelated rows. PG has no gap locks; phantom protection at SERIALIZABLE comes from SSI predicate locks (SIREAD), which never block.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      InnoDB row locks are actually index-record locks on whatever the statement scans. Without an index on the WHERE column it scans the whole clustered index and locks every row plus the gaps, so at repeatable read it behaves like a table lock until commit. The fix is an index on that column, or updating by primary key; read committed also helps because it drops gap locks and releases non-matching rows early.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪When does InnoDB use a record lock instead of a next-key lock?
          
      When the search uses a unique index with an equality condition on all its columns and the row exists — there can be only one matching row, so no gap needs protecting. Non-unique indexes, ranges and "not found" lookups use next-key or gap locks.
      
        
      ↪Do gap locks exist at READ COMMITTED?
          
      Mostly no. InnoDB disables gap locking for searches and index scans at RC; gap locks are used only for foreign-key and duplicate-key checks. That is why phantoms are possible at RC, and why RC has fewer deadlocks. (RC with statement-based binlog is not allowed for this reason — use row-based binlog.)
      
        
      ↪How do you SEE which locks a transaction holds?
          
      SELECT engine_transaction_id AS trx, object_name, index_name,
       lock_type, lock_mode, lock_status, lock_data
FROM performance_schema.data_locks;
-- waits: performance_schema.data_lock_waits  or  sys.innodb_lock_waits
      
          
      +------+-------------+------------+-----------+---------------+-------------+-----------+
| trx  | object_name | index_name | lock_type | lock_mode     | lock_status | lock_data |
+------+-------------+------------+-----------+---------------+-------------+-----------+
| 4321 | emp         | NULL       | TABLE     | IX            | GRANTED     | NULL      |
| 4321 | emp         | idx_age    | RECORD    | X             | GRANTED     | 20, 2     |
| 4321 | emp         | PRIMARY    | RECORD    | X,REC_NOT_GAP | GRANTED     | 2         |
| 4321 | emp         | idx_age    | RECORD    | X,GAP         | GRANTED     | 30, 3     |
+------+-------------+------------+-----------+---------------+-------------+-----------+
      
          
      That is example #3 above: IX on the table, next-key on age 20, record lock on PK 2, gap before age 30. (In MySQL 5.7 the equivalent tables were information_schema.innodb_locks/innodb_lock_waits.)
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      AUTO-INC lock
      
  
      To hand out AUTO_INCREMENT values, InnoDB uses a special table-level lock. How long it is held is controlled by innodb_autoinc_lock_mode:
      
  
      ModeNameBehaviourTrade-off
      
    
      0traditionalTable-level AUTO-INC lock held until the end of every INSERT statementConsecutive ids, safe for statement-based replication, poor concurrency
      
    
      1consecutive (default up to 5.7)Simple inserts (known row count) use a light mutex; bulk inserts (INSERT … SELECT, LOAD DATA) hold the table lock for the statementEach statement gets a consecutive block
      
    
      2interleaved (default in 8.0+)No table-level AUTO-INC lock; values come from a mutexFastest; ids of concurrent bulk inserts can interleave; needs row-based binlog (the 8.0 default) for safe replication
      
  
      

  
      Metadata locks (MDL) — the "ALTER TABLE froze production" story
      
  
      Besides row locks, MySQL takes a metadata lock on every table a transaction uses, to stop the table's structure from changing under it. DML takes a shared MDL; ALTER TABLE needs an exclusive MDL (at least briefly, even for "online" DDL). MDLs are held until the transaction ends, not the statement.
      
  
      
    
      TimeSession A (long txn)Session B (DBA)Sessions C, D, E… (app)
      
    
      t1BEGIN; SELECT * FROM orders LIMIT 1;  -- holds shared MDL, then idles
      
    
      t2ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note TEXT;  ⏳ "Waiting for table metadata lock"
      
    
      t3SELECT … FROM orders  ⏳ queued BEHIND the pending exclusive request ❗
      
    
      t4connection pool exhausted → site down
      
    
      t5COMMIT (or KILL)ALTER runseverything resumes
      
  
      
  
      🌍
      Why the whole app stops
      A pending exclusive MDL request has priority over new shared requests, so even plain SELECTs queue behind the waiting ALTER, which is waiting behind one idle transaction. Prevention: before DDL, check information_schema.innodb_trx for old transactions; run DDL with a short SET SESSION lock_wait_timeout = 5; (the default is one year!) and retry; prefer ALGORITHM=INSTANT (8.0+, e.g. adding a column) or tools like gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change. Diagnose with sys.schema_table_lock_waits or performance_schema.metadata_locks.
      
  
      🔀
      PostgreSQL has the same trap
      An ALTER TABLE needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; while it waits behind a long transaction, every new query on the table queues behind it. Use SET lock_timeout = '3s' before DDL and retry.
      

  
      Lock escalation (SQL Server) — and why MySQL/PG don't do it
      
  
      Lock escalation = replacing many fine-grained locks with one coarse lock to save memory. SQL Server escalates row/page locks to a table (or partition) lock when one statement holds roughly 5,000 locks on a single object, or under lock-memory pressure. Result: a big UPDATE can suddenly block the entire table. Controls: ALTER TABLE … SET (LOCK_ESCALATION = TABLE | AUTO | DISABLE), batching updates. InnoDB never escalates — it stores record locks as a compact bitmap per page, so millions of locks are cheap. PostgreSQL never escalates row locks — they live in the tuple header (xmax), not in a memory table. Oracle also stores row locks in the data block and never escalates.
      

  
      Explicit table locks: LOCK TABLES
      
  
      LOCK TABLES accounts WRITE, audit READ;   -- implicitly COMMITS any open txn
-- ... only these tables can be used now ...
UNLOCK TABLES;
      
  
      Rarely needed with InnoDB (row locks are better). Gotchas: it implicitly commits; you can only access the tables you locked; and mixing it with transactions is confusing (use SET autocommit=0 + LOCK TABLES + COMMIT + UNLOCK TABLES if you must). PostgreSQL has LOCK TABLE t IN SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE MODE etc. (8 table lock modes), released only at transaction end.
      

  
      FOR UPDATE NOWAIT / SKIP LOCKED — a job queue in SQL
      
  
      MySQL 8.0+ PG 9.5+ Normally a locking read waits if a row is locked. Two options change that:
      
  
        
    
      • NOWAIT — fail immediately (MySQL ERROR 3572) instead of waiting. Good for "seat is being booked by someone else, try another".
        • 
    
      • SKIP LOCKED — silently skip locked rows. Perfect for a work queue where many workers grab different jobs.
        • 
  
      
  
      -- each worker runs this in a loop
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT id, payload FROM jobs
 WHERE status = 'PENDING'
 ORDER BY id
 LIMIT 1
 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;             -- worker 2 skips the row worker 1 holds
UPDATE jobs SET status = 'RUNNING', worker = 'w2', started_at = NOW() WHERE id = 42;
COMMIT;                              -- then do the slow work OUTSIDE the transaction
-- ... process ... then: UPDATE jobs SET status = 'DONE' WHERE id = 42;
      
  
      🔀
      Elsewhere
      Oracle: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED / NOWAIT / WAIT n. SQL Server: table hints WITH (UPDLOCK, READPAST, ROWLOCK). Add an index on (status, id) so the locking read touches only a few index entries. SKIP LOCKED gives an inconsistent view on purpose — never use it for reports.
      

  
      Optimistic vs pessimistic concurrency
      
  
      
    
      🔒 Pessimistic
        
      
      • "Conflicts are likely — lock first."
        • 
      
      • SELECT … FOR UPDATE, then update, then COMMIT
        • 
      
      • Others wait; deadlocks possible
        • 
      
      • Best for hot rows with high contention (seat inventory, wallet balance)
        • 
      
      • Locks must not span user think-time
        • 
    
      
    
      🍀 Optimistic
        
      
      • "Conflicts are rare — check at write time."
        • 
      
      • Read row + version; later UPDATE … WHERE id=? AND version=?
        • 
      
      • Nobody waits; loser gets 0 rows → retry or show "data changed"
        • 
      
      • Best for low contention and long user edits (edit profile form, wiki page, admin screens)
        • 
      
      • Wasted work when conflicts are frequent
        • 
    
      
  
      
  
      
    QOptimistic vs pessimistic locking — how do you implement each and when do you pick which?
    
      
      
      -- 1. read (no lock; user may take minutes to edit)
SELECT id, title, body, version FROM articles WHERE id = 7;      -- version = 12

-- 2. save: compare-and-set
UPDATE articles
   SET title = 'New title', body = '...', version = version + 1
 WHERE id = 7 AND version = 12;
-- affected rows = 1 -> saved;  0 -> someone saved first: reload / merge / retry
      
      
      Pessimistic = SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside a short transaction (see Chapter 12 transfer). Pick pessimistic when contention is high and retries are expensive; pick optimistic when conflicts are rare or the "transaction" spans user think-time (you cannot hold DB locks across HTTP requests). A timestamp column (updated_at) can replace the version number, but clock resolution makes integers safer.
      
      
      🔀
      Frameworks
      JPA/Hibernate: @Version field → OptimisticLockException; LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE → FOR UPDATE. Django: select_for_update(). DynamoDB/MongoDB use the same compare-and-set idea with conditional writes.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Pessimistic locking locks the row up front with SELECT FOR UPDATE, so others wait — good for hot rows like inventory. Optimistic locking takes no lock; it keeps a version column and updates with WHERE version equals the value I read, and if zero rows change I know someone else won and I retry. I use optimistic when conflicts are rare or when the edit spans user think-time.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Is MVCC optimistic or pessimistic?
          
      MVCC is about reads (readers see snapshots and never wait). Writes in InnoDB are still pessimistic (X locks). PostgreSQL's SERIALIZABLE (SSI) is an optimistic layer on top: run freely, abort at commit if a dangerous pattern appeared.
      
        
      ↪A flash sale on one product — optimistic or pessimistic?
          
      Neither in the read-then-write form. Use one atomic conditional UPDATE (stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0); optimistic would cause a storm of retries, pessimistic a long lock queue. At extreme scale, move the counter to Redis or pre-split stock into buckets (see scenarios below).
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⚖️ Concurrency control protocols (the textbook side)
      
  
      A protocol is a set of rules that every transaction follows so that only serializable (and ideally recoverable) schedules can happen. Two families: lock-based (wait when in doubt) and timestamp/validation-based (abort when in doubt). Real engines mix them with MVCC.
      

  
      Two-phase locking (2PL)
      
  
      Rule: a transaction has a growing phase (it may acquire locks, never release) followed by a shrinking phase (it may release, never acquire). The moment it holds the most locks is its lock point.
      
  
  
      VariantRuleConflict-serializableNo cascading aborts (strict)Deadlock-free
      
    
      Basic 2PLGrow, then shrink✔✘✘
      
    
      Strict 2PLBasic + hold all X locks until commit/abort✔✔✘
      
    
      Rigorous 2PL (strong strict)Hold all locks (S and X) until commit/abort✔ (order = commit order)✔✘
      
    
      Conservative 2PL (static)Acquire all locks before starting (needs read/write set in advance)✔✘ by itself✔
      
  
      
  
      
    QWhat is two-phase locking and why does it guarantee serializability?
    
      
      
      Why it works (proof sketch): suppose 2PL produced a cycle T1 → T2 → … → T1 in the precedence graph. An edge Ti → Tj means Tj locked an item after Ti released it, so Ti's lock point comes before Tj's lock point. Following the cycle gives LP(T1) < LP(T2) < … < LP(T1) — impossible. So the graph is acyclic, and ordering transactions by lock point gives the equivalent serial order.
      
      
      What it does NOT give: deadlock freedom (two transactions in growing phase can wait on each other) and, for basic 2PL, recoverability (a released X lock lets others read uncommitted data). That is why real systems use strict (InnoDB, SQL Server under locking levels) or rigorous 2PL plus deadlock detection.
      
      
      ⚠️
      Classic confusion
      "Two-phase locking" (concurrency) ≠ "two-phase commit" (distributed atomicity, Chapter 19). Interviewers sometimes ask exactly this to see if you mix them up.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      In two-phase locking a transaction first only acquires locks, and once it releases any lock it can never acquire another. That guarantees conflict serializability: the transactions are equivalent to running in the order of their lock points. Strict 2PL also holds write locks until commit so nobody reads uncommitted data, which avoids cascading aborts. 2PL does not prevent deadlocks, so databases add deadlock detection.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Is every conflict-serializable schedule possible under 2PL?
          
      No. 2PL produces a subset of CS schedules. Example: R1(A) W2(A) R3(B) W1(B) is CS (edges T1 → T2 and T3 → T1, order T3 T1 T2). Under 2PL, T1 must release A before W2(A), so it must already hold its X lock on B at that moment — but then R3(B) would be blocked. So 2PL can never produce this schedule.
      
        
      ↪Does InnoDB use 2PL?
          
      For writes and locking reads, yes — locks are acquired as statements run and released together at COMMIT/ROLLBACK (strict, effectively rigorous for locking reads). Plain reads use MVCC instead of S locks, except at SERIALIZABLE where they become FOR SHARE reads and InnoDB behaves like classic rigorous 2PL.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Timestamp ordering (TO) and the Thomas write rule
      
  
      Idea: no locks. Each transaction gets a timestamp TS(T) when it starts (older = smaller). The schedule must be equivalent to the serial order of timestamps. Each item X remembers R-TS(X) (largest TS that read it) and W-TS(X) (largest TS that wrote it). If an operation arrives "too late", the transaction is aborted and restarted with a new timestamp.
      
  
      T wants to…CheckAction
      
    
      Read XTS(T) < W-TS(X)? (a younger txn already overwrote X)Yes → abort T. No → read, R-TS(X) = max(R-TS(X), TS(T))
      
    
      Write XTS(T) < R-TS(X)? (a younger txn already read the old value)Yes → abort T
      
    
      TS(T) < W-TS(X)? (a younger txn already wrote X)Basic TO → abort T. Thomas write rule → ignore this write (it is obsolete). Otherwise write, W-TS(X) = TS(T)
      
  
      
  
      🧠
      Thomas write rule in one line
      "If a younger transaction already wrote X and nobody younger read it, my older write would be overwritten in the serial order anyway — just skip it." Schedules allowed by Thomas are view-serializable but may not be conflict-serializable (the skipped write is a blind write — compare Chapter 12's VS example).
      
  
      Properties: conflict-serializable (basic TO), deadlock-free (nobody waits), but can starve long transactions (repeated restarts) and is not recoverable unless extended (strict TO delays reads/writes of items written by uncommitted transactions).
      

  
      Optimistic concurrency control (validation-based)
      
  
        
    
      1. Read phase — run the transaction on private copies; record its read set RS and write set WS. No locks.
        2. 
    
      2. Validation phase — at commit, check against every transaction Ti that validated earlier: either Ti finished before T started; or Ti finished its write phase before T's write phase and WS(Ti) ∩ RS(T) = ∅; or Ti finished its read phase before T's and WS(Ti) ∩ (RS(T) ∪ WS(T)) = ∅. Any failure → abort and restart T.
        3. 
    
      3. Write phase — copy private changes into the database.
        4. 
  
      
  
      Great when conflicts are rare (read-heavy workloads, in-memory engines like Hekaton/SQL Server In-Memory OLTP use an optimistic MVCC variant); terrible under high contention (lots of wasted work). The application-level "version column" is the same idea at row granularity.
      

  
      Multiversion protocols: MVTO, MV2PL, SI and SSI
      
  
      
    
      MVTO (multiversion timestamp ordering)
      Every write creates a new version stamped with the writer's TS. A read by T picks the newest version with W-TS ≤ TS(T) — reads never wait and never abort. A write by T is rejected if some younger transaction has already read the version T would be "inserting before".
      
    
      MV2PL
      Writers use 2PL; readers read committed versions. InnoDB at RC/RR is close to this: X locks for writes, snapshots for plain reads.
      
    
      Snapshot isolation (SI)
      Each transaction reads a snapshot from its start; at commit, first-committer (or first-updater) wins on write-write conflicts. Prevents dirty/non-repeatable reads, phantoms and lost updates, but allows write skew. PostgreSQL RR, Oracle "SERIALIZABLE", SQL Server SNAPSHOT.
      
    
      SSI (serializable snapshot isolation)
      SI + tracking of read-write anti-dependencies (T1 read something T2 later wrote). PostgreSQL (since 9.1) records reads as non-blocking SIREAD "predicate locks"; if it finds a dangerous structure — two consecutive rw-edges T1 → T2 → T3 among concurrent transactions — it aborts one with SQLSTATE 40001. Truly serializable, readers still never block, but you must retry. False positives are possible (it is conservative).
      
  
      
  
      ProtocolConflict handlingDeadlocks?Readers block writers?Best forUsed by
      
    
      Strict 2PLwaityes (detect)yeshigh contention writesInnoDB writes, SQL Server (locking levels), DB2
      
    
      Timestamp orderingabort + restartno—theory / distributedtextbooks; ideas in Spanner-like systems
      
    
      OCCabort at validationnonolow contentionin-memory engines, app-level version columns
      
    
      MVCC + SIfirst-updater-winspossible (writers lock)nomixed OLTPPostgreSQL RR, Oracle, SQL Server SNAPSHOT
      
    
      SSIabort on dangerous structurepossible (writers)noserializable without read locksPostgreSQL SERIALIZABLE, CockroachDB
      
  
      
  
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Lock-based protocols like strict 2PL make conflicting transactions wait, so they can deadlock. Timestamp ordering and optimistic validation never wait — they abort and restart the late transaction, so no deadlocks but possible starvation and wasted work. Modern engines combine MVCC for reads with locks for writes; PostgreSQL's serializable level adds SSI, which watches for dangerous read-write dependency patterns and aborts one transaction instead of blocking.
      

  
  
      ⛓️ Deadlocks
      
  
      A deadlock is a set of transactions where each one waits for a lock held by another in the set, so none can ever proceed. Locks + waiting = deadlocks are always possible; databases therefore detect and break them, and good application code makes them rare.
      
  
      
    
      TimeT1 (transfer 7 → 3)T2 (transfer 3 → 7)
      
    
      t1UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal-100 WHERE id=7;  🔒 X(7)
      
    
      t2UPDATE accounts SET bal=bal-50 WHERE id=3;  🔒 X(3)
      
    
      t3UPDATE … WHERE id=3;  ⏳ waits for T2
      
    
      t4UPDATE … WHERE id=7;  ⏳ waits for T1 → cycle!
      
    
      t5proceeds after T2 is rolled backERROR 1213 (40001): Deadlock found when trying to get lock; try restarting transaction
      
  
      

  
      The four Coffman conditions
      
  
      A deadlock needs all four. Break any one and deadlock is impossible.
      
  
      
    
      🔐
      1. Mutual exclusion
      A resource (X lock) can be held by only one transaction. Can't remove for writes.
      
    
      ✋
      2. Hold and wait
      Holding one lock while waiting for another. Break it: conservative 2PL — take all locks up front.
      
    
      🚫
      3. No preemption
      Locks can't be taken away. Break it: wound-wait / abort a victim.
      
    
      🔄
      4. Circular wait
      T1 waits for T2 … waits for T1. Break it: always lock in a global order (e.g. ascending id).
      
  
      
  
      🧠 "My Hungry Neighbour Circles"
      Mutual exclusion · Hold & wait · No preemption · Circular wait.
      

  
      Detection: the wait-for graph
      
  
      The lock manager keeps a wait-for graph: a node per transaction, an edge Ti → Tj when Ti waits for a lock Tj holds. A cycle = deadlock. (Compare with the precedence graph of Chapter 12: same picture, different meaning — that one is about conflict order, this one is about who is waiting right now.)
      
  

  
      
    QHow does MySQL detect and resolve deadlocks? How is it different in other databases?
    
      
      
      InnoDB: with innodb_deadlock_detect = ON (default), every time a transaction must wait, InnoDB checks the wait-for graph immediately. If a cycle exists it picks a victim — it prefers the smallest transaction, measured by rows inserted/updated/deleted — rolls the whole victim transaction back and returns ERROR 1213 (40001). Waits that are not deadlocks end after innodb_lock_wait_timeout (default 50 s) with ERROR 1205, which by default rolls back only the statement.
      
      
      On very high-concurrency systems detection itself can become a bottleneck (many threads waiting on the same hot row); some teams set innodb_deadlock_detect = OFF and rely on a short innodb_lock_wait_timeout instead.
      
      
      EngineWhen it checksVictimError
      
        
      MySQL InnoDBImmediately on each waitSmallest txn (fewest changed rows); whole txn rolled back1213 / SQLSTATE 40001
      
        
      PostgreSQLAfter waiting deadlock_timeout (default 1 s) — optimistic: most waits resolve on their ownThe transaction that ran the checkSQLSTATE 40P01 "deadlock detected"
      
        
      SQL ServerLock-monitor thread, every 5 s by default (more often when deadlocks are found)Lowest SET DEADLOCK_PRIORITY, then cheapest to roll back1205
      
        
      OracleAutomatic detectionRolls back only the statement that detected it; the transaction stays openORA-00060
      
      
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A deadlock is a cycle in the wait-for graph. InnoDB checks for a cycle every time a transaction has to wait, and if it finds one it rolls back the smaller transaction and returns error 1213, so the application must retry it. Plain long waits end with a lock wait timeout, 50 seconds by default. To avoid deadlocks I keep transactions short, access rows in a consistent order and make sure the queries use indexes so fewer rows are locked.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Deadlock vs lock wait timeout — what is the difference?
          
      A deadlock can never resolve by waiting (cycle), so it is detected and broken at once (1213, whole txn rolled back). A lock wait timeout is just a long wait for a lock someone holds — maybe a slow transaction; after 50 s the waiting statement fails (1205). Both should be retried, but a timeout often points to a long-running transaction to fix.
      
        
      ↪How do you find out what caused a deadlock?
          
      SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS\G → section LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK (only the last one). Set innodb_print_all_deadlocks = ON to log every deadlock to the error log. See the annotated output below.
      
        
      ↪Can a single-row UPDATE deadlock?
          
      Yes. A statement locks a secondary index entry and then the clustered (PK) record, while another statement may lock them in the opposite order (e.g. one searches via the PK, another via the secondary index). Also a single INSERT can deadlock through gap / insert-intention locks (classic scenario below).
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Reading SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS

LATEST DETECTED DEADLOCK

mysql tables in use 1, locked 1

RECORD LOCKS ... index PRIMARY ... lock_mode X locks rec but not gap waiting   <-- wants row 3
*** (2) TRANSACTION:
TRANSACTION 48212, ACTIVE 2 sec starting index read
UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 50 WHERE id = 7
*** (2) HOLDS THE LOCK(S):  ... row 3 ...
*** (2) WAITING FOR THIS LOCK TO BE GRANTED:  ... row 7 ...
*** WE ROLL BACK TRANSACTION (2)                           <-- the victim
      
  
      💡
      How to read it
      For each transaction: the SQL it was running, what it HOLDS, what it is WAITING FOR. Lock-mode phrases map to the lock types: locks rec but not gap = record lock, locks gap before rec = gap lock, plain lock_mode X = next-key lock, insert intention = insert-intention lock. Note: only the current statement is shown, not the earlier statement that took the held lock — you may need the application logs to reconstruct the order.
      

  
      Prevention: wait-die vs wound-wait
      
  
      Instead of detecting cycles, a system can prevent them using transaction timestamps (older = smaller TS = higher priority). Only one direction of waiting is allowed, so cycles cannot form. An aborted transaction restarts with its original timestamp, so it gets older over time and eventually wins — no starvation.
      
  
      SchemeOlder Ti requests lock held by younger TjYounger Ti requests lock held by older TjType
      
    
      Wait-dieTi waitsTi dies (aborts, restarts later with same TS)Non-preemptive
      
    
      Wound-waitTi wounds Tj (Tj is aborted)Ti waitsPreemptive
      
  
      
  
      Wait-Die · Wound-Wait
      The first word is what the OLD transaction does. Wait-die: old waits, young dies. Wound-wait: old wounds, young waits. In both, only the young one is ever killed.
      
  
      Other options: timeout-based (assume deadlock after N seconds — simple, but may kill innocent slow waits or wait too long), no-wait (abort immediately if the lock is busy), conservative 2PL (take all locks up front), resource ordering (global lock order). Distributed databases often use wound-wait (e.g. Google Spanner) because building a global wait-for graph is expensive.
      
  
      ℹ️
      Starvation and livelock
      Starvation: one transaction keeps losing — always picked as the deadlock victim or always overtaken in the lock queue. Fix: age-based priority (keep the original timestamp), fair FIFO lock queues. Livelock: transactions keep running and aborting each other without progress (e.g. two retries that collide again and again with identical timing). Fix: randomized (jittered) backoff before retrying.
      

  
      Classic deadlock scenarios and how to avoid them
      
  
      
    QTwo sessions each run "SELECT … FOR UPDATE; if not found, INSERT" for different new ids and deadlock. How?
    
      
      
      At REPEATABLE READ, a locking read that finds nothing takes a gap lock. Gap locks don't conflict with each other, so both sessions get the same gap. Then each INSERT needs an insert-intention lock on that gap, which conflicts with the other session's gap lock → each waits for the other.
      
      
      
        
      TimeT1T2
      
        
      t1SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 15 FOR UPDATE;  → empty, gap lock (10, 20)
      
        
      t2SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 16 FOR UPDATE;  → empty, gap lock (10, 20) ✔ (gaps don't conflict)
      
        
      t3INSERT INTO users(id, …) VALUES (15, …);  ⏳ blocked by T2's gap lock
      
        
      t4INSERT … VALUES (16, …);  blocked by T1's gap lock → DEADLOCK, one is rolled back
      
      
      
      
      Fixes: just INSERT and handle the duplicate-key error (or use INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE / INSERT IGNORE); or run at READ COMMITTED (no gap locks for searches); or accept and retry.
      
    
      
  
      
  
      ScenarioWhy it deadlocksFix
      
    
      Opposite-order transfers (A→B and B→A)Each locks its "from" row firstLock both rows in ascending id order (… WHERE id IN (a,b) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE)
      
    
      Read with FOR SHARE, then updateBoth hold S, both want X (upgrade deadlock)Read with FOR UPDATE from the start
      
    
      Check-then-insert on a missing keyGap locks + insert-intention (above)Insert directly, rely on UNIQUE; or RC
      
    
      Concurrent duplicate-key insertsOn a duplicate-key error the failed inserter takes an S lock on the existing entry; if the first inserter rolls back, two waiters both want XRetry; avoid hot-key insert races (generate ids differently)
      
    
      UPDATE without an indexLocks huge ranges, overlaps with everyoneIndex the WHERE columns
      
    
      Batch jobs touching rows in random orderOverlapping lock sets in different ordersSort keys before processing; smaller batches; commit per batch
      
  
      
  
      💡
      🛟 Deadlock avoidance checklist for application code
      (1) Keep transactions short; no user/network waits inside. (2) Touch tables and rows in a consistent order. (3) Index every column used in locking WHERE clauses. (4) Lock what you need up front with FOR UPDATE, not FOR SHARE + upgrade. (5) Consider READ COMMITTED if you don't need gap locks. (6) Always have a retry wrapper for 1213 / 40001 / 40P01 — deadlocks can be reduced, never fully eliminated.
      

  
  
      🎟️ Real-world concurrency scenarios
      
  
      Product-company interviews usually end with "design this so two users can't…". Each answer below follows the same recipe: name the anomaly → pick the cheapest correct mechanism → say how you verify success (affected rows / unique error) → say how you retry.
      

  
      
    QMovie seat booking: how do you make sure two users can never book the same seat?
    
      
      
      Anomaly: lost update / double booking — both users see the seat as FREE, both book. Mechanism: make the state change conditional and atomic, back it with a UNIQUE constraint, and use a temporary hold so payment happens outside the transaction.
      
      
      -- seats(show_id, seat_no, status ENUM('FREE','HELD','BOOKED'), held_by, hold_until,
--       PRIMARY KEY(show_id, seat_no))

-- 1. hold (one atomic statement; no read-then-write)
UPDATE seats
   SET status = 'HELD', held_by = 501, hold_until = NOW() + INTERVAL 5 MINUTE
 WHERE show_id = 88 AND seat_no = 'F12'
   AND (status = 'FREE' OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_until < NOW()));
-- ROW_COUNT() = 1 -> you have the seat;  0 -> "seat just taken, pick another"

-- 2. payment happens OUTSIDE any DB transaction

-- 3. confirm (only if the hold is still yours)
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE seats SET status = 'BOOKED'
 WHERE show_id = 88 AND seat_no = 'F12' AND held_by = 501 AND status = 'HELD';
INSERT INTO bookings(show_id, seat_no, user_id, payment_ref)
VALUES (88, 'F12', 501, 'pay_7Hq…');      -- UNIQUE(show_id, seat_no) = last line of defence
COMMIT;
      
      
      Multi-seat selection ("F12, F13, F14 together"): lock them with SELECT … WHERE show_id=88 AND seat_no IN (…) ORDER BY seat_no FOR UPDATE NOWAIT — sorted order prevents deadlocks, NOWAIT gives an instant "someone else is booking these" instead of a spinner.
      
      
      🌍
      At scale
      For a blockbuster release, the hot rows are a few thousand seats of one show. Holds with expiry keep lock time tiny; a background job (or the conditional WHERE above) recycles expired holds; Redis SET seat:88:F12 501 NX EX 300 can act as a fast pre-filter, but the database UNIQUE constraint stays the source of truth.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      I never read the seat status and then update it in two steps. I hold the seat with one conditional UPDATE — set it to HELD only where it is FREE or the old hold has expired — and check the affected row count. Payment happens outside the transaction; then a short transaction confirms the booking, and a unique constraint on show and seat guarantees no double booking even if there is a bug.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QFlash sale: 100 units, 10,000 buyers. How do you prevent overselling?
    
      
      
      UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1
 WHERE id = 42 AND stock >= 1;     -- atomic check-and-decrement
-- ROW_COUNT() = 1 -> create the order in the same transaction; 0 -> "sold out"
      
      
      Correct at any isolation level, because the UPDATE takes the row's X lock and evaluates stock >= 1 on the latest committed value. Add CHECK (stock >= 0) (enforced since MySQL 8.0.16) as a safety net.
      
      
      The real problem is throughput: every buyer queues on one row lock. Options: keep the transaction tiny (decrement + order insert only, payment later with a reservation timeout); split stock into N bucket rows (product_stock(product_id, bucket, qty)) and decrement a random non-empty bucket; or decrement in Redis (DECR is atomic) and write orders to the DB asynchronously via a queue, reconciling later.
      
      
      🚫
      Fails interviews
      "SELECT stock, if > 0 then UPDATE stock = stock - 1, all inside a transaction at REPEATABLE READ." The SELECT is a snapshot read with no lock: 10 buyers can all see stock = 1. A transaction alone is not a lock.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QA "likes" counter on a viral post is causing lock waits. What do you do?
    
      
      
      Every like runs UPDATE posts SET likes = likes + 1 WHERE id = 9, so all writers serialize on one row lock (a hot row). Fixes, from simplest:
      
      
        
        
      1. Sharded counter: post_likes(post_id, slot, cnt) with e.g. 16 slots; each like increments a random slot; read with SUM(cnt). Contention drops ~16×.
        2. 
        
      2. Buffer and batch: increment in Redis (INCR) and flush to the DB every few seconds in one UPDATE.
        3. 
        
      3. Event log + aggregation: insert a row per like (no contention — different rows) and compute counts asynchronously; also gives "who liked" and de-duplication via UNIQUE(post_id, user_id).
        4. 
      
      
      
      Accept that the displayed number is slightly stale — exact real-time like counts are rarely a business requirement.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QTwo users sign up with the same username at the same moment. Both pass the "is it taken?" check. How do you fix it?
    
      
      
      The check (SELECT) and the INSERT are separate; at any isolation level below SERIALIZABLE both can see "not taken" (it is a phantom-style race). Fix: a UNIQUE index on username and handle the duplicate-key error (ERROR 1062 / SQLSTATE 23000) as "username taken". The pre-check is still fine for nice UX, but the constraint is what guarantees correctness.
      
      
      ALTER TABLE users ADD CONSTRAINT uq_username UNIQUE (username);
INSERT INTO users(username, email) VALUES ('ravi_dev', 'r@x.in');
-- ERROR 1062 (23000): Duplicate entry 'ravi_dev' for key 'users.uq_username'  -> tell user
      
      
      ⚠️
      Watch the collation
      MySQL 8's default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is case- and accent-insensitive, so 'Ravi' and 'ravi' collide (usually what you want). In PostgreSQL the default is case-sensitive: use a unique index on lower(username) or the citext type.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      ScenarioAnomalyBest toolVerify / retry
      
    
      Seat / slot bookingDouble booking (lost update)Conditional UPDATE + hold expiry + UNIQUEROW_COUNT(); duplicate-key
      
    
      Inventory / flash saleOversellingUPDATE … SET stock = stock - n WHERE stock >= nROW_COUNT()
      
    
      Money transferLost update, deadlockFOR UPDATE in id order + ledger + idempotency key (Ch 12)Retry on 1213
      
    
      Hot counterLock contentionSharded counter / Redis batch—
      
    
      Unique username / emailCheck-then-insert raceUNIQUE constraintCatch 1062
      
    
      Job queue workersDouble processing / blockingFOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKEDStatus column + timeout reaper
      
    
      Doctors on call (≥ 1 must stay)Write skewSERIALIZABLE (PG SSI) or FOR UPDATE on all rows of the shiftRetry on 40001
      
    
      Wiki / profile edit formLost update across user think-timeOptimistic version column0 rows → "changed by someone else"
      
  
      
  
      ✏️ Pattern to say out loud: "atomic conditional write, check affected rows, unique constraint as a backstop, retry on deadlock". It answers 80% of these questions.
      

  
  
      📌 Key takeaways
        
    
      • Seven anomalies: dirty write, dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom, lost update, read skew, write skew. The ANSI table covers only three of them.
        • 
    
      • Defaults: InnoDB = REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server = READ COMMITTED. PG RR = snapshot isolation (catches lost updates); PG SERIALIZABLE = SSI; Oracle SERIALIZABLE = SI.
        • 
    
      • InnoDB MVCC: DB_TRX_ID + DB_ROLL_PTR → undo chain filtered by a read view (RC: new view per statement; RR: one per transaction). PG: xmin/xmax tuples + VACUUM.
        • 
    
      • InnoDB locks index records it scans: record, gap, next-key (record + gap before), insert-intention. No index ⇒ every row locked. Gap locks only at RR/SERIALIZABLE.
        • 
    
      • Intention locks (IS/IX) let table-level locks coexist cheaply with row locks; IS/IX never conflict with each other.
        • 
    
      • Long transactions hold metadata locks — an ALTER waiting behind one can freeze every query on the table. Use a short lock_wait_timeout.
        • 
    
      • 2PL ⇒ conflict-serializable; strict 2PL ⇒ also no cascading aborts; only conservative 2PL is deadlock-free. TO/OCC never wait (abort instead); Thomas write rule allows VS schedules.
        • 
    
      • Deadlock = cycle in the wait-for graph; InnoDB detects immediately and rolls back the smaller transaction (1213). Wait-die: old waits, young dies; wound-wait: old wounds, young waits.
        • 
    
      • Production recipe: atomic conditional UPDATE + check affected rows, FOR UPDATE in a fixed order, UNIQUE constraints as a backstop, SKIP LOCKED for queues, version columns for long edits, retry on 1213/40001.
        •
