      In MySQL InnoDB at the default level, two sessions run SELECT qty … ; UPDATE … SET qty = <value computed in app> concurrently. What can happen?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      InnoDB RR has no first-updater-wins check: the second UPDATE simply overwrites. PostgreSQL RR would raise 40001 instead.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      UPDATE emp SET age = 21 WHERE name = 'Ravi', with no index on name, at RR. What is locked?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      InnoDB locks what it scans; with no index it scans everything. It is not escalation (InnoDB never escalates) — it is many next-key locks.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which lock pair is compatible?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Two transactions intending to write different rows of the same table must both proceed, so IX–IX is compatible. IX–S, SIX–IX and IS–X conflict.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Which 2PL variant guarantees freedom from deadlock?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Conservative 2PL acquires all locks before starting, which breaks "hold and wait". Strict and rigorous only control when locks are released.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Under wait-die, a YOUNGER transaction requests a lock held by an OLDER one. What happens?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Wait-die: old waits, young dies. Keeping the original timestamp prevents starvation.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Under timestamp ordering with the Thomas write rule, T (TS = 5) wants to write X, where R-TS(X) = 3 and W-TS(X) = 8. What happens?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      TS(T) ≥ R-TS(X), so no younger reader saw the old value; TS(T) < W-TS(X), so a younger write already superseded it — Thomas skips the obsolete write.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      An ALTER TABLE orders … shows "Waiting for table metadata lock" and now every SELECT on orders hangs. Most likely cause?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      MDLs are held to transaction end. The pending exclusive MDL blocks new shared requests, so everything queues. Find and end the old transaction; use a short lock_wait_timeout for DDL.
      
    
      
    
      
      
      Best way to let 20 workers pull distinct jobs from a jobs table without blocking each other?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      SKIP LOCKED (MySQL 8.0+, PG 9.5+) makes each worker skip rows other workers have locked, so they never wait and never take the same job.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    
      Default isolation level: MySQL InnoDB vs PostgreSQL / Oracle / SQL Server?
      InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ. The other three: READ COMMITTED.
      
    
      Write skew — definition and an example?
      Two txns read an overlapping set, then update different rows based on it, breaking a joint rule. Doctors on call: both see 2 on call, both go off → 0. Allowed by SI.
      
    
      InnoDB hidden columns used by MVCC?
      DB_TRX_ID (last writer), DB_ROLL_PTR (pointer to undo record / older version); DB_ROW_ID only if no PK.
      
    
      RC vs RR read view timing in InnoDB?
      RC: new read view for each consistent read (statement). RR: one read view at the first consistent read, reused for the whole transaction.
      
    
      Next-key lock = ?
      Record lock + gap lock on the gap BEFORE that record, e.g. (10, 20]. Default for scans at RR; prevents phantoms.
      
    
      When does InnoDB take only a record lock (no gap)?
      Unique index, equality on all its columns, row exists.
      
    
      What is an insert-intention lock?
      A gap lock set by INSERT. Inserts at different positions in one gap don't block each other, but they wait for another txn's gap/next-key lock.
      
    
      Why do intention locks exist?
      So a table-level lock request can see "someone holds row locks inside" with one check, instead of scanning all row locks.
      
    
      Strict vs rigorous 2PL?
      Strict: hold X locks until commit/abort. Rigorous: hold ALL locks (S and X) until commit/abort.
      
    
      Thomas write rule?
      In TO, if TS(T) < W-TS(X) (and no younger read), ignore T's obsolete write instead of aborting. Allows VS-but-not-CS schedules.
      
    
      Four Coffman conditions?
      Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait ("My Hungry Neighbour Circles").
      
    
      Wait-die vs wound-wait?
      Wait-die: old waits, young dies. Wound-wait: old wounds (aborts) young, young waits. Restart keeps the original timestamp.
      
    
      InnoDB deadlock vs lock wait timeout errors?
      1213 deadlock: whole txn rolled back, immediately. 1205 timeout after innodb_lock_wait_timeout (50 s): only the statement rolled back by default.
      
    
      How to prevent overselling in one statement?
      UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock >= 1; then check affected rows.
      
  
      

      


      
  
      
    
      Chapter 14 · V · Storage & Performance
      
    
      💽 Storage, Pages, Buffer Pool & File Organization
      
    
      Explain how a row really lives on disk, why the database thinks in 16 KB pages, and how the buffer pool hides slow disks, so every indexing answer in the next chapter makes sense.
      
    
      ⏱ 30 minMySQL 8.4 / InnoDBPostgreSQLSQL ServerRocksDB · Cassandra
      
  
      

  
       
      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
      
    
        
      
      • The database reads and writes whole pages, not rows: InnoDB 16 KB, PostgreSQL 8 KB, SQL Server 8 KB. Query cost ≈ how many pages, and were they random or sequential?
        • 
      
      • A random disk read is thousands of times slower than RAM (HDD ≈ 4–10 ms, SSD ≈ 20–100 µs, RAM ≈ 100 ns). So every design tries to cut random page reads.
        • 
      
      • A slotted page = header + slot array (grows forward) + free space + rows (grow backward). Row address = (page no, slot no).
        • 
      
      • Big values go off-page: InnoDB DYNAMIC keeps a 20-byte pointer to overflow pages; PostgreSQL uses TOAST (rows above ~2 KB).
        • 
      
      • File organizations: heap (unordered), sorted, hashed, clustered / index-organized (InnoDB tables, Oracle IOT).
        • 
      
      • Buffer pool = RAM cache of pages. InnoDB uses LRU with midpoint insertion (5/8 young, 3/8 old, 1-second probation) so one big scan cannot flush hot data.
        • 
      
      • Dirty pages are flushed later; commit only forces the redo log (see Chapter 17).
        • 
      
      • Row store = OLTP (whole rows). Column store = OLAP (few columns, great compression).
        • 
      
      • B+ tree = update in place, fast reads. LSM tree = append + compaction, fast writes (RocksDB, Cassandra).
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ✏️ This chapter is the "why" behind indexing. Interviewers rarely ask "what is a slotted page?" alone, but they LOVE "why is a random read slow?" and "what does the buffer pool do?"
      

  
  
      🖥️ Memory hierarchy: why disk I/O dominates
      
  
      Storage comes in layers. Close to the CPU it is fast, small and costly. Far from the CPU it is slow, big and cheap. RAM is volatile (lost on power cut) and byte-addressable. Disks (HDD/SSD) are non-volatile and are read in blocks/pages. A database must keep its data on the slow layer (so it survives a crash), but wants to work on it in the fast layer. Almost every storage design in this chapter is about bridging that gap. ← the whole chapter in one line
      

  

  
      
    QWhy is disk I/O the dominant cost in query processing?
    
      
      
      What: When a query runs, the CPU work per row (compare a value, add to a sum) takes nanoseconds. Fetching a page that is not in RAM takes microseconds (SSD) to milliseconds (HDD). That is a gap of 1,000× to 40,000×.
      
      
      Why it matters: If a query must read 10,000 random pages from an HDD at ~4 ms each, that is 40 seconds, no matter how fast the CPU is. So textbook cost models count only I/O:
      
      
      cost  =  b × tT  +  S × tS
         b  = number of blocks transferred
         S  = number of seeks (random jumps)
         tT = time to transfer one block   (HDD ≈ 0.1 ms,  SSD ≈ 2–10 µs  for 4 KB)
         tS = time for one seek            (HDD ≈ 4 ms,    SSD ≈ 20–90 µs)
      
      
      How engines react: indexes (fewer pages), clustering (related rows on the same page), covering indexes (skip table pages), the buffer pool (keep hot pages in RAM), and sequential scans for big reports (no seeks).
      
      
      ℹ️
      Modern optimizers
      MySQL and PostgreSQL still weight I/O heavily, but they also add a CPU cost per row. With everything cached in RAM, CPU and memory bandwidth start to matter too.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      The database works in pages, and getting a page from disk is thousands of times slower than reading memory. A random HDD read is around 4 milliseconds; RAM is around 100 nanoseconds. So the cost of a query is mostly the number of page reads, especially random ones. Indexes, clustering and the buffer pool all exist to cut that number.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Random vs sequential I/O: why is sequential so much faster?
          
      On an HDD, a random read pays a seek (move the arm) plus rotational delay (wait for the sector), ~4–10 ms. A sequential read pays that once, then streams at 100–250 MB/s. On an SSD there is no arm, but random small reads still cost more than large sequential reads (internal parallelism, read-ahead, fewer requests). That is why MySQL docs say a scan can beat an index when the query needs most rows: "Sequential reads minimize disk seeks, even if not all the rows are needed."
      
        
      ↪Do SSDs make indexes useless?
          
      No. SSDs shrink the random-read penalty (≈ 100× better than HDD), but reading 4 pages is still far cheaper than reading 4 million pages. Indexes cut the number of pages; SSDs cut the price of each page. You want both.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      DeviceRandom 4 KB readSequential throughputMoving partsDB impact
      
    
      RAM (DRAM)~100 nstens of GB/snoneBuffer pool lives here; lost on crash
      
    
      NVMe SSD~20–100 µsGB/snoneRandom reads cheap-ish; huge parallel IOPS
      
    
      SATA SSD~50–100 µs~500 MB/snoneSame idea, interface-limited
      
    
      HDD (7200 rpm)~4–10 ms (seek + rotation)~100–250 MB/sarm + platter~100–200 random IOPS → avoid random I/O at all costs
      
  
      

  
      Pages, not rows · Seeks, not bytes
      🧠 When you estimate a query, count pages touched and ask how many were random. That one habit answers half of all performance questions.
      

  
  
      📓 Blocks and pages: the unit of I/O
      
  
      A block is what the disk/OS reads in one go (usually 4 KB). A database page is what the DBMS reads in one go. It is a fixed-size chunk of a data file, and every table and index is stored as a list of pages.
      

  
      
    
      🐬
      InnoDB: 16 KB
      Set by innodb_page_size when the instance is initialized (4/8/16/32/64 KB). Cannot be changed later.
      
    
      🐘
      PostgreSQL: 8 KB
      Chosen at compile time (BLCKSZ). Tables and indexes are arrays of 8 KB pages.
      
    
      🪟
      SQL Server: 8 KB
      96-byte header, slot array at the page end, max 8,060 bytes of in-row data. 8 pages = 64 KB extent.
      
    
      🔴
      Oracle: 8 KB (default)
      DB_BLOCK_SIZE is chosen at database creation; 8 KB is the common default.
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is a page? Why does InnoDB use 16 KB and not 4 KB?
    
      
      
      A page is the smallest unit the database reads from or writes to disk. To read one 100-byte row, InnoDB reads the whole 16 KB page that holds it into the buffer pool.
      
      
      Bigger pages help: an index page holds more keys, so the B+ tree has a higher fanout and fewer levels (≈1000 keys per 16 KB page → 3–4 levels for a billion rows; see Chapter 15). Scans also need fewer requests.
      
      
      Bigger pages hurt: changing one tiny row dirties 16 KB that must be written back (write amplification), and more memory is wasted on cold rows that share the page with a hot row. A 16 KB page is also larger than the disk's atomic 4 KB write, so a crash can leave a torn page. InnoDB fixes that with the doublewrite buffer; PostgreSQL with full-page writes in the WAL (Chapter 17).
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistake
      "The database reads the row from disk." No. It reads the page. Rows are never fetched alone.
      
      
      🧠
      Memory aid
      "MySQL is double": InnoDB 16 KB, PostgreSQL and SQL Server 8 KB.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      📋 Slotted page layout
      
  
      How do variable-length rows fit inside a page and still have a stable address? The answer used by almost every DBMS is the slotted page. Think of a notebook page: you write a list of line numbers from the top down, and the actual entries from the bottom up. The page is full when the two meet.
      

  

  
      
    
      Slot / line pointer
      A tiny (offset, length) entry pointing at a row inside the page. PostgreSQL calls it ItemId (4 bytes each, after a 24-byte page header).
      
    
      Record ID (RID / TID / ctid)
      The physical address of a row = page number + slot number. PostgreSQL shows it as ctid, e.g. (12,3) = page 12, item 3.
      
    
      Tuple header
      Per-row metadata before the column data: visibility info for MVCC (which transaction created/deleted the row) and a NULL bitmap.
      
  
      

  
      🔀
      Engine differences inside the page
      PostgreSQL: textbook slotted page; line pointers at the front, tuples from the back, a "special space" at the end for index pages. SQL Server: 96-byte header; the slot array sits at the end of the page (2 bytes per row). InnoDB: records inside an index page are kept in a singly-linked list in key order (from an infimum to a supremum system record), not physically sorted, plus a small page directory of slots pointing at every 4th–8th record so the page can be searched quickly.
      

  
      📊 Record formats: fixed vs variable length, overflow, TOAST
      
  
      
    
      Fixed-length record
      • Every column has a fixed size (INT, CHAR(10), DATE).
      • Field i is at a known offset: very fast to find.
      • Wastes space for short values; easy in-place updates.
      
    
      Variable-length record
      • Has VARCHAR, TEXT, JSON, BLOB.
      • Header stores a list of field lengths (or offsets) + NULL bitmap.
      • Saves space; an update that grows a row may not fit → move or split.
      
  
      

  
      InnoDB row formatLong column handlingNotes
      
    
      REDUNDANT768-byte prefix in the row, rest on overflow pagesOldest format; reserves fixed space even for NULLs
      
    
      COMPACT768-byte prefix in the row, rest off-pageSmaller header: variable-length list + NULL bitmap + 5-byte record header
      
    
      DYNAMIC defaultLong value fully off-page, only a 20-byte pointer in the rowValues ≤ 40 bytes stay inline; index key prefixes up to 3072 bytes
      
    
      COMPRESSEDLike DYNAMICPlus page compression (KEY_BLOCK_SIZE); not for pages above 16 KB
      
  
      

  
      Every InnoDB clustered-index row also carries hidden columns: DB_TRX_ID (6 bytes, last transaction that changed it), DB_ROLL_PTR (7 bytes, pointer to the undo record used by MVCC, see Chapter 13), and DB_ROW_ID (6 bytes, only if InnoDB had to invent a hidden primary key).
      

  
      
    QWhat happens when a row is bigger than a page, e.g. a 1 MB TEXT value?
    
      
      
      InnoDB's maximum row size is slightly less than half a page (~8,000 bytes for 16 KB pages, not counting off-page columns), because a B+ tree page must hold at least two rows. MySQL itself also caps the combined column size at 65,535 bytes. When a row is too long, InnoDB picks the longest columns and moves them to separately allocated overflow pages until the row fits. With DYNAMIC, the row keeps only a 20-byte pointer.
      
      
      Consequence: reading that column costs extra page reads. That is one reason SELECT * on tables with big TEXT/JSON columns is slow: you drag in overflow pages you did not need.
      
      
      🔀
      PostgreSQL TOAST, SQL Server row-overflow
      PostgreSQL never lets a tuple span pages. When a row is wider than ~2 KB (TOAST_TUPLE_THRESHOLD), big values are compressed and/or moved out-of-line into a TOAST table in ~2,000-byte chunks (max 1 GB per value). SQL Server moves variable-length columns, starting with the widest, into a ROW_OVERFLOW_DATA allocation unit when a row exceeds 8,060 bytes.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A row must fit in about half a page in InnoDB. If it does not, the biggest variable-length columns are pushed to overflow pages and the row keeps a 20-byte pointer. PostgreSQL does the same idea with TOAST, which also compresses. The practical lesson is to avoid SELECT * on wide tables, because reading those columns means extra page reads.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🗄️ Tablespaces, files, segments and extents (InnoDB)
      
  
      InnoDB groups pages into bigger units so related pages sit near each other on disk (good for sequential reads):
      
  
      
    
      Tablespacea file, e.g. shop/orders.ibd
      
    
      
    
      Segmenteach index gets 2: leaf pages + non-leaf pages
      
    
      
    
      Extent64 contiguous 16 KB pages = 1 MB
      
    
      
    
      Page16 KB, unit of I/O
      
    
      
    
      Rowrecord in a slotted page
      
  
      
  
      InnoDB on-disk fileWhat lives there
      
    
      ibdata1 (system tablespace)The change buffer; table data only if a table was created there. Historically also undo and doublewrite.
      
    
      db/table.ibd (file-per-table, default ON)One table's clustered index + all its secondary indexes. DROP/TRUNCATE give the space back to the OS; supports transportable tablespaces.
      
    
      mysql.ibdThe data dictionary (MySQL 8.0+).
      
    
      General tablespacesCREATE TABLESPACE ts1 ADD DATAFILE 'ts1.ibd', shared by several tables.
      
    
      undo_001, undo_002Undo logs (rollback + MVCC old versions).
      
    
      #innodb_redo/#ib_redoN (8.0.30+)Redo log (crash recovery, Chapter 17).
      
    
      #ib_16384_0.dblwr (8.0.20+)Doublewrite buffer files (torn-page protection).
      
  
      
  
      🔀
      PostgreSQL files
      Each table and each index is its own file under $PGDATA/base/<db_oid>/<relfilenode>, split into 1 GB segment files. Beside the main data file are "forks": _fsm (free space map: which pages have room) and _vm (visibility map: which pages are all-visible, used by VACUUM and index-only scans, see Chapter 15).
      

  
  
      📁 File organizations: how rows are arranged in a file
      
  
      A file organization decides where a new row goes and therefore how you find it later. Four classic choices:
      

  
      
    
      🧺
      Heap (unordered)
      Rows go wherever there is free space. Fast inserts. Finding a row needs a full scan or a separate index. PostgreSQL tables, Oracle default tables, SQL Server tables without a clustered index.
      
    
      📚
      Sequential (sorted)
      Rows kept sorted on a key. Great for range scans and binary search. Inserts must shift rows or use overflow chains, so it degrades and needs reorganizing.
      
    
      #️⃣
      Hashed
      A hash function on a key picks the bucket (page). Equality lookup in ~1 I/O. No range scans, no ordering; buckets can overflow.
      
    
      🌳
      Clustered / index-organized
      The rows themselves are stored in the leaf pages of a B+ tree on the key. Sorted and easy to insert into. InnoDB tables, Oracle IOT, SQL Server clustered index.
      
  
      

  
      OrganizationInsertEquality lookupRange scanFull scanMain weakness
      
    
      Heap✔ O(1), append to any page with room✘ full scan (needs an index)✘ full scan✔Every lookup needs a secondary index; rows may move (forwarding pointers)
      
    
      Sorted file✘ shift / overflow pages~ binary search, log₂(b)✔ excellent✔ in orderInserts and deletes are expensive; periodic reorganization
      
    
      Hashed✔ ~1 I/O✔ ~1 I/O✘~ unordered, may have half-empty bucketsOnly equality; growth needs rehashing (extendible/linear hashing)
      
    
      Clustered B+ tree~ log(N) + possible page split✔ 3–4 page reads✔ walk linked leaves✔ in key orderOnly one physical order; random keys cause page splits; secondary indexes need a second lookup
      
  
      

  
      
    QHeap table vs clustered (index-organized) table: what is the difference?
    
      
      
      Heap: rows are stored in no particular order. Every index (even the primary key index) is a separate structure that points to a physical row address (ctid in PostgreSQL, rowid in Oracle, RID in SQL Server).
      
      
      Clustered: the table is a B+ tree ordered by the key; the leaf pages hold full rows. Rows with nearby keys sit on the same page, so a key range scan reads few, contiguous pages. Secondary indexes store the key value (not a physical address), because rows move around when pages split.
      
      
      🔀
      Who uses what
      InnoDB: every table is clustered on the PRIMARY KEY (or first UNIQUE NOT NULL index, or a hidden 6-byte row id). PostgreSQL: always heap; CLUSTER reorders once but is not maintained. Oracle: heap by default, ORGANIZATION INDEX for an IOT. SQL Server: clustered on the PK by default; a table with no clustered index is a heap.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      In a heap, rows are dumped wherever there is space and every index points to a physical address. In a clustered table the rows live inside the primary key B+ tree, so they are physically sorted by key. MySQL InnoDB tables are clustered; PostgreSQL tables are heaps. Clustered tables are great for primary-key lookups and ranges, but secondary lookups need an extra hop through the primary key.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      📦 The buffer pool: the database's own RAM cache
      
  
      The buffer pool (InnoDB) / shared buffers (PostgreSQL) / buffer cache (Oracle, SQL Server) is a big area of RAM split into page-sized frames. Every page the engine reads or changes goes through it. The goal: serve most page requests from RAM, and touch disk as little as possible.
      

  

  
      
    QWhat is the buffer pool and how does it work?
    
      
      
      What: a cache of disk pages in RAM, managed by the DBMS. In InnoDB its size is innodb_buffer_pool_size (default 128 MB; on a dedicated server often up to ~80% of RAM).
      
      
      Why: RAM is ~1000× faster than disk. If the "working set" (hot pages) fits in the pool, most queries never touch disk.
      
      
      How (step by step):
      
      
        
        
      1. Lookup — the engine asks for page P; the page table (an in-memory hash) says whether P is in a frame.
        2. 
        
      2. Hit — pin the frame (pin count +1 so nobody evicts it while in use), read/modify it, unpin.
        3. 
        
      3. Miss — choose a victim frame with the replacement policy (LRU / clock). If the victim is dirty (modified in RAM, not yet on disk), it must be written first.
        4. 
        
      4. Load — read P from disk into the frame, update the page table.
        5. 
        
      5. Modify — a change sets the dirty flag and writes a redo log record. The page itself is written to disk later by background threads.
        6. 
      
      
      
      🚫
      Wrong answer that fails interviews
      "On COMMIT the changed data pages are written to disk." No! On commit only the redo log is flushed (with default durable settings). Dirty data pages are flushed later; after a crash, redo replays the changes (Chapter 17). Writing random data pages at every commit would be far too slow.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      The buffer pool is the database's own cache of disk pages in memory. Every read goes through it: on a hit we use the page in RAM, on a miss we evict a page using an LRU-like policy and load the new one. Changes are made in memory, which marks the page dirty, and the redo log makes them durable. Dirty pages are written to disk later in the background, at checkpoints.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Why not just use the OS page cache (or mmap)?
          
      The DBMS knows things the OS does not: (1) which pages are precious (B+ tree roots) and which come from a one-time report scan; (2) write ordering: with WAL, a dirty page may be written only after its log records are durable; (3) smarter prefetching. It also avoids caching every page twice. That is why InnoDB uses O_DIRECT on Linux (the 8.4 default for innodb_flush_method) to bypass the OS cache.
      
        
      ↪What is a "pinned" page?
          
      A page currently in use by some thread (pin count > 0). It cannot be evicted until every user unpins it. It is like a library book that is checked out: the librarian cannot put it into storage.
      
        
      ↪How do you know the buffer pool is too small?
          
      Watch the hit ratio: Innodb_buffer_pool_read_requests (logical reads) vs Innodb_buffer_pool_reads (reads that had to go to disk). If disk reads are a noticeable share and latency is I/O-bound, grow the pool (it can be resized online) or shrink the working set (better indexes, archiving old rows).
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      🧹 Eviction policies: LRU, clock, and InnoDB's midpoint LRU
      
  
      
    
      LRU (least recently used)
      Keep a list ordered by last access; evict from the tail. Simple, but every access must move a page to the head (lock contention), and one big scan can push out everything.
      
    
      Clock (second chance)
      An approximation of LRU. Frames sit in a circle, each with a reference bit set on access. A "clock hand" sweeps: bit = 1 → clear it and move on; bit = 0 → evict. Cheap, no list reordering. PostgreSQL uses a clock-sweep with a small usage counter.
      
    
      LRU-K
      Track the last K access times; evict the page whose K-th most recent access is oldest. Resists one-time scans.
      
    
      Sequential flooding
      The classic failure of plain LRU: a big sequential scan reads pages used only once, and they evict the whole hot working set.
      
  
      

  

  
      
    QA nightly report scans a 50 GB table. Why doesn't it wipe out the 10 GB buffer pool?
    
      
      
      Because InnoDB does not use plain LRU. A newly read page goes to the head of the old sublist (the midpoint), not the head of the whole list. It is promoted to the young sublist only if it is accessed again more than innodb_old_blocks_time (default 1000 ms) after its first access.
      
      
        
        
      1. The scan reads page after page; each lands in the old sublist (~3.7 GB of the 10 GB pool).
        2. 
        
      2. The scan touches each page a few times within milliseconds: inside the 1-second window, so no promotion.
        3. 
        
      3. New scan pages push older scan pages off the tail. The scan "recycles" only the old 3/8.
        4. 
        
      4. The ~6.3 GB young sublist with the OLTP working set survives.
        5. 
      
      
      
      💡
      Extra fixes
      Run heavy reports on a replica; or tune innodb_old_blocks_pct / innodb_old_blocks_time. PostgreSQL protects itself differently: large sequential scans use a small ring buffer (a few hundred KB) instead of the whole of shared_buffers.
      
      
      🧠
      Memory aid
      "3/8 old, 1 second probation." New pages are interns: they must prove themselves after a cooling-off period before they get a desk in the young area.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      ⏳ Dirty pages, flushing and checkpoints
      
  
      A dirty page is modified in memory but not yet written to its data file. InnoDB's page cleaner threads write them in the background:
      
  
        
    
      • Flushing starts gently at innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct_lwm (10% dirty) and gets aggressive near innodb_max_dirty_pages_pct (90).
        • 
    
      • Adaptive flushing matches the flush rate to how fast redo is being generated.
        • 
    
      • A checkpoint records "all changes up to LSN X are on disk", so redo before X is no longer needed and recovery can start from X. InnoDB uses fuzzy checkpoints (flush a bit at a time, no stop-the-world).
        • 
    
      • If the redo log is almost full, InnoDB must flush hard to free it (a sharp checkpoint): you see a write stall. That is why redo size (innodb_redo_log_capacity) matters for write-heavy systems.
        • 
    
      • Before writing a page in place, InnoDB writes it to the doublewrite buffer to survive torn pages. Details in Chapter 17.
        • 
  
      

  
      ✏️ Change buffer and adaptive hash index (InnoDB extras)
      
  
      
    
      Change buffer
        
      
      • Problem: an INSERT into a table with 5 secondary indexes may touch 5 random index pages that are not in RAM, so 5 random reads just to add entries.
        • 
      
      • Idea: write a "to-do note" for non-unique secondary index pages not in the pool; merge it later when the page is read anyway.
        • 
      
      • Lives in the buffer pool (max 25% by default) and the system tablespace.
        • 
      
      • MySQL 8.4 default innodb_change_buffering = none (it was all in 8.0).
        • 
    
      
    
      Adaptive hash index (AHI)
        
      
      • Problem: even a cached B+ tree lookup walks 3–4 pages and binary-searches each.
        • 
      
      • Idea: InnoDB watches hot lookups and builds an in-memory hash on key prefixes → direct jump to the record.
        • 
      
      • Automatic; you cannot create user hash indexes in InnoDB.
        • 
      
      • Can cause latch contention under heavy concurrency. MySQL 8.4 default innodb_adaptive_hash_index = OFF (ON in 8.0).
        • 
    
      
  
      
  
      ⚠️
      Common mistake
      "The change buffer is a write cache for all writes." No. It only buffers changes to secondary index pages that are not in memory, and only for non-unique indexes (a unique index must read the page to check for duplicates).
      

  
      🔀
      PostgreSQL: shared_buffers + OS page cache ("double buffering")
      PostgreSQL keeps its own cache, shared_buffers (default 128 MB; a common starting point is ~25% of RAM), but reads and writes data files through the operating system's page cache (buffered I/O). So a hot page may live twice: once in shared_buffers and once in the OS cache. That is why PostgreSQL is not tuned to 80% of RAM like InnoDB: the OS cache does the rest of the caching, and the planner is told about it with effective_cache_size. InnoDB, by contrast, uses O_DIRECT and one big buffer pool. Eviction: InnoDB = midpoint LRU; PostgreSQL = clock-sweep + ring buffers for big scans/VACUUM.
      

  
      InnoDB (MySQL)PostgreSQL
      
    
      Cache nameBuffer poolshared_buffers
      
    
      Typical size50–80% of RAM on a dedicated box~25% of RAM; the OS page cache holds more
      
    
      OS cacheBypassed (O_DIRECT)Used (double buffering)
      
    
      ReplacementLRU with midpoint insertionClock-sweep (usage count) + ring buffers
      
    
      Torn-page protectionDoublewrite bufferFull-page images in WAL
      
  
      

  
  
      📊 Row store vs column store
      
  
      So far every page held whole rows. That is a row store (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server by default). A column store flips it: each page holds the values of one column for many rows.
      

  

  
      
    
      Row store → OLTP
      • Many small transactions touching a few whole rows (place order, update balance).
      • One row = one place → fast point lookup, insert, update.
      • Pairs with B+ tree indexes.
      • Examples: MySQL InnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server.
      
    
      Column store → OLAP
      • Scans billions of rows but only a few columns (5 of 100 columns ≈ 5% of the data).
      • Compression: run-length, dictionary, delta → even less I/O.
      • Vectorized execution (process batches of values) + min/max zone maps to skip blocks.
      • Single-row updates and SELECT * lookups are slow.
      • Examples: ClickHouse, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, DuckDB; SQL Server columnstore indexes.
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhy are column stores faster for analytics but bad for OLTP?
    
      
      
      Use the memory aid RCVL: Read less (only the needed columns), Compress better (one data type per block, many repeats), Vectorized execution (tight CPU loops over arrays of values), Late materialization / block skipping (min/max per block).
      
      
      For OLTP it is the opposite: inserting one order means writing to every column file, and reading one full row means reading one block per column. Row stores keep the row together in one page.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A row store keeps all columns of a row together, which suits transactions that read or write whole rows. A column store keeps each column together, so an analytic query that sums one column over a billion rows reads only that column, and it compresses very well. That is why we use MySQL or PostgreSQL for OLTP and a columnar warehouse for reporting.
      
      
      More on warehouses and OLAP modelling in Chapter 20.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⚡ B-tree storage vs LSM-tree storage
      
  
      There are two big families of storage engines. A B+ tree engine (InnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) updates pages in place. An LSM-tree (log-structured merge tree) engine never updates in place: it buffers writes in memory and writes new sorted files sequentially, merging them in the background.
      

  

  
      
    
      Write amplification
      Bytes written to disk ÷ bytes the app wrote. B+ tree: change 100 bytes, rewrite a 16 KB page. LSM: data is rewritten once per level during compaction.
      
    
      Read amplification
      Disk reads per query. B+ tree: ~1 path from root to leaf. LSM: may check memtable + several files (Bloom filters cut this).
      
    
      Space amplification
      On-disk size ÷ logical data size. B+ tree pages are often 50–94% full (fragmentation). LSM keeps old versions until compaction, but files are packed full and compress well.
      
    
      Bloom filter
      A small bit array per file that answers "is key k maybe here?" with no false negatives and a small false-positive rate. It lets a point read skip files that cannot contain the key.
      
  
      

  
      B+ tree engineLSM-tree engine
      
    
      Write pathFind the leaf page, update in place (random I/O)Append to WAL + memtable; flush sorted files (sequential I/O)
      
    
      Point read✔ one root-to-leaf walk (3–4 pages)~ memtable + several levels; Bloom filters help
      
    
      Range scan✔ walk linked leaves~ merge iterators over all levels
      
    
      Write throughput~ limited by random page writes✔ very high ingestion
      
    
      Space~ fragmentation, coarse page compression✔ compact, compresses well
      
    
      Background workPage flushing, purge/VACUUMCompaction (CPU + I/O spikes)
      
    
      DeletesRemove/delete-mark in placeTombstones (too many hurt reads until compacted)
      
    
      ExamplesInnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, SQLiteRocksDB, LevelDB, MyRocks (MySQL), Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, TiKV
      
    
      Best forRead-heavy, latency-sensitive OLTPWrite-heavy, space-sensitive workloads (feeds, logs, IoT, time series)
      
  
      

  
      
    QB+ tree vs LSM tree: when would you choose an LSM-based engine?
    
      
      
      When the workload is write-heavy and you care about disk space: event logs, messaging, metrics, social graphs. LSM turns random writes into sequential ones and packs data tightly. Facebook's MyRocks (MySQL on RocksDB) used about half the space and wrote less than half the bytes of InnoDB in their LinkBench test (one vendor benchmark, so quote it carefully).
      
      
      Choose a B+ tree engine for read-heavy OLTP with point and range queries, where predictable low latency matters.
      
      
      🧠
      Memory aid
      LSM: "writes fast, reads search, compaction pays later". And the RUM idea: a storage structure can optimize at most two of Read, Update (write) and Memory/space amplification.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A B+ tree updates pages in place, so reads are cheap but every small write rewrites a whole page at a random place. An LSM tree buffers writes in a memtable and flushes them as sorted immutable files, then compacts them in the background. Writes become sequential and fast, but a read may check several files, which Bloom filters reduce. I would pick LSM, like RocksDB or Cassandra, for write-heavy ingestion, and a B+ tree engine like InnoDB for read-heavy OLTP.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🛡️ RAID levels (brief)
      
  
      RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) combines disks for speed and/or survival of a disk failure.
      
  
      LevelHowUsable capacity (N disks)SurvivesGood for
      
    
      RAID 0Striping only (blocks spread over disks)N✘ any 1 disk failure loses everythingScratch / temp data needing speed
      
    
      RAID 1Mirroring (same data on 2 disks)N/2✔ 1 disk per mirrorLogs, small critical volumes; reads can use both copies
      
    
      RAID 5Striping + distributed parityN − 1✔ 1 diskRead-mostly data; small writes pay a penalty (read old data + parity, write both = 4 I/Os); long risky rebuilds
      
    
      RAID 10Stripe across mirrored pairsN/2✔ 1 disk per pairThe usual pick for OLTP databases: fast random writes + redundancy
      
  
      
  
      🚫
      RAID is not a backup
      RAID protects against a disk dying. It happily mirrors a DROP TABLE, a bad UPDATE without WHERE, or ransomware. You still need backups + logs (Chapter 17).
      

  
  
      ✂️ Fill factor and page splits (teaser)
      
  
      If every page were 100% full, the very next insert or row growth in that page would force a page split: allocate a new page, move about half of the rows, and update the parent. So engines leave some room:
      
  
        
    
      • InnoDB tries to leave 1/16 of each index page free. Sequential inserts give ~15/16 (≈ 94%) full pages; random inserts give pages anywhere from 1/2 to 15/16 full. innodb_fill_factor controls sorted index builds; if a page drops below MERGE_THRESHOLD (50%), InnoDB tries to merge it with a neighbour.
        • 
    
      • PostgreSQL: table fillfactor defaults to 100 (lower it to make room for HOT updates); B-tree index fillfactor defaults to 90.
        • 
    
      • SQL Server: FILLFACTOR option on index builds.
        • 
  
      
  
      💡
      Why this matters for the next chapter
      A random primary key (UUIDv4) makes inserts land on random full pages → splits everywhere → half-empty pages and a bigger, slower index. A sequential key (AUTO_INCREMENT) only splits the right-most page. Full story in Chapter 15.
      

  
      📌 Key takeaways
        
    
      • The page is the unit of I/O: InnoDB 16 KB, PostgreSQL/SQL Server 8 KB. Count pages, especially random ones.
        • 
    
      • Random disk reads cost ms (HDD) or tens of µs (SSD) vs ~100 ns for RAM; that gap drives indexing, clustering and caching.
        • 
    
      • Slotted pages give rows a stable (page, slot) address while letting them move within the page.
        • 
    
      • Long values go off-page: InnoDB DYNAMIC (20-byte pointer), PostgreSQL TOAST (~2 KB threshold).
        • 
    
      • File organizations: heap, sorted, hashed, clustered. InnoDB tables are clustered on the PK; PostgreSQL tables are heaps.
        • 
    
      • The buffer pool caches pages; InnoDB's midpoint LRU (3/8 old, 1 s) resists scan flooding; dirty pages are flushed later, commit forces only the redo log.
        • 
    
      • 8.4 defaults: change buffering none, adaptive hash index OFF, O_DIRECT on Linux.
        • 
    
      • Row store for OLTP, column store for OLAP. B+ tree for read-heavy, LSM for write-heavy.
        • 
    
      • RAID 10 for OLTP databases; RAID is never a backup.
        •

      You run SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 7 in InnoDB. What is the smallest unit read from disk if the row is not cached?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      The page is the unit of I/O. InnoDB pages are 16 KB by default. Extents are allocation units, not read units.
      
    
      What is written to disk at COMMIT in InnoDB with default durable settings?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Commit forces the redo log (WAL). Dirty pages are flushed in the background; recovery replays redo for pages that did not make it.
      
    
      Where does InnoDB insert a page it has just read from disk into the LRU list?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      Midpoint insertion. It is promoted to the young sublist only if accessed again after innodb_old_blocks_time (1 s).
      
    
      PostgreSQL stores a 50 KB JSON value in a row. What happens?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      PostgreSQL never lets tuples span pages. Rows above ~2 KB trigger TOAST.
      
    
      Which workload fits an LSM-tree engine best?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      LSM turns writes into sequential appends. Analytics over one column is a column-store job.
      
    
      Which RAID level is the usual recommendation for a write-heavy OLTP database?
      
      
      
      
      
      
      RAID 10 gives redundancy with good random-write speed. RAID 5 has a small-write penalty; RAID 0 has no redundancy.
      
  
      

  
      
    
      Default page size: InnoDB vs PostgreSQL?
      InnoDB 16 KB (fixed at instance init); PostgreSQL 8 KB (compile time). SQL Server 8 KB.
      
    
      What is a slotted page?
      Header + slot array growing forward + rows growing backward. Row ID = (page, slot); rows can move inside the page without changing their ID.
      
    
      InnoDB DYNAMIC row format and long columns?
      Long values go fully to overflow pages; the row keeps a 20-byte pointer. Values ≤ 40 bytes stay inline.
      
    
      What is TOAST?
      PostgreSQL's oversized-attribute storage: values in rows above ~2 KB are compressed and/or stored out-of-line in ~2 KB chunks (max 1 GB).
      
    
      InnoDB extent size?
      1 MB = 64 contiguous 16 KB pages. Each index has 2 segments: leaf and non-leaf.
      
    
      Dirty page?
      A page changed in the buffer pool but not yet written to its data file. Flushed later by page cleaner threads / checkpoints.
      
    
      Sequential flooding?
      A big scan evicts the hot working set from a plain LRU cache. InnoDB avoids it with midpoint insertion (3/8 old sublist, 1 s probation).
      
    
      Change buffer?
      Buffers changes to non-unique secondary index pages not in memory; merged later. Default none in MySQL 8.4.
      
    
      Double buffering in PostgreSQL?
      Pages can sit both in shared_buffers and in the OS page cache, because PG uses buffered I/O. InnoDB avoids it with O_DIRECT.
      
    
      Row store vs column store?
      Row: whole rows per page → OLTP. Column: one column per block → OLAP, read less, compress more, vectorize.
      
    
      LSM tree in one line?
      Write to WAL + memtable, flush sorted immutable SSTables, compact in the background; Bloom filters speed reads.
      
    
      Three amplifications?
      Write (disk bytes ÷ app bytes), read (disk reads per query), space (disk size ÷ logical size). You can optimize at most two.
      
  
      

      


      
  
      
    
      Chapter 15 · V · Storage & Performance
      
    
      🌳 Indexing Deep Dive: B+ Trees, Clustered, Composite & Covering
      
    
      Explain exactly how an index finds a row in 3–4 page reads, design the right composite index for any query, and answer every "why is my index not used?" follow-up with confidence.
      
    
      ⏱ 75 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8.0 / 8.4 InnoDBPostgreSQLOracleSQL ServerGATE + product companies
      
  
      

  
       
      ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
      
    
        
      
      • An index is a separate, sorted structure: key → where the row is. It turns "read every page" into "walk 3–4 pages". Price: disk, RAM and extra work on every write.
        • 
      
      • Databases use B+ trees: data only in leaves, leaves linked left↔right, internal nodes hold only separator keys → fanout of hundreds to ~1000 → 3–4 levels for a billion rows. "Fat nodes, flat tree."
        • 
      
      • Clustered index = the table rows themselves stored in key order (max one per table). InnoDB: the table is the PRIMARY KEY B+ tree. PostgreSQL: every index is secondary, pointing into a heap.
        • 
      
      • InnoDB secondary index leaf = (indexed columns + PK). Lookup = secondary tree → PK → clustered tree (two traversals). Hence: keep the PK small, sequential, stable.
        • 
      
      • Composite INDEX(a,b,c) works for leftmost prefixes: (a), (a,b), (a,b,c). The first range is the last seek. Column order rule: Equality → Sort → Range.
        • 
      
      • Covering index = every needed column is in the index → no table lookup → EXPLAIN Using index. ICP = filter on index entries before fetching rows → Using index condition.
        • 
      
      • Index ignored when: function on column, implicit type cast, leading %, OR across columns, not a leftmost prefix, low selectivity, tiny table, stale stats.
        • 
      
      • Hash = equality only. Bitmap = low-cardinality OLAP. Full-text = inverted index. R-tree / GiST = spatial. BRIN = huge, naturally ordered tables. Partial / filtered / INCLUDE = PG / SQL Server extras.
        • 
      
      • "Why not index every column?" → every index is a tax on every write, eats buffer pool, and rarely helps multi-column filters.
        • 
    
      
  
      

  
      ✏️ This is the most-asked DBMS topic after transactions. Expect: "How does an index work?" → "Why B+ tree?" → "Clustered vs non-clustered?" → "Index on (a,b): does WHERE b=? use it?" → "Why is my index not used?"
      

  
  
      📖 Why indexes exist
      
  
      Without an index, finding WHERE email = 'asha@x.com' in a 10-million-row table means reading every page of the table (a full table scan). A database reads disk in whole pages (16 KB in InnoDB — see Chapter 14), so that could be hundreds of thousands of page reads. An index lets the engine jump to the right page in about 3 reads.
      
  
      Think of the index at the back of a textbook. Words are sorted, and each word lists page numbers. You don't read the whole book to find "deadlock". But every time the author adds a paragraph, the index must be updated too, and the index itself takes pages. ← reads get cheap, writes get dearer
      

  
      
    
      Search key
      The column(s) the index is built on (not necessarily a primary key).
      
    
      Index entry
      One (key value, pointer) pair. The pointer is a page/slot address, a rowid, or (in InnoDB) the primary key value.
      
    
      Full table scan
      Reading every page of the table in order. EXPLAIN type = ALL.
      
    
      Index seek / lookup
      Walking the tree from the root to the one leaf that holds the key.
      
    
      Index range scan
      Seek to the start key, then walk sideways along the leaves until the stop key.
      
    
      Fanout
      How many children one internal node points to. Bigger fanout → shorter tree.
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat is an index? Why does it speed up reads but slow down writes?
    
      
      
      What: a separate data structure (a B+ tree in almost every relational database) that keeps the values of some column(s) in sorted order, with a pointer to the row for each value.
      
      
      Why it speeds reads: because the keys are sorted in a very wide, shallow tree, the engine can find any key with about log1000(N) page reads — 3 or 4 even for a billion rows — instead of scanning every page. It also helps ORDER BY (rows already sorted), MIN()/MAX() (look at one end of the tree), joins (look up the matching key) and GROUP BY.
      
      
      Why it slows writes: every INSERT and DELETE, and every UPDATE that changes an indexed column, must also change every affected index: find the right leaf page, insert or remove an entry, sometimes split or merge pages, and write redo/undo log for those changes. A table with 6 indexes does roughly 7 tree modifications per insert.
      
      
      
        
      OperationWithout index (10M rows, ~100k pages)With B+ tree index
      
        
          
      WHERE id = 7Scan up to 100,000 pages~3 page reads (top levels usually cached → ~1 disk read)
      
          
      WHERE created_at BETWEEN … (500 rows)Scan 100,000 pagesSeek + walk a few leaf pages (+ row lookups)
      
          
      INSERT one rowAppend to a pageAppend + update every index (+ possible page splits)
      
              
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      Common mistakes
      Saying "an index stores a copy of the table" — only a clustered index holds full rows; a secondary index holds key + pointer. Saying "indexes always make queries faster" — for a query returning half the table, a full scan is cheaper (see selectivity).
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      An index is a separate sorted structure, usually a B+ tree, that maps column values to row locations. Because the tree is very wide and only three or four levels deep, the database can find a key in a few page reads instead of scanning the whole table, and it also gets sorted order for free. The cost is that every insert, delete, and update of an indexed column must also update each index, and the indexes take disk space and buffer-pool memory.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
      
        
      ↪Which columns would you index first in a new table?
          
      The primary key (automatic), columns used in JOIN … ON (foreign keys — InnoDB creates an index on FK columns automatically if none exists), columns in frequent, selective WHERE filters, and columns used in ORDER BY … LIMIT. Design composite indexes from the real queries, not one index per column.
      
        
      ↪Does an UPDATE always touch every index?
          
      No. Only indexes containing a column that changed. UPDATE orders SET amount = 99 WHERE id = 7 touches the clustered index only (if amount is not in a secondary index). In InnoDB, changing the primary key touches every index, because the PK is stored in all of them.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      📓 Textbook classification: dense, sparse, primary, clustering, secondary, multilevel
      
  
      University exams and GATE use the Silberschatz / Navathe vocabulary. Product companies use the engine vocabulary (clustered / non-clustered). Know both, and know where they differ.
      

  
      
    
      Dense index
        
      
      • One index entry for every search-key value (or every record).
        • 
      
      • Works whether or not the file is sorted on that key.
        • 
      
      • Bigger, but can answer "does key X exist?" from the index alone.
        • 
      
      • Secondary indexes must be dense.
        • 
    
      
    
      Sparse index
        
      
      • Entries for only some key values — typically one per data block (the block's first key).
        • 
      
      • Works only if the file is sorted on the search key.
        • 
      
      • To find key K: find the largest entry ≤ K, go to that block, scan it.
        • 
      
      • Much smaller. The internal levels of a B+ tree are sparse indexes.
        • 
    
      
  
      

  

  
      
    
      Textbook termMeaningDense / sparse?How many per file?
      
    
      
      Primary indexIndex on the ordering key field of a sorted file, where that field is unique (a key)Usually sparse (one entry per block)At most one
      
      
      Clustering indexIndex on the ordering field of a sorted file where that field is not unique (e.g. dept_id); one entry per distinct value, pointing at the first block holding itSparseAt most one (and not together with a primary index)
      
      
      Secondary indexIndex on any non-ordering field (unique or not)Must be denseMany
      
      
      Multilevel indexThe index itself is too big, so build a sparse index on the index, and again, until the top fits in one blockOuter levels sparse— (a B+ tree is a dynamic multilevel index)
      
          
  
      

  
      🚫
      Terminology trap
      Textbook "primary index" means "index on the field the file is physically sorted by". It does not automatically mean "the index on the PRIMARY KEY". In InnoDB both meanings coincide (the PK is the clustering key). In PostgreSQL they don't: the PK index is a secondary index over an unsorted heap. If an interviewer says "primary index", ask which meaning they want — that alone sounds senior.
      

  
      
    QDense vs sparse index — and why must a secondary index be dense?
    
      
      
      A dense index has an entry for every search-key value; a sparse index has an entry for only some values (usually one per block). Sparse lookup relies on "find the nearest smaller entry, then scan forward inside the block". That only works if the records are physically sorted by the key. A secondary index is on a column the file is not sorted by, so the record with key 50 could be in any block — skipping a key would lose it. Hence secondary indexes must be dense.
      
      
      🧠
      Memory aid
      "Secondary = dense; upper levels = sparse." And: one table, one physical order → one clustering index.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A dense index has one entry per key value, a sparse index has one entry per block. Sparse indexes are smaller but only work when the file is sorted on that key, because we find the closest lower entry and scan forward. A secondary index is on an unsorted column, so it must be dense. The upper levels of a B+ tree are exactly sparse indexes over the level below.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions
      
        
      ↪GATE: a file has 30,000 records, 10 records per block, sorted on the key. How many entries in a sparse primary index? In a dense one?
          
      Blocks = 30,000 / 10 = 3,000 → sparse index has 3,000 entries (one per block). Dense index has 30,000 entries. If 100 index entries fit per block, the sparse index needs 30 blocks; binary search over it costs ⌈log₂ 30⌉ = 5 block reads, plus 1 data block = 6. A second index level over those 30 blocks (1 block) reduces it to 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 reads — that is why we build multilevel indexes.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🌳 B-tree vs B+ tree: the structure behind (almost) every index
      
  
      A B-tree is a balanced, multi-way search tree (not binary!). Every node is one disk page and holds many keys, so the tree is wide and short, and every leaf is at the same depth. A B+ tree is a B-tree variant with two changes that matter enormously for databases:
      
  
        
    
      1. All data (rows or row pointers) lives only in the leaves. Internal nodes hold only separator keys and child pointers, so they are tiny per entry → more entries per page → huge fanout.
        2. 
    
      2. Leaves are linked to their neighbours (InnoDB: doubly linked). A range scan finds the first leaf, then just walks sideways.
        3. 
  
      
  
      InnoDB, SQL Server, Oracle, Db2, SQLite and PostgreSQL's default index all use B+ trees. MySQL's docs simply say "B-tree" — they mean a B+ tree.
      

  

  
      
    
      B-tree (textbook)B+ tree
      
    
      
      Where data / row pointers liveIn every nodeOnly in leaves
      
      
      Internal node contentkeys + data + child pointersseparator keys + child pointers
      
      
      FanoutLower (data takes space)✔ Higher → shallower tree
      
      
      Range scanIn-order walk up and down levels✔ Seek once, then follow leaf links
      
      
      Search costVaries (may stop early at an internal node)Always root → leaf (predictable)
      
      
      Keys repeated?No, each key appears onceYes, separators copy leaf keys
      
      
      Used bySome file systems / KV stores, textbooksInnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server, SQLite
      
          
  
      

  
      
    QWhy do databases use B+ trees and not hash tables, binary search trees, or plain B-trees?
    
      
      
      The real constraint: data lives on disk/SSD and is read in pages. The best structure is the one that needs the fewest page reads for the queries people actually run: equality, ranges, sorting, prefix matches.
      
      
      
        
      #️⃣
      vs Hash table
      O(1) equality, but no ranges (<, BETWEEN), no ORDER BY, no LIKE 'ab%', no leftmost-prefix use of a composite key, and no estimate of "how many rows between X and Y" for the optimizer.
      
        
      🌲
      vs BST / AVL / red-black
      Fanout 2 → ~30 levels for 10⁹ keys, and each level may be a separate random disk read. A node holds 1 key but a page is 16 KB: wasted I/O.
      
        
      🌳
      vs B-tree
      Data in internal nodes lowers fanout (deeper tree), and range scans bounce between levels. B+ keeps internals compact (cacheable) and leaves sequential.
      
        
      📜
      vs Sorted array
      Binary search is fine for reads, but every insert shifts half the file. A B+ tree changes one page (plus an occasional split).
      
      
      
      
      ℹ️
      Index lookup = 3 steps (Use The Index, Luke)
      (1) Tree traversal — bounded by height, cheap. (2) Following the leaf chain — unbounded: depends on how many entries match. (3) Fetching table rows — unbounded, often random I/O. When an "indexed query" is slow, it is almost always step 2 or 3, never step 1.
      
      
      🚫
      Answer that fails interviews
      "The index became unbalanced, so we rebuilt it." B+ trees are always height-balanced by construction. A rebuild can reclaim half-empty pages, but it does not fix a bad access path.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      Databases read whole pages, so we want the fewest page reads. A B+ tree puts hundreds of keys in each page, so even a billion rows need only three or four levels, and the top levels stay in memory. Because data lives only in linked leaves, a range query seeks once and then walks sideways. A hash index can't do ranges or sorting, and a binary tree would be about thirty levels deep, so the B+ tree is the best general-purpose choice.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions
      
        
      ↪Then why do some systems use LSM-trees instead?
          
      LSM-trees (RocksDB, Cassandra, MyRocks) turn random writes into sequential appends plus background compaction, so they win on write-heavy workloads and compress better. B+ trees win on read latency. See Chapter 14 for the full comparison.
      
        
      ↪Is the B+ tree in memory or on disk?
          
      On disk, as pages. Pages are cached in the buffer pool. In practice the root and internal levels are always cached (they are small), so a lookup usually costs about one physical read — the leaf — or zero if the leaf is hot.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Height and fanout: do the arithmetic out loud
      
  
      Fanout ≈ page size ÷ (separator key size + child pointer + per-record overhead). An InnoDB page is 16 KB. With a BIGINT key (8 B) + 4-byte page number + ~5 B header ≈ 16–17 B per entry → roughly 1,000 children per internal page. Each level multiplies capacity by the fanout.
      
  
      
    
      IndexLeaf capacityLevels for 10⁹ entriesSize of internal levels
      
    
      
      Narrow secondary index (BIGINT key + PK)~1,000 entries / leaf10⁹ → 10⁶ leaves → 10³ → 1 root = 3 levels~1,001 pages ≈ 16 MB (always cached)
      
      
      Clustered index, ~150-byte rows~100 rows / leaf (15/16 of 16 KB)10⁹ → 10⁷ leaves → 10⁴ → 10 → 1 = 4 levels~10,011 pages ≈ 160 MB (cacheable)
      
      
      Balanced binary tree (for contrast)1 key / nodelog₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30 levels—
      
          
  
      
  
      Jeremy Cole measured real InnoDB pages with an INT primary key: ~1,203 pointers per internal page, so height 3 holds ~677 million rows and height 4 holds hundreds of billions. "Most tables with sensible primary keys are 2 to 3 levels deep." ← 1000³ = a billion
      
  
      💡
      So what does one lookup cost?
      Point lookup by PK on 1 B rows: 4 page visits, but only the leaf is likely a real disk read. Secondary-index lookup in InnoDB: ~3 levels in the secondary tree + ~4 in the clustered tree = ~7 page visits, ~2 physical reads. This is why covering indexes matter (they skip the second tree).
      

  
      GATE corner: order of a B+ tree from block size
      
  
      GATE gives block size B, key size K, block (child) pointer P, record (data) pointer Pr, and asks for the order. Use the definition "order p = max child pointers in an internal node". Read the question carefully: some papers define order as max keys, or as the minimum (Knuth/Cormen style).
      
  
        
    
      1. Internal node holds p child pointers and p − 1 keys: p·P + (p − 1)·K ≤ B.
        2. 
    
      2. Leaf node holds pleaf (key, record pointer) pairs plus one next-leaf pointer: p_leaf·(K + Pr) + P ≤ B.
        3. 
    
      3. Take the largest integer that satisfies each inequality.
        4. 
  
      
  
      Internal:  6p + 9(p − 1) ≤ 512   →  15p ≤ 521  →  p = 34
Leaf:      p_leaf(9 + 7) + 6 ≤ 512  →  16·p_leaf ≤ 506  →  p_leaf = 31

Capacity if nodes are ~69% full (avg 23 pointers internal, 21 entries per leaf):
  root          1 node      23 pointers
  level 1      23 nodes    529 pointers
  level 2     529 nodes  12,167 pointers
  leaves   12,167 nodes × 21 entries = 255,507 record pointers   (3 internal levels + leaves)

Min occupancy (non-root): internal ⌈p/2⌉ = 17 children; leaf ⌈p_leaf/2⌉ = 16 keys.
      
  
      ⚠️
      GATE traps
      (1) Forgetting the next-leaf pointer in the leaf formula. (2) Using record pointers in internal nodes (they hold block pointers only). (3) Rounding up instead of down. (4) For a B-tree (not B+) every node also stores record pointers: p·P + (p − 1)(K + Pr) ≤ B. Same example gives 6p + 16(p − 1) ≤ 512 → 22p ≤ 528 → p = 24 — lower fanout, exactly why B+ wins.
      
  
      🧠
      Height bounds
      For N keys and order n, height ≤ ⌈log⌈n/2⌉ N⌉ (worst case: half-full nodes) and ≥ ⌈logn N⌉ (best case: full nodes). Silberschatz example: 1 M keys, n = 100 → at most ~4 node visits (log₅₀ 10⁶ ≈ 3.5), vs ~20 for a balanced binary tree.
      

  
      Search, insert (split) and delete (merge)
      
  
      
    
      
    
      
      
        
        
      1. Start at the root. Binary-search the separator keys inside the page.
        2. 
        
      2. Follow the child pointer for the interval that contains the key (key < first separator → leftmost child, and so on).
        3. 
        
      3. Repeat until you reach a leaf. Cost = height (usually 3–4 pages).
        4. 
        
      4. In the leaf, binary-search for the key. For a range (BETWEEN 40 AND 70), keep reading entries and follow the next-leaf pointer until a key exceeds 70.
        5. 
      
      
    
      
    
      
      
        
        
      1. Search for the leaf where the key belongs and insert it in sorted position.
        2. 
        
      2. If the leaf overflows, split it into two leaves (about half each) and copy the first key of the new right leaf up into the parent as a separator. (It stays in the leaf too, because leaves hold all keys.)
        3. 
        
      3. If the parent overflows, split it as well, but now the middle key is moved (pushed) up, not copied.
        4. 
        
      4. If the root splits, a new root is created: the tree grows at the top, so all leaves stay at the same depth. Height + 1.
        5. 
      
      
    
      
    
      
      
        
        
      1. Search for the leaf and remove the entry.
        2. 
        
      2. If the leaf drops below the minimum fill (textbook: half full; InnoDB: MERGE_THRESHOLD, default 50%), first try to borrow (redistribute) an entry from a sibling and update the parent's separator.
        3. 
        
      3. If the sibling is also at minimum, merge the two leaves and remove the separator from the parent.
        4. 
        
      4. Merges can cascade up. If the root ends up with a single child, that child becomes the new root: height − 1.
        5. 
      
      
      
      In practice many engines are lazy here: InnoDB first delete-marks records (MVCC needs old versions) and the background purge thread removes them later.
      
    
      
  
      

  

  
      
    QWhat is a page split and why is it bad for performance?
    
      
      
      Inserting into a full page forces the engine to allocate a new page, move about half the entries to it, and update the parent. Costs: extra page writes and redo log, a short latch on the affected pages, and two half-empty pages instead of one full one — so the index uses more pages per row and the buffer pool caches fewer rows.
      
      
      Who causes them: random keys (UUIDv4, hashed values, emails) insert all over the tree, splitting pages everywhere and leaving them ~50–70% full. Sequential keys (AUTO_INCREMENT, timestamps) always insert at the right edge; InnoDB detects this pattern and fills pages to about 15/16 before starting a new page.
      
      
      ℹ️
      Fill factor
      InnoDB leaves 1/16 of each page free for future updates (so ~93% full). PostgreSQL B-tree fillfactor defaults to 90. Lower fill factor = fewer splits for update-heavy tables but more pages. Details in Chapter 14.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A page split happens when we insert into a full B+ tree page: the engine creates a new page, moves half the entries, and adds a separator to the parent. It costs extra writes and leaves pages half empty, which wastes cache. Random keys like UUIDv4 cause splits all over the tree, while sequential keys like auto-increment only append at the right edge, which is why InnoDB prefers sequential primary keys.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🔑 Hash indexes vs B+ tree indexes
      
  
      A hash index runs the key through a hash function to get a bucket number, and stores (key, pointer) in that bucket. Lookup = hash the search value, go to the bucket: O(1) on average, no tree walk.
      
  
      
    
      #️⃣ Hash index
        
      
      • ✔ = and <=> only, very fast.
        • 
      
      • ✘ No <, >, BETWEEN, LIKE 'ab%'.
        • 
      
      • ✘ No ORDER BY, no MIN/MAX.
        • 
      
      • ✘ Only the whole key can be used — no leftmost-prefix of a composite key.
        • 
      
      • ✘ Optimizer cannot estimate "rows between two values".
        • 
    
      
    
      🌳 B+ tree index
        
      
      • ✔ Equality and ranges, prefix LIKE, IS NULL.
        • 
      
      • ✔ Sorted order → ORDER BY / GROUP BY / MIN / MAX.
        • 
      
      • ✔ Leftmost prefixes of composite keys.
        • 
      
      • ✔ Range estimates via index dives.
        • 
      
      • ~ O(logf N) — 3–4 pages, mostly cached.
        • 
    
      
  
      
  
      🔀
      Where hash indexes actually exist
      MySQL MEMORY engine: HASH is the default index type (BTREE also allowed). InnoDB: user-defined indexes are always B+ trees — writing USING HASH silently gives you a BTREE. InnoDB has only the internal Adaptive Hash Index (AHI): it watches hot B+ tree lookups and builds an in-memory hash on key prefixes to skip the tree descent. It can cause latch contention, and in MySQL 8.4 it is OFF by default (it was ON in 8.0). PostgreSQL: CREATE INDEX … USING hash exists (stores 32-bit hash codes, equality only; crash-safe since PG 10), but B-tree is usually just as good. Hash joins build temporary hash tables at query time — a different thing from a hash index (see Chapter 16).
      
  
      
    QWhen is a hash index better than a B+ tree?
    
      
      
      Only for pure exact-match lookups on in-memory data, where O(1) vs O(log N) matters and you never need ranges or sorting: session tables, caches, key-value lookups (MEMORY tables, Redis-style stores). For a general OLTP table the B+ tree is almost always the better choice, because real queries mix equality, ranges, sorting and composite prefixes — and B+ tree internal pages are cached, so the "log N" is about one real I/O anyway.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A hash index gives constant-time equality lookups, but it can't do ranges, sorting, prefix matching or leftmost-prefix use of a composite key, and it gives the optimizer no range estimates. So it only wins for pure in-memory point lookups. InnoDB only supports B+ tree indexes for users; it builds an adaptive hash index internally for hot pages, and that is disabled by default in MySQL 8.4.
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      🗄️ Clustered vs non-clustered (secondary) indexes
      
  
      A clustered index decides the physical order of the rows: its leaf pages are the table. A non-clustered (secondary) index is a separate tree whose leaves hold the key plus a pointer to the row. Rows can be physically sorted only one way, so a table has at most one clustered index, and any number of secondary ones.
      
  
      Analogy: a phone book sorted by surname is the data (clustered). A separate card file sorted by phone number that says "see surname Sharma" is non-clustered. You can have many card files, but the book itself has only one order.
      

  

  
      CREATE TABLE users (
  id    BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,
  email VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  city  VARCHAR(64)  NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),            -- clustered: leaves hold full rows, ordered by id
  UNIQUE KEY uk_email (email), -- secondary: leaf = (email, id)
  KEY idx_city (city)          -- secondary: leaf = (city, id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
      

  
      
    QClustered vs non-clustered index — explain with InnoDB.
    
      
      
      Clustered: in InnoDB the table is a B+ tree on the primary key. Leaf pages store the complete rows (plus hidden columns DB_TRX_ID and DB_ROLL_PTR for MVCC), sorted by PK. So WHERE id = 7 is one traversal, and WHERE id BETWEEN 100 AND 200 reads physically adjacent rows — very fast.
      
      
      Secondary: every other index is a separate B+ tree whose leaf entries are (indexed columns, primary key columns). Finding a row through it takes two traversals: secondary → PK → clustered. This second step is called a bookmark lookup / "back to table" (回表 in Chinese blogs).
      
      
        
        
      • Why store the PK and not a physical address? Rows move inside the clustered tree when pages split or merge. If secondary indexes stored physical addresses, every split would have to update every secondary index. Storing the PK makes secondary indexes immune to row movement.
        • 
        
      • Consequence 1: a long PK is copied into every secondary index → keep it short.
        • 
        
      • Consequence 2: PK columns are "free" in every secondary index → SELECT id FROM users WHERE city = 'Pune' is covered by idx_city.
        • 
        
      • Consequence 3: changing a PK value moves the row and rewrites every secondary entry → keep the PK stable.
        • 
      
      
      
      🔀
      Engine differences
      SQL Server: a PRIMARY KEY creates a clustered index by default unless one already exists (you can write PRIMARY KEY NONCLUSTERED); nonclustered indexes point to the clustering key, or to an 8-byte RID (file:page:slot) in a heap table. Oracle: heap tables by default (indexes store a rowid); an index-organized table (ORGANIZATION INDEX) is clustered on the PK, and its secondary indexes use a "logical rowid" = PK + a physical guess. PostgreSQL: no clustered indexes at all — see below.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      A clustered index stores the rows themselves in key order, so there can be only one per table. In InnoDB the primary key is the clustered index, and the table literally is that B+ tree. Secondary indexes are separate trees whose leaves store the indexed columns plus the primary key, so a lookup through a secondary index finds the primary key first and then searches the clustered index, which is two traversals. That's why the primary key should be small and stable, and why covering indexes are so valuable.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions
      
        
      ↪How many clustered indexes can a table have? Can it have zero?
          
      At most one, because the rows can be in only one physical order. Zero is possible in PostgreSQL, SQL Server heaps and Oracle heap tables. An InnoDB table always has exactly one, even if you don't define a PK (next question).
      
        
      ↪Is a clustered index always faster than a secondary one?
          
      For fetching full rows by key or by key range, yes. But a covering secondary index can beat it: its leaves are much narrower (only a few columns), so a scan reads far fewer pages. SELECT COUNT(*) in InnoDB scans the smallest secondary index for exactly that reason.
      
        
      ↪Why can a "covering" InnoDB query sometimes still visit the clustered index?
          
      MVCC. Secondary entries have no transaction id. If the entry is delete-marked or its page was changed by a transaction newer than your read view, InnoDB must visit the clustered record (which has DB_TRX_ID and the undo pointer) to decide what you are allowed to see. See Chapter 13.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      
    QWhat happens if an InnoDB table has no primary key?
    
      
      
        
        
      1. InnoDB uses the first UNIQUE index whose columns are all NOT NULL as the clustered index.
        2. 
        
      2. If there is none, it creates a hidden clustered index GEN_CLUST_INDEX on a hidden 6-byte, monotonically increasing DB_ROW_ID. You cannot query it, and the counter is shared across all such tables in the instance.
        3. 
        
      3. 8.0.30+ With sql_generate_invisible_primary_key = ON (default OFF), MySQL instead adds a real invisible PK column my_row_id BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT (GIPK), which tools and replication can use.
        4. 
      
      
      
      ⚠️
      Why "no PK" hurts in production
      Row-based replication must find each changed row on the replica; without a usable key that can mean a full scan per row event. Online schema-change tools and clusters (Group Replication requires a PK) also depend on it. Always declare a primary key.
      
    
      
  
      

  
      PostgreSQL: heap tables, ctid, index-only scans and HOT
      
  
      PostgreSQL stores rows in an unordered heap. Every index — including the primary key — is a secondary index whose entries point to a TID / ctid = (page number, item number). So every index lookup is "index → heap", but the second step is a direct jump to one page, not a second tree walk.
      
  
      
    
      🐬 InnoDB
        
      
      • Table = clustered B+ tree on PK.
        • 
      
      • Secondary leaf → PK value → second traversal.
        • 
      
      • PK range scans read contiguous rows (great).
        • 
      
      • Row moves on split: secondaries unaffected.
        • 
      
      • Updating a non-indexed column: in place in the clustered leaf; old version goes to undo.
        • 
    
      
    
      🐘 PostgreSQL
        
      
      • Table = heap (insertion order, roughly).
        • 
      
      • Every index leaf → ctid → one heap page fetch.
        • 
      
      • CLUSTER reorders the heap once; later writes are not kept in order.
        • 
      
      • An UPDATE writes a new tuple version (new ctid) → normally every index needs a new entry…
        • 
      
      • …unless it's a HOT update (below).
        • 
    
      
  
      
  
      
    
      Index-only scan (PG)
      Answer from the index without visiting the heap. Possible only if the page's bit in the visibility map says "all tuples visible to everyone". Otherwise PG must check the heap; EXPLAIN shows Heap Fetches: N. Frequent VACUUM keeps the visibility map fresh.
      
    
      HOT (heap-only tuple) update
      If the UPDATE changes no indexed column and the new version fits on the same heap page, no new index entries are created; the old line pointer redirects to the new version. Fewer indexes → more HOT updates; a lower table fillfactor leaves room for them.
      
    
      INCLUDE columns
      CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id) INCLUDE (amount); — amount is stored in the leaf as payload (not part of the search key) to make the index covering.
      
  
      

  
      
    
      InnoDB (MySQL)PostgreSQLOracleSQL Server
      
    
      
      Default table storageClustered on PKHeapHeap (IOT optional)Clustered on PK by default; heap if no clustered index
      
      
      Secondary index points toPK valuectid (page, item)rowid (heap) / logical rowid (IOT)Clustering key / RID (heap)
      
      
      No PK?First UNIQUE NOT NULL, else hidden DB_ROW_ID (or GIPK)Fine (heap)Fine (heap)Heap
      
      
      Covering extrasPK columns free in every secondaryINCLUDE + visibility mapColumns in indexINCLUDE
      
          
  
      
  
      🧠 "InnoDB: the table IS the index"
      InnoDB: Secondary → PK → row (two hops through trees). Postgres: index → ctid → heap (hop to an address).
      

  
  
      🎟️ Choosing the primary key: AUTO_INCREMENT vs UUID vs UUIDv7 vs Snowflake
      
  
      In InnoDB the PK is the clustered key and is copied into every secondary index, so PK choice is an indexing decision. The rule: Small, Sequential, Stable (the 3 S's).
      
  
      
    
      PK typeSizeInsert patternProsCons
      
    
      
      BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT8 B (INT: 4 B)Always the rightmost leaf; pages ~15/16 fullSmallest, fastest, cache-friendlyGuessable (/orders/1001 leaks volume), needs one central generator → awkward across shards
      
      
      UUIDv4 as CHAR(36)36 B+ (more under utf8mb4)Random leaf every timeGlobally unique, generate anywhereWorst: 9× bigger than INT in every index, page splits everywhere, ~50% fill, slow string comparisons
