      UUIDv4 as BINARY(16)16 BStill randomHalf the size of CHAR(36)Still random inserts and splits
      
      
      Time-ordered UUID (UUIDv7, or MySQL UUID_TO_BIN(UUID(), 1)) in BINARY(16)16 BNear the right edge (time in the high bits)Globally unique and mostly sequential2× a BIGINT; leaks creation time
      
      
      Snowflake ID (Twitter-style)8 BRoughly increasingBIGINT size, generated per node without coordinationNeeds a generator service/library and unique worker ids; clock-skew care
      
          
  
      
  
      
    
      UUIDv7
      RFC 9562 (2024): 48-bit Unix-millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits + random bits. Sorts by creation time. PostgreSQL 18 has uuidv7(); in MySQL generate it in the application (MySQL's UUID() returns version 1).
      
    
      UUID_TO_BIN(u, 1)
      MySQL 8.0 function that converts a UUID string to 16 bytes; the 1 swaps the time-low and time-high parts of a version-1 UUID so values become roughly sequential. Reverse with BIN_TO_UUID(b, 1). It does not make UUIDv4 sequential.
      
    
      Snowflake
      64-bit: 1 sign bit + 41-bit millisecond timestamp + 10-bit machine id + 12-bit per-ms sequence.
      
  
      
  
      CREATE TABLE orders (
  id         BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT,  -- internal, used in joins and FKs
  public_id  BINARY(16)      NOT NULL,                 -- UUIDv7 from the app, shown in URLs/APIs
  customer_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  created_at DATETIME        NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id),
  UNIQUE KEY uk_public (public_id),
  KEY idx_cust_created (customer_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
      
  
      
    QAuto-increment or UUID as the primary key in MySQL? Defend your choice.
    
      
      
      Size math: 1 billion rows, 5 secondary indexes → the PK is stored 6 times per row. BIGINT: 6 × 8 B × 10⁹ = 48 GB. BINARY(16): 96 GB. CHAR(36): 216 GB (Percona's figure) — just for key copies. Bigger keys also lower the fanout of every internal page.
      
      
      Insert math: with AUTO_INCREMENT, every insert hits the same hot rightmost page, already in memory. With UUIDv4, each insert lands on a random leaf among millions — once the index is bigger than the buffer pool, that is a disk read per insert, plus frequent splits that leave pages half empty. Percona measured roughly 2 I/Os per insert in that state.
      
      
      🌍
      Production story
      A payments team used CHAR(36) UUIDv4 PKs. Insert throughput was fine for months, then collapsed when the table outgrew the buffer pool: every insert became a random read + page split. Switching new tables to BIGINT internal PK + BINARY(16) UUIDv7 public id cut index size by ~60% and restored throughput.
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      In InnoDB I prefer a BIGINT auto-increment primary key, because the primary key is the clustered index and is copied into every secondary index, so small and sequential keys keep every index compact and inserts append at the right edge. A random UUIDv4 causes page splits all over the tree and bloats every index. If I need globally unique or non-guessable ids, I use a time-ordered UUIDv7 stored as BINARY(16), or keep a BIGINT internal key plus a separate unique public UUID column.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions
      
        
      ↪Does the PK choice matter as much in PostgreSQL?
          
      Less, because PG's table is a heap: rows are appended regardless of PK value, and other indexes store a ctid, not the PK. But the PK index itself still suffers random inserts with UUIDv4 (scattered leaf pages, more WAL from full-page writes), so UUIDv7 still helps.
      
        
      ↪Natural key (email, PAN, phone) as PK?
          
      Usually no: they are long, they can change (people change emails), and a change cascades into every FK and every secondary index. Use a surrogate PK and a UNIQUE constraint on the natural key.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
  
      ⛓️ Composite indexes and the leftmost-prefix rule
      
  
      A composite (multi-column) index on (a, b, c) is one B+ tree whose entries are sorted by a, then by b within equal a, then by c within equal (a, b) — exactly like a phone book sorted by (surname, first name). You can find "Sharma" or "Sharma, Priya" quickly, but not "everyone named Priya": the Priyas are scattered across every surname.
      

  

  
      The big truth table for INDEX(a, b, c)
      
  
      
    
      WHERE / ORDER BYSeek usesNotes
      
    
      
      a = 1✔ aref
      
      
      a = 1 AND b = 2✔ a, bref
      
      
      a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3✔ a, b, cref (const/eq_ref if UNIQUE)
      
      
      b = 2 AND a = 1✔ a, bOrder of conditions in WHERE does not matter
      
      
      b = 2✘ no seekNot a leftmost prefix. Maybe full index scan if covering, or skip scan (8.0.13+)
      
      
      b = 2 AND c = 3✘ no seekSame as above
      
      
      a = 1 AND c = 3~ a onlyGap at b: c is only filtered (via ICP)
      
      
      a > 1 AND b = 2~ a (range)First range stops the seek; b only filtered
      
      
      a = 1 AND b > 2 AND c = 3~ a, b (range)c filtered (ICP)
      
      
      a = 1 AND b IN (2, 5) AND c = 3✔ a, b, cIN = several equality ranges, so c still usable
      
      
      a LIKE 'ab%' AND b = 2~ a (range)Prefix LIKE is a range
      
      
      a LIKE '%ab'✘Leading wildcard
      
      
      a = 1 OR b = 2✘ (this index alone)Needs index merge with a separate index on b, or UNION
      
      
      a = 1 ORDER BY b✔ a + orderNo filesort
      
      
      a = 1 ORDER BY c~ aFilesort: b sits between
      
      
      a IN (1, 2) ORDER BY b~ aFilesort: two runs break the global b order
      
      
      ORDER BY a DESC, b DESCorderBackward index scan
      
      
      ORDER BY a ASC, b DESCorder only with INDEX(a ASC, b DESC)Descending indexes, 8.0+
      
          
  
      

  
      
    QI have an index on (a, b). Does WHERE b = 5 use it?
    
      
      
      Not for a normal seek. The index is sorted by a first, so all the b = 5 entries are scattered across every value of a; there is no single range to jump to. What can still happen:
      
      
        
        
      1. Full index scan (type = index, Using where; Using index) if the query is covered by (a, b): reading the narrow index is cheaper than reading the whole table.
        2. 
        
      2. Skip scan MySQL 8.0.13+ (Using index for skip scan): for each distinct value of a, do a small range scan for b. Conditions include: query is covering, single table, no GROUP BY/DISTINCT, and a range/equality on b. Good only when a has few distinct values. PostgreSQL 18 and Oracle also have skip scans.
        3. 
        
      3. The real fix: an index that starts with b, e.g. INDEX(b) or INDEX(b, a).
        4. 
      
      
      
      CREATE TABLE t (a INT NOT NULL, b INT NOT NULL, c INT, INDEX idx_ab (a, b));
EXPLAIN SELECT a, b FROM t WHERE b = 5;   -- covering
-- type: range   key: idx_ab   Extra: Using where; Using index for skip scan   (if a has few values)
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM t WHERE b = 5;      -- not covering (needs c)
-- type: ALL     key: NULL     Extra: Using where
      
      
      🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
      No, not for a seek, because a composite index is sorted by its first column first, so b values are spread across all values of a. That's the leftmost-prefix rule. If the query only needs a and b, MySQL may scan the whole index or, since 8.0.13, use a skip scan when a has few distinct values. The proper fix is an index that begins with b.
      
      
      
        
      ↪ Cross-questions
      
        
      ↪Does the order of conditions in the WHERE clause matter?
          
      No. WHERE b = 2 AND a = 1 and WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 are identical to the optimizer. The order of columns in the index is what matters.
      
        
      ↪INDEX(a) and INDEX(b) separately — same as INDEX(a, b)?
          
      No. For a = 1 AND b = 2 the optimizer picks one of them (or an index merge intersection, which reads both and intersects row ids — usually slower than one composite seek). A composite index finds exactly the matching entries in one seek.
      
        
      ↪How do you see how many columns of a composite index were used?
          
      key_len in EXPLAIN: add up the byte widths of the leading columns (INT 4, BIGINT 8, DATETIME 5, VARCHAR(n) utf8mb4 = 4n + 2, +1 if nullable). Try the calculator in Chapter 16.
      
      
      
    
      
  
      

  
      Choosing column order: Equality → Sort → Range
      
  
      🧠 E · S · R
      Equality columns first (any order among themselves) → Sort column next (so ORDER BY reads in index order and LIMIT stops early) → Range column last (anything after the first range is only filtered). Then optionally append SELECT columns to make it covering. "The first range is the last seek."
      
  
      SELECT id, created_at, amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'PAID' AND created_at >= '2026-10-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;

-- ❌ INDEX(created_at, customer_id, status): range first → scans every order since Oct-1 (all customers),
--    customer_id/status only filtered
-- ❌ INDEX(customer_id, created_at, status): status sits after the range → only filtered
-- ✅ INDEX(customer_id, status, created_at): E, E, then S/R on the same column
--    → seek to (42,'PAID','2026-10-01'), read backwards, stop after 20 rows, no filesort
-- ⭐ INDEX(customer_id, status, created_at, amount): + covering (id is the PK, free) → Using index
      
  
      🚫
      Myth: "Always put the most selective column first"
      For pure equality queries, the order barely changes the cost — the seek lands on the same entries. When a range is involved, equality-before-range beats selectivity every time (Use The Index, Luke shows two orders with identical selectivity where one is many times faster). Choose order by (1) E-S-R and (2) which prefixes other queries can reuse.
      

  
      
    
      🧪 Leftmost-prefix checker — INDEX idx_cs (customer_id, status, created_at) on orders
      
    
      Pick a condition for each column and an ORDER BY. The checker predicts which columns are used to seek, which are only filtered, the EXPLAIN type, key_len and whether a filesort is needed. (Column widths: customer_id INT NOT NULL = 4, status VARCHAR(16) utf8mb4 NOT NULL = 66, created_at DATETIME NOT NULL = 5.)
      
    
      
    
      
    
      
    
        
  
        
  
  

  
  
        🎯 Covering indexes, Index Condition Pushdown & index merge
        

  
        
    QWhat is a covering index and why is it so fast in InnoDB?
    
        
      
        What: an index that contains every column the query needs — in WHERE, SELECT, JOIN, ORDER BY and GROUP BY. The engine answers from the index alone and never visits the table rows. EXPLAIN shows Extra: Using index (PostgreSQL: Index Only Scan).
        
      
        Why it is fast: in InnoDB a secondary lookup normally costs a second B+ tree traversal per row (into the clustered index), and those are random reads. For 10,000 matching rows that is 10,000 extra probes. A covering index removes all of them. Its leaves are also narrow, so many entries fit per page.
        
      
        -- Hot query on the order-history page
SELECT id, created_at, amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;

ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_cust_created_amt (customer_id, created_at, amount);
-- id is the PK → already inside every secondary entry, no need to add it

EXPLAIN SELECT id, created_at, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
        

        type: ref   key: idx_cust_created_amt   key_len: 4   ref: const   rows: 120
Extra: Backward index scan; Using index        <-- no table access, no filesort
        
      
        ⚠️
        Don't overdo it
        Every extra column makes the index wider: more pages, more buffer pool, more write work, and the index must be updated when those columns change. Cover only hot, latency-critical queries. Adding id explicitly to an InnoDB secondary index "to cover it" is redundant (it's already there).
        
      
        🔀
        INCLUDE columns
        PostgreSQL (B-tree, GiST, SP-GiST) and SQL Server let you add non-key payload columns: CREATE INDEX ix ON orders (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (amount);. They are stored only in the leaves and don't affect sort order or uniqueness. MySQL has no INCLUDE — you append the columns to the key instead. PostgreSQL index-only scans also need the visibility map to say the heap page is all-visible.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        A covering index contains every column a query needs, so the database answers from the index alone, shown as Using index in EXPLAIN. In InnoDB that matters a lot, because otherwise every row found through a secondary index needs a second lookup in the clustered index. The primary key is stored in every secondary index, so it is covered for free. I use covering indexes for hot queries but keep them narrow, because each extra column adds write and memory cost.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is Index Condition Pushdown (ICP)? How is it different from a covering index?
    
        
      
        
        
        Without ICP
          
          
        • Storage engine uses the index only for the seek part.
          • 
          
        • For every entry in the range it fetches the full row from the clustered index.
          • 
          
        • The server then applies the rest of the WHERE and throws most rows away.
          • 
        
        
        
        With ICP (default on)
          
          
        • Conditions that use only index columns are pushed down into InnoDB.
          • 
          
        • InnoDB tests them on the index entry first.
          • 
          
        • Only entries that pass cost a row fetch → far fewer random reads.
          • 
        
        
      
        
      
        SELECT * FROM people
WHERE zipcode = '95054'
  AND lastname LIKE '%etrunia%'       -- leading % → cannot be part of the seek…
  AND address LIKE '%Main Street%';   -- …but CAN be checked on the index entry (ICP)
-- EXPLAIN Extra: Using index condition; Using where
        
      
          
        
        • Using index = covering: rows are never fetched.
          • 
        
        • Using index condition = ICP: rows are fetched, but fewer of them.
          • 
        
        • ICP applies only to secondary indexes in InnoDB (the clustered index already contains the row), to range, ref, eq_ref, ref_or_null access, and cannot push subqueries or stored functions. Switch: optimizer_switch='index_condition_pushdown=off' or hint NO_ICP.
          • 
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is index merge? Can MySQL use two indexes on one table?
    
        
      
        Yes — type = index_merge. MySQL scans several single-table indexes and combines the row ids:
        
      
          
        
        • Union (Using union(i1, i2)) for a = 1 OR b = 2 with separate indexes on a and b.
          • 
        
        • Sort-union for ORs of ranges: a < 10 OR b < 20.
          • 
        
        • Intersection (Using intersect(i1, i2)) for a = 1 AND b = 2 — a hint that you probably want a composite INDEX(a, b).
          • 
      
        
      
        Index merge is a rescue, not a design goal. It reads two indexes and merges in memory; one good composite index is almost always faster for AND. For OR, a UNION rewrite is the alternative (see Chapter 16).
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        ⚠️ "I have an index but it isn't used" — the full checklist
        
  
        This is the single most common follow-up. A B+ tree can seek only when the engine can compute a start key and stop key on the raw indexed value. Anything that hides the raw value, or makes the seek not worth it, disables the index.
        
  
        
    
        #CauseExample (index exists on the column)Fix
        
    
      
        1Function / expression on the columnWHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026, WHERE UPPER(email) = 'A@X.COM', WHERE price * 1.18 > 1000Range on the raw column (created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'); _ci collation already ignores case; functional index (8.0.13+)
        
      
        2Implicit type conversion (string column vs number)WHERE phone = 9876543210 on VARCHAR — every row is converted to a number ('98…', ' 98…', '98…abc' all equal it)Quote it: phone = '9876543210'. (Number column vs string literal is usually fine: the literal is converted)
        
      
        3Charset / collation mismatch in joinsutf8mb4 column joined to a latin1 columnSame type, length, charset and collation on both join columns
        
      
        4Leading wildcardWHERE name LIKE '%kumar'FULLTEXT index, reversed-string generated column + index, search engine. (LIKE 'kumar%' is fine — it is a range)
        
      
        5Not a leftmost prefixWHERE status = 'PAID' on INDEX(customer_id, status)New index starting with status; skip scan in narrow cases
        
      
        6OR across different columnsWHERE customer_id = 42 OR status = 'DISPUTED'Index on each column (index merge) or UNION rewrite
        
      
        7Low selectivityWHERE status = 'DELIVERED' matching 80% of rowsCorrect behaviour — a scan is cheaper. Query the rare values, or make the index covering
        
      
        8Tiny tableLookup table with 50 rows (1–2 pages)Nothing to fix
        
      
        9Stale / skewed statisticsBulk load of 20M rows, stats still say 10kANALYZE TABLE, more sample pages, histograms (Chapter 16)
        
      
        10ORDER BY + SELECT * on a non-covering indexWalking the index + row lookups for most rows costs more than scan + filesortAdd LIMIT, make it covering, or select fewer columns
        
      
        11!=, NOT IN, NOT LIKEWHERE status <> 'DONE'Usually low selectivity; rewrite as the positive set status IN ('NEW','PAID')
        
      
        12Invisible index or hintsALTER INDEX … INVISIBLE, IGNORE INDEXMake it visible / remove the hint
        
            
  
        
  
        🧠
        Memory aid: "Don't wrap the column"
        Keep the indexed column naked on one side of the comparison. Types, charsets and collations must match. And remember: the optimizer is allowed to say no when the index would touch too many rows — there is no fixed "30% rule" in modern MySQL; it compares estimated costs.
        

  
        
    QA query is slow even though the column is indexed. How do you debug it?
    
        
      
          
        
        1. EXPLAIN it. possible_keys empty → the predicate cannot use the index (function, cast, wildcard, prefix). possible_keys set but key = NULL → considered and rejected by cost.
          2. 
        
        2. Check the predicate against the checklist above: is the column wrapped, cast, or not a leftmost prefix?
          3. 
        
        3. Check selectivity: SELECT COUNT(*) … WHERE … vs table size. If it matches 40% of rows, the scan is right.
          4. 
        
        4. Check estimates: EXPLAIN ANALYZE — estimated vs actual rows. Big gap → ANALYZE TABLE / histogram.
          5. 
        
        5. Test the alternative: SELECT /*+ INDEX(t idx) */ … and compare actual time. If it is truly faster and stats are fine, consider a better index (composite / covering) before a permanent hint.
          6. 
        
        6. Optimizer trace if still unclear: SET optimizer_trace = 'enabled=on'; then read information_schema.OPTIMIZER_TRACE to see each plan's cost.
          7. 
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        First I run EXPLAIN to see whether the index is even possible and whether it was chosen. If it isn't possible, the predicate is usually non-sargable: a function on the column, a type mismatch, a leading wildcard, or the column isn't a leftmost prefix of the composite index. If it was possible but rejected, I check selectivity and statistics with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, refresh statistics if estimates are off, and only then consider a better composite or covering index, or a hint as a last resort.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪Why can the same query use the index for one value but not another?
          
        Because row estimates are per value (index dives / histograms). status = 'DISPUTED' (0.1%) → index. status = 'DELIVERED' (80%) → full scan. That is the optimizer working correctly.
        
        
        ↪Does IS NULL use an index?
          
        Yes in MySQL and PostgreSQL: B+ tree indexes store NULLs, and col IS NULL is an index lookup (ref / ref_or_null). Exception: Oracle B-tree indexes do not store entries whose key columns are all NULL, so IS NULL on a single-column Oracle index cannot use it.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        ⚖️ Cardinality vs selectivity: when is an index worth it?
        
  
        
    
        Cardinality (of a column / index)
        Number of distinct values. gender ≈ 3, city ≈ 500, email ≈ number of rows. SHOW INDEX shows an estimate in the Cardinality column.
        
    
        Selectivity (of a predicate)
        Fraction of rows it returns, 0 to 1. Lower = more selective. email = ? ≈ 1/N; is_active = 1 maybe 0.95. Rough equality estimate: rows ÷ cardinality.
        
  
        
  
        An index pays off when "seek + k random row fetches" is cheaper than "read every page sequentially". Since each secondary hit in InnoDB costs a clustered lookup, the break-even is often only a few percent to a few tens of percent of the table, depending on row size and caching.
        
  
        
    QShould you index a gender / boolean / status column?
    
        
      
        Usually not on its own. WHERE gender = 'F' matches ~50% of rows: half a table of random lookups is slower than one sequential scan, so the optimizer will ignore the index — and you still pay its write cost.
        
      
        Exceptions:
        
      
          
        
        • Skew, querying the rare value: is_deleted = 1 is 0.1% of rows, or a job queue's status = 'PENDING' → very selective, index helps.
          • 
        
        • As part of a composite index: INDEX(status, created_at) for "pending jobs, oldest first" — equality on status, then sorted by time.
          • 
        
        • Covering: SELECT COUNT(*) … GROUP BY gender can scan a tiny index instead of the table.
          • 
        
        • OLAP: Oracle bitmap indexes are designed for low-cardinality columns in read-mostly warehouses.
          • 
      
        
      
        🔀
        Partial indexes for the skewed case
        PostgreSQL: CREATE INDEX ON jobs (created_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING'; — indexes only the few pending rows. SQL Server calls these filtered indexes. MySQL has no partial indexes.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Not by itself. A column with very few distinct values usually matches a large fraction of rows, and fetching half the table through random index lookups is slower than a full scan, so the optimizer won't use it and we'd only pay the write cost. It makes sense if the data is skewed and we query the rare value, or as the first column of a composite index, or in a warehouse with bitmap indexes.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🔧 MySQL index flavours you should know
        
  
        
    
        
    
        
      
        A UNIQUE index enforces "no two rows with the same key" and speeds lookups. A PRIMARY KEY is a unique, NOT NULL index (and in InnoDB, the clustered one).
        
      
        ALTER TABLE users ADD UNIQUE KEY uk_phone (phone);   -- phone is NULLable
INSERT INTO users (email, phone) VALUES ('a@x.com', NULL), ('b@x.com', NULL);  -- ✅ both allowed
        
      
        🔀
        UNIQUE and NULL
        MySQL InnoDB and PostgreSQL allow many NULLs in a UNIQUE column (NULL ≠ NULL). PostgreSQL 15+ can say UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT to allow only one. SQL Server allows only one NULL in a UNIQUE constraint (workaround: a filtered unique index WHERE col IS NOT NULL). Oracle doesn't index all-NULL keys, so many NULLs are allowed.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Functional (expression) index MySQL 8.0.13+: indexes the result of an expression. Implemented as a hidden virtual generated column. Note the double parentheses.
        
      
        -- "Whose birthday is this month?" cannot be rewritten as one range on birth_date
ALTER TABLE users ADD INDEX idx_birth_month ((MONTH(birth_date)));
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE MONTH(birth_date) = 10;                 -- ✅ uses idx_birth_month
SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE DATE_FORMAT(birth_date, '%m') = '10';   -- ❌ different expression

-- Before 8.0.13: an indexed generated column does the same job
ALTER TABLE users ADD email_lower VARCHAR(255) AS (LOWER(email)) VIRTUAL, ADD INDEX (email_lower);
        
      
        The query must use exactly the indexed expression. Cannot be used for PRIMARY KEY or FOREIGN KEY. PostgreSQL and Oracle have had expression / function-based indexes for a long time: CREATE INDEX ON users (lower(email));.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Prefix index: index only the first N characters of a string. Required for TEXT/BLOB; optional for CHAR/VARCHAR. Max key size: 3072 bytes (InnoDB DYNAMIC / COMPRESSED row format), 767 bytes for the old REDUNDANT / COMPACT formats.
        
      
        -- How long a prefix is "unique enough"?
SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT LEFT(url, 20)) / COUNT(DISTINCT url) AS sel20,
       COUNT(DISTINCT LEFT(url, 40)) / COUNT(DISTINCT url) AS sel40
FROM pages;
ALTER TABLE pages ADD INDEX idx_url (url(40));
        
      
        Trade-offs: much smaller index, but it cannot be covering (the full value isn't there), cannot help ORDER BY, and a UNIQUE prefix index enforces uniqueness on the prefix only. Alternative for long values: index a short hash column (CRC32(url) or a stored SHA2) and compare both hash and value.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Descending index MySQL 8.0+: before 8.0, DESC in an index definition was parsed but ignored. Now keys are really stored in descending order. Main use: mixed directions.
        
      
        -- Leaderboard: highest score first, then earliest time for ties
ALTER TABLE scores ADD INDEX idx_board (game_id, score DESC, finished_at ASC);
SELECT player_id, score FROM scores
WHERE game_id = 7 ORDER BY score DESC, finished_at ASC LIMIT 10;   -- ✅ no filesort
        
      
        Same-direction ordering (ORDER BY a DESC, b DESC) never needed a DESC index: a normal index is read backwards (Backward index scan).
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Invisible index MySQL 8.0+: the optimizer ignores it, but it is still maintained on every write and still enforces UNIQUE. Use it to test "can I drop this?" safely; switching visibility is instant.
        
      
        ALTER TABLE orders ALTER INDEX idx_old_status INVISIBLE;   -- watch latency for a week
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER INDEX idx_old_status VISIBLE;     -- instant rollback if something regressed
-- or, if all is well:
ALTER TABLE orders DROP INDEX idx_old_status;
        
      
        A PRIMARY KEY cannot be made invisible. Invisible indexes do not save write cost — only dropping does.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        FULLTEXT index = an inverted index: for each word, the list of documents (and positions) containing it. That's what makes word search fast instead of LIKE '%word%' scanning every row.
        
      
        ALTER TABLE products ADD FULLTEXT INDEX ft_desc (title, description);
SELECT id, title, MATCH(title, description) AGAINST ('wireless earbuds') AS score
FROM products
WHERE MATCH(title, description) AGAINST ('wireless earbuds')
ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10;
-- Boolean mode: AGAINST ('+wireless -wired' IN BOOLEAN MODE)
        
      
        InnoDB keeps a hidden FTS_DOC_ID column and auxiliary index tables; new rows are visible to full-text search after commit. Minimum indexed word length is 3 characters by default (innodb_ft_min_token_size), plus a stopword list. For serious search (typos, synonyms, ranking) teams use Elasticsearch / OpenSearch. PostgreSQL: tsvector + GIN index.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        SPATIAL index uses an R-tree: nodes store bounding rectangles, so "which shops are inside this map rectangle?" is answered without scanning. Requires a NOT NULL geometry column with an SRID.
        
      
        Multi-valued index 8.0.17+: one row can have several index entries — one per element of a JSON array. Used by MEMBER OF(), JSON_CONTAINS(), JSON_OVERLAPS().
        
      
        ALTER TABLE customers ADD INDEX idx_zips ((CAST(info->'$.zipcodes' AS UNSIGNED ARRAY)));
SELECT id FROM customers WHERE 560001 MEMBER OF (info->'$.zipcodes');
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🧭 Beyond MySQL: bitmap, GIN, GiST, BRIN, partial, INCLUDE, filtered
        
  
        
    
        🟧
        Bitmap (Oracle)
        One bitmap per distinct value, one bit per row. gender='F' AND region='South' = bitwise AND of two bitmaps. Tiny and fast for low-cardinality, read-mostly warehouses. Bad for OLTP: one key covers many rows, so DML on it locks many rows.
        
    
        📚
        GIN (PostgreSQL)
        Generalized inverted index for values with many parts: array elements, JSONB keys (@>), full-text tsvector, trigrams (pg_trgm makes LIKE '%x%' indexable).
        
    
        🗺️
        GiST / SP-GiST (PostgreSQL)
        Frameworks for geometry, ranges, nearest-neighbour (ORDER BY location <-> point LIMIT 10), exclusion constraints. SP-GiST: quadtrees, k-d trees, tries.
        
    
        🧱
        BRIN (PostgreSQL)
        Stores only min/max per block range. Tiny (kilobytes for a huge table). Great when values follow physical order — e.g. created_at on an append-only log. Useless for random placement.
        
    
        ✂️
        Partial / filtered
        Index only a subset of rows: PG … WHERE status = 'PENDING'; SQL Server filtered index WHERE EndDate IS NOT NULL. Smaller, cheaper, better stats. Partial unique = "unique among active rows".
        
    
        ➕
        INCLUDE / included columns
        PG and SQL Server: payload columns in the leaf only, to make an index covering without widening the search key.
        
    
        🧮
        Columnstore (SQL Server)
        Column-oriented, compressed storage for analytics scans over billions of rows; batch-mode execution. See Chapter 20.
        
    
        📝
        LSM-tree (RocksDB / MyRocks)
        Not an index type but a storage engine design: sequential writes + compaction. Better write and space amplification, slower reads.
        
  
        
  
        
    
        I need to…UseWhere
        
    
      
        Equality + range + sort (default)B+ treeEverywhere
        
      
        Pure in-memory equalityHashMySQL MEMORY, PG hash, InnoDB AHI (automatic)
        
      
        Low-cardinality ad-hoc filters in a warehouseBitmapOracle
        
      
        Search words in textFull-text / invertedMySQL FULLTEXT, PG GIN on tsvector
        
      
        Elements inside arrays / JSONMulti-valued / GINMySQL 8.0.17+, PG
        
      
        Shapes, nearest neighbourR-tree / GiST / SP-GiSTMySQL SPATIAL, PG (PostGIS)
        
      
        Huge append-only, naturally orderedBRINPG
        
      
        Index only "interesting" rowsPartial / filteredPG, SQL Server (MySQL: none)
        
      
        Covering without widening the keyINCLUDEPG, SQL Server (MySQL: append to key)
        
            
  
        
  
        🧠 Pick the index by the question
        Hash = exact · B+ = anything ordered · Bitmap = few values, many reads · Inverted / GIN = words and elements · R-tree / GiST = shapes · BRIN = ordered and huge.
        

  
  
        🪙 The cost of indexes: why not index every column?
        
  
        
    QWhy not just index every column?
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Write cost — every INSERT/DELETE (and UPDATE of an indexed column) modifies every index: more page writes, redo/undo, page splits, more locks held. A table with a PK + 5 secondary indexes changes 6 B+ trees per insert; if those leaves aren't cached, that can mean up to 6 random reads first.
          2. 
        
        2. Space and memory — indexes consume disk and, more importantly, buffer pool. Cold index pages push hot data out of RAM.
          3. 
        
        3. They often don't help — single-column indexes rarely serve multi-column filters; one well-designed composite index beats five single ones.
          4. 
        
        4. Optimizer confusion — more candidate plans to evaluate, more chances to pick a bad one.
          5. 
        
        5. PostgreSQL-specific — every indexed column that changes kills a HOT update.
          6. 
      
        
      
        🧠
        Memory aid
        "Every index is a tax on every write." Index for the workload (the real, frequent queries), not for the schema.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Because every index has to be maintained on every write, so inserts and updates get slower and generate more log, and every index takes disk and buffer-pool memory that could cache hot data. Single-column indexes also rarely help queries that filter on several columns. I design a few composite indexes from the actual query patterns and drop indexes that are unused or redundant.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Redundant and duplicate indexes
        
  
        
    
        You have…VerdictWhy
        
    
      
        INDEX(a) and INDEX(a, b)✘ drop INDEX(a)(a, b) serves every seek on a (leftmost prefix). Small caveat: (a) is narrower for scans
        
      
        INDEX(a, b) and INDEX(b, a)✔ keep both if neededDifferent leftmost prefixes
        
      
        UNIQUE(a) and INDEX(a)✘ drop INDEX(a)Exact duplicate
        
      
        PRIMARY KEY(id) and INDEX(id)✘ drop INDEX(id)Exact duplicate
        
      
        InnoDB INDEX(a, id) (id = PK)~ same as INDEX(a)The PK is appended to every secondary entry anyway
        
            
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is index fragmentation and how do you fix it in InnoDB?
    
        
      
        Random inserts (page splits) and large deletes leave pages partly empty, and pages that are logically next to each other may not be physically adjacent. Result: more pages per row and less effective caching. Fix: OPTIMIZE TABLE t; — for InnoDB this is mapped to ALTER TABLE … FORCE, an online rebuild of the table and its indexes (it prints "Table does not support optimize, doing recreate + analyze instead").
        
      
        Use it after big purges or bulk random loads, not on a schedule "to fix slowness": some free space (1/16 per page) is intentional, and rebuilding doesn't fix a bad access path. For a big table, online schema-change tools (pt-online-schema-change, gh-ost) rebuild with less risk.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪Loading 100M rows: create indexes before or after?
          
        Usually load first (in PK order), then add secondary indexes. InnoDB then builds each index with a sorted bulk load (bottom-up, pages filled per innodb_fill_factor), which is much faster than 100M random inserts into each tree. In PostgreSQL use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on a live table so writes are not blocked.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🔍 Finding missing and unused indexes
        
  
        Never guess. Measure which queries are slow, which scan whole tables, and which indexes nobody reads.
        
  
        
    
        1. Catchslow query log / statement digests
        
    
        
    
        2. Ranktotal time = count × avg latency
        
    
        
    
        3. EXPLAINtype=ALL? filesort? rows examined ≫ sent?
        
    
        
    
        4. Fix & verifycomposite / covering index, rewrite, re-measure
        
  
        
  
        
    QHow do you find which indexes are missing and which are unused in MySQL?
    
        
      
        Missing = queries that read far more rows than they return. Unused = indexes with zero reads since the server started. MySQL 8 ships the sys schema, which turns Performance Schema counters into readable views.
        
      
        -- 1. Slow query log (catch the offenders)
SET GLOBAL slow_query_log = ON;
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 0.5;                  -- seconds
SET GLOBAL log_queries_not_using_indexes = ON;     -- noisy; use briefly
-- then summarise the log with: pt-query-digest slow.log

-- 2. Statements that did full table scans
SELECT query, exec_count, no_index_used_count, rows_examined_avg
FROM sys.statements_with_full_table_scans ORDER BY exec_count DESC LIMIT 10;

-- 3. Heaviest statements overall
SELECT query, exec_count, total_latency, rows_examined_avg, rows_sent_avg
FROM sys.statement_analysis ORDER BY total_latency DESC LIMIT 10;

-- 4. Indexes never read since startup
SELECT * FROM sys.schema_unused_indexes WHERE object_schema = 'shop';

-- 5. Redundant / duplicate indexes
SELECT table_name, redundant_index_name, dominant_index_name, sql_drop_index
FROM sys.schema_redundant_indexes WHERE table_schema = 'shop';
        
      
        ⚠️
        "Unused" depends on the time window
        The counters reset on restart. An index used only by the month-end report looks unused on day 10. Check after a full business cycle, check every replica (reads may go there), then make it INVISIBLE first and drop later.
        
      
        🔀
        Other engines
        PostgreSQL: pg_stat_statements for heavy queries; pg_stat_user_indexes where idx_scan = 0 for unused ones; auto_explain logs plans of slow queries. SQL Server: sys.dm_db_missing_index_details (optimizer's own suggestions — review, don't blindly create) and sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats (seeks/scans vs updates). Oracle: AWR reports, SQL Tuning Advisor, ALTER INDEX … MONITORING USAGE.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I start from data, not guesses. I turn on the slow query log, aggregate it with pt-query-digest, and rank queries by total time. For the top ones I run EXPLAIN and look for full scans, filesorts and a big gap between rows examined and rows returned, then add a composite or covering index and re-measure. For cleanup I use sys.schema_unused_indexes and schema_redundant_indexes, but I make an index invisible for a full business cycle before dropping it.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪The slow log is empty but the DB is at 100% CPU. Why?
          
        Death by a thousand cuts: one query taking 20 ms but running 5,000 times per second never crosses long_query_time. Rank by total latency in sys.statement_analysis / pg_stat_statements, not by per-call time.
        
        
        ↪Should you trust SQL Server's missing-index suggestions?
          
        As hints only. They are per-query, ignore write cost, often overlap each other and ignore column order for sorting. Merge them into a few well-ordered composite indexes.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🎯 Real-world scenario questions
        
  
        
    Q"My orders page is slow": WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20. Design the index.
    
        
      
        Apply Equality → Sort → Range: both equality columns first, then the sort column.
        
      
        ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_cust_status_time (customer_id, status, created_at);
EXPLAIN SELECT id, total, created_at FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'SHIPPED'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
        
      
        type: ref | key: idx_cust_status_time | rows: 20 | Extra: Backward index scan
        
      
        The engine seeks to (42, 'SHIPPED'), walks the leaf list backwards and stops after 20 entries: no filesort, no scanning all of the customer's orders. To make it covering, append total: (customer_id, status, created_at, total) (the PK id is already in every InnoDB secondary entry).
        
      
        🚫
        Wrong answer
        "Put created_at first because it is most selective." A column used for a range or sort in the middle stops the columns after it from being used for seeking or ordering.
        
    
        
  
        
  
        
    QThe index exists, EXPLAIN shows type: ALL. Walk me through your debugging.
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Is the predicate sargable? Function on the column, leading %, OR across different columns, or !=.
          2. 
        
        2. Type / collation mismatch? phone_varchar = 9876543210 (number) converts every row; joins on columns with different charsets or collations do the same.
          3. 
        
        3. Leftmost prefix? Index is (a, b) but the query filters only on b.
          4. 
        
        4. Selectivity? If the value matches a big share of rows, a full scan really is cheaper.
          5. 
        
        5. Stale statistics? Run ANALYZE TABLE t; and re-check rows in EXPLAIN.
          6. 
        
        6. Prove it: EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) with and without FORCE INDEX — compare real times, then fix the cause instead of shipping the hint.
          7. 
      
        
    
        
  
        
  
        
    QYou must add an index to a 500 GB table in production. How?
    
        
      
        MySQL 8 ALTER TABLE … ADD INDEX …, ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE builds it online (reads and writes continue), but it still costs I/O, a temporary sort area, and replicas apply it as one long statement that causes replication lag. Big shops use gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change (copy to a shadow table, throttle on lag, swap). PostgreSQL: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (cannot run inside a transaction; on failure it leaves an INVALID index you must drop). Always: test on a replica copy, run off-peak, watch lag and disk space.
        
      
        🌍
        Production story
        A team ran a plain ALTER on a busy primary; it finished fine, but every replica then spent hours applying it and fell far behind, so read traffic served stale data. The fix was a throttled online-schema-change tool that pauses when replica lag grows.
        
    
        
  
        
  
        ✏️ In every scenario answer, end with "…and I'd verify with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before and after."
        

  
        📌 Key takeaways
          
    
        • An index is a sorted copy of some columns + a pointer; B+ trees win because leaves are linked and fanout is huge (3–4 levels for billions of rows).
          • 
    
        • InnoDB table = clustered B+ tree on the PK; secondary leaves hold the PK, so a non-covering secondary lookup is a double lookup. PostgreSQL uses a heap + ctid instead.
          • 
    
        • Keep the PK short and increasing (auto-increment, UUIDv7 / ordered BINARY(16)); random UUIDv4 causes page splits and cache misses.
          • 
    
        • Composite indexes obey the leftmost prefix; the first range column ends seeking. Order columns Equality → Sort → Range.
          • 
    
        • Covering index = Using index (no table access); ICP = Using index condition (filter inside the index first).
          • 
    
        • Indexes are skipped for functions on columns, implicit type/collation conversion, leading %, low selectivity and stale stats — fix the query or add a functional index.
          • 
    
        • Every index is a tax on every write and on buffer-pool memory: index for the workload, then measure with the slow log, sys schema and EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
          •

        Table has INDEX(a, b, c). Which WHERE clause can seek on all three columns?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Order inside WHERE doesn't matter; equality on a, b, c uses the full prefix. A range on b stops seeking at b; skipping a or b breaks the leftmost prefix (c may only be filtered via ICP).
        
    
        
    
        
      
        In InnoDB, what does a secondary index leaf entry store besides the indexed columns?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        InnoDB secondary leaves hold the PK, so reaching the row needs a second lookup in the clustered index. ctid is PostgreSQL's heap pointer.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        EXPLAIN shows Extra: Using index. What does it mean?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        "Using index" = covering, no table rows read. "Using index condition" = ICP. Which index is used is shown in the key column.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        phone is VARCHAR and indexed. Why is WHERE phone = 9876543210 slow?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Implicit conversion applies to the column side. Quote the literal: phone = '9876543210'.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Which primary key choice causes the most page splits in a large InnoDB table?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Random keys insert all over the clustered tree, splitting half-full pages and missing the cache; CHAR(36) also bloats every secondary index.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        How should you safely check whether an index can be dropped in MySQL 8?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        An invisible index is ignored by the optimizer but still maintained, so switching back is instant. It does not save write cost — only dropping does.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        B-tree vs B+ tree: the key difference?
        B+ tree keeps all data/row pointers in leaves, internal nodes hold only keys, and leaves are linked → higher fanout and fast range scans.
        
    
        Dense vs sparse index?
        Dense: one entry per search-key value. Sparse: one entry per block; needs the file sorted on the key.
        
    
        What is a clustered index?
        An index whose leaves hold the table rows in key order; only one per table. InnoDB clusters on the PK.
        
    
        What is the "double lookup"?
        InnoDB secondary index → PK value → second descent in the clustered index to fetch the row. Avoided by a covering index.
        
    
        Leftmost-prefix rule?
        INDEX(a,b,c) can seek on (a), (a,b), (a,b,c); the first range column ends seeking for later columns.
        
    
        Using index vs Using index condition?
        Using index = covering, no table access. Using index condition = ICP: filter on index columns before fetching rows.
        
    
        Cardinality vs selectivity?
        Cardinality = number of distinct values. Selectivity = distinct / total rows (closer to 1 = better for an index).
        
    
        Functional index in MySQL?
        8.0.13+: INDEX ((LOWER(email))) — double parentheses; the query must use the exact same expression.
        
    
        BRIN index is good for…?
        Huge PostgreSQL tables where values follow physical order (append-only timestamps); stores min/max per block range.
        
    
        Find unused indexes in MySQL 8?
        sys.schema_unused_indexes (since restart), check replicas and a full cycle, make INVISIBLE, then drop.
        
  
        

        


        
  
        
    
        Chapter 16 · V · Storage & Performance
        
    
        🚀 Query Processing, Optimization & EXPLAIN
        
    
        Explain what the database does between "you press Enter" and "rows come back", read any MySQL or PostgreSQL plan line by line, and debug a slow production query like a senior engineer.
        
    
        ⏱ 50 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8.0 / 8.4PostgreSQLEXPLAIN ANALYZE 8.0.18+
        
  
        

  
         
        ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
        
    
          
      
        • Pipeline: Parse → Resolve (names, types, privileges) → Rewrite → Optimize (cost-based) → Execute as a tree of iterators (Open / Next / Close).
          • 
      
        • Rewrites are mostly rules (push selections and projections down, subquery → semi-join, merge derived tables). Physical choices are cost-based (which index, join order, join algorithm).
          • 
      
        • Cost comes from row estimates, and row estimates come from statistics (index cardinality, index dives, histograms). Bad estimates → bad plans. Most "the optimizer is dumb" stories are really "the statistics are wrong".
          • 
      
        • Joins: index nested loop (small outer, indexed inner), hash join (big + big, equality, no index; MySQL 8.0.18+, replaced BNL in 8.0.20), sort-merge (inputs already sorted; PostgreSQL / Oracle / SQL Server).
          • 
      
        • MySQL EXPLAIN: read type (system → const → eq_ref → ref → range → index → ALL), key, key_len (how many index columns are used), rows × filtered, and Extra (Using index = covering 🎉, Using filesort / Using temporary = extra work ⚠️).
          • 
      
        • EXPLAIN only estimates. EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the query and shows actual rows and time per step. Compare estimate vs actual.
          • 
      
        • Slow query playbook: Find (slow log, pt-query-digest) → Explain → Fix (sargable predicate, right composite / covering index, fresh stats, rewrite) → Verify.
          • 
      
        • Classic killers: N+1 queries, SELECT *, big OFFSET, functions on indexed columns, OR across columns, implicit type casts. MySQL 8.0 has no query cache (removed in 8.0.3).
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        ✏️ Interviewers love "This query is slow in production. What do you do?" The whole chapter is your answer, in order.
        

  
  
        ⚙️ The journey of a query: parse → optimize → execute
        
  
        SQL is declarative: you say what you want, not how to get it. The DBMS must turn your sentence into a step-by-step program. Think of a restaurant: you order "paneer butter masala" (SQL). The waiter checks the menu (parser), the head chef decides which cook, which pan and which order of steps (optimizer), and the kitchen cooks it (executor). ← same dish, many possible recipes
        

  
        
    
        1. Parsetokens → parse tree; syntax errors here
        
    
        
    
        2. Resolvetables, columns, types, privileges; "Unknown column" here
        
    
        
    
        3. Rewritelogical plan (relational algebra); push filters down; subquery → semi-join
        
    
        
    
        4. Optimizecost-based: access path, join order, join algorithm, sort strategy
        
    
        
    
        5. Executeiterator tree pulls rows through the buffer pool
        
  
        

  
        
    QWalk me through what happens when you run a SELECT.
    
        
      
        What: query processing is the set of steps that turn SQL text into result rows. Why it exists: the same SQL can be run in thousands of ways, and the cost difference between the best and worst way can be hours versus milliseconds.
        
      
          
        
        1. Connection & parse — the server receives text, splits it into tokens and builds a parse tree. A typo like SELEC fails here.
          2. 
        
        2. Resolve / bind — it checks that orders and customer_id exist, works out types, expands *, and checks your privileges. Unknown column 'x' fails here.
          3. 
        
        3. Logical plan + rewrite — the query becomes a relational-algebra tree (σ, π, ⋈). Rules then simplify it: constant folding (a < b AND b = 5 → a < 5 AND b = 5), removing always-true conditions, detecting Impossible WHERE, pushing filters down, converting IN (subquery) into a semi-join, merging views and derived tables, and turning an outer join into an inner join when a WHERE condition rejects NULLs.
          4. 
        
        4. Cost-based optimization — for each table it picks an access path (full scan, index range, index lookup...). It picks the join order and join algorithm. It decides how to sort and group. It estimates the cost of each candidate from statistics and keeps the cheapest.
          5. 
        
        5. Execution — the plan runs as a tree of iterators. Each operator offers Open(), Next(), Close(). The root asks its child for the next row, the child asks its children, and so on down to the table scans. Pages come from the buffer pool (disk only on a miss).
          6. 
        
        6. Send — rows stream to the client. A LIMIT can stop the whole tree early.
          7. 
      
        
      
        ℹ️
        The Volcano / iterator model
        "Open, Next, Next, Next, Close." Rows are pulled up one at a time, so operators are pipelined and memory stays small. Blocking operators (sort, hash-join build, aggregation) must eat all their input before they can output the first row. MySQL 8.0.20 finished replacing its old executor with an iterator executor, and EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE literally prints that iterator tree.
        
      
        🔀
        Engine differences
        MySQL: classic optimizer searches left-deep join orders; 9.7 LTS added the hypergraph optimizer to Community (bushy plans, off by default). PostgreSQL: parser → analyzer → rewriter (applies rules and views) → planner → executor; it uses exhaustive dynamic programming for small joins and a genetic optimizer (GEQO) for very many tables. Oracle / SQL Server: cost-based, and they cache plans globally in a shared plan cache, so parsing and optimizing are often skipped on a repeat query.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Common mistakes
        Saying "MySQL first checks the query cache" (gone since 8.0.3). Saying "the optimizer joins tables in FROM-clause order" (it reorders inner joins freely; only LEFT JOIN, STRAIGHT_JOIN or join-order hints constrain it). Confusing a parse error with a resolve error.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        First the parser checks syntax and builds a parse tree. Then the resolver checks that tables and columns exist and that I have privileges. The query becomes a relational-algebra tree, and rule-based rewrites push filters down and flatten subqueries. The cost-based optimizer then uses statistics to choose indexes, join order and join algorithms, and picks the cheapest plan. Finally the executor runs that plan as a tree of iterators that pull rows from the buffer pool and stream them to the client.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Where do statistics come in, and what if they are wrong?
          
        In step 4. The optimizer multiplies selectivity estimates to guess how many rows each step produces. If it thinks a filter returns 10 rows but it returns 2 million, it may choose nested loops instead of a hash join, or the wrong driving table. You see it in EXPLAIN ANALYZE as a big gap between estimated and actual rows. See statistics.
        
        
        ↪What is "pipelining" vs "materialization"?
          
        Pipelining: a row produced by one operator is passed straight to the parent (no temporary storage). Materialization: the whole intermediate result is written to a temporary table first, then read by the parent. Pipelining is cheaper and lets LIMIT stop early; materialization is unavoidable for sorts, some subqueries, and hash-join build sides. In MySQL EXPLAIN, select_type = MATERIALIZED and Using temporary are materialization clues.
        
        
        ↪Does a prepared statement skip some of these steps?
          
        Yes, partly. Parsing and resolving happen once at PREPARE. What happens to optimization depends on the engine — see prepared statement plan caching.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🌳 Query trees, equivalence rules & heuristic rewrites
        
  
        A query tree is the relational-algebra version of your SQL. Leaves are tables. Inner nodes are operators: σ (select = filter rows), π (project = keep columns), ⋈ (join). Data flows from the leaves up to the root. Two trees are equivalent if they return the same rows for every possible database. The optimizer moves operators around using equivalence rules to find a cheaper tree.
        

  
        SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-10-01'
  AND c.city = 'Pune';
        

  

  
        
    
        Equivalence rule (simple English)AlgebraWhy the optimizer cares
        
    
      
        Split an AND filter into stepsσp∧q(R) = σp(σq(R))Each piece can then move to a different place
        
      
        Filters can be applied in any orderσp(σq(R)) = σq(σp(R))Run the most selective / cheapest one first
        
      
        Push a filter below a join if it uses only one sideσp(R ⋈ S) = σp(R) ⋈ SThe big one. Smaller join inputs
        
      
        Only the last projection matters; project earlyπa(πa,b(R)) = πa(R)Narrower rows → less memory, can enable covering indexes
        
      
        Filter + Cartesian product = joinσR.x=S.y(R × S) = R ⋈x=y SNever compute the full cross product
        
      
        Inner joins are commutative and associativeR ⋈ S = S ⋈ R; (R ⋈ S) ⋈ T = R ⋈ (S ⋈ T)This is what makes join reordering legal
        
            
  
        

  
        
    QWhat are the heuristic (rule-based) rewrites every optimizer does?
    
        
      
          
        
        • Push selections down as close to the tables as possible (even into the storage engine: MySQL's Index Condition Pushdown).
          • 
        
        • Push projections down — drop columns nobody needs as early as possible.
          • 
        
        • Most restrictive operations first — joins that produce small results go first.
          • 
        
        • Replace σ over × with a join — never build a Cartesian product.
          • 
        
        • Flatten subqueries and views into joins / semi-joins so they can be reordered.
          • 
        
        • Simplify — constant folding, remove 1=1, detect impossible conditions, convert LEFT JOIN to INNER JOIN when the WHERE clause throws away NULL-extended rows anyway.
          • 
      
        
      
        These rules almost always help, so they are applied without costing. Choices that depend on the data (which index? which join order?) are costed.
        
      
        💡
        Join order explodes fast
        For n tables there are (2(n−1))!/(n−1)! possible join trees: 665,280 for just 7 tables. So optimizers use dynamic programming (System R style: best plan for every subset of tables), restrict the search to left-deep trees, or use greedy / genetic search for many tables. MySQL's optimizer_search_depth limits the exhaustive search.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        The optimizer uses equivalence rules to rewrite the query tree. The most important one is pushing selections and projections down, so that joins work on as few and as narrow rows as possible. Since inner joins are commutative and associative, it can also reorder joins, and it picks the order by cost because the number of possible orders grows factorially.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        ⚖️ Rule-based vs cost-based optimization
        
  
        
    
        📏 Rule-based (RBO)
          
      
        • Fixed priority list: "an index is always better than a full scan", "PK lookup beats everything".
          • 
      
        • Looks only at the query and schema, never at the data.
          • 
      
        • Predictable, but blind: it will use an index on gender even when it matches 50% of rows.
          • 
      
        • Historic: Oracle's old RBO (deprecated long ago).
          • 
    
        
    
        💰 Cost-based (CBO)
          
      
        • Enumerates alternatives, estimates each one's cost (I/O pages + CPU per row), picks the minimum.
          • 
      
        • Inputs: table and index sizes, row counts, distinct values, histograms, whether pages are likely cached.
          • 
      
        • Adapts to data, but is only as good as its statistics. Garbage in → garbage plan.
          • 
      
        • Every modern RDBMS (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server) is cost-based.
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHow does a cost model actually compute a "cost"?
    
        
      
        Cost is in abstract units, roughly "how many page reads plus how much CPU work". PostgreSQL makes it visible: seq_page_cost = 1.0, random_page_cost = 4.0, cpu_tuple_cost = 0.01. A sequential scan of a table with 345 pages and 10,000 rows costs 345 × 1.0 + 10,000 × 0.01 = 445. An index scan costs fewer pages, but each page is a random read (more expensive), plus index pages. The planner compares the totals.
        
      
        MySQL keeps similar constants in the tables mysql.server_cost and mysql.engine_cost (for example io_block_read_cost, row_evaluate_cost).
        
      
        🎯
        What they are really testing
        That you know the optimizer does not "know" the best plan. It guesses from estimates. Most bad plans come from bad cardinality estimates, not from bad cost formulas. Say that sentence.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪On SSDs, should random_page_cost stay at 4?
          
        Often it is lowered (for example to 1.1–2) because random reads on SSD are almost as cheap as sequential ones. Lowering it makes PostgreSQL choose index scans more often. Test before changing it in production.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        📊 Statistics, cardinality estimation & histograms
        
  
        
    
        Cardinality (of a column / index)
        Number of distinct values. country ≈ 200; email ≈ number of rows.
        
    
        Selectivity (of a predicate)
        Fraction of rows it returns (0 to 1). email = ? ≈ 1/N (very selective). status = 'ACTIVE' maybe 0.9 (not selective).
        
    
        Cardinality estimate (of a plan step)
        The optimizer's guess of how many rows that step outputs = table rows × selectivity. Textbook equality estimate: rows / distinct_values.
        
    
        Histogram
        Bucketed summary of how values are spread in a column, so the optimizer can see skew (e.g. 95% of orders are 'DELIVERED').
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhere do the optimizer's row estimates come from in MySQL and PostgreSQL?
    
        
      
        
        
        
        
        
          
          
            
        • Index statistics (persistent by default): per-index cardinality, stored in mysql.innodb_table_stats / mysql.innodb_index_stats. Built by sampling innodb_stats_persistent_sample_pages (default 20) random leaf pages. Auto-recalculated after ~10% of rows change.
          • 
            
        • Index dives: for a range or IN (...) on an indexed column, the optimizer actually walks the B+ tree to the start and end of the range and counts. Accurate, but costs a little. Beyond eq_range_index_dive_limit values it falls back to statistics.
          • 
            
        • Histograms 8.0.3+: for non-indexed columns. Singleton (one bucket per value) or equi-height (one bucket per value range). Up to 1024 buckets (default 100). Not used when the range optimizer can do index dives.
          • 
          
        
          
        ANALYZE TABLE orders;                                   -- re-sample index stats
ANALYZE TABLE orders UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON status WITH 64 BUCKETS;
SELECT column_name, JSON_EXTRACT(histogram, '$."histogram-type"') AS type
FROM information_schema.COLUMN_STATISTICS
WHERE table_name = 'orders';
ANALYZE TABLE orders DROP HISTOGRAM ON status;          -- remove it
        

        +-------------+-------------+
| COLUMN_NAME | type        |
+-------------+-------------+
| status      | "singleton" |   <-- 5 distinct statuses ≤ 64 buckets
+-------------+-------------+
        
        
        
        
        
          
          
            
        • ANALYZE (run by autovacuum too) samples rows and stores per-column stats in pg_statistic, readable through the view pg_stats.
          • 
            
        • Per column: null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals + most_common_freqs (MCV list), histogram_bounds (equi-height for the rest), and correlation (how well physical order matches value order — affects index scan cost).
          • 
            
        • default_statistics_target (100) controls the size; raise per column with ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN … SET STATISTICS 1000.
          • 
            
        • Extended statistics (CREATE STATISTICS … (dependencies, ndistinct, mcv)) teach it about correlated columns.
          • 
          
        
          
        SELECT attname, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs
FROM pg_stats
WHERE tablename = 'orders' AND attname = 'status';

CREATE STATISTICS orders_city_state (dependencies) ON city, state FROM orders;
ANALYZE orders;
        
        
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        The optimizer estimates rows from statistics. In MySQL that means sampled index cardinality, index dives into the B+ tree for ranges, and since 8.0 histograms for non-indexed columns, refreshed by ANALYZE TABLE. In PostgreSQL, ANALYZE fills pg_stats with distinct counts, most-common values and histograms. Better statistics mean better row estimates, and better row estimates mean better plans.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhy do cardinality estimates go wrong?
    
        
      
        
        
        CauseExampleFix
        
        
          
        Correlated columns (the optimizer assumes independence and multiplies selectivities)city='Mumbai' AND state='Maharashtra': 1/1000 × 1/30 = 1/30,000, but really ≈ 1/1000 → underestimate 30×PG: CREATE STATISTICS (dependencies). MySQL: a composite index on (city, state) gives combined stats; or hints
        
          
        Stale statisticsTable grew from 10k to 10M rows after a bulk load; auto-recalc not yet runANALYZE TABLE after big loads; raise sample pages
        
          
        Skew (non-uniform data)95% of orders are 'DELIVERED', 0.1% 'DISPUTED'; "rows / distinct" says 20% eachHistogram (MySQL 8.0+) / MCV list (PG)
        
          
        Functions and expressionsWHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026 — no stats on the expression → default guessSargable rewrite; functional index
        
          
        Parameter valuesA cached plan built for customer_id = 42 (5 rows) reused for a huge customer (2M rows)Re-optimize per value; avoid generic plans for skewed params
        
          
        Errors multiply across joins2× off at each of 5 joins → 32× off at the topFix the bottom-most wrong estimate first
        
                
      
        
      
        🌍
        Production story
        A nightly job bulk-inserted 20M rows into an empty staging table. The stats still said "0 rows", so the optimizer chose nested loops with that table as the outer side. The job went from 4 minutes to 3 hours. One ANALYZE TABLE staging_orders; after the load fixed it. Put ANALYZE in the job.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪How do you prove the estimate is wrong?
          
        EXPLAIN ANALYZE: compare rows= (estimate) with actual … rows= for each node. 10× or more apart means the plan above that node may be built on a lie. In MySQL you can also inspect the optimizer trace: SET optimizer_trace='enabled=on'; run the query, then SELECT * FROM information_schema.OPTIMIZER_TRACE;.
        
        
        ↪Should I add a histogram on an indexed column?
          
        Usually no. For indexed columns MySQL prefers index dives, which are more accurate. Histograms shine on non-indexed, skewed columns used in filters and joins: you get good estimates without paying index write cost. MySQL also refuses histograms on columns covered by a single-column unique index.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🔗 Join algorithms (and when each one wins)
        
  
        A join asks: "for each row on the left, which rows on the right match?" There are only a few basic ways to answer it. Let R be the outer (driving) table and S the inner table.
        

  
        
    
        🔁
        Simple nested loop
        for r in R: for s in S: if match → emit. Compares every pair. Cost ≈ |R| × |S|. OK only for tiny tables.
        
    
        📦
        Block nested loop (BNL)
        Load a big chunk of R into memory (the join buffer), scan S once per chunk. Fewer passes over S. MySQL used this before 8.0.20.
        
    
        🎯
        Index nested loop
        for r in R: seek S's index on the join key. Each probe ≈ tree height (1–3 page reads). MySQL shows it as eq_ref / ref on the inner table.
        
    
        #️⃣
        Hash join
        Build a hash table on the smaller input's join key, then probe it with each row of the bigger input. ~Linear time. Equality joins. MySQL 8.0.18+.
        
    
        🪢
        Sort-merge join
        Sort both inputs on the key, then walk them together like merging two sorted lists. Great if inputs are already sorted (index order) or sorted output is needed. PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server.
        
  
        

  

  
        
    
        AlgorithmI/O cost (pages)Example: R = 1000 pages / 100k rows, S = 500 pages, 100 buffer pages, 0.1 ms per I/O
        
    
      
        Simple nested loopM + m·N≈ 50,001,000 I/Os ≈ 1.4 hours
        
      
        Block nested loop (1-page block)M + M·N501,000 I/Os ≈ 50 s
        
      
        Block nested loop (98-page block)M + ⌈M/(B−2)⌉·N1000 + 11 × 500 = 6,500 ≈ 0.65 s
        
      
        Index nested loopM + m·C (C = cost per probe)Excellent when R is small after filtering; awful when m is huge
        
      
        Sort-mergesort(R) + sort(S) + (M + N)≈ 7,500 I/Os ≈ 0.75 s
        
      
        Hash join (Grace)3 · (M + N)4,500 I/Os ≈ 0.45 s
        
            
  
        
  
        Numbers from the CMU 15-445 join lecture. The lesson: memory is the multiplier, and the right algorithm turns hours into milliseconds.
        

  
        
    
        SituationBest choiceWhy
        
    
      
        Few outer rows after WHERE, index on inner join column🎯 Index nested loopEach probe is 1–3 page reads; nothing to build. Also best with LIMIT (first rows stream immediately)
        
      
        Two big inputs, equality join, no useful index#️⃣ Hash joinReads each input once (if build fits in memory)
        
      
        Inputs already sorted on the key, or ORDER BY on the key needed🪢 Sort-mergeNo sort cost; output already ordered
        
      
        Non-equality join (<, BETWEEN, band join)Nested loop with index range on inner (or merge/band join)Hash needs equality on the hash key
        
      
        Tiny tables, cross joinAny nested loopSetup cost of hashing/sorting is not worth it
        
            
  
        

  
        
    QExplain hash join. When is nested loop better than hash join?
    
        
      
        Hash join has two phases. Build: read the smaller input and put each row into an in-memory hash table keyed by the join column. Probe: stream the bigger input; for each row, hash its join key and look in that bucket for matches. If the build side fits in memory, the cost is just reading both inputs once: O(M + N). If not, both inputs are split into partitions on disk by hash value, and each partition pair is joined separately (Grace hash join). It only works for equality on the hash key, and it is blocking on the build side.
        
      
        Nested loop wins when the outer side is small and the inner side has an index on the join key. 100 filtered orders joined to customers by primary key = 100 PK lookups ≈ a few hundred page touches. Hashing a 10M-row customers table to answer that would be silly. Nested loop also returns the first row immediately, which is perfect for LIMIT 10.
        
      
        🔀
        MySQL history (asked a lot!)
        Before 8.0.18 MySQL had only nested-loop joins (simple, block, index, plus Batched Key Access). 8.0.18 added hash join for equi-joins with no usable index. 8.0.20 removed block nested loop completely: hash join is now used everywhere BNL used to be, including outer joins, semi-joins, anti-joins and joins without an equality condition (extra conditions become a filter). Memory is capped by join_buffer_size; beyond it, it spills to disk. MySQL does not offer a sort-merge join operator in the classic optimizer; PostgreSQL shows Merge Join, Oracle and SQL Server have it too.
        
      
        EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT e.name, d.dname
FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON d.code = e.dept_code;   -- no index on either code column
        

        -> Inner hash join (e.dept_code = d.code)  (cost=1.0e+6 rows=1e+6)
    -> Table scan on e  (cost=0.53 rows=998000)
    -> Hash
        -> Table scan on d  (cost=0.75 rows=5)          <-- build side = small table
        
      
        ⚠️
        Traps
        "Hash join needs an index" — no, it is used exactly when there is no usable index. "MySQL only supports nested loop joins" — true only before 8.0.18. Building the hash on the bigger table wastes memory.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Hash join builds a hash table on the smaller input using the join key, then streams the bigger input and probes the table for matches, so it is roughly linear and needs only equality. Nested loop is better when the outer side is small and the inner join column is indexed, because each outer row costs just one index lookup and the first rows come back immediately. In MySQL, hash join arrived in 8.0.18 and replaced block nested loop in 8.0.20.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪How do I tell which join algorithm MySQL used?
          
        Traditional EXPLAIN: inner table with type = eq_ref or ref → index nested loop. Extra: Using join buffer (hash join) → hash join. FORMAT=TREE prints Nested loop inner join or Inner hash join directly.
        
        
        ↪The hash join spills to disk. What can you do?
          
        Make the build side smaller (filter earlier, select fewer columns), raise join_buffer_size for that session (/*+ SET_VAR(join_buffer_size = 64M) */), or add an index on the join column so an index nested loop becomes possible.
        
        
        ↪What is a semi-join and anti-join?
          
        A semi-join returns each left row at most once if some match exists (that is IN / EXISTS). An anti-join returns left rows with no match (NOT EXISTS, NOT IN without NULLs). MySQL converts NOT IN/NOT EXISTS to anti-joins since 8.0.17.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Join order: who drives?
        
  
        For inner joins the optimizer is free to choose which table to read first (the driving or outer table). The goal is to keep the intermediate results small and to let the inner tables use index lookups. A good rule of thumb: drive from the table that is smallest after its own filters, and probe the others by indexed join keys.
        
  
        SELECT c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c                        -- 1,000,000 rows, 5,000 in Pune
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id   -- 50,000,000 rows, 10,000 this month
WHERE c.city = 'Pune' AND o.created_at >= '2026-10-01';
-- Good: drive from orders (10k rows via index on created_at), then 10k PK lookups into customers (eq_ref)
-- Bad:  drive from customers without an index on city → scan 1M rows first
        
  
        💡
        Forcing the order (last resort)
        SELECT STRAIGHT_JOIN … joins in FROM order. Newer, finer hints: /*+ JOIN_ORDER(o, c) */, JOIN_PREFIX, JOIN_SUFFIX, JOIN_FIXED_ORDER. A LEFT JOIN always reads the left (preserved) side first in MySQL's classic optimizer.
        

  
  
        🔍 Access methods: how one table is read
        
  
        
    
        Access methodWhat it doesGood whenMySQL EXPLAINPostgreSQL node
        
    
      
        Full table scanRead every page of the table (clustered index in InnoDB) in orderSmall table, or the query needs a big fraction of rowstype=ALLSeq Scan
        
      
        Index lookup (point)Walk the B+ tree to one keyEquality on PK / unique / selective columnconst, eq_ref, refIndex Scan
        
      
        Index range scanSeek to the start key, walk leaves to the stop keyBETWEEN, >, IN, LIKE 'ab%'rangeIndex Scan (with range cond.)
        
      
        Index-only (covering) scanAnswer from the index alone; never touch the table rowsEvery needed column is in the indexExtra: Using indexIndex Only Scan
        
      
        Full index scanRead the whole index in orderCovering, or to avoid a sorttype=indexIndex (Only) Scan without cond.
        
      
        Bitmap / MRRCollect row IDs from the index, sort them by physical location, then fetch pages in orderMedium selectivity; many rows scattered over the tableUsing MRRBitmap Index Scan → Bitmap Heap Scan
        
      
        Index mergeUse two+ indexes on one table, intersect/union row IDsa = 1 OR b = 2 with separate indexestype=index_mergeBitmapOr / BitmapAnd
        
            
  
        

  
        
    QWhy would the optimizer pick a full table scan even though an index exists?
    
        
      
        Because a scan can genuinely be cheaper. In InnoDB, each row found through a secondary index needs a second lookup into the clustered index (a random read). If the predicate matches, say, 40% of a large table, 40% × N random lookups cost more than reading all pages sequentially. There is no fixed "30% rule" in modern MySQL; it compares estimated costs using table size, row count and I/O block size. With a small LIMIT, it may use the index anyway.
        
      
        Other reasons: tiny table; the index is not a leftmost prefix; the column is wrapped in a function; implicit type conversion; a leading % wildcard; stale statistics; the index is INVISIBLE. Chapter 15 has the full checklist.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        An index is not always faster. If the predicate matches a large fraction of rows, many random index-plus-row lookups cost more than one sequential scan, so the cost-based optimizer correctly chooses the scan. I would check the estimate with EXPLAIN, and if it is wrong I would refresh statistics; if it is right, the real fix is a more selective or covering index.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        📋 Reading MySQL EXPLAIN, column by column
        
  
        EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose, with its estimates, without running the query. Traditional format prints one row per table access, in join order (top row = driving table). Here is every column in plain English.
        

  
        
    
        id
        Number of the SELECT this row belongs to. Same id = same join. Bigger ids are subqueries / union parts. NULL for a UNION result row.
