        select_type
        SIMPLE (no subquery/union), PRIMARY (outermost), SUBQUERY, DEPENDENT SUBQUERY (re-run per outer row ⚠️), DERIVED (subquery in FROM, materialized), MATERIALIZED (semi-join materialization), UNION, UNION RESULT, UNCACHEABLE SUBQUERY.
        
    
        table
        Table or alias read in this step; <derivedN>, <unionM,N>, <subqueryN> for internal temp results.
        
    
        partitions
        Which partitions are touched. Shows partition pruning. NULL for non-partitioned tables.
        
    
        type
        The access method ("join type"). The single most important column. Ladder below.
        
    
        possible_keys
        Indexes the optimizer could use. If it is non-NULL but key is NULL, an index was considered and rejected (cost, selectivity).
        
    
        key
        The index actually used. NULL = no index.
        
    
        key_len
        Bytes of the index key used for access. Tells you how many columns of a composite index are really working.
        
    
        ref
        What is compared to the index: const (a literal), db.c.id (a column from an earlier table), func. NULL for range scans.
        
    
        rows
        Estimated rows examined for this step (per loop of the outer table). Not the result size.
        
    
        filtered
        Estimated % of those rows that survive the remaining WHERE conditions. rows × filtered / 100 = rows passed to the next table.
        
    
        Extra
        Everything else: covering index, filesort, temp table, ICP, hash join... Table further below.
        
  
        

  
        The type ladder: best → worst
        
  

  
        
    
        typeMeaningExample (orders / customers)
        
    
      
        systemTable has exactly one row (special const)a one-row derived table
        
      
        constPK or UNIQUE NOT NULL fully compared to constants → at most 1 row, read once during optimizationWHERE id = 7
        
      
        eq_refJoin on a full PK / UNIQUE NOT NULL → exactly one row per row of the previous tableJOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id (c side)
        
      
        refEquality on a non-unique index or a leftmost prefix → possibly many rowsWHERE customer_id = 42
        
      
        fulltextFULLTEXT index used (MATCH … AGAINST)search in product descriptions
        
      
        ref_or_nullLike ref, plus an extra search for NULLWHERE coupon_id = 5 OR coupon_id IS NULL
        
      
        index_mergeSeveral indexes on one table combined (intersect / union / sort_union)WHERE customer_id = 42 OR status = 'DISPUTED'
        
      
        unique_subquery / index_subqueryIN-subquery replaced by an index lookup function… IN (SELECT id FROM …) when not converted to a semi-join
        
      
        rangeIndex range scan; ref column is NULLWHERE created_at >= '2026-10-01', IN (1,2,3), LIKE 'ab%'
        
      
        indexFull index scan (all leaves). Good only if covering (Using index) or it avoids a sortSELECT customer_id FROM orders
        
      
        ALLFull table scanWHERE note LIKE '%refund%'
        
            
  
        
  
        🚫
        Answer that fails interviews
        "type = index means it used an index, so it's good." No: it is a full index scan. Without Using index it also does a row lookup for every entry and can be slower than ALL.
        

  
        key_len: how many composite-index columns are used?
        
  
        MySQL adds up the byte width of each index column used for access. Compare the number with the column widths and you know which prefix of the index is working. ← super useful, rarely known!
        
  
        
    
        Column typeBytes in key_len
        
    
      
        TINYINT / SMALLINT / MEDIUMINT / INT / BIGINT1 / 2 / 3 / 4 / 8
        
      
        DATE / TIMESTAMP / DATETIME3 / 4 / 5 (+ fractional-second bytes if fsp > 0)
        
      
        CHAR(n)n × max bytes per char (utf8mb4 = 4, latin1 = 1)
        
      
        VARCHAR(n)n × max bytes per char + 2 (length bytes)
        
      
        Column is NULLable+ 1 (NULL flag)
        
            
  
        
  
        -- widths: customer_id = 4, status = 16*4 + 2 = 66, created_at = 5
WHERE customer_id = 42                                   -- key_len 4   → 1 column used
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'PAID'               -- key_len 70  → 2 columns
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND status = 'PAID'
  AND created_at >= '2026-10-01'                         -- key_len 75  → all 3
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-10-01'    -- key_len 4   → gap at status! created_at only filtered (ICP)
        

  
        
    
        🧮 key_len calculator — describe your composite index
        
    
        
    
        
    
        Match the key_len from your EXPLAIN against the prefix totals to see how many columns are used for access.
        
  
        
  
  

  
        The Extra column: good news and bad news
        
  
        
    
        Extra valueMeaningVerdict
        
    
      
        Using indexCovering index: all needed columns read from the index, no table row lookup✔ jackpot
        
      
        Using whereA WHERE filter is applied to rows after they are read. Does not mean "no index"~ normal; bad together with ALL on a big table
        
      
        Using index conditionIndex Condition Pushdown (ICP): parts of WHERE checked on index entries inside InnoDB before fetching full rows✔ fewer row lookups
        
      
        Using temporaryAn internal temp table is built (GROUP BY / DISTINCT / UNION / ORDER BY on different columns than GROUP BY)✘ watch it
        
      
        Using filesortAn extra sort step (in memory if it fits sort_buffer_size, else on disk). Not necessarily a file✘ watch it on big sets
        
      
        Using join buffer (hash join)Hash join (8.0.18+). Older: (Block Nested Loop), (Batched Key Access)~ fine for big unindexed joins; else add an index
        
      
        Impossible WHEREWHERE is always false (e.g. id = 1 AND id = 2, or NOT NULL column IS NULL); no table is readcheck your logic
        
      
        Select tables optimized awayAnswered during optimization (e.g. MIN(id) from the index end)✔
        
      
        Using index for group-byLoose index scan: GROUP BY reads only the first entry of each group from the index✔
        
      
        Using index for skip scan8.0.13+ skip scan on a composite index whose first column is not in WHERE~
        
      
        Backward index scanIndex read in reverse to satisfy ORDER BY … DESC without a sort✔
        
      
        Using MRRMulti-Range Read: row IDs sorted before fetching, so disk reads are more sequential✔
        
      
        Start temporary / FirstMatch(t) / LooseScanSemi-join strategies for IN/EXISTS subqueriesinfo
        
            
  
        
  
        🧠 "filesort, temporary = extra work; Using index = jackpot"
        And the ladder: Some Cats Eat Rats, Rarely In Alleys = system, const, eq_ref, ref, range, index, ALL.
        

  
        Annotated example: before and after adding an index
        
  
        EXPLAIN
SELECT id, created_at, amount
FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 10;
        

        +----+-------------+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+------+---------+----------+-----------------------------+
| id | select_type | table  | type | possible_keys | key  | key_len | ref  | rows    | filtered | Extra                       |
+----+-------------+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+------+---------+----------+-----------------------------+
|  1 | SIMPLE      | orders | ALL  | NULL          | NULL | NULL    | NULL | 1994322 |     3.33 | Using where; Using filesort |
+----+-------------+--------+------+---------------+------+---------+------+---------+----------+-----------------------------+
  type=ALL            -> reads all 2M rows
  key=NULL            -> no index available (possible_keys is NULL too)
  rows x filtered     -> 1,994,322 x 3.33% ≈ 66k rows expected to survive the WHERE
  Using filesort      -> then sorts the survivors just to return 10
        
  
        ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_cust_created (customer_id, created_at);   -- Equality first, then Range/Sort
        

        +----+-------------+--------+-------+------------------+------------------+---------+------+------+----------+----------------------------------------------+
| id | select_type | table  | type  | possible_keys    | key              | key_len | ref  | rows | filtered | Extra                                        |
+----+-------------+--------+-------+------------------+------------------+---------+------+------+----------+----------------------------------------------+
|  1 | SIMPLE      | orders | range | idx_cust_created | idx_cust_created | 9       | NULL |  120 |   100.00 | Using index condition; Backward index scan   |
+----+-------------+--------+-------+------------------+------------------+---------+------+------+----------+----------------------------------------------+
  type=range                 -> seek to (42, 2026-01-01) and walk the leaves
  key_len=9                  -> 4 (INT customer_id) + 5 (DATETIME created_at) = BOTH columns used
  rows=120                   -> 120 instead of 2M
  Backward index scan        -> DESC order comes free from the index: NO filesort, LIMIT stops after 10
        
  
        💡
        One more step: make it covering
        INDEX(customer_id, created_at, amount) holds every selected column (id is the PK and is stored in every InnoDB secondary index for free). Extra becomes Using where; Using index; Backward index scan: zero clustered-index lookups. key_len stays 9, because amount is only carried, not used for access.
        

  
        EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
        
  
        EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE 8.0.16+ prints the iterator tree: read it from the most indented line outwards. EXPLAIN ANALYZE 8.0.18+ actually executes the query and adds real numbers to every iterator: (actual time=first_row..all_rows rows=N loops=L). Times are per loop, so total ≈ last time × loops.
        

        -> Limit: 10 row(s)  (cost=201234 rows=10) (actual time=812..812 rows=10 loops=1)
    -> Sort: orders.created_at DESC, limit input to 10 row(s) per chunk  (cost=201234 rows=1.99e+6) (actual time=812..812 rows=10 loops=1)
        -> Filter: ((orders.customer_id = 42) and (orders.created_at >= TIMESTAMP'2026-01-01 00:00:00'))
                 (cost=201234 rows=66477) (actual time=0.9..811 rows=118 loops=1)      <-- estimate 66k, actual 118!
            -> Table scan on orders  (cost=201234 rows=1.99e+6) (actual time=0.05..640 rows=2e+6 loops=1)
        

        -> Limit: 10 row(s)  (cost=54.2 rows=10) (actual time=0.061..0.094 rows=10 loops=1)
    -> Index range scan on orders using idx_cust_created over (customer_id = 42 AND '2026-01-01 00:00:00' <= created_at) (reverse)
           (cost=54.2 rows=120) (actual time=0.059..0.091 rows=10 loops=1)
        
  
        812 ms → 0.09 ms. Note the first plan's filter estimate (66,477) vs actual (118): with no index and no histogram, MySQL used default guesses. That gap is exactly what you hunt for.
        
  
        ⚠️
        EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the statement
        It supports SELECT and multi-table UPDATE/DELETE. Never run it "just to see" on a production DELETE or a 2-hour report on the primary. Use a replica or a copy. EXPLAIN FOR CONNECTION <id> shows the plan of a query that is already running in another session.
        

  
        
    QEXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE — and what do you look at first?
    
        
      
        EXPLAIN = the plan + estimates; the query is not run; instant and safe. EXPLAIN ANALYZE = runs the query and reports actual time, actual rows and loops per step, so you see where the time goes and where estimates are wrong.
        
      
          
        
        1. type — any ALL or non-covering index on a big table?
          2. 
        
        2. key / possible_keys — index chosen? considered and rejected?
          3. 
        
        3. key_len — is the whole composite index used, or only a prefix?
          4. 
        
        4. rows × filtered — how much work, and how much of it is thrown away?
          5. 
        
        5. Extra — filesort / temporary on large sets? covering? ICP?
          6. 
        
        6. ANALYZE — estimate vs actual, and which node has the biggest actual time.
          7. 
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan with estimated rows and does not run the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows actual rows and timings per step. I read type first to spot full scans, then key and key_len to see how much of the index is used, rows times filtered for the amount of work, and Extra for filesort or temporary tables. With ANALYZE I compare estimated and actual rows, because a big gap means bad statistics and probably a bad plan.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪Is rows the number of rows returned?
          
        No. It is the estimated rows examined for that table, per loop of the outer table. For a join, the total work is roughly the product down the rows (adjusted by filtered).
        
        
        ↪What is the difference between Using index and Using index condition?
          
        Using index: index-only read, no row fetch at all (covering). Using index condition: ICP; rows are still fetched, but some WHERE conditions were tested on index entries first, so fewer rows are fetched.
        
        
        ↪What does SHOW WARNINGS after EXPLAIN give you?
          
        The query as the optimizer rewrote it (merged derived tables, semi-joins, folded constants). Great for seeing what your subquery actually became.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        PostgreSQL EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
        
  
        EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT id, created_at, amount FROM orders
WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01'
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;
        

        Limit  (cost=0.43..38.12 rows=10 width=22) (actual time=0.031..0.052 rows=10 loops=1)
  Buffers: shared hit=6
  ->  Index Scan Backward using idx_cust_created on orders  (cost=0.43..452.1 rows=120 width=22)
                                                       (actual time=0.029..0.048 rows=10 loops=1)
        Index Cond: ((customer_id = 42) AND (created_at >= '2026-01-01 00:00:00'))
        Buffers: shared hit=6                        <-- 6 pages, all from cache (read=N would mean disk)
Planning Time: 0.140 ms
Execution Time: 0.071 ms
        
  
        
    
        PostgreSQL nodeMeaningNearest MySQL wording
        
    
      
        Seq ScanRead the whole heaptype=ALL
        
      
        Index ScanWalk index, fetch each heap row (in index order)ref/range without Using index
        
      
        Index Only ScanAnswer from the index; heap visited only if the visibility map says the page is not all-visible (Heap Fetches)Using index
        
      
        Bitmap Index Scan → Bitmap Heap ScanCollect matching row locations into a bitmap, then visit heap pages in physical order (Recheck Cond)Using MRR / index_merge
        
      
        Nested LoopInner side run once per outer row (loops=N)eq_ref/ref inner table
        
      
        Hash Join + HashHash node = build sideUsing join buffer (hash join)
        
      
        Merge JoinBoth inputs sorted on the key, merged(no MySQL equivalent)
        
      
        Sort / HashAggregate / GroupAggregateSorting, groupingUsing filesort / Using temporary
        
            
  
        
  
        🔀
        Reading PostgreSQL plans
        cost=startup..total is in planner units, not ms. actual time and rows are per loop: multiply by loops. BUFFERS shows shared hit (cache) vs read (disk) — since PostgreSQL 18, EXPLAIN ANALYZE includes buffers by default. PostgreSQL has no optimizer hints in core (the pg_hint_plan extension adds them); you steer it with statistics, indexes and enable_* settings for testing. Oracle: EXPLAIN PLAN FOR … + DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY. SQL Server: graphical "actual execution plan" or SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON.
        

  
  
        🧭 Steering the optimizer: index hints & optimizer hints
        
  
        Sometimes the optimizer picks the wrong plan and you know a better one. Hints let you override it. Think of them as a seatbelt, not a steering wheel: use them after you have fixed statistics and indexes, never as the first move.
        

  
        
    
        Old-style index hints
          
      
        • USE INDEX (idx) — "only consider these indexes" (a table scan is still allowed).
          • 
      
        • FORCE INDEX (idx) — like USE, but a table scan is treated as very expensive, so the index is used if it can be used at all.
          • 
      
        • IGNORE INDEX (idx) — "pretend this index does not exist".
          • 
      
        • Can be scoped: FOR JOIN, FOR ORDER BY, FOR GROUP BY.
          • 
      
        • Written after the table name: FROM orders FORCE INDEX (idx_cust_created).
          • 
    
        
    
        Optimizer hints /*+ … */
          
      
        • Written right after SELECT / UPDATE / DELETE as a special comment.
          • 
      
        • Index-level 8.0.20+: INDEX(t idx), NO_INDEX, JOIN_INDEX, ORDER_INDEX, GROUP_INDEX — meant to replace the old index hints over time.
          • 
      
        • Join order: JOIN_ORDER, JOIN_PREFIX, JOIN_SUFFIX, JOIN_FIXED_ORDER.
          • 
      
        • Strategy: HASH_JOIN/NO_HASH_JOIN (8.0.18 only), BKA, MRR, NO_ICP, SKIP_SCAN, MERGE/NO_MERGE, SEMIJOIN(...).
          • 
      
        • Session knobs per query: SET_VAR(sort_buffer_size = 16M), MAX_EXECUTION_TIME(1000) (ms, SELECT only).
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        -- 1) old index hint
SELECT id, amount FROM orders FORCE INDEX (idx_cust_created)
WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

-- 2) optimizer hint (preferred in new code)
SELECT /*+ INDEX(orders idx_cust_created) */ id, amount
FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

-- 3) fix the join order and cap runtime at 2 seconds
SELECT /*+ JOIN_ORDER(o, c) MAX_EXECUTION_TIME(2000) */ c.name, o.amount
FROM customers c JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-10-01';
        

  
        
    QWhen would you use FORCE INDEX, and what is the risk?
    
        
      
        When: you have proven (with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, comparing actual times) that a specific index is faster, and fixing statistics (ANALYZE TABLE, histograms, more sample pages) did not make the optimizer choose it. Typical case: ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10 where MySQL picks a filter index plus filesort, but walking the created_at index and stopping after 10 rows is far faster.
        
      
        Risk: a hint freezes a decision that was right for today's data. When the data distribution changes, or someone renames/drops the index, the hint becomes wrong (a hint naming a missing index makes FORCE INDEX fail with an error; an optimizer hint with a bad name is just ignored with a warning). Hints also hide the real problem from the next engineer.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Order of fixes
        1) Rewrite the query to be sargable. 2) Fix statistics. 3) Fix the index design (composite / covering). 4) Only then a hint — with a comment saying why, and a ticket to revisit.
        
      
        🔀
        Other engines
        Oracle: rich hints /*+ INDEX(t idx) LEADING(a b) USE_NL(b) */, plus SQL Plan Baselines to pin plans. SQL Server: WITH (INDEX(idx)), OPTION (HASH JOIN, RECOMPILE), and Query Store "force plan". PostgreSQL: no hints in core by design; use the pg_hint_plan extension, or steer with statistics and (for testing only) SET enable_seqscan = off.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I treat hints as a last resort. First I check whether the query is sargable, whether statistics are fresh, and whether the index design is right. If the optimizer still picks a worse plan and I can prove it with EXPLAIN ANALYZE, I add an optimizer hint like INDEX or JOIN_ORDER with a comment, because a hint freezes the plan and can become wrong as the data changes.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🧩 Subquery optimization & derived-table merging
        
  
        Old MySQL (5.5 and earlier) was famous for running WHERE x IN (SELECT …) as a dependent subquery: once for every outer row. That is why old blogs say "never use IN with a subquery, always rewrite as JOIN". Since 5.6 / 8.0 the optimizer rewrites most subqueries itself. Know what it does, so you can read the plan.
        

  
        
    
        StrategyWhat it does (simple English)How it shows in EXPLAIN
        
    
      
        Table pulloutThe subquery table is unique on the join key, so it is turned into a normal inner joinBoth tables with the same id, no extra text
        
      
        FirstMatchJoin, but stop looking at inner rows after the first match per outer row (avoids duplicates)FirstMatch(o)
        
      
        LooseScanRead the subquery's index and take only the first entry of each key groupLooseScan
        
      
        Duplicate WeedoutDo a normal join, then remove duplicate outer rows with a temporary table of row IDsStart temporary … End temporary
        
      
        MaterializationRun the subquery once, store the result in an indexed temp table, then look up / join against itselect_type = MATERIALIZED, table <subquery2>
        
      
        IN → EXISTSFallback: push the outer value into the subquery and run it per outer row (good only if the subquery has an index)DEPENDENT SUBQUERY
        
      
        Anti-join 8.0.17+NOT IN / NOT EXISTS become anti-joinsNot exists / antijoin in FORMAT=TREE
        
            
  
        

  
        
    QIN vs EXISTS vs JOIN — which is faster?
    
        
      
        Modern answer: in MySQL 8 and PostgreSQL they usually produce the same plan, because the optimizer turns IN (subquery) and EXISTS (subquery) into a semi-join and then chooses the best strategy by cost. So choose by meaning:
        
      
          
        
        • JOIN when you need columns from both tables. Careful: if the right side has many matches, rows multiply (you may need DISTINCT, which costs a sort).
          • 
        
        • IN / EXISTS when you only ask "does a match exist?" — a semi-join never multiplies rows.
          • 
        
        • NOT EXISTS rather than NOT IN for "no match" — NOT IN returns nothing if the subquery yields a single NULL (see Chapter 8).
          • 
      
        
      
        SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE c.id IN (SELECT o.customer_id FROM orders o WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-10-01');

SELECT c.id, c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o
              WHERE o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at >= '2026-10-01');

SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at >= '2026-10-01';   -- DISTINCT needed!
        
      
        🚫
        Answer that fails interviews
        "EXISTS is always faster than IN" or "IN with a subquery is always slow, use JOIN." That was true for MySQL 5.5. Say: "it depends on the plan; modern optimizers convert both to semi-joins, so I check EXPLAIN."
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        In modern MySQL and PostgreSQL, IN and EXISTS subqueries are usually rewritten into a semi-join, so performance is often identical, and I confirm it with EXPLAIN. I pick by meaning: JOIN when I need columns from both sides, EXISTS or IN when I only test for a match, and NOT EXISTS instead of NOT IN because NOT IN breaks when the subquery returns a NULL.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪When can MySQL NOT use semi-join transformation?
          
        When the subquery has things like GROUP BY/aggregates, LIMIT, UNION, or sits inside an OR with other conditions, or the statement is a single-table UPDATE/DELETE in older versions. Then it falls back to materialization or IN→EXISTS. A DEPENDENT SUBQUERY row in EXPLAIN on a big outer table is your red flag.
        
        
        ↪What is a correlated subquery and why can it be slow?
          
        A subquery that refers to a column of the outer query (WHERE o.customer_id = c.id). Logically it runs once per outer row. If the optimizer cannot decorrelate it, 1M outer rows = 1M subquery executions; fast only if each one is an index lookup.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Derived tables, views and CTEs: merge or materialize?
        
  
        A derived table is a subquery in FROM. MySQL either merges it into the outer query (as if you had written one flat query — filters and indexes of the base table still work) or materializes it (runs it, stores the result in an internal temp table, then reads that). Merging is usually much better. Views and non-recursive CTEs follow the same rules.
        
  
        SELECT * FROM (SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders) t
WHERE t.customer_id = 42;
-- merged → becomes: SELECT id, customer_id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42  (uses the index)
        
  
          
    
        • Cannot be merged if the subquery has aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, HAVING, LIMIT, UNION, window functions, or subqueries in the select list. Then it is materialized (select_type = DERIVED, table <derived2>).
          • 
    
        • MySQL can add an auto-generated index on a materialized derived table (key = <auto_key0>) so joins against it are not full scans.
          • 
    
        • Derived condition pushdown 8.0.22+: an outer WHERE is pushed into a materialized derived table, so it materializes fewer rows.
          • 
    
        • Control: optimizer_switch derived_merge, hints /*+ MERGE(t) */ / NO_MERGE(t).
          • 
  
        
  
        🔀
        CTEs across engines
        PostgreSQL ≤ 11 always materialized CTEs (an "optimization fence"). Since PostgreSQL 12, a non-recursive CTE referenced once is inlined unless you write AS MATERIALIZED. MySQL 8 treats a CTE like a derived table: merged if possible, and materialized once (shared) if referenced several times. More in Chapter 9.
        

  
  
        🗄️ ORDER BY, LIMIT, filesort & GROUP BY
        
  
        Sorting is the most common "hidden" cost in a plan. There are only two ways to get rows in order: read them in index order (free, and LIMIT can stop early) or sort them afterwards (MySQL calls this filesort, even when it happens fully in memory).
        

  
        
    
        Is there an index whose order matches ORDER BYafter the equality columns of WHERE?
        
    
        
    
        Yes → read in index orderno sort; LIMIT 10 reads ~10 entries (Backward index scan for DESC)
        
    
        
    
        No → filesortcollect ALL matching rows, sort in sort_buffer_size, spill to disk in chunks + merge if too big
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is "Using filesort"? Is it always bad?
    
        
      
        What: MySQL could not get the rows in the requested order from an index, so it sorts them itself. How: it reads the matching rows, puts sort keys (plus either the needed columns or the row id) in the sort buffer, sorts, and if the data does not fit it writes sorted chunks to temporary files and merges them (Sort_merge_passes in SHOW STATUS counts these merges).
        
      
        Not always bad: sorting 200 rows in memory costs microseconds. It is bad when the input is large: sorting 2M rows to return the top 10 means reading and sorting all 2M first. With ORDER BY … LIMIT n MySQL can use a priority queue (keep only the best n in memory), which saves memory but still reads every matching row.
        
      
        
        
        Query (INDEX(customer_id, created_at))Filesort?Why
        
        
          
        WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at✔ no sortEquality on the first column → the second is already in order
        
          
        WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY created_at DESC✔ no sortBackward index scan
        
          
        WHERE customer_id IN (1,2,3) ORDER BY created_at✘ filesortThree separate sorted runs; the global order is broken
        
          
        WHERE customer_id > 40 ORDER BY created_at✘ filesortRange on the first column
        
          
        WHERE customer_id = 42 ORDER BY amount✘ filesortamount is not in the index
        
          
        ORDER BY customer_id, created_at (no WHERE, SELECT *)~ maybeIndex walk + 2M row lookups may cost more than scan + sort; the optimizer decides. With LIMIT 10 the index wins
        
                
      
        
      
        💡
        Fixes
        Design the index as Equality columns → Sort column (the "ESR" rule from Chapter 15). Select fewer columns so sort rows are smaller. Raise sort_buffer_size per query only (/*+ SET_VAR(sort_buffer_size = 8M) */), never globally to huge values — it is allocated per sorting session.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Using filesort means MySQL sorts the rows itself because no index gives them in the right order. It is fine for small inputs, but on a large input it must read and sort everything before returning even the first row, so LIMIT does not help much. The fix is usually a composite index with the equality columns first and the ORDER BY column next, so rows come out of the index already sorted and LIMIT stops early.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHow does MySQL execute GROUP BY? Why do I see "Using temporary"?
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Loose index scan (Using index for group-by) — best. For SELECT customer_id, MIN(created_at) … GROUP BY customer_id with INDEX(customer_id, created_at), it jumps to the first entry of each group and skips the rest.
          2. 
        
        2. Tight index scan — reads the index in group order and aggregates group by group. No temp table, but reads every entry.
          3. 
        
        3. Temporary table (Using temporary) — no index order fits, so MySQL builds an internal table keyed by the group columns and updates the aggregates as rows arrive. In 8.0 it lives in memory (TempTable engine) and spills to disk when it outgrows the limits (tmp_table_size, temptable_max_ram).
          4. 
      
        
      
        🔀
        MySQL 8.0 change that surprises people
        MySQL 5.7 sorted GROUP BY results implicitly. MySQL 8.0 does not. If you need order, write ORDER BY. (The old GROUP BY col DESC syntax was removed in 8.0.13.) PostgreSQL chooses between HashAggregate (hash table) and GroupAggregate (sorted input).
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🗃️ Query cache (gone) & plan caching / prepared statements
        
  
        Two different things get mixed up in interviews. A result cache stores the answer of a query. A plan cache stores the execution plan, so the next run can skip parsing and optimizing but still reads fresh data.
        

  
        
    QWhat happened to the MySQL query cache?
    
        
      
        The query cache stored the result set of a SELECT, keyed by the exact query text. An identical query got the stored result instantly. It was deprecated in 5.7.20 and removed in MySQL 8.0.3. Reasons:
        
      
          
        
        • Invalidation: any write to a table threw away every cached result that used that table. On a busy OLTP table the cache was mostly churn.
          • 
        
        • Global lock: one mutex protected the cache, so on many-core servers it became a bottleneck instead of a speed-up.
          • 
        
        • Exact text match: one extra space or a different comment = cache miss.
          • 
      
        
      
        What to use instead: cache in the application layer (Redis / Memcached) with explicit keys and TTLs, a proxy-level cache (ProxySQL), or read replicas. The InnoDB buffer pool still caches pages, which is a different thing.
        
      
        🚫
        Answer that fails interviews
        "Step 1 of query execution in MySQL is checking the query cache." Not since 8.0. Mention it only as history.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDo databases cache execution plans? What is parameter sniffing?
    
        
      
        
        
        EnginePlan caching behaviour
        
        
          
        MySQLNo shared, server-wide plan cache. A server-side prepared statement (PREPARE … EXECUTE, or the binary protocol used by most drivers) is parsed and resolved once per session; the cost-based choices are largely redone on each EXECUTE with the actual values. Benefit: less parsing, and safety from SQL injection.
        
          
        PostgreSQLPer-session prepared statements. The first five executions get custom plans (built for the actual parameter values); after that it may switch to a generic plan if that does not look more expensive. plan_cache_mode (PG 12+) can force force_custom_plan or force_generic_plan.
        
          
        OracleGlobal shared pool / library cache. A repeat query with bind variables = soft parse (reuse); new text = hard parse (expensive, latch-heavy). Using literals instead of binds floods the cache with hard parses.
        
          
        SQL ServerGlobal plan cache for procedures and parameterized queries. The plan is compiled for the first parameter values seen — parameter sniffing.
        
                
      
        
      
        Parameter sniffing problem: a plan built for customer_id = 42 (5 rows → index nested loop) is cached and reused for customer_id = 1 (a marketplace account with 3M rows), where a hash join or scan would be far better. Same SQL, same plan, 1000× slower for one customer. Fixes: recompile per execution (OPTION (RECOMPILE) in SQL Server), OPTIMIZE FOR, PostgreSQL plan_cache_mode = force_custom_plan, Oracle adaptive cursor sharing, or separate code paths for "big" tenants.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        A plan cache stores the execution plan, not the result, so repeated queries skip parsing and optimization but still read current data. Oracle and SQL Server have global plan caches; PostgreSQL and MySQL mostly work per session with prepared statements. The risk is parameter sniffing: a plan chosen for one parameter value is reused for a value with a very different number of rows. The MySQL query cache was a result cache, and it was removed in 8.0 because every write invalidated it and its global lock did not scale.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions
        
        
        ↪Besides speed, why use prepared statements?
          
        Security. Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so user input can never change the query structure. That is the main defence against SQL injection (Chapter 18).
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        ⏱️ The slow-query tuning workflow
        
  
        This is the answer to "This page is slow in production. What do you do?" Interviewers want a process, not a random list of tricks.
        

  
        
    
        1. Findslow query log (long_query_time), pt-query-digest, sys.statement_analysis / performance_schema digests, APM traces. Rank by total time = avg × calls.
        
    
        
    
        2. Reproduce & measuresame parameters, realistic data size; note rows examined vs rows sent
        
    
        
    
        3. ExplainEXPLAIN → type, key, key_len, rows×filtered, Extra; EXPLAIN ANALYZE on a replica → estimate vs actual
        
    
        
    
        4. Diagnosenon-sargable predicate? missing/wrong composite index? bad stats? filesort/temp on big set? N+1 / OFFSET / SELECT *?
        
    
        
    
        5. Fix (cheapest first)rewrite → ANALYZE / histogram → add or reorder index (covering?) → schema change / cache → hint
        
    
        
    
        6. Verify & watchcompare EXPLAIN ANALYZE and p95 latency; check write cost of the new index; keep monitoring
        
  
        

  
        SET GLOBAL slow_query_log = ON;
SET GLOBAL long_query_time = 0.5;               -- seconds (default 10)
SET GLOBAL log_queries_not_using_indexes = ON;  -- optional, noisy

-- Top statements by total latency (sys schema, built from performance_schema)
SELECT query, exec_count, total_latency, rows_examined_avg, rows_sent_avg
FROM sys.statement_analysis
ORDER BY total_latency DESC
LIMIT 5;
        
  
        🎯
        The killer metric
        rows_examined ÷ rows_sent. A query that examines 2,000,000 rows to send 10 has a ratio of 200,000 — it is begging for a better index. A ratio near 1 means the access path is already tight, and the problem is elsewhere (too many calls, network, locks).
        

  
  
        🐛 Classic performance anti-patterns (and the fixes)
        

  
        
    QWhat is a sargable predicate? Give examples of rewrites.
    
        
      
        Sargable = "Search ARGument ABLE". The indexed column stands alone on one side of the comparison, so the B+ tree can compute a start key and a stop key. If you wrap the column in a function, do arithmetic on it, or force a type conversion, the index sees a "black box" and cannot seek.
        
      
        
        
        ❌ Non-sargable✅ Sargable rewrite
        
        
          
        WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'
        
          
        WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-10-13'WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-13' AND created_at < '2026-10-14'
        
          
        WHERE price * 1.18 > 1000WHERE price > 1000 / 1.18
        
          
        WHERE LEFT(name, 3) = 'Ram'WHERE name LIKE 'Ram%'
        
          
        WHERE phone = 9876543210 (phone is VARCHAR)WHERE phone = '9876543210'
        
          
        WHERE IFNULL(coupon_id, 0) = 0WHERE coupon_id = 0 OR coupon_id IS NULL (ref_or_null)
        
          
        WHERE name LIKE '%kumar'Full-text index, reversed-string generated column, or a search engine
        
                
      
        
      
        If you cannot change the query, MySQL 8.0.13+ functional indexes (INDEX ((YEAR(created_at)))) let the exact same expression use an index. Full list of "index exists but not used" reasons: Chapter 15.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        A predicate is sargable when the indexed column is left untouched on one side of the comparison, so the database can seek directly to a key range. Wrapping the column in a function like YEAR or DATE, doing arithmetic on it, or comparing a string column to a number forces the engine to evaluate every row. I rewrite it as a range on the raw column, or, if I can't change the query, add a functional index on the exact expression.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is the N+1 query problem?
    
        
      
        What: the app runs 1 query to get a list (say 100 orders), then N more queries, one per item, to get related data (the customer of each order). 101 round trips instead of 1 or 2. Each query is fast alone — that is why it hides in the slow log — but 100 × (network round trip + parse + execute) adds up to a slow page. It usually comes from ORMs with lazy loading.
        
      
        orders = db.query("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE created_at >= %s LIMIT 100", day)
for o in orders:                                   # 100 extra queries!
    o.customer = db.query("SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id = %s", o.customer_id)
        
      
        -- Option A: a join
SELECT o.id, o.amount, c.name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2026-10-01' LIMIT 100;

-- Option B: two queries (what ORMs call eager loading / prefetch)
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (17, 42, 99 /* … ids from the first query */);
        
      
        ORM fixes: Django select_related / prefetch_related, Rails includes, Hibernate JOIN FETCH / batch fetching, SQLAlchemy joinedload / selectinload. Detect it by counting queries per request.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhy is LIMIT 10 OFFSET 1000000 slow? How do you paginate deep?
    
        
      
        Why: OFFSET does not "jump". The database must produce and throw away the first 1,000,000 rows (walking the index and, for SELECT *, fetching each row), then return 10. Page 100,000 is 100,000× more work than page 1. Results can also skip or repeat rows if data changes between pages.
        
      
        
        
        
        
        
          
        -- page 1
SELECT id, created_at, amount FROM orders
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10;
-- next page: pass the LAST row's (created_at, id) = ('2026-10-12 09:15:00', 88123)
SELECT id, created_at, amount FROM orders
WHERE created_at < '2026-10-12 09:15:00'
   OR (created_at = '2026-10-12 09:15:00' AND id < 88123)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 10;      -- needs INDEX(created_at, id)
        
          
        Every page is a seek + 10 rows, whether page 1 or page 100,000. Downsides: no "jump to page 537", and the sort key must be unique (add id as a tiebreaker). The expanded OR form uses the index fully in MySQL; the row-constructor form (created_at, id) < (…, …) is clearer but may use the index less well in MySQL.
        
        
        
        
        
          
        SELECT o.id, o.created_at, o.amount, o.note
FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT id FROM orders
      ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
      LIMIT 10 OFFSET 1000000) page USING (id);
        
          
        The inner query skips 1M entries using only the narrow covering index (no row fetches). Only the final 10 rows are fetched from the table. Still O(offset), but much cheaper. Use it when users really need page numbers.
        
        
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhy is SELECT * discouraged?
    
        
      
          
        
        • Kills covering indexes: the query needs every column, so every matching row requires a clustered-index lookup. SELECT id, created_at could have been Using index.
          • 
        
        • Moves more bytes: big TEXT/BLOB/JSON columns are read (even from overflow pages), sent over the network and held in memory.
          • 
        
        • Bigger sorts and temp tables: filesort and GROUP BY carry wider rows, so they spill to disk sooner.
          • 
        
        • Fragile code: adding or reordering a column can break code that reads columns by position.
          • 
      
        
      
        It is fine for ad-hoc exploration and for EXISTS (SELECT * …), where the select list is ignored.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhy is SELECT COUNT(*) on a big InnoDB table slow, when it was instant on MyISAM?
    
        
      
        MyISAM stores an exact row count in the table metadata, so COUNT(*) without WHERE is instant. InnoDB cannot do that because of MVCC: different transactions may see different numbers of rows at the same moment (one has inserted rows not yet committed, another is reading an old snapshot). So there is no single correct number to store. InnoDB must actually count the rows visible to your snapshot.
        
      
        How it counts: it scans an index — usually the smallest secondary index, because it has the most entries per page (fewest pages). If there is no secondary index it scans the clustered index; newer 8.0 releases can read the clustered index with parallel threads (innodb_parallel_read_threads). Either way it is still O(rows).
        
      
        💡
        Fixes
        Need an estimate? Use information_schema.TABLES.TABLE_ROWS or the rows from EXPLAIN (both approximate). Need an exact, frequent count? Keep a counter table updated in the same transaction (watch for a hot row), or a summary table refreshed periodically. Need a count with WHERE? Make sure an index covers the WHERE so it counts index entries only. And COUNT(*) = COUNT(1) in MySQL — no difference (see Chapter 7).
        
      
        🔀
        PostgreSQL
        Same reason (MVCC), same problem. It can use an Index Only Scan if the visibility map is mostly "all-visible" (recently vacuumed). For an estimate, read pg_class.reltuples.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QA query with OR on two different columns is slow. Why, and how do you fix it?
    
        
      
        WHERE customer_id = 42 OR status = 'DISPUTED': a single index on one column cannot answer the other half, so the optimizer may fall back to a full scan. Options:
        
      
          
        
        1. Index merge (union): if both columns have their own index, MySQL can scan both and union the row IDs (type = index_merge, Using union(idx_cust, idx_status)).
          2. 
        
        2. Rewrite as UNION: each branch uses its own best index. Use UNION (removes duplicates, for rows matching both) or UNION ALL with an exclusion condition (faster, no dedupe sort).
          3. 
      
        
      
        SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42
UNION ALL
SELECT id, amount FROM orders WHERE status = 'DISPUTED' AND customer_id <> 42;
        
      
        OR on the same column (status = 'A' OR status = 'B') is fine: it is the same as IN ('A','B'), a range on one index.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        🧮
        Function on column
        Rewrite as a range on the raw column, or a functional index.
        
    
        🔁
        N+1 queries
        JOIN or one batched IN (…); eager loading in the ORM.
        
    
        📄
        Deep OFFSET
        Keyset pagination; deferred join.
        
    
        ⭐
        SELECT *
        Select only needed columns → covering index possible.
        
    
        🔀
        OR across columns
        Index merge or UNION / UNION ALL rewrite.
        
    
        🔢
        COUNT(*) on huge table
        Estimate, counter table, or count a narrow index with a WHERE.
        
    
        🔤
        Type / collation mismatch
        Quote string literals; same type, charset and collation on join columns.
        
    
        📉
        Stale statistics
        ANALYZE TABLE after bulk loads; histograms for skewed columns.
        
  
        

  
        🌍
        Production story: the dashboard that timed out
        An admin dashboard ran SELECT * FROM orders WHERE DATE(created_at) = CURDATE() ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50 OFFSET ?. On 40M rows: type=ALL, filesort on the scan, and the OFFSET grew as admins clicked through. Three fixes took it from 9 s to 4 ms: (1) created_at >= CURDATE() AND created_at < CURDATE() + INTERVAL 1 DAY (sargable), (2) INDEX(created_at, id), (3) keyset pagination on (created_at, id) and selecting only the 6 columns shown on screen.
        

  
        🧠 F-E-F-V
        Find it (slow log) → Explain it (EXPLAIN / ANALYZE) → Fix the cheapest thing first (rewrite → stats → index → hint) → Verify (estimate vs actual, p95, write cost). "Find Every Fat Villain."
        

  
        📌 Key takeaways
          
    
        • Query journey: parse → resolve → rewrite (rules) → optimize (cost) → execute as an iterator tree. MySQL 8.0 has no query cache.
          • 
    
        • The optimizer guesses with statistics; most bad plans are bad row estimates (stale stats, skew, correlated columns, functions). Fix stats with ANALYZE TABLE and histograms.
          • 
    
        • Join algorithms: index nested loop (small outer + indexed inner, great with LIMIT), hash join (big + big, equality, MySQL 8.0.18+, replaced BNL in 8.0.20), sort-merge (sorted inputs; not in MySQL).
          • 
    
        • EXPLAIN reading order: type → key/possible_keys → key_len → rows × filtered → Extra. Using index good; Using filesort/Using temporary on big sets bad; type=index is a full index scan.
          • 
    
        • EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs the query: compare estimated vs actual rows per node.
          • 
    
        • Modern optimizers turn IN/EXISTS subqueries into semi-joins and merge derived tables; check EXPLAIN instead of repeating 2012 folklore.
          • 
    
        • Filesort is avoided by an index ordered as equality columns → sort column; then LIMIT stops early.
          • 
    
        • Hints are a last resort: they freeze plans. Plan caches can suffer from parameter sniffing.
          • 
    
        • Top killers: non-sargable predicates, N+1, deep OFFSET, SELECT *, OR across columns, type/collation mismatch, COUNT(*) on huge InnoDB tables.
          • 
  
        

  
        📚 Go deeper
          
    
        • MySQL 8.4 Reference: EXPLAIN Output Format — every type and Extra value, straight from the source.
          • 
    
        • MySQL 8.4 Reference: Optimization chapter — range optimizer, hash join, subquery strategies, ORDER BY / GROUP BY optimization, hints.
          • 
    
        • PostgreSQL docs: Using EXPLAIN — the best gentle tutorial on reading plans and cost numbers.
          • 
    
        • Use The Index, Luke! — free book on indexing and SQL performance for developers; the pagination and function chapters are gold.
          • 
    
        • CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems — lectures on join algorithms, query execution and optimization (cost formulas used in this chapter).
          • 
  
        

  
        
    
        
      
        EXPLAIN shows type = index and Extra is empty. What does that mean?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        type=index is a full index scan (second-worst on the ladder). Without Using index it is not covering, so every entry also costs a clustered lookup — it can be slower than ALL.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Index on (customer_id INT NOT NULL, created_at DATETIME NOT NULL). For WHERE customer_id = 42 AND created_at >= '2026-01-01', which key_len shows both columns are used?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        INT = 4 bytes, DATETIME (no fractional seconds) = 5 bytes, neither nullable: 4 + 5 = 9. key_len 4 would mean only customer_id is used for access.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Which statement about MySQL join algorithms is true?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Hash join arrived in 8.0.18 for equi-joins without a usable index, and in 8.0.20 BNL was removed and replaced by hash join everywhere. MySQL's classic optimizer has no sort-merge join operator.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Why did MySQL remove the query cache in 8.0?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        The query cache was correct but inefficient: heavy invalidation on write-heavy tables plus a single mutex. The buffer pool caches pages, not results.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Which predicate can use an ordinary B+ tree index on created_at for a seek?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Only the raw-column range is sargable. The others wrap the column in a function, which needs a functional index on that exact expression.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a node with rows=50000 (estimate) and actual … rows=12. What is the most likely root cause to check first?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        A big estimate-vs-actual gap means the optimizer's row estimate is wrong, which usually comes from statistics. B+ trees are always balanced.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Best way to serve page 50,000 of an infinite-scroll feed ordered by (created_at, id)?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        OFFSET still produces and discards a million rows. Keyset pagination seeks straight to the last seen key, so every page costs the same.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        5 stages of query processing?
        Parse → Resolve/bind → Rewrite (logical plan, rules) → Optimize (cost-based physical plan) → Execute (iterator tree).
        
    
        The most important heuristic rewrite?
        Push selections (and projections) down, below joins, so joins see fewer and narrower rows.
        
    
        Why do most bad plans happen?
        Bad cardinality (row-count) estimates: stale stats, skew, correlated columns, functions, parameter sniffing.
        
    
        MySQL EXPLAIN type ladder, best → worst
        system, const, eq_ref, ref, range, index, ALL — "Some Cats Eat Rats, Rarely In Alleys".
        
    
        key_len tells you…
        How many bytes (so how many leading columns) of a composite index are used for access. +1 for nullable, +2 for VARCHAR length.
        
    
        Using index vs Using index condition
        Using index = covering, no row fetch. Using index condition = ICP, rows still fetched but filtered on index entries first.
        
    
        Hash join vs index nested loop
        Hash: big + big, equality, no index, O(M+N). INL: small outer, indexed inner, first rows fast (great with LIMIT).
        
    
        EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE
        EXPLAIN = plan + estimates, not run. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (8.0.18+) = runs it, shows actual rows, time and loops per iterator.
        
    
        When is Using filesort avoided?
        When an index delivers rows in ORDER BY order after the equality columns: INDEX(eq_cols…, sort_col).
        
    
        Query cache status in MySQL 8?
        Removed in 8.0.3 (deprecated 5.7.20): write invalidation + global mutex. Cache in the app (Redis) instead.
        
    
        Parameter sniffing?
        A cached plan compiled for one parameter value is reused for a value with very different row counts → slow for some inputs.
        
    
        Why is COUNT(*) slow on InnoDB?
        MVCC: each snapshot can see a different row count, so no stored count; it must scan (smallest) index.
        
    
        Fix for deep OFFSET?
        Keyset/seek pagination on a unique sort key (e.g. (created_at, id)); or a deferred join on a covering index.
        
    
        Slow-query workflow?
        Find (slow log, digests) → Explain (EXPLAIN/ANALYZE) → Fix cheapest first (rewrite, stats, index, hint) → Verify.
        
  
        

        


        
  
        
    
        Chapter 17 · VI · Reliability & Security
        
    
        🛟 Recovery, Logging (WAL / ARIES) & Backups
        
    
        Explain exactly how a database keeps every committed transaction after a power cut, how ARIES puts the pieces back together, and how you would design backups that really restore.
        
    
        ⏱ 45 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8.4 / InnoDBPostgreSQLSQL ServerOracle
        
  
        

  
         
        ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
        
    
          
      
        • Three failure classes: transaction failure (undo it), system crash (RAM lost → redo + undo from the log), media failure (disk lost → restore backup + replay archived logs).
          • 
      
        • WAL rule: the log record describing a change reaches stable storage before the changed page does; a transaction is committed only when its commit record is on disk.
          • 
      
        • Real engines use STEAL + NO-FORCE: steal ⇒ need undo, no-force ⇒ need redo. Commit = one sequential log flush, shared by many txns via group commit.
          • 
      
        • Checkpoints bound recovery time. A fuzzy checkpoint does not stop work; it records the active-transaction table and dirty-page table.
          • 
      
        • ARIES = Analysis → Redo (repeat history, even losers, from the smallest recLSN) → Undo (losers backward, writing CLRs with undoNextLSN). pageLSN makes redo idempotent.
          • 
      
        • InnoDB: redo (crash recovery, circular, innodb_redo_log_capacity 8.0.30+), undo (rollback + MVCC), binlog (server layer: replication + PITR). An internal 2PC (Prepare → Binlog → Commit) keeps redo and binlog in agreement.
          • 
      
        • Doublewrite buffer (InnoDB) / full_page_writes (PostgreSQL) fix torn pages that redo alone cannot.
          • 
      
        • "Double 1" = innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 + sync_binlog=1 = fully durable (the default).
          • 
      
        • Backups: logical (mysqldump, pg_dump) vs physical (XtraBackup, pg_basebackup); full / incremental / differential; PITR = backup + binlog/WAL replay. Design from RPO and RTO. Replication is not a backup. Test your restores.
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        ✏️ The #1 question here is "How does a DB guarantee Durability?" If you can draw the WAL rule + steal/no-force matrix + ARIES's three passes, you beat 90% of candidates.
        

  
  
        ⚠️ What can fail? Failure classes & stable storage
        
  
        Recovery means: after something breaks, bring the database back to a state that keeps Atomicity (no half transactions) and Durability (no lost commits). What we must do depends on what was lost.
        
  
        Picture a person writing in a notebook (disk) while keeping some notes in their head (RAM). The diary next to the notebook is the log.
        

  
        
    
        FailureExampleWhat is lostRecovery tool
        
    
      
        Transaction failureConstraint violation, division by zero, deadlock victimNothing persistentUndo that one transaction (rollback)
        
      
        System crashPower cut, kernel panic, mysqld killedRAM: buffer pool, log bufferCrash recovery: redo then undo from the log
        
      
        Media (disk) failureDisk dies, file deleted, rm -rf, ransomwareDisk filesRestore backup + replay archived logs (binlog / WAL archive)
        
            
  
        

  
        
    
        Volatile storage
        Lost on crash (RAM, CPU cache).
        
    
        Non-volatile storage
        Survives a crash but can still fail (HDD, SSD).
        
    
        Stable storage
        An ideal store that never loses data. Approximated by several copies on independent devices (mirrored log disks, RAID, remote copies).
        
    
        Fail-stop assumption
        A crash stops the system without silently corrupting disk. Checksums detect when this is violated (torn page, bit rot).
        
  
        

  
        
    QClassify the types of failures and say what recovery each one needs.
    
        
      
        Transaction failure: one transaction cannot finish (logical error or system error like deadlock). Only that transaction is rolled back using its undo information. The server keeps running.
        
      
        System crash: memory contents vanish, disk is intact. On restart, the DBMS reads the log: it redoes committed work that had not reached the data files and undoes unfinished work that had.
        
      
        Media failure: the data files themselves are gone. Logs alone cannot help, because there is nothing to apply them to. You restore the latest backup and roll forward with archived logs.
        
      
        T → Take back · S → Script replay · M → Make from backup
        Transaction failure = undo. System crash = redo + undo. Media failure = restore + roll forward.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Is a deadlock a system crash?
          
        No. It is a transaction failure caused by a system error. The DBMS picks a victim, rolls it back, and everyone else continues.
        
        
        ↪Does stable storage really exist?
          
        No, it is an idealisation. We approximate it by writing the log to more than one independent device. Oracle, for example, recommends multiplexing online redo log groups on separate disks. That is what makes "the commit record is on stable storage" a believable promise.
        
        
        ↪Is RAID a backup?
          
        No. RAID survives a disk dying. It faithfully mirrors a DROP TABLE to every disk instantly. Same for replication. Only a separate, point-in-time copy protects against human and logical errors.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        📓 The log: records, WAL rule, undo & redo
        
  
        The log (journal) is an append-only file. Every change is described in it before it happens. Textbook record types:
        
  
        <Ti start>              -- Ti began
<Ti, X, V1, V2>          -- Ti changed item X from old value V1 (for UNDO) to new value V2 (for REDO)
<Ti commit>             -- Ti committed (durable once THIS record is on stable storage)
<Ti abort>              -- Ti rolled back
<Ti, X, V1>              -- redo-only "compensation" record written while undoing
<checkpoint L>          -- L = list of transactions active at checkpoint time
        
  
        Why a log at all? Writing a log record is a sequential append (fast). Writing the changed data pages means random writes all over the disk (slow). So we make the cheap thing mandatory at commit and the expensive thing lazy.
        

  
        
    QWhat is Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)? State its rules.
    
        
      
        What: WAL is the rule that the log record describing a change must reach stable storage before the changed data page does. In plain words: "write in the diary before you touch the house."
        
      
        The three rules:
        
      
          
        
        1. Order — log records reach stable storage in the order they were created.
          2. 
        
        2. Commit rule — a transaction is committed only after its <commit> record (and all earlier records) are on stable storage.
          3. 
        
        3. WAL rule proper — before a dirty data page is written to disk, all log records up to that page's latest change must be on stable storage. In ARIES terms: pageLSN ≤ flushedLSN.
          4. 
      
        
      
        Why it works: the log has the after-image (redo info) and the before-image (undo info) of every change. So whatever state the data files are in after a crash, the log can push them forward (redo) or pull them back (undo).
        
      
        Example — what happens on COMMIT in a WAL system:
        
      
        
        
        1. UPDATEchange page in buffer pool, append log record to log buffer
        
        
        
        
        2. COMMITappend commit record
        
        
        
        
        3. fsync logone sequential write, maybe shared with others
        
        
        
        
        4. "OK" to clientdata page still only in RAM — that's fine
        
        
        
        
        5. Laterbackground flush / checkpoint writes the page
        
      
        
      
        🔀
        Same idea, different names
        MySQL/InnoDB: redo log (#innodb_redo). PostgreSQL: WAL (pg_wal/) — "we do not need to flush data pages to disk on every transaction commit". Oracle: online redo logs written by LGWR. SQL Server: the transaction log (.ldf), "guarantees that no data modifications are written to disk before the associated log record". SQLite: rollback journal (default) or WAL mode.
        
      
        🚫
        Answer that fails interviews
        "On commit, the database writes the changed rows to the data file." No! Commit writes the log to disk. Data pages are written later (no-force).
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        WAL means the database writes a description of every change to an append-only log, and that log record must be on disk before the changed page is. At commit, only the log needs to be flushed, which is one fast sequential write. The data pages stay dirty in memory and are written later. If we crash, the log has both old and new values, so recovery can redo committed changes and undo uncommitted ones.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Why is just a commit record enough for durability?
          
        Because every update's after-image is already in the log before the commit record. Even if no data page was written, recovery can rebuild the committed state from the log.
        
        
        ↪Isn't an fsync on every commit slow?
          
        It would be, so engines use group commit: many transactions that commit at nearly the same moment share one fsync. See the internal 2PC section below for how MySQL batches it.
        
        
        ↪What if the page is half-written during the crash?
          
        That is a torn page. Redo cannot fix it, because redo assumes a valid page. InnoDB uses the doublewrite buffer; PostgreSQL logs full page images (full_page_writes).
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Undo vs redo — and which transactions get which
        
  
        
    
        ↩️ UNDO (roll back)
          
      
        • Uses the old value (before-image) V1.
          • 
      
        • Walk the log backward, restore old values.
          • 
      
        • Applied to transactions with <start> but no commit/abort ("losers").
          • 
      
        • Needed because uncommitted changes may already be on disk (steal).
          • 
      
        • Undo actions are themselves logged (redo-only records / CLRs).
          • 
    
        
    
        ↪️ REDO (roll forward)
          
      
        • Uses the new value (after-image) V2.
          • 
      
        • Walk the log forward, reapply new values.
          • 
      
        • Applied to transactions with commit (textbook: or abort, to replay compensation records).
          • 
      
        • Needed because committed changes may still be only in RAM (no-force).
          • 
      
        • Must be idempotent — applying twice = applying once.
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QClassic textbook question: given a log and a crash point, what are the final values?
    
        
      
        T0 transfers 50 from A to B. T1 withdraws 100 from C. Immediate modification (changes may hit disk before commit).
        
      
        <T0 start>
<T0, A, 1000, 950>
<T0, B, 2000, 2050>
<T0 commit>          ← crash point (b) is just after this line
<T1 start>
<T1, C, 700, 600>
<T1 commit>          ← crash point (c) is just after this line
        
      
        
        
        Crash pointActionABC
        
        
          
        (a) before <T0 commit> loggedundo T010002000700
        
          
        (b) after T0 commit, before T1 commitredo T0, undo T19502050700
        
          
        (c) after both commitsredo T0, redo T19502050600
        
                
      
        
      
        💡
        Order matters
        Textbook algorithm: do the redo pass first (forward), building the undo-list, then the undo pass (backward). Undo always goes in reverse log order so an item updated twice ends at its oldest value.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        ⚖️ Buffer policies: the steal / force matrix
        
  
        Two independent questions about the buffer pool decide whether recovery needs undo, redo, both or neither:
        
  
        
    
        STEAL
        May the buffer pool write a page holding uncommitted changes to disk (to free a frame)? Yes = steal. No = no-steal.
        
    
        FORCE
        Must all pages a transaction changed be written to disk before it commits? Yes = force. No = no-force.
        
  
        

  

  
        🧠 Steal → Undo · No-Force → Redo
        "Stolen goods must be undone." "Not forced now, redo later."
        

  
        
    QWhy do almost all databases choose STEAL + NO-FORCE, even though recovery becomes harder?
    
        
      
        STEAL lets the buffer pool evict any page when it needs room. Without it, a transaction that updates 50 GB would need 50 GB of RAM to hold its dirty pages until commit.
        
      
        NO-FORCE means commit costs one sequential log flush (shared via group commit) instead of many random page writes. A hot page updated by 1,000 transactions can be written once, not 1,000 times.
        
      
        The price: after a crash, the disk can contain uncommitted data (needs undo) and can miss committed data (needs redo). So recovery must do both. Recovery happens rarely; commits happen thousands of times per second. That trade is worth it.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Steal means uncommitted pages can be flushed, so we keep undo information. No-force means committed pages need not be flushed at commit, so we keep redo information. Together they give the best runtime performance: big transactions don't need to fit in memory, and commit is just one sequential log write. The cost is that crash recovery must both redo and undo, which is what ARIES does.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Map deferred and immediate modification onto the matrix.
          
        Deferred = changes reach the database only after commit → nothing uncommitted is ever on disk → no undo, redo only (NO-STEAL). Immediate = changes are written in place (after logging) before commit → undo + redo (STEAL + NO-FORCE).
        
        
        ↪Does deferred modification need undo?
          
        No. That is a classic trap. Deferred modification never writes uncommitted values to the database, so there is nothing to undo.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🚩 Checkpoints: sharp vs fuzzy
        
  
        Without checkpoints, recovery would have to scan the log from the very first record ever written. A checkpoint is a marker in the log that says "everything before this point is already safe on disk (or I know exactly what is not)". It does two jobs: it limits how far back recovery reads, and it lets the engine recycle old log space.
        

  
        
    QWhat is a checkpoint? Why is a fuzzy checkpoint better than a sharp one?
    
        
      
        
        
        Sharp (consistent) checkpoint
          
          
        • Stop accepting new updates.
          • 
          
        • Flush all dirty pages + log buffer to disk.
          • 
          
        • Write a <checkpoint L> record (L = active transactions).
          • 
          
        • Resume. Recovery starts at the checkpoint.
          • 
          
        • ✘ The database "freezes" for seconds to minutes on a big buffer pool.
        
        
        Fuzzy checkpoint (ARIES, InnoDB, PG)
          
          
        • Do not stop work.
          • 
          
        • Write begin_checkpoint, then end_checkpoint holding the transaction table and the dirty page table (DPT).
          • 
          
        • Pages are flushed lazily in the background.
          • 
          
        • Recovery starts redo at the smallest recLSN in the DPT, which may be before the checkpoint.
          • 
          
        • ✔ No pause. Small cost: redo may start a bit earlier.
        
      
        
      
        Where is "the last checkpoint"? A tiny fixed location (ARIES calls it the master record; InnoDB stores the checkpoint LSN in the redo file header; PostgreSQL keeps it in pg_control) points to it, so recovery finds it instantly.
        
      
        Trade-off: checkpoint more often → shorter recovery, but more background I/O. Bigger redo/WAL → fewer forced checkpoints, but longer recovery after a crash.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        A checkpoint bounds recovery work. A sharp checkpoint stops updates and flushes all dirty pages, which pauses the system. Real engines use fuzzy checkpoints: they just record which transactions are active and which pages are dirty, with each page's recLSN, while work continues. Recovery then redoes from the oldest recLSN instead of from the beginning of the log.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪What happens in InnoDB if the redo log fills up?
          
        Redo is circular. Space can be reused only after the checkpoint LSN moves past it, which needs the old dirty pages flushed. If writes outrun flushing, InnoDB does aggressive (synchronous) flushing and user writes stall. Fix: a bigger innodb_redo_log_capacity and better I/O capacity settings.
        
        
        ↪What is recLSN?
          
        For each dirty page, the LSN of the first log record that made it dirty since it was last flushed. Every change older than recLSN is already in the on-disk copy of that page.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🧩 ARIES: the algorithm every real engine borrows from
        
  
        ARIES (Mohan et al., IBM, 1992) = Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics. It supports STEAL + NO-FORCE, fine-grained (row) locking and fuzzy checkpoints. Three ideas: WAL, repeating history during redo, and logging changes during undo (CLRs).
        

  
        
    
        LSN
        Log Sequence Number. A unique, ever-increasing id of each log record (in InnoDB it is a byte offset in the log stream).
        
    
        pageLSN
        Stored inside every data page: the LSN of the latest log record applied to that page. It tells redo "has this change already reached this page?"
        
    
        prevLSN
        Stored in each log record: the previous record of the same transaction. It links a transaction's records into a backward chain, used by undo.
        
    
        flushedLSN
        Highest LSN already on disk. WAL rule: a page may be written only if pageLSN ≤ flushedLSN.
        
    
        Transaction table (ATT)
        One row per active transaction: status and lastLSN.
        
    
        Dirty page table (DPT)
        One row per dirty page in the buffer pool: recLSN.
        
    
        CLR
        Compensation Log Record. Written when an update is undone. It is redo-only (never undone itself) and carries undoNextLSN = the next record of that transaction still to undo.
        
  
        

  
        Worked example: one log, one crash, three passes
        
  
        Three transactions run. T1 commits. T2 and T3 are still running when the power fails. Read the log left to right.
        

  

  
        
    QExplain the three passes of ARIES.
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Analysis — read forward from the last checkpoint. Rebuild the transaction table and the DPT as they were at the crash. Output: the losers (no commit/end record), and RedoLSN = min(recLSN) in the DPT.
          2. 
        
        2. Redo ("repeat history") — read forward from RedoLSN. For each update or CLR, re-apply it unless: the page is not in the DPT, or its LSN < the page's recLSN, or the page's on-disk pageLSN ≥ LSN (already applied). Redo even the losers' changes. After redo, the DB is exactly as it was at the crash moment.
          3. 
        
        3. Undo — roll back all losers together. Always pick the largest LSN among them, undo it, write a CLR, follow prevLSN (or the CLR's undoNextLSN). When a transaction reaches its start, write an end record.
          4. 
      
        
      
        
        
        Analysiswho lost? which pages dirty?
        
        
        
        
        Redoreplay everything, idempotent via pageLSN
        
        
        
        
        Undoroll back losers, log CLRs
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        ARIES recovers in three passes. Analysis scans from the last fuzzy checkpoint to find the losing transactions and the dirty pages. Redo repeats history: it replays every logged change, even of losers, from the oldest recLSN, and uses pageLSN to skip changes already on the page. Undo then rolls back the losers from newest to oldest, writing compensation log records so the undo work itself is never repeated if we crash again.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Why redo the losers' changes if we are going to undo them anyway?
          
        Repeating history brings every page to one known state (the crash moment). Then undo can use the normal logical undo logic, which is needed with row-level locks: a page may hold changes from a winner and a loser mixed together. It also keeps redo simple — it does not need to know who won.
        
        
        ↪What if the system crashes again during recovery?
          
        Just restart recovery. Redo is idempotent thanks to pageLSN. Undo already done is recorded as CLRs; those get redone, and their undoNextLSN makes undo skip the work already done. So repeated crashes never cause repeated or "double" undo, and recovery always makes progress.
        
        
        ↪Why is a CLR never undone?
          
        A CLR describes an undo action. Undoing it would re-apply the loser's change — wrong. So CLRs are redo-only, and undoNextLSN jumps over the record that was already compensated.
        
        
        ↪Why does redo start before the checkpoint?
          
        A fuzzy checkpoint does not flush pages. A page dirtied at LSN 10 may still be unflushed at the checkpoint (LSN 30), so its change must be redone from 10.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🚫
        Answer that fails
        "Redo only committed transactions, then undo the uncommitted ones." That is the simple textbook (Silberschatz-style) idea, not ARIES. ARIES redoes everything first. Say which one you mean.
        

  
  
        📷 Shadow paging (the no-log alternative)
        
  
        
    QWhat is shadow paging? Why don't big OLTP databases use it?
    
        
      
        Idea: keep two page tables. The shadow page table (on disk) points to the old, committed pages and is never changed. A transaction writes modified pages to new locations and updates a current page table. Commit = flush new pages, then atomically switch one root pointer to the current table. Abort = throw the current table away.
        
      
          
        
        • ✔ No undo, no redo. Recovery is instant (the root pointer is always valid).
          • 
        
        • ✘ Data gets fragmented (related pages scattered), so range scans slow down.
          • 
        
        • ✘ Needs garbage collection of old pages.
          • 
        
        • ✘ Commit copies the page table; hard to support many concurrent writers.
          • 
      
        
      
        🔀
        Who uses the idea today
        LMDB and CouchDB use copy-on-write B-trees (a modern shadow paging). SQLite's old rollback journal is undo-only; its WAL mode is redo-only. ZFS/Btrfs file systems are copy-on-write too. InnoDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server use WAL.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        ⚙️ InnoDB in practice: redo, undo, binlog, doublewrite
        
  
        MySQL has two layers: the server layer (parser, optimizer, binlog) and the storage engine (InnoDB: redo, undo, buffer pool). So a committed change is written to three different logs. Interviewers love asking how they differ.
        

  
        
    
        LogLayerWhat it storesUsed forShape
