        Redo logInnoDBPhysical page changes ("page 42, offset 100, these bytes")Crash recovery (durability)Circular, fixed total size; LSN-based
        
      
        Undo logInnoDBOld row versions / how to reverse a changeROLLBACK, crash undo, MVCC consistent readsUndo tablespaces; cleaned by purge
        
      
        Binary logServerLogical events (ROW images or SQL statements)Replication, point-in-time recoveryAppend-only files, rotated, expire after 30 days by default
        
            
  
        

  
        
    QRedo log vs binlog — why does MySQL need both?
    
        
      
        Redo belongs to InnoDB. It is physical, small, circular, and only good for "bring pages back to the crash moment". It is overwritten after checkpoints, so it cannot rebuild yesterday's data.
        
      
        Binlog belongs to the server, works for any engine, keeps whole history files, and is logical, so a replica (even with different page layout) can apply it. That makes it right for replication and PITR — but it alone cannot repair half-written pages.
        
      
        Binlog formats: ROW (default; before/after row images, deterministic), STATEMENT (the SQL text; small, but NOW(), UUID(), LIMIT without ORDER BY can give different results on a replica), MIXED (statement, switching to row when unsafe). binlog_format itself is deprecated: new setups should just use ROW.
        
      
        SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'innodb_redo_log_capacity';   -- 8.0.30+
SHOW VARIABLES LIKE 'binlog_format';
SHOW BINARY LOGS;
SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS;         -- 8.4 name of SHOW MASTER STATUS
        
      
        +--------------------------+-----------+
| Variable_name            | Value     |
+--------------------------+-----------+
| innodb_redo_log_capacity | 104857600 |   -- 100 MiB default
+--------------------------+-----------+
        
      
        ℹ️
        Redo files changed in 8.0.30
        Before: two files ib_logfile0/1 sized by innodb_log_file_size × innodb_log_files_in_group. Since 8.0.30: one dynamic setting, innodb_redo_log_capacity, and 32 files #ib_redoN in the #innodb_redo directory. You can resize it online with SET GLOBAL.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        The redo log is InnoDB's physical, circular log for crash recovery. The binlog is the server's logical, append-only log for replication and point-in-time recovery. Redo can't give history because it is overwritten after checkpoints, and binlog can't fix half-written pages because it is logical. So MySQL keeps both and ties them together with an internal two-phase commit.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Internal two-phase commit: keeping redo and binlog in sync
        
  
        
    QWhat is MySQL's internal 2PC between redo and binlog, and why is it needed?
    
        
      
        
        
        1. PrepareInnoDB writes + fsyncs redo, marks txn PREPARED with XID
        
        
        
        
        2. Binlog writeevent group with same XID written + fsynced (the "decision point")
        
        
        
        
        3. CommitInnoDB writes commit mark in redo (lazy fsync is OK)
        
      
        
      
        Why: without it, the two logs can disagree after a crash.
        
      
          
        
        • Redo first, crash before binlog → primary has the row, replicas (and PITR) never see it.
          • 
        
        • Binlog first, crash before redo → replicas have the row, primary lost it.
          • 
      
        
      
        Recovery rule: for each transaction left in PREPARED state, look in the last binlog. XID present → commit it. XID absent → roll back. So the binlog is the source of truth.
        
      
        Group commit batches steps 1–3 for many transactions (flush, sync, commit stages), so one fsync serves many commits.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Is this the same as distributed 2PC?
          
        Same protocol idea (prepare, then commit), but both participants are inside one server process, so there is no network coordinator failure problem. Distributed 2PC is in Chapter 19.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Torn pages: doublewrite buffer and full_page_writes
        
  
        
    QWhy does InnoDB need a doublewrite buffer if it already has a redo log?
    
        
      
        An InnoDB page is 16 KB, but the disk/OS writes in 4 KB (or 512 B) pieces. A crash mid-write leaves a torn page: half new, half old, with a bad checksum. Redo records are mostly changes ("apply this to the page"), and you cannot apply a change to a corrupt page.
        
      
          
        
        1. When flushing, InnoDB first writes a batch of pages sequentially to the doublewrite file and fsyncs.
          2. 
        
        2. Then it writes each page to its real place.
          3. 
        
        3. On recovery, a page with a bad checksum is replaced by its good copy from doublewrite, then redo is applied.
          4. 
      
        
      
        The cost is low (one extra sequential write per batch, not 2× I/O). Since 8.0.20 it lives in separate #ib_*.dblwr files. You can turn it off only if the storage guarantees atomic 16 KB writes (e.g. ZFS, some cloud disks).
        
      
        🔀
        PostgreSQL does it differently
        full_page_writes = on: the first change to a page after each checkpoint writes the whole page image into WAL. Recovery restores that image, then replays later changes. Side effect: WAL volume jumps right after every checkpoint.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        What happens when InnoDB restarts after a crash
        
  
          
    
        1. Tablespace discovery — find the .ibd files referenced by redo.
          2. 
    
        2. Redo apply — from the checkpoint LSN, fix torn pages via doublewrite, re-apply redo. Done before any connection is accepted.
          3. 
    
        3. Resolve PREPARED txns against the binlog (internal 2PC rule).
          4. 
    
        4. Roll back incomplete transactions using undo — in the background, after the server is already open.
          5. 
    
        5. Purge old undo; change-buffer merge continues as pages are read.
          6. 
  
        
  
        🌍
        Production story
        A batch job deleted 50 million rows in one transaction and the server crashed. Restart was quick, but the rollback ran for hours in the background, holding locks and growing the history list. Lesson: break big DML into chunks (e.g. 10k rows per transaction).
        

  
  
        📘 PostgreSQL WAL in one screen
        
  
          
    
        • WAL = redo-only log in pg_wal/, 16 MB segment files. There is no undo log: old row versions stay in the heap (MVCC), and an aborted transaction's rows are simply invisible via the commit log (pg_xact). VACUUM cleans them later.
          • 
    
        • Recovery: start at the last checkpoint's redo point, replay WAL. No undo pass needed.
          • 
    
        • synchronous_commit: on (default, durable), off (may lose the last few hundred ms of commits on a crash, never corrupts).
          • 
    
        • fsync = off is dangerous: risk of real corruption, not just lost commits.
          • 
    
        • Archiving: wal_level = replica, archive_mode = on, archive_command / archive_library copies each finished segment to safe storage → enables PITR and replicas.
          • 
  
        
  
        🔀
        Engine comparison
        InnoDB: redo + undo (ARIES-like) + binlog. PostgreSQL: WAL (redo) only; versions in the heap. Oracle: online redo logs + undo tablespace; archived redo (ARCHIVELOG mode) for PITR. SQL Server: one transaction log (.ldf) with ARIES-style analysis/redo/undo; Accelerated Database Recovery (2019+) adds a persistent version store to make undo near-instant.
        

  
  
        🌡️ Durability knobs (and what you lose)
        
  
        
    
        SettingOn each commitmysqld crashOS crash / power loss
        
    
      
        innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 (default)write + fsync redo✔ no loss✔ no loss
        
      
        =2write to OS cache; fsync ~1/s✔ no loss✘ up to ~1 s lost
        
      
        =0nothing; write+fsync ~1/s✘ up to ~1 s lost✘ up to ~1 s lost
        
      
        sync_binlog=1 (default)fsync binlog✔✔
        
      
        sync_binlog=0 / NOS decides / every N groups✔~ last events lost → replica drift
        
            
  
        
  
        🔒 "Double 1" = safe
        innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 + sync_binlog=1. Relax them only for replicas you can rebuild, or bulk loads you can redo.
        
  
        ⚠️
        Hidden trap: the disk may lie
        fsync is only as honest as the hardware. A consumer SSD with a volatile write cache and no power-loss protection can acknowledge a write it hasn't stored. "Durable" settings + lying disks = lost commits.
        

  
  
        🛟 Backups: logical vs physical, full/incremental, PITR
        
  
        Crash recovery protects you from power cuts. It does nothing for a dead disk, a deleted table, ransomware, or a bad deploy. That is what backups are for.
        

  
        
    QLogical vs physical backup — what's the difference? Which would you use for a 2 TB database?
    
        
      
        
        
        Logical
          
          
        • SQL statements / CSV that recreate the data.
          • 
          
        • Tools: mysqldump, MySQL Shell util.dumpInstance(), mydumper, pg_dump.
          • 
          
        • ✔ Portable across versions/engines/OS; can restore one table.
          • 
          
        • ✘ Slow to restore (re-insert + rebuild every index). Hours to days for TBs.
        
        
        Physical
          
          
        • Copy of the actual data files + logs.
          • 
          
        • Tools: Percona XtraBackup, MySQL Enterprise Backup, pg_basebackup, file-system / cloud snapshots, Oracle RMAN.
          • 
          
        • ✔ Fast backup and restore (copy files back).
          • 
          
        • ✘ Same major version / platform; usually whole instance.
        
      
        
      
        For 2 TB: physical (XtraBackup or snapshots) + continuous binlog archiving for PITR. Keep an occasional logical dump for portability and single-table restores.
        
      
        How XtraBackup gets a consistent hot copy: it copies the .ibd files while they change (inconsistent!) and, in parallel, copies the redo log. The prepare step then runs crash recovery on the copy: redo committed work, roll back the rest. Same idea as pg_basebackup + WAL.
        
      
        mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 --routines --triggers \
          --databases shop > shop_2026-10-17.sql
        
      
        ⚠️
        Gotchas
        --single-transaction gives a consistent snapshot only for InnoDB (MyISAM tables are not protected), and a long dump is a long transaction that grows the undo history. mysqlpump was removed in 8.4 — use mysqldump or MySQL Shell dump utilities.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QFull vs incremental vs differential? Hot vs warm vs cold?
    
        
      
        
        
        TypeCopiesBackup time / sizeRestore needs
        
        
          
        Fulleverythingslowest / biggestjust that one
        
          
        Incrementalchanges since the last backup of any typefastest / smallestfull + every incremental in order
        
          
        Differentialchanges since the last fullgrows each dayfull + the latest differential
        
                
      
        
      
        Hot = DB fully online, reads and writes continue (XtraBackup, pg_basebackup). Warm = online but writes blocked / read-only for a while (e.g. FLUSH TABLES WITH READ LOCK). Cold = DB shut down, files copied (simplest, always consistent, needs downtime).
        
      
        Inc = since Last · Diff = since Full
        Incremental chain is long but small; differential is one file but grows.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QSomeone ran DROP TABLE orders at 14:05. How do you recover to 14:04:59?
    
        
      
      
          
        
        1. Restore the last full (physical) backup to a separate server — do not touch production yet.
          2. 
        
        2. Find the binlog position recorded with the backup (--source-data / xtrabackup_binlog_info).
          3. 
        
        3. Find the exact position of the bad event: mysqlbinlog --verbose binlog.000123 | grep -n "DROP TABLE".
          4. 
        
        4. Replay all needed binlogs in one connection up to just before it: mysqlbinlog --start-position=P --stop-position=X binlog.000120 binlog.000121 … | mysql. (Or with GTIDs, skip just that transaction.)
          5. 
        
        5. Verify, then copy the orders table back (or promote the server).
          6. 
      
        
      
        Binary logging must have been on before the backup, and the binlogs must still exist (archive them off the server!). PostgreSQL: restore a base backup, set recovery_target_time and restore_command, start the server.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I'd do point-in-time recovery on a separate instance: restore the last full backup, then replay the binary logs from the backup's recorded position up to just before the DROP event. Then I'd validate and copy the table back to production. That only works if binlogs were enabled and archived, which is why I'd always pair backups with continuous log archiving.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat are RPO and RTO? Is a replica a backup?
    
        
      
        
        
        RPO — Recovery Point Objective
        How much data (time) you can afford to lose. Daily backups only → RPO up to 24 h. Backups + archived binlogs/WAL → RPO of seconds.
        
        
        RTO — Recovery Time Objective
        How long you can be down. Restoring a 2 TB logical dump → RTO of a day. Promoting a standby → RTO of a minute.
        
      
        
      
        🚫
        "We have replication, so we don't need backups."
        Wrong. Replication copies mistakes instantly: a DROP TABLE or a bad UPDATE without WHERE reaches every replica within milliseconds. Replication improves availability (RTO); backups give you a past to go back to. A delayed replica (e.g. SOURCE_DELAY = 3600) helps a bit, but is still not a backup.
        
      
        
        
        📦
        3-2-1 rule
        3 copies of data, on 2 different media, 1 off-site (ideally immutable / offline against ransomware).
        
        
        ⏱️
        Test restores
        A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Schedule automatic restores + checks and time them (that is your real RTO).
        
        
        🛡️
        Protect backups
        Encrypt them, restrict access, keep them away from the DB host's credentials.
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        RPO is how much data I can lose, RTO is how long I can be down. I'd pick the backup design from those two numbers: nightly physical backups plus continuous binlog or WAL archiving for a small RPO, and a hot standby for a small RTO. Replication is not a backup because it replicates mistakes too, so I'd still keep off-site backups and regularly test restoring them.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪How would you back up a 5 TB, 24×7 MySQL database?
          
        Take hot physical backups from a replica (not the primary) with XtraBackup, weekly full + daily incremental, stream them compressed and encrypted to object storage. Archive binlogs continuously (e.g. mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --raw --stop-never). Restore-test weekly. Optionally keep a delayed replica for fast "undo" of human errors.
        
        
        ↪SQL Server recovery models?
          
        Simple: log truncates at checkpoint, no log backups, restore only to the last backup. Full: log backups, PITR possible. Bulk-logged: minimal logging for bulk ops, no PITR inside those log backups.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        📌 Key takeaways
          
    
        • Failure classes: transaction (undo), system crash (redo + undo from the log), media (backup + archived logs).
          • 
    
        • WAL rule: log before page; commit = commit record on stable storage. Group commit makes this cheap.
          • 
    
        • STEAL ⇒ undo, NO-FORCE ⇒ redo. Real engines choose both for speed.
          • 
    
        • Fuzzy checkpoints record the transaction table + DPT; redo starts at the smallest recLSN.
          • 
    
        • ARIES: Analysis → Redo (repeat history, idempotent via pageLSN) → Undo (losers, CLRs with undoNextLSN; safe under repeated crashes).
          • 
    
        • InnoDB: redo (crash), undo (rollback + MVCC), binlog (replication + PITR), tied by internal 2PC; doublewrite fixes torn pages. PostgreSQL: redo-only WAL + full_page_writes.
          • 
    
        • "Double 1" = fully durable. Relaxing trades lost seconds for throughput.
          • 
    
        • Backups: physical for big/fast, logical for portable; PITR = backup + log replay; design from RPO/RTO; replication ≠ backup; test restores; 3-2-1.
          • 
  
        

  
        📚 Go deeper
          
    
        • CMU 15-445/645 (Andy Pavlo) — the logging and recovery lectures explain ARIES with great slides.
          • 
    
        • MySQL 8.4: Redo Log — official redo, capacity and crash recovery details.
          • 
    
        • PostgreSQL: Continuous Archiving & PITR — base backups, WAL archiving, recovery targets.
          • 
    
        • Silberschatz, Recovery System slides — the textbook view (log-based recovery, checkpoints, ARIES).
          • 
    
        • Percona XtraBackup docs — how hot physical backups and "prepare" work.
          • 
  
        

  
        
    
        
      
        A buffer manager uses STEAL + NO-FORCE. What must the recovery system support?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        STEAL may put uncommitted data on disk (needs undo); NO-FORCE may leave committed data only in memory (needs redo).
        
    
        
    
        
      
        In ARIES, where does the Redo pass start?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        The oldest change that may be missing from disk is the smallest recLSN, which can be before the fuzzy checkpoint.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Why are CLRs never undone?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        CLRs are redo-only; undoNextLSN skips past the already-compensated record so repeated crashes never redo undo work twice.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        With innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=2, what can be lost?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        With 2, redo is in the OS page cache at commit, so a mysqld crash is fine, but the OS can lose up to ~1 s before the periodic fsync.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        To restore you need the full backup plus EVERY backup taken since it. Which scheme is that?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Incrementals each hold changes since the previous backup, so the whole chain is needed. A differential needs only full + latest differential.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        State the WAL rule.
        A log record must be on stable storage before the data page it describes; a txn is committed only when its commit record is flushed.
        
    
        STEAL needs…? NO-FORCE needs…?
        STEAL → undo. NO-FORCE → redo.
        
    
        Fuzzy checkpoint stores what?
        The active transaction table and the dirty page table (with recLSNs), without pausing work.
        
    
        ARIES's three passes?
        Analysis (find losers + dirty pages) → Redo (repeat history from min recLSN) → Undo (losers backward, writing CLRs).
        
    
        What makes ARIES redo idempotent?
        pageLSN: skip a record if the page's pageLSN ≥ the record's LSN.
        
    
        What is undoNextLSN?
        Field in a CLR pointing to the next record of that txn still to undo; lets recovery skip already-undone work.
        
    
        Redo vs undo vs binlog in MySQL?
        Redo: InnoDB physical, crash recovery. Undo: rollback + MVCC. Binlog: server logical, replication + PITR.
        
    
        Internal 2PC order?
        InnoDB prepare (redo fsync) → binlog write + fsync → InnoDB commit. Prepared txn in binlog ⇒ commit, else roll back.
        
    
        What problem does the doublewrite buffer solve?
        Torn (partially written) 16 KB pages that redo can't repair. PG uses full_page_writes for the same problem.
        
    
        RPO vs RTO?
        RPO = max data loss (time). RTO = max downtime. Replication helps RTO; backups + log archiving help RPO.
        
  
        

        


        
  
        
    
        Chapter 18 · VI · Reliability & Security
        
    
        🛡️ Security, SQL Injection & Access Control
        
    
        Explain who can do what in a database, why SQL injection happens, exactly why prepared statements stop it, and how data is protected in transit and at rest.
        
    
        ⏱ 25 minMySQL 8.4PostgreSQL
        
  
        

  
         
        ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
        
    
          
      
        • Authentication = who are you? Authorization = what may you do? DB users in MySQL are 'user'@'host'.
          • 
      
        • GRANT / REVOKE work at global, database, table, column and routine level. Roles (MySQL 8.0+) bundle privileges; they must be activated (default roles).
          • 
      
        • Least privilege: the app user gets only DML on its own schema — never ALL, SUPER, FILE or GRANT OPTION.
          • 
      
        • Views and stored procedures can be a security layer (expose only some rows/columns). Beware SQL SECURITY DEFINER = runs with the creator's rights.
          • 
      
        • Row-Level Security: PostgreSQL policies, Oracle VPD, SQL Server security policies. MySQL has none → emulate with views + CURRENT_USER() or in the app.
          • 
      
        • SQL injection = user input is concatenated into SQL text, so data becomes code. Fix: parameterized queries — the SQL structure is fixed before values arrive.
          • 
      
        • Escaping is not enough; identifiers (table/column/ORDER BY) can't be parameters → allow-list. Dynamic SQL inside procedures is still injectable.
          • 
      
        • Protect data: TLS in transit, TDE at rest, column encryption for very sensitive fields, bcrypt/argon2 for passwords (never plain or MD5), secrets out of code, audit logs, masking.
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        ✏️ The #1 question here: "What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?" The follow-up that separates candidates: "WHY do prepared statements prevent it?"
        

  
  
        🔑 Authentication vs authorization
        

  
        
    QWhat is the difference between authentication and authorization in a database?
    
        
      
        
        
        Authentication (AuthN)
          
          
        • "Who are you?"
          • 
          
        • Password, certificate, LDAP/Kerberos, IAM token.
          • 
          
        • MySQL: auth plugins — caching_sha2_password (default). mysql_native_password is disabled by default in 8.4.
          • 
          
        • PostgreSQL: pg_hba.conf rules (scram-sha-256, cert, …).
        
        
        Authorization (AuthZ)
          
          
        • "What are you allowed to do?"
          • 
          
        • Privileges: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE, DROP, EXECUTE…
          • 
          
        • Set with GRANT/REVOKE, roles, views, RLS.
          • 
          
        • Checked on every statement.
        
      
        
      
        Analogy: at an office, the ID card at the gate is authentication. Which floors your card opens is authorization.
        
      
        ℹ️
        MySQL account = user + host
        'app'@'10.0.%' and 'app'@'localhost' are two different accounts with separate passwords and privileges. The most specific host match wins.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Authentication proves identity, like logging in with a password or certificate. Authorization decides what that identity can do, through privileges, roles, views and row-level policies. The database authenticates once per connection but checks authorization on every statement.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🔒 GRANT, REVOKE, roles & least privilege
        

  
        
    QHow do GRANT and REVOKE work? At what levels can you grant?
    
        
      
        
        
        LevelSyntax (MySQL)Example use
        
        
          
        GlobalON *.*DBA only
        
          
        DatabaseON shop.*app user
        
          
        TableON shop.ordersreporting user
        
          
        ColumnGRANT SELECT (id, name) ON shop.customershide phone, pan_no
        
          
        RoutineGRANT EXECUTE ON PROCEDURE shop.place_ordercall but not touch tables
        
                
      
        
      
        CREATE USER 'shop_app'@'10.0.%' IDENTIFIED BY 'use-a-secret-manager';
GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON shop.* TO 'shop_app'@'10.0.%';

CREATE USER 'analyst'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '...';
GRANT SELECT (order_id, amount, created_at) ON shop.orders TO 'analyst'@'%';

REVOKE DELETE ON shop.* FROM 'shop_app'@'10.0.%';
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'shop_app'@'10.0.%';
        
      
        +-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| Grants for shop_app@10.0.%                                        |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
| GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO `shop_app`@`10.0.%`                         |
| GRANT SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE ON `shop`.* TO `shop_app`@`10.0.%`   |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------+
        
      
        USAGE means "no privileges", just the right to connect. WITH GRANT OPTION lets the user pass their privileges on — almost never give it to an app.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪If A grants to B WITH GRANT OPTION, and B grants to C, what happens when A revokes from B?
          
        In standard SQL, REVOKE … CASCADE also removes C's privilege (it depended on B's), while RESTRICT refuses if dependents exist. PostgreSQL follows this (needs CASCADE). MySQL does not track grant chains: C keeps the privilege until revoked separately.
        
        
        ↪Does REVOKE affect sessions already connected?
          
        In MySQL, table/column privilege changes apply to the next statement; global privilege changes and the active database are generally re-read only for new connections. To be safe, kill the old sessions.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat are roles and why use them? MySQL 8.0+
    
        
      
        A role is a named bundle of privileges. Grant privileges to roles, then roles to users. Onboarding = one grant; offboarding = one revoke; audits read cleanly.
        
      
        CREATE ROLE 'app_read', 'app_write';
GRANT SELECT ON shop.* TO 'app_read';
GRANT INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE ON shop.* TO 'app_write';

GRANT 'app_read', 'app_write' TO 'shop_app'@'10.0.%';   -- no ON clause
SET DEFAULT ROLE ALL TO 'shop_app'@'10.0.%';             -- roles are NOT active by default!
        
      
        ⚠️
        Classic trap
        You grant a role, the user logs in and gets "access denied". Granted roles are inactive until set as default (SET DEFAULT ROLE) or enabled in the session (SET ROLE), or activate_all_roles_on_login=ON. Check with SELECT CURRENT_ROLE();
        
      
        🔀
        Other engines
        PostgreSQL: users and groups are both "roles" (CREATE ROLE … LOGIN); membership inherits by default. Oracle / SQL Server: roles for years; SQL Server has fixed roles like db_datareader.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is the principle of least privilege? How do you apply it to an application's DB user?
    
        
      
        Give each account only the privileges it needs, and nothing more. If it is compromised (SQL injection, leaked password), the damage is limited.
        
      
          
        
        • Separate accounts: migration user (DDL), app user (DML only), read-only reporting user, DBA (humans, MFA, audited).
          • 
        
        • App user: no DROP, ALTER, GRANT OPTION, FILE (reads/writes server files!), SUPER/SYSTEM_VARIABLES_ADMIN, no access to mysql.*.
          • 
        
        • Restrict host: 'app'@'10.0.%', not '%'. Never let the app use root.
          • 
        
        • Review with SHOW GRANTS regularly; remove unused accounts.
          • 
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Least privilege means each account gets only what its job needs. For an app, I'd use a DML-only user on its own schema, restricted by host, with migrations run by a separate DDL account. Then even a successful SQL injection can't drop tables, read server files or grant itself more rights.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🔍 Views, procedures & row-level security
        

  
        
    QHow can views and stored procedures be used for security? What is the DEFINER pitfall?
    
        
      
        Views: grant SELECT on a view that shows only safe columns/rows, and grant nothing on the base table.
        
      
        CREATE SQL SECURITY DEFINER VIEW shop.v_customer_public AS
  SELECT id, name, city FROM shop.customers;     -- no phone, no email
GRANT SELECT ON shop.v_customer_public TO 'support'@'%';
        
      
        Procedures: grant only EXECUTE; the procedure does validated work (e.g. transfer_money checks balance) and the caller cannot run arbitrary UPDATEs.
        
      
        
        
        SQL SECURITY DEFINER (MySQL default)
        • Runs with the creator's privileges.
        • That is what makes the "only EXECUTE" pattern work.
        • Risk: if the definer is a powerful account and the code has a bug (or dynamic SQL), callers get that power.
        
        
        SQL SECURITY INVOKER
        • Runs with the caller's privileges.
        • Safer default for utility code.
        • Does not hide base tables.
        
      
        
      
        ⚠️
        DEFINER pitfalls
        Use a dedicated low-privilege definer account, not root. If the definer account is dropped, the object fails to run. Restoring a dump on another server can break on DEFINER=`x`@`host` lines. In 8.4, setting another user as definer needs SET_ANY_DEFINER.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is Row-Level Security (RLS)? How would you do it in MySQL?
    
        
      
        RLS filters which rows each user can see or change, enforced by the database for every query — the app cannot "forget" a WHERE tenant_id = ?. Great for multi-tenant SaaS.
        
      
        ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;      -- no policy yet = default deny
CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON orders
  USING      (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int)   -- rows you can see
  WITH CHECK (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int);  -- rows you can write
-- per request: SET app.tenant_id = '42';
        
      
        ⚠️
        Gotchas
        The table owner, superusers and BYPASSRLS roles skip policies (use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY for owners). If the app connects as the owner, RLS does nothing.
        
      
        🔀
        Engine differences
        Oracle: Virtual Private Database (VPD) — a policy function adds a predicate to queries. SQL Server 2016+: CREATE SECURITY POLICY with predicate functions. MySQL: no native RLS. Emulate with a view filtered by SUBSTRING_INDEX(CURRENT_USER(),'@',1) (or a mapping table) + grant only on the view, or enforce tenant filters in the app/ORM layer.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🐛 SQL injection: how it happens
        

  
        
    QWhat is SQL injection? Show a minimal example.
    
        
      
        SQL injection (SQLi) happens when an application builds a SQL string by gluing user input into it. The database receives one string and cannot tell which part the developer wrote and which part the user typed. If the input contains SQL syntax (a quote, a comment), it changes the meaning of the query. Data becomes code.
        
      
        user = request.form["username"]
pwd  = request.form["password"]
sql  = "SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '" + user + "' AND pwd_hash = '" + h(pwd) + "'"
cur.execute(sql)
        
      
        Normal input alice gives … WHERE name = 'alice' AND pwd_hash = '…'. Now the user types admin'-- as the name:
        
      
        SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = 'admin'-- ' AND pwd_hash = '...'
--                                         ^^^ everything after -- is a comment
        
      
        The quote closes the string early, -- comments out the password check, and the attacker logs in as admin without a password.
        
      
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        SQL injection happens when user input is concatenated into a query string, so input containing quotes or SQL keywords changes the query's structure. For example, a username like admin'-- can comment out the password check. The root cause is mixing code and data in one string; the fix is parameterized queries.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat types of SQL injection exist? What is the impact?
    
        
      
        Know the categories conceptually — interviewers want to see you understand why "it returns no error" doesn't mean "it's safe".
        
      
        
        
        TypeIdea (conceptual)Why it matters
        
        
          
        TautologyInput makes a condition always true (' OR '1'='1)Login bypass, dump all rows
        
          
        UNION-basedAppends UNION SELECT to read another table through the same pageReads data the page never meant to show
        
          
        Error-basedForces DB errors whose messages leak dataWhy you must never show raw DB errors to users
        
          
        Blind – booleanPage changes slightly when a condition is true/false; data leaks one bit at a timeNo visible output still ≠ safe
        
          
        Blind – timeCondition triggers a delay; attacker measures response timeWorks even when the page is identical
        
          
        Second-orderInput stored safely, later read from the DB and concatenated into another query"Trusted" data from your own DB can still be hostile
        
          
        Stacked queries; then a second statementOnly if the driver allows multi-statements (MySQL drivers usually disable it by default)
        
                
      
        
      
        Impact: data theft (PII, password hashes), auth bypass, data change/deletion, sometimes reading/writing server files (FILE privilege) or worse. It has been in the OWASP Top 10 for over a decade (under "Injection").
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🛡️ Preventing SQL injection
        

  
        
    QHow do you prevent SQL injection? WHY do prepared statements work?
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Parameterized queries / prepared statements — always, for every value.
          2. 
        
        2. Allow-list identifiers — table names, column names, ASC/DESC can't be parameters; map user input to a fixed set.
          3. 
        
        3. Least-privilege DB user — limits blast radius.
          4. 
        
        4. Safe stored procedures — no string-built dynamic SQL inside.
          5. 
        
        5. Input validation (type, length, format) as defence in depth; WAF as an extra net — never the main fix.
          6. 
        
        6. Generic error messages to users; detailed ones only in logs.
          7. 
      
        
      
        Why parameters work: the query text with placeholders (? or $1) is sent and parsed first. The parse tree is fixed: "compare column name with one string value". The values are sent separately (in the binary protocol) and are slotted in as literals. Whatever characters they contain — quotes, --, UNION — they are never parsed as SQL. The database "always distinguishes code from data".
        
      
        
        
        
        
        
          
        # placeholders + a separate tuple of values
cur.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = %s AND pwd_hash = %s", (user, h))

# ❌ NOT safe: this is still string formatting, done in Python
cur.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '%s'" % user)
cur.execute(f"SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '{user}'")
        
        
        
        
        
          
        // ❌ Statement + concatenation
stmt.executeQuery("SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '" + user + "'");

// ✔ PreparedStatement
PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(
    "SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = ? AND pwd_hash = ?");
ps.setString(1, user);
ps.setString(2, hash);
ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();
        
        
        
        
        
          
        // ❌ template literal = concatenation
await db.query(`SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = '${user}'`);

// ✔ placeholders + values array
const [rows] = await db.execute(
  'SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = ? AND pwd_hash = ?', [user, hash]);
        
        
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I prevent SQL injection mainly with parameterized queries. They work because the SQL with placeholders is parsed and its structure fixed before any user value arrives; the values are bound afterwards as pure literals, so they can never change the query's syntax. For things that can't be parameters, like column names or sort order, I use an allow-list. And I run the app with a least-privilege user as defence in depth.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Why isn't escaping quotes enough?
          
        Escaping depends on getting every context right: character sets (multi-byte encodings have caused real bypasses), numeric contexts where no quotes exist (WHERE id = 1 OR 1=1), identifiers, LIKE wildcards, and every developer remembering every time. OWASP calls escaping "strongly discouraged" as a primary defence. Parameters remove the whole class of bugs.
        
        
        ↪Can you parameterize a table name or ORDER BY column?
          
        No — placeholders hold values only. Use an allow-list:
        
          
        SORTABLE = {"price": "price", "date": "created_at"}
col = SORTABLE.get(request.args.get("sort"), "created_at")
direction = "DESC" if request.args.get("desc") == "1" else "ASC"
cur.execute(f"SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY {col} {direction} LIMIT %s", (limit,))
        
        
        ↪Does using an ORM make me safe?
          
        Mostly, for normal query-builder calls. But every ORM has a raw-SQL escape hatch (raw(), text(), whereRaw, $queryRawUnsafe, createNativeQuery). String-formatting input into those is injectable again. Use their bound-parameter forms.
        
        
        ↪Are stored procedures automatically safe?
          
        No. A procedure that builds SQL with CONCAT() and runs it with PREPARE … EXECUTE is injectable just like app code. Use EXECUTE stmt USING @param for values (and allow-lists for identifiers).
        
          
        -- ❌ SET @q = CONCAT('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = ''', p_status, '''');
-- ✔
SET @q = 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE status = ?';
SET @s = p_status;
PREPARE st FROM @q;  EXECUTE st USING @s;  DEALLOCATE PREPARE st;
        
        
        ↪Is a WAF enough?
          
        No. A Web Application Firewall pattern-matches requests; it can be bypassed by encodings and misses second-order injection. It is a safety net while you fix the code, not the fix.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🚫
        Answers that fail interviews
        "I validate input with a regex" or "I escape single quotes" as the main defence. Also: "prepared statements are faster, that's why we use them" — speed is a side benefit; the security reason is separating code from data.
        

  
        🧠 P-A-L-S
        Parameterize values · Allow-list identifiers · Least privilege · Safe errors (no raw DB errors to users).
        

  
  
        🔐 Protecting the data itself: encryption & passwords
        

  
        
    QEncryption in transit vs at rest vs column-level — what does each protect against?
    
        
      
        
        
        LayerHowProtects againstDoes NOT protect against
        
        
          
        In transitTLS between app and DB (and replicas, backups). MySQL: require_secure_transport=ON; client --ssl-mode=VERIFY_IDENTITY.Network sniffing, man-in-the-middleAnyone with valid DB credentials
        
          
        At rest (TDE)Engine encrypts data files, redo/undo, binlogs. InnoDB: master key in a keyring encrypts per-tablespace keys. CREATE TABLE … ENCRYPTION='Y'Stolen disks, copied files, lost backupsSQL injection, a logged-in attacker (data is decrypted for queries)
        
          
        Column / app-levelApp encrypts a field (e.g. Aadhaar, card token) before INSERT; key in a KMSDBAs, DB dumps, many SQLi leaks (attacker gets ciphertext)Can't index/search the plaintext easily; key management is hard
        
                
      
        
      
        🔀
        Engines
        MySQL: InnoDB tablespace encryption with keyring components (file keyring in all editions, KMS/Vault in Enterprise). PostgreSQL: no built-in TDE in community PG — use disk/filesystem encryption or pgcrypto for columns. Oracle TDE and SQL Server TDE + Always Encrypted (client-side column encryption).
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHow should user passwords be stored in a database?
    
        
      
        Never plain text, and never reversible encryption. Store a slow, salted hash made by a password-hashing function: Argon2id (modern first choice), bcrypt, or scrypt/PBKDF2.
        
      
          
        
        • Salt = random per-user value stored with the hash → equal passwords get different hashes; precomputed (rainbow) tables are useless.
          • 
        
        • Slow / memory-hard → each guess costs time, so offline brute force after a leak is expensive.
          • 
        
        • MD5 / SHA-256 alone are wrong: they are designed to be fast, so GPUs try billions per second.
          • 
        
        • Hash in the application, not with SQL functions like MD5() (they also put plaintext in query logs).
          • 
      
        
      
        CREATE TABLE users (
  id        BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  email     VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  pwd_hash  VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL   -- e.g. '$argon2id$v=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$...' (salt + params inside)
);
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I'd store passwords as salted, slow hashes using Argon2id or bcrypt, computed in the application. The salt defeats rainbow tables and the deliberate slowness makes brute force after a leak expensive. Fast hashes like MD5 or plain SHA-256 are not acceptable, and nothing should ever be stored in a reversible form.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        📋 Secrets, auditing, masking, PII & misconfigurations
        

  
        
    
        🔒
        Secrets
        No DB passwords in code or Git. Use a secret manager / env injection, rotate regularly, prefer short-lived IAM-based auth where the cloud offers it.
        
    
        📓
        Auditing
        Log who did what, when: logins, failed logins, DDL, privilege changes, access to sensitive tables. MySQL Enterprise Audit / Percona audit plugin, PostgreSQL pgaudit. Ship logs off the DB host.
        
    
        👤
        Masking
        Show XXXX-XXXX-1234 to support staff; use masked or synthetic data in dev/test copies. Static masking (copy) vs dynamic masking (at query time, e.g. SQL Server DDM).
        
    
        ⚖️
        PII & privacy law
        GDPR (EU), India's DPDP Act 2023: collect the minimum, know where PII lives, support deletion ("right to erasure" — remember backups and logs), encrypt, restrict access.
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat common database misconfigurations lead to breaches?
    
        
      
          
        
        • DB port (3306/5432/27017) open to the internet → keep it in a private network, firewall to app hosts only.
          • 
        
        • Default/empty/shared passwords; the app connecting as root/postgres.
          • 
        
        • Accounts with host '%' and broad GRANT ALL.
          • 
        
        • No TLS, or TLS without certificate verification.
          • 
        
        • Unencrypted, publicly readable backups (open cloud buckets are a classic leak source).
          • 
        
        • Verbose DB errors shown to end users; secure_file_priv empty + FILE privilege granted.
          • 
        
        • Unpatched versions; leftover test databases and anonymous users (run mysql_secure_installation style hardening).
          • 
        
        • Production data copied to dev without masking.
          • 
      
        
      
        🌍
        Real pattern
        Many large leaks were not clever hacks: an internet-exposed database or backup with no password, found by automated scanners within hours. Network isolation + auth + encryption of backups stop that whole class.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        Networkprivate subnet, firewall, TLS
        
    
        
    
        AuthNstrong auth, no shared creds
        
    
        
    
        AuthZleast privilege, roles, RLS
        
    
        
    
        Queryparameterized SQL
        
    
        
    
        DataTDE, column encryption, hashing, masking
        
    
        
    
        Detectaudit logs, alerts
        
  
        
  
        ← defence in depth: every layer assumes the one before it can fail
        

  
  
        📌 Key takeaways
          
    
        • AuthN = who you are; AuthZ = what you may do. MySQL accounts are 'user'@'host'.
          • 
    
        • GRANT/REVOKE at global, database, table, column and routine level; roles (8.0+) must be activated.
          • 
    
        • Least privilege: separate DDL, DML, read-only and admin accounts; never root for apps.
          • 
    
        • Views/procedures can hide data; DEFINER runs with the creator's rights — use a low-privilege definer.
          • 
    
        • RLS: PostgreSQL policies, Oracle VPD, SQL Server security policies; MySQL needs views or app logic.
          • 
    
        • SQLi = concatenating input into SQL. Parameterized queries fix it because structure is parsed before values are bound.
          • 
    
        • Allow-list identifiers; dynamic SQL in procedures and ORM raw queries can still be injectable; escaping and WAFs are not the fix.
          • 
    
        • TLS in transit, TDE at rest, column encryption for the most sensitive data, Argon2id/bcrypt for passwords, audit logs, masking.
          • 
  
        

  
        📚 Go deeper
          
    
        • OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet — the canonical list of defences, with code in many languages.
          • 
    
        • OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet — Argon2id/bcrypt parameters explained.
          • 
    
        • MySQL 8.4: Using Roles — roles, default roles and activation.
          • 
    
        • PostgreSQL: Row Security Policies — USING vs WITH CHECK, bypass rules.
          • 
    
        • PortSwigger Web Security Academy: SQL injection — clear explanations and legal practice labs.
          • 
  
        

  
        
    
        
      
        Why do prepared statements prevent SQL injection?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Code and data travel separately; bound values never reach the SQL parser as syntax.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        A user wants to sort by a column chosen in the UI. What is the safe approach?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Placeholders hold values, not identifiers. Only fixed, known column names should reach the SQL text.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        You granted a role to a MySQL user, but their queries still fail with "access denied". Most likely cause?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Granted roles are inactive until made default or enabled in the session (or activate_all_roles_on_login=ON).
        
    
        
    
        
      
        TDE (encryption at rest) protects against which threat?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Data is decrypted for any authenticated query; TDE protects the files themselves.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Which is the best way to store user passwords?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Password hashing must be one-way, salted, and deliberately slow; fast hashes and reversible encryption are wrong.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        AuthN vs AuthZ?
        Authentication = proving identity. Authorization = what that identity is allowed to do.
        
    
        GRANT levels in MySQL?
        Global (*.*), database (db.*), table, column, routine (EXECUTE).
        
    
        Principle of least privilege?
        Each account gets only the privileges its job needs — limits the blast radius of any compromise.
        
    
        SQL SECURITY DEFINER vs INVOKER?
        DEFINER runs with the creator's privileges (MySQL default); INVOKER with the caller's.
        
    
        Root cause of SQL injection?
        User input concatenated into SQL text, so data is parsed as code.
        
    
        What is second-order SQLi?
        Malicious input is stored safely, then later read from the DB and concatenated into another query.
        
    
        Blind SQLi?
        No data shown; attacker infers it from true/false page differences or response time delays.
        
    
        Can stored procedures be injectable?
        Yes — if they build SQL with CONCAT and PREPARE/EXECUTE it. Use EXECUTE … USING for values.
        
    
        Row-Level Security in MySQL?
        Not native. Emulate with filtered views + CURRENT_USER() or app-layer filters. PG has policies, Oracle VPD.
        
    
        Three places to encrypt data?
        In transit (TLS), at rest (TDE / disk), column/app-level (sensitive fields, keys in KMS).
        
  
        

        


        
  
        
    
        Chapter 19 · VII · Scale & Modern Data
        
    
        🌐 Distributed DBs: Replication, Sharding, CAP & Distributed Transactions
        
    
        Walk an interviewer from "the database is slow" to replicas, shards, quorums, CAP and sagas, and explain every trade-off on the way.
        
    
        ⏱ 70 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8.4PostgreSQLNoSQLadvanced
        
  
        

  
        ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
        
    
          
      
        • Scale in order of cost: fix queries and indexes → bigger box → cache → connection pool → read replicas → partition → functional split → shard. Shard last.
          • 
      
        • Replication = same data on many nodes (availability, read scaling). Sharding = different data on different nodes (write and storage scaling).
          • 
      
        • MySQL replication is asynchronous by default. Semi-sync waits for ≥1 replica to receive and flush (not apply). Group Replication uses Paxos and a majority.
          • 
      
        • Replica lag breaks read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix. Fixes: read from the leader after a write, sticky replica, GTID wait.
          • 
      
        • Shard key = high cardinality + even spread + present in most queries + not monotonic. Consistent hashing moves only ~1/n of keys when a node joins.
          • 
      
        • CAP: only during a network partition must you choose Consistency (linearizable) or Availability. "Pick 2 of 3" is misleading. PACELC adds: else Latency vs Consistency.
          • 
      
        • Quorum: N replicas, W write acks, R read replies. W + R > N ⇒ read set overlaps the latest write.
          • 
      
        • 2PC = vote then verdict; atomic but blocks if the coordinator dies. Saga = local transactions + compensations; no isolation. Outbox + CDC fixes the dual-write problem; consumers must be idempotent.
          • 
      
        • Raft/Paxos: majority agrees on a log. 2f+1 nodes tolerate f failures. Used by etcd, CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner, MySQL Group Replication.
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        ✏️ For SDE-2+ interviews this chapter IS the DBMS round. Cisco asked CAP + read/write quorum; Swiggy asked 2PC; Flipkart asked Saga/CQRS.
        

  
        🌐 Why distribute at all? Vertical vs horizontal scaling
        
  
        One database server has limits: CPU, RAM, disk I/O, network, and the fact that it can die. When one box is not enough, you have two choices. Make the box bigger, or add more boxes. ← every scaling answer starts here
        

  
        
    
        Node
        One database server (machine, VM or container) in a cluster.
        
    
        Replica
        A node that holds a copy of the same data as another node.
        
    
        Leader / primary / source
        The node that accepts writes. Old MySQL docs say "master". Followers are also called secondaries, standbys or replicas.
        
    
        Shard
        A node (or replica group) that holds a subset of the rows. Together all shards hold the whole table.
        
    
        Network partition
        A network fault where some nodes cannot talk to others. It is NOT the same as a table partition. Same word, different meaning.
        
    
        Quorum
        The minimum number of nodes that must agree for an operation to count, usually a majority.
        
  
        

  
        ⚠️
        Word trap: "partition"
        "Partitioning" a table = splitting data. A "network partition" in CAP = a broken network link. If the interviewer says "partition tolerance", they mean the network one.
        

  
        
    QWhat is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling for a database?
    
        
      
        Vertical scaling (scale up) = buy a bigger machine: more cores, more RAM, faster NVMe. Horizontal scaling (scale out) = add more machines and spread the data or the load across them.
        
      
        
        
        ⬆️ Vertical (scale up)
          
          
        • No code change. ACID, joins and foreign keys work as before.
          • 
          
        • More RAM ⇒ a bigger innodb_buffer_pool_size ⇒ more of the working set stays in memory.
          • 
          
        • Hard ceiling: the biggest machine you can buy.
          • 
          
        • Still a single point of failure.
          • 
          
        • Cost grows faster than capacity at the top end.
        
        
        ➡️ Horizontal (scale out)
          
          
        • No hard ceiling. Add nodes as you grow.
          • 
          
        • Fault tolerance: one node dies, others continue.
          • 
          
        • Adds distributed problems: replication lag, routing, cross-node joins, distributed transactions, CAP.
          • 
          
        • Two flavours: replicas (same data, scale reads) and shards (split data, scale writes and storage).
        
      
        
      
        🌍
        Real world
        Most products never need sharding. A well-indexed MySQL or PostgreSQL primary with a few replicas serves a very large app. Companies such as Notion (Postgres split into 480 logical shards on 32 hosts) and Figma sharded only after years of scaling up.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Vertical scaling means a bigger machine. It is simple and keeps all relational guarantees, but it has a ceiling and is still one point of failure. Horizontal scaling means more machines. Replicas scale reads and give failover; shards split the data to scale writes and storage. It has no hard ceiling, but I now have to deal with lag, routing, cross-shard queries and distributed transactions. So I scale up and tune first, and scale out when I must.
        
      
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Do read replicas help a write-heavy system?
          
        No. Every replica must apply every write, so replicas scale reads only. To scale writes you need sharding (or fewer, cheaper writes: batching, async processing).
        
        
        ↪Is "add more machines" always cheaper?
          
        Not in engineering cost. Sharding changes your schema, your queries, your deployment and your on-call life. A bigger box for a few more years is often the cheaper decision.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🚀 The scaling ladder
        
  
        When an interviewer says "the database is slow under load, what do you do?", they want a sequence, cheapest step first. Each step after "scale up" adds staleness or complexity that you must be ready to explain.
        

  
        
    
        0. Measureslow log, EXPLAIN, p99, read:write ratio
        
    
        1. Index & tunecomposite / covering indexes, kill N+1, keyset pagination
        
    
        2. Scale upmore RAM, bigger buffer pool
        
    
        3. CacheRedis cache-aside + TTL
        
    
        4. PoolProxySQL / PgBouncer
        
    
        5. Read replicasstale-tolerant reads
        
    
        6. Partitionone server, prune + drop old data
        
    
        7. Functional splitorders DB, users DB…
        
    
        8. ShardVitess / Citus / app-level
        
  
        

  
        🧠 I · U · C · P · R · P · S
        "I Usually Cache Plus Replicate Prior to Sharding" — Index, scale Up, Cache, Pool, Replicate, Partition, Shard.
        

  
        
    QYour database is slow under load. Walk me through how you would scale it.
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Measure first — which queries are slow (slow query log, performance_schema), what their plans are (EXPLAIN ANALYZE), the read:write ratio, p95/p99 latency, CPU vs I/O vs lock waits.
          2. 
        
        2. Fix queries and indexes — usually 10x–100x wins for free. Composite and covering indexes, no SELECT *, keyset pagination instead of big OFFSET, remove N+1 loops, archive cold rows.
          3. 
        
        3. Scale up — more RAM so the working set fits in the buffer pool; faster disks.
          4. 
        
        4. Cache hot, read-mostly data in Redis/Memcached (cache-aside + TTL + delete on write).
          5. 
        
        5. Pool connections so thousands of app threads share a few hundred DB connections.
          6. 
        
        6. Read replicas for read-heavy load (80–95% reads is common). Keep read-your-writes in mind.
          7. 
        
        7. Partition huge time-series tables inside one server (cheap DROP PARTITION, pruning).
          8. 
        
        8. Functional split — move unrelated tables to their own DB (users, orders, analytics). Also called vertical sharding.
          9. 
        
        9. Shard when write QPS or data size outgrows one primary. Move analytics to a columnar store (CQRS/CDC).
          10. 
      
        
      
        🚫
        Answer that fails
        "I would shard the database." Jumping to sharding before indexes, caching and replicas tells the interviewer you have never run a production database.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I measure first, because most slowness is a missing index or a bad query. Then I go up the ladder in order of cost: tune queries, scale up, add a cache for hot reads, pool connections, add read replicas for stale-tolerant reads, partition huge tables, split unrelated data into separate databases, and shard only when writes or storage outgrow one primary. At each step I say what I give up, like staleness with caches and replicas, or cross-shard joins with sharding.
        
      
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Reads must scale 10x tomorrow. What exactly do you do?
          
        (1) Check plans of the top 10 queries. (2) Cache-aside for hot keys with TTL and stampede protection. (3) Add replicas behind a router; send stale-tolerant reads there and keep a user's own recent reads on the primary or wait for the replica to reach the user's GTID. (4) Pool connections. (5) Precompute heavy aggregates (summary tables) or move them to a columnar store.
        
        
        ↪When would you NOT add a cache?
          
        When the hit ratio will be low (data changes on every read), when you need strict consistency (account balances), or when the real problem is a missing index — the slow query still runs on every miss.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        ⚡ The caching layer (Redis)
        
  
        A cache is a small, fast store (usually in RAM) that keeps copies of hot data so most reads never touch the database. Redis is the usual choice: an in-memory key-value store with TTLs, data structures (lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes), replication and clustering. Memcached is a simpler pure cache.
        

  
        PatternRead pathWrite pathGoodBad
        
    
        Cache-aside (lazy loading)App asks cache; on miss app reads DB and fills cacheApp writes DB, then deletes the keySimple; only hot data cached; cache crash ≠ outage3 trips on a miss; can serve stale data
        
    
        Read-throughApp asks cache; the cache library loads from DB—App code simplerCache must know the DB
        
    
        Write-through—Write cache and DB together, synchronouslyCache never staleSlower writes; caches data nobody reads (churn)
        
    
        Write-behind (write-back)—Write cache; flush to DB later in batchesFastest writes; absorbs burstsData loss if cache dies before flush
        
    
        Write-around—Write DB only; cache fills on next readWrite-once data never pollutes cacheFirst read is always a miss
        
  
        

  
        
    QExplain cache-aside. Why delete the key on write instead of updating it?
    
        
      
        What: the application owns the cache logic. How: read → try cache → on miss read DB → put in cache with a TTL. Write → update DB → delete the cache key.
        
      
        def get_user(uid):
    key = f"user:{uid}"
    cached = r.get(key)
    if cached is not None:              # 1. hit: no DB trip
        return json.loads(cached)
    row = db.fetch_one("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", (uid,))   # 2. miss: read DB
    r.set(key, json.dumps(row), ex=300)  # 3. fill cache, TTL 300 s
    return row

def update_email(uid, email):
    db.execute("UPDATE users SET email = %s WHERE id = %s", (email, uid))
    r.delete(f"user:{uid}")             # invalidate, do not overwrite
        
      
        Why delete, not update? Two writers can race. Writer A sets email=a, writer B sets email=b. If both then write the cache, the cache order can differ from the DB order, so the cache keeps "a" forever while the DB has "b". Deleting is order-independent: the next reader loads the true value.
        
      
        ⚠️
        The known race in cache-aside
        Reader misses and reads the OLD value from DB → writer updates DB and deletes the key → reader now SETs the old value. Mitigations: short TTL as a safety net, "delayed double delete" (delete again after a few hundred ms), versioned keys (user:42:v7), or lease tokens (Facebook's memcache design).
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        In cache-aside the app reads the cache first; on a miss it reads the database and fills the cache with a TTL. On a write it updates the database and deletes the key rather than updating it, because deletes cannot be reordered into a stale value. The TTL is a safety net so any stale entry dies on its own.
        
      
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪What happens if Redis goes down?
          
        Cache-aside degrades gracefully: all reads go to the DB. The danger is that the DB cannot take 100% of the load. Protect it with a circuit breaker, rate limiting, Redis replicas/Sentinel or Redis Cluster, and warm the cache before sending traffic.
        
        
        ↪How do several services keep their caches in sync with MySQL?
          
        Invalidate from the database's change stream: a CDC tool such as Debezium reads the MySQL binlog and publishes "row changed" events; a consumer deletes the matching keys. No service can "forget" to invalidate.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat are cache stampede (thundering herd), cache penetration and cache avalanche? How do you fix each?
    
        
      
        
        
        🐘
        Stampede / thundering herd
        A hot key expires. 10,000 requests miss at the same moment and all run the same expensive query. The DB falls over. Also called "dog-piling".
        
        
        🕳️
        Penetration
        Requests for keys that do not exist (e.g. user:-1 from a bot). Nothing is ever cached, so every request hits the DB.
        
        
        🌨️
        Avalanche
        Many keys expire at the same time (all set with TTL=3600 at deploy), or the cache cluster restarts. A wave of misses hits the DB.
        
      
        
      
        ProblemFixes
        
        
        StampedePer-key lock / single-flight: only the request that wins SET lock:key 1 NX EX 5 recomputes; others wait briefly or serve the stale value. Early refresh: recompute in the background before expiry (probabilistic early expiration, "XFetch"). Request coalescing: one DB query shared by all waiters (Discord does this).
        
        
        PenetrationCache the "not found" result with a short TTL; put a Bloom filter of valid IDs in front; validate input; rate-limit.
        
        
        AvalancheAdd random jitter to TTLs (3600 ± 300 s); keep the cache highly available; warm the cache; circuit-breaker on the DB.
        
      
        
      
        💡
        Retry storms are herds too
        When the DB is slow, clients retry and make it slower. Use exponential backoff plus random jitter (Stripe recommends exactly this).
        
    
        
  
        

  
        ⛓️ Connection pooling
        
  
        
    QWhy are database connections expensive, and what does a connection pool or proxy do?
    
        
      
        Why expensive: opening a connection costs a TCP handshake, often TLS, authentication, and server-side memory. MySQL gives each connection a thread (thread-per-connection by default). PostgreSQL forks a whole process per connection, so thousands of idle connections waste a lot of RAM. More active connections than CPU cores also means context switching and lock contention, so throughput drops.
        
      
        What a pool does: keeps a small set of open connections and lends them to requests. Two levels:
        
      
          
        
        • App-side pool (HikariCP, SQLAlchemy pool): per application instance.
          • 
        
        • Proxy pool: ProxySQL or MySQL Router in front of MySQL; PgBouncer in front of PostgreSQL. Many clients share few server connections. ProxySQL can also route reads to replicas and writes to the primary by query rules.
          • 
      
        
      
        PgBouncer modeServer connection held for…Breaks
        
        
        Sessionthe whole client sessionnothing, but little sharing
        
        
        Transactionone transactionSET, LISTEN, SQL-level PREPARE, session advisory locks, temp tables
        
        
        Statementone statementmulti-statement transactions are not allowed
        
      
        
      
        🌍
        Classic outage
        Autoscaling adds pods. 60 pods × pool size 20 = 1,200 connections, but MySQL max_connections is 151 by default (PostgreSQL 100). New pods get "Too many connections". Fix: a central proxy pool, smaller per-pod pools, and never hold a DB connection while calling a slow external API.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        A connection is costly to open and costly to keep: a thread in MySQL, a full process in PostgreSQL. A pool keeps a few warm connections and lends them out, so thousands of app threads share a few hundred DB connections. At scale I put a proxy like ProxySQL or PgBouncer in front, which also lets me split reads to replicas.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🖥️ Replication: same data, many nodes
        
  
        Replication means keeping a copy of the same data on several machines. Every copy is a replica. The hard part is not copying; it is deciding when to tell the client "committed" and what to do when copies disagree.
        
  
        H-A-R-D
        Why replicate? High availability (fail over), Analytics / backups offload, Read scaling, Distance (serve users from a nearby copy).
        

  
        Three topologies
        
  
        
    
        👑 Leader–follower (primary–replica)
        • All writes go to ONE leader.
        • Leader ships its change log to followers.
        • Reads can go to followers (may be stale).
        • No write conflicts. Default in MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB.
        
    
        👑👑 Multi-leader
        • Several nodes accept writes (often one per data centre).
        • They replicate to each other asynchronously.
        • Two leaders can change the same row → conflicts.
        • Use: multi-region writes, offline clients (calendar apps). MySQL Group Replication multi-primary mode.
        
    
        🕸️ Leaderless
        • Client (or a coordinator) sends writes to N replicas at once.
        • Success after W acks; reads ask R replicas.
        • Repair by read repair + anti-entropy.
        • Dynamo, Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Riak.
        
  
        

  

  
        
    QSynchronous vs asynchronous vs semi-synchronous replication — what exactly does the leader wait for?
    
        
      
        ModeLeader says "committed" after…Data loss on failover?Latency cost
        
        
        Async (MySQL default)its own local commit✘ yes — the lag windownone
        
        
        Semi-sync≥1 replica has received and logged the events (relay log)~ none with AFTER_SYNC, while it stays semi-sync+1 network round trip
        
        
        Sync / quorumreplicas (or a majority) durably agree✔ noneslowest node in the quorum; a dead standby can block commits
        
      
        
      
        How semi-sync works (MySQL 8.4): the source writes the binlog, sends events, and waits. With the default rpl_semi_sync_source_wait_point = AFTER_SYNC it waits after syncing the binlog but before the storage-engine commit, so no client can see a transaction that no replica has. With AFTER_COMMIT other clients may see data that is later lost on failover.
        
      
        -- on the source
INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_source SONAME 'semisync_source.so';
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_enabled = 1;
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout = 10000;   -- ms; then falls back to async!
-- on each replica
INSTALL PLUGIN rpl_semi_sync_replica SONAME 'semisync_replica.so';
SET GLOBAL rpl_semi_sync_replica_enabled = 1;
        
      
        🚫
        Two wrong answers that fail interviews
        (1) "Semi-sync means the replica has applied the change." No — it has only received and flushed it to the relay log. (2) "Semi-sync guarantees zero data loss." Only while it stays semi-sync. If no replica ACKs within rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout (10 s default) the source silently falls back to async.
        
      
        🔀
        Across engines
        PostgreSQL: async by default; synchronous_standby_names + synchronous_commit = on | remote_write | remote_apply chooses how far the standby must get. MongoDB: writeConcern: {w: "majority"}; a write acked with w: 1 can be rolled back after failover. MySQL Group Replication: Paxos-based, needs a majority.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        The difference is what the leader waits for before telling the client "committed". Async waits for nothing, so a crash can lose the last few transactions. Semi-sync waits until at least one replica has received and logged the change, which costs one round trip and is lossless with AFTER_SYNC — but it falls back to async on timeout. Fully synchronous or quorum replication loses nothing but every commit pays for the slowest node in the quorum.
        
      
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Group Replication vs semi-sync?
          
        Semi-sync: one primary waits for ≥1 ACK; failover is done by an external tool. Group Replication: members agree on transaction order with a Paxos-based protocol, a majority must be reachable, the primary is elected automatically, and conflicts are detected by certification. Cost: majority round trip, max 9 members. InnoDB Cluster = ≥3 servers with Group Replication + MySQL Shell + MySQL Router.
        
        
        ↪After a semi-sync primary crashes, can you just restart it as primary?
          
        No. It may hold transactions that no replica acknowledged. The MySQL manual says the failed source should be discarded (or rebuilt as a replica), not reused as the source.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QStatement-based vs row-based vs mixed binlog. What are GTIDs and the relay log?
    
        
      
        FormatWhat is loggedGoodBad
        
        
        STATEMENTthe SQL text; replica re-runs itsmall, readableunsafe for non-deterministic SQL: UUID(), RAND(), LIMIT without ORDER BY; trigger/routine issues
        
        
        ROW (default)before/after image of every changed rowdeterministic, safe; needed for CDC (Debezium)large for bulk updates (1M rows = 1M row events); reduce with binlog_row_image=MINIMAL
        
        
        MIXEDstatement normally, row for unsafe statementscompromiseharder to reason about
        
      
        
      
        Changing binlog_format is deprecated since MySQL 8.0; row-based is the default and the direction of travel.
        
      
        
        
        Relay log
        The replica's local copy of events received from the source. The I/O thread writes it; the applier threads read it. It decouples "download" from "apply".
        
        
        GTID
        Global Transaction ID = source_uuid:transaction_number. Every transaction gets one. A replica knows exactly which ones it has (gtid_executed).
        
        
        Auto-positioning
        SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION = 1: the replica says "I have these GTIDs" and the new source sends the rest. No binlog file name/offset maths during failover, and a transaction is never applied twice.
        
        
        Parallel apply
        replica_parallel_workers (default 4 in 8.4) appliers + a coordinator; replica_preserve_commit_order=ON keeps commit order. Single-threaded apply was a classic cause of lag.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Replication lag and its three anomalies
        
  
        With async replicas a follower can be seconds behind. Reading from it creates bugs that look like "data disappeared".
        
  
        AnomalyStoryFix
        
    
        Read-your-writes brokenYou update your profile photo, refresh, and see the old one (read hit a lagging replica).Read the user's own data from the leader for N seconds after a write; or wait until the replica has the write's GTID: WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET(gtid, 1).
        
    
        Monotonic reads brokenRefresh 1 shows a new comment; refresh 2 hits a more-lagged replica and the comment vanishes — time goes backwards.Sticky routing: same user → same replica (hash of user id).
        
    
        Consistent prefix brokenYou see the answer "Yes, 5 pm" before the question "Meeting at 5?" because they live on different partitions with different lag.Write causally related data to the same partition; carry causal tokens/versions.
        
  
        

  
        
    QThe primary dies. Walk me through failover. What is split-brain and how does fencing prevent it?
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Detect — health checks / heartbeats time out (Orchestrator, MySQL Router + InnoDB Cluster, Patroni for PG). Too short a timeout = false failovers; too long = long outage.
          2. 
        
        2. Choose the most up-to-date replica (largest gtid_executed).
          3. 
        
        3. Drain — let it apply everything already in its relay log.
          4. 
        
        4. Promote — STOP REPLICA; RESET REPLICA ALL; SET GLOBAL read_only = OFF;
          5. 
        
        5. Repoint other replicas with SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION = 1, and move the write endpoint (VIP / DNS / proxy).
          6. 
        
        6. Fence the old primary so it can never accept writes again.
          7. 
      
        
      
        Split-brain = two nodes both believe they are the leader and both accept writes. Data diverges and cannot be merged automatically. It happens when the old leader was only unreachable (network partition, long GC pause), not dead.
        
      
        Fencing stops the old leader: STONITH ("shoot the other node in the head" — power it off), revoke its VIP, set super_read_only, or use fencing tokens: every new leader gets a larger epoch number and storage rejects writes with an older token. Majority-based systems (Raft, Group Replication) avoid split-brain by design: a leader that cannot reach a majority steps down.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Async failover loses data
        Transactions committed on the old primary but not yet shipped are gone after promotion. If the old primary comes back, those "orphan" transactions conflict with new ones (e.g. duplicate auto-increment ids). GitHub's 2018 outage is the famous story of a cross-DC failover with writes on both sides.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Failover is detect, pick the most caught-up replica by GTID, let it drain its relay log, promote it, repoint the others with auto-positioning, and move the write endpoint. The real danger is split-brain: the old primary was only partitioned away and keeps taking writes. So I always fence it — STONITH, revoking its virtual IP, or fencing tokens — or I use a majority-based system where a leader without a majority steps down.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QPostgreSQL streaming (physical) vs logical replication?
    
        
      
        
        
        Streaming (physical)
