        • Ships WAL bytes: exact block changes.
        • Replica is a byte-identical, read-only hot standby of the whole cluster.
        • Same major version, same architecture.
        • Use: HA failover, read replicas.
        
        
        Logical
        • Decodes WAL into row changes, identified by replica identity (usually the PK).
        • CREATE PUBLICATION / CREATE SUBSCRIPTION; subset of tables.
        • Works across major versions → near-zero-downtime upgrades.
        • DDL is not replicated; subscriber writes can conflict.
        
      
        
      
        MySQL's binlog is already logical (row events), which is why one mechanism serves both replicas and CDC.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIn multi-leader or leaderless systems two writes hit the same key concurrently. How are conflicts resolved?
    
        
      
        
        
        Last-write-wins (LWW)
        Keep the value with the larger timestamp. Simple (Cassandra does this per cell) but silently drops the other write, and clock skew can make an older write "win".
        
        
        Version vectors / vector clocks
        Each replica keeps a counter per node: {A:2, B:1}. If one vector ≥ the other on every entry, it happened later; otherwise the writes are concurrent and both "siblings" are kept for the app to merge (Dynamo shopping cart, Riak).
        
        
        CRDTs
        Conflict-free Replicated Data Types: counters, sets, maps whose merge is commutative, associative and idempotent, so all replicas converge without coordination (G-Counter, OR-Set). Used in Riak, Redis Enterprise active-active, collaborative editors.
        
        
        Avoid conflicts
        Route all writes for one record to one "home" leader; use certification (Group Replication aborts the later conflicting transaction).
        
      
        
      
        🎯
        What they test
        That you know LWW loses data, and that "concurrent" means "neither knew about the other", not "same wall-clock time".
        
    
        
  
        

  
        ✂️ Partitioning vs sharding
        
  
        
    
        Partitioning (one server)
        • One big table split into pieces inside one database server.
        • App still sees one table.
        • Wins: partition pruning, instant DROP PARTITION for old data.
        • Does NOT add CPU, RAM or write capacity.
        
    
        Sharding (many servers)
        • Rows split across separate database servers (shards), each with its own CPU/disk.
        • Scales writes and storage.
        • Costs: cross-shard joins, distributed transactions, resharding, ops work.
        
    
        Vertical partitioning
        • Split columns: hot narrow columns in one table, big rarely-read blobs in another (1:1).
        • Or split by feature into separate DBs ("functional partitioning": users DB, orders DB).
        
  
        

  
        
    QHow does MySQL native partitioning work? What are RANGE, LIST, HASH and KEY, and what are the limits?
    
        
      
        TypeRuleTypical use
        
        
        RANGE / RANGE COLUMNSvalue falls in a rangetime series: one partition per month
        
        
        LIST / LIST COLUMNSvalue in a fixed listregion IN ('IN','US','EU')
        
        
        HASHMOD(expr, n) on an integer expressioneven spread
        
        
        KEYMySQL's own hash on one or more columns (any type)even spread on non-integer keys
        
      
        
      
        CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGINT NOT NULL,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  created_at  DATE   NOT NULL,
  amount      DECIMAL(10,2),
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created_at)          -- partition column MUST be in every unique key
)
PARTITION BY RANGE COLUMNS (created_at) (
  PARTITION p2026_08 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-09-01'),
  PARTITION p2026_09 VALUES LESS THAN ('2026-10-01'),
  PARTITION pmax     VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE)
);

EXPLAIN SELECT SUM(amount) FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-09-01' AND created_at < '2026-10-01';
-- partitions: p2026_09        ← pruning: only one partition is read

ALTER TABLE orders DROP PARTITION p2026_08;   -- deletes a month instantly (no row-by-row DELETE)
        
      
        ⚠️
        Limits people forget (MySQL 8.4, InnoDB)
        (1) Every column in the partitioning expression must be part of every unique key, including the PK. (2) Partitioned InnoDB tables support no foreign keys, in either direction. (3) Max 8192 partitions (incl. subpartitions). (4) No FULLTEXT or spatial indexes. (5) Queries that do not filter on the partition key scan all partitions — partitioning can make them slower.
        
      
        🔀
        PostgreSQL
        Declarative partitioning (PARTITION BY RANGE/LIST/HASH); each partition is a real table that can have its own indexes. A unique constraint must also include the partition key columns.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Sharding strategies
        
  
        StrategyHow a row finds its shardGoodBad
        
    
        Rangekey ranges: A–F → shard 1range scans stay on one shardhot spots on monotonic keys (all new rows hit the last shard)
        
    
        Hash (mod N)hash(key) % Neven spreadchanging N moves almost every key; range queries scatter
        
    
        Consistent hashingkey and nodes on a hash ring; next node clockwiseadding a node moves ~1/n of keysneeds virtual nodes for balance
        
    
        Directory / lookupa mapping table: tenant 42 → shard 7total flexibility; move one big tenant alonelookup service is a dependency (cache it)
        
    
        Geo / entityby region or by tenantdata residency, localityuneven region sizes
        
  
        

  

  
        
    QWhat is consistent hashing and why is it better than hash(key) % N?
    
        
      
        Problem: with hash % N, going from 3 to 4 servers changes the result for about 3 out of 4 keys, so almost all data must move (and a cache would lose most hits at once).
        
      
        How it works: map the hash space onto a circle. Hash each server onto the circle (several times — virtual nodes). Hash each key; walk clockwise to the first server: that server owns it. Adding a server only takes keys from its clockwise neighbour; removing one gives its keys to the next one. Expected movement ≈ K/n keys.
        
      
        Virtual nodes fix two issues: random positions give uneven arcs, and a dead server would dump all its load on one neighbour. With hundreds of points per server, load spreads evenly and a bigger machine can simply get more points.
        
      
        🌍
        Where it is used
        Dynamo/DynamoDB, Cassandra (token ring with vnodes), memcached client libraries (ketama), load balancers. Vitess and Citus instead use a fixed number of logical shards/ranges and move whole ranges, which achieves the same goal.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        With hash mod N, changing N remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing puts servers and keys on a ring and gives each key to the next server clockwise, so adding or removing a server only moves the keys in one arc — about 1/n of the data. Each server gets many virtual nodes so the load is even and a failed node's load spreads across many others.
        
      
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Is there a simpler way that gets most of the benefit?
          
        Pre-split into many logical buckets (say 4096) with hash(key) % 4096, and keep a small map bucket → physical shard. Resharding = moving whole buckets and updating the map. This is what most production systems actually do.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHow do you choose a shard key? What problems come with sharding?
    
        
      
        A good shard key has: high cardinality (many distinct values), even distribution of rows and traffic, is present in most queries (so a query goes to one shard), and is not monotonic under range sharding (timestamps and auto-increment send every insert to one shard).
        
      
        ProblemExampleFix
        
        
        Hot spot / celebrityA celebrity's posts get 1000× trafficsalt hot keys (post:123#0..9), cache, give big tenants dedicated shards
        
        
        Cross-shard query"Top 10 products across all users"scatter-gather + merge; or precompute into an analytics store
        
        
        Cross-shard joinorders by user, products globalco-locate related tables on the same key (Citus "colocation"); replicate small reference tables to every shard
        
        
        Cross-shard transactiontransfer between users on two shards2PC, saga, or redesign so it stays on one shard
        
        
        Secondary lookupsfind user by email when sharded by user_ida global index table email → user_id (itself sharded by email)
        
        
        Reshardingshard 3 is fulllogical buckets / online copy + catch-up + cutover (Vitess Reshard)
        
        
        Unique IDsauto-increment collides across shardsSnowflake IDs / UUIDv7 (below)
        
      
        
      
        🔀
        Tools
        Vitess (MySQL, from YouTube): VTGate router, keyspaces, vindexes, online resharding, failover. Citus (PostgreSQL extension): distributed and reference tables, colocation. MongoDB: built-in sharding with ranged or hashed shard keys. ProxySQL can route by rules but does not reshard.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I pick the key most queries filter on, with high cardinality and even traffic — usually user_id or tenant_id — and I avoid monotonic keys like timestamps under range sharding. Then I plan for the pain: cross-shard queries go scatter-gather or to an analytics store, related tables are co-located on the same key, IDs come from a Snowflake-style generator, and I pre-split into logical buckets so resharding means moving buckets, not rehashing everything.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHow do you generate unique IDs across shards?
    
        
      
        
        
        ❄️
        Snowflake (64-bit)
        1 sign bit + 41 bits milliseconds since a custom epoch + 10 bits machine id + 12 bits sequence (4096 ids/ms/machine). Roughly time-sorted, fits in BIGINT. Risk: clock moving backwards.
        
        
        🆔
        UUIDv7
        128-bit, timestamp first, then random bits (RFC 9562). No coordination and time-ordered, so B+ tree inserts stay at the right edge. Store as BINARY(16) in MySQL.
        
        
        🎲
        UUIDv4
        Fully random. Unique, but as an InnoDB clustered PK every insert lands on a random page → page splits, poor cache use, bigger secondary indexes.
        
        
        🔢
        Ranges / offsets
        Ticket server hands out blocks of ids; or auto_increment_increment = N + per-shard offset. Simple but needs care when adding shards.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        ⚖️ CAP, PACELC and consistency models
        
  
        
    QExplain the CAP theorem precisely. Why is "pick any 2 of 3" misleading?
    
        
      
        
        
        C — Consistency
        Linearizability: every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy. (NOT the "C" of ACID, which means "constraints hold".)
        
        
        A — Availability
        Every request to a non-failed node gets a non-error response (no time limit in the proof).
        
        
        P — Partition tolerance
        The system keeps working even when the network drops or delays messages between nodes.
        
      
        
      
        The theorem: if a network partition happens, a replicated system must choose: refuse some requests (stay C) or answer with possibly stale data (stay A). That's all.
        
      
        Why "2 of 3" misleads: partitions are not optional in a distributed system — cables, switches and GC pauses happen. So "CA" is not a real choice for a multi-node system. And when there is no partition, you can have both C and A. The choice is only made during a partition, and many systems make it per operation (tunable).
        
      
      
        Leans CP (during a partition)Leans AP
        
        
        etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul (majority consensus); HBase; Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB; MySQL Group Replication; MongoDB with majority read/write concernCassandra / ScyllaDB at CL=ONE; Riak; original Dynamo; DynamoDB eventually-consistent reads; DNS
        
      
        
      
        🚫
        Answers that fail
        "MySQL is CA." A single-node DB is not a distributed system, so CAP does not apply; a replicated MySQL must still choose during a partition. "Cassandra is AP" with no qualifier — with QUORUM reads and writes it behaves CP-ish. Always say which mode.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        CAP says that during a network partition a replicated system must choose between linearizable consistency and availability: either the cut-off nodes refuse requests, or they answer with possibly stale data. Partitions are unavoidable, so "CA" is not a real option, and when there's no partition you get both. Many databases make the choice per query, so I always say the configuration — for example Cassandra at QUORUM behaves CP-like, at ONE it is AP.
        
      
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Does Spanner beat CAP?
          
        No. It is CP. Google's private network makes partitions rare, so in practice availability is extremely high. TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks, bounded uncertainty of a few ms) lets it assign globally ordered commit timestamps — external consistency — at the cost of a short "commit wait".
        
        
        ↪Is MongoDB CP or AP?
          
        Depends on settings. A replica set has one primary; a primary cut off from the majority steps down, and with w: "majority" + majority reads it behaves CP. Reading from secondaries gives eventual consistency. PACELC lists it as PA/EC — proof that labels vary with configuration.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat does PACELC add to CAP?
    
        
      
        Partition → choose A or C; Else (normal operation) → choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the everyday cost: waiting for replicas to agree makes every request slower, even with a perfect network.
        
      
        ClassMeaningExamples
        
        
        PA/ELavailable in partition, fast otherwiseDynamo, Cassandra, Riak
        
        
        PC/ECconsistent always, pays latencyVoltDB, HBase/Bigtable, MySQL Cluster, Spanner/CockroachDB (usual classification)
        
        
        PA/ECavailable in partition, consistent otherwiseMongoDB (per the PACELC paper's list)
        
        
        PC/ELconsistent in partition, fast otherwiseYahoo PNUTS
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QStrong vs eventual consistency — and what lies in between?
    
        
      
        
        
        Linearizableone copy, real-time order
        
        
        Sequentialone global order, not real-time
        
        
        Causalcause before effect
        
        
        Session guaranteesread-your-writes, monotonic
        
        
        Eventualconverges "some day"
        
      
        
      
        Left = stronger, slower, less available. Right = weaker, faster. Eventual consistency only promises that if writes stop, all replicas end up equal. Serializability is a different axis: it is about transactions (as if run one at a time), while linearizability is about single objects in real time. Both together = strict serializability (Spanner, CockroachDB claim it / close to it).
        
      
        🧠
        ACID vs BASE
        BASE = Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent — the opposite trade-off to ACID. See Chapter 20.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        👥 Quorums: W + R > N
        
  
        
    QExplain read and write quorums. N=3, W=1, R=1 — is a read guaranteed to see the latest write?
    
        
      
        In a leaderless store each key lives on N replicas. A write succeeds after W replicas ACK. A read asks R replicas and takes the newest version (by timestamp/version).
        
      
        Rule: if W + R > N, the set of nodes you read from must overlap the set that took the latest write in at least one node (pigeonhole), so you see it. N=3, W=1, R=1 → 2 ≤ 3 → no guarantee. N=3, W=2, R=2 → 4 > 3 → overlap ✔. Tolerates 1 node down for both reads and writes.
        
      
        N/W/RBehaviour
        
        
        3 / 2 / 2balanced, the usual "QUORUM/QUORUM"
        
        
        3 / 3 / 1fast reads, but any node down blocks writes
        
        
        3 / 1 / 3fast writes, any node down blocks strong reads
        
        
        3 / 1 / 1fastest, eventual consistency only
        
      
        

      
        
        
        🧮 Quorum calculator
        
        
        
          
          
          
        
        
        
        
        
        
      
        
      
      

      
        ⚠️
        Quorum ≠ linearizable
        Even with W+R>N you can see anomalies: sloppy quorums (below) write to substitute nodes; concurrent writes resolved by LWW drop data; a write that reached only some nodes and "failed" is not rolled back, so later reads may or may not return it. Cassandra uses lightweight transactions (Paxos) for real compare-and-set.
        
      
        
        
        Sloppy quorum
        If some of the key's N "home" nodes are down, write to the first N healthy nodes on the ring instead (Dynamo). Higher write availability; W+R>N no longer guarantees overlap.
        
        
        Hinted handoff
        The stand-in node keeps a "hint" ("this belongs to node B") and replays it when B returns.
        
        
        Read repair
        A read that sees replicas disagree writes the newest value back to the stale ones.
        
        
        Anti-entropy with Merkle trees
        Background repair. Each replica builds a hash tree over key ranges; comparing roots and descending only into differing branches finds out-of-sync ranges while sending very little data.
        
      
        
      
        🔀
        Cassandra tunable consistency
        Per query: ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM (majority inside the local DC — avoids cross-region latency), ALL. RF=3 with QUORUM writes and reads → 2+2>3 → strong reads. ALL fails if any replica is down.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        With N replicas, a write waits for W acks and a read asks R nodes. If W plus R is greater than N, the read set and the write set must share at least one node, so the read sees the latest write. With N=3, W=1, R=1 there's no overlap guarantee, so reads can be stale; W=2, R=2 fixes that and still tolerates one node down. I'd add that quorums alone are not linearizable because of sloppy quorums and last-write-wins.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🚩 Consensus: Raft and Paxos
        
  
        
    QWhat problem does consensus solve? Explain Raft in simple steps.
    
        
      
        Problem: several nodes must agree on one ordered log of commands (and on who the leader is) even if some crash or messages are lost — without ever getting split-brain.
        
      
          
        
        1. Terms and election — time is split into numbered terms. A follower that hears no heartbeat within a random timeout becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself and asks others. A majority of votes → leader. Random timeouts avoid endless split votes.
          2. 
        
        2. Log replication — clients talk to the leader. The leader appends the command to its log and sends AppendEntries to followers.
          3. 
        
        3. Commit — once a majority has stored the entry, it is committed and applied to the state machine.
          4. 
        
        4. Safety — a node only votes for a candidate whose log is at least as up to date, so a new leader always has every committed entry. An old leader with a smaller term is ignored (built-in fencing).
          5. 
      
        
      
        Majority math: 2f+1 nodes survive f failures. 3 nodes → 1 failure; 5 nodes → 2. Even sizes add cost, not tolerance (4 nodes still survive only 1). Paxos solves the same problem; Raft was designed to be easier to understand. Used by: etcd, Consul, CockroachDB, TiDB/TiKV (Raft); Spanner (Paxos per split); ZooKeeper (ZAB); MySQL Group Replication (Paxos-based).
        
      
        🎯
        Consensus vs 2PC
        Consensus = replicas of the same data agree, progress needs only a majority. 2PC = different participants (different data) must all agree to commit; any one "no" aborts and a dead coordinator blocks. NewSQL databases combine both: Raft inside each range, 2PC across ranges.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🤝 Distributed transactions: 2PC, XA, 3PC, Saga
        
  

  
        
    QExplain two-phase commit. Why is it called blocking? How does MySQL support it (XA)?
    
        
      
        What: a protocol to make one transaction commit atomically on several databases/resource managers — all commit or all abort.
        
      
          
        
        1. Phase 1 — prepare/vote: coordinator asks every participant "can you commit?". Each does the work, writes a durable PREPARED record to its log, keeps its locks and votes YES (promising it can commit even after a crash) or NO.
          2. 
        
        2. Decision: all YES → coordinator durably logs COMMIT (the commit point); any NO or timeout → ABORT.
          3. 
        
        3. Phase 2 — commit/abort: coordinator sends the verdict; participants apply it, release locks, ACK.
          4. 
      
        
      
        Why blocking: a participant that voted YES has given up the right to abort alone. If the coordinator crashes before sending the verdict, the participant does not know whether others were told COMMIT or ABORT, so it must wait — holding row locks — until the coordinator recovers. Other transactions touching those rows stall.
        
      
        XA START 'transfer-981';
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 1;
XA END   'transfer-981';
XA PREPARE 'transfer-981';    -- phase 1: durable, locks held, survives a crash
-- ... coordinator collects votes from the other DB ...
XA COMMIT 'transfer-981';     -- phase 2 (or XA ROLLBACK 'transfer-981')

XA RECOVER;   -- lists transactions stuck in PREPARED state (in doubt) after a crash
        
      
        ⚠️
        Costs in production
        At least 2 round trips + forced log writes per participant; locks held across the network; coordinator is a single point of failure; in-doubt transactions found by XA RECOVER must be resolved by hand or by the TM. That is why microservices rarely use 2PC across services.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Two-phase commit has a prepare phase, where every participant makes its changes durable, keeps its locks and votes yes or no, and a commit phase, where the coordinator logs the decision and tells everyone. It's atomic, but it's blocking: once a participant votes yes it can't decide alone, so if the coordinator dies it sits on its locks waiting. MySQL exposes this as XA transactions, and XA RECOVER shows the in-doubt ones.
        
      
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Does 3PC fix the blocking?
          
        3PC adds a pre-commit phase so participants can finish without the coordinator — but only if the network has bounded delays and no partitions. Real networks have unbounded delays and process pauses, so 3PC can still break atomicity under a partition. It is rarely used. The practical fix is to make the coordinator itself highly available by replicating its decision with Raft/Paxos (what Spanner and CockroachDB do).
        
        
        ↪A participant voted YES and then crashed. What happens?
          
        On restart its recovery finds the PREPARED record in its log, re-acquires the state as "in doubt", and asks the coordinator for the verdict. It may not roll back on its own.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is the Saga pattern? Choreography vs orchestration? What does it give up?
    
        
      
        What: a long business transaction split into a sequence of local transactions, one per service. Each one commits on its own. If step k fails, run compensating transactions for steps k−1 … 1 in reverse ("refund", "release seat") — a semantic undo, not a rollback.
        
      
        
        
        1. Ordercreate PENDING
        
        
        2. Paymentcharge ₹500
        
        
        3. Inventoryreserve — FAILS
        
        
        Compensaterefund ₹500 → order CANCELLED
        
      
        
      
        
        
        Choreography
        • Services react to each other's events ("PaymentDone" → inventory reserves).
        • No central brain, loose coupling.
        • Hard to see the whole flow; cyclic dependencies as it grows.
        
        
        Orchestration
        • A saga orchestrator tells each service what to do and tracks state.
        • Flow is explicit, easy to monitor and test.
        • The orchestrator is extra infrastructure (Temporal, Step Functions, Camunda).
        
      
        
      
        🚫
        Sagas are ACD, not ACID
        No isolation: other transactions see intermediate states (payment taken, order still pending). Counter-measures: semantic locks (status = PENDING), commutative updates, re-reading values, and ordering steps so that the risky/irreversible ones come last ("pivot" transaction).
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        A saga breaks a cross-service transaction into local transactions, each committed in its own service, and if a step fails we run compensating actions in reverse — refund, release the seat. It can be choreographed through events or driven by an orchestrator; I prefer orchestration once there are more than three or four steps. The trade-off is no isolation, so I use pending states as semantic locks and make every step and compensation idempotent.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is the dual-write problem? How do the transactional outbox and CDC fix it? Why must consumers be idempotent?
    
        
      
        Dual write: the service does INSERT INTO orders and then kafka.send(OrderCreated). If it crashes in between, the DB has the order but nobody hears about it (or the event goes out for an order that was rolled back). Two systems cannot be updated atomically without 2PC.
        
      
        Outbox: write the event into an outbox table in the same local transaction as the business row. A relay then publishes outbox rows — either by polling, or by CDC (Change Data Capture: Debezium tails the MySQL binlog / PG WAL and publishes to Kafka).
        
      
        START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO orders (id, user_id, amount, status) VALUES (9001, 42, 500.00, 'PENDING');
INSERT INTO outbox (id, aggregate_id, type, payload)
VALUES (UUID_TO_BIN(UUID()), 9001, 'OrderCreated', JSON_OBJECT('order_id', 9001, 'amount', 500.00));
COMMIT;   -- both or neither
        
      
        The relay delivers at least once (it may resend after a crash), so consumers must be idempotent: processing the same message twice has the same effect as once.
        
      
        CREATE TABLE processed_messages (message_id BINARY(16) PRIMARY KEY);

START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO processed_messages VALUES (?);      -- duplicate → error 1062, skip the message
UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE user_id = 42;
COMMIT;
        
      
        🌍
        "User clicked Pay twice"
        The client sends an Idempotency-Key header (Stripe-style). The server stores key → result with a UNIQUE constraint; a retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging again.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is CQRS and when is it worth it?
    
        
      
        Command Query Responsibility Segregation: use one model for writes (normalized OLTP tables, enforcing invariants) and separate read models shaped for each screen (denormalized tables, Elasticsearch, Redis, a warehouse), kept up to date from the write side's events/CDC.
        
      
        Worth it when reads and writes have very different shapes or scale (feeds, search, dashboards). Cost: read models are eventually consistent (handle read-your-writes in the UI), more moving parts, replay/rebuild tooling. Often paired with event sourcing, but does not require it.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        📌 Key takeaways
          
    
        • Climb the scaling ladder in order; sharding is the last, most expensive step.
          • 
    
        • Replication copies data (availability, reads); sharding splits data (writes, storage). Partitioning stays on one server.
          • 
    
        • Async = possible loss; semi-sync waits for receipt (not apply) and falls back to async on timeout; quorum/consensus = majority durable.
          • 
    
        • Replica lag breaks read-your-writes, monotonic reads and consistent prefix; fix with leader reads, sticky replicas, GTID waits.
          • 
    
        • Failover must fence the old primary; majority-based systems prevent split-brain by design.
          • 
    
        • Good shard key: high cardinality, even traffic, in most queries, not monotonic. Consistent hashing / logical buckets make resharding cheap.
          • 
    
        • CAP is a choice made only during a partition; C = linearizability. PACELC adds latency vs consistency in normal times.
          • 
    
        • W + R > N gives overlap, not full linearizability. Repair via hinted handoff, read repair, Merkle trees.
          • 
    
        • 2PC is atomic but blocking; sagas trade isolation for availability; outbox + CDC + idempotent consumers kill the dual-write problem.
          • 
  
        

  
        📚 Go deeper
          
    
        • Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) — chapters 5–9 are the definitive source for replication, partitioning, consistency and consensus.
          • 
    
        • Jepsen: Consistency Models — a clickable map of linearizable, serializable, causal and friends, plus real database test reports.
          • 
    
        • MySQL 8.4 Manual: Replication — semi-sync, GTIDs, binlog formats, Group Replication.
          • 
    
        • The Raft Consensus Algorithm — paper plus an interactive visualization of elections and log replication.
          • 
    
        • Amazon's Dynamo paper — consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, vector clocks in one place.
          • 
  
        

  
        
    
        
      
        In MySQL semi-synchronous replication, the source commits after at least one replica has…
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Semi-sync only waits for receipt and flush of the relay log, not apply. And it falls back to async after rpl_semi_sync_source_timeout.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        N = 5 replicas. Which (W, R) guarantees that a read overlaps the latest write?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Need W + R > N: 3 + 3 = 6 > 5. The others sum to 4 or 5, which is not greater than 5.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        What does the "C" in CAP mean?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        CAP's C is linearizability (single-copy, real-time). ACID's C is about constraints — a classic mix-up.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Why is 2PC called a blocking protocol?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        After voting YES a participant is "in doubt" until it hears the verdict; its locks stay held.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Adding a 4th node to a 3-node cluster sharded with consistent hashing moves roughly what fraction of keys?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        The new node takes its share (~1/4) from neighbours. With hash mod N going 3 → 4, about 75% of keys move.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Which statement about MySQL partitioned InnoDB tables is TRUE?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        That is the key rule. Partitioned InnoDB tables support no foreign keys at all, and queries missing the key scan every partition.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        Replication vs sharding?
        Replication = same data on many nodes (HA, read scaling). Sharding = different rows on different nodes (write + storage scaling).
        
    
        Three replica-lag anomalies?
        Read-your-writes, monotonic reads, consistent prefix. Fixes: leader reads after write, sticky replica, GTID wait, causal partitioning.
        
    
        What is a GTID?
        source_uuid:txn_no — a global id per transaction. With SOURCE_AUTO_POSITION=1 failover needs no binlog file/offset maths.
        
    
        Split-brain + fix?
        Two nodes both act as leader and accept writes. Fix: fencing (STONITH, revoke VIP, fencing tokens) or majority-based leadership.
        
    
        Good shard key?
        High cardinality, even data AND traffic, used in most queries, not monotonic (for range sharding).
        
    
        Why virtual nodes?
        Even load on the hash ring, and a failed node's keys spread across many nodes instead of one neighbour.
        
    
        PACELC?
        If Partition: Availability vs Consistency; Else: Latency vs Consistency. Cassandra PA/EL; Spanner-like PC/EC.
        
    
        Sloppy quorum + hinted handoff?
        Write to the first N healthy nodes when home nodes are down; the stand-in keeps a hint and replays it when the home node returns.
        
    
        2f+1 rule?
        A majority-consensus group of 2f+1 nodes tolerates f failures: 3 → 1, 5 → 2. Four nodes still tolerate only 1.
        
    
        Transactional outbox?
        Write the event to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the data; CDC/poller publishes it. At-least-once → idempotent consumers.
        
  
        

        


        
  
        
    
        Chapter 20 · VII · Scale & Modern Data
        
    
        🍃 NoSQL, NewSQL & Data Warehousing (OLTP vs OLAP)
        
    
        Pick the right store for the job — key-value, document, wide-column, graph, NewSQL or a columnar warehouse — and defend the choice with trade-offs, not hype.
        
    
        ⏱ 45 min🔥 Asked a lotNoSQLMySQL 8.4
        
  
        

  
        ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
        
    
          
      
        • NoSQL = non-relational stores built for horizontal scale, flexible schemas and specific access patterns. Usually trades joins and (some) consistency for scale and latency.
          • 
      
        • ACID vs BASE: BASE = Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent.
          • 
      
        • Families: key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j), time-series, search (Elasticsearch), vector.
          • 
      
        • NoSQL modelling is query-first: design tables around the queries; denormalize; embed what is read together.
          • 
      
        • MongoDB is ACID for single-document writes always, and multi-document transactions since 4.0 (replica sets) / 4.2 (sharded).
          • 
      
        • NewSQL (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB) = SQL + ACID + horizontal scale via ranges replicated by Raft/Paxos.
          • 
      
        • OLTP = many small row-level transactions (row store, normalized). OLAP = big scans and aggregates (column store, star schema).
          • 
      
        • Star schema = one fact table + denormalized dimensions; snowflake = dimensions normalized into sub-dimensions. Know the grain and SCD Type 2.
          • 
    
        
  
        

  
        ✏️ "SQL vs NoSQL — which would you choose?" is a favourite opener. Never answer with a product; answer with access patterns, consistency needs and scale.
        

  
        ☁️ Why NoSQL exists
        
  
        
    QWhat is NoSQL and what problems was it created to solve?
    
        
      
        What: "Not only SQL" — databases that do not use the relational table model as their core. Each family is optimized for one shape of data and one set of access patterns.
        
      
        Why (mid-2000s web scale):
        
      
          
        
        • Scale-out writes: one relational primary could not take Amazon/Google/Facebook write volumes; sharding MySQL by hand was painful. Dynamo and Bigtable were built to partition and replicate automatically.
          • 
        
        • Availability: stay writable during node or data-centre failures (AP designs — see Chapter 19).
          • 
        
        • Flexible schema: semi-structured JSON, fields that differ per record, fast iteration without ALTER TABLE on billions of rows.
          • 
        
        • Specialized access: sub-millisecond key lookups (Redis), graph traversals (Neo4j), full-text search, time-series.
          • 
      
        
      
        What you give up (usually): joins, ad-hoc queries, multi-row transactions, strong consistency by default, and the schema as a safety net (the schema moves into application code — "schema-on-read").
        
      
        
        
        ACID
        • Atomic, Consistent, Isolated, Durable.
        • Correctness first; pessimistic.
        • Banking, inventory, bookings.
        
        
        BASE
        • Basically Available — answers even during failures.
        • Soft state — state may change without input (replicas converging).
        • Eventually consistent — replicas agree once writes stop.
        • Feeds, likes, carts, sessions.
        
      
        
      
        🧠
        Chemistry trick
        ACID and BASE are chemical opposites — and so are their priorities: ACID = correctness over availability, BASE = availability over immediate consistency.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        NoSQL databases were built for problems relational databases handled badly at web scale: automatic horizontal scaling of writes, staying available across failures, flexible schemas, and specialized access like key lookups or graph traversal. The price is usually fewer joins, weaker or tunable consistency, and moving schema rules into the application. So I choose based on access patterns and consistency needs, not on hype.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        📦 The NoSQL families
        
  
        
    
        🔑
        Key-value
        key → opaque value. O(1) get/put. Redis, Memcached, DynamoDB, Riak. Caches, sessions, carts, rate limits, leaderboards.
        
    
        📄
        Document
        key → JSON/BSON document with nested fields, queryable and indexable. MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore. Catalogs, profiles, CMS.
        
    
        🧱
        Wide-column
        Partition key → sorted rows of columns. Huge write throughput. Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase, Bigtable. Time series, messaging, IoT.
        
    
        🕸️
        Graph
        Nodes + edges with properties; traversals without joins. Neo4j, Neptune. Social graphs, fraud rings, recommendations.
        
    
        ⏱️
        Time-series
        Append-mostly timestamped points, downsampling, retention. InfluxDB, TimescaleDB (PG extension). Metrics, sensors.
        
    
        🔎
        Search
        Inverted indexes, relevance scoring. Elasticsearch, OpenSearch. Full-text search, logs.
        
    
        🧭
        Vector
        Nearest-neighbour search over embeddings (HNSW, IVF). Pinecone, Milvus, pgvector. Semantic search, RAG.
        
  
        

  
        FamilyData modelStrengthWeaknessPick when…
        
    
        Key-valuekey → blobfastest, simplest to partitionno query by value (except secondary indexes, e.g. DynamoDB GSIs), no joinsyou always know the key
        
    
        Documentnested JSONmatches app objects; rich queries + indexesjoins weak ($lookup); 16 MB doc limit (MongoDB)aggregate read as a whole (an order with its items)
        
    
        Wide-columnpartition → sorted rowsmassive writes, linear scale, multi-DCqueries must follow the key; no joins; limited ad-hocknown query patterns at huge volume
        
    
        Graphnodes + edgesmulti-hop traversalsharder to shard; bulk analyticsrelationships ARE the data
        
    
        Searchinverted indextext relevance, facetsnot a primary system of recordfuzzy text search over another DB's data
        
  
        

  
        ✏️ Modelling data in NoSQL
        
  
        
    QHow is NoSQL data modelling different? When do you embed vs reference in MongoDB?
    
        
      
        Relational modelling is data-first: normalize entities, then write any query with joins. NoSQL modelling is query-first: list the access patterns, then shape documents/tables so each query hits one partition and needs no join. Duplication is accepted.
        
      
        
        
        Embed (nest inside the parent)
        • One-to-one or one-to-few (user → 2 addresses).
        • Data read together and owned by the parent (order → line items).
        • One read, atomic single-document update.
        
        
        Reference (store the id)
        • One-to-many unbounded (viral post → 2M comments) — would blow the 16 MB limit.
        • Many-to-many (products ↔ orders).
        • Child is read or updated on its own; data shared by many parents.
        
      
        
      
        {
  "_id": 9001,
  "user_id": 42,
  "status": "PAID",
  "created_at": "2026-10-01T10:15:00Z",
  "shipping": { "city": "Bhubaneswar", "pin": "751003" },
  "items": [
    { "sku": "BK-101", "name": "DBMS Book", "qty": 1, "price": 499 },
    { "sku": "PN-007", "name": "Pen",       "qty": 3, "price": 20 }
  ]
}
        
      
        Note the item name and price are copied into the order: that is intentional — it is the price at the time of purchase.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Common mistake
        Porting a normalized MySQL schema 1:1 into MongoDB collections and then doing $lookup everywhere. You get the costs of NoSQL and none of the benefits.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QExplain Cassandra's partition key and clustering key. Model "messages in a chat".
    
        
      
        
        
        Partition key
        Hashed onto the token ring; decides which nodes store the row. All rows with the same partition key live together.
        
        
        Clustering key
        Sorts rows inside a partition on disk, so range scans within one partition are cheap.
        
      
        
      
        CREATE TABLE messages_by_channel (
  channel_id  bigint,
  bucket      int,          -- e.g. 10-day time bucket: keeps partitions bounded
  message_id  timeuuid,
  author_id   bigint,
  body        text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((channel_id, bucket), message_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC);

-- Query: latest 50 messages in a channel → hits ONE partition, already sorted
SELECT * FROM messages_by_channel
WHERE channel_id = 7 AND bucket = 2026 LIMIT 50;
        
      
        The composite partition key (channel_id, bucket) prevents one busy channel from becoming a giant hot partition (Discord used exactly this bucket idea). A second access pattern ("messages by author") gets a second table, written alongside.
        
      
        🔀
        DynamoDB single-table design
        DynamoDB has a partition key + optional sort key too. Advanced designs put several entity types in ONE table with generic keys (PK = USER#42, SK = ORDER#2026-10-01#9001) so one Query fetches a user and their orders together — "pre-joined" data. Extra access patterns use Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs), which are eventually consistent.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🧭 SQL vs NoSQL: how to decide
        
  
        
    
        Need multi-row ACID invariants, joins, ad-hoc queries?money, inventory, bookings, reporting → relational (PostgreSQL / MySQL)
        
    
        
    
        Will one well-tuned relational primary + replicas + cache handle the load?most apps: yes → stay relational
        
    
        
    
        Access patterns known and simple, at huge scale or multi-region writes?yes → key-value / wide-column (DynamoDB, Cassandra)
        
    
        
    
        Data is nested and read as a whole, schema varies?yes → document (MongoDB)
        
    
        
    
        Specialized need?relationships → graph · text → search · embeddings → vector · metrics → time-series. Need SQL + ACID + scale-out → NewSQL
        
  
        

  
        
    QSQL or NoSQL for an e-commerce site? Bust the common myths.
    
        
      
        Use both (polyglot persistence): orders, payments and inventory in a relational DB (ACID, constraints); product catalog with varied attributes in a document store or a JSON column; carts and sessions in Redis; search in Elasticsearch; analytics in a warehouse fed by CDC.
        
      
        MythReality
        
        
        "NoSQL is faster."Faster for its designed access pattern. Off-pattern queries (ad-hoc filters, joins) are slower or impossible.
        
        
        "SQL doesn't scale."Read replicas, partitioning, Vitess/Citus and NewSQL scale SQL very far. Most companies never outgrow one primary.
        
        
        "NoSQL has no schema."It has an implicit schema in your code (schema-on-read). MongoDB even supports JSON-schema validation.
        
        
        "NoSQL has no transactions."MongoDB has multi-document ACID transactions; DynamoDB has TransactWriteItems; Cassandra has lightweight transactions (Paxos).
        
        
        "Relational can't do JSON."MySQL JSON type + generated-column indexes; PostgreSQL JSONB with GIN indexes.
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        I'd start from the data and the access patterns. Orders, payments and stock need ACID and constraints, so they go in a relational database. The catalog has varied attributes and is read as a whole, so a document store or JSON column fits. Sessions and carts go in Redis, search in Elasticsearch, and analytics in a warehouse. Speed and scale claims are pattern-specific, so I'd only add a NoSQL store where a real access pattern needs it.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs MongoDB ACID?
    
        
      
        Yes, with caveats. A write to a single document (including its embedded arrays) has always been atomic. Multi-document ACID transactions arrived in 4.0 for replica sets and 4.2 for sharded clusters.
        
      
          
        
        • Default transaction runtime limit is 60 seconds (transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds); longer ones are aborted.
          • 
        
        • For durability across failover use writeConcern: {w: "majority"}; for a consistent view use readConcern: "snapshot". A write acked with w: 1 can be rolled back after a failover.
          • 
        
        • Transactions cost performance — design documents so most invariants live in one document, and use transactions for rare cross-document cases (transfer between two wallets).
          • 
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🚀 NewSQL: SQL that scales out
        
  
        
    QWhat is NewSQL and how does it give ACID + SQL + horizontal scale at the same time?
    
        
      
        Goal: keep SQL and serializable ACID transactions, but scale horizontally and survive node, zone and region failures automatically — without hand-sharding.
        
      
          
        
        1. Split every table (and index) into key ranges ("ranges", "regions", "tablets") of a few hundred MB.
          2. 
        
        2. Replicate each range with Raft or Paxos (usually 3 or 5 copies); the range leader serves writes. A majority = durable.
          3. 
        
        3. Rebalance automatically: ranges split when large or hot, and move between nodes.
          4. 
        
        4. Transactions touching several ranges use 2PC, but the coordinator's state is itself replicated, so it does not block forever like classic 2PC.
          5. 
        
        5. Ordering with MVCC timestamps: Spanner uses TrueTime (GPS + atomic clocks, uncertainty of a few ms, "commit wait"); CockroachDB uses hybrid logical clocks; TiDB uses a central timestamp oracle (PD).
          6. 
      
        
      
        SystemWire compatibilityConsensusNote
        
        
        Google SpannerGoogleSQL / PostgreSQL dialectPaxos per splitexternal consistency via TrueTime
        
        
        CockroachDBPostgreSQL wireRaft per rangeserializable by default
        
        
        TiDBMySQL wireRaft (TiKV)TiFlash columnar replicas → HTAP
        
        
        YugabyteDBPostgreSQL (YSQL) + Cassandra-like (YCQL)Raft per tabletreuses PG's query layer
        
      
        
      
        ⚠️
        Trade-offs
        Every write pays a consensus round trip (more for cross-region), cross-range transactions cost 2PC, and some features (certain locking or sequence behaviours) differ from the engine they imitate. PACELC: PC/EC — they pay latency for consistency.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        NewSQL databases like Spanner, CockroachDB and TiDB split tables into ranges, replicate each range with Raft or Paxos, and run 2PC across ranges with a replicated coordinator. So you keep SQL and serializable transactions while capacity grows by adding nodes and failures are handled by majority. The cost is latency: every write needs a consensus round trip.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        📊 OLTP vs OLAP
        
  
        AspectOLTP (transactions)OLAP (analytics)
        
    
        Purposerun the business: place order, pay, book seatanalyse the business: revenue by region by month
        
    
        Query shapemany short reads/writes touching few rows by keyfew huge read-only scans + aggregates over millions/billions of rows
        
    
        Usersthousands of app users concurrentlyanalysts, dashboards, ML pipelines
        
    
        Schemanormalized (3NF) to avoid anomaliesdenormalized star/snowflake
        
    
        Storagerow store (InnoDB, PostgreSQL heap)column store (Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse)
        
    
        Datacurrent statehistory over years
        
    
        Metrictransactions/sec, p99 latencyquery throughput, scan speed
        
    
        SizeGB to a few TBTB to PB
        
  
        
  
        🎯
        What they test
        Why you should not run heavy analytics on the production MySQL primary: long scans fight for buffer pool and I/O, hold MVCC snapshots open (undo grows), and slow customer transactions. Offload to a replica at minimum, or to a warehouse.
        

  
        
    QWhy are column stores so much faster for analytics?
    
        
      
        A row store keeps all columns of a row together on a page. A column store keeps all values of one column together.
        
      
      
          
        
        1. Read only needed columns — a query on 3 of 100 columns reads ~3% of the data.
          2. 
        
        2. Compression — similar values sit together: run-length encoding (IN,IN,IN → IN×3), dictionary encoding, delta encoding for dates. 5–10× smaller is common, so less I/O.
          3. 
        
        3. Vectorized execution — process batches of column values with tight CPU loops / SIMD.
          4. 
        
        4. Zone maps / min-max per block — skip blocks that cannot match WHERE date = '2026-09-01'.
          5. 
      
        
      
        Downside: single-row inserts and updates are expensive, so warehouses load in batches and buffer small writes.
        
      
        🔀
        MPP warehouses
        Massively Parallel Processing: data is distributed across many nodes, each scans its slice in parallel, results are merged. Redshift (distribution keys), BigQuery and Snowflake (storage separated from compute; scale compute independently), ClickHouse, Databricks SQL. File formats in lakes: Parquet / ORC (columnar).
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🗄️ Warehouse, mart, lake, lakehouse
        
  
        
    
        Data warehouse
        Central, cleaned, integrated, historical store for analytics with a fixed schema (schema-on-write). Subject-oriented, time-variant, non-volatile (Inmon's definition).
        
    
        Data mart
        A smaller, subject-specific slice of the warehouse for one team (sales mart, finance mart).
        
    
        Data lake
        Cheap object storage (S3, GCS, ADLS) holding raw data of any format — JSON, logs, images, Parquet. Schema-on-read. Risk: becomes a "data swamp" without governance.
        
    
        Lakehouse
        Lake storage + warehouse features via an open table format (Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi): ACID commits, schema enforcement, time travel, fast SQL engines on top.
        
  
        

  
        
    QETL vs ELT — what is the difference and why did ELT become popular?
    
        
      
        
        
        Extractfrom MySQL, APIs, logs (batch or CDC)
        
        
        Transformclean, dedupe, join, conform
        
        
        Loadinto warehouse tables
        
      
        
      
        
        
        ETL
        • Transform on a separate ETL server, then load the clean result.
        • Born when warehouse compute was expensive and fixed.
        • Only curated data lands; raw data is lost.
        • Tools: Informatica, SSIS, Talend.
        
        
        ELT
        • Load raw data first, transform inside the warehouse with SQL.
        • Cloud warehouses have elastic compute, so this is cheap and simple.
        • Raw data kept → re-run transforms any time.
        • Tools: Fivetran/Airbyte to load + dbt to transform.
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        In ETL the data is transformed on a separate engine before it is loaded, which made sense when warehouse compute was scarce. In ELT we load raw data straight into the warehouse or lake and transform it there with SQL, usually with dbt. Cloud warehouses made compute elastic, so ELT is simpler and keeps the raw history so transformations can be re-run.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        ⭐ Dimensional modelling: facts, dimensions, star & snowflake
        
  
        
    
        Fact table
        Measurable events — numbers you add up: quantity, amount, discount. Very tall (billions of rows), narrow; holds foreign keys to dimensions.
        
    
        Dimension table
        Descriptive context you filter and group by: who, what, where, when — customer, product, store, date. Wide, relatively short.
        
    
        Grain
        What ONE fact row represents, e.g. "one line item of one order". Declare it first; every measure and dimension must match it. Mixing grains causes double counting.
        
    
        Surrogate key
        Warehouse-generated integer key for a dimension row (customer_sk), separate from the source system's natural key (customer_id). Needed for history (SCD Type 2).
        
  
        

  

  

  
        
    QStar schema vs snowflake schema — which would you choose and why?
    
        
      
        StarSnowflake
        
        
        Dimensionsdenormalized (one table each)normalized into sub-dimensions
        
        
        Joins per queryfewer (fact → dim)more (fact → dim → sub-dim)
        
        
        Query speed / simplicity✔ faster, BI-tool friendly~ slower, harder SQL
        
        
        Storage / redundancymore duplication (category repeated)✔ less duplication
        
        
        Dimension maintenanceupdate many rows if a category is renamedupdate one row
        
      
        
      
        SELECT d.year, d.month, p.category, SUM(f.amount) AS revenue
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date    d ON d.date_sk    = f.date_sk
JOIN dim_product p ON p.product_sk = f.product_sk
WHERE d.year = 2026
GROUP BY d.year, d.month, p.category;
        
      
        💡
        Default answer
        Star, because dimension tables are small compared with the fact table, so the storage saved by snowflaking is tiny while every query pays extra joins. Snowflake a dimension only when it is huge or has a deep, shared hierarchy. (A galaxy / fact constellation = several fact tables sharing conformed dimensions.)
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Both have a central fact table of measurable events. In a star, each dimension is one denormalized table, so any question is one join away and BI tools love it. In a snowflake, dimensions are normalized into sub-tables, which saves a little space and makes updates easier but adds joins. Since dimensions are tiny compared with facts, I'd default to a star.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat are Slowly Changing Dimensions? Explain SCD Type 1, 2 and 3 with an example.
    
        
      
        Dimension attributes change slowly over time: a customer moves from Bhubaneswar to Bengaluru. Should last year's sales be reported under the old city or the new one? SCD types are the standard answers (Kimball).
        
      
        TypeWhat happens on changeHistory?
        
        
        0never change (original value kept, e.g. date of birth)—
        
        
        1overwrite the old value✘ lost; old sales now show the new city
        
        
        2insert a NEW row with a new surrogate key + valid_from / valid_to / is_current✔ full history
        
        
        3add a column previous_city~ only one previous value
        
        
        4current row in the dimension, history in a separate table✔
        
        
        61 + 2 + 3 hybrid: new row per change AND a current-value column overwritten on all rows✔ + easy "as of now" reporting
        
      
        
      
        customer_sk | customer_id | name | city        | valid_from | valid_to   | is_current
------------+-------------+------+-------------+------------+------------+-----------
        101 | C42         | Asha | Bhubaneswar | 2024-01-01 | 2026-06-30 | N
        245 | C42         | Asha | Bengaluru   | 2026-07-01 | 9999-12-31 | Y
        
      
        START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE dim_customer SET valid_to = '2026-06-30', is_current = 'N'
WHERE customer_id = 'C42' AND is_current = 'Y';
INSERT INTO dim_customer (customer_id, name, city, valid_from, valid_to, is_current)
VALUES ('C42', 'Asha', 'Bengaluru', '2026-07-01', '9999-12-31', 'Y');
COMMIT;
        
      
        Facts loaded before July point to customer_sk = 101, later facts to 245, so "sales by city" stays historically correct. This is exactly why surrogate keys matter: the natural key C42 now maps to two rows.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Type 1 overwrites and loses history. Type 2 closes the current row and inserts a new one with a new surrogate key and validity dates, so old facts keep pointing to the old version. Type 3 keeps just a previous-value column. I'd use Type 2 for anything we report on historically, like customer city or product category.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🎲 OLAP operations on a cube
        
  
        Think of sales as a cube with axes Time × Product × Region; each cell holds a measure (revenue).
        
  
        
    
        ⬆️
        Roll-up
        Aggregate up a hierarchy: city → region → country; day → month.
        
    
        ⬇️
        Drill-down
        Go to finer detail: year → quarter → month.
        
    
        🔪
        Slice
        Fix ONE dimension: Year = 2025 → a 2-D slab.
        
    
        🎲
        Dice
        Filter on SEVERAL dimensions: Year ∈ {2024, 2025} AND Region ∈ {East, West} AND Category = Electronics → a sub-cube.
        
    
        🔄
        Pivot
        Rotate axes: regions as rows, months as columns.
        
  
        
  
        R-D-S-D-P
        "Really Deep Sandwiches Don't Pivot" — Roll-up, Drill-down, Slice, Dice, Pivot. Slice = one knife cut; dice = many cuts.
        

  
        
    QHow do you produce subtotals and grand totals in SQL? ROLLUP vs CUBE vs GROUPING SETS.
    
        
      
        SELECT
  IF(GROUPING(region), 'ALL regions', region) AS region,
  IF(GROUPING(year),   'ALL years',   year)   AS year,
  SUM(amount) AS revenue
FROM sales
GROUP BY region, year WITH ROLLUP;
        
      
        +-------------+-----------+---------+
| region      | year      | revenue |
+-------------+-----------+---------+
| East        | 2025      |     500 |
| East        | 2026      |     700 |
| East        | ALL years |    1200 |   ← subtotal per region
| West        | 2025      |     300 |
| West        | 2026      |     400 |
| West        | ALL years |     700 |
| ALL regions | ALL years |    1900 |   ← grand total
+-------------+-----------+---------+
        
      
          
        
        • ROLLUP(a, b) → groups (a,b), (a), () — hierarchical subtotals.
          • 
        
        • CUBE(a, b) → all combinations: (a,b), (a), (b), () — 2ⁿ groupings.
          • 
        
        • GROUPING SETS ((a), (b), ()) → exactly the groupings you list.
          • 
        
        • GROUPING(col) returns 1 when the NULL in that row is a "super-aggregate" NULL, not a real NULL value.
          • 
      
        
      
        🔀
        Engine support
        MySQL supports only GROUP BY … WITH ROLLUP (and GROUPING() since 8.0) — no CUBE or GROUPING SETS; emulate them with UNION ALL. PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server and warehouses support ROLLUP(...), CUBE(...) and GROUPING SETS.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Trap
        Using IFNULL(region, 'ALL') to label totals mislabels rows where region is genuinely NULL. Use GROUPING().
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QA dashboard query over 2 billion rows is slow. What do you do?
    
        
      
          
        
        1. Move it off OLTP — run it in a columnar warehouse fed by CDC/ELT, not on the MySQL primary.
          2. 
        
        2. Pre-aggregate — summary tables or materialized views (daily revenue by store) refreshed incrementally. MySQL has no materialized views: emulate with a summary table maintained by a scheduled job/event. PostgreSQL has REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW [CONCURRENTLY]; Oracle and warehouses can refresh incrementally.
          3. 
        
        3. Partition / cluster by date so filters prune most of the data.
          4. 
        
        4. Select only needed columns (column stores reward this) and check the grain to avoid fan-out double counting.
          5. 
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat is HTAP?
    
        
      
        Hybrid Transactional/Analytical Processing: one system serves OLTP and real-time analytics on fresh data, without a nightly ETL. Usually it keeps a row store for transactions and a columnar replica kept in sync for analytics, and the optimizer routes each query.
        
      
        Examples: TiDB (TiKV row store + TiFlash columnar replicas), SingleStore, Oracle Database In-Memory column store, SQL Server columnstore indexes on OLTP tables, MySQL HeatWave (Oracle Cloud). Trade-off: resource isolation between the two workloads is the hard part.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        📌 Key takeaways
          
    
        • NoSQL exists for scale-out writes, availability, flexible schemas and specialized access; it usually gives up joins and default strong consistency.
          • 
    
        • Know the families and one product + use case each: KV, document, wide-column, graph, time-series, search, vector.
          • 
    
        • NoSQL modelling is query-first: embed what is read together, reference unbounded or shared data; Cassandra = partition key (where) + clustering key (order).
          • 
    
        • Choose by access patterns and invariants, not hype. Polyglot persistence is normal.
          • 
    
        • MongoDB: single-document atomic always; multi-document ACID since 4.0 / 4.2.
          • 
    
        • NewSQL = ranges + Raft/Paxos + 2PC with replicated coordinators + MVCC timestamps.
          • 
    
        • OLTP = row store, normalized, small transactions. OLAP = column store, star schema, big scans.
          • 
    
        • Star (default) vs snowflake; declare the grain; SCD Type 2 + surrogate keys keep history correct.
          • 
    
        • MySQL has only WITH ROLLUP (+ GROUPING()); CUBE and GROUPING SETS exist in PG/Oracle/SQL Server.
          • 
  
        

  
        📚 Go deeper
          
    
        • Designing Data-Intensive Applications — ch. 2–3 compare data models and explain column storage beautifully.
          • 
    
        • MongoDB Manual: Data Modeling — embed vs reference with official patterns.
          • 
    
        • Apache Cassandra: Data Modeling — query-first design with partition and clustering keys.
          • 
    
        • Kimball Group: Dimensional Modeling Techniques — grain, facts, dimensions, SCD types from the source.
          • 
    
        • MySQL 8.4: GROUP BY Modifiers — WITH ROLLUP and GROUPING().
          • 
  
        

  
        
    
        
      
        BASE stands for…
        
      
      
      
      
      
        BASE is the availability-first counterpart of ACID.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        A viral post can have millions of comments. In MongoDB you should…
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Unbounded one-to-many → reference. Embedding would hit the 16 MB document limit and make every post read huge.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        In Cassandra, which part of the primary key decides which nodes store a row?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        The partition key is hashed to a token on the ring; clustering keys only order rows inside the partition.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        A customer moves city and you must keep reporting old sales under the old city. Which SCD type?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Type 2 adds a new row with a new surrogate key, so old facts keep pointing to the old version. Type 3 keeps only one previous value.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Which grouping feature does MySQL 8 support natively?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        MySQL has only WITH ROLLUP (plus GROUPING()). CUBE and GROUPING SETS need UNION ALL emulation.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Why is a column store faster for SELECT SUM(amount) FROM sales?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Column pruning + compression + vectorized execution mean far fewer bytes read and processed.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        Five NoSQL families + example each?
        Key-value (Redis), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra), graph (Neo4j), search (Elasticsearch). Also time-series (InfluxDB), vector (Milvus).
        
    
        Embed vs reference rule?
        Embed one-to-few, read-together, owned data. Reference unbounded one-to-many, many-to-many, independently accessed data.
        
    
        Partition key vs clustering key?
        Partition key → which nodes (hashed). Clustering key → sort order inside the partition.
        
    
        Is MongoDB ACID?
        Single-document: always. Multi-document transactions: since 4.0 (replica sets), 4.2 (sharded). 60 s default limit.
        
    
        NewSQL in one line?
        SQL + ACID + horizontal scale: ranges replicated by Raft/Paxos, 2PC across ranges, MVCC timestamps (Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB).
        
    
        OLTP vs OLAP storage?
        OLTP: row store, normalized, index lookups. OLAP: column store, star schema, compressed scans, MPP.
        
    
        ETL vs ELT?
        ETL transforms before loading (separate engine). ELT loads raw first and transforms inside the warehouse (dbt).
        
    
        Lake vs warehouse vs lakehouse?
        Lake: raw files, schema-on-read. Warehouse: curated, schema-on-write. Lakehouse: lake + ACID table format (Delta, Iceberg, Hudi).
        
    
        What is the grain?
        What one fact row represents (e.g. one order line). Declare it first; mixing grains double counts.
        
    
        Slice vs dice?
        Slice fixes one dimension (Year = 2025). Dice filters several dimensions → a sub-cube.
        
  
        

        


        
  
        
    
        Chapter 21 · VII · Scale & Modern Data
        
    
        🏗️ Schema Design & Real-World Scenario Questions
        
    
        Walk into "Design the database for BookMyShow" with a repeatable framework, ready-made DDL for the classic systems, and crisp answers to every modeling pattern the interviewer pokes at.
        
    
        ⏱ 60 min🔥 Asked a lot
        
  
        

  
         
        ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
         
          
    
        • Framework: clarify requirements → list entities → relationships & cardinality → tables + keys → access patterns → indexes → concurrency hot spots → scale & evolution.
          • 
    
        • Never overwrite history you must explain later: copy price into order_items, keep money movements as immutable ledger rows.
          • 
    
        • Let the database enforce invariants: UNIQUE(show_id, seat_id) stops double booking; UPDATE … SET stock = stock - ? WHERE stock >= ? stops overselling.
          • 
    
        • Money: DECIMAL(19,4) or integer minor units (paise) — never FLOAT. Double-entry: every transfer = debit row + credit row, sum = 0.
          • 
    
        • Retries are normal: idempotency key with a UNIQUE constraint turns "charged twice" into "duplicate ignored".
          • 
    
        • Feeds: fan-out-on-write for normal users, fan-out-on-read for celebrities (hybrid).
          • 
    
        • Keys: BIGINT auto-increment PK inside + random/UUIDv7 public_id outside. Random UUIDv4 as InnoDB PK = page splits.
          • 
    
        • Patterns to know cold: trees (adjacency + recursive CTE, closure table), polymorphic associations, EAV vs JSON, soft delete + UNIQUE, audit tables, multi-tenancy, UTC time, hot counters, expand–contract migrations.
          • 
  
         
        

  
        🧭 The schema-design framework (use it every single time)
        
  
        A schema-design round is not a test of whether you remember the "correct" table list. It is a test of how you think. The interviewer wants to see you ask questions, make choices, state trade-offs, and protect the data from bugs and races. So follow the same eight steps every time, out loud.
        

  
        
    
        1. Clarifycore features, scale, read/write ratio, consistency needs
        
    
        
    
        2. Entitiesnouns → tables
        
    
        
    
        3. Relationships1:1, 1:N, M:N → FK or junction
        
    
        
    
        4. Tables + keysPK, FK, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK
        
  
        
  
        
    
        5. Access patternsthe top 3–5 queries
        
    
        
    
        6. Indexescomposite, leftmost prefix, covering
        
    
        
    
        7. Concurrencywhere can two users collide?
        
    
        
    
        8. Scale & evolvecaching, sharding key, archiving, migrations
        
  
        

  
        
    QThe interviewer says "Design the database for X". What do you do in the first two minutes?
    
        
      
        Ask, don't draw. Spend the first 1–2 minutes on requirements. You are showing that you design for a real business, not for a textbook.
        
      
          
        
        1. Scope the features — "For e-commerce, should I cover catalog, cart, orders and payments, or also returns, coupons and sellers?" Pick 3–5 core features.
          2. 
        
        2. Ask the scale — users, rows per day, peak QPS. "10k orders/day" and "10M orders/day" lead to different designs (one MySQL vs sharding).
          3. 
        
        3. Ask read vs write ratio — feeds are read-heavy; ledgers and logs are write-heavy.
          4. 
        
        4. Ask the consistency need — money and seats need strong consistency; like counts can be eventually consistent.
          5. 
        
        5. State assumptions — "I'll assume one currency, MySQL 8 InnoDB, single region first; I'll discuss scaling at the end."
          6. 
      
        
      
        Then list entities (the nouns in the requirements), draw relationships, write the core DDL, name the top queries and their indexes, and only then talk about scale.
        
      
        🎯
        What is really being tested
        (1) Can you turn vague requirements into entities and keys? (2) Do you know normalization but also when to denormalize? (3) Do you spot the race condition (overselling, double booking, double charge)? (4) Do you pick indexes from queries, not from columns?
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "Before I draw tables, let me confirm the scope. I'll cover users, products, cart, orders and payments. Roughly how many orders per day, and is it read-heavy? I'll assume MySQL 8 with InnoDB. I'll start normalized to 3NF, list the main queries, add indexes for them, then look at where two users can collide, and finally talk about scaling."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Why start normalized instead of designing for performance directly?
          
        Normalized tables (3NF, see Chapter 6) have one source of truth per fact, so updates can't create contradictions. Denormalize later only for a measured hot read path (e.g., a cached like_count), and say how you keep the copy in sync.
        
        
        ↪The interviewer refuses to give numbers. What now?
          
        Pick a reasonable number and say it: "I'll assume 1M daily users and 100k orders per day — that fits on one primary with replicas. If it grows 100×, I'll shard by user_id." Making a clear assumption is better than stalling.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Design checklist itemQuestion to ask yourself
        
    
        Primary keysEvery table has one? BIGINT for anything that grows?
        
    
        Foreign keysChild rows can't point to missing parents? ON DELETE behavior chosen on purpose?
        
    
        UniquenessWhat must never be duplicated? (email, seat per show, idempotency key)
        
    
        HistoryDo I need the value "as it was" (price at purchase, address at delivery)?
        
    
        Money & timeDECIMAL / integer minor units? Stored in UTC?
        
    
        StatusIs there a state machine? Which transitions are legal?
        
    
        IndexesOne index per top query; composite order = equality columns first, then range/sort.
        
    
        ConcurrencyWhere can two requests collide? Atomic UPDATE, row lock, UNIQUE, or version column?
        
    
        GrowthWhich table becomes huge? Partition/archive/shard key?
        
  
        

  
        ✏️ The single most impressive thing you can do in a design round: spot the race condition before the interviewer asks.
        

  
  
        🛒 Design 1: E-commerce (Amazon / Flipkart)
        
  
        Requirements: users browse products (with variants like size/colour), add to cart, place orders, pay, and leave reviews. Inventory must never go negative. Order history must show the price the user actually paid, even if the product price changes later.
        

  

  
        CREATE TABLE users (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  email       VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  name        VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  created_at  DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  UNIQUE KEY uq_users_email (email)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE products (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  category_id BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  title       VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  is_active   BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  KEY idx_products_cat (category_id, is_active)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE product_variants (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  product_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  sku         VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  price       DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (price >= 0),
  attrs       JSON,                       -- {"size":"M","color":"red"}
  UNIQUE KEY uq_variant_sku (sku),
  FOREIGN KEY (product_id) REFERENCES products(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE inventory (
  variant_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED PRIMARY KEY,
  qty         INT NOT NULL CHECK (qty >= 0),   -- CHECK enforced from MySQL 8.0.16
  version     INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  FOREIGN KEY (variant_id) REFERENCES product_variants(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id            BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id       BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  status        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',  -- PENDING/PAID/SHIPPED/DELIVERED/CANCELLED
  total_amount  DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,
  ship_address  JSON NOT NULL,            -- snapshot, not FK to addresses
  idem_key      CHAR(36) NOT NULL,        -- client-generated, stops double orders on retry
  created_at    DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  UNIQUE KEY uq_orders_idem (user_id, idem_key),
  KEY idx_orders_user_time (user_id, created_at),
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id    BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  variant_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  qty         INT NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price  DECIMAL(12,2) NOT NULL,     -- price AT PURCHASE TIME
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, variant_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (order_id)   REFERENCES orders(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (variant_id) REFERENCES product_variants(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
        

  
        
    QWhy store unit_price in order_items when the product table already has a price? Isn't that redundant?
    
        
      
        It looks redundant but it is not the same fact. product_variants.price = "price today". order_items.unit_price = "price this customer agreed to pay on that day". Prices change, discounts end, sellers edit listings. If the order looked up the current price, last year's invoice would silently change. That breaks accounting, refunds and tax reports.
        
      
        Same idea for the shipping address: copy it into the order. If the user edits their address book later, the parcel that was already shipped still went to the old address.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Common mistake
        Saying "this violates 3NF, so I'll remove it". It does not violate 3NF: unit_price depends on the key (order_id, variant_id), not on variant_id alone, because it is frozen at order time.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
