        "An order is a historical record. I snapshot the unit price and the shipping address into the order, because the live product price and the user's address book can change later. It's not duplication — it's a different fact: the price at purchase time."
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QTwo users buy the last unit at the same time. How do you prevent overselling?
    
        
      
        This is the concurrency question of e-commerce. Without care, both requests read qty = 1, both decide "enough stock", both write qty = 0 — two orders, one item. That is a lost update (see Chapter 13).
        
      
        
        
        TimeT1 (Asha)T2 (Ravi)
        
        
        t1SELECT qty → 1
        
        
        t2SELECT qty → 1
        
        
        t3UPDATE qty = 0; COMMIT
        
        
        t4UPDATE qty = 0; COMMIT ❗ oversold
        
      
        
      
        Three correct fixes, best first:
        
      
        
        
        
        
        
          
        UPDATE inventory
   SET qty = qty - 1
 WHERE variant_id = 42 AND qty >= 1;
-- affected rows = 1 → success; 0 → out of stock, abort the order
        
          
        The check and the write happen in one statement. InnoDB takes an exclusive row lock, so the second transaction waits, then re-evaluates qty >= 1 on the latest committed value and updates 0 rows. Shortest lock time, no extra round trip.
        
        
        
        
        
          
        START TRANSACTION;
SELECT qty FROM inventory WHERE variant_id = 42 FOR UPDATE;  -- X lock
-- app checks qty >= 1
UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE variant_id = 42;
INSERT INTO orders ...; INSERT INTO order_items ...;
COMMIT;
        
          
        Pessimistic locking. Good when the app needs to read several values before deciding. Lock order matters: if an order has many items, lock variants in ascending id order to avoid deadlocks.
        
        
        
        
        
          
        SELECT qty, version FROM inventory WHERE variant_id = 42;  -- qty=5, version=7
UPDATE inventory SET qty = 4, version = 8
 WHERE variant_id = 42 AND version = 7;
-- 0 rows → someone else changed it → retry
        
          
        No lock held while the user thinks. Good for low contention. Under a flash sale it causes many retries — prefer the atomic update there.
        
        
        
      
        
      
        🌍
        Flash sale (Big Billion Days)
        One popular SKU becomes a hot row: thousands of transactions queue on the same row lock. Fixes: reserve stock in Redis with an atomic DECR and write orders asynchronously; or split stock into N "buckets" rows and decrement a random bucket; or put buyers in a queue. The DB constraint CHECK (qty >= 0) stays as the last safety net.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "A read-then-write lets two buyers both see one unit. I'd make the check and decrement a single atomic statement — UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = ? AND qty >= 1 — and look at affected rows. InnoDB's row lock serializes the two buyers. A CHECK constraint qty >= 0 is my safety net. For a flash sale I'd move the counter to Redis or split it into buckets."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪When do you deduct stock — at add-to-cart, at checkout, or after payment?
          
        Usually reserve at checkout (with an expiry, e.g. 10–15 minutes) and confirm on payment success; a background job releases expired reservations. Deducting at add-to-cart lets people hoard stock; deducting only after payment can oversell during the payment window.
        
        
        ↪Does REPEATABLE READ alone stop overselling in MySQL?
          
        No. A plain SELECT under RR reads a snapshot, so both transactions can see qty=1. What saves you is that the UPDATE is a locking, current read. Write the condition inside the UPDATE, or use FOR UPDATE. (PostgreSQL's RR would instead raise a serialization error on the second update.)
        
        
        ↪The user double-clicks "Place order". How do you avoid two orders?
          
        The client sends an idempotency key (a UUID generated when the checkout page loads). UNIQUE(user_id, idem_key) makes the second insert fail with a duplicate-key error; the server then returns the first order. See the banking design for the full pattern.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QKey indexes and scale follow-ups for e-commerce?
    
        
      
        QueryIndex
        
        
        "My orders", newest firstorders(user_id, created_at)
        
        
        Products in a categoryproducts(category_id, is_active)
        
        
        Lookup by SKUUNIQUE(sku)
        
        
        Items of an orderPK (order_id, variant_id) — leftmost prefix
        
        
        Reviews of a productreviews(product_id, created_at) + UNIQUE(user_id, product_id)
        
      
        
      
        Scale: catalog search goes to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch (full text, facets), not LIKE '%phone%'. Product pages are cached. Orders shard well by user_id (all of one user's orders on one shard). Old orders move to an archive table or a warehouse (Chapter 20). Variant attributes that differ per category go in a JSON column — see EAV vs JSON.
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🎟️ Design 2: Movie seat booking (BookMyShow)
        
  
        Requirements: cities → theatres → screens → seats (fixed layout). Movies play in shows (screen + start time). A user selects seats, they are held for ~10 minutes while the user pays, then confirmed. No seat can ever be sold twice for the same show.
        

  

  
        CREATE TABLE shows (
  id         BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  movie_id   BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  screen_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  starts_at  DATETIME NOT NULL,                       -- UTC
  UNIQUE KEY uq_screen_time (screen_id, starts_at),
  KEY idx_movie_time (movie_id, starts_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE show_seats (
  show_id         BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  seat_id         BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  price           DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  status          ENUM('AVAILABLE','HELD','BOOKED') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE',
  held_by         BIGINT UNSIGNED NULL,
  hold_expires_at DATETIME NULL,
  booking_id      BIGINT UNSIGNED NULL,
  version         INT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (show_id, seat_id),                     -- one row per seat per show
  KEY idx_expiry (status, hold_expires_at)            -- for the cleanup job
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  show_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  status      ENUM('PENDING','CONFIRMED','CANCELLED','EXPIRED') NOT NULL,
  amount      DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL,
  idem_key    CHAR(36) NOT NULL,
  created_at  DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  UNIQUE KEY uq_booking_idem (user_id, idem_key),
  KEY idx_user_time (user_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
        

  
        
    QTwo users click the same seat at the same second. Walk me through how you stop double booking.
    
        
      
        The seat for a show is one row: show_seats(show_id, seat_id). Holding it is a conditional atomic UPDATE — only flip it if it is free (or its old hold has expired):
        
      
        START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE show_seats
   SET status = 'HELD', held_by = 501,
       hold_expires_at = UTC_TIMESTAMP() + INTERVAL 10 MINUTE
 WHERE show_id = 9001
   AND seat_id IN (107, 108)
   AND (status = 'AVAILABLE'
        OR (status = 'HELD' AND hold_expires_at < UTC_TIMESTAMP()));
-- app: if affected rows <> 2 → ROLLBACK ("seat just got taken")
COMMIT;
        
      
        START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO bookings (user_id, show_id, status, amount, idem_key)
VALUES (501, 9001, 'CONFIRMED', 500.00, 'c1a6...');
UPDATE show_seats
   SET status = 'BOOKED', booking_id = LAST_INSERT_ID()
 WHERE show_id = 9001 AND seat_id IN (107, 108)
   AND status = 'HELD' AND held_by = 501
   AND hold_expires_at >= UTC_TIMESTAMP();
-- affected rows <> 2 → hold expired → ROLLBACK and refund
COMMIT;
        
      
        Why it works: the second user's UPDATE blocks on the row X-lock held by the first, then re-checks the WHERE on the committed row, sees HELD with a future expiry, and updates 0 rows. The primary key (show_id, seat_id) guarantees there is only one row to fight over.
        
      
        
        
        TimeT1 (user 501)T2 (user 777)
        
        
        t1UPDATE … seat 107 WHERE AVAILABLE → locks row
        
        
        t2UPDATE … seat 107 → waits for lock
        
        
        t3COMMIT (seat HELD)
        
        
        t4re-checks → 0 rows ✔ "seat taken"
        
      
        
      
        💡
        Alternative design: a booked-seats table with UNIQUE
        Instead of pre-created rows, insert into booked_seats(show_id, seat_id, booking_id) with UNIQUE(show_id, seat_id). The second INSERT fails with a duplicate-key error. Simple and bullet-proof, but holds with expiry need a separate table or a cleanup delete.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Lock ordering
        If user A holds seats 107→108 and user B holds 108→107 in the same transaction, they can deadlock. A single UPDATE … WHERE seat_id IN (…) walks the PK in order, which avoids most of this. InnoDB detects deadlocks and rolls one back — the app should retry or show "seat taken". See Chapter 13.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "I keep one row per seat per show, keyed by (show_id, seat_id). Holding is a single conditional UPDATE: set HELD with a 10-minute expiry only where the seat is AVAILABLE or its hold expired, and I check affected rows. The row lock serializes two users, so exactly one wins. On payment I flip HELD to BOOKED in the same transaction that writes the booking, and a background job — or the expiry check itself — frees stale holds."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Why not lock the seats with SELECT … FOR UPDATE and keep the transaction open while the user pays?
          
        A DB transaction must be short (milliseconds). Payment takes minutes. Holding a lock that long blocks other users, eats connections and grows undo history. Model the hold as data (status + expiry), not as a long-lived lock.
        
        
        ↪Who releases expired holds?
          
        Two layers: (1) the hold query itself treats an expired hold as free, so correctness never depends on cleanup; (2) a job runs UPDATE show_seats SET status='AVAILABLE', held_by=NULL WHERE status='HELD' AND hold_expires_at < UTC_TIMESTAMP() LIMIT 1000 so the seat map looks right. Index (status, hold_expires_at) makes it cheap.
        
        
        ↪Payment succeeded but the hold had already expired and someone else took the seat. Now what?
          
        The confirm UPDATE returns fewer rows, so the booking is rolled back and an automatic refund is triggered. Say it out loud: "external payments can't be in my DB transaction, so I design for this compensation path".
        
        
        ↪A blockbuster opens and 1 million users hit the seat map. How do you scale?
          
        Serve the seat map from a cache (Redis bitmap per show), refreshed on change. Use Redis SET key NX EX 600 as a fast pre-hold to shed load, but keep the DB row as the source of truth. Put users in a virtual waiting room. Shard by show_id — every seat of a show lives on one shard, so a booking never spans shards.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🏦 Design 3: Banking / wallet ledger (Paytm, UPI wallet)
        
  
        Requirements: accounts hold money; users transfer money; every rupee must be traceable forever; network retries must never move money twice; the balance must be correct even under heavy concurrency.
        

  
        
    
        ❌ Naive: balance column only
          
      
        • UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100
          • 
      
        • No history: "why is my balance ₹340?" can't be answered
          • 
      
        • A bug or bad UPDATE destroys information forever
          • 
      
        • Auditors and regulators will reject it
          • 
    
        
    
        ✔ Ledger: immutable double-entry
          
      
        • Every transfer = one transactions row + ≥2 ledger_entries
          • 
      
        • Debits and credits of a transaction sum to zero
          • 
      
        • Rows are INSERT-only; corrections are new reversing entries
          • 
      
        • Balance = SUM(entries), cached on the account for speed
          • 
    
        
  
        

  

  
        CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  currency    CHAR(3) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'INR',
  balance     BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,          -- cached; source of truth = ledger
  version     BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  CHECK (balance >= 0)                             -- no overdraft for wallets
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE transactions (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  idem_key    VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL,
  type        VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,               -- TRANSFER / TOPUP / REVERSAL
  status      VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,               -- POSTED / FAILED
  created_at  DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  UNIQUE KEY uq_txn_idem (idem_key)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE ledger_entries (
  id             BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  txn_id         BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  account_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  amount         BIGINT NOT NULL,                 -- +credit / -debit, in paise
  balance_after  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  created_at     DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  KEY idx_acct_time (account_id, id),             -- statement / passbook query
  FOREIGN KEY (txn_id) REFERENCES transactions(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (account_id) REFERENCES accounts(id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
-- App DB user gets INSERT, SELECT only on ledger_entries (no UPDATE/DELETE).
        

  
        START TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO transactions (idem_key, type, status)
VALUES ('req-7f3a', 'TRANSFER', 'POSTED');          -- duplicate key → already done, return old result
SET @t = LAST_INSERT_ID();

-- lock BOTH accounts in a fixed order (lower id first) → no deadlock
SELECT id, balance FROM accounts WHERE id IN (1, 2) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 10000 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 10000;
-- affected rows = 0 → insufficient funds → ROLLBACK
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 10000 WHERE id = 2;

INSERT INTO ledger_entries (txn_id, account_id, amount, balance_after)
SELECT @t, 1, -10000, balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;
INSERT INTO ledger_entries (txn_id, account_id, amount, balance_after)
SELECT @t, 2, +10000, balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 2;
COMMIT;
        

  
        
    QThe client times out and retries the transfer. How do you make sure money moves only once?
    
        
      
        Idempotency key. The client creates a unique key per intent (not per HTTP attempt) and sends it with every retry. The server inserts it into a table with a UNIQUE constraint inside the same transaction as the money movement.
        
      
          
        
        1. First attempt — INSERT key succeeds → transfer happens → COMMIT. The response is lost on the network.
          2. 
        
        2. Retry — INSERT key fails with duplicate-key error 1062 → the server looks up the stored result and returns it. No second transfer.
          3. 
        
        3. Two retries arrive at the same time — the second INSERT waits on the first one's lock on the unique index entry; when the first commits, it gets a duplicate error. Exactly-once effect.
          4. 
      
        
      
        🚫
        Failing answer
        "I'll check SELECT … WHERE idem_key = ? first and insert if not found." Two concurrent retries both see "not found". Only a UNIQUE constraint (or a lock) makes check-and-insert atomic.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "Money is stored as an immutable double-entry ledger: each transfer writes a transaction row and a debit and credit entry that sum to zero, and corrections are reversing entries, never updates. I cache the balance on the account and update it in the same transaction, locking both accounts in id order to avoid deadlocks. Retries carry an idempotency key with a UNIQUE constraint, so a duplicate request fails on insert and returns the original result."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪If the balance is cached, how do you know it is correct?
          
        A nightly reconciliation job checks accounts.balance = SUM(ledger_entries.amount) per account and that every transaction's entries sum to 0. Any mismatch raises an alert. The ledger wins; the cache is rebuilt from it.
        
        
        ↪The two accounts are on different shards. Now what?
          
        A single local transaction is no longer possible. Options: 2PC (blocking, rarely used across services), or a saga — debit A with a "pending outgoing" entry, credit B, then finalize; on failure, write a compensating credit back to A. An outbox table makes "DB write + event publish" atomic. Details in Chapter 19.
        
        
        ↪Why BIGINT paise instead of DECIMAL rupees?
          
        Both are exact. Integer minor units are fast, language-independent (no float parsing in JSON) and common in payment APIs. DECIMAL(19,4) is fine when you need fractional units (FX rates, interest). FLOAT/DOUBLE is never fine: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3.
        
        
        ↪The ledger_entries table grows to billions of rows. How do you show a balance fast?
          
        Read the cached accounts.balance or the latest balance_after (index (account_id, id), read 1 row descending). For history, page with keyset pagination (WHERE account_id=? AND id < ?). Partition by month and archive old partitions; keep periodic balance snapshots so recomputation starts from a checkpoint.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        📸 Design 4: Social feed (Twitter / Instagram)
        
  
        Requirements: users post, follow others, like and comment; the home feed shows recent posts from people I follow. Very read-heavy (people scroll far more than they post). Like counts can be a few seconds stale.
        

  

  
        CREATE TABLE follows (
  follower_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  followee_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  created_at   DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  PRIMARY KEY (follower_id, followee_id),        -- "whom do I follow?"
  KEY idx_followee (followee_id, follower_id),   -- "who follows me?"
  CHECK (follower_id <> followee_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE posts (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED PRIMARY KEY,       -- time-sortable (Snowflake-style) id
  author_id   BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  body        VARCHAR(2200) NOT NULL,
  media_url   VARCHAR(500),                      -- file lives in object storage (S3)
  like_count  INT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  created_at  DATETIME(6) NOT NULL,
  KEY idx_author_time (author_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE likes (
  post_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  user_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  created_at  DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  PRIMARY KEY (post_id, user_id),                -- one like per user per post
  KEY idx_user (user_id, created_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE feed_items (
  user_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,          -- the reader
  post_id     BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,          -- sortable id ⇒ newest = largest
  author_id   BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, post_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;
        

  
        
    QHow do you build the home feed? Fan-out on write or fan-out on read?
    
        
      
        
        
        Fan-out on READ (pull)
          
          
        • At read time: get followees, fetch their recent posts, merge, sort
          • 
          
        • SELECT p.* FROM posts p JOIN follows f ON p.author_id = f.followee_id WHERE f.follower_id = ? ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 20
          • 
          
        • Writes are cheap; reads are expensive (follow 1,000 people → 1,000 index ranges)
          • 
          
        • Good for: celebrities' posts, inactive users
          • 
        
        
        
        Fan-out on WRITE (push)
          
          
        • At post time: insert the post id into every follower's feed_items
          • 
          
        • Read = one PK range scan: WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY post_id DESC LIMIT 20
          • 
          
        • Reads are cheap; a post by someone with 50M followers = 50M writes
          • 
          
        • Good for: normal users (most have < 1,000 followers)
          • 
        
        
      
        
      
        Real answer: hybrid. Push for normal authors (async, via a queue). For celebrity authors (followers above a threshold) skip the push; at read time, merge the precomputed feed with a pull of the few celebrities the user follows. Feed inboxes usually live in Redis (capped list of the latest ~800 ids) or a wide-column store, not in MySQL.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "Feeds are read-heavy, so I precompute: when a normal user posts, a worker pushes the post id into each follower's feed list. That makes reading one range scan. The problem is celebrities — one post would mean millions of writes — so for them I switch to pull and merge their recent posts at read time. That hybrid is what large networks describe using."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪How do you store like counts without a hot row?
          
        Insert into likes (the truth, deduplicated by PK). The counter is derived: increment in Redis (INCR) and flush to posts.like_count in batches, or use sharded counter rows. Exact count is always recomputable from likes. See hot counters.
        
        
        ↪How do you paginate the feed?
          
        Keyset (cursor) pagination, not OFFSET: WHERE user_id = ? AND post_id < :last_seen ORDER BY post_id DESC LIMIT 20. OFFSET 10000 reads and throws away 10,000 rows, and new posts shift pages so users see duplicates.
        
        
        ↪What is the shard key?
          
        posts by author_id ("my profile" stays on one shard); feed_items by reader user_id; follows stored twice (by follower and by followee) so both directions are single-shard queries. See Chapter 19.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        💬 Design 5: Chat / messaging (WhatsApp, Slack)
        
  
        Requirements: 1:1 and group conversations, send messages, load history newest-first, unread counts, read receipts. Extremely write-heavy; history is append-only.
        

  

  
        CREATE TABLE conversations (
  id           BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  type         ENUM('DM','GROUP') NOT NULL,
  dm_key       VARCHAR(41) NULL,                 -- 'minId:maxId' for DMs only
  last_msg_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NULL,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_dm (dm_key)                      -- only ONE DM per pair (NULLs allowed for groups)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE participants (
  conversation_id   BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  user_id           BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  last_read_msg_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  joined_at         DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, user_id),
  KEY idx_user_conv (user_id, conversation_id)   -- "my chats"
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

CREATE TABLE messages (
  conversation_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  msg_id           BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,     -- per-conversation increasing / Snowflake
  sender_id        BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  client_msg_id    CHAR(36) NOT NULL,            -- dedupe resends from flaky mobile networks
  body             TEXT,
  created_at       DATETIME(6) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (conversation_id, msg_id),
  UNIQUE KEY uq_client (sender_id, client_msg_id)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Last 50 messages (cursor = smallest msg_id already shown)
SELECT * FROM messages
 WHERE conversation_id = 77 AND msg_id < 120345
 ORDER BY msg_id DESC LIMIT 50;

-- Unread count for me in conversation 77
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM messages m
  JOIN participants p ON p.conversation_id = m.conversation_id AND p.user_id = 501
 WHERE m.conversation_id = 77 AND m.msg_id > p.last_read_msg_id;
        

  
        
    QHow do you store read receipts without writing one row per message per reader?
    
        
      
        Store a watermark: participants.last_read_msg_id. Since messages in a conversation are ordered, "read up to 120345" means every earlier message is read too. One UPDATE per "user opened chat", not one row per message. For a group, "seen by" for message M = participants whose last_read_msg_id >= M.
        
      
        Per-message delivery state (sent ✓, delivered ✓✓) for 1:1 is often a small separate table or lives only in the device; at WhatsApp scale, the server keeps undelivered messages in a queue and deletes after delivery.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "Messages are clustered by (conversation_id, msg_id), so loading history is one range scan with a cursor. Read receipts are a watermark per participant — last_read_msg_id — so unread count is just messages above it. Mobile clients resend, so each message carries a client-generated id with a unique constraint to dedupe. At scale I'd shard by conversation_id and likely move messages to a wide-column store like Cassandra, which is built for this append-and-range-read pattern."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪How do you guarantee message order?
          
        Order within a conversation only (global order is unnecessary and expensive). Generate msg_id on the server: per-conversation sequence (e.g. UPDATE conversations SET seq = LAST_INSERT_ID(seq + 1)) or a time-ordered Snowflake id from the node owning that conversation. Never trust device clocks.
        
        
        ↪How do you list "my chats sorted by latest message"?
          
        Denormalize last_msg_id / last_msg_at onto conversations (or onto participants per user, to sort by an index on (user_id, last_msg_at)). Update it in the same transaction as the message insert. A very active group then becomes a hot row — batch that update.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🔗 Design 6: URL shortener (bit.ly)
        
  
        Requirements: long URL → short code (7 chars); redirect fast; optional custom alias and expiry; click analytics. Reads (redirects) outnumber writes 100:1 or more.
        

  
        CREATE TABLE urls (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  code        VARCHAR(16) CHARACTER SET ascii COLLATE ascii_bin NOT NULL,  -- case-sensitive!
  long_url    VARCHAR(2048) NOT NULL,
  url_hash    BINARY(32) NOT NULL,              -- SHA-256(long_url): dedupe without indexing 2 KB text
  owner_id    BIGINT UNSIGNED NULL,
  expires_at  DATETIME NULL,
  created_at  DATETIME(6) NOT NULL DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP(6),
  UNIQUE KEY uq_code (code),
  KEY idx_hash (url_hash)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- clicks: append-only, high volume → usually Kafka → ClickHouse/warehouse, not this OLTP DB
CREATE TABLE click_daily (
  url_id  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  day     DATE NOT NULL,
  clicks  BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  PRIMARY KEY (url_id, day)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

INSERT INTO click_daily (url_id, day, clicks) VALUES (42, '2026-10-17', 1)
  ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE clicks = clicks + 1;   -- upsert counter (better: batch from a stream)
        

  
        
    QHow do you generate the short code, and how do you avoid collisions?
    
        
      
        ApproachHowProsCons
        
        
        Base62(id)Insert row, take AUTO_INCREMENT id, encode in [0-9a-zA-Z]No collisions ever; 627 ≈ 3.5 trillion codesSequential = guessable; needs id service when sharded
        
        
        Hash + truncateFirst 7 chars of base62(MD5/SHA(url))Same URL → same codeCollisions possible → retry with salt; UNIQUE catches them
        
        
        Random + UNIQUERandom 7 chars; INSERT; on duplicate-key retryNot guessable, statelessRetries grow as space fills
        
        
        Pre-generated key poolOffline job fills unused codes; servers grab batchesFast, no collisions at write timeExtra service to run
        
      
        
      
        ⚠️
        Collation trap
        MySQL 8's default collation utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is case-insensitive, so aB3 and Ab3 would collide under the UNIQUE index. Base62 needs a binary/case-sensitive collation such as ascii_bin.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "The core table is tiny: code, long URL, owner, expiry, with a UNIQUE index on code using a case-sensitive collation. I'd generate codes by base62-encoding a unique 64-bit id, so there are no collisions, or random codes with retry if guessability matters. Redirects are 99% of traffic, so they hit a cache first. Click analytics are streamed out to an analytics store instead of updating a counter row per click."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪301 or 302 redirect?
          
        301 (permanent) lets browsers cache it — less load but you lose click counts. 302 (temporary) means every click reaches you — needed for analytics and expiry.
        
        
        ↪How would you scale it to billions of URLs?
          
        It's a key-value lookup, so shard by hash of code (or use DynamoDB/Cassandra). Cache hot codes in Redis/CDN. Id generation via Snowflake-style ids or ranges handed to each app server, so no single sequence is a bottleneck.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🗺️ More scenarios — the short versions
        
  
        For these, interviewers usually want the core tables plus one sharp idea. Learn the sharp idea.
        

  
        
    
        🚕
        Ride-sharing
        Sharp idea: trip state machine + live locations kept out of the main DB.
        
    
        🏨
        Hotel / flight booking
        Sharp idea: date-range overlap check, or one row per room-night.
        
    
        📚
        Library
        Sharp idea: book vs copy (title vs physical item).
        
    
        🏥
        Hospital appointments
        Sharp idea: slot table + UNIQUE stops double booking a doctor.
        
    
        🍔
        Food delivery
        Sharp idea: menu snapshot + order status history.
        
    
        🏆
        Leaderboard
        Sharp idea: RANK() for small, Redis sorted set for big.
        
  
        

  
        
    QDesign the database for ride-sharing (Uber / Ola).
    
        
      
        Tables: riders, drivers (vehicle, status ONLINE/OFFLINE/ON_TRIP), trips (rider_id, driver_id, pickup/drop lat-lng, status, fare, timestamps), trip_events (append-only status history), payments, ratings.
        
      
        CREATE TABLE trips (
  id          BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  rider_id    BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL,
  driver_id   BIGINT UNSIGNED NULL,
  status      ENUM('REQUESTED','ACCEPTED','ARRIVED','STARTED','COMPLETED','CANCELLED') NOT NULL,
  pickup      POINT NOT NULL SRID 4326,
  dropoff     POINT NOT NULL SRID 4326,
  fare_paise  BIGINT NULL,
  requested_at DATETIME(6) NOT NULL,
  KEY idx_rider_time (rider_id, requested_at),
  KEY idx_driver_time (driver_id, requested_at)
) ENGINE=InnoDB;

-- Driver accepts: only if still REQUESTED (two drivers tap "accept" together)
UPDATE trips SET driver_id = 88, status = 'ACCEPTED'
 WHERE id = 5001 AND status = 'REQUESTED';      -- affected rows 0 → someone else got it
        
      
          
        
        • State machine: every transition is a conditional UPDATE WHERE status = <expected> plus an insert into trip_events. Illegal jumps (COMPLETED → STARTED) are impossible.
          • 
        
        • Nearby drivers: driver GPS updates every few seconds — far too many writes for an OLTP row. Keep live locations in Redis GEO (or an in-memory index by geohash / H3 cell); query "drivers within 2 km". Store only trip route summaries durably.
          • 
        
        • One driver, one trip: UPDATE drivers SET status='ON_TRIP' WHERE id=? AND status='ONLINE' in the same transaction as accepting.
          • 
      
        
      
        🔀
        Geo support
        MySQL 8 has SRID-aware spatial types and SPATIAL indexes (R-tree) with ST_Distance_Sphere. PostgreSQL + PostGIS is the stronger choice for heavy geo (GiST indexes, ST_DWithin). Redis GEOSEARCH is the common choice for live positions.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHotel booking: how do you check if a room is free for 10–13 Oct and stop overlapping bookings?
    
        
      
        Two date ranges [a_in, a_out) and [b_in, b_out) overlap when a_in < b_out AND b_in < a_out. Use half-open ranges: check-out day is free for the next guest.
        
      
        START TRANSACTION;
SELECT id FROM rooms WHERE id = 12 FOR UPDATE;        -- serialize bookings for this room
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM reservations
 WHERE room_id = 12 AND status = 'CONFIRMED'
   AND check_in < '2026-10-13' AND '2026-10-10' < check_out;
-- 0 → INSERT INTO reservations (room_id, check_in, check_out, ...) ; else ROLLBACK
COMMIT;
        
      
        Why lock the room row? Without it, two transactions both count 0 overlaps (the new rows don't exist yet — a phantom/write-skew problem, see Chapter 13) and both insert.
        
      
        Alternative (inventory per night): table room_nights(room_id, night, reservation_id) with PRIMARY KEY(room_id, night). Booking 3 nights inserts 3 rows; an overlap is a duplicate-key error. For hotels that sell "room types" not specific rooms, keep room_type_inventory(hotel_id, room_type, night, total, booked) and use the atomic UPDATE … SET booked = booked + 1 WHERE booked < total for each night.
        
      
        🔀
        PostgreSQL does it declaratively
        An exclusion constraint: EXCLUDE USING gist (room_id WITH =, daterange(check_in, check_out) WITH &&) (needs the btree_gist extension) rejects overlapping rows at the database level. PostgreSQL 18 also adds WITHOUT OVERLAPS for temporal primary/unique keys. MySQL has no equivalent — use locking or per-night rows.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDesign a library management system.
    
        
      
        The classic beginner trap is one books table. A library owns several copies of the same title. Separate them.
        
      
        CREATE TABLE books  (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, isbn CHAR(13) UNIQUE, title VARCHAR(300) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE authors(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE book_authors (book_id BIGINT, author_id BIGINT, PRIMARY KEY (book_id, author_id));  -- M:N
CREATE TABLE copies (id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, book_id BIGINT NOT NULL, barcode VARCHAR(32) UNIQUE,
                     status ENUM('AVAILABLE','LOANED','LOST') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'AVAILABLE');
CREATE TABLE members(id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), max_loans TINYINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 3);
CREATE TABLE loans (
  id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  copy_id BIGINT NOT NULL, member_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  issued_at DATE NOT NULL, due_at DATE NOT NULL, returned_at DATE NULL,
  open_copy BIGINT AS (IF(returned_at IS NULL, copy_id, NULL)) STORED,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_one_open_loan (open_copy),            -- a copy can't be loaned twice at once
  KEY idx_member_open (member_id, returned_at)
);
-- Overdue list
SELECT m.name, b.title, l.due_at FROM loans l
  JOIN copies c ON c.id = l.copy_id JOIN books b ON b.id = c.book_id
  JOIN members m ON m.id = l.member_id
 WHERE l.returned_at IS NULL AND l.due_at < CURRENT_DATE;
        
      
        The generated column trick: open_copy is the copy id only while the loan is open, NULL after return. UNIQUE allows many NULLs, so history is kept but only one open loan per copy is possible. Fines and reservations (holds queue) are extra tables.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHospital / clinic: how do you stop two patients booking the same doctor slot?
    
        
      
        Tables: patients, doctors, departments, doctor_schedules (weekly template), appointments, prescriptions + prescription_items, medical_records.
        
      
        CREATE TABLE appointments (
  id          BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  doctor_id   BIGINT NOT NULL,
  patient_id  BIGINT NOT NULL,
  slot_start  DATETIME NOT NULL,                 -- fixed 15-min slots, UTC
  status      ENUM('BOOKED','CANCELLED','DONE','NO_SHOW') NOT NULL,
  active_slot DATETIME AS (IF(status = 'BOOKED', slot_start, NULL)) STORED,
  UNIQUE KEY uq_doctor_slot (doctor_id, active_slot),   -- cancelled rows don't block re-booking
  KEY idx_patient (patient_id, slot_start)
);
        
      
        With fixed slots, double booking is a duplicate-key error. With variable-length appointments, fall back to the hotel overlap check with a lock on the doctor row. Medical records are sensitive: audit every read, encrypt at rest, restrict by role (Chapter 18), and never hard-delete.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDesign food delivery (Swiggy / Zomato).
    
        
      
        Three sides: customers, restaurants, delivery partners. Tables: restaurants, menu_items (price, is_available), orders (customer, restaurant, partner, status, totals), order_items (name and price snapshot), order_status_history, delivery_partners, payments, ratings.
        
      
          
        
        • Snapshot again: restaurants change menus hourly; the order keeps item_name and unit_price as they were.
          • 
        
        • Status history: order_status_history(order_id, status, at) powers "ordered 7:02, picked up 7:21" and SLA analytics. The current status is also cached on orders.
          • 
        
        • Partner assignment: conditional UPDATE so one order gets exactly one partner and one partner holds a limited number of orders.
          • 
        
        • Discovery ("restaurants near me that are open") uses a geo index + search engine, not the OLTP DB.
          • 
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDesign a game leaderboard. How do you get a player's rank?
    
        
      
        CREATE TABLE scores (
  game_id   INT NOT NULL,
  player_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  score     INT NOT NULL,
  updated_at DATETIME(6) NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (game_id, player_id),
  KEY idx_game_score (game_id, score DESC)
);
-- Top 10
SELECT player_id, score, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rnk
  FROM scores WHERE game_id = 1 ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 10;
-- One player's rank without ranking everyone
SELECT 1 + COUNT(*) AS my_rank FROM scores
 WHERE game_id = 1 AND score > (SELECT score FROM scores WHERE game_id = 1 AND player_id = 501);
        
      
        "My rank" counts everyone above me — O(N) in the index range. At millions of players with constant updates, use a Redis sorted set: ZADD to update, ZREVRANK for rank and ZREVRANGE 0 9 for top-10, all O(log N). The DB keeps the durable score history; Redis serves ranks. Daily/weekly boards = one sorted set per period with a TTL. (Window functions: Chapter 9.)
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🧩 Modeling patterns & anti-patterns
        
  
        After the main design, interviewers drill into one detail: "How would you store categories?", "What if users delete things?", "Why not UUIDs?". These are the answers.
        

  
        Trees & hierarchies (categories, comments, org chart)
        
  
        
    QHow do you store a category tree (Electronics → Phones → Android) in a relational DB?
    
        
      
        ModelStoresGet subtreeMove a nodeUse when
        
        
        Adjacency listparent_idRecursive CTE✔ 1 UPDATEDefault choice (MySQL 8+, PG)
        
        
        Materialized pathpath = '/1/4/9/'LIKE '/1/4/%' (index prefix)~ rewrite subtree pathsRead-heavy, breadcrumbs
        
        
        Nested setlft, rgtBETWEEN lft AND rgt✘ renumber half the treeStatic trees only
        
        
        Closure tableAll (ancestor, descendant, depth) pairsOne join~ delete + insert pairsDeep trees, fast ancestor/descendant queries
        
      
        
      
      
        CREATE TABLE categories (
  id        INT PRIMARY KEY,
  parent_id INT NULL,
  name      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL,
  KEY idx_parent (parent_id),
  FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES categories(id)
);
WITH RECURSIVE sub AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS depth FROM categories WHERE id = 1
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.name, s.depth + 1 FROM categories c JOIN sub s ON c.parent_id = s.id
)
SELECT * FROM sub;
        
      
        +----+-------------+-------+
| id | name        | depth |
+----+-------------+-------+
|  1 | Electronics |     0 |
|  4 | Phones      |     1 |
|  5 | Laptops     |     1 |
|  9 | Android     |     2 |
+----+-------------+-------+
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "I'd start with an adjacency list — a parent_id foreign key — and use a recursive CTE for subtrees, which MySQL supports from 8.0. If the tree is deep and read-heavy, I'd add a closure table with every ancestor-descendant pair, so subtree and breadcrumb queries are one indexed join. Nested sets read fast but every insert renumbers the tree, so I avoid them for data that changes."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪What stops a cycle (A is parent of B, B is parent of A)?
          
        A FK can't. Check in the app before moving a node ("is the new parent inside my subtree?"), and guard recursive CTEs with a depth limit (MySQL also stops at cte_max_recursion_depth, default 1000).
        
        
        ↪How do you model threaded comments (Reddit)?
          
        comments(id, post_id, parent_id, path, …). Fetch all comments of a post with WHERE post_id = ? (one index range) and build the tree in the app. A materialized path ordered by path gives display order directly.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Polymorphic associations
        
  
        
    QComments can belong to a post, a photo or a video. How do you model that?
    
        
      
        
        
        ❌ commentable_type + commentable_id
          
          
        • Rails/Laravel style: ('PHOTO', 42)
          • 
          
        • No real FK possible — id 42 may point at nothing
          • 
          
        • Every join needs a CASE on the type
          • 
        
        
        
        ✔ Exclusive FKs + CHECK
          
          
        • post_id NULL, photo_id NULL, video_id NULL, each a real FK
          • 
          
        • CHECK ((post_id IS NOT NULL) + (photo_id IS NOT NULL) + (video_id IS NOT NULL) = 1)
          • 
          
        • Integrity enforced; fine for a few parent types
          • 
        
        
        
        ✔ Common supertype
          
          
        • commentable(id); posts, photos, videos each have a 1:1 FK to it
          • 
          
        • comments.commentable_id → real FK
          • 
          
        • Scales to many types; one extra table
          • 
        
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "The type-plus-id pattern is easy but the database can't enforce the foreign key, so orphans creep in. With a few parent types I'd use one nullable FK column per type and a CHECK that exactly one is set. With many types I'd add a shared supertype table that every commentable entity references, so comments get a real foreign key."
        
    
        
  
        

  
        EAV vs JSON (variable attributes)
        
  
        
    QPhones have RAM and screen size, shirts have size and fabric. How do you store product attributes?
    
        
      
        EAV (Entity–Attribute–Value) = a table (product_id, attr_name, value). Infinitely flexible, but: every value is a string (no types), no NOT NULL/CHECK per attribute, and "phones with 8 GB RAM and 6.5-inch screen" needs one self-join per attribute. It is a well-known anti-pattern for general use.
        
      
        ALTER TABLE product_variants
  ADD COLUMN ram_gb INT AS (CAST(attrs->>'$.ram_gb' AS UNSIGNED)) VIRTUAL,
  ADD INDEX idx_ram (ram_gb);

SELECT id, sku FROM product_variants
 WHERE ram_gb = 8 AND attrs->>'$.color' = 'black';
-- MySQL 8.0.13+ also allows functional indexes; 8.0.17+ multi-valued indexes on JSON arrays
        
      
        OptionIntegrityQueryPick when
        
        
        Real columns✔ full✔ easyAttributes known, few, shared
        
        
        JSON + generated columns~ JSON schema / app✔ index hot keysVaries per category (most catalogs)
        
        
        EAV✘✘ self-joinsUsers define attributes at runtime, rarely filtered
        
        
        Table per type✔~ union across typesFew, stable subtypes
        
      
        
      
        🔀
        PostgreSQL
        JSONB with a GIN index answers containment queries (attrs @> '{"color":"black"}') without declaring each key. MySQL needs a generated column or functional index per key you filter on.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Soft delete
        
  
        
    QYou use deleted_at for soft delete. A user deletes their account and signs up again with the same email — the UNIQUE index blocks it. Fix?
    
        
      
        Soft delete = mark the row (deleted_at = NOW()) instead of deleting it, so you can restore, audit, and keep FKs valid. The catch: UNIQUE(email) still sees the dead row.
        
      
        ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN deleted_at DATETIME(6) NULL,
  ADD COLUMN live_email VARCHAR(255) AS (IF(deleted_at IS NULL, email, NULL)) STORED,
  DROP INDEX uq_users_email,
  ADD UNIQUE KEY uq_live_email (live_email);   -- many NULLs allowed → deleted rows don't clash
        
      
        🔀
        Partial index
        PostgreSQL: CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON users(email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL; SQL Server: filtered index with WHERE deleted_at IS NULL. MySQL has no partial indexes, hence the generated-column trick.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Other soft-delete costs
        Every query must remember WHERE deleted_at IS NULL (use a view); tables keep growing; FKs with ON DELETE CASCADE no longer fire; and privacy laws (GDPR / India's DPDP Act) may require real erasure of personal data. Alternative: hard delete + copy the row into an archive table.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Audit trails & history
        
  
        
    Q"We need to know who changed an order's status and when." How do you design it?
    
        
      
          
        
        • History table written by the app (order_status_history(order_id, old, new, changed_by, changed_at)) in the same transaction — knows the actor, explicit.
          • 
        
        • Trigger AFTER UPDATE copying OLD into orders_history — catches every SQL path, but adds write latency, can't see the app user unless passed in a session variable, and cascaded FK actions don't fire triggers in MySQL.
          • 
        
        • CDC (Debezium reading the binlog) → Kafka → audit store. Zero app changes, async.
          • 
        
        • Temporal tables: SQL Server and MariaDB have system-versioned tables (FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF); MySQL does not — emulate with valid_from/valid_to columns.
          • 
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Multi-tenancy (SaaS)
        
  
        
    QYou're building a SaaS used by 5,000 companies. One database per tenant, schema per tenant, or a shared table with tenant_id?
    
        
      
        ModelIsolationCost / opsBest for
        
        
        DB per tenantStrongest; easy per-tenant backup/restoreHigh: 5,000 DBs to migrateFew, large, regulated customers
        
        
        Schema per tenantGoodMedium; catalog bloat at thousandsHundreds of tenants
        
        
        Shared tables + tenant_idWeakest — one missing WHERE leaks dataLowest; one migrationMany small tenants (most SaaS)
        
      
        
      
        For shared tables: put tenant_id first in every PK and index (PRIMARY KEY (tenant_id, id)), include it in FKs, enforce it in a data-access layer, and shard by it later. PostgreSQL Row-Level Security can enforce it inside the DB. A common hybrid: shared tables for the long tail, dedicated DBs for enterprise customers.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Money, time zones, ENUMs, NULLs
        
  
        
    QQuick-fire: which type for money, timestamps, and status values?
    
        
      
        
        
        Money
        DECIMAL(19,4) (exact) or BIGINT minor units (paise/cents) + a currency CHAR(3) column. Never FLOAT/DOUBLE — binary floating point can't represent 0.1 exactly.
        
        
        Instants (when something happened)
        Store UTC. DATETIME(6) filled with UTC by the app, or TIMESTAMP with the session time_zone='+00:00'. MySQL TIMESTAMP converts using the session time zone and ends at 2038-01-19 03:14:07 UTC — avoid for far-future dates. Convert to local time only for display.
        
        
        Future local events
        A 9 AM clinic appointment next year: store local time + IANA zone ('Asia/Kolkata'), because DST rules can change before the date.
        
        
        Status
        ENUM is compact and fast, but adding a value in the middle rebuilds the table and reordering is painful. A lookup table (order_statuses) + FK is flexible and can carry labels; VARCHAR + CHECK is the portable middle ground.
        
        
        NULL vs sentinel
        Use NULL for "unknown / not applicable", not 0, '' or '1970-01-01'. Sentinels silently pollute AVG, MIN and joins.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        IDs: AUTO_INCREMENT vs UUID vs Snowflake
        
  
        
    QShould the primary key be AUTO_INCREMENT or UUID?
    
        
      
        In InnoDB the PK is the clustered index (Chapter 15): rows are stored in PK order, and every secondary index stores the PK.
        
      
        IDSizeInsert patternGenerate without DB?Leaks info?
        
        
        BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT8 B✔ append at the end✘Count & growth rate guessable
        
        
        UUIDv4 (random)16 B (BINARY) / 36 B (CHAR)✘ random → page splits, half-full pages, cache misses✔No
        
        
        UUIDv7 (RFC 9562)16 B✔ time-ordered prefix✔Creation time
        
        
        Snowflake (64-bit: time + machine + seq)8 B✔ mostly ordered✔ needs worker idsCreation time
        
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "InnoDB clusters rows by primary key, so random UUIDv4 keys insert all over the B+ tree, causing page splits and a bigger, colder index — and every secondary index carries that 16-byte key. I'd use a BIGINT auto-increment PK internally and expose a separate random or UUIDv7 public_id with a unique index, so URLs aren't enumerable. If IDs must be generated across shards, I'd use time-ordered ids like Snowflake or UUIDv7."
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Natural key (email, PAN, ISBN) or surrogate key?
          
        Surrogate as PK, natural key as UNIQUE. Natural keys change (emails do), may be long, and are sometimes sensitive (PAN, Aadhaar) — you don't want them copied into every FK and index. Exception: junction tables use the composite natural key (a_id, b_id).
        
        
        ↪INT or BIGINT?
          
        Signed INT tops out at 2,147,483,647. Fast-growing tables (events, messages, likes) hit that, and changing a PK type on a huge table is a painful migration. Default to BIGINT.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Hot counters
        
  
        
    QA viral post gets 50,000 likes per minute. UPDATE posts SET like_count = like_count + 1 is timing out. Why, and what do you do?
    
        
      
        Every increment needs the exclusive lock on one row. Transactions line up behind each other — throughput is limited by lock hold time, no matter how many cores you have.
        
      
          
        
        1. Sharded counter rows — post_counters(post_id, slot 0..15, cnt); increment a random slot; read = SUM(cnt). Contention drops ~16×.
          2. 
        
        2. Buffer and batch — INCR in Redis, flush every few seconds with one UPDATE + n.
          3. 
        
        3. Event log + aggregate — append like events (Kafka), a consumer aggregates. The likes table stays the truth for "did I like this?".
          4. 
      
        
      
        Trade-off: the displayed count is a few seconds stale — fine for likes, not for bank balances.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        Zero-downtime schema changes
        
  
        
    QYou need to rename a column on a 500 GB table that serves live traffic. How?
    
        
      
        Never rename in place — old app servers still running during a deploy would break. Use expand → migrate → contract:
        
      
        
        
        1. ExpandADD new column (nullable)
        
        
        
        
        2. Dual-writeapp writes old + new
        
        
        
        
        3. Backfillcopy in chunks, throttle on replica lag
        
        
        
        
        4. Switch readsread new column
        
        
        
        
        5. Contractstop writing old, then DROP
        
      
        
      
        -- Adding/dropping a column is INSTANT in MySQL 8.0+ (metadata-only; default algorithm in 8.4)
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN delivery_note VARCHAR(500) NULL, ALGORITHM=INSTANT;
-- Adding an index: online, concurrent DML allowed
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_status_time (status, created_at), ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;
-- Backfill in small chunks
UPDATE orders SET new_col = old_col WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 10000 AND new_col IS NULL;
        
      
        For changes that would copy the whole table (changing a column type, PK changes), use gh-ost (triggerless, reads the binlog) or pt-online-schema-change (trigger-based): they build a shadow table, copy rows in chunks, replay ongoing changes, then swap tables with a short atomic rename. Before dropping an index, make it INVISIBLE first so you can undo instantly.
        
      
        ⚠️
        The metadata lock trap
        Even an INSTANT ALTER needs a brief exclusive metadata lock. If a long-running transaction holds the table, the ALTER waits — and every new query queues behind the ALTER. Set a short lock_wait_timeout and kill or wait out long transactions first.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        "I'd do expand-and-contract: add the new column, which is instant in MySQL 8, have the app write both, backfill in throttled chunks, switch reads, and only after everything is on the new column drop the old one. Each step is backward compatible, so I can roll back the app at any point. For a change that rebuilds the table, I'd use gh-ost, and I'd set a low lock_wait_timeout so a metadata lock can't freeze traffic."
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhere do images/videos go, and what do you do with 5 years of old orders?
    
        
      
          
        
        • Blobs: files go to object storage (S3/GCS) behind a CDN; the DB stores the key/URL, size, content type and checksum. Large BLOBs bloat the buffer pool, backups and replication.
          • 
        
        • Archiving: partition big append-only tables by month (PARTITION BY RANGE) so old data is dropped or moved with a cheap partition operation instead of a massive DELETE. Or move cold rows to an archive table / warehouse in small batches.
          • 
        
        • Rate limiter in SQL? Possible (INSERT … ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE hits = hits + 1 per user per minute window) but a hot path — Redis INCR + EXPIRE is the usual answer.
          • 
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
  
        🚩 Red flags that sink design rounds
        
  
        🚩 Red flag✔ Say this instead
        
    
        Drawing tables before asking a single question"Let me confirm scope, scale and consistency needs first."
        
    
        Comma-separated ids in a column (tags = '1,4,9')"That's a many-to-many — I'll use a junction table post_tags(post_id, tag_id)."
        
    
        FLOAT for money"DECIMAL or integer paise — money must be exact."
        
    
        Read-then-write stock/seat checks"Atomic conditional UPDATE, or a UNIQUE constraint, decides the winner."
        
    
        Order joins live product price"Orders snapshot price and address at purchase time."
        
    
        UPDATE/DELETE on financial history"Ledger is append-only; corrections are reversing entries."
        
    
        Holding DB locks while the user pays"Holds are data with an expiry, not long transactions."
        
    
        "Add an index on every column""One composite index per top query; each index slows writes."
        
    
        "We'll use NoSQL because it scales""Relational fits here; I'd move only the feed/chat/hot-counter piece to a specialised store."
        
    
        Random UUIDv4 as InnoDB PK without comment"BIGINT PK internally, UUID as public id."
        
    
        No mention of retries / double-clicks"Idempotency key with a UNIQUE constraint."
        
  
        

  
        S-L-U-I-C-E
        Snapshot history · Ledger, never overwrite money · UNIQUE decides races · Idempotency keys for retries · Conditional atomic UPDATE · Expand–contract migrations. The six moves that turn an average design answer into a strong one.
        

  
        🗣️ Say it like this — closing any design question
        "To summarise: the core tables are normalized with real foreign keys and unique constraints for the business rules. The top queries each have a matching composite index. The race on X is handled by an atomic conditional update, and retries are safe because of an idempotency key. If we grow 100×, I'd add read replicas and caching first, then shard by Y because most queries are scoped to Y, and move Z to a specialised store."
        

  
        ✏️ Cross-links: isolation & locks → Ch 13, index design → Ch 15, sharding & sagas → Ch 19.
        

  
        📌 Key takeaways
          
    
        • Use the 8-step framework every time: clarify → entities → relationships → tables/keys → access patterns → indexes → concurrency → scale.
          • 
    
        • Snapshot what must not change (order price, shipping address, menu item name).
          • 
    
        • Money: exact types, double-entry immutable ledger, idempotency keys, lock accounts in a fixed order.
          • 
    
        • Races are solved by the database: conditional atomic UPDATE + affected-rows check, UNIQUE constraints, or FOR UPDATE — never by "check in app, then write".
          • 
    
        • Seat/room holds are rows with an expiry, not long transactions; overlap = a_in < b_out AND b_in < a_out.
          • 
    
        • Feeds: hybrid fan-out; chat: cluster by (conversation, msg_id) + read watermark; counters: shard or batch.
          • 
    
        • BIGINT PK + public UUID; UTC timestamps; adjacency list + recursive CTE for trees; JSON + generated columns over EAV.
          • 
    
        • Schema changes on live tables: expand–contract, INSTANT/INPLACE DDL, gh-ost for table rebuilds.
          • 
  
        

  
        📚 Go deeper
          
    
        • Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) — the Twitter fan-out story, data models, and why derived data exists.
          • 
    
        • SQL Antipatterns (Bill Karwin) — EAV, polymorphic associations, jaywalking (comma lists), naive trees — the source of most "red flag" questions.
          • 
    
        • MySQL 8.4 Manual: Online DDL Operations — exactly which ALTERs are INSTANT, INPLACE or COPY.
          • 
    
        • gh-ost (GitHub) — how triggerless online schema migration works in production.
          • 
    
        • Stripe: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency — the idempotency-key pattern explained by a payments company.
          • 
  
        

  
        
    
        
      
        Two buyers race for the last unit. Which approach reliably prevents overselling in MySQL InnoDB?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        The conditional UPDATE is a locking current read: the second transaction waits for the row lock, re-evaluates qty >= 1 on the committed value and updates 0 rows. A plain SELECT under RR reads a snapshot, so both buyers can see qty = 1.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Why does order_items store unit_price?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        It's a different fact — the agreed price frozen at order time. Invoices, refunds and tax reports must not change when the catalog price changes.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        Booking A is [10 Oct, 13 Oct) and booking B is [13 Oct, 15 Oct) for the same room. With the condition a_in < b_out AND b_in < a_out, do they overlap?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        With half-open ranges, b_in (13) < a_out (13) is false, so no overlap. This is why hotels use [check_in, check_out).
        
    
        
    
        
      
        What is the main problem with random UUIDv4 primary keys in InnoDB?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Rows are stored in PK order, so random keys insert everywhere. Time-ordered UUIDv7/Snowflake ids or a BIGINT PK + separate public UUID avoid this.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        A celebrity with 50M followers posts. In a hybrid feed design, what happens?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        Fan-out-on-write is used for normal authors; celebrities are handled with fan-out-on-read to avoid millions of writes per post.
        
    
        
    
        
      
        With soft delete via deleted_at, how do you keep emails unique only among live users in MySQL?
        
      
      
      
      
      
        MySQL has no partial indexes (that's PostgreSQL / SQL Server syntax). UNIQUE(email, deleted_at) fails the other way: two live rows both have deleted_at NULL, and NULLs never conflict, so duplicates slip in. The generated column is NULL for deleted rows, and UNIQUE allows many NULLs.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    
        The 8 steps of a schema-design answer?
        Clarify → entities → relationships → tables + keys → access patterns → indexes → concurrency → scale/evolution.
        
    
        How does BookMyShow-style booking stop double booking?
        One row per (show_id, seat_id); hold = conditional UPDATE to HELD with expiry where AVAILABLE or expired; check affected rows; confirm HELD→BOOKED with the booking insert.
        
    
        Double-entry ledger rule?
        Every transaction writes ≥2 entries whose amounts sum to zero; entries are insert-only; corrections are reversing entries.
        
    
        What makes an idempotency key actually work?
        A UNIQUE constraint on it, inserted in the same transaction as the side effect. A SELECT-then-INSERT check races.
        
    
        Date-range overlap condition?
        a_start < b_end AND b_start < a_end (half-open ranges).
        
    
        Fan-out on write vs read?
        Write: push post id to followers' feeds (cheap reads, expensive for celebrities). Read: merge followees' posts at read time. Hybrid uses both.
        
    
        Four ways to store a tree?
        Adjacency list (parent_id + recursive CTE), materialized path, nested set, closure table.
        
    
        Why is EAV an anti-pattern?
        No types or constraints per attribute, one self-join per filtered attribute. Prefer JSON + indexed generated columns.
        
    
        Fix for a hot like-counter row?
        Sharded counter rows (SUM on read), or Redis INCR flushed in batches; keep the likes table as truth.
        
    
        Expand–contract migration steps?
        Add new column → dual-write → backfill in chunks → switch reads → stop old writes → drop old column.
        
  
        

        


        
  
        
    
        Chapter 22 · VIII · Interview Arsenal
        
    
        ⚡ Rapid-Fire, Tricky Questions & Common Mistakes
        
    
        Answer 160+ rapid-fire questions in one or two lines, see through the classic gotchas, avoid the answers that fail interviews, and keep a one-page cheat sheet in your head.
        
    
        ⏱ 60 min🔥 Asked a lotMySQL 8PostgreSQLOracleSQL ServerNoSQL
        
  
        

  
         
        ⚡ TL;DR — 60-second revision
        
    
          
      
        • Most traps are engine behaviour stated as universal: TRUNCATE rollback, NULLs in UNIQUE, "PK = clustered index", default isolation level.
          • 
      
        • The rest come from three-valued logic (NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, NOT IN + NULL = zero rows) and evaluation order (no aliases or aggregates in WHERE).
          • 
      
        • And from over-generalised theory: "indexes always help", "SERIALIZABLE = one at a time", "MVCC = no locks", "CAP = pick 2 of 3", "denormalization is bad".
          • 
      
        • Winning pattern: "It depends on the engine — in MySQL X, in PostgreSQL Y, the standard says Z."
          • 
      
        • Rapid-fire rounds sample 1–2 questions per subject. Crisp beats long: one definition + one example, then stop and let them drill.
          • 
      
        • Defaults to know cold: InnoDB = REPEATABLE READ; PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server = READ COMMITTED.
          • 
      
        • Ranking: ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3,4 · RANK 1,2,2,4 · DENSE_RANK 1,2,2,3.
          • 
      
        • Deadlock error codes: MySQL 1213, PostgreSQL 40P01; PG serialization failure 40001 → retry.
          •

        🎯
        What a rapid-fire round is really testing
        Fresher rounds are "broad and fast": one or two questions per subject, usually a definition plus a small task (normalize a table, explain a join). The interviewer checks precision (partial vs transitive dependency, not "less redundancy") and whether you can give one real example. Then they push one level deeper. That deeper step is where most people fall.
        
  
        Frequency chips: 🔥 hot = shows up in almost every DBMS segment (normalization, SQL queries, ACID, joins, keys). common = frequent or role-dependent. rare = GATE-style or senior/DBA. They are judged from about 25 interview reports and 7 popular question lists, so treat them as direction, not statistics. Use the shell's 🔥 Hot questions only filter for a 15-minute pass.
        

  
        ⚡ Rapid-fire bank (166 questions)
        
  
        Grouped by topic. Each answer is 1–4 lines — exactly how long your spoken answer should be. Say it, then stop talking ← and let them ask the follow-up.
        
  
        🗄️ Basics & architecture
        
  
        QWhat is a DBMS, and why not just use files?
        A DBMS is software that defines, stores, queries and protects shared data. Plain files give you bytes only.
        A DBMS adds a query language, integrity constraints, concurrency control (many users at once), crash recovery, security and less redundancy. With files, every app must rebuild all of that itself.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 01 · DBMS Essentials
        
  
        QDBMS vs RDBMS?
        DBMS is the general category (hierarchical, network, document, key-value...). An RDBMS stores data as relations (tables), enforces keys and referential integrity, and uses SQL. Examples: MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 01 · DBMS Essentials
        
  
        QDatabase vs DBMS?
        The database is the organised data itself (your shop's orders). The DBMS is the software that manages it (MySQL). One DBMS server can host many databases.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 01 · DBMS Essentials
        
  
        QSchema vs instance?
        Schema = the structure (table names, columns, types, constraints). It rarely changes. Instance = the data stored at one moment. It changes with every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 02 · Architecture & Schemas
        
  
        QWhat is the three-schema (ANSI/SPARC) architecture?
        External level (user views), conceptual level (logical schema of the whole DB), internal level (physical storage, files, indexes). Mappings between levels give data independence.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 02 · Architecture & Schemas
        
  
        QPhysical vs logical data independence — which is harder?
        Physical: change storage or indexes without changing the logical schema. Logical: change the logical schema (add a column/table) without breaking views or apps. Logical is harder, because apps depend directly on the logical structure.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 02 · Architecture & Schemas
        
  
        QWhat is the data dictionary (system catalog)?
        Metadata the DBMS keeps about itself: tables, columns, types, constraints, indexes, users, privileges. MySQL exposes it as information_schema; PostgreSQL as pg_catalog (plus information_schema).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 02 · Architecture & Schemas
        
  
        Q2-tier vs 3-tier architecture?
        2-tier: the client talks to the DB directly. 3-tier: client → application server → DB. 3-tier is safer (DB not exposed), scales better and reuses business logic. Web apps are 3-tier.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 02 · Architecture & Schemas
        
  
        QRelation, tuple, attribute, domain, degree, cardinality?
        Table, row, column, set of allowed values for a column, number of columns, number of rows.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QWhat is NULL?
        A marker for missing, unknown or not-applicable data. It is not 0 and not ''. Any comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN, so use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QName the main data models.
        Hierarchical (tree, IMS), network (graph of records, CODASYL), relational (tables, Codd 1970), object/object-relational, and NoSQL models: document, key-value, wide-column, graph.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 01 · DBMS Essentials
        
  
        🔑 Keys, constraints & relational algebra
        
  
        QSuper key vs candidate key vs primary key?
        Super key: any set of columns that uniquely identifies a row. Candidate key: a minimal super key (drop any column and it is no longer unique). Primary key: the one candidate key you pick as the row identity.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QWhat is an alternate key?
        A candidate key that was not chosen as the PK. Declare it UNIQUE NOT NULL, e.g. email when user_id is the PK.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QWhat is a foreign key?
        Column(s) whose values must match a PK or UNIQUE key in the referenced table (maybe the same table), or be NULL. It enforces referential integrity.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QPrimary key vs UNIQUE key?
        PK: one per table, never NULL, the row identity (and the clustered index in InnoDB). UNIQUE: many per table, NULLs allowed. NULL count is engine-specific: many in MySQL/PostgreSQL/Oracle, one in SQL Server.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QWhat is a composite key?
        A key made of two or more columns, e.g. (order_id, line_no) or a junction table's (student_id, course_id).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QSurrogate vs natural key?
        Surrogate: system-made (AUTO_INCREMENT, UUID); stable and compact. Natural: a business value (email, PAN); meaningful but can change. Common practice: surrogate PK + UNIQUE on the natural key.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints · Ch 21 · Schema Design
        
  
        QTypes of integrity constraints?
        NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, DEFAULT. Plus the two rules: entity integrity (PK unique and not NULL) and referential integrity (every non-NULL FK value exists in the parent).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QWhat do ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL / RESTRICT do?
        They decide what happens to child rows when the parent row is deleted (or its key updated). CASCADE deletes/updates children, SET NULL nulls the FK, RESTRICT/NO ACTION blocks the parent change. InnoDB rejects SET DEFAULT.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QSelection (σ) vs projection (π)?
        σ picks rows that satisfy a condition (like WHERE). π picks columns and, in pure algebra, removes duplicates (like SELECT DISTINCT col).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QWhich relational algebra operators are fundamental?
        Six: select σ, project π, union ∪, set difference −, Cartesian product ×, rename ρ. Intersection, joins and division are derived from them.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        QWhat is relational division used for?
        "For all" questions: students who took all courses, suppliers who supply every part. In SQL you write it with double NOT EXISTS or GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT x) = (SELECT COUNT(*) ...).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 04 · Keys & Constraints
        
  
        🧩 ER modelling
        
  
        QWhat are the components of an ER model?
        Entities/entity sets, attributes (simple/composite, single/multivalued, derived, key), and relationships with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N) and participation (total/partial).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 03 · ER Model
        
  
        QWhat is a weak entity?
        An entity with no key of its own. It is identified by its owner's key plus a partial key (discriminator), through an identifying relationship. Example: Dependent of Employee. Drawn with double rectangle.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 03 · ER Model
        
  
        QCardinality vs participation?
        Cardinality = how many: 1:1, 1:N, M:N. Participation = must every entity take part? Total (double line) or partial (single line).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 03 · ER Model
        
  
        QHow do you map an M:N relationship to tables?
        Create a junction table with both FKs, usually a composite PK on the pair, plus any relationship attributes (e.g. enrollment(student_id, course_id, grade)).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 03 · ER Model
        
  
        QMinimum number of tables for an ER diagram?
        1:N → 2 tables (FK on the N side). M:N → 3. 1:1 with total participation on one side → can merge into 1. Each multivalued attribute → its own table.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 03 · ER Model
        
  
        QGeneralization vs specialization vs aggregation?
        Generalization: bottom-up, merge common features into a superclass. Specialization: top-down, split into subclasses. Aggregation: treat a relationship as an entity so it can join another relationship.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 03 · ER Model
        
  
        QHow are derived and multivalued attributes mapped?
        Derived (age from DOB): usually not stored; compute it. Multivalued (phone numbers): a separate table (person_id, phone) with a composite key.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 03 · ER Model
        
  
        🧹 Functional dependencies & normalization
        
  
        QWhat is normalization and why do it?
        Splitting tables using functional dependencies to remove redundancy and the insert, update and delete anomalies it causes, without losing information (lossless).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QInsert, update and delete anomalies?
        Insert: cannot add a department until it has an employee. Update: renaming a department means changing many rows. Delete: deleting the last employee loses the department's data.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QWhat is a functional dependency?
        X → Y means: any two rows that agree on X must agree on Y. It is a business rule, not something you guess from sample data.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 05 · Functional Dependencies
        
  
        QDefine 1NF.
        Every column holds atomic (single) values. No repeating groups, no lists in one cell, and each row is identifiable by a key.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QDefine 2NF.
        1NF and no partial dependency: no non-prime attribute depends on only part of a candidate key. It only matters when a key is composite.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QDefine 3NF.
        2NF and no transitive dependency of non-prime attributes on a key. Formal test: for every non-trivial X → A, X is a superkey or A is prime.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QDefine BCNF and how it differs from 3NF.
        BCNF: for every non-trivial X → Y, X is a superkey. It drops 3NF's "or A is prime" escape. They differ only with overlapping composite candidate keys.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QWhat do 4NF and 5NF remove?
        4NF removes non-trivial multivalued dependencies (independent facts like a student's hobbies and languages in one table). 5NF removes join dependencies not implied by keys.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QWhat is a lossless-join decomposition?
        Joining the parts gives back exactly the original table, no spurious rows. Binary test: the common attributes are a key of at least one part: (R1 ∩ R2) → R1 or (R1 ∩ R2) → R2.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 05 · Functional Dependencies · Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QWhat is dependency preservation?
        Every original FD can be checked inside a single decomposed table without joins. 3NF synthesis always keeps it; BCNF decomposition may lose it.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 05 · Functional Dependencies · Ch 06 · Normalization
        
  
        QHow do you find candidate keys from FDs?
        Compute attribute closures X⁺. X is a key if X⁺ = all attributes and no proper subset works. Attributes that never appear on any right-hand side must be in every key — start from them.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 05 · Functional Dependencies
        
  
        QArmstrong's axioms?
        Reflexivity (Y ⊆ X ⇒ X → Y), augmentation (X → Y ⇒ XZ → YZ), transitivity (X → Y, Y → Z ⇒ X → Z). Sound and complete. Union, decomposition and pseudo-transitivity are derived.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 05 · Functional Dependencies
        
  
        QWhat is a canonical (minimal) cover?
        An equivalent FD set with single attributes on the right, no extraneous left-side attributes and no redundant FDs. It is the input to the 3NF synthesis algorithm.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 05 · Functional Dependencies
