        QWhat is denormalization and when is it right?
        Adding redundancy on purpose (copied columns, summary tables, counters) to make reads faster. You pay with harder writes and possible anomalies. Right for read-heavy paths and OLAP, after measuring.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 06 · Normalization · Ch 21 · Schema Design
        
  
        ✍️ SQL core
        
  
        QSQL command categories?
        DDL: CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME. DML: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE. DQL: SELECT. DCL: GRANT, REVOKE. TCL: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QDELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP — one line each?
        DELETE: DML, row by row, WHERE allowed, fires triggers, can roll back. TRUNCATE: removes all rows by deallocating pages, no DELETE triggers; rollback is engine-specific. DROP: removes the table itself (data, indexes, constraints).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QSQL vs MySQL?
        SQL is the standard language. MySQL is one RDBMS product that implements a dialect of SQL.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QCHAR vs VARCHAR?
        CHAR(n) is fixed length and padded with spaces; good for fixed codes like country codes. VARCHAR(n) stores only the actual characters plus a 1–2 byte length prefix.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QWHERE vs HAVING?
        WHERE filters rows before grouping and cannot use aggregates. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates like COUNT(*) > 5.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QWhat is the logical order of query evaluation?
        FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT (window functions here) → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET. This is why a SELECT alias is not visible in WHERE.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QWhat is the GROUP BY rule?
        Every non-aggregated column in SELECT must be in GROUP BY (or functionally dependent on it). MySQL enforces this with ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY, on by default since 5.7.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QLIKE wildcards?
        % = any number of characters (including zero), _ = exactly one character. Use ESCAPE to match a literal % or _.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QIs BETWEEN inclusive?
        Yes, both ends. For DATETIME ranges prefer >= '2025-01-01' AND < '2025-02-01', otherwise you miss times after midnight on the last day.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QCOALESCE vs IFNULL vs NULLIF?
        COALESCE(a,b,c) returns the first non-NULL (standard). IFNULL (MySQL) / ISNULL (SQL Server) are 2-argument versions. NULLIF(a,b) returns NULL when a = b — handy to avoid divide-by-zero: x / NULLIF(y,0).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QHow do aggregate functions treat NULL?
        COUNT(*) counts rows. COUNT(col), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX skip NULLs. So AVG(col) can differ from SUM(col)/COUNT(*).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core
        
  
        QWhere do NULLs go in ORDER BY?
        Engine-specific. MySQL and SQL Server put NULLs first in ASC. PostgreSQL and Oracle put them last in ASC, and support NULLS FIRST/LAST.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core · Ch 11 · SQL Dialects & Engines
        
  
        QConstraint vs index?
        A constraint is a logical rule (must be unique). An index is a physical access structure. PK and UNIQUE constraints are enforced using unique indexes.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 07 · SQL Core · Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        🔗 Joins, subqueries & set operations
        
  
        QTypes of joins?
        INNER (matches only), LEFT/RIGHT OUTER (all rows of one side + NULLs), FULL OUTER (all rows of both), CROSS (Cartesian product), SELF (table with itself). Also semi-join (EXISTS) and anti-join (NOT EXISTS).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QWhen does a LEFT JOIN behave like an INNER JOIN?
        When WHERE filters on a right-table column, e.g. WHERE o.status = 'PAID'. The NULL-extended rows fail it and vanish. Put that condition in ON instead.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QGive a self-join example.
        Employees who earn more than their manager: FROM emp e JOIN emp m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QHow many rows does a CROSS JOIN return?
        m × n. A 1,000-row table crossed with a 1,000-row table gives 1,000,000 rows.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QEqui-join vs non-equi (theta) join?
        Equi-join uses =. Non-equi uses other operators, e.g. e.salary BETWEEN g.lo AND g.hi to find a salary grade. Theta join is the general form.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QHow do you do a FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL?
        MySQL has no FULL OUTER JOIN. Emulate it: LEFT JOIN ... UNION ... RIGHT JOIN (or UNION ALL with an anti-join on the second branch to keep real duplicates).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries · Ch 11 · SQL Dialects & Engines
        
  
        QWhy did my join produce duplicate rows?
        Fan-out: one row matched many rows on the other side (1:N or M:N). Fix it by aggregating before the join, using EXISTS for filtering, or joining on the full key — not by slapping DISTINCT on top.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QUNION vs UNION ALL?
        UNION removes duplicates (needs a sort or hash). UNION ALL keeps all rows and is faster. Use UNION ALL unless you really need de-duplication.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QIN vs EXISTS?
        IN compares a value against a list/subquery result. EXISTS checks whether a (usually correlated) subquery returns any row and can stop at the first match. Modern optimizers often turn both into a semi-join.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QWhat is a correlated subquery?
        A subquery that uses the outer row's columns, so it logically runs once per outer row. Example: employees above their department's average salary.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries
        
  
        QINTERSECT and EXCEPT in MySQL?
        Supported from MySQL 8.0.31. Before that, emulate INTERSECT with an inner join/EXISTS and EXCEPT with an anti-join (NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL). Oracle calls EXCEPT MINUS.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries · Ch 11 · SQL Dialects & Engines
        
  
        QJoin vs subquery — which is better?
        Use a join when you need columns from both tables; use EXISTS/IN when you only test existence. Optimizers often rewrite one into the other, so pick the clearer one and check EXPLAIN.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 08 · Joins & Subqueries · Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        🪟 Window functions, CTEs, views, procedures & triggers
        
  
        QWhat is a window function?
        A function computed over a set of related rows without collapsing them: f() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... ROWS ...). Used for ranking, running totals, moving averages, LAG/LEAD. MySQL has them since 8.0.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK?
        Salaries 100, 90, 90, 80 → ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3,4; RANK 1,2,2,4 (gap after tie); DENSE_RANK 1,2,2,3 (no gap).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat do LAG and LEAD do?
        Read a value from the previous (LAG) or next (LEAD) row in the window order. Used for day-over-day change and streak detection.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWindow function vs GROUP BY?
        GROUP BY returns one row per group. A window function keeps every row and puts the group value beside it (e.g. each employee with their department's average).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat is a CTE?
        WITH name AS (...) — a named temporary result for one statement. Improves readability, can be referenced several times, and enables recursion. MySQL since 8.0.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat is a recursive CTE used for?
        Hierarchies (org chart, category tree), graph walks, generating number or date series. Shape: anchor member UNION ALL recursive member, with a stop condition.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat is a view?
        A named stored query (virtual table). It stores no data. Used for abstraction, reuse and security (expose only some columns/rows).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat is a materialized view?
        A view whose result is stored physically, so reads are fast, but it must be refreshed and can be stale. Native in PostgreSQL and Oracle; SQL Server has indexed views; MySQL has none (use a summary table).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL · Ch 11 · SQL Dialects & Engines
        
  
        QCan you UPDATE through a view?
        Yes, if each view row maps to exactly one base-table row: no aggregates, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, UNION, and (mostly) no joins. WITH CHECK OPTION blocks changes that would make the row leave the view.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat is a stored procedure?
        A named routine stored in the DB (SQL + procedural logic) with IN/OUT parameters, run with CALL/EXEC. Fewer round trips, central logic, and security via EXECUTE privilege.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QFunction vs stored procedure?
        A function returns a value and can be used inside SQL expressions; it generally cannot have side effects or control transactions. A procedure is called on its own, can return result sets/OUT params and (engine-dependent) commit or roll back.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat is a trigger?
        Code that runs automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE (BEFORE/AFTER, row- or statement-level). Uses: audit logs, updated_at, complex rules. Downsides: hidden logic, slower bulk writes, hard debugging.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QTrigger vs stored procedure?
        A trigger fires implicitly on a table event and cannot be called directly or take parameters. A procedure is called explicitly and takes parameters.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        QWhat is a cursor and why avoid it?
        A pointer for row-by-row processing in procedural code (DECLARE, OPEN, FETCH, CLOSE). It is much slower than set-based SQL; use it only when per-row logic is unavoidable.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        💳 Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QWhat is a transaction?
        A logical unit of work — a group of reads/writes that must run all-or-nothing and in isolation. Example: transfer = debit A + credit B.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QExplain ACID with one example.
        Bank transfer of ₹500. Atomicity: debit and credit both happen or neither (undo log). Consistency: rules hold, e.g. balance ≥ 0 (constraints). Isolation: other transfers never see half the transfer (locks/MVCC). Durability: after COMMIT it survives a crash (redo/WAL + fsync).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QTransaction states?
        Active → partially committed → committed. Or active/partially committed → failed → aborted (rolled back), then restart or kill.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QCOMMIT vs ROLLBACK vs SAVEPOINT?
        COMMIT makes changes permanent. ROLLBACK undoes the whole transaction. SAVEPOINT marks a point you can ROLLBACK TO without undoing everything.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QWhat is autocommit?
        Each statement is its own transaction and commits immediately. On by default in MySQL and PostgreSQL clients. Use START TRANSACTION / BEGIN to group statements.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QHow are atomicity and durability implemented?
        Atomicity: undo information (InnoDB undo log; old row versions in PostgreSQL) to roll back. Durability: write-ahead log (redo/WAL) flushed to disk at COMMIT, replayed after a crash.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID · Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        QWhat is a serializable schedule?
        An interleaving of operations whose result equals some serial (one-after-another) order. It is the correctness goal for concurrent transactions.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QConflict vs view serializability?
        Conflict-serializable ⇔ the precedence graph has no cycle (easy, polynomial test). View serializability is broader (allows blind writes) but NP-complete to test, so real systems use protocols (2PL, SSI) instead.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        QRecoverable vs cascadeless vs strict schedule?
        Recoverable: commit only after the transactions you read from commit. Cascadeless: read only committed data, so no cascading aborts. Strict: no read or write of an item until its last writer ends. Strict 2PL gives strict schedules.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 12 · Transactions & ACID
        
  
        🚦 Isolation, locking, MVCC & deadlocks
        
  
        QName the concurrency anomalies.
        Dirty read (read uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (same row changes between reads), phantom (re-run range query sees new rows), lost update (two read-modify-writes, one overwrites the other), write skew (two txns read overlapping data, write different rows, break an invariant together).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QANSI isolation levels and what each prevents?
        READ UNCOMMITTED: nothing. READ COMMITTED: dirty reads. REPEATABLE READ: + non-repeatable reads (ANSI still allows phantoms). SERIALIZABLE: all of them. Real engines differ — see the cheat sheet.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QDefault isolation level in MySQL vs PostgreSQL?
        MySQL InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server: READ COMMITTED.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QShared vs exclusive lock?
        S (read) locks are compatible with other S locks. X (write) locks are compatible with nothing. So: many readers or one writer.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QWhat is two-phase locking (2PL)?
        Growing phase (only acquire locks), then shrinking phase (only release). It guarantees conflict-serializability. Strict 2PL holds X locks until commit (no cascading aborts); rigorous 2PL holds all locks until commit. 2PL can still deadlock.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QOptimistic vs pessimistic locking?
        Pessimistic: lock first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE); good under high contention. Optimistic: no lock; check a version column at write time (UPDATE ... WHERE id=? AND version=? → 0 rows = conflict, retry); good for low contention and web apps.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QWhat is MVCC?
        Multi-version concurrency control: keep several versions of a row so readers see a consistent snapshot without read locks. Readers don't block writers and writers don't block readers; writers still block writers. InnoDB keeps old versions in undo logs; PostgreSQL keeps them as dead tuples cleaned by VACUUM.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QWhat are intention locks?
        Table-level markers (IS, IX, SIX) saying "I hold or will hold row locks below". They let a table-lock request be checked quickly. IX is compatible with IX, so many row-lockers coexist.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QWhat are gap and next-key locks?
        InnoDB locks on index records: a gap lock locks the space between records; a next-key lock = record lock + the gap before it. Locking reads at REPEATABLE READ use them to stop phantom inserts.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QDeadlock and the four Coffman conditions?
        Transactions wait for each other in a cycle. All four must hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QDeadlock prevention vs avoidance vs detection?
        Prevention: break a condition (lock ordering, conservative 2PL, wait-die/wound-wait). Avoidance: grant only if the state stays safe (rare in DBs). Detection: find a cycle in the wait-for graph and abort a victim.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QHow does InnoDB handle a deadlock?
        It detects the cycle immediately and rolls back the transaction that modified the fewest rows (ERROR 1213). The app must catch it and retry. PostgreSQL checks after deadlock_timeout (1 s default) and raises 40P01.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QHow do you reduce deadlocks in app code?
        Lock rows in a consistent order (e.g. ascending account id), keep transactions short, add indexes so fewer rows get locked, take FOR UPDATE up front instead of upgrading S→X, and retry on deadlock errors.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QWait-die vs wound-wait?
        Both use start timestamps. Wait-die: older waits for younger; younger asking older dies. Wound-wait: older wounds (aborts) the younger holder; younger waits. Both prevent cycles; restarted txns keep their timestamp, so no starvation.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        QSELECT ... FOR UPDATE, NOWAIT, SKIP LOCKED?
        FOR UPDATE takes X locks for a read-modify-write. NOWAIT fails immediately instead of waiting. SKIP LOCKED skips locked rows — perfect for many workers pulling jobs from a queue table. MySQL 8.0+ and PostgreSQL support both options.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control
        
  
        🌳 Indexing
        
  
        QWhat is an index?
        A separate sorted (or hashed) structure that maps key values to row locations. It turns a full scan into a few page reads, at the cost of extra space and slower writes.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QClustered vs non-clustered index?
        Clustered: the table rows themselves are stored in key order — at most one per table. Non-clustered: a separate structure with keys + row locators. In InnoDB the locator is the PK, so a secondary lookup walks two B+ trees.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QB-tree vs B+ tree — why do databases use B+?
        B-tree keeps data in all nodes. B+ tree keeps data only in leaves, and leaves are linked. Internal nodes hold only keys → higher fan-out → shallower tree, and range scans just walk the leaf chain.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QWhy not a binary search tree or a hash table?
        A BST has fan-out 2, so it is too deep (one disk read per level). A hash supports only equality — no ranges, no ORDER BY, no prefix search. A B+ tree with hundreds of keys per page reaches billions of rows in 3–4 levels.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QDense vs sparse index?
        Dense: one entry per search-key value (or record). Sparse: one entry per block, so it only works when the file is sorted on that key. Secondary indexes must be dense.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QComposite index and the leftmost-prefix rule?
        Index on (a,b,c) serves filters on a, (a,b), (a,b,c). It generally cannot seek on b alone, and a range on b stops c from being used for seeking. Put equality columns first, then range/sort columns.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QWhat is a covering index?
        An index that contains every column the query needs, so the engine answers from the index alone (index-only scan; MySQL EXPLAIN shows Using index).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QWhen should you NOT add an index?
        Small tables, low-selectivity columns (boolean, gender), write-heavy tables, columns rarely filtered, and redundant indexes ((a) when (a,b) exists). Every index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and uses memory.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QWhen will the optimizer NOT use an index?
        Function or arithmetic on the column (YEAR(dt)=2025), leading wildcard (LIKE '%abc'), implicit type conversion, skipping the leftmost column, low selectivity (a scan is cheaper), stale statistics, some ORs across columns.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive · Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QCardinality vs selectivity?
        Cardinality = number of distinct values in a column. Selectivity = fraction of rows a predicate returns. Indexes help most when selectivity is small (few rows).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QWhat is a hash index good and bad at?
        Good: O(1) equality lookups. Bad: no ranges, no ORDER BY, no partial-key use. Examples: MySQL MEMORY engine, InnoDB adaptive hash index (internal), PostgreSQL hash indexes.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QAUTO_INCREMENT vs UUID primary key in InnoDB?
        Sequential ids append at the right edge of the clustered B+ tree: compact, few page splits. Random UUIDv4 inserts land everywhere: page splits, fragmentation, and a fat 16-byte (or 36-char) PK copied into every secondary index. Prefer BIGINT or time-ordered UUIDs (v7).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive · Ch 21 · Schema Design
        
  
        QBitmap index vs full-text index?
        Bitmap (Oracle): one bitmap per distinct value; great for low-cardinality analytic filters, bad for concurrent OLTP writes. Full-text: an inverted index (word → documents) for MATCH ... AGAINST or PostgreSQL tsvector search.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        🚀 Query processing & optimization
        
  
        QSteps of query processing?
        Parse and validate → translate to relational algebra → logical rewrites (push selections down, reorder joins) → pick a physical plan by cost → execute (iterator/Volcano model).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QCost-based vs rule-based optimizer?
        Rule-based applies fixed heuristics. Cost-based estimates I/O and CPU from statistics (row counts, histograms) and chooses the cheapest plan. All modern RDBMSs are cost-based.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QWhat does EXPLAIN show?
        The chosen plan: access type (const, ref, range, index, ALL...), key used, estimated rows, filtered, and Extra notes (Using index, Using filesort, Using temporary). EXPLAIN ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+) also runs it and shows real times and row counts.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QName the join algorithms.
        Nested loop (O(m·n), fine with a small outer side), index nested loop (probe an index on the inner table), sort-merge (sort both, then merge), hash join (build a hash table on the smaller input, probe with the larger; equi-joins only — MySQL since 8.0.18).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QWhat is a sargable predicate?
        One the engine can answer with an index seek: the bare column compared to a value. WHERE dt >= '2025-01-01' is sargable; WHERE YEAR(dt) = 2025 is not (unless you add a functional index).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QHow do you optimize a slow query?
        Reproduce, read EXPLAIN. Then: add/fix composite or covering index, make predicates sargable, avoid SELECT *, fix N+1, replace big OFFSET with keyset pagination, update statistics. Cache or denormalize only after that.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QWhy is LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000000 slow?
        The engine still reads and throws away a million rows. Keyset (seek) pagination WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 costs the same on every page.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        QWhat is the N+1 query problem?
        An ORM loads N parents, then runs one more query per parent for its children (N+1 round trips). Fix with a JOIN, IN (...) batching or eager loading.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 16 · Query Optimization
        
  
        🛟 Recovery & backups
        
  
        QWhat is write-ahead logging (WAL)?
        Log records describing a change reach stable storage before the changed data page does. After a crash: redo committed work, undo uncommitted work.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        QWhat is a checkpoint?
        A periodic point where dirty pages are flushed and recorded, so recovery only scans the log from there. Fuzzy checkpoints do this without stopping the world.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        QARIES in one breath?
        Analysis (find dirty pages and active txns), Redo (repeat history from the oldest dirty-page LSN), Undo (roll back losers, writing compensation log records). Uses WAL with steal/no-force.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        QWhat do steal and no-force mean?
        Steal: a dirty page of an uncommitted txn may be written to disk (so undo is needed). No-force: committed pages need not be flushed at commit (so redo is needed). This combo is fastest and is what ARIES/InnoDB/PostgreSQL use.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        QWhat is shadow paging?
        Copy-on-write pages plus an atomic switch of the page-table pointer at commit. No undo/redo log needed, but data gets scattered and concurrency is hard.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        QFull vs incremental vs differential backup?
        Full: everything. Incremental: changes since the last backup of any kind. Differential: changes since the last full backup. Also logical (SQL dump) vs physical (file copy).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        QWhat are point-in-time recovery, RPO and RTO?
        PITR = restore a base backup, then replay the binlog/WAL up to a chosen moment (e.g. just before a bad DROP). RPO = how much data you may lose. RTO = how long recovery may take.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 17 · Recovery & Logging
        
  
        💽 Storage & engines
        
  
        QWhat is a page, and what are the default sizes?
        The fixed-size unit the DB reads and writes. InnoDB default 16 KB, PostgreSQL 8 KB, SQL Server 8 KB.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 14 · Storage & Buffer Pool
        
  
        QWhat is the buffer pool?
        The DB's in-memory cache of pages (InnoDB innodb_buffer_pool_size, PostgreSQL shared_buffers). Reads hit memory; dirty pages are flushed later; eviction uses an LRU variant.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 14 · Storage & Buffer Pool
        
  
        QHeap file vs clustered (index-organized) table?
        Heap: rows in no particular order, indexes point to physical row ids (PostgreSQL, SQL Server heaps). Clustered/index-organized: rows live in the PK B+ tree leaves (InnoDB, Oracle IOT, SQL Server clustered index).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 14 · Storage & Buffer Pool · Ch 15 · Indexing Deep Dive
        
  
        QInnoDB vs MyISAM?
        InnoDB: transactions, row-level locks, MVCC, foreign keys, crash recovery — the default since MySQL 5.5. MyISAM: no transactions, table-level locks, no FKs, but stores an exact row count.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 11 · SQL Dialects & Engines · Ch 14 · Storage & Buffer Pool
        
  
        QWhy does PostgreSQL need VACUUM?
        An UPDATE writes a new tuple version and leaves the old one as a dead tuple. VACUUM reclaims dead tuples and freezes old transaction ids to prevent wraparound.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 13 · Concurrency Control · Ch 14 · Storage & Buffer Pool
        
  
        QTop differences between MySQL and PostgreSQL?
        Default isolation (RR vs RC), clustered PK in InnoDB vs heap tables in PG, transactional DDL only in PG, PG has richer types (JSONB, arrays) and features (partial indexes, materialized views, FULL OUTER JOIN), MySQL is simpler to run with many replicas.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 11 · SQL Dialects & Engines
        
  
        QOracle quirk with empty strings?
        Oracle treats '' as NULL, so WHERE name = '' finds nothing and '' IS NULL is true. MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server treat '' as a real empty value.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 11 · SQL Dialects & Engines
        
  
        🛡️ Security
        
  
        QWhat is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?
        Untrusted input is glued into a SQL string and changes the query's meaning (' OR '1'='1). Prevent with parameterized queries/prepared statements, least-privilege DB users and input validation. Escaping alone is not a fix.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 18 · Security
        
  
        QGRANT / REVOKE and least privilege?
        DCL commands that give or remove privileges (SELECT, INSERT, EXECUTE...) on objects to users or roles. The app user should get only what it needs — never root/superuser.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 18 · Security
        
  
        QHow can views help security?
        Grant SELECT on a view instead of the base table, so a user sees only some columns (no salary) or some rows (only their region).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 18 · Security · Ch 09 · Advanced SQL
        
  
        🌐 Distributed databases & CAP
        
  
        QWhat is the CAP theorem?
        In a replicated system, during a network partition you must choose consistency (every read sees the latest write — linearizable) or availability (every live node answers). Partitions can't be wished away, so it is really C vs A when P happens.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QWhat is PACELC?
        If Partition: Availability vs Consistency; Else: Latency vs Consistency. It captures the everyday trade-off. Cassandra = PA/EL; HBase/Bigtable = PC/EC; MongoDB is listed PA/EC.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QACID vs BASE?
        BASE = Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent: favours availability and scale. ACID favours correctness of every transaction.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs · Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QPartitioning vs sharding vs replication?
        Partitioning: split a table into parts, often inside one server. Sharding: horizontal partitioning across servers, each holding a subset of rows. Replication: copies of the same data on several nodes for read scaling and high availability.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QHow do you choose a shard key?
        High cardinality, even spread, and most queries hitting one shard (e.g. workspace_id, tenant_id, user_id). Bad keys cause hot shards (celebrity users, timestamps) and cross-shard joins.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QWhat is consistent hashing?
        Nodes and keys are hashed onto a ring; a key goes to the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys. Virtual nodes even out the load.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QSync vs async replication, and replication-lag problems?
        Sync: commit waits for the replica (safer, slower). Async: faster, but replicas lag → stale reads, read-your-writes violations, possible lost writes on failover. Fix: read from the primary after a write, or wait for a GTID/LSN.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QWhat is two-phase commit (2PC)?
        Atomic commit across several databases. Phase 1: the coordinator asks all participants to PREPARE (vote yes/no). Phase 2: if all say yes, COMMIT; else ABORT. Weakness: if the coordinator dies after prepare, participants block holding locks.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QWhat is a Saga, and Saga vs 2PC?
        A Saga is a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it on failure. Non-blocking and scalable, but no isolation and only eventually atomic. 2PC is atomic but blocking and slow.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QWhat is a read-write quorum (R + W > N)?
        With N replicas, write to W and read from R. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps the latest write set, so a read can see the newest value. Cassandra QUORUM/QUORUM with RF=3 is 2 + 2 > 3.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        QVertical vs horizontal scaling?
        Vertical: a bigger machine — simple but has a ceiling. Horizontal: more machines — needs replication/sharding and adds complexity. Usual path: fix queries/indexes → cache → read replicas → partition → shard.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 19 · Distributed DBs
        
  
        🍃 NoSQL, NewSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QSQL vs NoSQL?
        SQL: fixed schema, joins, ACID, strong consistency; scales up first. NoSQL: flexible schema, data modelled around access patterns, built to scale out; consistency often tunable/eventual. Choose by data shape, queries, consistency needs and scale.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QTypes of NoSQL databases?
        Key-value (Redis, DynamoDB), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra, ScyllaDB, HBase), graph (Neo4j). Also time-series and search engines (Elasticsearch).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QDoes MongoDB support ACID transactions?
        Yes. Single-document writes are always atomic; multi-document ACID transactions exist since 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters), with a performance cost.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QWhen is MongoDB a good or bad fit?
        Good: document-shaped data read together, evolving schema, horizontal scale. Bad: many-to-many relations, heavy joins, multi-entity invariants (payments, inventory) — use PostgreSQL/MySQL there.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP · Ch 21 · Schema Design
        
  
        QOLTP vs OLAP?
        OLTP: many short read/write transactions on few rows; normalized; row stores; ACID. OLAP: big scans and aggregations over history; denormalized star schemas; column stores.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QStar vs snowflake schema?
        Star: one fact table surrounded by denormalized dimension tables — fewer joins, faster. Snowflake: dimensions normalized into sub-dimensions — less redundancy, more joins.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QFact vs dimension table?
        Fact: measurable events at a declared grain (sale amount, qty) + FKs to dimensions. Dimension: descriptive context (product, date, customer, store).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QSlowly changing dimension types?
        Type 1: overwrite (no history). Type 2: add a new row with valid-from/valid-to or a current flag (full history). Type 3: keep a 'previous value' column (limited history).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QETL vs ELT?
        ETL transforms data before loading the warehouse. ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse with SQL (dbt style) — natural for elastic cloud warehouses.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QRow store vs column store?
        Row store keeps whole rows together — good for point lookups and writes (OLTP). Column store keeps each column together — reads only needed columns and compresses well (Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake, ClickHouse).
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        
  
        QWhat is NewSQL?
        Distributed SQL databases that keep SQL + ACID while scaling out: Google Spanner, CockroachDB, TiDB, YugabyteDB.
        🔎 Depth: Ch 20 · NoSQL & OLAP
        

  
        ⚠️ Tricky & gotcha questions
        
  
        Each gotcha shows the common wrong answer first, then the precise one. Most of them are "it depends on the engine" — say which engine does what, and you win.
        
  
        💡
        The 3-part shape of a perfect gotcha answer
        (1) Short verdict: "Yes, but…" / "No — that's a common myth." (2) The mechanism in one sentence. (3) The engine difference or the fix. Ten seconds each.
        

  
        🔑 Keys, constraints & NULLs
        

  
        
    QCan a table have no primary key? What does InnoDB do then?
    
        
      
        🚫
        Wrong answer
        "No, every table must have a primary key."
        
      
        Yes, SQL allows it. But InnoDB always stores rows in a clustered B+ tree, so it must cluster on something:
        
      
          
        
        1. PK defined → the PK is the clustered index.
          2. 
        
        2. No PK → the first UNIQUE index whose columns are all NOT NULL becomes the clustered index.
          3. 
        
        3. Neither → InnoDB adds a hidden 6-byte row id and builds GEN_CLUST_INDEX on it. You can't use it in queries.
          4. 
      
        
      
        🔀
        Engine differences
        MySQL 8.0.13+ has sql_require_primary_key (default OFF) to forbid PK-less tables. PostgreSQL tables are heaps, so a PK-less table is just a heap with no unique row identity. Replication tools and ORMs often need a PK anyway.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        SQL allows it, but it's bad practice. In InnoDB the table is still clustered: on the PK if there is one, else on the first NOT NULL unique index, else on a hidden 6-byte row id. So I always define a small PK, usually a BIGINT.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan a foreign key be NULL? Can it reference a UNIQUE column instead of the PK? Its own table?
    
        
      
        Yes, yes and yes.
        
      
          
        
        • NULL: unless declared NOT NULL, an FK column may be NULL — meaning "no parent". PostgreSQL docs: a referencing row need not satisfy the FK if any referencing column is NULL (composite FKs with MATCH FULL change this).
          • 
        
        • UNIQUE target: an FK may reference any PK or UNIQUE key (PostgreSQL also accepts a non-partial unique index; SQL Server docs say a UNIQUE constraint can be referenced).
          • 
        
        • Same table: emp.manager_id → emp.id is a self-referencing FK.
          • 
      
        
      
        ⚠️
        Gotcha inside the gotcha
        An FK to a non-unique column is not standard SQL. MySQL 8.4 rejects it by default (restrict_fk_on_non_standard_key=ON); older InnoDB allowed it as a deprecated extension.
        
      
        CREATE TABLE emp (
  id         BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
  email      VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  manager_id BIGINT NULL,                        -- NULL = the CEO has no manager
  FOREIGN KEY (manager_id) REFERENCES emp(id)    -- self-reference
);
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes a UNIQUE column allow multiple NULLs?
    
        
      
        🚫
        Wrong answer (repeated on popular prep sites)
        "UNIQUE allows exactly one NULL."
        
      
        It depends on the engine. The SQL standard left this implementation-defined.
        
      
        EngineMultiple NULLs in a UNIQUE column?
        
        
        MySQL (InnoDB)✔ many — "permits multiple NULL values"
        
        
        PostgreSQL✔ many by default; UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (PG 15+) allows only one
        
        
        Oracle✔ many (all-NULL keys are not indexed)
        
        
        SQL Server✘ only one NULL per UNIQUE constraint (use a filtered unique index WHERE col IS NOT NULL for "many")
        
      
        
      
        Why many? Because NULL = NULL is not TRUE, so two NULLs are never "equal duplicates".
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs NULL = NULL true? Does WHERE col = NULL find NULL rows?
    
        
      
        No and no. Any comparison with NULL gives UNKNOWN (SQL has three truth values). WHERE keeps only TRUE rows, so col = NULL returns zero rows, even for rows where col is NULL.
        
      
        SELECT NULL = NULL, NULL <> 1, NULL IS NULL, NULL <=> NULL;
-- NULL       NULL      1             1      (MySQL)
-- <=> is MySQL's NULL-safe equal; standard SQL: IS NOT DISTINCT FROM
        
      
        ANDTRUEFALSEUNKNOWN
        
        
        TRUETRUEFALSEUNKNOWN
        
        
        FALSEFALSEFALSEFALSE
        
        
        UNKNOWNUNKNOWNFALSEUNKNOWN
        
      
        
      
        OR mirrors it: TRUE OR UNKNOWN = TRUE, FALSE OR UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN. NOT UNKNOWN = UNKNOWN.
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Does a CHECK constraint reject NULL?
          
        No. A CHECK fails only when the expression is FALSE. NULL makes it UNKNOWN, which passes. So CHECK (age >= 18) accepts a NULL age — add NOT NULL if you mean it. (MySQL enforces CHECK only from 8.0.16; before that it was parsed and ignored.)
        
        
        ↪Is NULL the same as 0 or ''?
          
        No — NULL means unknown/missing. Oracle is the odd one: it treats '' as NULL.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhy does WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM emp) return zero rows?
    
        
      
        Because manager_id contains a NULL (the CEO). x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL) means x<>1 AND x<>2 AND x<>NULL. The last part is UNKNOWN, so the whole AND is never TRUE. Every row is dropped.
        
      
        -- employees who manage nobody
SELECT e.id, e.name
FROM emp e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM emp r WHERE r.manager_id = e.id);

-- or
WHERE e.id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM emp WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL);
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        NOT IN with a subquery that can return NULL gives no rows, because comparing with NULL is UNKNOWN and the AND chain never becomes TRUE. I default to NOT EXISTS for anti-joins; it is NULL-safe and the optimizer turns it into an anti-join.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan a primary key be a VARCHAR? Should it?
    
        
      
        Yes, it can (email, ISBN, country code). Should it? Usually not in InnoDB:
        
      
          
        
        • Every secondary index leaf stores the PK value. A 100-byte VARCHAR PK makes every index fat.
          • 
        
        • String comparison is slower than integer comparison, and depends on collation (case-insensitive by default in MySQL: 'A@x.com' = 'a@x.com').
          • 
        
        • Natural values change (people change email), and changing a PK cascades to every FK.
          • 
        
        • Random strings insert all over the B+ tree → page splits.
          • 
      
        
      
        Good compromise: id BIGINT PK + UNIQUE(email). Short fixed codes (CHAR(2) country code) are fine as PKs.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan a table have two primary keys? Is every super key a candidate key?
    
        
      
        No and no. One PK per table — but it may be composite (two columns is still one key). You can have many candidate/UNIQUE keys. Every candidate key is a super key, but a super key is a candidate key only if it is minimal: {id, name} is a super key, not a candidate key, because {id} alone already works.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes declaring a foreign key create an index? Does an FK make joins faster?
    
        
      
        Engine-specific, and no. InnoDB requires an index on FK columns and creates one if missing. PostgreSQL does not auto-index the referencing columns (its docs say indexing them is often a good idea, e.g. for deletes on the parent). An FK is an integrity rule; it does not speed up a join by itself — the index does. You can also join tables with no FK at all.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        ✂️ DELETE / TRUNCATE / DROP & DDL
        

  
        
    QCan you ROLLBACK a TRUNCATE?
    
        
      
        🚫
        Wrong answer
        "TRUNCATE is DDL, so it can never be rolled back." (Also wrong: "TRUNCATE is not logged at all.")
        
      
        EngineTRUNCATE inside a transaction
        
        
        MySQL✘ causes an implicit commit (like all DDL) — cannot roll back
        
        
        Oracle✘ DDL commits implicitly
        
        
        PostgreSQL✔ "transaction-safe" — rolled back if the transaction doesn't commit
        
        
        SQL Server✔ can be rolled back inside an explicit transaction
        
      
        
      
        TRUNCATE is minimally logged, not unlogged: SQL Server records only page deallocations, while DELETE logs every row.
        
      
        BEGIN;
TRUNCATE orders;
ROLLBACK;            -- orders is back, every row
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        It depends on the engine. In MySQL and Oracle, TRUNCATE is DDL with an implicit commit, so no rollback. PostgreSQL and SQL Server can roll it back inside a transaction. It's fast because it deallocates pages instead of logging each row.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes TRUNCATE fire DELETE triggers? Reset AUTO_INCREMENT? Work on an FK-referenced table?
    
        
      
          
        
        • Triggers: no ON DELETE triggers anywhere. PostgreSQL has separate ON TRUNCATE triggers; SQL Server says TRUNCATE can't activate a trigger.
          • 
        
        • Identity: MySQL resets AUTO_INCREMENT; SQL Server resets to the seed; PostgreSQL keeps going (CONTINUE IDENTITY) unless you write RESTART IDENTITY.
          • 
        
        • FK parent: generally refused. PostgreSQL needs all referencing tables in the same command or CASCADE; SQL Server forbids it; InnoDB fails if other tables reference it.
          • 
      
        
      
        🌍
        Real-world
        An audit trigger "logs every deletion". Someone cleans a table with TRUNCATE. The audit table shows nothing. That's why triggers alone are not a reliable audit.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QYou ran DELETE FROM orders; (no WHERE) inside a transaction. Are you doomed?
    
        
      
        No — if you are inside an explicit transaction (or autocommit is off), ROLLBACK brings every row back. DELETE is DML and is fully logged. If autocommit was on, it is already committed: restore from backup + point-in-time recovery (binlog/WAL). A replica won't save you — the DELETE replicated too.
        
      
        START TRANSACTION;
DELETE FROM orders;       -- oops
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders;   -- 0 (you see your own change)
ROLLBACK;                 -- all rows back

SET sql_safe_updates = 1; -- MySQL: refuse UPDATE/DELETE without a key in WHERE (or LIMIT)
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs DELETE FROM t the same as TRUNCATE t?
    
        
      
        Same end state, different mechanics. DELETE: per-row logging, fires triggers, keeps the AUTO_INCREMENT counter, can be filtered, can roll back everywhere, slower, and space is reused rather than released. TRUNCATE: drops and re-creates (or deallocates) the data pages — fast, no DELETE triggers, resets identity in MySQL.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan DDL (CREATE/ALTER/DROP) be rolled back?
    
        
      
        Engine-specific. MySQL and Oracle: DDL commits implicitly (and also commits whatever you had open before it!). PostgreSQL has transactional DDL: BEGIN; ALTER TABLE ...; ROLLBACK; undoes the ALTER. That makes PostgreSQL migrations safer.
        
      
        ⚠️
        MySQL trap
        START TRANSACTION; UPDATE ...; CREATE INDEX ...; ROLLBACK; — the UPDATE is already committed by the implicit commit of CREATE INDEX.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QA transaction inserts a row, gets AUTO_INCREMENT id 101, then rolls back. What id does the next insert get?
    
        
      
        102. Auto-increment values are never handed back on rollback, so gaps are normal. Allocating ids must not wait for other transactions to finish, so InnoDB does not reuse them (default innodb_autoinc_lock_mode=2 since 8.0). PostgreSQL sequences behave the same: nextval() is never rolled back.
        
      
        🚫
        Fails a design round
        "I'll use the AUTO_INCREMENT id as the gap-free invoice number." Use a separate counter row updated under a lock if the law requires gap-free numbers.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        ✍️ SQL semantics
        
  
        Half of these traps disappear once you remember the logical order in which a SELECT is evaluated:
        
  
        
    
        FROM / JOINbuild rows
        
    
        
    
        WHEREfilter rows (no aggregates, no aliases)
        
    
        
    
        GROUP BYmake groups
        
    
        
    
        HAVINGfilter groups
        
    
        
    
        SELECTcompute + aliases + windows
        
    
        
    
        DISTINCTdedupe
        
    
        
    
        ORDER BYsort (aliases OK)
        
    
        
    
        LIMITcut
        
  
        

  
        
    QCOUNT(*) vs COUNT(1) vs COUNT(col) — which is fastest?
    
        
      
        🚫
        Wrong answers
        "COUNT(1) is faster" · "COUNT(*) reads all columns".
        
      
        COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) are the same — the MySQL manual says InnoDB handles them identically, with no performance difference. * here means "count rows", not "read every column". COUNT(col) is different in meaning: it counts only non-NULL values of col.
        
      
        -- emp: (1, 'Asha', 10), (2, 'Ravi', NULL), (3, 'Meera', 10)
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(1), COUNT(dept_id), COUNT(DISTINCT dept_id) FROM emp;
-- 3        3         2               1
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪Is SELECT COUNT(*) instant on a 100M-row InnoDB table?
          
        No. InnoDB keeps no exact row count, because under MVCC different transactions see different counts. It scans the smallest available index. MyISAM stores an exact count (instant). For dashboards, use an approximate count or a maintained counter.
        
        
        ↪Department count including empty departments — COUNT(*) or COUNT(e.id)?
          
        COUNT(e.id). After a LEFT JOIN, an empty department still produces one NULL-extended row, so COUNT(*) shows 1 instead of 0. (This exact problem appeared in a Swiggy online test.)
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan WHERE use a column alias from SELECT?
    
        
      
        No (standard SQL). WHERE runs before SELECT, so the alias doesn't exist yet. MySQL's manual: when WHERE is evaluated, "the column value may not yet have been determined". MySQL does allow aliases in GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY (PostgreSQL allows them in GROUP BY and ORDER BY, not HAVING).
        
      
        SELECT name, salary * 12 AS annual FROM emp WHERE annual > 600000;   -- ERROR 1054 unknown column
SELECT name, salary * 12 AS annual FROM emp WHERE salary * 12 > 600000;  -- OK: repeat the expression
SELECT * FROM (SELECT name, salary * 12 AS annual FROM emp) t WHERE annual > 600000; -- OK: derived table
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan you use an aggregate in WHERE? Can HAVING be used without GROUP BY?
    
        
      
        No, and yes. WHERE filters rows before groups exist, so WHERE COUNT(*) > 5 is an error — use HAVING (or a subquery/CTE). HAVING without GROUP BY treats the whole result as one group:
        
      
        SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders HAVING COUNT(*) > 1000;   -- one row, or no rows
SELECT * FROM emp WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM emp);  -- aggregate via subquery
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes ORDER BY inside a subquery, view or CTE guarantee the final order?
    
        
      
        No. A table (and a derived table) is an unordered set. Only the outermost ORDER BY guarantees order. MySQL's optimizer may simply drop an ORDER BY in a derived table or view when it merges it. SQL Server rejects ORDER BY in views, subqueries and CTEs unless TOP, OFFSET or FOR XML is also used. Inner ORDER BY only matters together with LIMIT/TOP (it picks which rows).
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs LIMIT 10 without ORDER BY deterministic?
    
        
      
        No. Without ORDER BY the order is undefined — it often looks like insertion or PK order, until a plan changes or a parallel scan kicks in. Also order by a unique column (add id as tie-breaker), or pagination will skip/duplicate tied rows.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDISTINCT vs GROUP BY — any difference?
    
        
      
        For plain de-duplication, same result and usually the same plan: SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM emp ≡ SELECT dept FROM emp GROUP BY dept. GROUP BY is for when you also need aggregates per group. (Old MySQL 5.x GROUP BY sorted implicitly; MySQL 8 does not — always write ORDER BY.)
        
      
        ⚠️
        Red flag
        Adding DISTINCT to "fix" duplicates from a join hides a fan-out bug. Fix the join or pre-aggregate instead.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QWhat does SELECT 1 mean inside EXISTS? Is SELECT * slower there?
    
        
      
        EXISTS only asks "is there at least one row?". The select list is ignored, so SELECT 1, SELECT * and even SELECT NULL behave the same — no columns are fetched. SELECT 1 is just a readable convention meaning "I only care about existence".
        
      
        SELECT c.name FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id);  -- customers with ≥1 order
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QMy LEFT JOIN returns fewer rows than the left table. Why?
    
        
      
        A condition on the right table sits in WHERE. NULL-extended rows fail it (UNKNOWN) and are removed, so the LEFT JOIN behaves like an INNER JOIN.
        
      
        -- wrong: customers without PAID orders disappear
SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'PAID';
-- right: keep every customer, attach only PAID orders
SELECT c.name, o.id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'PAID';
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs 'abc' = 'abc   ' (trailing spaces) true?
    
        
      
        Depends on type and collation.
        
      
          
        
        • CHAR(n) is padded with spaces on storage. MySQL strips trailing spaces from CHAR on retrieval; PostgreSQL treats trailing spaces in char(n) as insignificant when comparing. So for CHAR, effectively true.
          • 
        
        • VARCHAR/TEXT in MySQL: depends on the collation's pad attribute. Older collations (utf8mb4_general_ci, utf8mb4_unicode_ci) are PAD SPACE → trailing spaces ignored → true. MySQL 8's default utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is NO PAD → false. In PostgreSQL varchar/text, trailing spaces count → false.
          • 
        
        • SQL Server follows ANSI padding for = → true (but LIKE differs).
          • 
      
        
      
        Interview point: this matters for UNIQUE checks on usernames — 'ravi' and 'ravi ' may collide or not.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes a view store data? Is querying a view faster than the base query?
    
        
      
        No and usually no. A view is a stored query. When you query it, the engine merges the view text into your query (or materializes a temp result for complex views). Same work as writing the query yourself. Only materialized views (PostgreSQL, Oracle) and indexed views (SQL Server) store results and can be faster — at the cost of refresh and staleness. MySQL has no native materialized view.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs reading your own uncommitted changes a dirty read?
    
        
      
        No. A dirty read is reading another transaction's uncommitted data. Every transaction always sees its own writes.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🌳 Indexing
        

  
        
    QDoes an index always speed things up? Why not index every column?
    
        
      
        🚫
        Wrong answer
        "Yes — just add indexes everywhere."
        
      
          
        
        • Writes get slower: every INSERT/DELETE (and UPDATE of an indexed column) must also update every index — more I/O, more locks, more redo.
          • 
        
        • Space and memory: indexes compete with data for the buffer pool.
          • 
        
        • Low selectivity: for WHERE is_active = 1 matching 90% of rows, a full scan is cheaper than 90% random lookups; the optimizer ignores the index.
          • 
        
        • Small tables: one or two pages — scanning is cheapest.
          • 
        
        • Non-sargable predicates (YEAR(dt)=2025, LIKE '%x') can't use the index anyway.
          • 
        
        • Redundant indexes: (a) is redundant if (a,b) exists.
          • 
      
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        No. An index speeds up selective reads but costs on every write, uses memory, and is ignored when a predicate matches a large fraction of rows or wraps the column in a function. I index for the actual query patterns — usually a few composite indexes — and confirm with EXPLAIN.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QHow many clustered indexes can a table have? Is the PK always the clustered index?
    
        
      
        At most one — the rows can be physically ordered only one way. Is the PK always it? Engine-specific:
        
      
        EngineClustered index
        
        
        MySQL InnoDBAlways clustered; the PK is the clustered index (fallbacks above)
        
        
        SQL ServerPK becomes clustered by default "unless a clustered index already exists"; tables without one are heaps
        
        
        PostgreSQLNo clustered index — tables are heaps; CLUSTER is a one-time reorder, not maintained
        
        
        OracleHeap by default; clustered only as an index-organized table (IOT)
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIndex on (city, age). Does WHERE age = 30 use it?
    
        
      
        Generally no — leftmost-prefix rule. The index is sorted by city first; ages are scattered across cities, so there is no single range to seek. Exceptions: MySQL 8.0.13+ skip scan (and Oracle's) when city has few distinct values, or a full index scan if the index covers the query.
        
      
        PredicateSeeks on (city, age)?
        
        
        city='Pune'✔
        
        
        city='Pune' AND age=30✔ both columns
        
        
        city='Pune' AND age>30✔ equality then range
        
        
        city>'P' AND age=30~ range on city; age used only as a filter
        
        
        age=30✘ (skip scan aside)
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan both LIKE 'abc%' and LIKE '%abc' use a B-tree index?
    
        
      
        Only the prefix one. 'abc%' is a range (>= 'abc' AND < 'abd'). '%abc' can start anywhere, so no range exists. Use a full-text index, PostgreSQL trigram (pg_trgm) index, or store the reversed string with its own index.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes Extra: Using index in MySQL EXPLAIN mean "an index was used"?
    
        
      
        No. The key column tells you which index was used. Using index means a covering (index-only) read — the table rows were never touched. Using index condition is different again: index condition pushdown.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes B-tree mean binary tree? Can a hash index serve BETWEEN or ORDER BY?
    
        
      
        No and no. A B-tree is a balanced multi-way tree with hundreds of keys per page (high fan-out, 3–4 levels for billions of rows). A hash index answers only =; MySQL's manual says it cannot speed up ORDER BY, cannot do ranges, and only whole keys can be used.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🧹 Normalization gotchas
        

  
        
    QIs every relation with only two attributes in BCNF?
    
        
      
        Yes, always. Take R(A, B). The only possible non-trivial FDs are A → B and B → A. If A → B holds, then A determines both columns, so A is a key. Same for B. So every determinant is a superkey, which is the BCNF rule.
        
      
        🎯
        What is being tested
        Can you prove it from the definition in two lines, instead of guessing? Say: "any non-trivial FD in a 2-column table has the whole table on its closure, so its LHS is a key". See Chapter 06.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QBCNF is "stricter" than 3NF. So should you always go to BCNF?
    
        
      
        Not always. A 3NF decomposition (synthesis algorithm) is guaranteed to be lossless and dependency-preserving. A BCNF decomposition is always lossless, but it may lose a dependency. Then that FD can only be checked by joining tables (or a trigger).
        
      
        Classic example: R(student, course, teacher) with teacher → course and (student, course) → teacher. Key = (student, course). teacher → course breaks BCNF (teacher is not a superkey). Splitting into (teacher, course) and (student, teacher) is BCNF, but (student, course) → teacher can no longer be enforced inside one table.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        BCNF removes more redundancy, but sometimes the split loses a functional dependency. 3NF always keeps both lossless join and dependency preservation. So in practice I go to BCNF when no dependency is lost, and stop at 3NF when it would be.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan a table in BCNF still have redundancy?
    
        
      
        Yes — from multi-valued dependencies. emp(name, skill, language) where skills and languages are independent. No FDs at all, so it is in BCNF, yet every skill is repeated for every language. 4NF fixes it: split into (name, skill) and (name, language). Join dependencies that are not MVDs need 5NF.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes normalization always make queries faster?
    
        
      
        No. Normalization reduces redundancy and update anomalies, and makes writes cheaper and safer. Reads that need many tables now need joins, which can be slower. That is why read-heavy systems and warehouses denormalize on purpose (star schema, cached counters, materialized views). Say "normalize for correctness, denormalize measured hot paths".
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🚦 Isolation, locking & MVCC gotchas
        

  
        
    QCan phantom reads happen at REPEATABLE READ?
    
        
      
        Depends who you ask — and that is the point.
        
      
          
        
        • SQL standard: yes, REPEATABLE READ allows phantoms. Only SERIALIZABLE forbids them.
          • 
        
        • MySQL InnoDB (RR is the default): plain SELECTs read from one snapshot, so re-running a range query shows no new rows. Locking reads (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, UPDATE, DELETE) take next-key locks (row + gap), which block inserts into the range.
          • 
        
        • Catch in InnoDB: a snapshot read and a locking read in the same transaction can disagree. Your SELECT shows 3 rows, but UPDATE … WHERE on the same range touches 4 (it reads the latest committed data) — and after that your SELECT sees the 4th row too.
          • 
        
        • PostgreSQL RR: snapshot isolation; phantoms do not appear (the PG docs mark them "allowed by the standard, but not in PG").
          • 
      
        
      
        
        
        ↪ Cross-questions the interviewer will ask next
        
        
        ↪So is InnoDB RR equal to SERIALIZABLE?
          
        No. It still allows lost updates (read-then-write from the snapshot) and write skew. See the next two questions and Chapter 13.
        
      
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan a lost update happen at REPEATABLE READ?
    
        
      
        In MySQL InnoDB, yes (default settings). In PostgreSQL, no — it throws an error instead.
        
      
        
        
        TimeT1 (withdraw 50)T2 (deposit 50)
        
        
        t1BEGIN; SELECT bal → 100
        
        
        t2BEGIN; SELECT bal → 100
        
        
        t3UPDATE … SET bal = 150; COMMIT;
        
        
        t4UPDATE … SET bal = 50; COMMIT; ❗ deposit lost
        
      
        
      
        The app computed the new value from a stale snapshot. InnoDB simply waits for T2's lock, then overwrites. PostgreSQL RR notices the row changed after T1's snapshot and fails T1 with could not serialize access due to concurrent update; the app must retry.
        
      
        Fixes (any engine): atomic UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 50 WHERE id = 1; or SELECT … FOR UPDATE before computing; or optimistic locking with a version column (WHERE id = 1 AND version = 7, check rows affected).
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs SERIALIZABLE the same in MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server?
    
        
      
        EngineHow "SERIALIZABLE" worksWhat you see
        
        
        MySQL InnoDBLike RR, but plain SELECTs become SELECT … FOR SHARE (when autocommit is off) — pessimistic lockingMore blocking, more deadlocks
        
        
        PostgreSQL (9.1+)SSI — Serializable Snapshot Isolation: snapshot reads + tracking of read/write dependencies; optimisticNo extra blocking; some txns fail with SQLSTATE 40001 → retry
        
        
        OracleReally snapshot isolationWrite skew still possible
        
        
        SQL ServerKey-range locks (pessimistic). Separate SNAPSHOT level for versioned readsBlocking
        
      
        
      
        🚫
        Failing answer
        "SERIALIZABLE means transactions run one after another." No — they run concurrently; the result must equal some serial order.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QCan two transactions deadlock on a single row?
    
        
      
        Yes — by lock upgrade. T1 and T2 both run SELECT … FROM acct WHERE id = 1 FOR SHARE. Shared locks are compatible, so both get one. Now both run UPDATE acct … WHERE id = 1. Each needs an exclusive lock and waits for the other's shared lock. Cycle → InnoDB detects it and rolls back one (ERROR 1213).
        
      
        Fix: if you will write the row, take the exclusive lock at once: SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Keep a consistent lock order for multi-row work.
        
      
        ⚠️
        Also wrong: "2PL prevents deadlocks"
        Basic and strict 2PL guarantee conflict-serializability, not deadlock freedom. Only variants like conservative (static) 2PL, or wait-die / wound-wait, avoid deadlocks.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDoes MVCC mean "no locks at all"?
    
        
      
        No. MVCC means readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers for plain reads. Two writers on the same row still take row locks; the second one waits. Locking reads, DDL (metadata locks) and gap locks still exist.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🌐 Distributed & NoSQL gotchas
        

  
        
    Q"CAP says pick any 2 of 3." True?
    
        
      
        Misleading. In a distributed system, network partitions will happen; you cannot opt out of P. So the real choice is: during a partition, either refuse some requests (stay Consistent — CP) or answer with possibly stale data (stay Available — AP). A "CA" system is just a single-node (non-distributed) system.
        
      
        Two more traps: the C in CAP means linearizability (every read sees the latest write), not the C in ACID (constraints hold). And PACELC adds the normal case: Else (no partition) you still trade Latency against Consistency.
        
      
        🗣️ Say it like this in the interview
        Partitions are not optional, so CAP is really a choice made during a partition: reject requests to stay consistent, or serve possibly stale data to stay available. When there is no partition, PACELC says we still trade latency against consistency, for example synchronous vs asynchronous replication.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QIs NoSQL faster than SQL?
    
        
      
        Not inherently. A NoSQL store is fast for the access patterns you modeled it for (key lookups, one partition, pre-joined documents) and scales out more easily. Ad-hoc queries, joins and multi-entity transactions are usually slower or harder. A well-indexed PostgreSQL/MySQL on one big machine handles a lot.
        
      
        Related traps: "NoSQL has no transactions" — MongoDB has multi-document ACID transactions (since 4.0 on replica sets, 4.2 on sharded clusters). "NoSQL has no schema" — it is schema-on-read: the schema lives in your code. See Chapter 20.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        
    QDo read replicas make writes faster? Do they give strong consistency?
    
        
      
        No and no (by default). Every write still goes to the primary, and replicas must apply it too. Async replicas lag, so a user can write and then read old data from a replica (fix: read-your-writes routing, or read from the primary right after a write). Scale writes with sharding. See Chapter 19.
        
    
        
  
        

  
        🐞 Common mistakes & failing answers
        
  
        Candidates lose DBMS points in four ways: fuzzy definitions (often copied from prep sites), SQL execution errors, knowing only one approach, and poor communication. Delete these wrong answers from memory.
        

  
        ❌ Theory answers that fail
        
  
        Wrong answerCorrect answerWhere
        
    
        "UNIQUE allows only one NULL."MySQL, PostgreSQL (default), Oracle allow many NULLs. SQL Server's UNIQUE constraint allows one; PG 15+ can opt in with NULLS NOT DISTINCT.04
        
    
        "TRUNCATE can never be rolled back."True in MySQL/Oracle (implicit commit, DDL). PostgreSQL and SQL Server can roll it back inside a transaction.07
        
    
        "2PL avoids deadlocks."2PL guarantees conflict-serializability; deadlocks are still possible.13
        
    
        "A foreign key makes joins faster."An FK is an integrity rule. Speed comes from an index on the FK column (InnoDB creates one automatically; PostgreSQL does not).04
        
    
        "Primary key = clustered index."True in InnoDB and by default in SQL Server. PostgreSQL tables are heaps (no clustered index); Oracle uses heaps unless you choose an IOT.15
        
    
        "Every DB defaults to REPEATABLE READ."Only MySQL InnoDB. PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server default to READ COMMITTED.13
        
    
        "3NF means no transitive dependency" (only).Precise: for every non-trivial FD X → A, X is a superkey or A is a prime attribute.06
        
    
        "Durability means data is in RAM safely."Durability = once COMMIT returns, the change survives a crash — because the WAL/redo log was flushed to disk.17
        
    
        "Indexes always speed up queries."They speed up selective reads; they slow writes, cost space, and low-selectivity indexes are ignored.15
        
    
        "Views store data."A normal view stores only the query. A materialized view (PG, Oracle) or indexed view (SQL Server) stores results.09
        
  
        

  
        🚫
        The definition-only answer
        "ACID is Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability." Full stop. That is a fail at product companies. Interviewers want a one-line real example for each letter and how the engine delivers it (undo log, constraints, locks/MVCC, redo log + fsync).
        

  
        ❌ SQL-round mistakes
        
  
        MistakeFix
        
    
        WHERE col = NULLWHERE col IS NULL (three-valued logic)
        
    
        NOT IN (subquery) where the subquery can return NULLNOT EXISTS, or filter IS NOT NULL in the subquery
        
    
        Filtering the right table of a LEFT JOIN in WHERE (turns it into an INNER JOIN)Move that condition into ON
        
    
        COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN, so empty departments show 1COUNT(e.id) — counts only matched rows
        
    
        UNION to stack tablesUNION ALL unless you really need de-duplication
        
    
        LIMIT without ORDER BY; or ordering on a non-unique columnOrder by a unique tie-breaker (ORDER BY salary DESC, id)
        
    
        Ignoring join fan-out, then "fixing" duplicates with DISTINCTCheck the cardinality; aggregate before joining
        
    
        Nth highest with LIMIT onlyAlso know DENSE_RANK() and the correlated-subquery version — "now without LIMIT" is a standard follow-up
        
    
        Non-aggregated column in SELECT with GROUP BYEvery SELECT column must be grouped or aggregated (MySQL's ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY enforces this)
        
    
        Dates stored/compared as strings; functions on indexed columns (YEAR(dt) = 2025)Use DATE types and sargable ranges: dt >= '2025-01-01' AND dt < '2026-01-01'
        
  
        

  
        -- ❌ departments with no 2025 hires vanish
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS hires
FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e ON e.dept_id = d.id
WHERE e.hired >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY d.name;

-- ✅ keep every department; filter inside ON
SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) AS hires
FROM dept d LEFT JOIN emp e
  ON e.dept_id = d.id AND e.hired >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY d.name;
        

  
        ❌ Communication mistakes
        
  
        
    
        🏃
        Writing SQL before clarifying
        Ask: duplicates? ties? NULLs? include zero counts? expected output columns?
        
    
        🤐
        Silent coding
        Think aloud: "First I join, then group, then filter groups with HAVING."
        
    
        🎭
        Bluffing
        Say what you know, reason from first principles, mark the guess as a guess.
        
    
        📏
        Engine fact as universal
        Add "in MySQL InnoDB…" — it turns a trap into a bonus point.

        Index rules
          
      
        • Leftmost prefix for composite indexes
          • 
      
        • Equality columns first, then the range column
          • 
      
        • Range stops later columns from seeking
          •

        • LIKE 'x%' ✔, LIKE '%x' ✘

        • A — undo log / rollback
